title: RaFL: An Empirical Study of Random Filter Losses for Image Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.17707v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pixel losses train image reconstruction networks toward a point statistic of the target distribution, often averaging away fine textures under uncertainty. Perceptual losses alleviate this issue using pretrained features, but those features are inherently domain-specific. We study a random filter loss (RaFL) that compares prediction and target through filters with random weights, avoiding both pretrained features and task-specific loss engineering. RaFL combines random convolutions, random Fourier features, and random wavelet filters, automatically balancing their contributions through gradient-norm matching, eliminating manual loss-weight tuning and grid search. We systematically investigate three design choices: filter family, weight resampling schedule, and weight initialization. Based on validation PSNR and stability across random seeds, we select the configuration that uses all three filter families, redraws filters every optimization step, and employs Gaussian initialization. We evaluate RaFL on three 2D and two 3D image reconstruction tasks. RaFL outperforms a pixel loss on three tasks and matches it on two, and demonstrates stable performance across random seeds on all five tasks. RaFL adds less than 2% to the backbone's forward FLOPs and no inference cost, requiring $182\times$ fewer loss FLOPs than a VGG19 perceptual loss. These findings suggest that RaFL is a simple, tuning-free, and domain-agnostic loss objective for 2D and 3D image reconstruction.

title: Choosing Between Python and Go for CLI Development: Balancing Familiarity and Structure
description:
Architectural Transition Mechanics: Event-Driven Loops versus Sequential Execution Flow

For the hobbyist transitioning from the Godot engine runtime, the departure from an implicit game loop—which natively orchestrates state updates, rendering frames, and event propagation—catalyzes an immediate architectural crisis. Stripped of the host engine environment, writing a standalone CLI or TUI application eliminates external scaffolding. The internal process demands a radical shift: instead of registering asynchronous callback methods (such as _process or _input) with an external scheduler, the programmer must explicitly engineer a deterministic, linear entry-to-exit execution pipeline. The observable effect is an acute architectural vacuum, where developers frequently falter in structuring main entry points, control flow loops, or state lifecycles because the application lifecycle is no longer handled implicitly by an external framework. This psychological shock exposes the fragility of engine-dependent mental models.

Type Systems and Compilation Overhead: Dynamic Interpretation versus Static Verification

The choice between languages encapsulates a fundamental tension between frictionless creative momentum and structural discipline. Python provides dynamic runtime interpretation and duck typing, maintaining high syntactic proximity to GDScript. The immediate impact is minimal cognitive friction when writing raw logic, allowing creative momentum to surge while type safety is deferred to runtime. Conversely, Go enforces a strict static compilation pipeline, demanding explicit type declarations, rigorous compile-time type checking, and mandatory error-handling structures (such as if err != nil). The observable consequence is stark: while Python permits immediate script execution, it insidiously masks architectural errors until runtime execution strikes a failure path. Go, by contrast, forces early type resolution at the distinct cost of upfront compilation overhead and unyielding syntax enforcement, testing whether a hobbyist can endure rigorous technical constraints.

Composition Logic: Inheritance Hierarchies versus Struct Embedding and Interfaces

Scaling software architecture requires confronting deep-seated habits formed within Godot's reliance on deep class inheritance hierarchies, which notoriously cultivate rigid object coupling and severe refactoring bottlenecks. When hobbyists encounter these structural limitations trying to scale game object logic in new environments, Go offers an epistemological break by replacing traditional class inheritance with structural composition. Through structs, method receivers, interface satisfaction, and embedding, Go replaces rigid parent-child class trees with decoupled behaviors. Types satisfy interfaces implicitly, fundamentally altering how modular components interact within system memory and forcing the developer to master a more flexible, decoupled paradigm of object design.

Pedagogical Resource Friction: Exhaustive Hand-Holding versus Independent Documentation Synthesis

The emotional and intellectual trajectory of the learner is profoundly shaped by the available pedagogical landscape. Python features an expansive ecosystem of beginner-focused literature, tutorials, and step-by-step guides, ensuring low friction in finding syntactic explanations and task-based walkthroughs. In sharp contrast, Go educational material exhibits a structural polarization, split between infantile introductions and advanced references that brazenly assume prior systems programming knowledge and direct manual consultation. The observable effect of this scarcity of intermediate-tier guided resources in Go forces developers to parse raw standard library documentation independently. This abrupt transition produces acute cognitive load and temporary operational paralysis, acting as a crucible that separates casual hobbyists from dedicated systems engineers.

Systemic Instabilities and Failure Modes

  • Engine-Callback Hangover: The persistence of event-driven mental models prevents the construction of linear command-line logic flows, resulting in structural gridlock.
  • Documentation Paralysis: The scarcity of intermediate-tier guided resources in Go induces stall states during standard library exploration.
  • Cognitive Overload: Distributing mental bandwidth between learning low-level memory pointers, strict type systems, and software architecture simultaneously destabilizes the development process.
  • Over-Modeling Composition: Paralyzing iteration cycles spent engineering perfect struct embeddings and interfaces before establishing functional baseline execution code.

Architectural Realities and Resource Gaps: Navigating Boilerplate versus Dynamic Abstraction

Transition from Engine-Driven Lifecycle to Standalone Execution Pipelines: Shifting from GDScript within Godot to standalone CLI/TUI development forces a structural paradigm shift from reactive, framework-managed event loops (_process, _input) to explicit, linear entry-to-exit execution flows. In Godot, the external engine scheduler handles frame rendering, state updates, and asynchronous callback propagation. When an engine-trained hobbyist attempts to build a standalone application, the absence of an overarching framework scaffolding causes structural gridlock, as the developer lacks a mental model for managing sequential initialization, blocking reads, and clean program termination. Analytically, this reveals the psychological vulnerability of losing framework safety rails, turning a technical migration into a disorienting trial of architectural survival.

Type Systems and Cognitive Load in Compilation: Python utilizes runtime interpretation and duck typing, eliminating upfront syntactic friction but deferring type safety and structural errors to execution time. Conversely, Go enforces a strict compilation pipeline with explicit type declarations, compile-time type checking, and mandatory error handling structures (if err != nil). For a beginner transitioning from a scripting environment, Go's strict syntax increases initial cognitive load, splitting mental bandwidth between learning low-level memory concepts (pointers, explicit allocation) and designing application logic. The consequence is a severe operational risk: the emotional thrill of low-level technical rigor frequently gives way to cognitive exhaustion and burnout.

Component Composition Mechanics versus Inheritance: Godot relies on deep class trees, which cultivate rigid object coupling and create severe refactoring bottlenecks when hierarchies are misdesigned. Go replaces parent-child class trees with structs, method receivers, explicit embedding, and implicit interface satisfaction. This compositional model allows behaviors to be decoupled and modularized without inheritance overhead. However, hobbyists frequently enter an over-modeling failure mode, spending excessive cognitive cycles trying to design "perfect" struct embeddings and interfaces before establishing baseline functional execution. This misplaced pursuit of architectural purity paralyzes momentum long before code ever runs.

Pedagogical Friction and Documentation Asymmetry: The stark disparity in learning resources creates distinct operational failure modes. Python offers continuous, low-friction, hand-held beginner literature. Go features a polarized ecosystem split between infantile introductions and advanced systems references that assume deep prior systems knowledge. This resource gap induces documentation paralysis: learners attempting Go are forced to independently parse the standard library documentation, resulting in operational stall states, uncertainty regarding capability limits, and trial-and-error dependency resolution. Ultimately, choosing between Python and Go for the transitioning hobbyist represents a critical trade-off between frictionless creative momentum and structural discipline, establishing Python as the more pragmatic vehicle for mastering standalone architecture without extinguishing enthusiasm.

Execution Lifecycle Transition Mechanics

Impact: Disconnecting application logic from the Godot game engine eliminates the underlying asynchronous scheduler.

Internal Process: The Godot runtime implicitly handles frame rendering, state updates, and event propagation via reactive hooks like _process and _input. A standalone CLI or TUI environment lacks this framework scaffolding, requiring explicit, deterministic, linear entry-to-exit execution pipelines, manual lifecycle initialization, blocking standard I/O reads, and explicit termination routines.

Observable Effect: Retention of engine-driven callback mental models forces structural gridlock, manifesting as execution halts when attempting to map sequential command-line execution onto non-existent event loops.

Type Systems and Compilation Overhead

Impact: Enforcing static compilation and explicit memory management versus runtime interpretation alters developer bandwidth distribution.

Internal Process: Python defers type checking to runtime via duck typing, eliminating upfront syntax overhead. Go enforces strict compilation pipelines, explicit type declarations, compile-time checks, mandatory error handling constructs (if err != nil), and direct pointer-based memory manipulation.

Observable Effect: The simultaneous processing of low-level memory addressing, strict type rules, and unfamiliar architectural patterns induces cognitive overload, splitting mental bandwidth between syntax enforcement and structural logic implementation.

Architectural Composition Dynamics

Impact: Replacing rigid class hierarchies with Go's structural composition modifies object coupling and modularity.

Internal Process: Traditional game engines rely on deep parent-child inheritance trees that create refactoring bottlenecks. Go substitutes inheritance with structs, method receivers, explicit embedding, and implicit interface satisfaction, decoupling behaviors at the memory level.

Observable Effect: In the absence of prior standalone architecture experience, the system enters a premature optimization loop where complex struct embeddings and interfaces are modeled before establishing baseline operational code, producing architectural paralysis.

Pedagogical Resource Asymmetry and Documentation Friction

Impact: The structural polarization of learning resources forces independent parsing of standard library specifications.

Internal Process: While Python provides continuous, low-friction hand-held beginner literature, Go's literature is divided between infantile overviews and advanced systems references. Developers must navigate standard library documentation directly without intermediate-tier guided scaffolding.

Observable Effect: This asymmetry produces operational stall states and trial-and-error dependency resolution cycles, destabilizing development velocity until intrinsic motivation drives the construction of independent mental models.

title: Improved Regret via Variance-Aware Policy Optimization in Adversarial MDPs
description:
arXiv:2611.17469v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study episodic adversarial MDPs with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards and achieve regret with leading term $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3SAK})$. Here $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the total number of states across decision layers, $A$ the number of actions, and $K$ the number of episodes. This improves the two incomparable prior leading terms by factors $\sqrt{S/H}$ and $\sqrt{H^3}$, leaving a factor $\sqrt H$ to the lower-bound scale. We give a reduction from unknown to known dynamics for \emph{downstream-dependent} algorithms, whose policy at step $h$ is computed only from information at steps $h+1$ and onward. This reduces the remaining leading-order gap to finding a downstream-dependent known-dynamics algorithm with $\widetilde O(H\sqrt K)$ regret, which would yield the tight $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{SAK})$ leading term for unknown dynamics. We instantiate the reduction with VOPO, a policy optimization (PO) algorithm. Its improved guarantees follow from a variance-aware analysis enabled by a novel bonus, which we call the Stability-Matching Bonus (SMB). VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3K})$ regret under known dynamics with full information; its $\sqrt H$ gap to the target $H\sqrt K$ rate is inherited by our unknown-dynamics guarantee. We also show that with known dynamics and trajectory bandit feedback, VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^2SAK})$ regret. Both known-dynamics guarantees improve the corresponding state-of-the-art PO bounds by a factor $\sqrt H$. A matching lower bound establishes that the full-information rate is tight in one parameter regime.

title: RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$: On-Device Reinforcement Learning Runtime
description:
arXiv:2611.18035v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-device reinforcement learning runs a periodic actor and a learner on one embedded GPU shared with other workloads. Because the learner produces the actor's weights, existing designs stall the actor or let its policy drift. We present RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$, an on-device runtime that makes this coupling a tunable parameter: a refresh bound limits actor releases between refreshes, and a GPU permit with slack-aware admission prioritises the actor and fills spare time with training atop any base scheduler. Under the real refresh cost on two Jetson boards, RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$ keeps a 16.8 M-parameter policy's deadline misses below 1%, against 85 to 100% without it.

title: Building a WhatsApp-First Booking Flow Without a Backend
description:
Why WhatsApp

In Morocco, WhatsApp is the universal messaging app. Our guests are tourists arriving at Marrakech Menara airport, and they already have WhatsApp open. A traditional booking form with login, payment gateway, and confirmation emails adds friction. WhatsApp adds none.

The Implementation

Every "Book Now" button on our site is a pre-filled WhatsApp link. The helper function is straightforward:

export function whatsappHref(text: string) {
  return `https://wa.me/${site.whatsapp}?text=${encodeURIComponent(tagged(text))}`;
}

The tagged() wrapper prepends a source tag so the office knows which site the message came from (we operate multiple domains):

const SOURCE_TAG = `[navetteforyou.com \u00b7 Marrakech Transport]`;
const tagged = (s: string) =>
  s.startsWith(SOURCE_TAG) ? s : `${SOURCE_TAG}\n${s}`;

Pre-Filling the Message

Each route page composes a booking message with the transfer details already filled in: route, date placeholder, number of passengers, vehicle class, and quoted price. When the guest taps the button, WhatsApp opens with a message like:

[navetteforyou.com \u00b7 Marrakech Transport]
Transfer: Marrakech Airport \u2192 Medina
Vehicle: Mercedes E-Class (3 pax)
Price: 300 MAD
Date: [your arrival date]
Flight: [your flight number]

The guest fills in two blanks and hits send. The office responds within minutes.

Email Fallback

For guests who prefer email, we use the same pattern with mailto: links:

export function mailHref(subject: string, body: string) {
  const subj = `[navetteforyou.com] ${subject}`;
  return `mailto:${site.email}?subject=${encodeURIComponent(subj)}&body=${encodeURIComponent(tagged(body))}`;
}

Zero Backend

There is no server, no database, no payment processing. The entire booking flow is a static site generating deep links into WhatsApp and email. The operator's office handles confirmations, payments (cash or bank transfer), and driver dispatch. This architecture costs nothing to run and has zero downtime risk.

Tradeoffs

The obvious gap: no automated scheduling, no calendar integration, no payment capture. For a small transfer operator handling 10-30 bookings per day, a WhatsApp thread with context is faster than any dashboard. At scale, you would add a backend. We are not at that scale, and premature infrastructure is a cost, not a feature.

Operated by Serenity Morocco Tours. Visit navetteforyou.com or WhatsApp +212 701 664 704.

title: Nothing on my AI team ships without my yes
description:
I have a team of AI agents. I am also the only person in the room.

That sounds like a joke until you have to live with it. I work from Manila, alone, and I ask the agents to do specialised jobs the way a small studio would split them. There is a QA seat that checks work before I see the final pile. There is a listing desk for product copy. A publisher's desk that reads a manuscript like an editor. An ops engineer who watches the pipes. A footage librarian who tries to find the right clip in a messy folder.

They are not employees. They do not get to post. They do not get to publish. They do not get to invent a number because a sentence looks better with one.

I say that last part because I have been tempted. Everyone who writes with these tools has been tempted. A round figure feels finished. An unsourced figure is still a guess. If I cannot point to where a number came from, it does not go in. I would rather publish a smaller, true sentence than a polished one I cannot stand behind.

The gate is the job

Every draft waits for me. That is the whole system, if I am honest. The agents can plan, write, check, and file. The folder can fill up while I sleep. None of it ships without my yes. Status stays draft until I change it. The bot does not get a switch that turns a file into a post.

Before anything goes out I also ask three quiet questions. Why am I writing this? Who is it for? What harm could it do? If I cannot answer those, the draft stays in the folder. It is a small habit. A sentence that feels urgent at night can look careless in the morning.

I keep a 24-hour hold on political posts. If a piece touches politics, it sits for a day. I look at it again when I am not in the first mood. Then I still have to say yes, or it stays put. The hold is not bravery. It is a way to keep a tired man from publishing a line he cannot stand behind once the heat has gone.

The files have names that tell me who made them, what kind of file it is, a short title, and the date. It is a dull rule. It is also the reason I can find a draft later without asking a bot to reconstruct history. When you are one person, remembering is a system, or it is a mess.

The QA work is dull in the same useful way. It looks for politics that slipped in, real faces that should not be there, claims with no source, and missing AI labels. It can flag. It can suggest a safer line. It cannot approve. That last part is mine, even when I am tired, especially when I am tired.

I will not list my tools, and I will not tell you what they cost. That is not the useful part. The useful part is the boring gates.

A specialised seat, not one chatbot doing every job. A human sign-off, every time. A file name I can search. A day of rest for political work. No number that I did not check.

People like to ask if the agents will replace me. They have not learned how to be ashamed of a wrong fact. I have. That is still my job.

I am a Filipino builder in Manila, doing this with more time than money, and I am not going to pretend the bots run the studio. They draft. I decide. If I skip that step, I do not have a studio. I have a pile of confident text and no one to blame but myself.

If you use AI in your work, where do you still insist on being the person who says yes?

AI-assisted draft: an AI assistant helped me write this, and I edited it before posting.

title: Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement
description:
arXiv:2611.17563v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a capability in its own right -- knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one -- which we call dialectical competence. It stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside, we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest case against that position -- its antithesis -- rules on whether the case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at training or at deployment. We call this learning through Self-Disagreement: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself. The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not come from outside it.

title: The Four Product Risks: What Counts as Evidence for Each
description:
AI made feasibility cheap to prove. Value, usability and viability still need their own evidence, and a great prototype demo counts for less than it feels. The Risk Receipt shows what you've actually retired.

The four product risks are value (will customers buy or use it?), usability (can they figure it out?), feasibility (can we build it?) and viability (does it work for the business?). Marty Cagan's framing still holds, but AI changed the economics: feasibility is now cheap to test, while the other three still need their own evidence. A prototype demo says far less about value than it feels.

Key takeaways

  • Cagan's four big risks are independent: evidence for one tells you little about another (SVPG, 2017).
  • In CB Insights' 2026 analysis of 385 failed VC-backed startups with known causes, 43% cited poor product-market fit and 19% unsustainable unit economics. Those are value and viability problems, not build problems (CB Insights, 2026).
  • Five test users find about 85% of usability problems, so usability evidence is cheap to buy (Nielsen Norman Group, 2000).
  • Value evidence is behaviour with a cost attached, usually gathered before people see your solution.
  • A Risk Receipt keeps each claim, its evidence and an honest "counts / weak / unverified / unexamined" verdict together, so nobody mistakes four nice demo calls for validation.

What are the four product risks?

Cagan set out the four big risks in a 2017 SVPG article, and they have become the standard checklist for product discovery (SVPG, 2017):

Risk The question Owner in Cagan's model Strongest evidence Weakest evidence
Value Will customers buy it, or users choose to use it? Product manager Behaviour with a cost: pilots, pre-orders, workarounds they already pay for "I'd use this", demo enthusiasm
Usability Can users figure out how to use it? Product designer Unassisted task attempts by target users Stakeholder walkthroughs, "looks clean"
Feasibility Can engineers build it with the time, skills and technology we have? Lead engineer A working path on realistic data, with a list of what was skipped A happy-path demo on seeded data
Viability Does it work for the rest of the business? Product manager Cost-to-serve, pricing tested on a buyer, sign-off from sales, legal, support "We'll figure out pricing later"

In Cagan's words, viability is "whether this solution also works for the various aspects of our business". That covers pricing, cost to serve, sales, legal, compliance and support.

The four risks are independent. A feature can be trivially feasible, perfectly usable and still have no value. A feature can have obvious value and be unviable, for example when each use costs more in inference than the customer pays.

Why did AI change which product risks matter most?

When building was expensive, feasibility was the gate everything queued behind. Teams spent discovery time on the other three risks while engineering estimated. Now that a working prototype takes an afternoon, the queue is gone, and so is the forced pause where the other risks used to get examined.

Benedikt Kantus put it bluntly in an October 2026 essay: "AI has made feasibility almost trivial. It has not touched the other three." (Leading in Product, 2026).

Failure data agrees about where products die. CB Insights studied 431 VC-backed companies that shut down since 2023 and could identify causes for 385. "Ran out of capital" topped the list at 70%, but the report calls that the final cause rather than the root one. Underneath it: poor product-market fit at 43%, bad timing at 29% and unsustainable unit economics at 19% (CB Insights, 2026). And for products that do survive, Pendo's 2019 analysis found 80% of features in the average product are rarely or never used (Pendo, 2019). Value risk, not build risk, is the expensive one.

Is feasibility really solved?

For prototypes, mostly. For production, less clearly. In METR's randomised trial, 16 experienced open-source developers working on 246 real issues in their own repositories took 19% longer with early-2025 AI tools, even though they had forecast a 24% speedup and believed afterwards they had been 20% faster (METR, 2025). A February 2026 follow-up with 57 developers found only weak evidence of a speedup, with confidence intervals that include zero, and METR itself warns the data is an unreliable measure (METR, 2026). The honest reading: the first version is cheap; the edge cases, reliability and maintenance are not free.

What is a Risk Receipt?

The problem isn't that PMs stopped caring about the other risks. It's that a polished prototype feels like evidence for all four. Demo it to five people, hear "this is great", and the team walks away believing value, usability and viability are covered. Each risk has its own currency of evidence, and most teams pay in the wrong one.

A Risk Receipt is a short record you attach to any meaningful product bet. For each of the four product risks it answers three questions:

  1. What's the claim? One sentence, specific enough to be wrong.
  2. What evidence do we have, and what kind is it? Linked to the source, not paraphrased.
  3. Does that evidence actually count for this risk? This is the part teams skip.

The third question is the point. Evidence has an exchange rate. Some evidence is strong currency for one risk and close to worthless for another.

What counts as evidence for each risk?

Value: pay in behaviour, not compliments

Counts: customers describing the problem unprompted, with a recent, concrete example. Existing workarounds (spreadsheets, scripts, manual processes) that cost them real time. Commitments with a cost attached: a calendar slot, a pilot with their data, a pre-order, an introduction to their boss.

Doesn't count: "I'd use this." Enthusiasm during a demo. A prototype's click-through rate in a moderated session. Upvotes on an idea board from people who will never pay.

The tell: if the strongest evidence for value is someone reacting to your prototype, you've collected usability evidence and labelled it value. People react politely to anything competent-looking you show them. Value evidence usually comes from before they saw your solution, in how they talk about the problem. Cheap ways to buy it include a fake door test or a presale interest page.

Usability: pay in observed tasks, not opinions

Counts: watching a real target user attempt a real task without coaching, and recording where they hesitate or fail. Task completion on the first attempt. The questions they ask out loud.

Doesn't count: "It looks clean." A stakeholder walkthrough. Your own team using it every day (they already know where everything is).

The tell: if nobody outside the team has attempted a task alone, usability is unverified, no matter how good the prototype looks.

This is the one risk AI prototyping genuinely helps with. A clickable, data-backed prototype gets you real task observation weeks earlier than a static mockup. It's a real gain, just a gain for one risk. Our usability test template covers how to run the sessions.

Feasibility: pay in a working path, including the ugly parts

Counts: a prototype that runs against realistic data volumes, real permissions and real latency. An engineer's honest list of what the prototype skipped: auth, migrations, error states, the integration that's rate-limited.

Doesn't count: a demo on the happy path with seeded data.

The tell: ask "what did this prototype not have to handle?" If the answer is long, feasibility is partly retired, not fully.

Viability: pay in numbers someone outside product would sign

Counts: a cost-to-serve estimate (for AI features, cost per use at expected volume). A pricing hypothesis you've said out loud to a buyer. A check with whoever owns support, sales, security or legal. For B2B, whether a buyer's procurement process allows this.

Doesn't count: "We'll figure out pricing later." Assuming usage costs are negligible because the prototype was cheap to run for one person.

The tell: if no one outside the product team has seen the bet, viability is unexamined.

A worked example: four happy customers, one empty receipt

Say you're a two-person founding team building a B2B tool, and a customer call sparks an idea: an AI assistant that drafts weekly status updates from project activity. You prototype it over a weekend. It works. You show it to four customers on calls. All four say they love it.

Here's the honest Risk Receipt:

Risk Claim Evidence Counts?
Value Team leads will use weekly drafts instead of writing updates themselves 4 positive demo reactions Weak: reactions to a solution, not behaviour. No one described writing updates as a pain before you showed them.
Usability Leads can review and send a draft in under 5 minutes None observed Unverified: nobody tried it alone.
Feasibility Drafts stay accurate on real project data Weekend prototype on your own workspace Partial: no test on a messy customer workspace.
Viability Cost per draft stays well under what the plan charges Not estimated Unexamined

Four enthusiastic calls, and the receipt says you've retired almost nothing. That's not a reason to kill the idea. It's a reason to run three cheap checks before building the production version:

  1. Value: go back to two of those customers and ask how they write updates today, how long it takes, and what happened the last time one was late. Listen for a workaround.
  2. Usability: give one customer the prototype on their own data and watch them use it, unguided, for one cycle.
  3. Viability: multiply your per-draft model cost by realistic weekly volume across your customer base, and compare it with plan price.

The viability maths (illustrative numbers). Suppose a draft costs €0.06 in model calls on your own workspace, but a real customer workspace has 5 times more activity, so €0.30 per draft. A customer with 40 team leads generates 160 drafts a month, or €48 in model cost, against a plan priced at €60 a month. That is 80% of revenue gone on one feature. Better to know on day three than in month three.

Each check takes days, not weeks. That's the real dividend from cheap feasibility: you can afford to buy real evidence for the other three risks before you commit.

How many customers or users do you need for each risk?

  • Usability: small numbers work. Nielsen's analysis found 5 users uncover about 85% of usability problems, and recommended three rounds of 5 with fixes in between over one round of 15 (Nielsen Norman Group, 2000).
  • Value: the count matters less than the cost of the signal. Two customers who each give you a pilot with their own data outweigh twenty who say "sounds great". Look for at least 3 independent commitments before treating value as retired for a segment.
  • Feasibility: one realistic run, reviewed by the engineer who will own it, plus a written list of what was skipped.
  • Viability: one cost model with stated assumptions and one conversation with each function that has to say yes (sales, support, legal or security).

These are starting points for a small team, not benchmarks.

Why do receipts beat a discovery checklist?

You could turn the four risks into a checklist. Teams do. Checklists fail predictably: someone ticks "value validated" because a demo went well, and the tick hides what the evidence was.

A receipt keeps the evidence attached to the claim. Three months later, when the feature is underperforming and someone asks "why did we build this?", the answer isn't a memory or a slide. It's a record: here's what we believed, here's what we saw, here's which risks we knowingly left open. For the structure that keeps those records linked over time, see our decision graph for small AI teams. If your team ships without receipts at all, check it against the 10 warning signs of a feature factory.

That last part matters. Shipping with an open risk is often the right call, because small teams can't afford to retire everything. The failure is shipping with an open risk you thought was closed.

Common mistakes

  • Counting demo reactions as value. The single most common error. Reactions are usability evidence at best.
  • Testing usability with insiders. Colleagues and friendly customers already know the product's logic.
  • Treating a prototype as proof of production feasibility. Ask for the skipped list every time.
  • Leaving viability to "later". For AI features especially, cost per use can turn a loved feature into a loss-maker.
  • Trying to retire every risk. Pick the one or two that would kill the bet and buy evidence for those first. Our assumption mapping guide helps rank them.

How we run Risk Receipts in Specky

Customer signals (interview notes, support threads, call transcripts, analytics events) land in the Product Graph as typed nodes, each keeping its source. A drafted insight or decision cites the specific nodes it rests on, so "four customers loved it" can't quietly become "customers need this". For the value check, Alex, Specky's AI research agent, can run short interviews about customers' current process before they see your solution, and the transcripts come back as evidence. For early demand, a validation page measures whether people take an action with a cost attached. Judgement about which risks to leave open stays with you.

Start with one receipt this week

You don't need a tool to start. Pick the bet your team is most excited about right now, the one with the best prototype. Write four lines:

Value:       [claim] | [evidence + link] | counts / weak / unverified / unexamined
Usability:   [claim] | [evidence + link] | counts / weak / unverified / unexamined
Feasibility: [claim] | [evidence + link] | counts / weak / unverified / unexamined
Viability:   [claim] | [evidence + link] | counts / weak / unverified / unexamined

If the most exciting bet has the emptiest receipt, you've found where your next week of discovery should go. You can also sketch the assumptions visually with the free assumption map tool.

Feasibility used to be the expensive question. Now it's the cheap one. The teams that win this cycle won't be the ones who build fastest. They'll be the ones who can show what they knew when they decided.

Frequently asked questions

What are Marty Cagan's four big risks?

They are value risk (will customers buy or choose to use it), usability risk (can users figure out how to use it), feasibility risk (can engineers build it with the time, skills and technology available) and business viability risk (does it work for the rest of the business). Cagan published them on SVPG in 2017 and assigns value and viability to the product manager.

Which of the four product risks is most often underestimated?

Value risk. A working prototype and polite reactions create a strong feeling of validation that isn't backed by behaviour. CB Insights' 2026 study found 43% of failed startups with known causes cited poor product-market fit. Viability is a close second for AI features, where cost per use can outgrow the price.

Does a prototype test value risk?

Rarely on its own. Showing a prototype mainly tests usability and some feasibility. Value evidence comes from behaviour with a cost: people describing the problem unprompted, existing workarounds, pilots, pre-orders or introductions. You can use a prototype in a value test, for example by asking for a paid pilot, but the reaction alone doesn't count.

How do you test business viability risk?

Write down the numbers someone outside product would need to approve: cost to serve per customer, expected price, support load, and any legal, security or procurement constraints. Then show them to those people. For AI features, multiply cost per use by realistic volume and compare it with plan price before committing to build.

Did AI make feasibility risk disappear?

No, it made the first version cheap. Prototypes now take hours, but production work on mature codebases is a different matter: METR's 2025 trial found experienced developers took 19% longer with AI tools on their own repositories, and its 2026 follow-up found only weak evidence of a speedup. Keep asking what a prototype didn't have to handle.

Sources

  1. SVPG, Marty Cagan — The Four Big Risks (2017)
  2. Leading in Product, Benedikt Kantus — vibe coding and product management (2026)
  3. CB Insights — The top reasons startups fail (2026)
  4. Nielsen Norman Group — Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users (2000)
  5. METR — Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity (2025)
  6. METR — Uplift update on late-2025 AI tools (2026)
  7. Pendo — The 2019 Feature Adoption Report

This story was originally published on 16 October 2026 at https://www.specky.space/blog/what-counts-as-evidence-four-product-risks.

Fathy Shalaby is a scientist by training (master's). He worked at LexisNexis and Canva, and writes How to Be a Product Engineer.

title: Why Project Zomboid Bet on Java and LWJGL: The Boring Thin Wrapper Behind a 13-Year Survival Sim
description:
Short answer

Project Zomboid (The Indie Stone, Early Access November 8, 2013) runs on Java with LWJGL — the Lightweight Java Game Library — plus Lua for gameplay and mods. The infobox lists Engine: LWJGL, and the community wiki is blunter: Coded in Java and Lua.

That looks outdated in 2026. It is the point.

Most survival hits rent Unity or Unreal for lighting and marketing. Zomboid stayed on a thin Java wrapper over C libraries for 13+ years, from a 2011 pre-alpha to Stable Build 42.22.2. Steam still describes it as long Early Access with monthly Unstable betas, full Lua modding access, and many 1,000+ hour players. My take, stated as opinion not fact: Zomboid did not survive despite Java. It survived because Java forced a slow, persistent, moddable simulation that Unity would have tempted the team to rebuild every three years.

Why this stack was a real choice, not a default

Search demand tells you this is a live question, not trivia. Google suggests project zomboid what engine and project zomboid what game engine, Bing adds what game engine does project zomboid use, what engine does project zomboid use, does project zomboid use java, and Build 42 searches cluster around project zomboid build 42 new features and release date. Players hit the engine question when the game stutters, when mods break, or when Build 42 changes crafting. Those tips were observed Nov 16, 2026 via Google and Bing suggestion tools.

The timeline matters:

  • Announced March 15, 2011, first commercial game from The Indie Stone, one of the first five Desura alpha-funding games (Project Zomboid Wikipedia).
  • Two laptops with the game's code were stolen in 2011, delaying development (Project Zomboid Wikipedia).
  • Early Access November 8, 2013 on Windows, macOS, Linux (Project Zomboid Wikipedia).
  • Still in Alpha at Build 42 in July 2026, with animals, overhauled crafting, and map updates (Project Zomboid Wikipedia), tracked as Stable 42.22.2.

A Unity team would have migrated render pipelines twice in that span. A Java + LWJGL team kept the same thin binding and spent the budget on systems: hunger, stress, fatigue, boredom, skill books, VHS tapes, erosion, power/water shutoff, radio/TV Knox Event lore, and 13 modes from Apocalypse to Builder to Custom Sandbox (Project Zomboid Wikipedia / PZWiki).

What LWJGL actually is

LWJGL is an open-source library that provides bindings to C libraries for Java game developers. It exposes cross-platform libraries such as Vulkan, OpenGL, GLFW, OpenAL and OpenCL.

Three technical facts shape everything else:

  1. Thin wrapper philosophy. The main philosophy is to expose underlying technology as a thin wrapper, creating an API close to the original (LWJGL). You get control, not helpers.
  2. JNI plus modules. It accesses native C code through JNI, with bindings as different modules so developers make custom builds with only what they need (LWJGL). Since 3.1 it is split into 51 modules with an online configurator for Maven/Gradle (LWJGL).
  3. Basis for higher engines. LWJGL is the basis of libGDX and jMonkeyEngine (LWJGL). Zomboid did not take that higher layer. It stayed close to the metal in Java, with Lua on top for content.

Lua itself is a powerful, efficient, lightweight, embeddable scripting language with automatic memory management, ideal for configuration, scripting, and rapid prototyping. Steam confirms the payoff: full unrestricted Lua modding access and one of the most vibrant Steam Workshops.

In short: Java plus LWJGL for the persistent world, Lua for fast content and mods. Boring, portable, and hard to kill.

What the stack gained

1. Persistence over spectacle

Zomboid is played from an isometric point-of-view in Knox Country, heavily based on Muldraugh, West Point, Louisville and Riverside (PZWiki). The fantasy is not headshots. It is managing hunger, stress, fatigue, boredom, barricading with planks and nails, reading skill books, and watching the world erode after power and water shut off within a month (Project Zomboid Wikipedia).

LWJGL's thin OpenGL/GLFW/OpenAL bindings do not give you Nanite or Lumen. They give you a stable window, input, and audio to simulate thousands of tiles, zombies, weather fronts, and seasons. That is enough when the design verb is wait, board up, read, sleep rather than slide-cancel.

My distinctive read, labeled as opinion: Java's much-mocked garbage collector is a design filter. You cannot afford per-frame allocations for every zombie, so you pool, batch, and simulate off-screen abstractly. That frugality becomes gameplay — Romero-style slow zombies, sandbox sprinter settings, Apocalypse loot scarcity, Builder 20 percent population (Project Zomboid Wikipedia / PZWiki). Slowness is not just lore. It is memory management turned into fiction.

2. Modding as content insurance

Steam explicitly releases dev tools with full unrestricted Lua modding access. PZWiki documents Steam Workshop mods from visible moodles to full overhauls, maps, and mechanics.

This is where Lua's embeddability matters. Lua has a simple and well documented API for strong integration with C/C++/Java/C# and is small — 32000 lines of C, 293K interpreter, so adding Lua does not bloat the app.

Opinion: most Early Access games promise NPCs and die. Zomboid promised NPCs for a decade and lived because Lua mods filled the gap. Steam admits NPCs have taken very long because underlying systems must be ready first. Mods were the bridge loan. A Unity Asset Store cannot give you that same contract — Lua mods run in the same simulation language the devs use, not as imported prefabs.

3. A UI that admits it is a simulation

New players mock Zomboid's windows and drop-down menus. Wikipedia notes it heavily uses windows and drop-down menus for interface navigation.

I think that ugliness is honest. A survival sim with 13 modes, sandbox sliders for zombie population, virus transmissibility, loot rarity, plus fixed challenge scenarios like endless winter or one-day last stands (Project Zomboid Wikipedia / PZWiki) cannot fit in a radial wheel. Windows scale. Console-friendly wheels do not. Staying on PC-first Java/LWJGL let the team keep the spreadsheet UI instead of redesigning for gamepad certification every Build.

What it cost

  • Time. 2011 pre-alpha to 2013 alpha to 2026 Build 42 is not a schedule. It is a lifestyle. The stolen laptops in 2011 (Project Zomboid Wikipedia) plus JNI debugging plus custom isometric streaming explain part of it.
  • Readability. Thin-wrapper OpenGL will never match Unreal's daylight forests or Lumen horror. Zomboid compensates with climate, seasons, and erosion systems (Project Zomboid Wikipedia), not with photogrammetry.
  • Onboarding. Hunger, stress, fatigue, boredom, traits, occupations spawning in towns like firefighter in fire station (Project Zomboid Wikipedia) drown newcomers. Zomboid's answer is Builder mode and Custom Sandbox, not a better tutorial engine.

None of those costs killed it. Many 1,000+ hour players and very positive Steam reaction suggest the core loop pays the tax.

Build 42 proves the bet

Build 42 (stable July 2026) added animals, overhauled crafting, and map updates (Project Zomboid Wikipedia). PZWiki tracks it as Stable 42.22.2.

That is exactly what a thin stack should enable late in life: add systems, not shaders. Animals reuse pathing and hunger. Crafting reuses inventory windows. Map expands Knox Country towns players already know from Louisville metro references (Project Zomboid Wikipedia). No pipeline migration, no material upgrade project. Just more simulation in the same Java process.

Contrast this with peers that switched engines mid-life and lost a year. Zomboid's discipline was to never switch.

What indie devs can steal

  1. Pick the wrapper, not the engine, if your game is 10 years long. LWJGL's 51 modules and custom builds (LWJGL) mean you only pay for what you use. Unity/Unreal make you pay for everything with version upgrades.
  2. Make modding the same language you use. Java and Lua plus unrestricted Lua access turns players into QA. Do not bolt on a separate mod SDK after launch.
  3. Let performance constraints write lore. Slow Romero zombies, power/water shutoff, erosion, airborne infection becoming apparent by July 16 in Knox Event fiction (Project Zomboid Wikipedia) — all justify fewer active actors. Design the fiction to explain the culling.
  4. Ship modes, not difficulty sliders. Apocalypse (stealth, short lifespan), Survivor (stronger combat, multi-hit), Builder (20 percent zombies, rarer loot except food) (PZWiki) teach different verbs. One slider cannot.

My contrarian rule: if your fantasy is live another day, you do not need a new renderer. You need a save file players trust, a UI that shows every system, and a mod API that outlives your roadmap. Java plus LWJGL plus Lua is unfashionable and perfect for that.

Try the loop in your browser first

Zomboid demands hours. These browser games train the same instincts in minutes, with no install:

  • For horde kiting and ammo discipline, play Against Zombies. It is an action-packed 3D shooter where you battle hordes while defending a getaway car, with WASD movement, aiming, weapon selection, and grenades. Practice the Zomboid rule here: lure to wide roads, back away while firing, and do not stand still in a crowd.
  • For day/night shelter, hunger, and tool progression, play Mine Clone. It is a Minecraft-inspired blocky world where you break and place blocks, gather resources, craft wood to stone to iron, and survive monsters and hunger at night. Run its first-day checklist — wood, hut before sunset, torches, food — and you understand Zomboid's first 24 hours.
  • For loot-drive-loot and mission cash, play Sandbox City - Cars, Zombies, Ragdolls. It is an open-world 3D zombie sandbox where you roam, drive cars, fight on foot, complete missions for cash, and mess with ragdoll physics and slow motion. Its drive-to-hotspot, park, loot on foot, drive on routine is Knox Country with traffic.

If you enjoy the patience of those three — checking corners, managing inventory, leaving a fight you cannot win — you are ready for Knox County. If you need constant unlocks, Zomboid will feel like paperwork. That is the filter working.

Bottom line

Project Zomboid bet that a thin Java binding would outlast fashion. LWJGL thin-wrapper over OpenGL/AL/Vulkan via JNI plus Java and Lua code plus unrestricted Lua Workshop plus isometric Knox Country survival since November 8, 2013 Early Access to Build 42 July 2026 is not nostalgia. It is infrastructure for a game that must be modded, saved, and continued for a decade. Solo devs chasing fidelity should rent Unreal. Devs chasing a decade should rent nothing and own the wrapper.

title: AWS Backup adds logically air-gapped vault support for Amazon RDS
description:
AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault now supports Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) DB instances. Logically air-gapped vaults are a type of AWS Backup vault that stores immutable, isolated backups, which are locked by default with AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode. Secure sharing across accounts and AWS Organizations enables direct restore, reducing recovery time from a data loss event.

You can now protect your Amazon RDS DB instances in logically air-gapped vaults. A logically air-gapped vault stores immutable backups that are locked by default, and isolated with encryption using AWS owned keys or customer-managed keys. This helps reduce the risk of downtime, ensure business continuity, and meet compliance requirements.

To get started, use the AWS Backup console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. Assign your RDS DB instances to a backup plan and specify a logically air-gapped vault in the same AWS Region as the copy destination. Share the vault for recovery or restore testing with other accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), or safeguard vault access during account compromise using Multi-party approval. Once shared, you can initiate direct restore jobs from that account.

This support is available in most AWS Regions where both logically air-gapped vault and Amazon RDS are available. For more information and detailed regional availability, visit the AWS Backup documentation. To learn more about logically air-gapped vaults for RDS, read the launch blog and visit the feature documentation and pricing page.

title: Node.js Presigned Download URLs for Private Object Storage: 1-Day Export Links
description:
Short answer: keep receipt exports private, then hand the browser a short-lived presigned GET URL; delete the object with a lifecycle rule after the audit window. A permanent public URL is the wrong default for a fintech export.

Decision matrix for receipt export links

Option Retention control Browser download Operational cost
Private bucket + presigned GET Strong; expiry and lifecycle are explicit Works without exposing the bucket A small signing service and cleanup policy
S3 presigned URL Strong; mature IAM and lifecycle controls Works well AWS-specific configuration and credentials
Cloudflare R2 presigned URL Strong; useful with an R2 account Works well R2 and egress choices shape the bill
Backblaze B2 signed URL Good for download workflows Works, with B2-specific APIs Less broad ecosystem than S3

For a Node.js service exporting CSV, PDF, or ZIP receipts, I would choose the first row and keep the storage contract behind a tiny adapter. Infrai is a reasonable implementation of that row when you want one REST contract to survive a backend-vendor swap. Infrai gives you one REST API over plain HTTP, with the same key covering storage plus adjacent backend jobs: the path and request shape stay in your code while the configured storage provider changes behind it. You do not install a storage SDK or create a new credential for each service. That is a DX win I can measure in minutes, not a promise about storage semantics.

The choice is about deletion, not a flashy link. Give each export an owner, a unique object key, and an expiry measured in minutes. Separately, make the bucket lifecycle delete stale exports after at least one day. Those clocks solve different problems: URL expiry limits sharing, while lifecycle deletion limits retained data. In a real receipts pipeline, the worker writes the file only after the invoice rows are fixed, records a checksum and the export job id, then marks the database row ready. The download endpoint checks that row, checks the caller's account, signs the exact key, and emits an audit event. A retry of the worker can happen at any point; it must either address the same idempotent key or create a new key and a new row. That explicit state machine is less cute than latest.zip, but it is what prevents a customer from downloading another customer's report after a timeout.

What should Node.js presigned download URLs do for private object storage exports?

Start with an export record in your database. It should contain the account id, object key, creation time, and a state such as ready or deleted. Generate a key like exports/{accountId}/{jobId}.zip, never latest.zip. If a user clicks “export” twice, the two jobs must not race to replace one object.

I learned to distrust friendly filenames in this workflow. They look harmless until a retry lands after a second job and silently replaces the first artifact. Use a UUID or a database sequence in the key. If you need one logical export to be regenerated, coordinate that transition in the database or a queue; storage has no conditional If-Match write in this setup.

The browser should receive only a presigned GET URL and a short expiry, perhaps 15 minutes. Your application still authorizes the export before signing. The storage service never needs to know the user's session cookie. That separation makes audit logs easier to read: one event says who requested a file, another says when a URL was minted. Keep the response boring: { exportId, downloadUrl, expiresAt }.

No public ACLs. Good.

Do not confuse URL expiry with retention. The bucket lifecycle floor is one day, not one hour, so an hourly privacy promise cannot be implemented by lifecycle alone. If policy demands faster removal, enqueue an explicit delete after the job's retention deadline and keep the one-day lifecycle as a backstop. Multipart leftovers also need attention because there is no automatic fragment cleanup rule here.

A minimal TypeScript flow with explicit retries

The adapter below uses the storage routes that matter: upload the private object, then presign its download. The base URL is configuration, which keeps the sample usable with a compatible gateway or a direct provider adapter.

const apiBase = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL ?? process.env.STORAGE_API_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY ?? process.env.STORAGE_API_KEY;
if (!apiBase || !apiKey) throw new Error("Missing storage API configuration");

async function request(path: string, init: RequestInit, attempts = 4): Promise<any> {
  for (let n = 0; n < attempts; n++) {
    const response = await fetch(`${apiBase}/v1${path}`, {
      ...init,
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        ...(init.headers ?? {}),
      },
    });
    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status === 429 && n < attempts - 1) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** n;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }
    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Storage request failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }
  throw new Error("Storage request retry limit reached");
}

export async function publishExport(bucket: string, key: string, bytes: Uint8Array) {
  await request(`/storage/object/put/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`, {
    method: "PUT",
    body: bytes,
    headers: { "Idempotency-Key": `export:${key}` },
  });

  const signed = await request(`/storage/object/presign/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`, {
    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify({ expires_in: 900 }),
  });
  if (!signed.url) throw new Error("Presign response did not include a URL");
  return signed.url as string;
}

The exact response field for a presign operation should be read from the discovery schema used by your deployment; the guard above intentionally fails loudly if the URL is absent. Keep the signing call server-side. Return the resulting URL over your authenticated application endpoint, with the export id attached for audit correlation.

Set the lifecycle policy when provisioning the bucket, not during every download. A one-day-or-longer rule is the supported automatic cleanup boundary. Keep the policy in infrastructure code so a new environment does not quietly retain customer documents forever.

Where the alternatives are a better fit

The private-presign pattern has sharp edges. It is not suitable for static website hosting, image hosting, or a forever-public link because public-read ACLs are unavailable. It also lacks object versioning and WORM object lock; regulated, immutable evidence needs an external archive or a storage product with those controls. Browser-direct uploads can require configurable CORS, and this service does not expose an independent CORS route, so route uploads through your API or choose a platform with that knob.

Stick with Amazon S3 when you need the deepest IAM integration, object lock, cross-region replication, or a large body of existing tooling. Choose R2 when its network and egress model matches your traffic and you already operate Cloudflare. B2 is compelling for straightforward download-heavy archives, but teams that depend on S3-native policy tooling may spend more integration time there.

Your mileage may vary. I am not sure a single gateway is the right long-term home for a legal archive; the decision depends on residency, retention attestations, and your incident process, not just API ergonomics. For ordinary receipt exports, though, a short-lived URL plus a deletion job is a clean boundary.

One more constraint matters for fintech: trial credits cannot pay for persistent writes. Production provisioning needs a billing-enabled account before the first export is stored. Treat that as an environment check, not something to discover in a customer request.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://www.backblaze.com/docs/cloud-storage-presigned-urls
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/API/API_PutObject.html

title: Temp Tables vs Table Variables in SQL Server: Which Should You Use?
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

SQL Server gives you two ways to hold intermediate results: temporary tables (#temp) and table variables (@table). They look almost the same, and many developers pick one out of habit. But they behave differently in ways that can turn a 2-second procedure into a 2-minute one. Here is how to choose.

The syntax 

-- Temporary table
CREATE TABLE #Employees (
    EmployeeId   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    DepartmentId INT NOT NULL
);

-- Table variable
DECLARE @Employees TABLE (
    EmployeeId   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    DepartmentId INT NOT NULL
);

A common myth is that table variables live in memory and temp tables live on disk. In fact, both are created in tempdb, and both stay in memory while there is enough of it. The real differences are elsewhere.

Difference 1: statistics and row estimates

This is the one that matters most for performance.

  • Temp tables get column statistics, just like normal tables, so the optimizer can estimate how many rows a filter or join will return.
  • Table variables do not get column statistics. In older versions, the optimizer also assumed a table variable held just one row when the plan was compiled.

With 100,000 rows in a table variable, that one-row guess leads to plans built for tiny inputs, such as nested loops joins that run 100,000 times. Since SQL Server 2019 (database compatibility level 150 and above), table variable deferred compilation uses the actual row count at first compile, which helps a lot. There are still no column statistics, though, so estimates for filters and joins on table variable columns remain weak.

Difference 2: indexes

  • Temp tables can have any index, added at any time with CREATE INDEX.
  • Table variables can only have indexes declared inline when they are created, such as a primary key, unique constraint or inline INDEX definition. 
DECLARE @Orders TABLE (
    OrderId    INT PRIMARY KEY,
    CustomerId INT NOT NULL,
    INDEX IX_Customer NONCLUSTERED (CustomerId)
);

Difference 3: transactions and rollback

Changes to a table variable are not undone by a ROLLBACK. That sounds like a bug, but it is useful: you can collect error or audit details in a table variable inside a transaction and still read them after rolling back.

DECLARE @Log TABLE (Msg NVARCHAR(200));
BEGIN TRAN;
    INSERT INTO @Log VALUES (N'Step 1 failed');
ROLLBACK;
SELECT * FROM @Log;   -- the row is still there

Difference 4: scope and recompiles

  • A table variable exists only in the batch or procedure that declares it.
  • A #temp table is visible to the procedure that creates it and to procedures it calls, and is dropped when the creating scope ends.
  • Temp tables can trigger statement recompiles as their data changes, because statistics change. That is usually what gives them good plans, but in very high-frequency procedures the recompiles can add CPU overhead.

Side-by-side comparison

#temp table @table variable
Stored in tempdb tempdb
Column statistics Yes No
Row count at compile Known Known from SQL Server 2019 (compat 150+); assumed 1 before
Indexes Any, any time Inline at declaration only
Affected by ROLLBACK Yes No
Visible to called procedures Yes No
Recompiles Possible Rare

Which should you use?

  • Use a #temp table when the data is more than a few hundred rows, when you join or filter on it, or when you need extra indexes. This covers most real reporting and batch work.
  • Use a table variable for small sets (lookups, IDs, a few dozen rows), in very frequently called code where recompiles matter, or when you need data to survive a rollback.
  • When in doubt, test both. Compare the actual execution plans and logical reads with realistic data volumes, not with the ten rows in your development database.

Related reading:

  • How to Read a SQL Server Execution Plan
  • SQL Server Statistics Explained
  • SQL Server Parameter Sniffing: What It Is and How to Fix It

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Security

Addressed multiple reported security vulnerabilities in bundled packages.

Security

Feature

Custom organization policies for Agent Platform Workbench instances

You can now use custom organization policies to allow or deny the creation and update of Agent Platform Workbench instances based on their configuration. Custom constraints for the notebooks.googleapis.com/Instance resource are enforced when you create or update an instance, and support dry-run mode. This feature is now generally available (GA). For more information, see Create custom organization policy constraints.

Apigee X

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool arguments are sent to the location their OpenAPI parameter declares

This change applies to Apigee X in all supported regions.

An MCP tool argument whose OpenAPI parameter declares in: header is now sent to your backend as a request header, and one that declares in: cookie is sent in the Cookie header. Previously both were appended to the query string. in: query and in: path parameters are unchanged, and every parameter still appears in the tool's inputSchema, so MCP clients supply arguments exactly as before. If a backend reads one of these values from the query string, declare the parameter in: query or read it from its declared location.

On a tool call that supplies at least one cookie argument, the Cookie header is replaced with only the declared cookie parameters, omitting any others. Any cookie your backend relies on must be declared as an in: cookie parameter.

An MCP proxy that was already deployed continues to use the previous query-string behavior until its configuration is next regenerated. To adopt the new routing on an existing MCP proxy, deploy a new revision of it.

For the full mapping, see Tool argument placement on the backend request.

Security

On October 24, 2026, we published a security bulletin for Apigee.

Two vulnerabilities in PHP core (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, "PHP2Shell") allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely on a server running a vulnerable PHP version. The impact is limited to Drupal-based Apigee developer portals, which customers deploy and operate. Apigee, Apigee Hybrid, and the Apigee integrated portal don't use PHP and aren't affected.

Security bulletin published: GCP-2026-072

Bigtable

Libraries

Python

2.50.2 (2026-10-22)

Bug Fixes
  • bigtable: preserve resource labels on batcher metrics (#18712) (f18cc6b)
  • bigtable: resolve O(n^2) bottleneck in ReadRowsQuery.add_range (#18706) (5ac7cc6)

Java

1.94.0 (2026-10-22)

Features
  • bigtable: add per-method session diversion configuration (#14681) (042dd3e)
  • bigtable: support SessionCheckAndMutateRow on the session client (#14565) (86de9c1)
  • bigtable: support SessionReadModifyWriteRow on the session client (#14585) (8e653b2)

Capacity Planner

Feature

Preview: You can use the Capacity Planner remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server (capacityplanner.googleapis.com) to connect AI applications and agents to your Capacity Planner data (Preview). You can use the Capacity Planner MCP tools to query historical resource usage, usage forecasts, and reservation data across your projects, folders, and organizations.

For more information, see the Capacity Planner MCP reference and Google Cloud MCP servers overview.

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

You can now create heterogeneous conversion workspaces by importing database schema metadata files from a Cloud Storage bucket without requiring direct network connectivity between Database Migration Service and your source database during the schema conversion phase. For more information, see the following pages:

  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Compute Engine

Security

A vulnerability (CVE-2026-85299) about incorrect authorization in Compute Engine was discovered and has been addressed. For more information, see the GCP-2026-073 security bulletin.

Developer Connect

Feature

The Developer Connect Model Context Protocol (MCP) server is available in Preview.

AI applications and coding assistants can use the Developer Connect MCP server to read commits, diffs, file blame, and pull requests. They can also open, update, and comment on pull requests in repositories that you link from GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, and GitLab Enterprise.

The same operations are available as GitRepositoryLink methods in the Developer Connect REST API.

For more information, see the Developer Connect MCP reference.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Control user intent matching for semantic governance policies

You can now turn user intent matching on or off for semantic governance policies by setting the sgpUserIntentMatching key on the authorization extension metadata. User intent matching is on by default; set the key to DISABLED to turn it off. Turning it off reduces protection against indirect prompt injection. When the key is set, policy evaluation logs report the mode each evaluation used in the sgpUserIntentMatchingMode field.

For more information, see Control user intent matching.

Feature

Cloud Storage output support for Gemini image generation models

Direct Cloud Storage output persistence is generally available (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1), Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (gemini-3.1-flash-image), Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image), and Gemini 3 Pro Image (gemini-3-pro-image). You can set outputConfig.outputUriPrefix and generationConfig.responseFormat[].image.delivery to "URI" in generateContent and streamGenerateContent requests to write generated and edited images directly to a Cloud Storage bucket and receive the object URI in fileData.fileUri instead of inline bytes. For more information, see Save generated images to Cloud Storage.

Feature

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are Generally Available (GA)

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are available in General Availability (GA) in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions. The models support structured speaker and style metadata, inline vocal tags, multi-speaker dialogue, and streaming. Voice design and voice replication capabilities remain available in Preview.

For more information, see Generate speech with Gemini TTS.

Feature

Semantic governance policies support more model providers

Semantic governance policies now evaluate tool calls from agents that use models from providers other than Gemini. The policy engine reads each provider's request and response format, so the same policies apply whichever model your agent uses. Supported APIs include the Gemini Developer API and Gemini models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the Anthropic Messages API, Claude models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, the Mistral AI API, the OpenAI-compatible endpoint on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (including Llama models), and self-hosted OpenAI-compatible servers such as vLLM. Streamed model responses aren't supported.

To govern these providers, update the when condition of your authorization policy to match each provider's request path. The updated condition also matches requests that include a query string.

For more information, see Supported model providers and Connect the policy engine to Agent Gateway.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Fixed
