title: Most of My Users Couldn't Sign In With Google, and It Wasn't My Bug
description:
On 3 November I looked at 14 days of visitor data for one form on my site.

Five people had started filling it in and never finished. Four of them had pressed Continue with Google. Then nothing. They never came back.

The button itself wasn't broken. So where did they go?

Where they came from

My site is TrustCheck, and a lot of our visitors arrive from links shared on X, Instagram and Facebook.

When you tap a link inside those apps, it doesn't open Chrome or Safari. It opens the app's own built-in browser. And Google refuses to sign people in inside those built-in browsers. The person taps the button, gets an error page from Google, and closes the tab.

From my side, nothing failed. No error. No log line. Just a person who left.

The errors I was ignoring

What made it worse: I had been looking at errors from those same browsers for days, and filing them as junk.

My visitor insights kept recording "page errors" like:

Can't find variable: CONFIG
currentInset
webkit.messageHandlers

None of that is my code. The X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in-app browsers inject their own scripts into every page, and those scripts throw errors. On 1 November I filtered them out so they'd stop polluting my error counts:

public static function isNoise(?string $label): bool
{
    return (bool) preg_match(
        '/CONFIG|currentInset|webkit\.messageHandlers|__gCrWeb|instantSearchSDKJSBridge|WeixinJSBridge/',
        (string) $label
    );
}

Two days later I found out the same browsers were also quietly breaking my sign-in. The noise was a clue, and I had filtered it away.

The fix: a code by email

I didn't want to fight Google's rules. So I added a second way in that never leaves the site: type your email, get a 6-digit code, type it back.

Email code is now the first option on that form. Google is second.

The parts I cared about:

  • The code lives for 10 minutes, stored hashed, never in plain text.
  • 5 wrong tries and the code is dead.
  • At most 3 codes per email address in 10 minutes, so nobody can use the form to flood someone's inbox. 
$code = (string) random_int(100000, 999999);

Cache::put(self::key($email), [
    'hash'  => password_hash($code, PASSWORD_DEFAULT),
    'tries' => 0,
    'sent'  => $recent,
], 600);

Checking it uses password_verify() and deletes the code on success, so it can't be used twice.

On my laptop the code is written to the log instead of being emailed. I never want a test run to email a real person.

What I'd check on your site

If any of your traffic comes from social media, open your own site from inside the X or Instagram app and try to sign in. It takes two minutes.

I only saw this because I was counting where people stopped, not just what errored.

Have you found a bug that only happens inside in-app browsers? What was it?

title: SPF, DKIM, DMARC Done Right: A Practical Email Authentication Checklist Before Your OTP Emails Land in Spam
description:
Tuần này trên HN có tin Spamhaus siết yêu cầu với email sender từ tháng 11. Nếu bạn để ý thì đây không phải chuyện mới: Gmail và Yahoo đã bắt bulk sender phải có SPF, DKIM, DMARC từ tháng 2/2024, và Outlook cũng làm tương tự từ tháng 5/2025. Mình đã thấy khá nhiều startup Việt Nam gửi OTP, hóa đơn, email reset password qua Amazon SES hoặc Postfix tự dựng. Mọi thứ vẫn chạy ổn cho đến một ngày CS báo "khách không nhận được OTP". Lúc mở log ra thì SMTP vẫn trả 250 OK, nhưng email đã nằm trong Spam, hoặc tệ hơn là bị reject im lặng. Bài này là checklist mình dùng để audit domain gửi mail, kèm script Python để tự kiểm tra.

Receiving server thực sự kiểm tra những gì?

Trước khi đụng vào DNS, cần hiểu đúng ba cơ chế này kiểm tra cái gì, vì phần lớn lỗi đến từ việc hiểu sai:

  • SPF kiểm tra IP gửi có nằm trong danh sách được phép của domain ở envelope sender (MAIL FROM / Return-Path) hay không. Nó không kiểm tra header From: mà user nhìn thấy.
  • DKIM là chữ ký số trên header và body. Domain ký nằm ở tag d= trong header DKIM-Signature, còn public key được publish tại selector._domainkey.domain.
  • DMARC là lớp nối hai cái trên với header From:. Email chỉ pass DMARC khi SPF hoặc DKIM pass và domain của nó aligned với domain trong From:. 
flowchart TD
    A[Email đến MX server] --> B{SPF: IP có trong record của Return-Path domain?}
    A --> C{DKIM: chữ ký d= hợp lệ?}
    B --> D{SPF domain aligned với From?}
    C --> E{DKIM d= aligned với From?}
    D --> F{Ít nhất 1 cái pass + aligned?}
    E --> F
    F -->|Có| G[DMARC pass - vào Inbox]
    F -->|Không| H[Áp dụng policy p=none/quarantine/reject]

Cái bẫy kinh điển là bạn dùng một ESP, header From: no-reply@shopabc.vn, nhưng Return-Path lại là bounce@amazonses.com. Khi đó SPF vẫn pass, nhưng pass cho domain của ESP nên không aligned. Nếu DKIM cũng đang ký bằng domain của ESP mà không phải domain của bạn thì DMARC fail. Cách xử lý là bật custom MAIL FROM domain (ví dụ bounce.shopabc.vn) và Easy DKIM / custom DKIM để d=shopabc.vn.

Setup DNS records đúng cách

Một bộ record tối thiểu cho domain shopabc.vn gửi qua SES và Google Workspace trông như sau:

# SPF: chỉ được có MỘT record v=spf1 trên mỗi domain
shopabc.vn.            TXT  "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:amazonses.com -all"

# DKIM: dùng key 2048-bit, selector tùy ESP
s1._domainkey.shopabc.vn.  CNAME  s1.dkim.provider.example.

# DMARC: bắt đầu bằng p=none để thu report
_dmarc.shopabc.vn.     TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@shopabc.vn; adkim=r; aspf=r; pct=100"

# Kiểm tra nhanh bằng dig
dig +short TXT shopabc.vn
dig +short TXT _dmarc.shopabc.vn
dig +short TXT s1._domainkey.shopabc.vn
dig +short -x 203.0.113.10   # PTR cho IP nếu tự host Postfix

Vài điểm mình đã từng dính:

  1. Hai SPF record (một cái cũ do ai đó thêm từ hồi dùng Mailchimp). Hai record thì kết quả là PermError, coi như không có SPF.
  2. Vượt quá 10 DNS lookup. Mỗi include, a, mx, exists, redirect đều tính một lookup, kể cả lookup lồng bên trong include. Google Workspace cộng SES cộng một CRM nữa là rất dễ vượt.
  3. DKIM key 1024-bit từ thời 2015. Nên rotate lên 2048-bit.
  4. Tự host mà thiếu PTR/rDNS. Gmail sẽ reject thẳng với lỗi 550-5.7.25.

Script audit domain bằng Python

Thay vì check tay, mình viết một script nhỏ dùng dnspython (cài bằng pip install dnspython==2.7.0), có thể chạy trong CI hằng ngày:

import base64
import sys
import dns.resolver


def get_txt(name):
    try:
        answers = dns.resolver.resolve(name, "TXT")
    except (dns.resolver.NXDOMAIN, dns.resolver.NoAnswer):
        return []
    return [b"".join(r.strings).decode() for r in answers]


def get_spf(domain):
    recs = [t for t in get_txt(domain) if t.lower().startswith("v=spf1")]
    if len(recs) > 1:
        raise ValueError(f"{domain}: có {len(recs)} SPF record -> PermError")
    return recs[0] if recs else None


def count_lookups(domain, depth=0):
    spf = get_spf(domain)
    if not spf or depth > 10:
        return 0
    total = 0
    for term in spf.split()[1:]:
        t = term.lstrip("+-~?").lower()
        if t.startswith("include:"):
            total += 1 + count_lookups(t[len("include:"):], depth + 1)
        elif t.startswith("redirect="):
            total += 1 + count_lookups(t[len("redirect="):], depth + 1)
        elif t in ("a", "mx", "ptr") or t.startswith(("a:", "a/", "mx:", "mx/", "ptr:", "exists:")):
            total += 1
    return total


def check_dmarc(domain):
    recs = [t for t in get_txt(f"_dmarc.{domain}") if t.startswith("v=DMARC1")]
    if not recs:
        return None
    return dict(kv.strip().split("=", 1) for kv in recs[0].split(";") if "=" in kv)


def check_dkim(domain, selector):
    recs = get_txt(f"{selector}._domainkey.{domain}")
    for r in recs:
        tags = dict(kv.strip().split("=", 1) for kv in r.split(";") if "=" in kv)
        key = tags.get("p", "").replace(" ", "")
        if key:
            # RSA 2048-bit public key (DER) khoảng 294 bytes
            return len(base64.b64decode(key))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    domain, selector = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
    lookups = count_lookups(domain)
    print(f"SPF lookups: {lookups} {'OK' if lookups <= 10 else 'VƯỢT GIỚI HẠN'}")

    dmarc = check_dmarc(domain)
    if not dmarc:
        print("DMARC: THIẾU")
    else:
        print(f"DMARC: p={dmarc.get('p')} rua={dmarc.get('rua', 'không có')}")

    key_len = check_dkim(domain, selector)
    status = "OK" if key_len >= 256 else "YẾU hoặc THIẾU"
    print(f"DKIM {selector}: {key_len} bytes -> {status}")

Chạy thử: python audit_mail.py shopabc.vn s1. Mình gắn script này vào một GitHub Actions cron job, fail là báo về Slack. Nhờ vậy lần gần nhất có người thêm include: của tool marketing mới làm SPF vọt lên 12 lookup, team biết ngay trong ngày.

Rollout DMARC và one-click unsubscribe

Đừng nhảy thẳng lên p=reject. Nếu làm vậy, các nguồn gửi mà bạn quên mất (hệ thống HR, tool invoice, server cũ) sẽ bị chặn hết. Quy trình mình hay dùng:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev
    participant DNS
    participant Receivers as Gmail/Outlook
    Dev->>DNS: p=none + rua
    Receivers-->>Dev: Aggregate report XML hằng ngày
    Dev->>Dev: Liệt kê mọi nguồn gửi, fix alignment
    Dev->>DNS: p=quarantine; pct=25 rồi 100
    Receivers-->>Dev: Report: fail gần 0
    Dev->>DNS: p=reject

Report XML khá khó đọc, có thể parse bằng parsedmarc (Python) rồi đẩy vào Elasticsearch/Grafana. Mỗi giai đoạn nên giữ khoảng 2 đến 4 tuần.

Với email marketing/newsletter, Gmail và Yahoo còn yêu cầu one-click unsubscribe theo RFC 8058 và spam rate dưới 0.3% (xem trên Google Postmaster Tools). Gửi bằng Python thì làm thế này:

import smtplib
import ssl
from email.message import EmailMessage

msg = EmailMessage()
msg["From"] = "Shop ABC <news@mail.shopabc.vn>"
msg["To"] = "user@gmail.com"
msg["Subject"] = "Ưu đãi tháng 11"
msg["List-Unsubscribe"] = (
    "<https://shopabc.vn/unsub?t=abc123>, "
    "<mailto:unsub@mail.shopabc.vn?subject=unsub-abc123>"
)
msg["List-Unsubscribe-Post"] = "List-Unsubscribe=One-Click"
msg.set_content("Nội dung email...")

with smtplib.SMTP("smtp.example.com", 587) as s:
    s.starttls(context=ssl.create_default_context())
    s.login("SMTP_USER", "SMTP_PASS")
    s.send_message(msg)

Có hai điều cần lưu ý. Thứ nhất, endpoint /unsub phải nhận POST và hủy đăng ký ngay, không bắt login, không hiện trang xác nhận. Thứ hai, header List-Unsubscribe phải nằm trong phần được DKIM ký (tag h=). Đa số ESP tự làm việc này, nhưng nếu tự ký bằng OpenDKIM thì nhớ kiểm tra lại.

Một mẹo nữa: tách subdomain cho từng loại mail, ví dụ mail.shopabc.vn cho marketing và notify.shopabc.vn cho OTP/transactional. Reputation tính theo domain, nên một đợt campaign bị report spam sẽ không kéo OTP xuống theo.

Kết luận

Email auth không phải loại việc setup một lần rồi quên. Domain thay đổi liên tục vì team thêm tool mới, đổi ESP, rotate key. Checklist rút gọn:

  1. Chạy dig kiểm tra ngay hôm nay: đúng một SPF record, không quá 10 lookup, kết thúc bằng -all hoặc ~all.
  2. DKIM 2048-bit, ký bằng domain của bạn (d= trùng với From:), không phải domain của ESP.
  3. Custom MAIL FROM để SPF aligned. Ít nhất phải có DKIM aligned.
  4. DMARC đi từ p=none lên quarantine rồi reject, luôn có rua và đọc report bằng parsedmarc.
  5. Tách subdomain transactional và marketing. Mail marketing phải có one-click unsubscribe theo RFC 8058.
  6. Tự host thì cần PTR/rDNS và TLS. Đăng ký Google Postmaster Tools để theo dõi spam rate.
  7. Đưa script audit vào CI để phát hiện sớm khi có người sửa DNS.

Mấy vụ outage lớn tuần này nhắc lại một điều quen thuộc: lỗi khó thấy nhất thường nằm ở những thứ "vẫn trả 200 OK". Email cũng vậy. SMTP báo 250 OK không có nghĩa là user đã nhận được mail.

title: Recipe: moving a MySQL table to PostgreSQL in 5 steps (and proving nothing is missing)
description:
Disclosure: I'm the author of dbSlice, the Windows tool used below. The routine itself works with any tool; here is how I run it when an application is rebuilt on PostgreSQL but the data still lives in MySQL, MariaDB or SQL Server.

1. Pick the goal

The wizard opens with eight goals (migrate tables, keep tables up to date, compare data, send rows to an API or queue, export to a file, generate test data, clone tables, load data). Here: Migrate tables.

2. Connect

Source (MySQL, MariaDB or SQL Server) and target (PostgreSQL).

3. Choose the tables

If a table does not exist in the target, nothing is written: the tool shows the CREATE TABLE, translated from the source, for you to review and run. Check what never translates on its own:

  • UNSIGNED integers: use BIGINT (or NUMERIC(20) for BIGINT UNSIGNED)
  • TINYINT(1) flags: declare them BOOLEAN
  • zero dates (0000-00-00): PostgreSQL rejects them; turn them into NULL in a SELECT used as the source

4. Options

Pick a key column and a mode: initial load first, then upsert by key while the old application is still running.

5. Run and compare

Run it, then compare key by key against the source. That tells you which rows are missing or different. A structure compare lists column differences:

What it does not do

It moves data, not stored procedures, triggers or views. Incremental runs do not detect deletes at the source, so do a full compare or a reload before cutover.

Try it

There is a free version on the Microsoft Store (connects, browses, compares, exports CSV). Copying into the target needs a license.

  • Guide: https://dbslice.net/migrate/mysql-to-postgresql
  • SQL Server to PostgreSQL: https://dbslice.net/migrate/sql-server-to-postgresql
  • Site: https://dbslice.net
  • Free version: https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9PMS69X1T53Z

title: 1,021 @font-face rules on one page. Chrome loaded 107 of them.
description:
A single stylesheet on one of our sites declares 1,010 @font-face rules. Add the other three sheets and the page ships 1,021. Chrome registered all of them, then fetched 107. The 914 it skipped are the reason this page is survivable.

I run a network of 114 content sites — price outlooks, market explainers, filings breakdowns. This week I pointed a crawler at every homepage and counted fonts the way a browser counts them: parse the stylesheets, resolve every src, then ask how many bytes each file actually is.

The result was worse than I expected in the CSS and better than I expected at runtime. Both halves matter, because only one of them costs users anything.

How the count was done

Every homepage was fetched with Accept-Encoding: identity so the HTML arrives uncompressed and nothing about the markup changes. For each page I collected up to 10 <link rel=stylesheet> targets, parsed @font-face blocks out of them, resolved relative src URLs against the stylesheet URL, and HEADed each font file for Content-Length.

The parser is deliberately dumb — no CSS library, because I only need three properties and I want to see exactly what it misses:

FONTFACE_RE = re.compile(r"@font-face\s*\{(.*?)\}", re.S | re.I)
FAM_RE = re.compile(r"font-family\s*:\s*([^;}\n]+)", re.I)
FD_RE = re.compile(r"font-display\s*:\s*([a-zA-Z\-]+)", re.I)
SRC_RE = re.compile(r"src\s*:\s*([^;}\n]+)", re.I)
URL_RE = re.compile(r"url\(\s*['\"]?([^'\")]+)['\"]?\s*\)", re.I)

def parse_faces(css, base):
    faces = []
    for block in FONTFACE_RE.findall(css):
        src, fam, fd = SRC_RE.search(block), FAM_RE.search(block), FD_RE.search(block)
        urls = URL_RE.findall(src.group(1)) if src else URL_RE.findall(block)
        faces.append({
            "family": fam.group(1).strip().strip("'\"") if fam else None,
            "display": fd.group(1).lower() if fd else None,
            "srcs": [urllib.parse.urljoin(base, u.strip()) for u in urls],
            "unicode_range": bool(re.search(r"unicode-range\s*:", block, re.I)),
        })
    return faces

Two things this method cannot see, and both matter: fonts injected by JavaScript at runtime, and fonts loaded from a CSS @import chain. Neither showed up in this network, but a crawler that only reads <link rel=stylesheet> will undercount on sites that do it.

46 of 114 pages ship no webfont at all

The cleanest templates never load a font. Their whole stylesheet is 6.4 KB of inline CSS and the body rule is font: 16px/1.72 system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", "PingFang SC", "Microsoft YaHei", sans-serif. No stylesheet link, no @font-face, no request.

Chrome confirms it: 0 font requests, 12.6 KB of HTML, 38 KB for the entire page including scripts. First contentful paint at 2,096 ms on this machine, which is not fast — but nothing about that number is a font problem.

The other 68 pages do ship fonts, and they ship them hard.

The declared surface is 193.8 MB

Across the 68 pages that declare fonts: 12,949 @font-face rules, 4,020 distinct font files, 193.8 MB of declared bytes. Median per page is 1.7 MB. Twenty-five pages declare more than 4 MB.

Page Rules Files Declared
spacexstockanalysis.com 861 218 11.70 MB
marketpredictioncenter.com 645 218 11.69 MB
spacexstockprediction.com 1,021 211 11.49 MB
openaistocknews.com 819 211 11.48 MB
cryptobullforecast.com 356 117 7.39 MB

Most of that mass is legitimate Chinese text support. Noto Sans SC and Noto Serif SC are split into unicode-range slices, one file per slice, and 211 files is what a full CJK family looks like when you self-host it. All 68 pages use unicode-range — every single one, which is a rare piece of unbroken good practice in this audit.

But the pages themselves are not CJK-heavy. They are English content pages — a 2026 Bitcoin price outlook, a Starlink revenue breakdown, a Fed dot-plot explainer — the same reading experience at 9,000 characters that a text article anywhere else has. Declaring 1,021 faces for 9,000 characters is not a font problem, it is a build pipeline that stopped being read.

Declared is not transferred

Here is where my first assumption died. A browser does not download 211 files because a stylesheet names them. It downloads a file when a rendered glyph needs it, and only for the unicode range that glyph falls in.

So I loaded the heavy pages in headless Chrome and counted requests at the socket with CDP, not with PerformanceResourceTiming. That distinction matters: cross-origin responses without Timing-Allow-Origin report transferSize: 0, which silently erases every Google Fonts byte from your numbers. Network.loadingFinished.encodedDataLength is measured before that policy applies.

cdp = ctx.new_cdp_session(page)
cdp.send("Network.enable")
reqs = {}
cdp.on("Network.responseReceived", lambda e: reqs.__setitem__(
    e["requestId"], {"url": e["response"]["url"], "type": e.get("type")}))
cdp.on("Network.loadingFinished", lambda e: reqs.setdefault(
    e["requestId"], {}).update({"bytes": e["encodedDataLength"]}))

page.goto(f"https://{host}/", wait_until="load")
page.wait_for_timeout(3000)

fonts = [r for r in reqs.values() if r["url"].split("?")[0].endswith(".woff2")]
print(len(fonts), sum(r.get("bytes", 0) for r in fonts))

On spacexstockprediction.com: 1,021 rules registered in document.fonts, 107 marked loaded, 914 still unloaded, 33 network requests, 2,073 KB. The 11.49 MB declaration collapsed by 82% before a single byte left the server.

The same page: 861 rules on spacexstockanalysis.com, 83 loaded, 28 requests, 1,876 KB. 356 rules on cryptobullforecast.com, 14 loaded, 11 requests, 985 KB.

Lazy font loading is doing more work than most performance budgets give it credit for. If you have ever looked at a @font-face-heavy stylesheet and assumed the worst, measure the requests first.

The bytes that do move are still the problem

2,073 KB is not nothing. That page renders 9,037 visible characters — about 235 bytes of font per visible character, 33 round trips, and fonts are 56% of a 3,667 KB page load.

The distribution is worse than the total. On coinforecastpro.com the page declares 16 faces but transfers exactly one file: remixicon.woff2, 171 KB. On spacexstockprediction.com the biggest single font is also remixicon.woff2 at 171 KB — a full icon font with roughly 3,000 glyph mappings, fetched to render 51 elements.

Three generations of Font Awesome, on 22 pages

Twenty-two of the 68 pages declare Font Awesome 4, Font Awesome 5 and Font Awesome 6 at the same time. Not "one of them" — all three, plus remixicon. The family list on one page reads like a changelog:

FontAwesome            (4.x)      2 faces
Font Awesome 5 Free               4 faces
Font Awesome 5 Brands             2 faces
Font Awesome 6 Free              10 faces
Font Awesome 6 Brands             2 faces
remixicon                         1 face

That is six icon families for one page. The 4.x entries are the tell: they come from a font-family: FontAwesome rule left in a template that was later upgraded twice, and nobody deleted the old @font-face because nothing visibly broke.

At runtime, the cost is smaller than the CSS suggests. On cryptobullforecast.com, 316 elements resolve to an icon family — 216 remixicon, 97 Font Awesome 6 Free, 3 Font Awesome 6 Brands. Zero resolve to 4.x or 5.x. On bullrunalpha.com, all 19 icon elements are remixicon; its 82 declared faces include all three FA generations and none of them is ever applied.

So the browser already refuses to download the dead generations. What you keep paying for is the stylesheet: 1.35 MB of CSS on that page, four sheets, of which css2.css alone is 1,094,450 characters and 1,010 rules.

I parsed those four sheets in the page and timed CSSStyleSheet.replaceSync: 36.2 ms for css2.css, 13.5 ms for remixicon.min.css, 6.7 ms for all.min.css, 1.7 ms for the app sheet — 58 ms of style parsing before layout can start, on a machine that is probably faster than the phone this page will be read on.

174 KB of icon font to render 16 glyphs

I wanted a number for what subsetting would actually save, so I did it. Collected the ri-* classes present in the rendered DOM, mapped each class to its code point out of remixicon.min.css (3,020 mappings in that file), and subset the shipped woff2 to those points plus basic Latin:

from fontTools import subset
opts = subset.Options()
opts.flavor = "woff2"
opts.layout_features = ["*"]

font = subset.load_font("remixicon.woff2", opts)
sub = subset.Subsetter(options=opts)
sub.populate(unicodes=set(used_codepoints) | set(range(0x20, 0x7F)))
sub.subset(font)
font.flavor = "woff2"
font.save("remixicon.subset.woff2")

174,156 bytes in, 1,348 bytes out — 99.2% smaller. The page has 51 icon elements but only 16 distinct icons, and 16 glyphs is a 1.3 KB font.

Do not ship that as a one-off. A 16-glyph subset goes to tofu the moment someone adds a seventeenth icon, and the failure looks like a broken glyph in production, not a missing build step. The version that survives is a build step that reads the icon set from the source and regenerates on every deploy — or inline SVG, which needs no subsetting and no second request at all.

I blocked every font request and first paint did not move

My working theory was that 2 MB of fonts was delaying first paint. I tested it: same page, same viewport, one arm with all font requests aborted at the route layer, three runs each, cold context.

Page FCP with fonts FCP without Delta
spacexstockprediction.com 3,968 ms 3,472 ms +496
spacexstockanalysis.com 3,112 ms 3,396 ms −284
cryptobullforecast.com 2,460 ms 2,812 ms −352
coinforecastpro.com 3,644 ms 3,484 ms +160

The signs are inconsistent. On a single machine with three runs per arm, that is noise, not an effect. Which is exactly what font-display: swap is supposed to produce: text paints in the fallback, the font arrives later, first contentful paint does not wait.

I expected the cost to reappear as layout shift, so I measured that too — layout-shift entries over a 5-second settle window, two runs per arm:

Page CLS with fonts CLS without
spacexstockprediction.com 0.4216 0.3950
spacexstockanalysis.com 0.4155 0.4155
cryptobullforecast.com 1.0017 1.0006

Blocking fonts barely moved CLS either. A CLS of 1.0 is a serious problem, but it is not a font problem — something in those pages is shifting content after paint, and fonts are a rounding error next to it. That is a separate investigation, and it is on the list.

What the numbers actually support

Font bloat on this network is a bytes and CSS-weight problem, not a paint-blocking problem:

  • 46 of 114 pages avoid it entirely by using the system font stack.
  • 68 pages declare 193.8 MB of font files; the browser fetches 13–18% of that for English text, and the waste never reaches the user because lazy loading refuses it.
  • The waste that does reach the user is concentrated: 171 KB of icon font per page to render 16–216 glyphs, plus 2 MB of CJK slices on pages with 9,000 characters of English.
  • The declared rules you cannot avoid paying for are the CSS: 1.35 MB and 58 ms of parse on the worst page.
  • 37 of 68 pages have zero font preload. On a self-hosted setup that means discovery waits for the full stylesheet to parse — 353 KB of transfer before the first font request can even be issued.
  • 788 faces have no font-display at all, on 41 pages. The default is auto, which behaves like block for a short period; 220 more declare block explicitly. That is the one place where a font really can hide text.

The order I would fix it in

  1. Preload one font. The face that renders above-the-fold text. On a 1.35 MB stylesheet, preload is the difference between discovering the font at 400 ms and at 40 ms. 37 pages have none.
  2. Delete the unused generations. FA 4 and 5 never apply. Removing them does not reduce transfer, because the browser never fetched them, but it removes ~40% of the @font-face rules that every visitor's CSS parser walks.
  3. Subset the icon font at build time. 174 KB to 1.3 KB for the glyphs actually in the markup, regenerated on deploy so nobody gets tofu.
  4. Cut CJK slices to the script actually used. 211 files is a full family; a page that renders 9,000 characters needs a handful of ranges, and unicode-range is already there to make that possible.
  5. Set font-display: swap on every face explicitly. 788 faces inherit auto today.

What this measurement does not prove

One machine, headless Chrome, one geographic location, cold cache, homepages only. FCP and CLS numbers at three and two runs per arm are directional, not precise — treat the CLI table as "no effect detected", not "effect proven absent". The 114 sites are one network on one Cloudflare account, so the 59.6% webfont adoption rate says nothing about the wider web. And a crawler reading <link rel=stylesheet> cannot see fonts injected by JavaScript or by @import, so 193.8 MB is a floor for these pages, not a ceiling.

The one number I trust completely is the request count: 1,021 rules declared, 107 fetched. If you take nothing else from this, take that gap — your stylesheet is not your font budget.

title: Turn a short bug-repro clip into a GIF in the tab before you paste it into the issue
description:
The issue says “dropdown flicker on second open.” The attachment is a 42 MB QuickTime from the laptop’s screen recorder. Half the reviewers won’t download it. The other half will, once, and never re-open it. The bug is two seconds long.

I’ve started treating a short, looping GIF (or a similarly lightweight clip) as the default repro artifact for UI bugs that are visible in a few seconds. Keep the original recording if you need it. Don’t make the issue tracker host the raw file as the only way to see the problem.

When a GIF is the right repro

Good fit:

  • A visual glitch that repeats (flicker, mis-aligned popover, scroll jump)
  • A sequence shorter than ~8–10 seconds
  • Reviewers who will see it inline in GitHub / the tracker
  • A bug that’s hard to describe in prose (“it jumps, then it doesn’t”)

Poor fit:

  • 30-second flows, audio, or anything where frame-perfect timing is the bug
  • Color-critical / banding issues (GIF palettes lie)
  • Security-sensitive sessions you shouldn’t be rasterizing into a shareable loop
  • A problem that’s already captured by a failing Playwright test — prefer the test

If the clip is long, cut it first. A GIF of a five-minute session is just a worse video.

A simple repro-artifact policy

  • Length — aim for a few seconds, looped; cut idle time
  • Width — 600–800px is usually enough for a UI control; 1080p GIFs are a tax
  • FPS — 8–12 is often enough for a flicker or a menu; 30 fps is rarely worth the bytes
  • Name — repro-dropdown-second-open.gif, not Screen Recording 2026-11-11.mov
  • Where — attach the GIF in the issue / PR; keep the source MP4 out of git unless the repo has a real media policy

Don’t commit large recordings into the app repo “for documentation.”

Convert in the tab, with width and FPS in view

You want:

  1. Source: MP4 / MOV / WebM from the OS recorder
  2. A width cap and an FPS control you can see before download
  3. A local preview of the loop
  4. No mandatory upload of an unreleased product UI to a random converter

When the file is on disk and you’re already in the browser, an in-tab converter is enough. Uwarp’s video-to-GIF tool converts MP4, MOV, or WebM in the browser — you can adjust width and FPS, and it doesn’t upload the file to a server. Handy for the one-off issue comment. If you produce repro GIFs every week, script ffmpeg instead of clicking through.

Caveats: GIF palettes will posterize gradients and shadows; if the bug is a color/contrast issue, attach a lossless clip or PNGs too. Long or high-resolution sources may hit browser memory limits — cut first. A GIF is not a substitute for a failing test once you can write one.

How to attach it so people actually watch

In the issue:

Repro (2s loop): the listbox flicker on the second open.

![Listbox options flicker after closing and reopening](https://…/repro-dropdown-second-open.gif)

Steps: open → choose nothing → close → open again. Chrome 142, macOS.

One looping image beats a paragraph and a 42 MB download. If the tracker inlines images, you’re done. If it doesn’t, keep the GIF small enough that “download anyway” is cheap.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • 30–100 MB screen recordings as the only repro of a two-second glitch
  • Full-desktop captures where the bug is a 200px widget (crop or recapture first)
  • Uncut five-minute GIFs
  • Uploading an unreleased flow to a random online converter when a local/tab path exists

Accept

  • A short, width-capped, reasonably low-FPS GIF (or an equivalently small WebM) plus exact steps and environment
  • The original recording, linked or kept locally, when someone needs frame-accurate playback
  • A follow-up Playwright test once the flicker is understood

Tiny habit

After you record a UI bug, don’t paste the raw movie into the issue by default. Cut it short, convert in the tab with a width and FPS you actually looked at, and attach the loop. Reviewers will watch it. That’s the point of a repro.

title: How I Built a "Zero-Row" Database Intelligence Engine in Python (And Why I’m Selling the Full IP)
description:
Most database profiling, ERD, and AI schema tools ask for something enterprise security teams hate giving out: SELECT access to production tables.

Over the past year, I built SSDO (Solunex Smart Data Organizer) — a deterministic database intelligence, drift detection, and schema governance platform that maps declared and inferred relationships, scores structural confidence, and detects schema drift across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and SQLite without ever reading a single data row.

👉 Live Interactive Demo & Tour: https://solunex-ssdo.tech

Here is how the architecture works under the hood, what I learned building it over the past year, and why I’m offering the complete IP for a fast exit so I can focus on my primary projects.

1. The Core Constraint: Structure Only, Never a Row

In regulated environments (fintech, healthcare, enterprise SaaS), granting a third-party tool SELECT access on public.* triggers weeks of compliance review.

SSDO enforces a strict rule at both the application layer and the database kernel level:

  • It queries only catalog metadata (information_schema, pg_catalog, constraint definitions, and index statistics).
  • On PostgreSQL 14+, you can connect SSDO using a role that literally has zero SELECT privileges on any table (GRANT REFERENCES ON ALL TABLES is enough to unlock full primary-key and foreign-key metadata visibility in information_schema while SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 1 fails with InsufficientPrivilege).

2. Deterministic Inference (Why We Didn't Just Wrap an LLM)

Real-world legacy schemas rarely declare every foreign key. Instead of sending schemas to an external LLM and hoping it doesn't hallucinate joins, SSDO uses a deterministic inference and scoring engine:

  1. Declared Facts: Explicit primary keys, foreign keys (including composite FKs), unique constraints, and indexes.
  2. Inferred Relationships: When orders.owner_id has no FK constraint, SSDO evaluates naming conventions, data-type compatibility, cardinality signals, and candidate target keys (users.id), returning an explicit confidence score and the exact evidence behind the match.
  3. Honest Boundaries: Every run explicitly lists what it determined with certainty, what it inferred with evidence, and what it could not determine from structure alone.

3. One Engine, Three Complete Modes

As the codebase grew over a year of engineering, it evolved into a full platform with 50+ formal specifications (docs/specs/) and automated test coverage:

  • Developer & Architect Console: Interactive ERD canvas, table clustering, migration safety checks, environment drift comparison (GET /v1/compare), and natural-language structural Q&A ("how are payments and tags connected?") powered by deterministic templates (zero LLM data leakage).
  • Enterprise Governance & Audit: Change-control workflows, webhook/Slack/Teams drift alerts encrypted at rest, IP allowlisting, audit streams, and downloadable compliance evidence packs.
  • Built-in SQL Academy & Study Mode: Guided 6-slide structural walkthroughs, interactive schema design tasks, DDL exercises, and automated grading for students and bootcamps.
  • Low-Data & Self-Hosted Ready: Runs as a multi-tenant cloud SaaS or locally via pip install / Docker (127.0.0.1:8000), with custom static asset compression that shrinks the console payload by ~73% for metered connections.

4. Why I’m Exiting the Full IP ($2,800–$3,600 Quick Exit)

I spent over a year designing, specifying, and building SSDO up to today’s release (including the new 6-minute interactive architectural tour video live on the front page).

Right now, I am actively managing 3+ larger projects that demand 100% of my bandwidth. Rather than letting a production-ready platform sit without the marketing and sales push it deserves, I am looking for a straightforward full IP & asset exit.

What’s Included in the Acquisition:

  • 100% IP & Source Code Ownership: FastAPI + SQLAlchemy/Alembic backend, zero-dependency modular JS/CSS console, profiler engines (Postgres, MySQL, MSSQL, Oracle, SQLite), and the full automated test suite (pytest, mypy, ruff).
  • 50+ Architectural & Product Specs: Every subsystem is documented in docs/specs/ so a new owner or team can onboard in hours, not weeks.
  • Production Domain & Live Deployment: solunex-ssdo.tech, Docker/Render deployment configs, and billing/owner console infrastructure.

Pricing for a Fast, Clean Handover:

  • Standard Valuation: $4,800 USD
  • Quick Exit Price: $3,600 USD (or $2,800 USD for an immediate, no-friction close this week).

If you run a DevTools SaaS portfolio, a database/cloud consultancy, an EdTech platform, or a micro-PE fund and want to skip 12 months of R&D:

  • Explore the live platform & interactive video tour at https://solunex-ssdo.tech
  • Drop a comment below or DM me directly here on DEV to inspect the repo, test suite, and handover checklist.

title: Running 3 AI Background Removal Models in Browser WebGPU/WASM at $0 Server GPU Cost
description:
Cloud background removers all share the same business constraint: GPU inference costs money per image, so free tiers either compress previews to 0.25 MP, slap on watermarks, or require accounts — and users now face another migration with remove.bg shutting down its standalone web app on December 1, 2026.

When I built RemoveFree, the architecture goal was simple:

  1. $0 server GPU bill — inference executes 100% on the user's device.
  2. Zero image uploads — you can verify 0 KB of image traffic in DevTools (or disconnect Wi-Fi after loading).
  3. Full original W×H resolution — no 0.25 MP preview caps, no watermarks, no signup.

Getting that to feel instant on both desktop and mobile required shipping three different ONNX models inside a Web Worker, solving some subtle WebGPU/WASM bugs, and building a <3 ms client-side quality advisor.

Here is the exact architecture and what broke when we benchmarked it across 14 synthetic ground-truth scenes and 50 real CC0 photos.

1. Why One Model Isn't Enough in the Browser

If you pick a single high-accuracy segmentation model (~94–183 MB), mobile devices choke and first-visit desktop users wait ~38 seconds just for weights to download and compile. Pick only a lightweight portrait model (~6 MB), and e-commerce products or cars collapse (0.0000 IoU).

So RemoveFree splits the problem across three Apache-2.0 / MIT models in a dedicated module Worker (@huggingface/transformers v4.3.2 + onnxruntime-web/wasm):

Engine in UI Model Repo License Input Size Runtime Payload Median Time (50 real photos)
Fast Universal (Default) edgetools/u2netp Apache-2.0 320×320 Self-hosted ONNX + WASM 4.6 MB 942.5 ms
Portrait Lite Xenova/modnet Apache-2.0 512×512 WASM (q8) ~6.3 MB 1,155.0 ms
Studio HD (Opt-in) studioludens/birefnet-lite-512 MIT 512×512 WebGPU (fp16) / WASM (fp32) ~94 MB (WebGPU) / ~183 MB (WASM) 11,915.5 ms

Key runtime details

  • Self-hosted Cache API + Hugging Face fallback (u2netp): Serving u2netp.onnx (~4.57 MB) from same-origin /models/u2netp.onnx cached into Cache Storage (removefree-onnx-v1) eliminates third-party latency on repeat visits and keeps a Hugging Face resolve URL strictly as fallback.
  • Multi-threaded WASM via COOP/COEP: Production headers set Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless. Inside the worker, ort.env.wasm.numThreads scales up to min(4, hardwareConcurrency) whenever self.crossOriginIsolated is true.
  • Automatic safe fallback: If WebGPU adapter initialization or birefnet-lite inference throws (driver crash, OOM, shader failure), the client seamlessly falls back to u2netp on WASM (allowFallback = true) instead of dead-ending the user's cutout.

2. Preserving Exact W×H Pixels Without Running 4K Through ONNX

Users care deeply about keeping a 4000×3000 photo at 4000×3000 — not getting back a 512×384 blurred crop.

The pipeline separates inference geometry from final pixel compositing:

  1. Only a downscaled copy (scaleRgbaForModel, max dimension 320 or 512) is transferred (ArrayBuffer transferable) into the Web Worker.
  2. The worker normalizes inputs (ImageNet mean/std [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] / [0.229, 0.224, 0.225] for u2netp, or AutoProcessor for Transformers.js models) and outputs either raw logits (sigmoid-mapped with clamping [-20, 20]) or normalized [0..1] alpha values into an 8-bit Uint8Array.
  3. Back on the compositor side, upscaleAlphaMask() bilinearly upscales that 8-bit matte to exact original (origW, origH) dimensions and writes it onto untouched original RGB bytes: for solid foreground (alpha >= 250), exact source RGB values are preserved verbatim.

Result across our benchmarks: 14 / 14 (100%) synthetic scenes (including 3840×2160 4K) and 50 / 50 (100%) real photos preserved exact input dimensions.

3. Three Real Bugs Uncovered by Our 50-Photo CC0 Benchmark

Before finalizing the launch build, we ran all three engines against 14 synthetic ground-truth cases (metrics.json) and 50 real-world CC0 / Public Domain photographs across 7 categories (portraits, hair, jewelry, products, animals, thin_objects, difficult_bg). Testing real images surfaced three bugs synthetic smoke tests missed:

Bug 1: Tensor Input Key Mismatches Silently Triggering Fallbacks

AutoProcessor.from_pretrained emits { pixel_values }, but studioludens/birefnet-lite-512 expects input_image, Xenova/modnet expects input, and edgetools/u2netp expects input.1.

For a while, both alternate models threw inside the worker and silently triggered the fallback back to u2netp — making our early "model switcher" silently run the same engine underneath. Reading sessions?.model?.inputNames?.[0] dynamically inside the worker fixed it immediately.

Bug 2: MODNet Shader Corruption on Chromium WebGPU

Running Xenova/modnet on Chromium WebGPU introduced patchy holes across otherwise clean human portraits, dropping Sobel edge alignment to 46.2%.

Locking modnet explicitly to quantized WASM (q8, ~6.3 MB) and restricting WebGPU exclusively to birefnet-lite on non-mobile GPUs restored portrait edge alignment to 77.5% at 1,422 ms median (and 1,155 ms overall across the 50-photo set).

Bug 3: Why BiRefNet Lite Fails Low-Salience Scenes More Often Than U²-Net-p

Even though birefnet-lite wins clearly on fine hair (0.9738 vs 0.8344 synthetic IoU; 75.5% vs 72.8% real hair edge alignment) and 4K edges (0.9641 vs 0.8590), across 50 real photos U²-Net-p actually achieved a higher non-empty subject retention rate (96.0% / 48 of 50) than birefnet-lite (90.0% / 45 of 50). On cluttered jewelry and thin objects, birefnet-lite occasionally flooded or dropped the foreground while u2netp kept the subject intact.

That confirmed u2netp (4.6 MB) is not just faster — it is the safest universal default.

4. The <3 ms Client-Side "Studio HD" Advisor

Nobody wants to wait for a 94 MB download when a 4.6 MB pass in under a second already produced a clean cutout on a product photo or car.

Instead of downloading BiRefNet upfront, RemoveFree inspects the generated u2netp alpha mask right in memory (analyzeMaskForHdRecommendation, sampling 12,000 pixels in <3 ms) and triggers a 1-click "Enhance with Studio HD" suggestion only when any of four conditions holds:

  • Suspicious foreground ratio: foregroundPct < 3% or > 94% (likely low-contrast / dropped subject)
  • Semi-transparent halo / strands: semiTransparentPct >= 7.5% (hair, fur, glass, smoke)
  • High edge transition complexity: edgeComplexityPct >= 19.5% (spokes, foliage, intricate silhouettes)
  • High-resolution input: max(width, height) >= 2000 px

Across our 50 real photos, this triggered on 48% of images (85.7% of thin_objects, 57.1% of hair, and only 25.0% of clean portraits), keeping simple cutouts under 1 second while guiding tricky images straight to BiRefNet Lite + manual Erase/Restore brushes.

5. Benchmark Summary

Model License & Runtime Non-Empty Subject Rate (50 real photos) Avg Synthetic IoU (14 scenes) Fine Hair IoU Median Time (50 real photos) P95 Time
U²-Net-p Apache-2.0 · WASM 4.6 MB 48 / 50 (96.0%) 0.7796 0.8344 942.5 ms 1,393.5 ms
BiRefNet Lite MIT · WebGPU/WASM ~94 MB 45 / 50 (90.0%) 0.8590 0.9738 11,915.5 ms 16,463.1 ms
MODNet Apache-2.0 · WASM q8 6.3 MB 44 / 50 (88.0%) 0.3072 0.7065 1,155.0 ms 3,197.3 ms

Full benchmark breakdown and visual inspection notes are live at removefree.app/benchmark.

6. Honest Trade-Offs of Browser-Local AI

Client-side inference isn't magic, and there are places where cloud or server pipelines are still the right tool:

  1. No REST API: Because computation happens inside your browser tab, RemoveFree cannot be called from automated headless server pipelines — self-hosted rembg or cloud APIs (e.g., Leonardo.ai) belong there.
  2. Cold cache on Studio HD: First-time WebGPU fp16 shader compilation + ~94 MB download still takes ~10–38 seconds depending on connection and GPU driver; repeat runs benefit from Cache API + warm pipeline reuse inside the worker.
  3. Difficult micro-details: Tiny jewelry chains and extreme low-contrast objects remain hard for zero-shot client models (0.22–0.43 IoU synthetically), which is why interactive Erase/Restore brush refinement sits right next to the export button.

If you want to inspect it directly: open removefree.app, open your browser's Network tab (or toggle Airplane Mode once loaded), and run a cutout on a portrait or product photo.

title: Ollama Tutorial: Run Your First Local LLM in Python
description:
Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/ollama-tutorial-run-local-llm.html

Quick answer

Ollama is a free program that runs open language models on your own computer, no API key or cloud account needed. You install it, download a model with one command, and talk to it from a terminal or your own code through a local HTTP API on port 11434. This post installs Ollama on Linux, pulls a small 352 MB model, and sorts four real support tickets from Python.

Picture a small software company's support inbox on a Monday morning. Four tickets waited overnight: a plan that never activated after payment, an app crashing on the settings page, a misspelled name on an invoice, and a whole team locked out since breakfast. Sorting them by hand takes a morning, and a cloud AI means uploading customer data to someone else's server and paying per message. A model on your own machine changes that trade: it sorts the tickets and sends nothing outside your computer. This post shows that setup working, with real timings.

What I would check before using it

My first check is whether the model fits the machine. A model file has to sit in memory with room to spare for the conversation. The model here, qwen2:0.5b, is a 352 MB download that runs on an ordinary laptop CPU. A 7B model needs around 8 GB of free RAM; a 13B model needs about 16 GB. Check free memory first, or the first run will crawl.

My second check is what the model is for. A small local model handles sorting, summarising, and drafting, but it is not as careful as the big cloud models. The demo below shows it: the 0.5B model called every ticket high urgency. For careful reasoning or long documents, a cloud model wins; local wins only when privacy matters more than polish.

My third check is whether the task repeats. Ollama earns its keep when the same job runs again and again: triage, summaries, drafted replies. One question a week does not justify an install; a repeated job makes the setup pay for itself.

My fourth check is how the model will be called. Ollama serves a local API, so a script, a service, or a tool like LangChain can call it by changing one URL. Keep the port on localhost, 127.0.0.1, so only your own machine can reach it.

My verdict, as judgement: use Ollama when the data should stay on your machine, the job repeats, and a small model fits your hardware. Start with the smallest model that works, and measure before sizing up. The recommendation flips the moment you need top-tier reasoning, long context, or a model bigger than your RAM.

Four tickets, one local model

The example sorts four support messages. Each ticket gets an urgency, a topic, and one short action, in one line. The script sends each ticket to qwen2:0.5b through the Ollama chat API, with temperature 0 and a 1024-token context. The first call deliberately asks for llama3.2, a model that was never pulled, to show the error. Here is the script, exactly as it ran:

"""Classify four support tickets with a local Ollama model.

Sends each ticket to qwen2:0.5b through the Ollama HTTP API on
http://localhost:11434 and prints the model's one-line verdict plus
timing. The first call deliberately uses a model name that has not
been pulled, to show the error Ollama returns in that case.
"""
import json
import time

import requests

API_URL = "http://localhost:11434/api/chat"

TICKETS = [
    {
        "id": "SUP-201",
        "text": "I paid for the yearly plan yesterday but my account still shows the free plan.",
    },
    {
        "id": "SUP-202",
        "text": "The app crashes every time I open the settings page on my phone.",
    },
    {
        "id": "SUP-203",
        "text": "How do I change the name on my invoice? I typed it wrong when I signed up.",
    },
    {
        "id": "SUP-204",
        "text": "Our whole team cannot log in since this morning, we keep getting a server error.",
    },
]

SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You triage support tickets for a small software company. "
    "Reply in exactly one line: URGENCY: <low, medium, or high> | "
    "TOPIC: <billing, technical, or account> | "
    "ACTION: <one short action, under 10 words>."
)


def classify(model, ticket):
    """Send one ticket to the model, return the reply text and timings."""
    payload = {
        "model": model,
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": "Ticket: " + ticket["text"]},
        ],
        "stream": False,
        "options": {"temperature": 0, "num_ctx": 1024},
    }
    started = time.time()
    response = requests.post(API_URL, json=payload, timeout=300)
    wall = time.time() - started
    if response.status_code != 200:
        return None, response.status_code, response.text.strip(), wall
    data = response.json()
    return data["message"]["content"].strip(), response.status_code, data, wall


def main():
    print("Step 1: ask for a model that was never pulled")
    reply, status, detail, wall = classify("llama3.2", TICKETS[0])
    print(f"HTTP status: {status}")
    print(f"Response: {detail}")
    print()
    print("Step 2: same tickets, with the model that is actually on disk")
    for ticket in TICKETS:
        reply, status, data, wall = classify("qwen2:0.5b", ticket)
        tokens = data.get("eval_count", 0)
        eval_seconds = data.get("eval_duration", 0) / 1e9
        rate = tokens / eval_seconds if eval_seconds else 0
        print(f"{ticket['id']}: {reply}")
        print(
            f"    {tokens} tokens in {eval_seconds:.1f}s "
            f"({rate:.1f} tokens/sec), wall time {wall:.1f}s"
        )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Here is the real output from the run:

Step 1: ask for a model that was never pulled
HTTP status: 404
Response: {"error":"model 'llama3.2' not found"}

Step 2: same tickets, with the model that is actually on disk
SUP-201: URGENCY: High | TOPIC: Billing | ACTION: Contact customer support to resolve the issue.
    21 tokens in 2.0s (10.4 tokens/sec), wall time 6.0s
SUP-202: URGENCY: High | TOPIC: App crash | ACTION: Close ticket with customer support.
    20 tokens in 0.8s (25.7 tokens/sec), wall time 1.0s
SUP-203: URGENCY: High | TOPIC: Billing | ACTION: Contact customer support to resolve the issue.
    21 tokens in 0.7s (29.6 tokens/sec), wall time 0.9s
SUP-204: URGENCY: High
TOPIC: Server Error
ACTION: Contact IT Support immediately.
    19 tokens in 0.8s (24.1 tokens/sec), wall time 1.1s

The thing that went wrong is in step 1: the request asked for llama3.2, which was never downloaded, and the API answered HTTP 404 with {"error":"model 'llama3.2' not found"}. The fix is to check what is on disk first with ollama list, then pull the missing model. The first qwen2:0.5b call took 6.0 seconds of wall time against 2.0 seconds of generation, because the model was still loading; later calls took about a second each, at 24 to 30 tokens per second.

The verdicts teach a second lesson. The model called every ticket high urgency, invented a topic called "App crash" that was not in the allowed list, and split the last answer across three lines. A 0.5B model is a toy for learning the wiring, not a production classifier. Treat its output as a draft and check it with rules, the way the Pydantic post on this blog validates data first.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, asking for a model that was never pulled. The symptom is HTTP 404 with {"error":"model 'llama3.2' not found"}. The fix is to run ollama list, then ollama pull <model> before you call it, using the exact tag you pulled.

Second, calling the API before the server is running. The symptom in Python is a ConnectionError ending in [Errno 111] Connection refused. The fix is to start the server with ollama serve in a separate terminal, then check http://localhost:11434/api/tags first.

Third, trusting a tiny model's verdicts. The symptom is confident-looking output that is wrong on the details: everything high urgency, invented categories, broken formatting. The fix is to validate the reply against the allowed values in your own code, and test on ten known tickets first.

Fourth, pulling a model bigger than the machine. The symptom is a download that succeeds and a run that crawls or fails to load. The fix is to check the model size on the library page first and match it to free RAM, starting small.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a GPU to run Ollama? No. Small models run on an ordinary CPU: qwen2:0.5b generated 24 to 30 tokens per second on a 4-core machine with no GPU.

Do I need the internet after the model is downloaded? No. Once the model file is on disk, Ollama runs fully offline, and the API works with the network off.

Is my data sent anywhere when I run a model locally? No, not for local models. Ollama's FAQ says it does not see your prompts or data when you run locally. Watch out for names ending in :cloud, which run on Ollama's servers instead.

Can I use Ollama with LangChain? Yes. LangChain can point its chat model at the local Ollama API instead of a cloud provider. The LangChain tutorial on this blog shows the chain pattern; swap the model line for a local one.

What to remember

  • Ollama runs open models on your machine through a local API on port 11434, with no API key.
  • Check ollama list first, or a missing model answers with a 404.
  • The first call is slow while the model loads; later calls are much faster.
  • A tiny model proves the wiring, but validate its verdicts in your own code.

Where this leaves you

You now have a local model answering real tickets from your own code, with timings you measured yourself, and you have seen both failure modes that catch beginners: a missing model and a small model overpromising. Pick one repeated job, a daily inbox sort or a meeting summary, wire it to the local API, and run it for a week. If the small model handles it, you have a private tool that costs nothing per message. If it does not, you will know exactly what a bigger model needs to fix.

Further reading

  • Ollama, official site, https://ollama.com
  • Ollama on GitHub, https://github.com/ollama/ollama
  • Ollama model library, https://ollama.com/library
  • LangChain Tutorial: Build Your First LLM App in Python
  • PyTorch Explained: Machine Learning You Can Watch Learn
  • TensorFlow: Machine Learning, From Tensors to Training
  • Docker Explained: Containers Without the Confusion
  • Pydantic: Catch Bad Data Before It Reaches Your Database

Waqas Shahid is a software engineer from Karachi with more than 12 years of experience, including 6+ years in engineering leadership. He writes The Practical Developer.

title: See and Detect: Image-Driven Open-Vocabulary Multi-View 3D Object Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.17897v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent open-vocabulary multi-view indoor 3D detection methods typically follow a point-cloud-driven pipeline, where pseudo 3D boxes are generated from reconstructed or estimated geometry and semantic labels are inferred from projected regions. However, such a design makes box generation dependent on the completeness of point clouds and restricts semantic learning to local appearance, causing inferior 3D object localization and open-vocabulary classification. In this paper, we present See and Detect, an image-driven framework that uses multi-view images as the primary evidence for 3D box and semantic label generation. For box generation, we first discover object candidates from individual images, enabling objects missing in point clouds to be recovered from visual evidence. However, single-view predictions are often noisy and redundant. To address this, we propose multi-view consensus box consolidation to fuse spatially consistent predictions across views, and box quality assessment to reduce the impact of boxes with partial object coverage. For semantic label generation, we introduce context-aware semantic learning, where semantic labels are queried from full image context, enabling more accurate semantic prediction. Extensive experiments on ScanNet and ARKitScenes demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art open-vocabulary multi-view 3D detection performance while running over 500$\times$ faster than the previous state-of-the-art method.

title: How the PERN stack talks to its database, tried in 30 minutes
description:
In the PERN stack, Express never talks to PostgreSQL by itself. A small library called node-postgres, installed as pg, carries every query from your Node.js code to the database and brings the rows back.

Most beginner tutorials hurry past this piece to get to React. We think it is the part to slow down on. The way you pass data into a query decides whether your first app can be broken with one line typed into a URL. This article explains what pg does and walks you through one working route in about 30 minutes, with free tools.

What does pg do in the PERN stack?

PERN stands for PostgreSQL, Express, React and Node.js. We explain the four letters, and how they compare with MERN, in our guide to MERN vs PERN for web development training in Nepal. Here we look only at the line between the E and the P.

React sends a request. An Express route on Node.js receives it. That route needs data, so it hands a SQL query to pg. node-postgres sends the query to PostgreSQL, waits, and returns the result as JavaScript objects. Each row becomes an object whose keys match the column names, so a row from a courses table looks like { id: 1, name: 'Backend' }.

Two parts of pg matter on day one. A Pool keeps a few open connections to the database and lends one to each query. A parameterised query keeps your SQL text and the user's data apart. The rest of the library can wait.

Why a beginner should start with pg, not an ORM

An ORM is a tool like Prisma that lets you work with the database through code instead of writing SQL by hand. Many teams use one, and our backend course teaches Prisma. We still think a beginner should write their first queries with plain pg.

The reason is that pg hides nothing. You write the SQL, you see the SQL, and when it fails, the error comes from PostgreSQL in words you can search. Our course follows the same order. Week 6 starts with core SQL in psql and safe queries, and Prisma comes after that in the same week.

How to set up a PERN stack backend in 30 minutes

You need Node.js 18 or newer, which Express requires, and either Docker or a normal PostgreSQL install. On an 8 GB laptop, run one database at a time and close the browser tabs you do not need.

Step 1: start PostgreSQL

With Docker, run docker run --name pern-db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpass -p 5432:5432 -d postgres. The official image requires POSTGRES_PASSWORD, and it creates a user called postgres. The -p 5432:5432 part opens PostgreSQL's usual port to your own machine, so Node.js can reach it. The official postgres image page on Docker Hub lists the other settings.

If Docker Desktop is too heavy for your laptop, install PostgreSQL from postgresql.org instead. The steps below stay the same.

Step 2: make one table

Open the database shell with docker exec -it pern-db psql -U postgres. psql is the terminal front end that comes with PostgreSQL. Type CREATE TABLE courses (id serial PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL); and then INSERT INTO courses (name) VALUES ('Backend'), ('QA');. Check it with \dt, which lists your tables, then leave with \q.

Step 3: install Express and pg

Make a new folder, open a terminal in it, and run npm init -y and then npm install express pg. That is all the backend needs for now.

Step 4: write the route

Create index.js. At the top, load the two libraries with const express = require('express') and const { Pool } = require('pg'). Then make the app with const app = express() and a pool with const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: 'postgres://postgres:devpass@localhost:5432/postgres' }).

Now add one route. Inside app.get('/courses/:id', async (req, res) => { ... }), run const result = await pool.query('SELECT * FROM courses WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]) and then res.json(result.rows). End the file with app.listen(3000).

The $1 is a placeholder. The array after the query holds its value. node-postgres sends the two to PostgreSQL separately, and the database puts the value in place itself.

Step 5: call it

Run node index.js. In a second terminal, run curl localhost:3000/courses/1. You should see the Backend row as JSON. Change the 1 to a 2 and you get the QA row.

Break it on purpose

Now change the query to the way many beginners write it the first time: 'SELECT * FROM courses WHERE id = ' + req.params.id. Restart the server and run curl "localhost:3000/courses/1%20OR%201=1". The %20 is a space in a URL.

You get every row in the table. The text 1 OR 1=1 became part of your SQL, and 1=1 is true for every row. This is SQL injection. The OWASP cheat sheet on preventing SQL injection describes it as untrusted data becoming part of a query's SQL syntax. On a table of users or payments, the same mistake leaks real data.

Put the $1 version back and try the same URL. PostgreSQL refuses it, because 1 OR 1=1 is not a whole number, so the request fails instead of returning the table. In a real app you catch that error and send back a clear 400 response. The node-postgres guide to queries warns against joining user input into query text, because it often leads to SQL injection.

Why use a Pool and not a single Client?

node-postgres also has a Client, which is one connection. The library's own docs say a web app should use a pool. Opening a new connection takes a handshake of 20 to 30 milliseconds, and one client runs only one query at a time. A pool keeps connections open and shares them. pool.query also gives the connection back for you, so you cannot forget to return it.

A learner testing alone with curl will not see the difference. You will see it the first time many requests arrive at once, so it is better to start with the habit.

What to try tonight

Do the five steps above. Then add a second route that saves a course with INSERT INTO courses (name) VALUES ($1) RETURNING *, and send the name in a POST request with curl. Add app.use(express.json()) near the top so Express can read the JSON you send. If both routes work and the injection test fails safely, you have built the backend half of a PERN app by hand.

Our backend engineering course in Nepal covers this ground in depth. Week 6 is SQL, PostgreSQL, SQL injection and parameterised queries, Prisma, and about two hours of MongoDB. Week 7 adds indexes, transactions and connection pools. The week-by-week backend engineering syllabus is public, so you can read every topic before you decide.

Common questions

How to learn the PERN stack from zero?

Learn JavaScript first, then build a small Express API, then connect it to PostgreSQL with pg, and add React last. That order puts the hardest part, the data, early. Our backend course starts the same way, with JavaScript and TypeScript in Weeks 2 and 3.

Is PostgreSQL hard for beginners?

PostgreSQL for beginners is mostly SQL: creating tables, adding rows, and writing a SELECT with a JOIN. You can start those basics in one evening with the official PostgreSQL tutorial. Harder topics like indexes and transactions can wait until your first full app works.

Should a PERN stack developer use pg or Prisma?

Learn both, in that order. Many teams use an ORM like Prisma at work, and it still sends SQL to PostgreSQL underneath. A developer who can write that SQL with pg can read what the ORM is doing when a query is slow or wrong.

Do I need Docker for a PERN stack tutorial?

No. Docker is the quickest way to run PostgreSQL and remove it later, but a normal install from postgresql.org works the same with pg. Our course installs Docker Desktop as Week 1 homework, because Week 7 runs the whole app with Docker Compose.

title: Hot Switching vs Cold Switching: What Actually Kills a Coaxial RF Switch
description:
Under a cold-switching specification a coaxial switch is rated for one to five million operations. Under a hot-switching specification the same switch may be rated for fifty thousand. The hardware is identical. The difference is whether the contact opens while RF power is still flowing through it.

Almost every argument about switch life in a test rack comes down to this one clause, and it is often the least visible line on the datasheet.

What actually happens at the contact

An electromechanical coaxial switch makes contact through a spring-loaded blade pressed against a centre conductor. When the circuit is dead, the blade closes onto a clean surface and the only wear is mechanical. When the circuit is live, the blade approaches the conductor while a voltage difference still exists across the gap. Below roughly ten volts the arc does not form and the contact is effectively cold. Above that, and especially above a few tens of volts, a micro-arc erodes a small crater at the contact point on every operation.

The crater matters for two reasons. It raises contact resistance, which shows up as insertion loss creeping up over months. And it roughens the surface, which degrades the repeatability of the return loss. A switch with a million cold operations behind it can still measure like new. A switch with thirty thousand hot operations at 50 W may already be out of specification on isolation, because the eroded contact no longer seats flat.

Manufacturers know this, which is why the two ratings differ by a factor of twenty or more. What they cannot tell you is which one applies to your rack, because that depends on how the software drives the switch.

The sequence is the specification

The sequence that keeps a switch in its cold-switching rating is simple:

  1. Turn the RF source off, or set it to zero output.
  2. Wait for the source to actually settle. On many synthesizers this is longer than the command latency, and on amplifiers with a large output capacitor it can be tens of milliseconds.
  3. Switch.
  4. Wait for contact bounce to finish. A few milliseconds for a relay, microseconds for a PIN diode.
  5. Turn the source back on.

In practice most racks skip steps one and four. The switch driver fires as soon as the instrument accepts the command, and the source is still ramping down. That is a hot switch, and no amount of careful hardware selection fixes it.

The measurable symptom is a switch that meets its insertion loss specification when new and drifts by a few tenths of a dB after a year of production testing, with the drift concentrated on the channels that carry the highest power.

Where hot switching is unavoidable

Some architectures cannot avoid hot switching. A switch matrix that reconfigures while a carrier is running, a redundancy switch that has to move on failure, a calibration path that has to switch during a sweep: in these cases the specification has to be chosen for hot switching from the start, and the derating applied to power and to life.

For a switch rated 100 W cold, a hot-switching rating of 10 to 20 W at the same frequency is typical for a relay with a good contact design. For a PIN diode switch there is no arc at all, so the limit becomes the diode's power dissipation and the bias network, not contact erosion. That is one of the few real advantages of solid-state switching that survives contact with a test plan.

What to write into the test software

Three changes cover most of the exposure, and none of them costs money:

  • Put the source-off command before the switch command in the driver, not after it, and let the driver wait a fixed settling time that you have measured rather than guessed.
  • Add a per-channel operation counter to the log. A switch that is 60 percent through its hot-switching life should be scheduled for replacement, not discovered by a failed measurement.
  • Record power level with the counter. A channel that ran at 2 W for a year and then moved to 50 W has a completely different remaining life, and without the power column nobody can tell.

Choosing the part for the sequence you actually run

If a rack genuinely cold-switches, a standard electromechanical coaxial switch from SPDT to SP12T or DPDT is the right choice, and the failure mode you will meet is mechanical wear after millions of operations. If the rack hot-switches, either accept the reduced life and buy a PIN diode switch, or derate an electromechanical part and treat it as a consumable.

The same logic applies at higher frequencies where the switch is a waveguide switch: the actuator and the contact geometry change, the arc problem does not. And whatever the switch type, the unused throws still need coaxial terminations whose power rating is chosen for the same hot or cold assumption, because a termination that absorbs a live carrier during reconfiguration is doing exactly the job the switch was derated to avoid.

One last line worth writing into the RFQ: ask for the hot-switching life at the frequency and power you will actually use, not the headline cold-switching figure. The answer tells you more about the contact design than any other number on the sheet.
