title: Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-View 3D Transformers via Regime-Aware Attention Approximation
description:
arXiv:2611.17629v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.

title: Federated Soft Poly-Level Learning Over a Distributed Network with Guaranteed Convergence
description:
arXiv:2611.17722v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-level learning/optimization, e.g., bilevel optimization, has been recognized for its versatile applicability across a broad array of domains, spanning from signal processing to machine learning. However, most existing works focus on bilevel and trilevel optimization. In contrast, multi-level optimization problems involving four or more hierarchical levels, which we term poly-level learning (PLL) problems, remain largely unexplored.In addition, in practical PLL, data may be distributed across multiple nodes over a distributed network. Nevertheless, extant studies on PLL predominantly focus on the non-federated setting, necessitating the collection of data to central servers and thereby posing potential privacy risks. To this end, we propose a Federated Poly-Level Learning (FPLL) framework over a distributed network to tackle the PLL problems with soft constraints in a federated manner. FPLL hinges on a novel non-linear cut, i.e., $L$-cut, for the level-wise relaxation to the PLL problems. Additionally, the proposed federated algorithm is designed with adjustable parameters that allow for a flexible trade-off between its computational complexity and performance efficiency, enabling users to tune it according to specific application requirements. We also carry out non-asymptotic analysis to derive the iteration complexity for the proposed FPLL to achieve the $\epsilon$-Pareto stationary point. Extensive experiments have been undertaken to elucidate the superior efficacy of the proposed method.

title: Dockerizing Python APIs for Local and Production
description:
A Python API that works on one laptop can still be painful to deploy if the image is bloated, runs as root, or rebuilds dependencies on every copy change. A clear multi-stage Dockerfile, plus a slightly different compose setup for local work, gives you the same service in development and in production without copying build tools into the runtime image.

This guide is a practical pattern for FastAPI and other Python APIs. It is not a full Kubernetes guide. The aim is a small, non-root image, fast rebuilds, and a local workflow that does not pretend to be production.

A production multi-stage Dockerfile

The builder stage installs compilers and Poetry, then creates a virtualenv. The runtime stage copies only that virtualenv and the application code, and runs as a non-root user.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder

WORKDIR /app

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        build-essential \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir poetry

COPY pyproject.toml poetry.lock ./
RUN poetry config virtualenvs.in-project true \
    && poetry install --only main --no-interaction --no-ansi --no-root

FROM python:3.11-slim AS runtime

WORKDIR /app

RUN groupadd --system --gid 999 appuser \
    && useradd --system --uid 999 --gid appuser --no-create-home appuser

COPY --from=builder /app/.venv /app/.venv
COPY src /app/src

ENV PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH" \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["uvicorn", "src.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

Install Poetry with pip in the builder, not by piping an installer script from the internet at build time. Copy pyproject.toml and poetry.lock before the application source so dependency layers stay cached when you only change code. The runtime image should not include build-essential or Poetry.

Add a .dockerignore that excludes .venv, .git, tests you do not need in the image, and local env files. Accidental copies are a common way to bloat an image or leak a secret.

Why these choices matter

  • Multi-stage builds. Compilers and packaging tools stay in the builder. The runtime image is smaller and has a smaller attack surface.
  • A non-root user. The process does not need to run as root to bind to port 8000 inside the container. If the app is compromised, a root process gives the attacker more room.
  • Layer caching. Code changes should not reinstall every dependency. Lock files should change only when dependencies change.
  • Unbuffered output. PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 makes logs show up promptly in container platforms.

Do not treat a typical image size as a guarantee. The point is to keep build tools and virtualenv sources out of the final image, and to measure the result in your own CI.

Local development should not be a fake production

Locally, you want a fast feedback loop: bind-mount the source, reload the app, and talk to dependent services such as Postgres or Redis. In production, you want the built image, no bind mounts of application code, and no reload. Those are different compose files, or at least different service definitions, on purpose.

# docker-compose.yml (local)
services:
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      target: builder
    command: poetry run uvicorn src.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --reload
    working_dir: /app
    volumes:
      - .:/app
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      - PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
    depends_on:
      - redis


python

The local service above is a sketch: it uses the builder context so Poetry is available, and it mounts the project. Your exact local target may differ. What should not differ is the rule: --reload and live source mounts stay in development. Production should run the runtime image, with a pinned tag, and a process manager or platform restart policy around it.

For production you may also want more than one Uvicorn worker, or a process manager in front of Uvicorn. Choose that based on the service, and keep reload disabled. A health endpoint that does not call a third-party API is useful for both compose and a later orchestrator.

# a simple health route in the app
@app.get("/healthz")
async def healthz():
    return {"status": "ok"}

Production habits

  • Pin base image versions. python:3.11-slim should be a digest or a known tag in CI, not a moving target you never review.
  • Pass secrets as environment variables or mounted secret files, never as layers copied into the image.
  • Run the same image you tested, not a rebuild on the server with different dependencies.
  • Set resource limits in compose or in the platform so one process cannot eat the host.
  • Consider a healthcheck that hits /healthz, but keep it cheap.

If the API also needs a worker, give it the same runtime image and a different command. Do not invent a second, looser Dockerfile for the worker. Shared images keep local and production closer together.

Common mistakes

  • A single-stage image that installs build tools and then never removes them. If you must stay on one stage, at least uninstall compilers in the same layer you used them. Multi-stage is cleaner.
  • Copying the whole repo, including .env and local virtualenvs. A tight .dockerignore is part of the Dockerfile, not an afterthought.
  • Running Uvicorn with --reload in production. Reload is a development convenience. It adds a watcher and is not how you want a public process to start.
  • Building on the server from whatever is on the branch. Build in CI, scan or at least inspect the image, and deploy a tag you already ran tests against.
  • Forgetting the lock file. A build that reads only pyproject.toml can resolve a different set of packages tomorrow.

If you use pip instead of Poetry, the same structure applies: a builder installs into a virtualenv from a pinned requirements file, and the runtime copies that virtualenv. Tools such as uv can make the install faster, but they do not change the layout. Keep the runtime slim, non-root, and reproducible.

For a service that also serves static files or needs system libraries, add those packages in the runtime stage on purpose, not by reusing the builder image. Every package in the final image should have a reason to be there.

Summary

Dockerizing a Python API well is mostly discipline: multi-stage builds, a non-root runtime user, dependency layer caching, and a local compose setup that does not copy production habits such as bind mounts and reload. Do that, and the same service can move from a laptop to a production host without a one-off image for each environment.

If you want help containerizing a FastAPI or Python API for local work and production, get in touch.

Originally published at https://prakashtank.com/blog/dockerizing-python-apis-for-local-and-production.

title: Rounding money in Uniface ProcScript - why the modulo operator was the wrong tool
description:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 got a credit module in stage 31. One operation suggests a credit limit per customer: two months of revenue, rounded down to full 10 euros, half of it if the customer paid late once or twice, and nothing at all from three late payments on.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. The app uses SQLite through the SLE driver (SQLite 3.50.2).

The amounts

All money columns of the app are integer cents. Two months of revenue are the revenue of the last 12 months divided by 6, and "full 10 euros" is a multiple of 1000 cents.

What went wrong

The first version did the rounding in ProcScript with the modulo operator. The test service of the stage ran the operation against fixed test data and compared with the expected amount. Two of 60 tests failed: the suggestion came back with a fraction (1000,33) instead of a multiple of 1000 cents.

revenue / 6 is not an integer in most cases. In these tests % only worked with the integer part of the value, so subtracting the remainder from the value kept the fraction. Instead of looking for the right combination of ProcScript functions, the rounding moved to the place where the numbers come from anyway.

The working version

The helper COUNT_SQL runs a statement that returns one number:

entry COUNT_SQL
params
    string pSql : IN
    numeric pCount : OUT
endparams
    pCount = -1
    sql pSql, "CUSTOMERS"
    if ($status >= 0)
        pCount = $result
    endif
    return 0
end

The rounding is one SELECT. With integer cents, / in SQLite is already an integer division; CAST(... AS INTEGER) keeps the result an integer even if a value ever arrives as REAL. For positive amounts both mean rounding down:

    call COUNT_SQL("SELECT CAST(%%(vRevenue) / 6000 AS INTEGER) * 1000 FROM (SELECT 1 AS X)", vBase)

Half of it, again on full 10 euros:

        call COUNT_SQL("SELECT CAST(%%(vBase) / 2000 AS INTEGER) * 1000 FROM (SELECT 1 AS X)", vBase)

The whole entry:

entry SUGGEST_OF
params
    numeric pCustomerId : IN
    numeric pSuggestCents : OUT
    string pReason : OUT
endparams
variables
    string vCond, vPaid, vText
    numeric vRevenue, vLate, vLateOpen, vBase
endvariables
    pSuggestCents = 0
    pReason = ""
    call REV_COND(vCond)
    call PAID_SQL(vPaid)
    call COUNT_SQL("SELECT COALESCE(SUM(d.GROSS_CENTS), 0) FROM SALES_DOC d WHERE %%(vCond) AND d.CUSTOMER_ID = %%(pCustomerId) AND d.DOC_DATE > date('now', 'localtime', '-1 year')", vRevenue)
    call COUNT_SQL("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM SALES_DOC d JOIN %%(vPaid) p ON p.DOC_ID = d.DOC_ID WHERE d.CUSTOMER_ID = %%(pCustomerId) AND d.DOC_TYPE = 'INVOICE' AND d.STATUS = 'PAID' AND d.DUE_DATE IS NOT NULL AND p.LASTPAY > d.DUE_DATE AND d.DOC_DATE > date('now', 'localtime', '-1 year')", vLate)
    call COUNT_SQL("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM SALES_DOC d WHERE d.CUSTOMER_ID = %%(pCustomerId) AND d.DOC_TYPE = 'INVOICE' AND d.STATUS IN ('ISSUED', 'PARTLY_PAID') AND d.DUE_DATE < date('now', 'localtime')", vLateOpen)
    vLate = vLate + vLateOpen
    if (vRevenue <= 0)
        pReason = "No revenue in the last 12 months."
        return 0
    endif
    call COUNT_SQL("SELECT CAST(%%(vRevenue) / 6000 AS INTEGER) * 1000 FROM (SELECT 1 AS X)", vBase)
    call FMT_CENTS(vRevenue, vText)
    if (vLate >= 3)
        pReason = "Revenue %%(vText) in 12 months, %%(vLate) late payment(s): no limit suggested (prepayment)."
        return 0
    endif
    if (vLate > 0)
        call COUNT_SQL("SELECT CAST(%%(vBase) / 2000 AS INTEGER) * 1000 FROM (SELECT 1 AS X)", vBase)
        pReason = "Revenue %%(vText) in 12 months, %%(vLate) late payment(s): one month of revenue."
    else
        pReason = "Revenue %%(vText) in 12 months, paid on time: two months of revenue."
    endif
    pSuggestCents = vBase
    return 0
end

The same pitfall in a median

The lifecycle module computes the median of "days until the first order". The obvious way to find the middle of a sorted list uses % 2. The tested version uses a comparison that is true for the middle element of an odd list and for the lower middle of an even list:

    vI = 0
    forlist vRow in vData
        vI = vI + 1
        if (vI * 2 >= pWithOrder & vI * 2 <= pWithOrder + 1)
            getitem vDays, vRow, 1
            pMedianDays = vDays
        endif
    endfor

Notes

  • $concat takes at most five arguments; a sixth argument is a compile error (1000). Longer texts are built in several steps.
  • After the change, the test service ran 60 tests with 0 failures. The tests roll back at the end, and the database file had the same MD5 before and after.

title: Certified Improvements to Best-Known Thomson-Problem Configurations with a Search Pipeline Built with Large Language Model Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.17776v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Thomson problem asks for N unit charges on a sphere with minimum Coulomb energy; for large N the best configurations known are curated in the Cambridge Cluster Database, whose largest-N entries were set in October 2026. We report configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502 with energies 0.0036186, 0.0109730 and 0.0614033 below the database values, certified by exact integer arithmetic. All three are numerically strict local minima modulo rotations and keep the defect inventory and scar compositions of the database configurations; the database value for N = 912 had been reached by two different methods. Our search runs unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from the database configurations, with a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions after relabelling by geometry, and gradient-only polishing; replica-exchange basin hopping alone found the N = 912 and 1382 configurations, the former in one of five runs. We built and ran it with large language model agents (Claude, through a chat interface and the Claude Code agent), and we report every search, including those that failed. Two findings matter for others who search the database. Polishing alone lowers two entries by more than the threshold at which our pipeline reports a candidate, which produced two spurious records until candidates were compared with the polished database energies (the polished baseline). A local-relaxation speed-up passed its exactness test yet found nothing in a controlled comparison in which every arm with full relaxation went below the database value within 15 minutes. We distil three practices for computational discovery with large language model agents: calibrate the search code and verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare candidates with the polished baseline, and test design changes in controlled comparisons with pass criteria fixed in advance.

title: Hybrid post-quantum E2EE in a messenger: what is hybrid, and how to check it yourself
description:
Hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-65, layer by layer, with tests you can run.

Umbera is an end-to-end encrypted messenger. This post walks through every place where it uses post-quantum cryptography, points to the file and the test behind each one, and ends with an equally explicit list of what you can't verify yet. All code excerpts come from the public repository and are Apache-2.0.

A 90-second look at the app before the details:

What is open, and what isn't

Open, in UmberaAPP/UMBERA:

  • core/: the Rust crypto core (ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-65, X25519, Ed25519, secp256k1, AES-GCM, key derivation, MLS groups with X-Wing, call frame keys, QR device linking, message franking), plus tests, vectors and fuzz targets. The same code is published on crates.io as umbera-core 1.1.0.
  • kotlin/: the protocol layer of the apps (envelopes, Double Ratchet, mailbox addresses, group signatures, safety number, the second call layer, meetings by link).
  • communities/: Communities cryptography, with an independent Go reference implementation.
  • docs/: PROTOCOL.md, PROOF.md, and PQ_STATUS.md, which lists every post-quantum mechanism with its file, line and test.

Not open: the server, the app UI, the network and storage layers. The full code will go to trusted independent auditors when the project is audited, and we'll publish the report afterwards. Builds aren't reproducible yet.

Why hybrid, and why now

Harvest now, decrypt later. Anyone can record ciphertext today, whether from the wire, the server or a database backup. If the session keys were agreed with elliptic curves only, a large enough quantum computer could later recover them with Shor's algorithm and read the archive. For messages that should stay private for years, the timeline of that computer barely matters, because the recording already exists.

Why not pure post-quantum? ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) were standardised in 2024. The math has been studied for a long time, but the implementations are young, and timing leaks have already turned up in Kyber implementations (KyberSlash). X25519 is the opposite: very well understood, and broken by a quantum adversary. A hybrid feeds both secrets into one key derivation, so an attacker has to break both. Signal's PQXDH, Apple's PQ3 and the X25519MLKEM768 key exchange in browsers' TLS make the same choice.

From docs/PROTOCOL.md, section 4:

ss_classical = X25519(ephemeral_private, recipient_x25519_public)
(ct, ss_pq)  = ML-KEM-1024.Encapsulate(recipient_kyber_public)
okm = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = ss_classical || ss_pq, salt = HYBRID_LABEL, info = "key-derivation", L = 64)

What exactly is hybrid

1:1 messages: envelope v3 and sealed sender

A message is encrypted by the Double Ratchet, packed together with the sender's identity, and sealed to the recipient. Because the sender is inside the ciphertext, the server never learns who sent it (sealed sender). In 2.1 the seal is envelope v3: an ephemeral X25519 key plus an ML-KEM-1024 encapsulation, HKDF-SHA256 salted with a hash of the transcript (ephemeral key, KEM ciphertext, both recipient public keys), then AES-256-GCM and padding to a size class. Each transcript part is length-prefixed:

// core/src/sealv3.rs, lines 8–20 · Apache-2.0
fn part(h: &mut Sha256, x: &[u8]) {
    h.update((x.len() as u32).to_be_bytes());
    h.update(x);
}

fn th(label: &str, parts: &[&[u8]]) -> Vec<u8> {
    let mut h = Sha256::new();
    part(&mut h, label.as_bytes());
    for p in parts {
        part(&mut h, p);
    }
    h.finalize().to_vec()
}

An ML-KEM-1024 ciphertext is 1,568 bytes, so not every message carries one. A full v3 envelope has a fresh capsule. Up to 49 short v3s envelopes (24 hours at most) then use a fresh ephemeral X25519 key plus a one-way chain from the hybrid pair secret of the last confirmed full envelope. Measured sizes: 21,682 bytes for the previous v2 format, 5,038 for full v3, 3,078 for short v3s, and 3,117 on average over 50.

The ratchet itself runs on X25519, and a fresh ML-KEM-1024 secret is mixed into the root key at session start and then every 20 new chains or every 24 hours. File keys are wrapped with X25519 + ML-KEM-1024 and bound to the transcript (file wrap v2).

Mailboxes: where an envelope goes

The server has no "from" or "to" fields. An envelope goes to a mailbox address that only the two people in the conversation can compute, with one address per direction. Between two 2.1 apps, the address mixes the X25519 pair secret with a direction secret derived from the hybrid v3 exchange, so someone who later breaks X25519 still can't compute it. The address also rotates weekly, at the same second for everyone:

// kotlin/src/commonMain/kotlin/app/umbera/core/crypto/RendezvousV2.kt, lines 39–40 · Apache-2.0
    fun ridEpoch(ssX25519: ByteArray, dir: ByteArray, fromId: String, toId: String, epoch: Long): String =
        hex(RustCore.hkdfSha256(ssX25519 + dir, SALT, "rdv-e|$fromId|$toId|$epoch".encodeToByteArray(), 32u))

If either side still runs 2.0.x, the pair keeps its previous, fixed address.

Groups: MLS with X-Wing, plus ML-DSA-65 on top

Groups use MLS (RFC 9420) through OpenMLS 0.9.2. New groups are created on MLS_256_XWING_CHACHA20POLY1305_SHA256_Ed25519 (0x004D), where the KEM is X-Wing (X25519 + ML-KEM-768). An existing group moves to X-Wing by itself once every member supports it, and keeps its members and history. A group with a 2.0.x member stays on suite 0x0001.

MLS member signatures are still Ed25519, as the standard defines today. On top of them, every Commit, Proposal and Welcome carries an ML-DSA-65 signature. Ordinary messages form a per-sender hash chain that is closed by an ML-DSA-65 checkpoint every 20 messages or after 30 seconds of silence. Once a member has announced these signatures, an unsigned change in their name is refused. The cost is +4,429 bytes per signed Commit and about +275 bytes per message on average.

Calls: a second post-quantum layer over DTLS-SRTP

DTLS-SRTP agrees its key classically, so a call recorded today could be decrypted later. That's why every audio, video and screen-sharing frame is encrypted a second time, with keys from a fresh X25519 + ML-KEM-1024 exchange per call. The exchange is carried inside the encrypted, caller-signed call setup, the keys are bound to a hash of the whole exchange, and each direction gets its own key:

// core/src/callkey.rs, lines 74–86 (excerpt) · Apache-2.0
    let th = transcript(call_id, public, answer);
    let ikm = Zeroizing::new([ss_x, ss_k].concat());
    let prk = Zeroizing::new(hkdf::Hkdf::<Sha256>::extract(Some(&th), &ikm).0.to_vec());
    let exp = |info: &str, n: u32| p::hkdf_sha256_expand(prk.to_vec(), info.as_bytes().to_vec(), n);
    let i2r = exp("umbera-call-v1/frames/initiator->responder", 32)?;
    let r2i = exp("umbera-call-v1/frames/responder->initiator", 32)?;

Frames use AES-128-GCM in WebRTC's frame-encryptor format. The key is PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (100,000 rounds) of the 256-bit hybrid output. If AES-128 here bothers you, that's a fair thing to push on. In group calls, every pair of participants runs its own exchange, and no server mixes media. In meetings by link, a 256-bit room key lives only in the URL fragment after #, so the server sees only a random room number.

Stopping key substitution

  • Safety number v2 hashes all four identity keys (secp256k1, X25519, ML-DSA-65, ML-KEM-1024), each one length-prefixed. v1 covered only the first two, which meant a server could have swapped the post-quantum keys without changing the number. 
// kotlin/src/commonMain/kotlin/app/umbera/core/crypto/SafetyNumber.kt, lines 51–55 · Apache-2.0
    fun identityV2(secp256k1: ByteArray, x25519: ByteArray, mlDsaPk: ByteArray, mlKemPk: ByteArray): String {
        var buf = V2_LABEL
        for (k in listOf(secp256k1, x25519, mlDsaPk, mlKemPk)) buf += lenBE(k.size) + k
        return HashUtils.sha256(buf).toHexLower()
    }
  • The key transparency log is an append-only Merkle tree. Since 16 November 2026, the server signs each tree head with Ed25519 and ML-DSA-65; the ML-DSA message includes the Ed25519 key. The client side is open (KeyTransparencyVerifier.sthAuthentic): once the log's ML-DSA-65 key is pinned, a tree head without a valid PQ co-signature is rejected. Pinning happens on first use, so the very first contact with the log is the weak point.
  • No silent downgrade. A new format is sent only after the contact has announced support inside an end-to-end encrypted message. If that announcement later disappears, the app shows "key changed" instead of quietly falling back.

Linking a computer by QR follows the same pattern: X25519 + ML-KEM-1024, transcript-salted HKDF, key confirmation in both directions, a 6-digit code on both screens, and a device certificate signed with both secp256k1 and ML-DSA-65.

Try it yourself

You need Rust 1.91 or newer.

git clone https://github.com/UmberaAPP/UMBERA
cd UMBERA/core
cargo test --release
# 8 test binaries, 114 passed, 0 failed

cargo test --release --test proof          # 1:1 seal: 7 tests
cargo test --release --test proof_groups   # MLS groups: 6 tests
cargo test --release --test compat_v06     # new core vs. the previous core (OpenMLS 0.6)
cargo test --release --lib sealv3::        # envelope v3 vectors, shared with Kotlin
cargo test --release --lib callkey::       # call frame keys
cargo test --release --lib xwing_hundred_leaves_and_sizes -- --nocapture

cd ../communities/pqc && go test -v ./...  # independent Go check of the Communities vectors

tests/proof.rs models the hybrid seal and checks each property directly. Here's the one that matters for post-quantum:

// core/tests/proof.rs, lines 87–94 · Apache-2.0
fn breaking_only_x25519_is_not_enough() {
    // An attacker who somehow learned Bob's X25519 key (for example with a future
    // quantum computer) still cannot open the message without his Kyber key.
    let bob = new_recipient();
    let eve = new_recipient();
    let sealed = seal(&bob, MESSAGE);
    assert_eq!(open(&bob.x25519_private, &eve.kyber_private, &sealed), None);
}

The mirror test, breaking_only_kyber_is_not_enough, is right below it. tests/proof_groups.rs checks that every member can read a message, that an outsider can't even with a group under the same ID, that a removed member can't read new epochs, and that a new member can't read old ones. One caveat: these tests prove properties of the scheme on the core's primitives. They don't prove what a store build runs.

Known-answer vectors pin each formula byte for byte. core/tests/vectors/seal-v3-vectors.txt covers the v3/v3s envelope, the file key, mailbox addresses and their weekly epochs. It's computed in Rust with sha2 + hkdf directly and checked by the Kotlin tests too. primitives-golden.json pins SHA-256, HKDF, AES-GCM, X25519, Ed25519, ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-65 and more. The strongest review is to implement a formula from PROTOCOL.md yourself and diff it against these files.

Capture your own traffic. On a network you control, use Wireshark with the filter dtls || rtp || srtp during a call. You should see a DTLS handshake followed only by SRTP, with no plain RTP. Send a one-letter message and then a long paragraph, and the upload sizes fall into the same few fixed classes. Turn on Tor and repeat: nothing goes to the server directly any more.

Since the server code is closed, that table describes what reaches the server according to the open client code. In short, the server sees mailbox addresses and when they're used, public keys, the number of linked computers and your IP address (unless Tor is on). It doesn't see content, the sender, the recipient account, group membership, exact sizes or meeting keys.

What we don't claim

  • No independent audit yet.
  • No reproducible builds yet. Until they exist, "the app runs this code" rests on our word and on what you can observe.
  • The server and the apps aren't open.
  • Without Tor, the server sees your IP address. Tor is off by default, and Tor itself has no post-quantum handshake yet.
  • Older apps (2.0.x) use older schemes: no second call layer, the previous MLS suite, safety number v1, and a fixed mailbox address. Everything is still end-to-end encrypted.
  • A key change warns, it doesn't block, and a missing transparency log entry doesn't raise a warning yet.
  • Mailbox reads are authorised with Ed25519, so that part is classical today. PQ_STATUS.md covers end-to-end encryption, not the transport to the server.
  • A compromised device is out of scope.

Break it

If the code does less than PQ_STATUS.md says, that's a security report. Email the address in SECURITY.md with the subject SECURITY (acknowledgement within 72 hours), and use GitHub Discussions for questions. There's no paid bounty yet, but confirmed findings are credited. Good places to start: the v3s inheritance window, trust-on-first-use pinning of the log's ML-DSA key, and the call frame format.

Links: repository · PQ_STATUS.md · PROTOCOL.md · PROOF.md · crates.io/umbera-core · umbera.app/verify

title: SceneAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Portable Game Scene Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.17821v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Moving a scene generator to a new game engine requires more than exporting its final output: planning, construction tools, and stored experience may also depend on the original backend. We present SceneAgent, a multi-agent framework for reusing the construction process and its experience across backends. A canonical SceneContext maintains the evolving world, while backend adapters isolate coordinate conventions, asset bindings, and export. Structured handoffs let fresh Builder sessions query this persistent state without inheriting the full construction transcript. Across generations, human-approved traces are distilled into asset-ID-free Layout skills and semantic Content skills that can be retrieved and recombined. We introduce GameSceneBench, comprising 69 indoor and outdoor prompts. Under a common asset and evaluation protocol, SceneAgent obtains human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2-89.4% against five baselines. Ablations show that reusable skills and the multi-agent protocol primarily improve prompt alignment and scene completeness, with additional runtime. Deployment in a second engine preserves the shared construction protocol and skill library while replacing backend integration components. Together, these results support separating persistent scene state, task-local reasoning, and reusable experience for portable scene construction.

title: Invoice PDF page breaks: a row split in half, and the total alone on the last page
description:
An invoice template gets tested with five line items. It fits on one page and looks fine. Then a customer orders thirty things, and the PDF comes back with a row cut in half across the page break, or with Subtotal and Tax at the bottom of page one and TOTAL sitting by itself at the top of page two.

It's an old problem. The Stack Overflow question about keeping a table row off a page break has about 240,000 views and was still getting edits in 2025, and the invoice-specific versions of it (this one, this one) have no answers at all. A Hacker News comment from October puts the mood well: headless Chrome, Puppeteer, wkhtmltopdf all tried, and "it really feels like it shouldn't be this hard".

It's less hard than it looks once you know which four rules matter. We measured each one rather than repeat the folklore.

The setup

Playwright 1.63 driving Chromium 153 headless, page.setContent() then page.pdf() on US Letter with half-inch margins. A plain HTML table, 14px sans-serif, each line item three lines tall, followed by a totals block (a <div> with Subtotal, Tax and TOTAL). We read every page back with pdftotext and rendered the page boundaries to images. Puppeteer's page.pdf() drives the same print engine, so the results should carry over; we didn't run it separately.

Failure 1: a row cut in half

With no page-break CSS at all, 60 line items, Chromium cuts rows wherever the page ends. Item 27 gets its first two lines on page 2 and its "third line" on page 3:

Note the header, though. Description / Qty / Amount is repeated at the top of the next page without any CSS, because it's in a <thead>. Chromium repeats <thead> on every page of a table that spans pages. If your header is a plain first <tr> inside <tbody>, it won't be repeated. Move it into <thead>.

The fix for the row:

tr { break-inside: avoid; }

Same 60 items with that rule: none of the four page boundaries cut a row. Each one ends on a row's last line and the next page starts with the header and a complete row. The older spelling, page-break-inside: avoid, is an alias and does the same thing in Chromium.

Flex rows behave the same way. We rebuilt the table as display: flex divs: without a rule they split mid-row too, and with break-inside: avoid on the row div they stopped splitting. What you lose with divs is the repeated header, since only a real <thead> gets that.

Failure 2: TOTAL alone on the last page

Now a 13-item invoice whose totals block only just doesn't fit. Rows are whole (the rule above is on), but the block after the table splits like any other text:

This one reaches the customer looking like a mistake. The page they look at first has no total on it.

The obvious fix doesn't fully work:

.totals { break-inside: avoid; }

The block stays together now, but the whole thing moves to page 2. In our runs, page 2 was Subtotal, Tax and TOTAL with no line item above them. A total that doesn't sit under anything isn't much better.

What does work is telling Chromium the totals must not be separated from what comes before them:

.totals {
  break-inside: avoid;
  break-before: avoid;
}

With that, Chromium carries the last line item over to page 2 along with the totals, and repeats the header above it:

Putting break-after: avoid on the last row (tbody tr:last-child { break-after: avoid; }) gave the same result in our runs. Use whichever reads better in your stylesheet.

Don't put the total in <tfoot>

It's tempting, since <tfoot> looks like it was made for totals. But Chromium repeats <tfoot> at the bottom of every page the table spans, just as it repeats <thead> at the top. A grand total in <tfoot> prints on page 1 as if it were the total for page 1. Use <tfoot> for something that should repeat, like "continued on next page", and keep the real totals in a block after the table.

Where the rules stop

A row taller than a page still splits. We gave one line item a 70-line description. With tr { break-inside: avoid; } Chromium first pushed that row to a fresh page, leaving page 1 mostly empty, and then split it across pages 2 and 3 anyway, because it can't fit anywhere. The CSS can't help a row that's bigger than the page. If your descriptions can get that long, cap them in the table and print the full text in a notes section underneath.

wkhtmltopdf is a different engine. It's built on an old QtWebKit, not Chromium, and the unanswered question above is someone finding page-break-inside ignored on rows there. Nothing we measured here says anything about wkhtmltopdf. If you're still on it, that's one more reason to move.

Test with the longest invoice you have. Every one of these failures depends on where the page happens to end, so a template that passes with 5 rows and with 60 can still fail at 13. Generate a few lengths in a loop, open the boundaries, and look.

The short version 

thead { display: table-header-group; } /* the default; only needed if something reset it */
tr { break-inside: avoid; }
.totals { break-inside: avoid; break-before: avoid; }

Header in <thead>, totals in a block after the table, never in <tfoot>.

Where we fit

None of this needs a service. It's CSS, and it works in the Chromium you may already be running. We make iReceipt PRO, an API that takes a template and JSON and returns the PDF, so you don't run a browser at all. The CSS above is still yours to write either way, and still worth testing against whatever renders your invoices: the page break lands wherever your content puts it.

Originally published at https://ireceipt.pro/blog/invoice-pdf-table-row-split-across-pages.

title: Why AI Search Crawlers Hate Single-Page Apps (and What They Actually See)
description:
If your web app relies on client-side rendering (CSR)—like a standard React Vite SPA, Vue CLI build, or Angular app without SSR—you might be completely invisible to modern AI search engines and autonomous crawler agents.

Many developers assume: "Googlebot executes JavaScript, so ChatGPT and Perplexity probably do too."

In reality, autonomous agents and real-time AI retrieval pipelines operate under completely different latency and compute budgets than legacy search indexers.

Here is why client-side SPAs struggle with AI crawlers, what these bots actually receive, and how to verify what you're serving them.

1. The Real-Time Retrieval Problem

When a user asks Perplexity, ChatGPT Search, or Claude a question requiring real-time web context, the engine needs to:

  1. Dispatch queries to multiple URLs in parallel.
  2. Fetch the page contents.
  3. Extract clean text, facts, and structure.
  4. Synthesize the answer and stream it back to the user within 2–3 seconds.

Spinning up a headless Chromium instance, waiting 800ms for your React bundle to download, executing your JavaScript chunks, waiting for client-side API requests to resolve, and capturing the final hydrated DOM is computationally expensive and too slow for interactive search.

As a result, most AI retrieval bots perform fast, lightweight HTTP GET requests and extract content directly from raw HTML.

2. What the Bot Actually Sees

If you ship a client-side SPA, your server returns something like this:


html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <title>My SaaS Platform</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <div id="root"></div>
    <script type="module" src="/assets/index-C8a12x.js"></script>
  </body>
</html>


Some teams try to patch this by adding rich meta tags (og:description, description) via packages like react-helmet on the client.

However, if those tags are injected into the <head> after JavaScript mounts, the initial raw HTTP response still lacks them! The bot reads an empty <head> or default template tags before hydration ever runs.

You don't need fancy tools to run a baseline check. Open your terminal and run:


curl -A "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; PerplexityBot/1.0)" -L https://yourdomain.com


Look at the output:


Can you read your actual value proposition, pricing, and feature headings directly in the terminal output?


Or do you just see script bundles and an empty container <div id="root"></div>?


If you see an empty container, search crawlers that don't execute JS are getting zero context from your domain.


Have You Tested Your Domain?

We built a free diagnostic scanner over at AI-Primed that analyzes how edge bots, AI search crawlers, and LLM parsers extract your site's data (including WAF rules, robots directives, and machine readability).

title: Why is my landing page not converting?
description:
We build Opti-Behavior, the WordPress plugin used in the examples.

Your landing page gets visits, but nobody clicks the button. Before you redesign it, find which of nine usual causes is hurting your page: each one leaves a trace you can check in your own data. Below, the 9 reasons and where to look, then how we read them page by page in WordPress: the modules collect (heatmaps, scroll, funnels, forms, errors), Smart Insights ranks the problems, and the Page X-Ray report (Pro) lists what to fix first. On our demo store it found a home page where « Go to checkout » got 0 clicks over 4,236 visits.

You have traffic. You have a page. But nobody clicks the button. If you keep asking yourself “why is my page not converting?”, Page X-Ray gives you the answer, for every page of your site, in one report.

Most analytics tools show you numbers: visits, bounce rate, time on page. They do not tell you what is wrong, or what to fix first. So you open a heatmap, then a recording, then the funnel report, then the error log. An hour later, you are still guessing.

Landing page not converting? Start with these 9 reasons

Before we look at Page X-Ray, here is the short list. When a landing page is not converting, it is almost always one of these nine things. Each one leaves a clear trace in your data.

Reason What you see in the data Where to look
People do not understand the offer in 5 seconds Short visits, quick exits from the top of the page Scroll heatmap, time on page
The main button is hard to find Few clicks on the button, clicks on other things Click heatmap
The button is below where most people stop Scroll depth ends before the button Scroll heatmap
Clicks on things that are not links Hot spots on images, icons or text Click heatmap, rage clicks
The form asks too much People start the form and quit on one field Form analytics
Something is broken JavaScript errors, dead clicks, slow load Error tracking, recordings
The page is slow on mobile High mobile exit rate, poor Core Web Vitals Performance report
Not enough trust People scroll to reviews or price, then leave Recordings, attention heatmap
Wrong visitors One traffic source converts much worse than the others Funnel filtered by source

Checking all nine by hand takes time. That is exactly why we built Page X-Ray. It reads the same data for one page and tells you which of these problems is the biggest. Here is how it works.

Page X-Ray is the new per-page report of Smart Insights in Opti-Behavior Pro 1.9.2. It reads every module for one page (heatmaps, scroll depth, session recordings, funnels, forms, errors and broken links) and turns them into one answer: what is wrong, how many visits it costs, and the one button that opens the right report.

In this article we walk through a real report from our live demo store, section by section. Every screenshot comes from the plugin, not from a mockup.

Page not converting? The short answer

A page not converting almost always has one of five causes. Page X-Ray checks each of them, on each page, with your real visitors:

  • The main button is not seen or not clicked. It sits too low, says something vague, or competes with other links.

  • Visitors leave before the offer. They stop scrolling before the part of the page that matters.

  • Something is broken. A link leads to a missing page, a script error freezes a button, a form field makes people give up.

  • The page does not earn trust. No reviews, no testimonials, no legal pages, no human to contact.

  • Something changed. A plugin, theme or WordPress update, or a page edit, happened just before the numbers moved.

Instead of five reports to cross-check for every page not converting, you get one report that ranks these problems by the visits they cost and tells you what to do about each one. For the whole site, see our website analytics report.

Start with the list: which page should you fix first?

Open Smart Insights → Page X-Ray. Every tracked page of the period is listed with a health score, its number of visits and its number one problem. The list is sorted from the page to fix first to the healthiest, so the first row is where your time pays off most.


Every tracked page, from the one to fix first to the healthiest, with the problem that costs it the most visits.

A healthy page with a lot of traffic can still sit high in the list if one problem touches many visits. A page with a low score but very few visits stays lower. The score is about what visitors actually hit, not about a theoretical checklist.

One report per page: health score and page goal

Click Open on a page and its report starts with the essentials. Here is the home page of our demo coffee store.


The health score (46, Fix), what the page is, its goal, and the numbers that matter compared with the rest of the site.

  • Health score. Built from the problems visitors actually hit, with the points lost per area: Content & UX, Errors, Forms, Funnel, Links.

  • What this page is. Page X-Ray reads the live page and recognises its type (home page, product, article, contact page and more) and how sure it is.

  • Goal of the page. The main button it found, here “Go to checkout”, and the share of visits that reach it. Here: 0%. That single number explains why this page is not converting.

  • On the page. Words, reading time, calls to action, price shown, page height and menu links, read from the live page.

  • Vital signs. Visits, visitors, page views, time on page, scroll depth, bounce and mobile share, each compared with the previous period or with the site average.

What to fix, most costly first

This is the heart of the report, and where a page not converting shows its real cause. Each problem is a card with the visits it touched, why it matters, what to do, and one button that opens the exact report you need. The most costly problem comes first.


Six problems on one page, ranked by the visits they cost, each with why it matters, what to do and a button to the right report.

Why nobody clicks your main button

“Nobody clicks Go to checkout, the goal of this page. Over 4,236 visits, not one click.” When the goal of a page is never taken, nothing else on the page matters. Page X-Ray tells you to make it the only prominent button, move it above the fold and say what happens after the click, and opens the click heatmap so you can see where visitors click instead.

Broken links that cost you clicks

A link that leads to a missing page is a dead end for the visitor and for search engines. The card shows the link text, the address, how many visits clicked it and since when, so you can fix or remove it in minutes.

Visitors who click the menu, not the content

When most clicks land on the menu, the header or the footer, visitors are looking for something the page does not give them. Page X-Ray measures that share and points you to the user journeys to see where they go next.

Forms that visitors abandon, and the field that stops them

Visitors who start a form have intent. Losing them is the most expensive loss on a page. The card names the field where most people give up, here “author”, and suggests making it optional or clearer.

JavaScript errors: which plugin broke the page?

A failing script can freeze a button, a form or a menu without any visible message. Page X-Ray lists each error with the message, the file and the line, the plugin or theme that ships it (here WooCommerce), the browsers and devices, and the number of visits affected.

The WordPress page audit: a checklist made for this type of page

Below the problems comes the page audit. It works like a landing page audit, done automatically for every page of your WordPress site. It compares what the page contains with the checklist for its type: a product page is not checked like an article or a contact page. It is split into tabs, each with a score, the missing items and one clear action per item.

Understand: can visitors and Google tell what the page is?


Meta description, title length, a single H1, a clear goal, the offer visible without scrolling, and a mobile-ready page.

Missing meta description (see Google’s guide to meta descriptions), a title that is too long, three H1 headings on one page: small things that decide what people see in Google and whether they understand the page in the first seconds.

Buttons: which calls to action are really clicked?


Every call to action with its position on the page, the share of visitors who reach it, its clicks and a verdict.

Page X-Ray finds the buttons automatically. For each one you see where it sits, how many visitors scroll that far and how many click. If it picked the wrong buttons, choose them yourself on the page: the goal, the verdicts and the action plan follow your choice.

Behaviour: where visitors look, click and leave


Viewing time for each tenth of the page, how many visitors are still there, and where they click.

This tab answers “why do visitors leave my website?” with numbers, page by page. Here, 36% of the viewing time is spent in the first tenth of the page, but the main button sits at 20%. Page X-Ray suggests moving it up, repeating it after the section where visitors spend their time, and adding a reason to continue before the point where 20% of them leave. It also flags elements that people click but that are not links, like a “30-day taste guarantee” heading.

Trust: would you buy from this page?


Reviews, testimonials, legal pages and a way to reach a human.

No reviews, no testimonials, no privacy policy linked: visitors hesitate. Each missing item comes with a precise fix, like adding two or three short testimonials just before the main button.

Content: is there enough, and is it easy to read?


Images without alt text, what the main button says, enough words to decide, sub-headings, author and date.

Here on a blog article: 1,314 words where about 600 are expected for this kind of page, 12 sub-headings, author and date shown, but 3 of 17 images without alternative text.

Sharing: what people see when they share your page


A preview of the shared link, and the missing share title, description, image and large card.

When a page has no share title, description or image (the Open Graph tags), Facebook, LinkedIn, X or Discord pick one at random. Page X-Ray shows the preview people see and what to set, usually from your SEO plugin.

Evolution: did a change really move your visitors?


Visits per day over 90 days, and the last 14 days against the 14 days before, with a verdict.

Numbers move every day. The Evolution tab compares two periods and tells you if the difference is real or just normal day-to-day noise, using simple statistical tests. Here: no real change.

Did a plugin update break my page? The WordPress change log

“My traffic dropped after a WordPress update.” “Conversions fell after I edited the page.” Page X-Ray keeps a log of plugin, theme and WordPress updates and of page edits. Each change is listed with its date and marked on the charts as a dashed line, so you can see at a glance whether a problem started right after it.


Every plugin, theme and WordPress update of the period, with the version before and after.

When a change has enough visits on each side, the report compares the days before and after it. No more guessing whether the new theme version is the reason your page stopped converting.

Your funnels, seen from the page

A page is often one step of a longer path: product page, cart, checkout. Page X-Ray shows every funnel the page belongs to, how many visitors reach this step, how many are lost here and how many reach the goal, day by day. To find where WooCommerce shoppers drop their cart, read our WooCommerce abandoned cart guide. On a shop, the cart and the checkout are often the steps that leak: see how to reduce cart abandonment on WooCommerce.


Two funnels from the page: 125 visitors enter, 118 are lost at this step in the first one.

The action plan, in order

The report ends with what to do, in order, with the effort each step needs and a button that takes you straight to it.


Fix now: quick wins with a clear fix. Change, then compare: bigger changes you measure before and after.

“Fix now” steps are clear fixes, like a broken link or a missing description. “Change, then compare” steps are bigger changes. When the page goal converts at 0%, an A/B test would have nothing to compare, so Page X-Ray tells you honestly to change the page and compare 14 days before and after instead.

How Page X-Ray fits in Smart Insights

Smart Insights works in four steps: your modules collect, Smart Insights finds what to fix, you fix it, and an A/B test or a before and after comparison proves the fix. The Insights tab lists problems across the whole site. The Page X-Ray tab looks at the same data page by page.


Collect, understand, fix, prove: the Insights and Page X-Ray tabs read the same data.

Landing page analysis with Page X-Ray (Pro), step by step

A landing page analysis answers three questions: what the page is for, where visitors stop before that goal, and which problem costs the most visits. Page X-Ray, in Opti-Behavior Pro, puts the three answers in one report. Here is the order we use.

  • Collect a few days of visits. Install Opti-Behavior from WordPress.org and activate Opti-Behavior Pro (a free trial is available). A problem is only raised when enough visitors are measured; reports built on few visits are marked as provisional.

  • Pick the page to analyse. Go to Opti-Behavior → Smart Insights, open the Page X-Ray tab and choose the period. The list ranks your pages by health score with the main problem of each. Start with the pages where visitors from search or ads land first. You can also open a page report from the Dossier button of the Heatmaps list.

  • Check the goal of the page. Click Open. Page X-Ray reads what the page is (home page, product, article, contact page and more) and the goal that follows: the button to click, the form to send, the file to download. If the goal it found is not the right one, change it before you read the rest.

  • Read what to fix, most costly first. The problems are ranked by the visits they touch. Each one says why it matters, what to do, and has a button to the report already filtered on this page: heatmap, recordings, errors or forms.

  • Look at what changed in WordPress. Plugin, theme and WordPress updates and edits of the page over the period are marked on the charts. If a problem starts the day of an update, test that update first.

  • Follow the action plan, one change at a time. The plan sorts the work into Fix now and Change, then compare. Make one change, then open the report again on a period of the same length and compare. To share the analysis, use Print / Save as PDF.

What Page X-Ray does not do

We would rather be clear about the limits. Page X-Ray explains a page not converting with what visitors really did, so it needs visits: a problem is only raised when enough visitors are measured, and cards built on few visits are marked as provisional. It does not rewrite your page for you. And money figures are only shown when they come from real orders, never from a guess.

Page X-Ray also does not slow your site down. Reports are built in your WordPress admin from data you already collect, and the trackers on the public site load late. We measured it: 100/100 on Google PageSpeed Insights with tracking on. If you are comparing tools, see also our Hotjar alternative for WordPress guide.

Choosing a tool? See our WordPress heatmap plugin comparison of 8 options.

Questions people ask

Why is my landing page not converting?

A landing page not converting usually has one of four problems: visitors never see or never click the main button, they do not trust the page, something on the page is broken (a link, a script or a form), or they leave before they reach the offer. Page X-Ray checks all four on each page and ranks them by the visits they cost, so you know which one to fix first.

Why is my page not converting even though it gets traffic?

Traffic only means visitors arrive. A page not converting despite good traffic usually loses people after they land: the main button sits below the point where most visitors stop scrolling, the page does not answer the question they came with, or something broken gets in the way. Page X-Ray shows which one it is, with the share of visits each problem touches.

How do I know which page on my site to fix first?

Open the Page X-Ray tab in Smart Insights. It lists every tracked page with a health score, its number of visits and its most costly problem, sorted from the page to fix first to the healthiest.

How can I see why visitors leave my website?

Page X-Ray splits the page into ten parts and shows how much of their time visitors spend on each part, how many are still there, and the exact point where most of them leave. It then tells you what to put before that point.

Why does nobody click my button?

It is the most common cause of a page not converting: the button is too low on the page, says something vague like Submit, or competes with other links. Page X-Ray measures where each call to action sits, how many visitors reach it and how many click it, and flags the buttons that are never clicked.

How do I find broken links and JavaScript errors on a WordPress page?

With Opti-Behavior Pro, broken links and script errors are recorded when real visitors hit them. Page X-Ray shows them in the report of the page they happen on, with the number of visits affected and, for script errors, the file, the line and the plugin or theme that ships it.

Did a plugin update hurt my conversions?

Page X-Ray logs plugin, theme and WordPress updates and page edits. Each change is drawn on the charts, and the report compares the two weeks before and after it, with a verdict that says whether the change really moved visitors or stayed inside normal day-to-day noise.

Is Page X-Ray free?

Page X-Ray is part of Opti-Behavior Pro. The free plugin shows the Page X-Ray tab with a lock and an example report, so you can see what you get before you upgrade.

Does Page X-Ray slow down my website?

No. Page X-Ray builds its reports inside your WordPress admin from data you already collect. On the public site, the Opti-Behavior trackers load late and scored 100/100 on Google PageSpeed Insights with tracking on.

Where is my data stored?

On your own server. Opti-Behavior is self-hosted: the data behind Page X-Ray stays in your WordPress database and is never sent to a third-party analytics service.

The bottom line

Knowing that you have a page not converting is easy. Knowing why, and what to do first, used to take hours of cross-checking reports. Page X-Ray does that work for every page not converting, and for the healthy ones too: it reads what visitors really did, ranks the problems by the visits they cost, and gives you an ordered plan with a button for each step. Try it on the live demo, then on your own site.

Original article, kept up to date: https://optiuser.com/go/devto-not-converting

Drafted with AI assistance, reviewed by the Opti-Behavior Team.

title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
description:
Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done.

Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery, Selection, Access, and Success.

You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success: whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.

That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change.

That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one.

The agentic testing pyramid

If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?”

We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid, the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite.

To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success, that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome.

An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, are E2E evals.

Example

Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans.

Here’s a typical request from one of your customers:

Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission.

Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am:

  • Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature)

  • 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget)

  • Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time)

  • Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three)

Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans:

How to build an end-to-end eval

We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor, an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.

Here are the terms we’ll use:

  • Task: one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded

  • Variant: the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills

  • Trial: one attempt by one variant at one task

  • Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each

  • Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output

Step 1: Set a goal

Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier).

Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places:

  • Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail

  • Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn

  • Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate

For example, your goal might be to:

  • Increase the success rate on a specific task

  • Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal

  • Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it

  • A/B test a prompt

  • Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why

Example

We looked in all three places for sfbeans:

  • Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.

  • Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.

  • Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.

That gives us our goal:

Goal

Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for

Agents

Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from.

In scope

Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans.

Out of scope

Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later.

Done when

Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time.

Step 2: Define metrics

Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals:

Success

  • Success rate: the share of trials that pass

  • Pass@k: the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”)

  • Pass^k: the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”)

Efficiency (measured on successful trials only)

  • Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task

  • Time: how long the trial took

  • Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars

Example

Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 on AI Gateway) on the iced latte order could look like:

Trial

Result

What happened

Steps

Time

Cost

1

Pass

Compared quotes from 3 cafes, ordered at Valencia

9

3:40

$0.52

2

Fail: over budget

Skipped quote, ordered at 24th St: $9.27

5

1:50

$0.31

Pass

Compared quotes from 4 cafes, ordered at Valencia

11

4:30

$0.68

4

Fail: late

Ordered at Dolores, ready 9:20

5

Pass

What the numbers mean:

  • Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.

  • Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.

  • Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.

  • Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials.

  • Time: ~3:50 on successful trials.

  • Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too.

So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5.

Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters:

Product

What a failed attempt costs the user

Metric to lead with

Order my morning coffee

Paid for the wrong drink, late for work, lost trust

Pass^k

Coding agent with a test suite

Extra time and model cost; the agent uses test feedback to revise its code and try again

Pass@k

Draft an email the user reviews

A quick edit before hitting send

Success rate

Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”

Step 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Example

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/.

  • Common case: iced-latte-mission, the order from earlier

  • Edge case: usual-unavailable, where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: team-order, with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: impossible-request, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user

impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

Here’s iced-latte-mission:

The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection, keeping the eval focused on Success.

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:

To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json:

The actual check lives in check_orders.py. It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score:

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:

Step 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers.

Example

Two agents, Claude Code and Codex, with two models each, make four variants.

Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job:

This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 (Sandbox limits).

To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway.

Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Step 5: Analyze traces

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

Example

The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/. Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:

Run harbor view jobs to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative).

For each variant, we calculate success rate and estimate pass^5 separately for each task, then average each metric across the four tasks. Each task counts equally.

Variant

Success

That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials.

Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke:

Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json. The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order. No quote. It treated the menu price as the final price.

Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money.

We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”

When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring:

  • Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.

  • Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one.

  • Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.

Automated trace analysis

For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it.

Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An analysis.md file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.

Model calls go through AI Gateway. Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage.

Iterate to greatness

Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it.

Pick the fix the traces point to, like the --max-total flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.

Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it.

Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. A saturated eval still catches regressions, but it can’t tell you what to improve next.

Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again. Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace.

description:
STATERA Library · Series 08 · Volume 06 · Chapter 09 · EN
Source: https://github.com/Statera-Library/08_Vol_06_Robot_Communication_and_APIs/blob/main/Chapter_09_Fleet_APIs/Chapter_09_Fleet_APIs_EN.md

Volume 06 Robot Communication and APIs

09. Fleet APIs

09.01 Fleet API Design Principles: Multi-Robot Orchestration

A fleet API transforms a collection of individually autonomous robots into a coordinated operational system. While a robot API exposes the capabilities, state, and commands of one machine, a fleet API represents shared resources, missions, traffic constraints, priorities, and operational policies across many robots. Its primary design objective is therefore orchestration rather than direct low-level control.

Multi-robot orchestration requires a clear separation between fleet-level intent and robot-level execution. The fleet management layer should specify what must be accomplished, such as transporting material between locations or performing an inspection route, while each robot retains responsibility for local navigation, obstacle avoidance, motion control, and immediate safety behavior. This separation reduces coupling between central services and heterogeneous robot implementations.

A useful fleet API is based on stable abstractions such as robot, mission, task, location, route, resource, traffic zone, charging station, and operational state. These abstractions create a common vocabulary between fleet management servers, warehouse systems, manufacturing systems, hospital applications, and robots. Hardware-specific concepts should remain behind adapters whenever possible so that applications are not tightly coupled to individual robot vendors or platforms.

Robot identity is the foundation of fleet orchestration. Every robot should have a persistent identifier associated with its type, capabilities, software configuration, current availability, and authorization scope. A fleet service can then discover which robots are eligible for a task without assuming that all machines are equivalent. Capability-based selection becomes especially important when AMRs, towing robots, manipulators, inspection robots, and other specialized platforms share one environment.

Mission APIs should express operational objectives rather than sequences of actuator commands. A mission may contain pickup, delivery, inspection, waiting, charging, docking, or interaction tasks connected by dependencies and execution constraints. The fleet orchestrator converts this mission into robot assignments and execution plans.
