title: TypeScript `declare module` Augmentation in 2026: Adding Types to Untyped npm Packages Without DefinitelyTyped
description:
TypeScript declare module Augmentation in 2026: Adding Types to Untyped npm Packages Without DefinitelyTyped

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

TypeScript projects frequently depend on npm packages that ship no type definitions. The package works at runtime, but every import triggers compiler errors. The @types namespace exists for popular libraries, yet thousands of smaller packages remain untyped. When npm install @types/your-package returns a 404, developers face a choice: abandon type safety for that dependency or write declarations manually.

The standard advice points to DefinitelyTyped, a central repository where contributors submit type definitions for review and publication. This process takes weeks and requires ongoing maintenance as the underlying package evolves. For internal tools, proprietary packages, or rapidly changing APIs, DefinitelyTyped becomes a bottleneck rather than a solution.

TypeScript provides declare module for local augmentation, which adds types directly in the consuming project. The declaration file lives alongside application code, versioned in the same repository, and remains under direct control. Changes to the package API require only a local edit, no pull request to an external repository.

This post demonstrates the mechanics of declare module, the critical distinction between global scripts and module augmentation, and the setup required to make TypeScript recognize local type declarations. The patterns here apply to TypeScript 5.x and 6.0, with references to the official tsconfig documentation for configuration fields.

Key Takeaways

  • declare module creates type definitions for untyped npm packages without submitting to DefinitelyTyped.
  • A declaration file MUST contain at least one import or export statement to function as module augmentation; files without either become global scripts where declare module creates new ambient modules that do not merge with existing types.
  • Place declaration files in a types/ directory and configure typeRoots in tsconfig.json to include that path (the typeRoots field accepts an array of directory paths relative to the tsconfig file).
  • Interface declarations inside declare module merge with existing package types, while type aliases and classes overwrite them completely.
  • The types field in package.json points to the main declaration file when bundling types with a published package (as documented in Publishing Declaration Files).

Understanding Module Augmentation vs Ambient Declarations

TypeScript distinguishes between two uses of declare module: ambient module declarations and module augmentation. Ambient declarations create new modules from scratch, typically for global scripts or libraries that define global variables. Module augmentation extends existing modules by merging new declarations with the original type definitions.

The difference determines whether TypeScript merges the new declarations or treats them as separate definitions. When a file contains no import or export statements, TypeScript treats it as a global script. A declare module in a global script creates a new ambient module. If the module name matches an installed package, the ambient declaration shadows the package's original types rather than augmenting them.

When a file includes at least one import or export statement, TypeScript treats it as a module. A declare module in a module file becomes augmentation. The compiler merges the new declarations with the package's existing types, preserving original definitions while adding new members.

This distinction surfaces in a common failure mode: developers write a declaration file with declare module "some-package", place it in the project, but omit any import or export. The file becomes a global script. The declared module takes precedence over the actual package types, and existing typed members disappear. Adding a single export {} at the top of the file converts it to a module, enabling augmentation behavior.

The official tsconfig documentation does not explicitly label this import/export requirement in a single section, but the behavior follows from TypeScript's module system semantics. A file without imports or exports exists in the global scope, where declare module introduces a new identifier. A file with imports or exports becomes a module, where declare module extends an existing identifier.

Creating Declaration Files for Untyped Packages

An untyped package exports functions, classes, or objects with no accompanying .d.ts files. TypeScript infers the module as any, providing no autocomplete or error checking. A declaration file supplies the missing type information.

Consider an untyped utility package csv-helpers that exports a single function:

// node_modules/csv-helpers/index.js
module.exports.parseCSV = function(input) {
  return input.split('\n').map(line => line.split(','));
};

TypeScript sees this import as any:

import { parseCSV } from 'csv-helpers';
// parseCSV has type any
const result = parseCSV(data);

Create a declaration file in types/csv-helpers/index.d.ts:

export {};

declare module 'csv-helpers' {
  export function parseCSV(input: string): string[][];
}

The export {} statement converts this file into a module, enabling augmentation. The declare module block specifies the module name exactly as it appears in imports. The export function declaration provides the function signature.

TypeScript module augmentation workflow

After adding the declaration file, configure TypeScript to recognize it. The typeRoots option in tsconfig.json tells TypeScript where to look for type declarations. By default, TypeScript searches node_modules/@types directories. Adding a custom path includes local declarations:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "typeRoots": [
      "./node_modules/@types",
      "./types"
    ]
  }
}

This configuration searches both the standard @types packages and the local types/ directory. The typeRoots field accepts relative paths from the tsconfig.json location. When typeRoots is set, TypeScript includes only packages under those directories, excluding all other @types locations unless explicitly listed.

TypeScript now recognizes parseCSV with its declared signature. Autocomplete suggests the function, the compiler validates argument types, and return values receive proper inference.

For packages with multiple exports, declare each member:

export {};

declare module 'csv-helpers' {
  export function parseCSV(input: string): string[][];
  export function serializeCSV(data: string[][]): string;
  export const CSV_DELIMITER: string;
}

Class-based packages require class declarations:

export {};

declare module 'legacy-logger' {
  export class Logger {
    constructor(name: string);
    log(message: string): void;
    error(error: Error): void;
  }
}

Generic functions and interfaces work the same way:

export {};

declare module 'cache-lib' {
  export interface Cache<T> {
    get(key: string): T | undefined;
    set(key: string, value: T): void;
  }

  export function createCache<T>(): Cache<T>;
}

The structure matches standard TypeScript module syntax. The declare module wrapper scopes all declarations to the specified module name. The export keyword on each member makes it available to consumers.

The Critical Import Rule: Global Script vs Module Augmentation

The import/export requirement determines whether augmentation succeeds or fails. A declaration file without import or export becomes a global script, where declare module creates a new ambient module instead of merging with existing types.

This appears most commonly when augmenting packages that already ship partial types. Express.js provides base types in @types/express, but applications need to add custom properties to request objects. A declaration file extends the Request interface:

declare module 'express-serve-static-core' {
  interface Request {
    user?: { id: string; email: string };
  }
}

Without an import or export, this file becomes a global script. TypeScript treats the declare module as a new ambient module declaration. The original Express types remain unchanged, and req.user stays untyped.

Adding a single export statement fixes the issue:

export {};

declare module 'express-serve-static-core' {
  interface Request {
    user?: { id: string; email: string };
  }
}

The export {} exports nothing but converts the file into a module. Now declare module functions as augmentation, and the Request interface merges with the existing definition from @types/express. The user property becomes available on all request objects with full type support.

The same pattern applies to any package with existing types. Augmenting a typed package requires the import/export conversion. Augmenting an untyped package from scratch also requires it, because the absence of types does not change TypeScript's module resolution behavior.

A common variation uses an actual import instead of export {}:

import type { Request } from 'express-serve-static-core';

declare module 'express-serve-static-core' {
  interface Request {
    user?: { id: string; email: string };
  }
}

The import type statement serves dual purposes: it converts the file into a module and provides type references for use in the augmentation. This approach makes sense when the augmentation references types from the package being extended.

Projects often collect multiple augmentations in a single file:

export {};

declare module 'express-serve-static-core' {
  interface Request {
    user?: { id: string; email: string };
  }
}

declare module 'csv-helpers' {
  export function parseCSV(input: string): string[][];
}

One export {} at the top suffices for the entire file. Each declare module block augments a different package. The file remains a module throughout, enabling augmentation for all declarations.

Augmenting Existing Types in Third-Party Libraries

Packages with partial type coverage need augmentation to fill gaps. A library might type core functionality but omit newer features, or expose untyped plugin hooks. Augmentation adds the missing pieces without forking the package or waiting for upstream changes.

Consider a charting library with typed chart creation but untyped configuration options:

// Existing types from @types/chart-lib
export function createChart(config: any): Chart;
export interface Chart {
  render(): void;
}

The config parameter accepts any, losing all type safety. Augmentation defines the configuration shape:

export {};

declare module 'chart-lib' {
  interface ChartConfig {
    width: number;
    height: number;
    data: Array<{ x: number; y: number }>;
    options?: {
      title?: string;
      colors?: string[];
    };
  }

  export function createChart(config: ChartConfig): Chart;
}

The augmented createChart declaration overwrites the original. For functions, TypeScript uses the most recently declared signature. The new signature replaces the any parameter with a structured interface.

Interface augmentation uses merging instead of replacement. When augmenting an interface, TypeScript combines both definitions:

export {};

declare module 'chart-lib' {
  interface Chart {
    // Original members remain available
    exportImage(): Blob;
    setTheme(theme: 'light' | 'dark'): void;
  }
}

The augmented Chart interface includes render() from the original definition plus the two new methods. Both old and new members coexist. This merging behavior applies only to interfaces and namespaces, not to type aliases or classes.

Real-world augmentation often extends plugin systems. Testing libraries provide hooks for custom matchers:

export {};

declare module 'vitest' {
  interface Assertion<T = any> {
    toBeWithinRange(floor: number, ceiling: number): T;
  }
}

After this augmentation, custom matchers appear in autocomplete and pass type checking:

import { expect } from 'vitest';

expect(value).toBeWithinRange(10, 20);

TypeScript declaration merging in action

Some packages expose global namespaces that need extension. A utility library might define a global namespace for configuration:

export {};

declare global {
  namespace UtilConfig {
    interface Settings {
      apiEndpoint: string;
      timeout: number;
    }
  }
}

The declare global block augments the global scope rather than a specific module. This pattern works for libraries that add properties to Window, global, or other global objects.

Augmenting deep module paths follows the same rules:

export {};

declare module 'framework/internal/helpers' {
  export function internalHelper(param: string): void;
}

The module path must match exactly as it appears in imports. TypeScript resolves nested paths like framework/internal/helpers the same way it resolves top-level module names.

Project Structure and tsconfig Setup for Declaration Files

TypeScript discovers declaration files through the typeRoots and types options. A standard project structure places all custom declarations in a dedicated directory:

project/
├── src/
│   ├── index.ts
│   └── app.ts
├── types/
│   ├── csv-helpers/
│   │   └── index.d.ts
│   ├── legacy-logger/
│   │   └── index.d.ts
│   └── express/
│       └── index.d.ts
├── package.json
└── tsconfig.json

Each subdirectory under types/ corresponds to a package name. The index.d.ts file contains the augmentation for that package. This mirrors the structure of node_modules/@types and helps TypeScript resolve the correct declarations.

The tsconfig.json includes this directory in typeRoots:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "typeRoots": [
      "./node_modules/@types",
      "./types"
    ]
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*", "types/**/*"]
}

The typeRoots field lists all directories to search for type packages. Order matters: TypeScript searches from first to last, and the first matching package wins. Including ./types after ./node_modules/@types allows local declarations to override installed packages when needed.

The include array must list both source files and type declaration files. TypeScript compiles everything matching these patterns. Omitting types/**/* from include causes the compiler to ignore the declarations.

For projects that augment only a few packages, a single declaration file works:

project/
├── src/
├── types.d.ts
├── package.json
└── tsconfig.json

The types.d.ts file at the project root contains all augmentations:

export {};

declare module 'csv-helpers' {
  export function parseCSV(input: string): string[][];
}

declare module 'legacy-logger' {
  export class Logger {
    constructor(name: string);
    log(message: string): void;
  }
}

This approach eliminates the need for typeRoots configuration. TypeScript automatically includes .d.ts files from the include pattern. For small projects or quick prototypes, this structure reduces overhead.

Monorepos require careful path configuration. Packages sharing type augmentations place them in a shared location:

monorepo/
├── packages/
│   ├── app-a/
│   ├── app-b/
│   └── shared-types/
│       └── index.d.ts
└── package.json

Each package's tsconfig.json references the shared types:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "typeRoots": [
      "../../node_modules/@types",
      "../../packages/shared-types"
    ]
  }
}

Relative paths resolve from the tsconfig.json location. This setup allows multiple packages to share augmentations without duplication.

The types field restricts which @types packages TypeScript includes. By default, all visible @types packages load automatically. Setting types to a specific list limits inclusion:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "types": ["node", "jest"],
    "typeRoots": ["./node_modules/@types", "./types"]
  }
}

This configuration includes only @types/node and @types/jest from node_modules/@types, plus all packages from the local types/ directory. The types array applies only to @types packages, not to custom typeRoots entries. Local declarations always load when their directory appears in typeRoots.

Projects publishing packages with bundled types set the types field in package.json:

{
  "name": "my-package",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "./dist/index.js",
  "types": "./dist/index.d.ts"
}

The types field in package.json points to the main declaration file. TypeScript resolves imports from this package using the specified .d.ts file. The typings field serves as a synonym for types and works identically.

Common Pitfalls: When Augmentation Overwrites Instead of Merges

TypeScript merges interface declarations but overwrites type aliases, classes, and function signatures. This difference causes frequent confusion when augmenting packages with mixed declaration types.

Consider a package that exports a type alias for configuration:

// Original package types
export type Config = {
  apiKey: string;
  timeout: number;
};

Augmentation attempts to add a field:

export {};

declare module 'config-package' {
  export type Config = {
    debug: boolean;
  };
}

This augmentation completely replaces the original type. The augmented Config contains only debug, losing apiKey and timeout. Type aliases do not merge. The augmentation overwrites the entire definition.

The same failure mode affects classes:

// Original package
export class Logger {
  log(message: string): void;
}

// Augmentation
export {};

declare module 'logger-package' {
  export class Logger {
    setLevel(level: string): void;
  }
}

The augmented Logger class replaces the original. The log method disappears, and only setLevel remains. Class declarations do not support merging.

Converting type aliases to interfaces enables merging:

// Original package (if you control it)
export interface Config {
  apiKey: string;
  timeout: number;
}

// Augmentation
export {};

declare module 'config-package' {
  export interface Config {
    debug: boolean;
  }
}

Now Config includes all three properties. Interface augmentation merges declarations, preserving original members while adding new ones.

When the original package uses type aliases and cannot be modified, augmentation requires a workaround. Intersection types combine the original type with new properties:

export {};

import type { Config as OriginalConfig } from 'config-package';

declare module 'config-package' {
  export type Config = OriginalConfig & {
    debug: boolean;
  };
}

The augmentation imports the original type and creates a new type that intersects it with the additional properties. This preserves the original shape while extending it. The technique works but introduces coupling to the package's internal structure.

Declaration Type Augmentation Behavior Workaround if Not Mergeable
Interface Merges with original None needed
Type Alias Overwrites completely Use intersection type with import
Class Overwrites completely Extend class or use interface augmentation for methods
Namespace Merges with original None needed

Function overloads experience similar issues. A package exports a function with multiple signatures:

// Original package
export function request(url: string): Promise<Response>;
export function request(url: string, options: RequestOptions): Promise<Response>;

Augmentation adds a third signature:

export {};

declare module 'request-package' {
  export function request(config: RequestConfig): Promise<Response>;
}

The augmentation replaces all existing overloads with the single new signature. TypeScript does not merge function overload lists across augmentation boundaries. Adding overloads requires redeclaring all signatures:

export {};

declare module 'request-package' {
  export function request(url: string): Promise<Response>;
  export function request(url: string, options: RequestOptions): Promise<Response>;
  export function request(config: RequestConfig): Promise<Response>;
}

This duplication introduces maintenance risk. When the package updates its signatures, the augmentation must update as well. For packages that change frequently, this becomes unsustainable.

Namespace augmentation follows interface merging rules. A package defines a namespace:

// Original package
export namespace Utils {
  export function helper(): void;
}

Augmentation extends it:

export {};

declare module 'utils-package' {
  export namespace Utils {
    export function newHelper(): void;
  }
}

The augmented namespace merges with the original. Both helper and newHelper remain available. Namespaces support the same merging behavior as interfaces.

Augmentation order matters when multiple declaration files modify the same module. TypeScript processes files in the order they appear in the compilation. Later augmentations build on earlier ones. Circular augmentation dependencies create resolution errors:

// file-a.d.ts
import type { TypeFromB } from './file-b';
declare module 'package' {
  export type A = TypeFromB;
}

// file-b.d.ts
import type { TypeFromA } from './file-a';
declare module 'package' {
  export type B = TypeFromA;
}

This circular reference causes a compilation error. Breaking the cycle requires restructuring the augmentations or consolidating them into a single file.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I augment built-in TypeScript types like Array or Promise?

TypeScript allows augmentation of built-in types through the global scope. Use declare global with an export {} statement to ensure module mode, then augment the interface. For example, adding a method to Array requires declare global { interface Array<T> { myMethod(): T; } }. This pattern applies to any global type, but changes affect the entire project and may conflict with libraries that make similar augmentations.

What happens if I declare a module that matches a real package but forget the import/export statement?

The declaration file becomes a global script, and the declare module creates a new ambient module that shadows the real package. TypeScript uses the ambient declaration instead of the package's actual types, and existing typed members from the package disappear. Adding export {} at the top of the file converts it to a module and enables proper augmentation that merges with the package types.

How do I augment a package that has no types at all versus one that ships partial types?

The approach remains identical for both cases. Create a declaration file with export {} at the top, then use declare module 'package-name' to define or extend types. For packages with no types, the augmentation creates the entire type definition. For packages with partial types, the augmentation merges with existing definitions if using interfaces or overwrites them if using type aliases or classes.

Can I split augmentations for a single package across multiple files?

TypeScript merges all augmentations for a module across the entire compilation. Multiple files can contain declare module 'same-package' blocks, and TypeScript combines them. Each file must include export {} to function as a module. The augmentations accumulate in the order TypeScript processes the files, determined by the include patterns in tsconfig.json.

Why does my augmentation work in VSCode but fail during tsc compilation?

VSCode and the TypeScript compiler may use different tsconfig.json files or different file inclusion patterns. Check that the declaration file appears in the include array or that its directory is listed in typeRoots. Running tsc --listFiles shows which files TypeScript includes in the compilation. If the declaration file is missing from that list, adjust the include or typeRoots configuration.

Production Patterns: Maintaining Type Safety Without DefinitelyTyped

Module augmentation enables full type safety for untyped dependencies without external coordination. The declaration files live in source control, version alongside application code, and remain under direct team control. When the underlying package changes, updating the local declarations requires a single commit rather than a pull request to an external repository.

This approach scales to dozens of untyped packages in large codebases. A dedicated types/ directory organizes augmentations by package name, mirroring the structure of @types and making maintenance straightforward. Teams can establish conventions for augmentation reviews, testing type coverage, and updating declarations when dependencies change.

The import/export rule determines success or failure. Every declaration file must contain at least one import or export statement to function as module augmentation. A file without either becomes a global script where declare module creates ambient modules that shadow rather than merge with package types. The single line export {} suffices to enable augmentation behavior.

Interface augmentation merges with original definitions, preserving existing members while adding new ones. Type aliases, classes, and function signatures overwrite completely, requiring intersection types or redeclaration of all signatures when extending them. Understanding these merging rules prevents data loss and maintains type accuracy across package updates.

The patterns demonstrated here apply to both untyped packages and partially typed packages that need extension. TypeScript treats both cases identically once the declaration file structure is correct. Local augmentation provides complete flexibility to define types that match actual runtime behavior, regardless of whether upstream maintainers have published types or plan to do so.

title: A Heterogeneous Scheduling System for 18 Billion Tests---Writing a COW Filesystem from Scratch，Part 9
description:
Scale is complexity.

Exhaustively verifying the correctness of a file system is, in theory, impossible. So what singlefs does is creep closer bit by bit, with pruning and a reuse database: anything already judged never needs judging again, and equivalent cases are judged only once. One layer up sits a multi-agent scheduling and scripting system: a main agent dispatches the work, following the gate scripts to run verifications and experiments.

Is the system stable? Reasonably so — like bolting a steering wheel onto a bare chassis. When things go well it runs fast, but life always has its rainy days. Running it for real, we hit problems like these:

  • The main agent dispatches tasks within milliseconds. Several tasks start at once, fight each other, and eat all the memory: OOM.
  • Tasks that look perfectly reasonable hold onto resources for ages, and the agent's own scheduled check-ins are unreliable, so nobody comes back to look.
  • Every script writes straight into the database, with a real risk of corrupting it; task records are scattered everywhere and slow to look up. And so on.

So we need two things: a task management system and a database service. The task management system coordinates resources and dispatches tasks; the database service validates and writes the data. In the repository the former is called task-server and the latter prune-server.

0. The starting point: every task goes through one entrance

There is exactly one rule: every task that runs project code is launched through the task service. Builds, tests, gates, experiments — light or heavy, CPU or GPU — all go into the same queue.

# Submit a task: the command goes verbatim after --
task-server/task submit -- cargo test --release -p singlefs-verification --test crash_enumeration_fixed_script_stream

# Get the outcome: exits on completion, with the task's exit code
task-server/task wait <task-id>

The parameters that used to be passed at submission — thread count, memory cap, which machine, which card — are all gone. The service decides these. If a command specifies one, it is rejected on the spot, and the agent is told which parameter to remove. The reason is simple: one of the things agents are best at is asking for a little more resource for their own tasks.

The service itself is a user-level systemd service: FastAPI on uvicorn, listening only on a unix socket. Tasks and every attempt are recorded in an embedded SQLite database, and each row carries an HMAC check column. Each attempt is its own systemd unit, wrapped in a cgroup memory cap: if it goes over, the kernel kills only that unit and nobody else.

The "just launch it directly" path is blocked at the tool layer. Every Bash command an agent runs passes through a hook first; any cargo, gate, or experiment script not launched via task submit is rejected on the spot. Sub-agents have had their right to run verifications revoked: they write the commands they want run into their report and hand it to the main agent to submit.

Results come back as a code table, each outcome mapped to a fixed exit code, so the agent knows what to do next just from the exit code:

# task-server/task_server_lib.py (excerpt)
# Outcome types: name → (exit code of wait, None means the command's own; description)
OUTCOME_TYPES = {
    "succeeded": (0, "command exited 0"),
    "command-failed": (None, "command itself exited non-zero"),
    "memory-cap-hit": (250, "hit this task's own cap"),
    "memory-cap-at-maximum": (236, "hit the cap, already at the max of both hosts"),
    "card-fault": (237, "scrub found the card faulty"),
    "never-fits": (241, "won't fit on any host no matter how long it waits"),
    "stalled": (233, "log didn't grow for 10 minutes; the service stopped it"),
    "over-four-hours": (229, "cumulative or projected time reached the 4-hour hard limit; bounced by the service"),
    "killed-externally": (228, "killed by a TERM or KILL not sent by the service"),
    # ...
}

Another key point: the agent's scheduled check-ins are unreliable. So the service can't rely on the agent remembering to come back. When a task reaches an outcome, has been queued too long, or looks stuck, the service sends a message straight to the inbox socket of the session that submitted the task, waking the agent up. The first line says whether this is an outcome or a reminder; what follows is the evidence and the way forward. The agent never has to poll or set an alarm.

At first everything went very smoothly. The task management system launched tasks centrally within the configured resource limits, queued what didn't fit, and bounced failures and errors back — in short, it handed results back to the agent, which carried on according to what came back. On top of that, a periodic sweep checked task states and terminated anything abnormal.

Then the problems arrived right on cue.

1. Can tasks cut in line?

Say memory is 50GB. Task A is using 32GB, and the next task, B, needs 24GB, so clearly B can't start yet. But C, behind B, needs only 16GB. Can C cut in? What about D after it? If we keep letting later tasks cut in, when will B ever get done?

Design: cutting in is allowed, but it's a matter of time. C's estimated runtime must not exceed A's remaining runtime. On top of that, there's a maximum queue time: once a task has waited two hours, it gets top priority and nobody may cut in front of it.

In the implementation this is called "gap-filling." How much longer the task in the way still has to run is called the "blocking time":

# task-server/task_server.py (excerpt)
def attempt_remaining(self, attempt):
    """How much longer (seconds) this running attempt has: estimate minus elapsed;
    with no estimate, or once past the estimate, take elapsed."""
    estimate = self.attempt_estimate(attempt)
    elapsed = max(0.0, self.now - float(attempt.get("started_at") or self.now))
    if estimate is not None and estimate > elapsed:
        return estimate - elapsed
    return elapsed

The second half is a small trick: if a task has no runtime history, or has already run past its estimate, we guess it will run "at least as long again as it already has."

Whether a task can cut in is decided in two steps:

# gap_fill in task-server/task_server.py (excerpt, self-test branches removed)
# Step 1: after B at the head starts, does the share still free on this host fit C?
left = snapshot.total(host) - margin - head_booked - beside
if booked <= left:
    return True, "gap-fill: fits, estimate not consulted"

# Step 2: only tasks that would eat into B's share are compared by time
estimate, _ = self.task_estimate(task)
if estimate is None:
    return False, "no gap-fill: this task has no estimate"
blocking, blocker = self.blocking_seconds(host)   # blocking time
if estimate <= blocking:
    return True, "gap-fill: estimate within blocking time"
return False, "no gap-fill: estimate exceeds blocking time"

If C never touches the memory B needs, however long it runs it won't delay B, so it starts right away. Only tasks that would eat into B's share are compared by time: C must finish before A does.

The two-hour rule takes just two lines:

def aged(self, task, now):
    """Still queued aged_seconds after submission: high priority."""
    return now - float(task.get("submitted_at") or now) >= self.aged_seconds

def queue_order(self, queued, now):
    """Queue order: high priority first, each keeping its original order (stable sort)."""
    return sorted(queued, key=lambda row: not self.aged(row[0], now))

Big and small tasks alternate per host. A task whose booked amount reaches 85% of a host's usable limit counts as a "whole"; everything else is a "fragment." Fragments fill a batch, the batch is sealed, and the whole gets its turn; once the whole has started, the next batch of fragments is filled. Otherwise fragments keep arriving one after another and the whole never gets to see the host empty.

2. Where does the runtime come from, and is it accurate?

Cutting in requires comparing times. Where do the times come from?

From the database. When each attempt wraps up, the service records its runtime. The estimate is the runtime of the most recent successful run of the same command; if, among the last five runs, one ran longer before failing, that longer one is taken. Failures that exited right at the start don't count: they say nothing about how long the command takes.

Tasks with no record may not cut in. That's the estimate is None → False in the code above.

Is it accurate? No. The same command runs fast when it reuses a lot from the verdict database and slow when it reuses little. So for entry points that run item by item, the service estimates more finely: before the real run, it launches an estimation sub-task in which the entry point reports, for each item, "how many to judge fresh and how many can be reused":

ITEM_PLAN item=<item name> to_judge=<count to judge fresh> reusable=<count reusable>

After each run, the entry point also reports how long each item actually took:

ITEM_DONE item=<item name> seconds=<seconds> judged=<count judged fresh> reused=<count reused> exit=<code>

From this the service records, per item, "seconds per fresh judgment, seconds per reuse," and the next estimate is the sum of counts times rates. It's still just an estimate, so it's only used to decide whether to cut in. Sadly, this isn't very accurate either. Ha.

3. How much memory does a task need?

For a task that has never run, first look for its kin; if there's no kin either, give it 4GB. If it hits the cap midway, raise the cap by 1.5× and requeue it.

"Kin" is identified by a command key. For cargo test, for example, the same package, same features, and same build profile make one key; which test target is named does not go into the key — they build the same thing, and most of the memory goes into compilation.

With a record, take the largest of the peaks measured in the last five runs:

# task-server/task_server.py (excerpt)
RECORD_WINDOW = 5

def recorded_prediction(self, task, base):
    """Peaks measured over the last RECORD_WINDOW runs of the same command key:
    prediction, cap and booking all equal the largest one, not multiplied by 1.5."""
    window = sorted(self.recorded_measurements(task), reverse=True)[:RECORD_WINDOW]
    ...
    predicted = max(value for _, value in window)
    cap = math.ceil(predicted / lib.MEBIBYTE) * lib.MEBIBYTE

Without a record, start at 4GB and grow on each hit:

# task-server/task_server_lib.py
CAP_GROWTH_FACTOR = 1.5
UNRECORDED_MEMORY_DEFAULT_BYTES = 4 * GIBIBYTE

def grown_cap(cap_bytes):
    return math.ceil(cap_bytes * CAP_GROWTH_FACTOR / MEBIBYTE) * MEBIBYTE

4096M → 6144M → 9216M, bumping up one step at a time. If multiplying by 1.5 would reach the whole host's limit, the task is no longer requeued; it's bounced back to the session that submitted it, with suggested fixes: verify the scope, shrink it, or shard it.

For tasks that hit the cap several times in a row, the service adds a paragraph to the message — "check the code for logic loops or memory leaks" — and lists every cap and peak in order: is the peak growing each time, is it pinned at the cap every time? Not fitting in 4GB may mean the task really is big; still not fitting after climbing to 40GB usually means something is wrong with the code.

There's a pitfall we stepped in here: what exactly is the peak measuring? cgroup's memory.peak counts page cache too. One build task used under 1GB in its own processes, but page cache pushed the reading to 50GB. Setting quotas from that number would mean handing the entire machine to that one task. So the peak the service records counts only memory the processes themselves use (anon plus shmem), not page cache.

At this point, the main agent's concurrency problem and the problem of misbehaving tasks hogging resources were solved. And with a task database in place, the lookup and record-keeping problems were solved too. Most importantly, verdicts accumulated from small everyday tests can be reused by later tests, and bit by bit they fill in coverage for the whole project.

But it wasn't over. New problems came hard on the heels of the old.

4. Gate results that couldn't be reused

In the original design, a light gate ran day to day and a heavy gate ran at commit time. Then I discovered the light gate was actually a completely separate codebase. That meant every run started from scratch, reused nothing, and its results were useless to the heavy gate.

Hooking the light gate into the pruning database would amount to rewriting a scaled-down heavy gate. Merging it into the heavy gate instead would mean the heavy gate had to allow runs scoped by range and by named item.

Solution: take the heavy gate's whole verification system apart and make it addressable by name. Delete the light gate.

Now there is just one gate, with two ways to run it:

Mode How to launch When
Unscoped No selection flags; the gate picks what to judge by key on its own At commit
Scoped --item <item>, --check <cell>, named test targets Any time 
# List the items that can be named; no build, no run
bash .claude/gate.d/crash-point-replay.sh --list-items

# Judge only the one crash-enumeration case changed this time
bash .claude/gate.d/crash-point-replay.sh --check crash-case-replay --crash-cases-only --item crash-case:<case name>

The crucial point: both modes are the same script and the same verdict database; only the scope differs. Verdicts produced by everyday named runs are written to the database, and the commit-time run reads them by key and reuses them directly. Each verdict's key consists only of what it depends on: the fingerprint of the function unit with comments stripped, the toolchain, dependency versions, and its own inputs. Paths, line numbers, and which commit — none of these go into the key.

There is only one verdict database, too: the RocksDB held by prune-server. Tasks on both machines read and write through it, and each kind of verdict gets its own key prefix. Any script that opens a separate directory or writes a separate table to store verdicts is bounced in review, no exceptions. This is the database service mentioned at the start.

To keep "everyday" from quietly turning back into "everything," the service added a confirmation step at the entrance. After submission a task doesn't enter the queue right away; the service prints a confirmation slip: how many items it recognized from the command, estimated memory, estimated time. The agent has to copy two of those numbers back verbatim before the task enters the queue:

task-server/task confirm <task-id> --items <N> --tasks <M>

Unscoped runs and whole-package tests are rejected on the spot anywhere other than at commit.

5. Waiting on very long verifications

What if a verification takes 7 hours? Everything behind it is stuck. One verification, and no other development can happen.

Solution: sharding. Cut the task into small pieces.

The entry script declares it in a header line, and the service knows the job should be sharded:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# task-server-shards: *
# task-server-compiles: yes
# task-server-card-lease: on-demand

The service splits a job into three stages, each an ordinary sub-task that queues, picks a machine, sets its memory, and retries on its own:

  1. Plan: the entry point writes a plan.json into the plan directory saying how many shards to cut.
  2. Shards: one sub-task per shard, with TASK_SERVER_SHARD=<shard>/<count> in its environment; it judges only its own share and writes verdicts straight into the verdict database.
  3. Merge: starts only once all shards have succeeded. The merge judges nothing fresh; it only reconciles: everything each shard was supposed to judge can be read from the database right now. If one shard fails, its siblings still run to the end and their verdicts still go into the database. On resubmission, only what hasn't been judged gets filled in.

Beyond sharding there are two hard time rules:

  • After two hours of running, the service doesn't stop the task, but it sends the submitting session a reminder: is the scope right? Does it really need to run this long?
  • At four hours cumulative, the service stops it and bounces it, no negotiation. There's only one way forward: split the item, or optimize the algorithm. Shrinking the verification domain or naming fewer items doesn't count as splitting. ### 6. The crashing GPU

Small pieces brought a new problem. Code bugs plus scheduling problems crashed the GPU outright. And when the GPU goes down, it takes the network with it.

I wrote two separate GPU articles about this a couple of days ago, if you're interested.

  • Before handing over a card, the service scrubs it and reads it back before giving it to the task.
  • After a task ends, the service reclaims the card first: reads VRAM, reads compute processes, reads the kernel log for that period. A card that threw an Xid is benched for 60 minutes, and the task is requeued onto another card.
  • A card judged faulty gets the outcome card-fault, and a human is asked on the spot to reset it. No waiting, no retrying. ### 7. Tasks that could only run on one machine

Because of resource constraints, some tasks could, believe it or not, only run on one machine. Copy the project to the second machine? Changes are far too frequent; every copy and every reconciliation makes token consumption explode.

Solution: share the codebase over NFSv4, with both machines mounting it at the same absolute path.

# This host: /etc/exports, one line per shared root
<root> <second host address>(rw,sync,no_subtree_check)

# Second host: /etc/fstab, mount at the same absolute path as this host
<this host address>:<root> <root> nfs4 rw,hard,nofail,_netdev,x-systemd.automount,x-systemd.mount-timeout=30 0 0

Three things are shared: the repository itself, the data root (working directories and shard artifacts live under it), and the session log directory. The second machine runs in the same live tree — no copying, no sending, no fetching back, not a single character of any path rewritten. What one machine writes, the other reads directly.

The only exception is the build directory: it lives on each machine's own local disk, is created fresh for every run, and is deleted afterwards. It never goes in a shared directory.

In the service this is a startup condition. On startup the service checks four things: is the configuration present, has this host exported, has the second host mounted, and can each side read a probe file written by the other in both directions. If any check fails, the service doesn't start.

The matching principle went into the project rules: no task must be bound to one machine; if one is, that's a defect. The service has no "this host only" list. If a task dispatched to the second machine goes red, let it go red and go fix the script — don't add exceptions to the service.

Well, that's more or less it. The service's own verification tasks had to queue behind those very long tasks, which made verifying and developing the service very slow. The classic awkward situation: the condition for getting in can only be met once you're in. But in the end these problems were solved.

And then, a new storm appeared.
CPU tasks were in fact solved by this point: CPU and memory form a single resource pool, and scheduling is fairly stable. But GPU tasks held their cards hostage.

8. CPU and GPU tied together

A crash-point replay task first builds and records on the CPU, and only at the very end goes onto a card to judge. Yet it holds the card from the moment it starts. Much of the time, the GPU is just waiting.

Solution: decouple. Assign no card at start; lease one only when the task reaches the step that needs it, and return it immediately after use.

The # task-server-card-lease: on-demand line in the entry file header is that declaration. For such tasks the service assigns no card and does no scrub at start, judging memory and CPU like any ordinary task. In the gate it looks like this:

# .claude/gate.d/crash-point-replay.sh (excerpt)
crash_point_replay_take_card() {
  local cards lease_exit
  [[ -z "$crash_point_replay_card_leased" ]] || return 0      # already holding one: use it
  if cards="$(crash_point_replay_card_lease take)"; then lease_exit=0; else lease_exit=$?; fi
  if (( lease_exit != 0 )) || [[ -z "$cards" ]]; then
    echo "  ✗ $1: $2 needs a card; on-demand lease refused, this run did not start"
    return 1
  fi
  crash_point_replay_card_leased="$cards"
  echo "  · $1: $2 needs a card; leased $cards on demand (returned when this run ends)"
}

Behind lease take, the service picks a free card by card priority, scrubs it, reads it back, and only then hands it over. If all cards are taken, the request waits in line, first come first served. Any card not returned when a task ends is reclaimed by the service.

The tests in the verification package were split into two stages accordingly:

  1. Record only: runs on the CPU and writes the inputs to be judged into the verdict database. Holds no card.
  2. Judge only: leases a card, reads the inputs back from the database, judges them on the card, and returns the card when done. The other half was done too: once a task has a card and enters its GPU stage, its CPU accounting switches to the number of cores actually in use during that card-holding stage. While it waits on the card's results, its CPU slots go to others.

The time a card spends in hand shrank from "the whole task" to "the part that's actually computing."

Finally, more or less there

  • Memory no longer gets eaten by several tasks starting at once. Admission is decided in exactly one place, the service, and only what qualifies gets started.
  • No task holds resources indefinitely. Stuck ones are stopped, long ones get reminders, four-hour ones are bounced.
  • Every outcome has a name, an exit code, and a next step, and it's delivered to the session that started it.

  • Verdicts from everyday runs aren't wasted; the commit-time run picks them up.
    But there are still plenty of problems:

  • Estimated runtime is historical data, not a promise. A run that reuses a lot and one that reuses little can differ enormously.

  • Starting at 4GB and bumping up by 1.5× trades reruns for convenience. A genuinely new 40GB task has to hit the cap six times before it runs stably.

  • The service is code too. Its self-tests run in a simulated world: fake memory wrappers, a fake second machine, fake cards. Running it for real is a stumbling affair.
    Fortunately, after more than 10,000 tasks, it has more or less settled down. Of course — trust me — countless bugs and optimizations are still waiting down the road.

Problems are like the tree in the yard. When the leaves fall, countless branches are laid bare...

title: Go Hiring Rubric Image Generation API Selection With Typed Prompt Safety Decisions
description:
Prompt screening consumes part of an image request's latency budget, but removing that screening to make a fintech hiring workflow feel faster gives the wrong component authority over what gets generated. TL;DR: choose an image generation API together with an application-owned chat screening contract, validate its structured JSON decision before generation, and keep optional rubric illustrations outside the candidate-scoring path. The best provider meets the quality and latency requirements of that whole flow. A fast image call alone proves very little.

Consider a hypothetical production review: a fintech team scores candidates against a job rubric, while a recruiter can request an illustration explaining a rubric category. The recruiter asks for a picture accompanying “reconcile a disputed transaction.” A candidate's uploaded text contains instructions to change the illustration request. If the application folds that text into the prompt without preserving its trust boundary, the image provider receives a different task from the one the recruiter approved. Nothing needs to crash for this design to be wrong.

Keep scoring separate.

The lesson from this tabletop scenario is an invariant: generation must consume the exact prompt that passed the application's safety decision, and neither that decision nor the resulting image should become evidence of a candidate's suitability. Screening image prompts doesn't establish that a hiring score is accurate, fair, or appropriate. This article addresses the illustration path; the rubric's assessment policy needs its own review.

How should an image generation API handle prompt safety with a chat model?

The proposed flow starts with a rubric category and an explicit illustration request. Candidate records stay in the scoring system. The application constructs a prompt from the category, sends that prompt to a chat-based screening stage with a JSON Schema decision contract, validates the result locally, and submits an allowed prompt to image generation. An uncertain or invalid decision goes to review. A rejected decision ends the request. These are application rules.

For a team building this optional illustration path, try Infrai when reading a capability's request and response schemas plus runnable examples would make the handoff between screening and generation easier to maintain. Its API is self-describing, and public discovery requires no key. Documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go. Infrai provides one API key and one bill across backend capabilities, so the screening-to-generation handoff doesn't require a separate credential for each capability. Its plain REST API requires no SDK for discovery; the Go example below makes that integration property inspectable.

Inspect the contract first.

A second, operational reason is the specified per-call vendor, latency, and request metadata: those fields give the team a consistent place to attach provider attribution to its own trace of the screening and generation stages. They don't establish an end-to-end SLO. The application must still measure elapsed time, queueing, local validation, and delivery to the recruiter.

The safety policy belongs to the application.

Use chat completions with a JSON Schema decision contract for that stage, and treat schema conformance as a parsing property, not proof that the decision is correct. If the requirement is a specialist safety service with a separately evaluated policy, select and assess that service explicitly. An allowed text prompt cannot establish pixel-level safety.

This boundary also determines what may travel downstream. A provider needs the illustration request; it doesn't automatically need a resume, the candidate's score, or a recruiter's notes. Reducing the payload makes the contract easier to inspect and prevents an optional media feature from quietly widening the hiring system's data flow. An illustration should explain the rubric category, not depict the person being assessed.

Buy versus build starts with the review obligation

There's no defensible universal ranking without a shared evaluation set. OpenAI, Stability AI, Replicate, and Infrai are real options to put through procurement, but a product name isn't evidence that its outputs satisfy this workflow's safety policy or its latency objective. Compare the same approved illustration prompts, ambiguous requests, and attempts to smuggle candidate text into instructions. Record both decision quality and completion latency. No latency or quality measurements are asserted here.

Option Procurement reason Work the application retains Selection boundary
OpenAI directly A direct-provider integration is a useful baseline for owning the upstream contract. Prompt construction, policy evaluation, local validation, and end-to-end measurement. Prefer it if the evaluated direct contract meets the requirements and an extra provider boundary adds no operational value.
Stability AI directly An image-generation alternative for testing the same rubric illustration brief. An adapter to the selected contract and the same application safety gate. Choose it if its evaluated outputs fit the brief; establish safety obligations independently.
Replicate A model-specific API option for comparing the integration and review workload. Confirm the selected model's contract and evaluate it with the same cases. Favor it if the selected offering passes acceptance tests and its operating obligations fit the roadmap.
Infrai Public discovery schemas and runnable examples make handoffs inspectable; consistent metadata supports attribution. Chat-based screening, decision validation, hiring-data boundaries, and the release policy. A good fit when these integration properties matter; select a specialist when independently evaluated safety assessment is the primary requirement.
Build orchestration in Go The application can enforce one decision contract across evaluated providers. Contract versioning, evaluation data, concurrency controls, review handling, and on-call ownership. Build this policy boundary when required; it does not replace an image model or independent safety evaluation.

The distinction is ownership. Direct-provider integration concentrates the contract with the selected provider; a common HTTP surface can standardize the application's handoff, but introduces another dependency to assess. Model-level selection still requires model-level evaluation. These are architectural trade-offs, not measured claims that one vendor generates better illustrations.

The direct options deserve a fair test: if OpenAI or Stability AI already fits the chosen quality threshold and integration practices, a common surface may not remove enough work to justify another dependency. Conversely, a platform team maintaining several capabilities may value a discoverable contract more than another client library. Replicate belongs in that test when its selected offering matches the required brief; verify the exact model contract rather than treating the platform's name as an output guarantee.

Who approves a policy revision? Who reviews an uncertain result? Who can release a held image? A procurement scorecard that can't answer those questions hasn't compared the operating models, however detailed its feature columns look.

Budget latency for the whole decision

For the serial illustration path, the planning model is screening time plus local validation plus generation time plus any review and delivery time. That's a dependency relationship, not a benchmark. Optional review of metadata or a user-visible description introduces another stage; it can improve the release workflow, but reviewing a description is not equivalent to inspecting the generated image.

As a synthetic capacity example, suppose accepted traffic is 2 illustration requests per second and the planning assumption is 3 seconds of total in-flight processing per request. The starting estimate is 6 concurrent requests. Those numbers are assumptions for sizing an experiment, and burst arrivals, retries, and slow requests can invalidate that simple average quickly. Measure the distribution before setting a concurrency limit.

Tail latency matters.

Define the interactive SLO around a recruiter receiving either a completed illustration or a clear held-for-review state. Track those outcomes separately so that a quick refusal doesn't disguise poor generation availability. If image quality requires a slower path, keep the candidate score usable while the optional illustration completes. A strict immediate-render requirement may favor another product design, including a reviewed static illustration library.

Provider switching needs the same discipline. An allowed decision concerns a particular prompt under a particular policy. Changing prompt construction during a switch invalidates the assumption that the earlier review still applies; reconstruct the screening input and obtain a fresh decision. A replacement provider also needs acceptance testing, because a stable JSON shape doesn't establish equivalent image output.

Make the prevention path inspectable before integration

Start by inspecting the API contract. This standalone Go program retrieves the public discovery document, checks the HTTP status, and prints the document for inspection. The response lets the integrator locate capabilities and inspect their declared contracts before building the screening-to-generation adapter. The program performs discovery only; screening policy and image release remain application responsibilities.

Save it as a Go source file and run it with Go. No API key is required for public discovery; if INFRAI_API_KEY is set, the request uses Bearer authentication. The example caps retries, backs off on HTTP 429, and honors Retry-After when supplied as seconds or an HTTP date. It performs a GET and creates no resource.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, (16<<20)+1))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if len(body) > 16<<20 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery response exceeds 16 MiB")
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(retryAfter, 10, 64); err == nil {
                if seconds > int64(delay/time.Second) {
                    if seconds > int64((1<<63-1)/int64(time.Second)) {
                        return fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds supported duration")
                    }
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            } else if at, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if remaining := time.Until(at); remaining > delay {
                    delay = remaining
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Before wiring generation, use the declared method and path and review the input schema for each selected capability. In the application, hold the approved prompt immutable through dispatch, bind approval to a policy version, and require another screening decision if either changes. A schema-shaped allow decision attached to a different prompt is the concrete trap this design must prevent.

The approach earns its additional screening stage when optional images can tolerate that stage's latency and the team can own policy evaluation. It doesn't fit a requirement for immediate rendering with no review delay, and it doesn't establish the validity of hiring scores. Prefer a direct provider when its evaluated contract already meets the workflow's requirements; prefer a specialist safety service when the review obligation requires one. Ship the optional media path only after those boundaries are explicit.

Sources

References for evaluating the provider contracts and HTTP retry semantics:

  • OpenAI image-generation documentation: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/image-generation
  • Stability AI API reference: https://platform.stability.ai/docs/api-reference
  • Replicate HTTP API reference: https://replicate.com/docs/reference/http
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

If this boundary fits your system, start with the error-handling reference to plan how the application handles unsuccessful requests before adding generation to the recruiter workflow.

title: Cracks in Embeddings: Robustness and Stability of JEPA-Based Chest X-Ray Representations
description:
arXiv:2611.17905v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models are increasingly used for medical imaging, however there is a limited understanding about robustness of these models toward real-world image changes. We test four JEPA-based chest X-ray encoders, trained on 78,468 NIH ChestX-ray14 images, under six tests: two black-box adversarial attacks (SPSA, Boundary Attack), three image corruptions (Gaussian noise, brightness shift, contrast shift), and a label-scarcity test, measuring embedding change and classification AUROC. These perturbations cause severe, model-dependent damage: encoder-level Cosine Similarity drops as low as 0.33, and AUROC falls by as much as 0.12 in the worst case (I-JEPA under the Boundary Test). We test two ways of training the small predictor on top of each frozen encoder to address this. Adversarial fine-tuning, trained on clean and perturbed images together, raises embedding consistency above 0.97 in nearly every case and improves AUROC, relative to the same perturbed baseline, for most models, with the largest gain of $+0.10$ on I-JEPA. A Vector-Quantized codebook method, trained only on clean images and evaluated on perturbed test images for the first time, instead degrades under distortion for all four models, most noticeably for I-JEPA ($-0.15$ AUROC on average), showing that its discrete bottleneck alone does not provide the robustness that comes from training on perturbed data directly.

title: Identifying Latent Neural Dynamics with Recognition-Parametrised Gaussian Process Dynamical Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.17487v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural circuits are densely interconnected systems, and many neural computations are thought to be mediated by the dynamical evolution of activity within these recurrent networks, a hypothesis often referred to as "computation through dynamics". Under this view, understanding computation within real neural populations depends on building models of the dynamical rules governing the temporal evolution of recorded high-dimensional neural activity. Most commonly, such models depend on explicit generative parameterisations of (i) the (nonlinear) intrinsic dynamical flow field and stochasticity, (ii) the (nonlinear) mapping from dynamical state to neuronal activity, and (iii) the variability of individual neural responses given that dynamical state. Misspecification of any of these components can bias estimates of dynamics and latent trajectories. In this paper, we circumvent generation-related issues by introducing the Recognition-Parametrised Gaussian Process dynamics (RP-GPdyn) model. RP-GPdyn models the dynamical flow field using a nonparametric Gaussian Process-defined transition function and models the relationship of dynamics to neural activity implicitly using the Recognition-Parametrised Model (RPM) framework. We show that this generation-free approach uncovers meaningful, behaviourally relevant latent variables and dynamics from both synthetic and experimental datasets.

title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render
description:
You can now stream generative UI from your Chat SDK agent with json-render.

With a typed catalog of components, the agent writes a JSON spec that json-render converts into a Chat SDK card. Each adapter then posts the card in its platform’s native format, such as Block Kit on Slack and Adaptive Cards on Teams.

The catalog covers tables, charts, buttons, and more, so there’s no separate tool to build and maintain for each message shape.

Stream cards as the model writes

streamCard posts the card once its root element has content and updates the message as new elements stream in. Edits go out at most once every 500 ms by default, which matches Chat SDK’s streaming interval. Once the stream ends, the message shows the final, validated card.

Validate specs and enforce platform limits

toCard checks every element’s props against its component schema and throws CardSpecError for an invalid spec. Each problem gets its own readable issue, so you can send the list back to the model for a corrected spec.

Platforms cap what a single message can hold, and Chat SDK adapters degrade content past those caps. The Slack adapter, for example, turns a second table into a code block. Pass limits to reject those specs instead.

title: Delayed Effects of Temporary Weight Decay in Muon Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2611.17876v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A temporary optimization intervention can increase validation loss when it ends yet reduce it at the final training budget. We demonstrate this with temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers with 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 3.4B parameters. For models up to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect. At 162M, changing window duration alters final loss even at approximately matched total shrinkage. Most strikingly, a schedule selected at 162M and transferred without retuning to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay when removed, overtakes it only after 73% of training, and ultimately finishes 0.028 nats better while also outperforming the best sampled constant-decay baseline. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger after the intervention ends. An approximate norm-dynamics recurrence captures the slow convergence of these relative steps, and fixed-norm replays of the measured trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference. At 162M and 405M, norm-reset experiments show that smaller weight norms at the end of the decay window explain most of the final loss improvement. A separate Gram intervention exhibits related post-removal norm and relative-step dynamics. These results show that temporary optimization schedules can have delayed effects long after removal and should therefore be evaluated at the intended final training budget, not only at removal.

title: Scheduled Data Cleanup: Choosing a Cheap, Easy Queue for a Small SaaS
description:
Short answer

Short answer: the right choice for scheduled data cleanup is the design that preserves a recovery contract across a missed tick, a lost acknowledgement, and a duplicate delivery. A database-backed scheduler, a hosted queue, BullMQ, and RabbitMQ can all carry work; none of them makes the cleanup idempotent for you. Cost and ease follow from the amount of delivery state your team must operate.

The shipment example matters here. A cleanup job may delete expired rows, archive records, or fan out a shipment update to many subscribers. In all three cases, a timeout can leave the producer unsure whether the consumer finished. Treat every delivery as at-least-once unless the system explicitly proves otherwise.

The decision starts with the recovery boundary

The first decision is where recovery state lives. Separate four concerns: deciding that work is due, claiming a unit of work, performing it, and recording the result. A cron expression answers only the first question. Cron has long been a Unix scheduling convention, but the convention does not give an application a durable job state, a retry policy, or a deduplication key.

For scheduled cleanup, the database is often the most useful source of truth. Store a row for each cleanup window or tenant, with a stable key such as tenant_id + cleanup_date. A scheduler finds due rows and enqueues work. The worker claims the row, processes a bounded batch, and records completion. If the enqueue call or worker process is interrupted, the next attempt can use the same key.

A hosted queue reduces the amount of queue infrastructure the team operates. That can be the easiest choice when the team does not want to own broker upgrades, persistence settings, dashboards, and alerting. It is not automatically the cheapest: the real comparison includes the queue charge, the scheduler, observability, network paths, and the engineering time spent proving recovery behavior.

The catch is operational ownership. If the hosted service cannot meet your data residency, retention, private-network, or regional delivery requirements, use a component you can run inside the required boundary. If a hosted queue does not expose the retry, visibility, or delivery semantics your cleanup needs, it is the wrong fit even if its first invoice is small.

How should a small SaaS worker claim scheduled data cleanup safely?

A missed tick is visible. Duplicate work is quieter and can be worse: two workers can both decide that a shipment update is ready, or two cleanup attempts can delete and then recreate the same derived record. I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I put the retry contract ahead of the scheduler brand.

Use a stable idempotency key at the business boundary. For a shipment update, that might be shipment_id + event_version; for cleanup, it might be tenant_id + cleanup_window. Persist the key where the side effect is committed. A retry then becomes a lookup and a no-op, rather than a second irreversible action.

A queue's retry count is not an idempotency system. Exponential backoff reduces pressure during a dependency failure, but it does not tell you if the first attempt committed just before its response was lost. The worker needs a durable record and a transaction boundary that the team can explain during a postmortem.

Three words: assume duplicates happen.

For database-backed claiming, PostgreSQL documents FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED as useful for avoiding lock contention with multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table. The claim should be short; do not hold a row lock while calling a slow external subscriber. Claim a batch, commit the claim, perform the work, and update the result with a guarded transition.

type CleanupJob struct {
\tID        int64
\tTenantID  int64
\tWindowKey string
\tStatus    string
\tAttempts  int
}

func claimSQL(limit int) string {
\treturn `
WITH due AS (
  SELECT id
  FROM cleanup_jobs
  WHERE status = 'pending'
    AND run_after <= now()
  ORDER BY run_after, id
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT $1
)
UPDATE cleanup_jobs AS j
SET status = 'running',
    attempts = attempts + 1,
    claimed_at = now()
FROM due
WHERE j.id = due.id
RETURNING j.id, j.tenant_id, j.window_key, j.status, j.attempts`
}

The SQL is a claiming pattern, not a complete queue implementation. Add a lease timeout so a worker process that disappears does not hold work forever. Keep the cleanup batch bounded, and make the completion update conditional on the job still belonging to that attempt. Your mileage may vary with transaction isolation and workload; verify those choices against the PostgreSQL behavior in your deployment.

Consider one tenant whose cleanup window contains 18,000 records and whose shipment subscribers are split across email, webhook, and an internal analytics consumer. The scheduler should publish references to bounded slices, not one heroic message. Suppose the worker claims slice 12, commits that claim, sends the webhook, and loses its connection before recording completion. A lease expiry makes slice 12 visible again. The second worker sees the same operation key, checks the durable side-effect record, and records a duplicate attempt without sending a second webhook. If the first worker had not committed the side effect, the second worker performs it and writes the result. Now add a deployment during that window: old and new workers can overlap because both respect the claim transition and the lease owner. Finally, a policy change marks the tenant exempt after the scheduler selected the slice; the worker re-checks eligibility before deletion and records an exemption rather than treating the stale selection as authority. This is why the job row, the idempotency key, and the audit result belong in the design before the queue is selected. A queue can transport the reference, but it cannot infer whether a legal hold, shipment cancellation, or prior commit should win.

What does each operating model leave your team owning?

The comparison should start with the failure you need to control, not feature count. BullMQ is a queue library built around Redis, so it is a natural fit when the application already has a Redis operational path and a Node.js worker. For a Go service, that choice adds a runtime and ownership boundary unless another service already owns the queue. That is a team-shape trade-off, not a quality verdict.

A hosted queue is attractive when the team wants a managed delivery layer and a small operational surface. Ask for concrete answers about retry delays, dead-letter handling, message visibility, ordering, maximum payloads, regional placement, and metrics. “It retries” is not enough. You need to know what happens after a worker receives a message and then loses its connection.

RabbitMQ is a broker option when routing, exchanges, acknowledgements, consumer coordination, and explicit delivery controls matter. Those controls also create operational work: persistence, capacity, upgrades, topology, and alerts become part of the service you run. A small SaaS may accept that work when message routing is central to the product; it may be a poor fit for one nightly cleanup table.

Option Good fit Main cost or risk Questions to answer
Database-backed scheduler Small cleanup volume, strong transactional ownership Database contention and custom worker logic How are leases, retries, and retention implemented?
BullMQ Existing Redis and Node.js operations Redis and runtime coupling Which team owns Redis durability and the worker?
Hosted queue Small team, low broker-operations appetite Provider semantics and boundary constraints Are retry, visibility, region, and dead-letter behavior sufficient?
RabbitMQ Rich routing and acknowledgement controls Broker operations and topology Who drills recovery and manages capacity?

No option wins in the abstract. For this Go-shaped cleanup worker, the relevant boundary is the one the team can operate, observe, and recover. A database-backed scheduler has a small starting surface; a hosted queue moves delivery operations outside the application; a broker adds explicit routing and acknowledgement machinery. Those are different ownership contracts, not a leaderboard.

Rehearse failure, then make rollback boring

Test the ambiguous edges before production. Kill the worker after it claims a job. Delay the database response after the side effect commits. Deliver the same shipment event twice. Run two schedulers at once. Advance the clock across a daylight-saving transition for each region you serve. The expected result is either one durable side effect or a recorded, inspectable failure that can be retried safely.

Instrument the state transitions, not just queue depth. Track due jobs, claimed jobs, age of the oldest lease, attempts by reason, dead-letter volume, cleanup rows affected, and idempotency-key collisions. Alert on work age and repeated attempts. A queue with zero visible messages can still have a stuck running set.

Rollback needs a business rule. If a cleanup version is wrong, stop claiming new rows, preserve the job records, and make the operation reversible where possible. Do not “fix” the queue by deleting messages before you know whether their side effects committed. For shipment fan-out, replay from the durable event or outbox record; for destructive cleanup, prefer a staged mark-and-delete window when the retention policy allows it.

The recommendation is not suitable when the database cannot absorb the claim traffic, when external delivery requires broker features you do not have, or when strict cross-region guarantees exceed the chosen component. Stick with a more capable broker or hosted service when those constraints are real. I'm not sure any cost estimate stays stable long enough to be a selection criterion by itself, so use a measured workload and a recovery exercise to settle the decision.

References

  • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html
