title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
description:
Interfaze on Vercel

  • 50 million requests a month

  • Backend running on Fluid compute

  • Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway

Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification.

As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does.

Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down.

The backend required no infrastructure work

Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox, which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up.

Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs

Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box.

AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale

Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else.

The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality.

When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there.

Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months

Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK, with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence.

The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long.

Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers

Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up.

Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part.

What's next

Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite, an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gateway for web search, one API that routes to whichever search provider a developer picks, the way AI Gateway does for models. It launches on the same Vercel backend as everything else.

About Interfaze: Interfaze builds models for deterministic tasks, including OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. Its customers are engineering teams in legal, healthcare, and finance.

title: Your 27-model ensemble has 1.5 opinions: measuring diversity with Fleiss' kappa and lineage-weighted voting
description:
An ensemble is a claim about independence. You put k models in a room, they vote, and errors unique to each member cancel out. That only works if members actually disagree. If they all came from the same handful of prompts, voting is theatre.

Our platform has 3,784 model records and 46,807 graded calls over 16,787 fixtures. On paper that is a deep committee. I measured how deep with three estimators: stance concentration, pairwise contradiction, and Fleiss' kappa converted to effective ensemble size.

On the 2,722 fixtures with five or more voters, the average ballot held 10.34 models and 1.46 effective opinions. A majority vote over those ballots scored 56.95% — slightly worse than the 57.00% average of the members it aggregated.

The data

Everything below comes from one append-only table. The relevant columns:

column meaning
match_id / model_id fixture key, model record
training_word_id prompt lineage that model was built from
prediction_direction home, draw, away, home/draw, away/draw
direction_arity single (70.18%) or double (29.76%)
confidence 1–10 integer, not a probability
hit / actual_result settled once, home / draw / away

Two properties matter. First, 29.76% of calls are two-outcome leans, so "agreement" is not string equality — two members can differ in label yet stay logically compatible. Second, training_word_id exposes the pedigree behind each ballot, where the collapse originates.

Estimator 1: how concentrated is a ballot?

If ten members split 9/1/0, the committee has one opinion and one dissenter. The Herfindahl index over stance shares gives a "number of effective stances" directly:

WITH per_match AS (
  SELECT match_id, count(*) AS n,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE prediction_direction='home')      AS h,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE prediction_direction='draw')      AS d,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE prediction_direction='away')      AS a,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE prediction_direction='home/draw') AS hd,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE prediction_direction='away/draw') AS ad
  FROM ai_predictions WHERE hit IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1
), scored AS (
  SELECT *, (h*h + d*d + a*a + hd*hd + ad*ad)::numeric / (n*n) AS hhi,
         greatest(h,d,a,hd,ad)::numeric / n AS top_share
  FROM per_match WHERE n >= 5
)
SELECT count(*) AS fixtures, round(avg(n),2) AS mean_ballot,
       round(avg(top_share),4) AS mean_top_share,
       round(avg(hhi),4) AS mean_hhi,
       round(avg(1.0/hhi),3) AS effective_stances,
       round(100.0*count(*) FILTER (WHERE top_share=1)/count(*),2) AS pct_unanimous,
       round(100.0*count(*) FILTER (WHERE h>0 AND a>0)/count(*),2) AS pct_home_and_away
FROM scored;

Read the last two columns together. A third of ballots are unanimous, and only 3.99% of fixtures have at least one member on each side of the home/away divide. The 358-call maximum ballot we once recorded is not a debate; it is a chorus. Mean top share is 0.8119 and mean HHI 0.7486, so 1/hhi = 1.455 effective stances against a 10.34-member roster.

Estimator 2: are disagreements real or cosmetic?

Label identity is too strict. home and home/draw are compatible; home and away are not. So classify each pair by outcome set, not string:

WITH ballots AS (
  SELECT match_id, model_id, prediction_direction AS dir
  FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE hit IS NOT NULL AND match_id IN (
    SELECT match_id FROM ai_predictions WHERE hit IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) BETWEEN 2 AND 40)
), pairs AS (
  SELECT a.dir AS d1, b.dir AS d2
  FROM ballots a JOIN ballots b
    ON a.match_id = b.match_id AND a.model_id < b.model_id
)
SELECT count(*) AS pairs,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE d1 = d2) / count(*), 2) AS identical_pct,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT (
         (d1 IN ('home','home/draw') AND d2 IN ('home','home/draw')) OR
         (d1 IN ('draw','home/draw','away/draw')
          AND d2 IN ('draw','home/draw','away/draw')) OR
         (d1 IN ('away','away/draw') AND d2 IN ('away','away/draw'))
       )) / count(*), 2) AS contradictory_pct
FROM pairs;

Across 115,084 member pairs: 71.66% carry the identical label, 28.34% differ, and 24.93% are irreconcilable — one member says the home side wins, another says it does not. A quarter of all pairs are in direct logical conflict, yet ballot concentration is 0.81. Both are true: disagreement lives in the tail, and the tail almost never decides the vote.

Estimator 3: kappa to effective sample size

Concentration is a per-fixture view. Fleiss' kappa corrects observed agreement for what chance alone would produce given the label marginals — here home 19,072, away/draw 11,116, away 10,249, home/draw 6,010, draw 360, across 46,807 rows.

from math import comb

marginals = {"home": 19072, "away/draw": 11116, "away": 10249,
             "home/draw": 6010, "draw": 360}
total = sum(marginals.values())
p_exp = sum((v / total) ** 2 for v in marginals.values())   # 0.2869
p_obs = 0.7166                                              # identical-label rate
kappa = (p_obs - p_exp) / (1 - p_exp)                       # 0.6026

n = 10.34                                                   # mean ballot size
n_eff = n / (1 + (n - 1) * kappa)                           # 1.56
print(round(p_exp, 4), round(kappa, 4), round(n_eff, 3))

# What a genuinely independent committee of 57% members would score
p = 0.5700
for k in (1, 5, 11, 21):
    acc = sum(comb(k, i) * p**i * (1 - p)**(k - i)
              for i in range(k // 2 + 1, k + 1))
    print(k, round(acc * 100, 2))

0.2869 0.6026 1.56
1  57.00
5  62.95
11 68.34
21 74.30

Two independent estimators land in the same place: Herfindahl says 1.455 effective stances, kappa says 1.56 effective members. Eleven independent 57% members would score 68.34%. Ours score 56.95%. The theoretical gain is 11.4 points of accuracy; the realised gain is negative 0.05.

Where the collapse comes from: the pedigree column

The ballot average is 10.34 models but only 4.10 distinct training_word_id values — 0.439 lineages per model, and on 94.31% of multi-model fixtures there are strictly fewer lineages than models. Models are not independent individuals; they are re-parameterisations of a few prompts, so their errors are shared by construction. That suggests a fairer vote: one ballot per lineage, not per model. Take each lineage's modal stance, then vote across lineages.

WITH base AS (
  SELECT match_id, max(actual_result) AS res FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE hit IS NOT NULL AND actual_result IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) >= 5
), rows AS (
  SELECT p.match_id, p.training_word_id AS tw, p.prediction_direction AS dir
  FROM ai_predictions p JOIN base b USING (match_id)
), lineage AS (
  SELECT match_id, tw, mode() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY dir) AS stance
  FROM rows GROUP BY 1, 2
), tallied AS (
  SELECT match_id, count(*) AS lineages,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE stance='home')      AS h,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE stance='draw')      AS d,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE stance='away')      AS a,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE stance='home/draw') AS hd,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE stance='away/draw') AS ad
  FROM lineage GROUP BY 1
), voted AS (
  SELECT t.*, b.res, h + 0.5*hd AS hv,
         d + 0.5*hd + 0.5*ad AS dv, a + 0.5*ad AS av
  FROM tallied t JOIN base b USING (match_id)
), picked AS (
  SELECT *, CASE WHEN hv > dv AND hv > av THEN 'home'
                 WHEN dv > hv AND dv > av THEN 'draw'
                 WHEN av > hv AND av > dv THEN 'away' END AS pick
  FROM voted
)
SELECT count(*)                                            AS fixtures,
       round(avg(lineages), 2)                             AS mean_lineages,
       round(100.0 * count(pick) / count(*), 2)            AS pct_decisive,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE pick = res)
             / count(pick), 2)                             AS accuracy_on_decisive
FROM picked;

fixtures 2722 | mean_lineages 4.10 | pct_decisive 72.44 | accuracy_on_decisive 57.35

Model-level voting on the same fixtures: 78.18% decisive, 56.95% accurate. Lineage-level: 72.44% decisive, 57.35% accurate. Deduplicating the ballot buys 0.40 points and costs 5.74 points of decisiveness, because a smaller, more honest electorate ties more often.

Consensus tells you the fixture is easy, not that you are right

One more diagnostic, because "agreement predicts accuracy" is the assumption teams lean on hardest. Split fixtures by unanimity and look at the average accuracy of individual members in each group:

ballot share of fixtures mean member accuracy
unanimous 33.43% 65.36%
contested (top share < 0.70) 800 fixtures 50.14%

Unanimity does correlate with being right — but just as strongly with the fixture being easy. On the contested set, where a committee would add value, member accuracy is 50.14% and the disagreements do not resolve. The aggregate is brutal: committee 56.95% against members 57.00%. Aggregation over clones is not free; it is a small tax.

Practical rules I now apply

  1. Report effective size, not roster size. 1/hhi or the kappa conversion belongs next to every "we have N models" claim. Ours reads 1.46 out of 10.34.
  2. Deduplicate by lineage before voting. Weight each member 1 / members_in_its_lineage, otherwise you sample one prompt many times.
  3. Track the contradiction rate, not just disagreement. 28.34% of pairs differ; 24.93% are strictly incompatible. The gap is the cosmetic part.
  4. Never read consensus as confidence. Log the top share with every aggregated call so you can split unanimity from easiness later.
  5. Publish the negative result. "Committee is 0.05 points worse than its members" is the sentence that stops someone shipping an ensemble as a feature.

Limits

Observational statistics on our own settled history, not a controlled experiment. Ballot composition is not random — high-profile fixtures attract more models, so the ≥5-model subset over-represents them. training_word_id approximates pedigree; two models on one word can diverge through temperature and version drift. Condorcet figures assume independence and are arithmetic ceilings, not forecasts; the correlated-vote simulation at kappa 0.6–0.81 reproduces only the flat 56.8–57.3% band we observe — evidence about mechanism, not proof. Every number is recomputable from ai_predictions with the queries above.

An ensemble's value is a property of its pedigree graph, not its member count — and the graph is measurable in about forty lines of SQL.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

title: Java - this & final keywords
description:
this Keyword in Java

The this keyword in Java is a reference variable that refers to the current object of a class. It is commonly used to distinguish instance variables from local variables when they have the same name.

  • Refers to the current class object.
  • Used to access current class instance variables and methods.
  • Used to invoke another constructor of the same class using this().

Example

`class Student {
String name;
int age;

Student(String name, int age) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
}

void display() {
    System.out.println(this.name);
    System.out.println(this.age);
}

}`

public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) {
Student s1 = new Student("Gowtham", 20);
s1.display();
}
}

Output:

Gowtham
20

Explanation

  • this.name refers to the instance variable.
  • name refers to the constructor parameter.
  • this.age refers to the instance variable.
  • age refers to the constructor parameter.
  • The this keyword helps us avoid confusion when variable names are the same.

Common Uses of this Keyword

  1. Referring to current class instance variables.
  2. Calling another constructor using this().
  3. Calling a method of the current object.
  4. Passing the current object as an argument.

final Keyword in Java

In Java, the final keyword is used to restrict changes and make code more secure and predictable. It can be applied to variables, methods, and classes to prevent modification, overriding, or inheritance. This helps in creating constant values, stable methods, and immutable classes.

1. Final Variable

A final variable cannot be reassigned after it has been initialized.

Example:

`public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) {
final int age = 20;

    System.out.println(age);
}

}`

Output:

20

Here, age is a final variable, so we cannot assign another value to it.

2. Final Method

A final method cannot be overridden by a subclass.

Example:

`class Parent {
final void display() {
System.out.println("This is a final method");
}
}

class Child extends Parent {
// Cannot override display()
}`

public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) {
Child obj = new Child();
obj.display();
}
}

Output:

This is a final method

Here, the display() method is declared as final, so the child class cannot override it.

3. Final Class

A final class cannot be extended by another class.

Example:

final class Student {
void display() {
System.out.println("Hello Java!");
}
}

public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) {
Student s1 = new Student();
s1.display();
}
}

Output:

Hello Java!

Here, Student is a final class, so another class cannot inherit from it.

title: Your Classifier Scored Ninety Six Percent Because the Same Emails Were in Both Halves
description:
We trained a small model
to route support emails.

Delivery.

Billing.

Damaged goods.

Account changes.

Forty thousand labelled emails.

Shuffle them.

Eighty percent to train,
twenty percent to test.

The test score was ninety six percent.

We celebrated.

We shipped it.

In the first month
it routed about three in four correctly.

Same model.

Same kind of emails.

The test set was not lying.

It was answering
a different question
from the one we asked.

Here is what we found
when we finally read the data.

Our biggest customers
send the same email
over and over.

Their systems use templates.

Only the order number changes.

Some threads
had been labelled twenty times,
once per reply,
each one quoting the last.

A random split
puts copies of the same email
on both sides.

So the test was full
of emails the model had already seen
in training,
with a different number in them.

It did not have to understand
damaged goods.

It only had to remember
this customer's wording.

That is leakage.

Information from the test
reached the training,
and the score measured memory.

Production has no copies.

Next month's emails
are new.

The fix is to split
the way the future arrives.

Group by customer,
or by thread,
so everything from one source
lands on one side.

In scikit-learn
that is GroupShuffleSplit,
or GroupKFold for cross validation.

Remove near duplicates
before you split,
not after.

And when the data has dates,
train on the past
and test on the most recent weeks.

Our honest score
came out at seventy nine.

Lower,
and true.

It matched production
within a point or two,
and for the first time
we knew which number to improve.

This does not only apply
to models you train.

If you test a prompt
on examples you also put in the prompt,
or tune it on the cases
you then grade it on,
the same thing happens.

Before you trust a score,
ask what the test had
that tomorrow will not.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: Why your Codex plugin doesn't show up: a plugin.json checklist
description:
Disclosure: I run PickAPlugin, an independent catalog of ChatGPT and Codex plugins. This is adapted from our guide on the same topic.

Codex is pretty quiet when a manifest is wrong. The plugin just doesn't show up, and there's no error to chase. Here's what the manifest needs and the mistakes that trip people up most.

What it needs

  • name: kebab-case (my-plugin, not My Plugin). It's the id.
  • version: semver, like 0.1.0.
  • description: one clear sentence.
  • The file lives at .codex-plugin/plugin.json. Only that file goes in that folder. Skills, .mcp.json and hooks live at the plugin root.

A minimal manifest:

{
  "name": "my-plugin",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Does one useful thing for your agent."
}

The mistakes we see most

  1. Paths that don't start with ./, or absolute paths like /Users/me/....
  2. Paths with .. that point outside the plugin.
  3. Marketplace entries missing source or policy.
  4. Secrets pasted into the manifest. Use environment variables instead.

Check it quickly

We keep a free plugin.json validator. It runs in your browser (nothing is uploaded) and flags errors, warnings and nice-to-haves. It also checks marketplace.json.

Is there an official schema?

OpenAI documents the fields in its plugin build docs, and many manifests reference the agent-plugins.org schema in $schema. The validator checks the commonly documented rules.

The full guide is at pickaplugin.com/guides/validate-plugin-json.

title: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
description:
When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits.

Last year, we shipped just that, with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it.

More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged.

  • The first is automation: Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines.

  • The second is agents and harnesses: Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too.

As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance.

Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three.

More secure workflows

The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection.

Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end, before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools.

Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel

On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change:

Because Vercel manages the keys by default, observability keeps working. Names, timings, and statuses are always visible, and when you need to see a payload, you can decrypt it in the dashboard or the CLI. Decryption happens in your browser or terminal, follows the same permissions as the project’s environment variables, and every request is recorded in your team’s audit log.

Encryption on self-hosted Worlds

Encryption is implemented in the SDK, so it can also protect payloads on self-hosted Worlds before they reach storage, queues, or streams.

A custom World enables encryption by implementing getEncryptionKeyForRun() with your key management. Return the same 32-byte key for each run on every call so the SDK can encrypt new payloads and decrypt them during replay:

More security work in v5

Cross-run writes are sealed too. When code resumes another run’s hook, starts a run in another deployment, or writes into a stream forwarded from another run, the payload is encrypted to the target run’s public key. The writer can encrypt for that run without reading its existing payloads.

You can also limit how long sensitive data is stored. With payload retention set to experimental_retention: 0, inputs, outputs, and stream contents are deleted as soon as a run completes or fails. The run’s metadata stays visible in observability.

A redesigned trace viewer

The redesigned trace viewer makes runs easier to navigate, with span search, zoom, a minimap, and local inspection during development.

Run attributes are new in v5. They let you attach searchable context to a run, such as an order ID, and then find runs by it. Attributes are plaintext, so they should not contain secrets.

Workflows in every region

In Workflow SDK 4, every run lived in iad1. Even when a project was deployed to several regions, each run’s event log, queue, and streams were only stored in one region, so a step running anywhere else made cross-region requests to record its progress.

For v5, we deployed Workflow infrastructure to every Vercel Function region. Each run has its own home region: its state, queue dispatch, and streams are served from the region where it started, without cross-region round trips on the hot path.

By default, a run starts in the region of the function that starts it. Deploy to several regions, and each run stays close to the user who triggered it, with no configuration:

To place a run somewhere else, pass a region to start(). That lets a workflow run next to the database it reads and writes, or keep a customer’s data in the region where it has to stay:

The region option decides where a run’s data lives. Your steps run where your app is deployed, so deploy to that region too if you want them to execute there. Existing v4 runs stay in iad1.

Infrastructure reliability

Regional isolation also improves reliability. A disruption in one region does not have to stop new runs in healthy regions. For projects with Vercel Function failover configured, steps can execute in a fallback region while continuing to use the run’s original home region for state. That state remains pinned to its home region; it does not migrate during failover.

With the help of anonymized telemetry and close collaboration with many customers, we found and fixed dozens of rare bugs and race conditions in the Workflow runtime. Workflow SDK also recovers on its own from more kinds of intermittent network errors.

As a result, with Workflow SDK 5, we’ve seen almost no runs fail or stall because of a platform or runtime bug.

Agent-ready performance

In Workflow SDK 4, every step invocation involved a queue hop to start the step and another to continue the workflow. That is acceptable for slow background automations, but adds latency to the AI workloads developers are building today.

Agent loops and harnesses can contain thousands of sequential events, high-throughput token streams, tool chains, and dynamic subagents. At that scale, the networking and CPU work around every step became a limit.

In Workflow SDK 5, we rewrote large parts of the engine to minimize extra queue hops, unnecessary networking, and CPU work. Across the measured workloads, we saw 1.6× to 25× improvements in measured latency and overhead, while preserving the same developer experience and introducing no major breaking changes.

The benchmarks below compare v5.2.0 with v4.8.12 on Vercel. Pick a measurement to see how v5 compares with v4, then play or scrub through the explainer to see exactly what each benchmark measures.

Workflow SDK 5 includes hundreds of performance improvements to achieve this. Here are some of the major changes behind these numbers:

Fewer queue hops

In v4, each step handed execution back through the queue. In v5, an invocation can execute several steps inline, including parallel steps, before yielding for a wait, a hook, or an approaching timeout.

The runtime also avoids unnecessary persistence round trips and folds step creation into execution. Fewer queue and network requests mean less CPU work and lower runtime overhead. In a five-step benchmark, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 618 ms to 109 ms.

Incremental replay

Over a 1,020-step benchmark, v4’s p75 overhead grew with the event log: replaying the full event history took time proportional to its size. In the final sampled range, overhead reached 1,748 ms. On v5.2.0, it was 70 ms. The median time to finish all 1,020 steps fell from 21.0 minutes to 3.0 minutes.

WebSocket streaming

Durability should not make a streamed response fall behind its producer. On the Vercel World, v5.2.0 writes streams over WebSockets by default. In a benchmark replaying a 52.4-second agent response, median delivery dropped from 226.1 seconds to 53.5 seconds.

Payload compression reduces the data stored and transferred. AI token streams average around 80% smaller after compression.

These measurements describe one workload, in one region, against the Vercel World. They are a useful view of runtime overhead, rather than a prediction for every application.

Benchmark results and methodology

Measured October 8, 2026, on Vercel production in iad1, against the managed Vercel World. Each version uses a separate deployment of the same app. Steps take 1 KB of JSON in and out.

The full results, including tails, are in the performance documentation.

Worlds: the shared durability primitive

Workflow SDK’s durable functions sit on a World: the interface for storing progress, dispatching work, and delivering streams. That same foundation also now supports fx and durable-harness, which adds durability to existing agent harnesses.

Improvements to the shared storage, queue, and streaming infrastructure can benefit any consumer of a World. Optimizations inside the Workflow replay runtime apply to Workflow SDK; they do not automatically apply to every harness.

Choose the integration around how you want to build:

  • Workflow SDK: write durable application logic with use workflow and use step.

  • WorkflowAgent: use @ai-sdk/workflow for an AI SDK agent loop inside a workflow.

  • fx: embed and extend a native coding agent with libfx.

  • durable-harness: keep an existing supported harness and add durability beneath it.

    • Supports Pi and OpenCode, with experimental integrations for Claude Code and Codex in Vercel Sandbox.

  • eve: build agents with durable sessions powered natively by Workflow SDK and Worlds.

We’ll soon be adding more offerings to our catalog of SDKs and frameworks backed by Worlds for durability.

Build with Workflow SDK 5

Besides the improvements above, Workflow SDK 5 also adds:

  • In-flight cancellation with AbortController

  • Searchable run attributes

  • More framework integrations

  • And more

The v5 upgrade docs cover what changed. To start building a new workflow, install the SDK:

Workflow SDK also has a Python SDK, now in beta, with the same durable workflows, steps, sleeps, and hooks.

title: Tenant-Safe Fintech Exports: Presigned Download URL 403s, Clock Skew, and Key Encoding
description:
Short answer: treat a 403 on a presigned download URL as a signature disagreement about the exact object-storage bytes and time used for signing, then trace those inputs before changing permissions.

That rule matters in a fintech system serving generated reports to authenticated customers. A link can be authorized for the right tenant and still fail because a proxy decoded %2F, a worker's clock is ahead, or the signer used a different object key than the uploader. The storage service is doing what it should: it verifies a precise request, not your intention.

The decision record: preserve these invariants

I start the design with four invariants. The authenticated request determines tenant_id; that value selects a storage prefix, never a user-supplied path. The object key is stored as data and passed unchanged to the signer. The application signs and serves from UTC time. Finally, the download response never reveals a bucket listing or another tenant's metadata.

The export worker writes an immutable object such as tenants/acme/reports/2026-09-07/statement-1842.csv. The API records the canonical key and a checksum in its database. At download time it checks the caller's tenant and report row, creates a short-lived URL, and logs a request identifier rather than the full query string (the signature itself is a credential).

Here is the useful comparison I put in an architecture decision record:

Option Isolation boundary Failure you can diagnose Good fit
Direct presigned URL Storage key plus signed parameters Canonical-request mismatch, expiry, clock drift Browser downloads of private exports
Application streaming proxy Application authorization on every byte Proxy timeout, range handling, memory pressure Strict egress policy or per-download auditing
Public object with random name Name secrecy URL leakage and retention mistakes Non-sensitive, disposable artifacts
Signed CDN URL CDN policy and storage origin Policy/key-group mismatch Large files with edge caching

For customer reports, the first option is usually the smallest attack surface when the key prefix is tenant-scoped and the URL lifetime is conservative. It is not suitable when every byte must pass through a data-loss-prevention scanner; use an application proxy there. That trade-off belongs in the record, before the first 403 arrives.

How do presigned download URLs, 403 signatures, expiry, and object keys fail together?

Signature verification is an equality test. The signer canonicalizes the HTTP method, path, selected headers, and query parameters, hashes that string, and derives a signature with a secret key. The verifier repeats the process. One character of difference is enough for a 403.

The path is the common trap. A key containing a space, +, Unicode, or a literal %2F has several representations. A framework may decode once while a reverse proxy decodes again. Do not build a URL by concatenating a bucket, slash, and raw filename. Keep the key canonical in storage, let the storage SDK perform its canonical encoding, and treat the returned URL as opaque. In Node.js, pass the same string to upload and signing; avoid a second decodeURIComponent in a download controller. I also compare the URL's path before and after every gateway hop, because a helpful normalization middleware can turn one valid byte sequence into a different one while preserving a perfectly plausible filename in logs. That mismatch is easy to miss during a code review and obvious in a hex dump.

It failed.

I keep a redacted trace beside each export: method, canonical key hash, signer region, X-Amz-Date, X-Amz-Expires, and the server's UTC offset. Never log X-Amz-Signature, access keys, or the complete URL. A 403 then becomes a comparison exercise instead of a guess.

This tiny Python helper checks the inputs without contacting storage:

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlsplit


def inspect_presigned_url(raw_url: str, now: datetime) -> dict:
    query = parse_qs(urlsplit(raw_url).query)
    signed_at = query.get("X-Amz-Date", [""])[0]
    expires = int(query.get("X-Amz-Expires", ["0"])[0])
    issued = datetime.strptime(signed_at, "%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ").replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    age_seconds = (now.astimezone(timezone.utc) - issued).total_seconds()
    return {
        "has_signature": bool(query.get("X-Amz-Signature")),
        "age_seconds": age_seconds,
        "expires_seconds": expires,
        "expired": age_seconds > expires,
        "credential_present": bool(query.get("X-Amz-Credential")),
    }

If expired is false but the request still fails, compare the canonical path and method next. A GET signed in the worker and followed as a HEAD by a client library is a different request. A browser can also add a header that was included in the signed-header list but changed in transit. Strip optional headers from the signing policy unless you truly need them.

Clock skew deserves its own alarm. NTP keeps machines close, but containers, suspended laptops, and isolated build workers drift. Compare the signer timestamp with a trusted UTC source and alert before the allowed window is consumed. A longer expiry hides the symptom and extends the blast radius of a leaked link; it does not repair a bad clock.

A tenant-isolated export path that stays observable

The API should resolve a report ID to a database row, not accept an arbitrary object key from the browser. The row contains the tenant and canonical key. Authorization happens before signing, and the audit event records success or denial without secrets.

from datetime import timedelta
from hashlib import sha256


def create_download_link(user, report_id, reports, signer, clock):
    report = reports.find(report_id)
    if report is None or report.tenant_id != user.tenant_id:
        raise PermissionError("report is not available")

    # The key came from the database, after tenant authorization.
    expires_in = timedelta(minutes=5)
    url = signer.presign_get_object(key=report.object_key, expires=expires_in)
    audit("report_link_issued", user_id=user.id, report_id=report.id,
          key_hash=sha256(report.object_key.encode()).hexdigest())
    return url

The critical path has two independent clocks: the report's creation time and the URL's issue time. Use the latter for expiry. If a queue retries an old job, it must not silently overwrite the canonical key with a newly encoded variant. Make the object write idempotent, then sign only after the database says the object is complete.

For operations, split metrics by tenant and outcome: authorization denial, signer rejection, expired link, and client cancellation. A spike in signature mismatches across every tenant points to deployment or clock configuration. One tenant alone suggests a key with unusual bytes or a bad migration. This distinction saves hours.

What should the team test before blaming storage?

Build a matrix around bytes and time, not just a happy-path filename. Include spaces, +, %, repeated slashes, non-ASCII names, and a key that literally contains %2F. Generate and consume each URL through the same proxy path used in production. Assert that the resolved tenant prefix matches the database row and that a URL for tenant A cannot fetch tenant B's report.

Freeze the clock in unit tests. Add an integration test at the exact expiry boundary, then one second after it. Test GET and HEAD separately. Test a client that preserves the URL byte-for-byte and another that normalizes it, so the team can see which layer changed the request.

There is a practical limit here: storage providers differ in canonicalization details and maximum expiry windows. Your mileage may vary across SDK versions and gateways, so pin the signer version, document the provider's signing specification, and run a canary against the real endpoint during upgrades. A generic retry on 403 is dangerous; retry only after classifying the cause, and never mint a new link for an unauthorized report.

Keep the rejected option visible. Making every object public and hiding the name removes signature mismatches, but it turns a leaked export URL into an authorization bypass and complicates retention. It is valid for public documentation or non-sensitive assets, not customer financial reports.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/API/sig-v4-authenticating-requests.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986

title: How I handle ~1M requests a day on 1 vCPU and 2GB RAM (and keep bots out without user accounts)
description:
I run a Tempgbox : free temporary email service on one vCPU and 2GB of RAM. Django, PostgreSQL, Redis, Celery. It serves around a 1 million+ requests a day. Still i notice that backend use only 500 Mb ram and 1.5 GB ram free.

Four changes made the biggest difference for such a small server.

Cloudflare in front. I put Cloudflare in front of everything as a proxy. Most requests are for frontend pages, and Cloudflare caches those, so they never reach my server. That alone took a lot of load off it.

DRF to Django Ninja. I migrated the API from Django REST Framework to Django Ninja, which has built-in async support. I’m still learning how much that gives me, but it was the right direction for an API that does a lot of waiting.

Cleaning up guest users. Most of my users are guests, so guest accounts pile up fast. Now I delete a guest user as soon as their token expires. The database stays small, and I stopped paying to store people who were gone anyway.

Redis, with regular cleanup. I use Redis for short-lived data, and I clean it up on a schedule instead of letting it grow. With only 2GB of RAM, Redis can quietly eat memory that the rest of the stack needs, so I treat it like a cache that must stay small, not a place to dump things.

I’m curious what other people with tiny servers did first. Caching, cleanup, or something else?

title: Open-World Scene Deocclusion
description:
arXiv:2611.17695v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recovering the complete appearance of occluded objects from a single image is a fundamental problem for scene understanding and image editing. Real-world scenes are challenging due to clutter, complex spatial occlusions, and diverse object categories. Existing methods often struggle when occlusion involves background surfaces or objects that are not explicitly detected, and fail to resolve the cyclic occlusion dependencies that frequently occur in natural scenes. We introduce a training-free, open-world scene deocclusion framework that recovers the full amodal appearance of detected or user-selected objects from a single RGB image, decomposing the scene into depth-ordered RGBA layers that are geometrically plausible, semantically faithful, and visually consistent with the visible scene. Extensive experiments show that our approach improves scene-level deocclusion, producing coherent and realistic reconstructions in real-world settings. Code will be available on the project page: https://sashjk.github.io/owsd/

title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
description:
arXiv:2611.17583v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs.
  In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better.
  These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. $I(W;R)$ measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.

title: Understanding the MERN Stack: A Complete Guide to Modern Full-Stack Web Development
description:
Introduction
Modern web development requires powerful, scalable, and efficient technologies to build interactive web applications. One of the most popular technology stacks used by developers today is the MERN Stack.

MERN is an acronym for four powerful JavaScript-based technologies: MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, and Node.js. Together, these technologies provide a complete environment for developing full-stack web applications using JavaScript across both the frontend and backend.

The MERN Stack has gained popularity because of its flexibility, developer-friendly ecosystem, reusable components, and ability to build scalable applications.
What Is the MERN Stack?
The MERN Stack is a full-stack JavaScript technology stack consisting of four major technologies:

  1. MongoDB – Database Layer

MongoDB is a NoSQL document-oriented database that stores application data in flexible, JSON-like documents called BSON documents.

Unlike traditional relational databases, MongoDB does not require a fixed table structure. This makes it easier to manage dynamic application data.

Key features:

  • Flexible document-based data storage.
  • High scalability.
  • Efficient data retrieval.
  • Support for complex data structures.
  • Easy integration with Node.js.
  • Express.js – Backend Framework

Express.js is a lightweight and flexible web application framework built on top of Node.js.

It simplifies backend development by providing tools for handling HTTP requests, managing routes, implementing middleware, and building RESTful APIs.

Key features:

  • Routing and request handling.
  • Middleware integration.
  • REST API development.
  • Error-handling mechanisms.
  • Simplified server-side development.
  • React.js – Frontend Library

React.js is a JavaScript library used to build interactive and dynamic user interfaces.

It follows a component-based architecture, allowing developers to divide an application into smaller, reusable components.

Key features:

  • Component-based architecture.
  • Virtual DOM.
  • Reusable UI components.
  • State management.
  • Efficient rendering.
  • Node.js – Runtime Environment

Node.js is a JavaScript runtime environment that allows developers to execute JavaScript outside the browser.

It uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model, making it suitable for building scalable network applications.

Key features:

  • Asynchronous programming.
  • Non-blocking I/O.
  • Large npm package ecosystem.
  • Cross-platform compatibility.
  • Efficient server-side execution. How Does the MERN Stack Work? The four technologies work together to create a complete web application.

The general application workflow is:

  1. A user interacts with the React.js frontend.
  2. React sends an HTTP request to the backend API.
  3. Express.js receives and processes the request.
  4. Node.js executes the backend JavaScript code.
  5. The backend communicates with MongoDB when database operations are required.
  6. MongoDB returns the requested data.
  7. The backend sends a response to React.
  8. React updates the user interface with the received information. Advantages of the MERN Stack
  9. Single programming language: JavaScript can be used throughout the application.
  10. Open-source technologies: All four technologies have strong open-source ecosystems.
  11. Reusable components: React improves development efficiency through reusable UI components.
  12. Scalability: MongoDB and Node.js support applications with growing requirements.
  13. Large community: Developers can access extensive documentation, tutorials, and community support.
  14. Cost-effective development: The stack offers many free tools and libraries. Applications Built Using MERN The MERN Stack can be used to develop various types of applications, including:
  15. E-commerce platforms.
  16. Social networking applications.
  17. Learning management systems.
  18. Food delivery applications.
  19. Real-time chat applications.
  20. Content management systems.
  21. Portfolio websites.
  22. Business management dashboards. Conclusion The MERN Stack is a powerful choice for modern full-stack web development. Its JavaScript-based architecture, flexibility, scalability, and extensive ecosystem make it suitable for beginners as well as experienced developers.

By mastering MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, and Node.js, developers can build complete web applications, from interactive user interfaces to secure backend systems and database management.

title: Checkout Validation for UnionPay Cards: BINs, 19 Digits, and Missing CVVs
description:
Most card-validation code was written with an implicit template in mind: 16 digits, a 3-digit CVV, a postal code, and a number that passes the Luhn check. That template fits most Visa and Mastercard traffic. It does not fit UnionPay well. When the template is wrong, the failure is silent. The shopper sees "invalid card number," leaves, and your processor never logs an attempt you could investigate.

This article covers the client-side and server-side validation logic needed so valid UnionPay cards reach your processor. It also covers how to account for the weaker fraud signals those transactions can carry. For background on the network itself, see How China UnionPay Cards Work Online & What Merchants Should Expect.

The four assumptions that break

Before writing any code, list the assumptions your current form makes. In most legacy checkouts, four of them cause UnionPay rejections:

  1. Fixed length. UnionPay card numbers typically run from 16 to 19 digits. A maxlength="19" attribute that counts spaces, or a regex like ^\d{16}$, rejects valid cards.
  2. Brand detection by first digit. UnionPay numbers typically start with 62 or 81. Detection code that maps only 4, 5, 3, and 6 can mislabel these numbers or drop them into a reject branch.
  3. CVV is always present. Some UnionPay cards have no card verification value. If the form requires the field, the shopper cannot complete it.
  4. Postal code is always meaningful. Shoppers outside the US, UK, and Canada often have no postal code that address verification can check. A required ZIP field blocks them or invites junk input.

A possible fifth: some processors have documented that certain UnionPay numbers do not pass the Luhn checksum. Do not treat that as a universal rule. Check your processor's current documentation, because it determines whether a Luhn failure on a 62 number should block submission.

Data flow: where validation actually happens

The flow is easier to reason about when you separate it into stages:

[Input field] -> normalize -> detect brand -> client checks -> tokenize (processor JS/SDK)
      -> your server -> processor -> network route (e.g., Discover in the US) -> issuer

The key point is that your code should block only inputs that are definitely invalid. Brand-specific rules beyond length and character checks belong to the processor and the issuer. Each extra rule you enforce is a chance to reject a card the network would have approved.

If you use a processor's hosted fields or tokenization library, most of this is handled for you. You still need to audit your own wrapper code. Custom formatting, analytics hooks, and "helpful" pre-submit checks often reintroduce the bugs.

Step-by-step implementation

Step 1: Normalize before anything else

Strip spaces and dashes, then confirm that only digits remain. Run every length check against the normalized string, not the raw input.

function normalizePan(raw: string): string | null {
  const digits = raw.replace(/[\s-]/g, "");
  return /^\d+$/.test(digits) ? digits : null;
}

If your input applies display formatting, set the HTML maxlength to the formatted length. For 19 digits grouped as 4-4-4-4-3, that is 23 characters with spaces. Don't set it to 19.

Step 2: Detect brand with ordered prefix ranges

Use a range table and match the longest prefix first. The overlap matters here: the BIN range 622126–622925 is allocated to Discover, and UnionPay can also issue cards in it. A detector that checks 62 before the narrower range, or the other way round with no clear intent, gives inconsistent labels.

type Brand = "unionpay" | "discover" | "visa" | "mastercard" | "unknown";

interface BrandRule {
  brand: Brand;
  from: number;      // inclusive prefix start
  to: number;        // inclusive prefix end
  prefixLen: number;
  lengths: number[];
}

const RULES: BrandRule[] = [
  // Discover/UnionPay overlap: label it, but accept either outcome downstream
  { brand: "discover", from: 622126, to: 622925, prefixLen: 6, lengths: [16,17,18,19] },
  { brand: "unionpay", from: 62,     to: 62,     prefixLen: 2, lengths: [16,17,18,19] },
  { brand: "unionpay", from: 81,     to: 81,     prefixLen: 2, lengths: [16,17,18,19] },
  { brand: "visa",     from: 4,      to: 4,      prefixLen: 1, lengths: [13,16,19] },
  // ...other brands
];

function detectBrand(pan: string): BrandRule | null {
  const sorted = [...RULES].sort((a, b) => b.prefixLen - a.prefixLen);
  for (const r of sorted) {
    if (pan.length < r.prefixLen) continue;
    const p = Number(pan.slice(0, r.prefixLen));
    if (p >= r.from && p <= r.to) return r;
  }
  return null;
}

The brand label should drive UI hints only: the logo, the CVV field's visibility, and grouping. It should not be the reason a card is rejected. An unknown brand with a plausible length should still go to tokenization. The processor knows the current BIN tables, and your hard-coded list will drift out of date.

Step 3: Apply Luhn as a soft check for UnionPay 

function luhnValid(pan: string): boolean {
  let sum = 0;
  let double = false;
  for (let i = pan.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    let d = pan.charCodeAt(i) - 48;
    if (double) { d *= 2; if (d > 9) d -= 9; }
    sum += d;
    double = !double;
  }
  return sum % 10 === 0;
}

function clientVerdict(pan: string): "block" | "warn" | "allow" {
  const rule = detectBrand(pan);
  if (pan.length < 12 || pan.length > 19) return "block";
  if (rule && !rule.lengths.includes(pan.length)) return "warn";
  if (!luhnValid(pan)) {
    return rule?.brand === "unionpay" ? "warn" : "block";
  }
  return "allow";
}

warn means the form shows an inline hint ("Please double-check your card number") but still lets the shopper submit. Use a hard block only for lengths no card brand uses.

Step 4: Make CVV and postal code conditional

On the client, keep the CVV field visible but optional when the detected brand is UnionPay. Add a short hint such as "Leave blank if your card has no security code."

On the server, two changes are required:

  • Your request schema must accept a missing CVC for these cards. Many teams relax the frontend and forget that a backend validator such as cvc: z.string().length(3) still rejects the request.
  • Your processor's CVC and AVS rules must not auto-decline when the result is unavailable or not checked. Check whether your risk rules treat "no result" the same as "mismatch."

Ask for a postal code only when the billing country uses one.

Decision table

Condition Client action Server action
Length outside 12–19 after normalization Block Reject
Prefix 62/81, length 16–19, Luhn passes Allow Forward
Prefix 62/81, Luhn fails Warn, allow submit Forward; let processor decide
Prefix 622126–622925 Allow; show either logo Forward; don't assert brand
UnionPay, CVV empty Allow Accept null CVC; don't auto-decline on "unavailable"
Unknown prefix, plausible length, Luhn passes Allow Forward

Compensating for weaker fraud signals

Accepting cards with no CVV and no AVS means you lose two checks that many rule sets depend on. Don't respond by blocking UnionPay outright. Move the weight to signals you still have:

  • 3-D Secure. Request authentication on UnionPay transactions where your processor supports it. For card-not-present payments, authentication is what shifts fraud liability. Treat an authenticated result as the primary trust signal.
  • Device and behavior data. Device fingerprint, account age, velocity of attempts per device, and shipping-address reuse work regardless of card brand.
  • Funding type. Many UnionPay cards are debit. If your processor returns a funding field (debit/credit/prepaid), store it. You will need it in the next section.

Write rules in terms of signal availability, for example "CVC result unavailable AND not 3DS-authenticated AND new device." Avoid rules like "brand == unionpay." Rules keyed to availability also hold up when other brands send incomplete data.

Recurring billing: check before you store

UnionPay International's product documentation lists recurring transactions and pre-authorization for credit and signature-based debit cards, but not for PIN-based debit cards. For subscription products, that leads to a concrete failure mode. The first charge succeeds, the card is saved, and the first renewal fails.

Mitigations:

  1. Record funding type and brand when the card is saved.
  2. If your processor exposes it, check whether the card supports merchant-initiated transactions before you mark the subscription as auto-renewing.
  3. Route renewal failures for these cards to a dunning flow that asks the customer to authorize payment, rather than retrying silently.

Common mistakes and how to catch them

  • Formatted maxlength too short. Catch it with an E2E test that types a 19-digit number and checks the field value.
  • Backend schema stricter than frontend. Catch it with a contract test that posts a tokenized payment with no CVC.
  • Analytics hooks that validate. Some form-tracking scripts flag "invalid" fields and block submission. Search your bundle for duplicated Luhn or regex logic.
  • Hard-coded BIN tables going stale. Log every unknown brand detection that still authorizes successfully. A rising count means your table needs updating.
  • Risk rules treating "unavailable" as "fail." Pull declines for UnionPay-detected cards and group them by CVC and AVS result code.

Test matrix

Use your processor's published UnionPay test numbers, not numbers you construct yourself. Cover at least:

Case Expected
16-digit UnionPay, CVV present Authorizes
19-digit UnionPay Field accepts all digits; authorizes
UnionPay, CVV omitted Submits; no client or server validation error
Number in Discover overlap range Accepted regardless of displayed logo
Non-US billing, no postal code Submits
Saved UnionPay debit card, renewal Handled by MIT check or dunning path

If every row passes, your checkout no longer depends on the 16-digit, 3-digit-CVV template. UnionPay shoppers will reach your processor, and the decline decisions will come from the network and issuer instead of your form code.

title: Betsson Casino Perú y Bolivia: por qué el símbolo de moneda no basta
description:
Suponemos que una persona en La Paz abre una página con el teléfono móvil. La portada habla de bolivianos; el formulario de pago tiene una cifra y el signo de dólar; la ventana de confirmación hay otro importe. No es necesario realizar una operación real para descubrir el asunto. Le bastará seguir el recorrido como si se tratara de una prueba del software apuntando la información que viene acompañada de cada cantidad.

Un directorio dirigido específicamente a los lectores de Bolivia, por ejemplo, casinosonlinebolivia.com , muestra la clase de oferta que un usuario podría hallar al comenzar a buscar. Para esta prueba me interesa algo más modesto que la posibilidad de elegir un sitio: comprobar si la moneda, el importe y la identidad del comercio que se están manejando en cada pantalla son todavía reconocibles. La página de Betsson Casino Perú sirve aquí como referencia de otro mercado. La prueba de La Paz es ficticia y no describe la caja de Betsson.

Captura uno: la promesa de la portada

Imagina una "demo" donde han puesto el texto "desde 100". La tarjeta que está al lado tiene "Bs" pero no se sabe si ese símbolo corresponde a ese número o a la cifra del otro producto. Anota exactamente lo que hay, ya que las capturas ayudan porque mañana puede que haya cambios en el diseño o en la disposición del texto. En una pantalla pequeña puede ser que la etiqueta acabe en una línea y quede como vos pensás en el diseño de otra tarjeta, por lo tanto, anotar es muy importante.

Me parece muy mala idea poner el símbolo sólo una vez y confiar en que el visitante aplique ese símbolo a los demás importes. Además, el nombre completo de la moneda en el paso 1 ocupa poco espacio. En la pantalla de confirmación, por otro lado, un código como BOB hace la diferenciación entre el boliviano y una cuantía que en la especificidad de la comunicación el comercio ha puesto en dólares americanos.

Captura dos: el importe editable

El segundo punto de control lo encontramos en el formulario. Si una persona escribe 100, la pantalla tiene que hacer ver muy claro qué quiere decir eso antes de continuar. Debes comprobar si la aplicación acepta una coma decimal y qué pasa si haces borrar y vuelves a escribir. En el caso de una prueba de la interfaz, el caso más sorprendente suele ser el error silencioso: si la aplicación interpreta un carácter de otra forma, el usuario puede ser capaz de llegar a la siguiente pantalla con un importe que no era el que pensaba.

Hay una nueva prueba fácil: vuelve al paso anterior. Si el selector cambia de moneda o si se pierde el valor, se anota. La prueba sirve para comprobar si la persona puede revisar lo que ha escrito para entender la operación antes de llegar a un botón para formalizarlo.

Cuando una página me obliga a deducir la moneda por el propio diseño o por la lengua, cierro esa parte de la prueba. Unas deducciones tan básicas no deberían depender del lector.

Captura tres: el resumen antes de confirmar

En el caso del resumen, debería ser posible leer por separado el importe inicial, cualquier tipo de cargo que se exprese y la cifra final. En el caso de que haya conversión, el lector necesita información sobre cuál es la parte que se aplica el tipo de cambio. A lo mejor la pantalla sólo incorpora una estimación o la conversión hace referencia a un tercero. En dicho caso, al defecto se le denomina hacer pasar una estimación por una cifra cerrada.

No me gusta un botón de confirmación que tapa el nombre del receptor al desplazar la página; el comercio y el total deberían estar cerca del botón. Un diseño donde el usuario tenga que subir y bajar para recordarlos separa dos datos que deberían ser de la misma unidad informativa. Un formulario puede ser rápido y estar mal resuelto.

No mezcles la revisión técnica con el marco aplicable

El hecho de que un sitio muestre bolivianos o funcione en español indica algo acerca de su interfaz, pero hay que buscar la situación de un operador particular de manera separada. Para iniciar ese tipo de consulta la Autoridad de Fiscalización del Juego de Bolivia publica la información institucional y la legislación en su página oficial, que mejor será realizarla con el nombre legal y la situación exacta de una forma distinta a la de una portada antes de hacer inferencias.

Una vez concluido, simplemente queda añadir una nota que recoja el importe total, la moneda y el nombre que aparecen en las tres pantallas, y si uno de ellos cambia sin explicación, esa sería la respuesta. Ya se puede cerrar el formulario en ese momento. La prueba ya respondía la pregunta inicial, que era ver si el valor conservaba el mismo sentido de pantalla a pantalla.
