title: Camera-to-Print Node.js Pipeline: How to Normalize Orientation and Validate Output
description:
The safest camera-to-print pipeline reads orientation metadata, chooses an explicit rotation that makes the pixels upright, converts the corrected image to the required print format, and validates the resulting dimensions before an order can proceed. In a Node.js application, I would put those operations behind one job boundary and persist the input checksum, chosen angle, target format, and output checksum. The decisive trade-off is quality versus bandwidth: inspect once and retain enough evidence to reverse a bad decision, but do not repeatedly move an original camera file across services just to discover that a converted asset has the wrong shape.

TL;DR: Treat metadata as an instruction, not proof that the pixels are already upright. Make the rotation explicit, validate after conversion, and make retries converge on the same output. A request that times out may still have completed, so recovery must never mean blindly applying another 90-degree rotation.

Infrai is a concrete fit at the remote inspection boundary because its one REST API and one key let an application switch providers without changing code. That contract covers 295 routes across 20 modules, requires no SDK, and has a self-describing public discovery surface; here, the useful result is less provider-specific recovery glue, not a claim that network processing is always preferable.

How should Node.js normalize camera image orientation metadata for print?

Conversion answers a format question; it does not, by itself, settle orientation or print geometry. A camera can store pixels in one direction and attach metadata describing how viewers should display them. The pipeline therefore has to read that metadata, map it to explicit degrees, rotate to upright when required, and only then convert. Reversing those stages makes diagnosis harder because the output can be a valid file and still be unsuitable for the intended print.

That distinction matters in a fintech media library that auto-tags receipt, identity-document, and dispute-evidence images for search. Search tags may be technically correct while a downstream case packet prints sideways. Worse, a retried job can rotate an already corrected derivative again if the worker uses the mutable output as its next input.

Success is not enough.

The record for each transformation should include the immutable source identifier or checksum, the orientation value observed, the explicit angle applied, the requested output format, and the final dimensions. Those fields are operational evidence: they let an operator distinguish a bad metadata interpretation from a wrong print preset and undo a rotation without guessing.

Derive the recovery contract before choosing a processor

Start with a stable job identifier derived by the application, not by the image vendor. The Node.js API can enqueue print_asset:{source_checksum}:{preset_version} and let the worker claim that identity exactly once at the storage boundary. If a response is lost, a retry looks up the same job and output rather than minting another transformation. Infrai's platform convention specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities, so the application must still retain its own durable job identity beyond that limit. Rate limiting belongs in the same state machine: HTTP 429 moves the job to delayed retry, honoring Retry-After where available, while permanent input errors stop the order.

The processing state is small: received, inspected, rotated, converted, validated, or rejected. Store the evidence at each transition. Do not infer validated from a 2xx conversion response, because the required check happens against the converted artifact, where a swapped width and height or an unexpected size can still be caught before fulfillment.

The request shape should come from discovery rather than an article that will go stale. Save a payload conforming to the current schema as metadata-request.json; this runnable client then performs the inspection call, uses Bearer authentication from the environment, honors Retry-After on 429, and surfaces the actual error body. It makes no guesses about undocumented fields.

import json
import os
import random
import sys
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request


def retry_delay(headers, attempt):
    value = headers.get("Retry-After")
    if value and value.isdigit():
        return float(value)
    return min(2 ** attempt, 30) + random.random()


def inspect_metadata(payload_path, attempts=5):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    with open(payload_path, "rb") as payload_file:
        payload = payload_file.read()
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/image/metadata",
        data=payload,
        method="POST",
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
    )
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=60) as response:
                return json.load(response)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Infrai returned HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error
            time.sleep(retry_delay(error.headers, attempt))
    raise RuntimeError("metadata inspection exhausted its retry budget")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        raise SystemExit("usage: python inspect_metadata.py metadata-request.json")
    print(json.dumps(inspect_metadata(sys.argv[1]), indent=2))

The next runnable local reference worker uses Pillow as the concrete processor, normalizes the common EXIF orientation values into pixels, records the applied degrees, converts to a requested print format, reopens the output, and rejects dimensions that do not match the preset. The surrounding Node.js service only needs to submit and observe the stable job; keeping image mutation in one worker prevents a retry from crossing two partially completed implementations.

import argparse
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path

from PIL import Image


ROTATION_BY_ORIENTATION = {1: 0, 3: 180, 6: 270, 8: 90}


def checksum(path: Path) -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    with path.open("rb") as stream:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: stream.read(1024 * 1024), b""):
            digest.update(chunk)
    return digest.hexdigest()


def build_print_asset(source: Path, output: Path, width: int, height: int) -> dict:
    source_hash = checksum(source)
    with Image.open(source) as image:
        orientation = int(image.getexif().get(274, 1))
        if orientation not in ROTATION_BY_ORIENTATION:
            raise ValueError(f"unsupported mirrored EXIF orientation: {orientation}")
        degrees = ROTATION_BY_ORIENTATION[orientation]
        upright = image.rotate(degrees, expand=True) if degrees else image.copy()
        if upright.mode not in ("RGB", "CMYK"):
            upright = upright.convert("RGB")
        upright.save(output, format="TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw")

    with Image.open(output) as converted:
        actual = converted.size
    if actual != (width, height):
        output.unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise ValueError(f"print dimensions {actual} do not match {(width, height)}")

    return {
        "job_id": f"print_asset:{source_hash}:v1",
        "source_sha256": source_hash,
        "orientation_seen": orientation,
        "rotation_degrees": degrees,
        "output_format": "TIFF",
        "output_dimensions": [width, height],
        "output_sha256": checksum(output),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("source", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("output", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("--width", type=int, required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--height", type=int, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    print(json.dumps(build_print_asset(args.source, args.output, args.width, args.height)))

Run it against a preset whose dimensions have already been approved for the print product:

# Execute as: python print_worker.py camera.jpg print.tiff --width 2400 --height 3000

This deliberately rejects mirrored EXIF orientations rather than pretending that rotation alone handles them. The supplied media operations take explicit rotation degrees; a mirror requires a transform that is outside this narrow contract. A production queue should classify that rejection for review, not repeatedly retry it.

Choose the boundary by failure mode, not feature count

There are at least four credible processors, and their useful differences appear at the recovery boundary rather than in a checklist of image effects.

Option Operational fit Quality/bandwidth consequence Better choice when
Sharp In-process processing close to a Node.js API Avoids an extra network transfer; the application owns native-library deployment and retry state Images can be processed near their source and the team wants direct control
ImageMagick Mature command-line or worker boundary Keeps transformation local but requires careful command construction and resource isolation The print workflow needs a broad specialist toolchain
Cloudinary Managed image transformation service Moves originals or derivatives over the network; centralizes managed transformations Delivery workflows and managed media operations matter more than a vendor-neutral contract
ImageKit Managed image optimization and delivery service Trades local processing control for a hosted media path Existing delivery and optimization requirements already align with its service
Infrai One REST boundary that can keep application code stable while the vendor behind a capability changes Reduces capability-specific integration glue, though remote processing still spends bandwidth A team values one consistent contract across media operations and wants transformation evidence at its own job boundary

Sharp and ImageMagick are not lesser fallbacks. They are often the stronger answer when originals already sit beside the worker, bandwidth is constrained, or a print specialist needs exact control over the local processing build. Cloudinary and ImageKit are reasonable managed choices when their media delivery models match the system. Infrai fits a different constraint: its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples, and its platform convention specifies idempotency for supported capabilities. The application can keep its contract while the implementation behind that capability moves.

Teams with a Node.js order service should try Infrai for the metadata/rotation/conversion boundary when they expect providers to change and want to remove per-vendor integration glue; the stable REST contract matters because retry and audit state can remain in the application. A second, concrete benefit is that one key spans a broad capability surface, so the worker does not need another vendor-specific SDK and credential lifecycle for each adjacent media operation.

There is still a limit. If the source and printer pipeline share a local network, or the print vendor mandates a tightly controlled color-management toolchain, a local Sharp or ImageMagick worker is the better design. A consistent remote API does not erase upload time, and no conversion response replaces validation against the print preset.

Make bandwidth loss visible

Quality and bandwidth should become fields in the decision, not opposing slogans. Retain the immutable original where policy permits, because reprocessing from a derivative compounds loss and makes a mistaken rotation harder to reverse. Send the original to a remote processor once per stable job identity, then retain or address the corrected result by checksum. Do not download the same result merely to learn whether the job succeeded if stored metadata can answer that question.

For auto-tagging, derive the search asset from the upright pixels. A small search derivative can reduce later transfer, while the print artifact remains tied to its validated dimensions. The tags and the print file should point back to the same source checksum and transformation record; otherwise a search result can quietly refer to a different orientation than the file included in the customer packet.

Observability needs only a few high-value facts: job identity, attempt number, processor, stage, response class, applied angle, and input/output checksums. Do not log credentials or the image itself. Alert on exhausted retries, repeated 429 responses, and validation rejection rates, but avoid interpreting one delayed attempt as a failed order.

Roll out without gambling on existing orders

Begin in shadow mode: inspect metadata and calculate the intended angle without changing the fulfillment asset. Compare the recorded decision with the current approved output, then enable mutation for one print preset. The promotion gate is mechanical: a job reaches fulfillment only after conversion and dimension validation, and a retry with the same source checksum and preset version returns the same recorded outcome.

Next, test the cases that damage recovery logic: lost responses, duplicate queue delivery, a 429 with a retry delay, orientation values for 0, 90, 180, and 270-degree outcomes, mirrored metadata, corrupt input, and a converted file with reversed dimensions. Roll back by disabling the new preset version; undo an individual bad result by replaying the immutable source with a corrected explicit angle. That is why the transformation record is part of the product, not incidental logging.

Finally, move one adjacent operation at a time. Keep the application-owned job identity and evidence schema unchanged when switching among local processing, a specialist provider, or a consistent API boundary. The processor is replaceable. The recovery contract is not.

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation
  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • Sharp documentation
  • ImageMagick documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • ImageKit documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current discovery schema before wiring the worker.

title: I replaced my budget app with a 16-page PDF
description:
Every budget app I tried wanted a subscription and a category tree before it would show me one useful number. So I built the version I actually wanted: one printable PDF, a pen, and ten minutes a week.

The Quiet Money Planner is 16 US Letter pages. It does not connect to your bank, does not ask for an email, and does not tell you what you should want. It gives you one place to write down what comes in, what goes out, and what you decide to do about the difference.

What is on the pages:

  • money in: expected and irregular income
  • fixed costs and variable costs, planned vs actual
  • the gap between in and out, with three decision prompts
  • a 31-day bill calendar
  • debt list and payoff order
  • sinking funds for known future costs
  • a weekly spending log and a no-spend week tracker
  • a subscription audit
  • a month review and a one-page year view

It is black and white with a green accent, so it photocopies cleanly. One PDF, print-ready, also readable on a tablet.

What it is not: not financial advice, not a promise that you will save a particular amount, not a bank connection, and not a course. If you have debt, tax or investment questions, talk to a qualified adviser.

I made it with reportlab, mostly because I wanted to see whether a paper tool could be simpler than the apps I kept abandoning. The numbers on the pages are yours; the workbook only asks the questions.

The Quiet Money Planner is $14: https://itfabers.lemonsqueezy.com/checkout/buy/971ae8d5-bc70-4140-9027-a66d84246380

title: Is Framer built on React? Getting React code from a Framer site
description:
Yes. Published Framer sites are rendered with React, Framer's code components are React components, and its animation library started life as Framer Motion, now published as Motion. But Framer doesn't give you the React source of your site. To get React code, you either rebuild the design in React, or convert the published site with a tool such as Deframer, which writes React 19 components in TypeScript inside a Next.js, TanStack Start, Astro, React Router or Vite project.

What you get from a conversion is real React, with a few particulars worth knowing before you plan to reuse it.

How React shows up in Framer

  • Published sites. Each page you publish is made of modules that Framer's runtime renders with React, on the server and then in the browser. That's why a converter can read a published site as components rather than as flat HTML.
  • Code components and overrides. When you write code in Framer, you write React: a code component is a React component, and an override is a function that changes a layer's props. Framer's developer documentation covers both.
  • Motion. The animation library many React developers know as Framer Motion is now published as motion, imported from motion/react (Motion). Framer's springs, transitions and gestures are built on it.

None of that means Framer is "a React app you can open". The editor stores your design in its own format, and the published output is built for Framer's runtime, the framer package, not for a React project of your own.

Your options for getting React code

Rebuild in React

Use your Framer site as the reference and build the components yourself. You get exactly the structure you want, at the cost of matching every breakpoint, variant and animation by hand.

Export components from the editor

Framer's marketplace lists plugins aimed at this, such as React Export, whose listing describes it as bridging "Framer's intuitive design environment and your production-ready React codebase" (Framer Marketplace). Plugins work on components inside your project; check what each one covers before relying on it for a whole site.

Convert the whole published site

Deframer converts the entire published site into a Next.js, TanStack Start, Astro, React Router or Vite project: every page, layout, component, style, CMS collection, form and animation. It reads only the public files the site serves, so it needs no access to your Framer account. See how to export a Framer site to Next.js for the steps.

What the React code looks like after converting

A converted project is a standard React 19 app in the framework you picked (Next.js 16 by default), where every file is .ts or .tsx (plus .astro pages in Astro). The components are the same in all four:

  • Design components in src/components/, in the designer's own folders, each with a CSS module. Their props use human names: variants are called what the designer called them, such as "Desktop" or "D / Light", not Framer's internal ids.
  • Pages as components in src/views/, wired to the framework's routes (src/app/ in Next.js, src/routes/ or src/pages/ in the others).
  • Your own code components and overrides in src/code/; marketplace code in src/vendor/.
  • Styles in src/styles/: color styles as CSS variables, shared text styles as classes, fonts as @font-face rules.

Two details matter if you want to use these components outside the project.

They're client components. Every generated module starts with "use client", because the design components use state, effects and animation. Your route files stay server components and render them.

They use the project's kit. Instead of the framer package, the code imports a small helper kit that ships in the project at src/lib/deframer/, imported as @/deframer. The kit reproduces what Framer's runtime does for published sites: variants, breakpoints, effects, routing, CMS, forms. The project's tsconfig.json also points JSX at it:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "jsxImportSource": "@/deframer",
    "paths": {
      "@/deframer": ["./src/lib/deframer"],
      "@/deframer/*": ["./src/lib/deframer/*"],
      "@/*": ["./src/*"]
    }
  }
}

That JSX runtime applies defaultProps to function components as React 18 did, which code written for Framer relies on, and passes DOM elements only the props they can render.

Reusing components in another React app

The simplest path is to keep working in the converted project and build new features there, since it's an ordinary React app. If you do want to move a component into another codebase, bring what it depends on:

  1. the component's .tsx file and its .module.css;
  2. the components it imports, and their CSS modules;
  3. the styles it uses from src/styles/ (color tokens, text styles, fonts);
  4. the kit, src/lib/deframer/, plus the @/deframer path alias and jsxImportSource setting in your tsconfig.json.

Then render the component inside a client boundary and check it at each breakpoint. Deframer's terms let you use, change and distribute the kit as part of the project and its derivatives; read the terms for the exact wording.

For a component you'll maintain long-term, it can be cleaner to treat the converted version as the reference and rewrite it in your app's own conventions. Framer code components and overrides in a Next.js project covers the code you wrote in Framer, and what you get in a converted Next.js project tours every folder.

Types and strictness

Framer's editor never type-checks code components, so code you wrote there can contain real type errors. A project that contains such code builds with typescript: { ignoreBuildErrors: true } in next.config.ts, with a comment saying why. npx tsc --noEmit still lists the errors, so you can fix them file by file and then remove the setting. Generated components get explicit prop and ref types where TypeScript can't infer them.

Cost and ownership

Converting is free; downloading a converted project uses one credit: $10 for one, $25 for five or $100 for thirty, on the pricing page. You own the converted code of your own site. Deframer is an independent tool, not affiliated with Framer, and gives the code only of sites you own or have the owner's permission to download.

FAQ

Is Framer made with React?

Yes. Published Framer sites are rendered with React, code components are React components, and Framer's animations build on the library now called Motion. The editor itself stores designs in Framer's own format.

Can I export React code from Framer?

Not natively. Marketplace plugins can export some components, and Deframer converts a whole published site into a Next.js, TanStack Start, Astro, React Router or Vite project with React 19 components in TypeScript (Framer to React).

Is Framer Motion the same as Framer?

No. Framer is the website builder. Framer Motion was its open-source animation library for React and is now published as motion, imported from motion/react. You can use it in any React project, and converted Framer sites use it for their animations.

Can I use converted Framer components in my existing Next.js app?

Yes, if you bring their dependencies: the CSS modules, the styles they use and the project's @/deframer kit with its tsconfig settings. Building inside the converted project is simpler, and if your app uses Next.js, convert to Next.js so the routes match.

Do converted components need the Framer runtime?

No. The project contains no Framer runtime. A small, readable helper kit in src/lib/deframer/ replaces it, and you can read and change it like the rest of your code. See the FAQ.

Originally published on the Deframer blog. Deframer converts a published Framer site into Next.js, Astro, React Router, TanStack Start, Vite, Nuxt or static HTML code.

title: Agentic induction of common data elements and information extraction from sarcoma case report abstracts
description:
arXiv:2611.18506v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Common data elements (CDEs) support clinical data comparability but are usually defined manually. We investigated whether large language model agents could derive a CDE schema from sarcoma case report abstracts and apply it at scale. An agent proposed 72,909 candidate CDEs from 24,588 PubMed abstracts; agentic consolidation yielded 1,570 CDEs. We retained 53 supported by at least 50 abstracts and attempted evidence-linked extraction across the corpus. Processing succeeded for all retained CDEs in 79.2% of abstracts, including responses indicating non-mention. Two human reviewers approved 83.0% of retained CDEs for relevance, 67.9% for clarity, and 56.6% for correctness. In 100 sampled abstracts, exact agreement with the value extracted by the LLM was 94.9% among 1,116 pairs with a non-empty answer (abstract-level bootstrap 95% CI, 93.0-96.4%). Errors concentrated in anatomical and temporal fields. These findings support agent-assisted schema drafting followed by expert curation before large-scale extraction.

title: Node.js Multipart ZIP Exports with 2-Step Retention and Signed Downloads
description:
Short answer: for a large customer-support ZIP export, have a Node.js worker use multipart object storage, explicitly complete the upload, and issue a short-lived signed download link only after completion. Keep the document's deletion deadline in durable job data. Link expiry controls access; it does not prove deletion.

For teams that value a replaceable HTTP boundary, Infrai is a reasonable adapter candidate for this job. Its public discovery endpoint exposes the request schema, response schema, billing data, and runnable examples without requiring a key. That makes the first integration step unusually concrete: inspect the contract, generate a thin adapter, then keep vendor details out of the export worker.

The second advantage operates at a different level. Infrai's discovery surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. A support platform that later connects its export worker to scheduling or observability can keep one credential and one bill instead of adding another set for each capability. The storage adapter still needs to remain narrow. That's what preserves the option to move.

How should a Node.js worker upload a large ZIP export and return a signed download link?

Think in two timelines. The support case might carry delete_after = 2026-09-16T12:00:00Z, while the download link should live only long enough for an authorized agent to retrieve the archive. These controls answer different questions. The deadline says when the signed documents must cease to exist. The link lifetime says how long one access grant remains usable.

Different clocks.

The worker assigns every attempt a unique key such as support-exports/case-1842/run-7f3c.zip, creates a multipart upload, and durably records its upload ID. It uploads each ZIP chunk and stores the returned part identifier. Only after every part is present does it explicitly complete the upload. If the job is cancelled, the worker explicitly aborts it. Unfinished parts don't disappear under an hourly lifecycle rule: lifecycle has a one-day minimum, and multipart fragments aren't cleaned automatically.

Keep those states boring.

The frontend never owns upload state. It receives a short-lived presigned GET URL after completion, and it must not attach the Infrai authorization header when following that URL. A separate deletion worker reads delete_after, removes the object at the deadline, and records the outcome in the application's audit trail. Use a queue or database lock around that transition because strict If-Match conditional writes aren't available. Unique object keys also stop two concurrent export jobs from overwriting the same archive.

Only then.

Here is a copyable contract check for the adapter. It calls the public discovery endpoint with a complete URL and an explicit method, verifies the exact operation the worker intends to use, and leaves request fields to the returned JSON Schema rather than freezing guessed fields into application code.

type Discovery = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
  params: unknown;
};

async function loadMultipartCreateContract(): Promise<Discovery> {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.multipart.create",
    { method: "GET" },
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery request failed with ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
  }

  const contract = (await response.json()) as Discovery;
  if (
    contract.method !== "POST" ||
    contract.path !== "/v1/storage/multipart/create/{bucket}" ||
    !contract.available
  ) {
    throw new Error("Multipart create contract did not match the required adapter boundary");
  }

  return contract;
}

loadMultipartCreateContract()
  .then((contract) => console.log(JSON.stringify(contract.params, null, 2)))
  .catch((error: unknown) => {
    console.error(error);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  });

Run that check in CI when the adapter changes, then implement the adapter from the published TypeScript example. For authenticated calls, read process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY, send Authorization: Bearer <key>, set an explicit method, and inspect every response status. On 429, honor Retry-After or use exponential backoff. Writes need a stable idempotency key so a retry can't apply the same transition twice. The returned presigned upload or download URL is a separate trust boundary and receives no Infrai bearer token.

In words, the diagram is: API creates export job -> Node.js worker streams ZIP parts -> object store assembles the object -> application marks the job ready -> frontend receives signed GET URL -> deletion worker removes the object at delete_after. The job database holds intent and progress. Storage holds bytes. The signed URL carries temporary authority.

The before-and-after migration boundary

Before the adapter, vendor assumptions tend to leak everywhere: controllers construct object keys, workers know multipart calls, and UI code treats a URL expiration as document retention. A migration then touches three layers at once.

After the adapter, the application depends on a small contract: begin an upload for a unique key, write parts, complete or abort, sign a GET, and delete at a deadline. Provider-specific request shapes live behind that contract. The distinction matters because compatibility claims are cheap; a bounded interface, a discovery assertion, and stored multipart state are concrete evidence that the application can change providers without rewriting its case workflow.

Don't hide the upload ID in process memory. A worker can be restarted between parts, and another worker should be able to continue from the durable record instead of restarting a large archive. The same record should distinguish uploading, ready, deletion_due, and deleted. If an upload never reaches ready, a cleanup job aborts it explicitly. If it does reach ready, only then may the API mint a download link.

Persist it.

This is also where observability earns its keep. Count jobs by state, alert on uploads that remain unfinished beyond the worker's expected window, and track deletion deadlines that have passed without a deleted state. I'm not sure what deletion evidence your auditor will accept; that depends on policy, and the answer should determine what the deletion worker records before production rollout. A signed URL expiring is never enough evidence by itself.

Which object storage choice keeps the export worker replaceable?

There isn't one universal winner. Amazon S3 has a mature multipart and lifecycle ecosystem. Google Cloud Storage fits teams already committed to Google IAM and regional controls. Cloudflare R2 is worth considering when an S3-compatible client boundary matches the surrounding system. Infrai fits when a self-describing REST contract and one credential across backend capabilities remove more friction than a provider-specific SDK would.

Option Fit for this support-export flow Migration and retention trade-off
Amazon S3 Multipart upload, signed access, and specialist lifecycle controls Strong choice when AWS IAM, object lock, versioning, or replication must be first-class
Google Cloud Storage Resumable transfer and signed URL patterns in the Google ecosystem Strong choice when Google IAM and regional policy already define the application boundary
Cloudflare R2 Familiar S3-compatible tooling for multipart object workflows Check required regions, governance controls, and replication before standardizing
Infrai storage Multipart completion and presigned GET behind a self-describing REST surface Thin adapter is easy to inspect; specialist immutability and cross-region controls are outside its fit

My recommendation is specific: teams building replaceable Node.js support-export workers should try Infrai for the storage adapter when public discovery and runnable TypeScript examples matter more than adopting another SDK. The supporting reason is operational: the same credential spans a broad backend surface, reducing key rotation and billing reconciliation if the workflow later adds adjacent capabilities. Neither point eliminates the need for an application-owned retention state machine.

What are the limits of signed links and lifecycle deletion?

A signed URL is temporary access, not retention enforcement. It can expire while the ZIP remains stored. Conversely, deleting the object ends future retrieval even if a previously issued URL has time remaining. Design, log, and alert on those controls separately.

The catch is that Infrai storage has no object versioning or object lock, so it isn't suitable for a financial-grade WORM archive or any workflow that must recover an overwritten object. It also lacks automatic cross-region replication and cross-cloud bulk migration tooling. Stick with a specialist such as Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage when immutable retention, automatic geographic copies, or provider-native compliance controls are requirements.

There are narrower boundaries too. Public-read ACLs aren't supported, so this pattern isn't for permanent public links, image hosting, or static websites. Browser-direct upload is a poor fit when the team must self-configure CORS. Hour-level storage expiry doesn't fit the one-day lifecycle minimum, and server-side metadata search isn't available beyond prefix-based listing. For signed customer documents, those constraints push control back where it belongs — into the worker, queue, and job database.

The final decision rule is crisp. Choose the self-describing adapter when exports are private, the application can own deletion scheduling, and reversible integration is the priority. Choose specialist storage when the storage layer itself must enforce immutability, replication, or richer governance.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the runnable multipart guide at https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/large-zip-export-multipart-upload-signed-download-link/ and keep the adapter small.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/objects/multipart-objects/

title: The Wasteful JOIN I Was Afraid to Write? GORM Wrote It for Me.
description:
In my last article I wrote an unnecessary JOIN by hand to see what it cost. That test came from a worry: after a long time of letting GORM write my SQL, I didn't trust myself to write it efficiently.

I ended that article with a promise to check the other half of the worry, which was my assumption that GORM's own SQL is efficient.

So I took the same task and wrote it three ways in GORM. The version I would have reached for at work, GORM's association joins, generated the same wasteful join I had been afraid of writing myself. It also finished first in every run with default settings, which makes it easy to miss.

Limited to one CPU core, it took about twice as long as the alternatives.

The task, written three ways

The data is the same as last time: users, addresses (one per user, with a city) and orders, with 5 million rows in each. The task is also the same: fetch every order placed by a user who lives in Pune.

The GORM models:

type User struct {
    ID      int64
    Name    string
    Address Address
    Orders  []Order
}

type Address struct {
    ID     int64
    UserID int64
    City   string
}

type Order struct {
    ID        int64
    UserID    int64
    Total     float64
    CreatedAt time.Time
    User      User
}

1. Association joins. This uses GORM's own relationship handling, and it is the one I would have written by default.

db.Joins("User").
    Joins("User.Address").
    Where(`"User__Address"."city" = ?`, "Pune").
    Find(&orders)

2. A hand-written join string.

db.Joins("JOIN addresses ON addresses.user_id = orders.user_id").
    Where("addresses.city = ?", "Pune").
    Find(&orders)

3. A subquery.

sub := db.Model(&Address{}).Select("user_id").Where("city = ?", "Pune")
db.Where("user_id IN (?)", sub).Find(&orders)

The SQL GORM generated

I printed each statement with db.ToSQL, which builds the SQL without running it. The line breaks below are mine; the SQL is GORM's.

1. Association joins

SELECT "orders"."id", "orders"."user_id", "orders"."total", "orders"."created_at",
       "User"."id" AS "User__id", "User"."name" AS "User__name",
       "User__Address"."id" AS "User__Address__id",
       "User__Address"."user_id" AS "User__Address__user_id",
       "User__Address"."city" AS "User__Address__city"
FROM "orders"
LEFT JOIN "users" "User" ON "orders"."user_id" = "User"."id"
LEFT JOIN "addresses" "User__Address" ON "User"."id" = "User__Address"."user_id"
WHERE "User__Address"."city" = 'Pune'

2. Hand-written join string

SELECT "orders"."id", "orders"."user_id", "orders"."total", "orders"."created_at"
FROM "orders"
JOIN addresses ON addresses.user_id = orders.user_id
WHERE addresses.city = 'Pune'

3. Subquery

SELECT * FROM "orders"
WHERE user_id IN (SELECT "user_id" FROM "addresses" WHERE city = 'Pune')

The first statement goes from orders through users to addresses. That is the route I called wasteful in the last article, where I wrote it by hand as Query A. It also selects every column of the user and the address for each order.

The other two never mention users.

Run it yourself

Everything is in the same GitHub repository as the last article. You need Docker and nothing else, because the Go program runs in a container too.

# start PostgreSQL 16
docker compose up -d --wait db

# load 5 million users, addresses and orders
docker exec pgtest psql -U postgres -v users=5000000 -v orders=5000000 -f /setup.sql

# print GORM's SQL for each way, then its plan
docker compose run --rm gorm

# the same three statements, limited to one CPU core
docker exec pgtest psql -U postgres -f /gorm-single-core.sql

main.go prints the SQL for each of the three ways and runs it with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). That executes the query and reports the plan PostgreSQL used, the real timings and how many pages it touched.

All three return the same rows, 999,696 orders in my first set of runs. Your count will differ slightly, because orders are assigned to users at random.

Round 1: default settings

With PostgreSQL's default settings, association joins finished first in all four runs. The median was 1,478 ms, against 1,960 ms for the hand-written join and 1,985 ms for the subquery, so it looked about 25% faster.

Run 1. Association joins 2. Hand-written join 3. Subquery
1 1,573 ms 2,111 ms 2,000 ms
2 1,405 ms 1,850 ms 1,971 ms
3 1,455 ms 2,010 ms 1,891 ms
4 1,501 ms 1,910 ms 2,031 ms
Median 1,478 ms 1,960 ms 1,985 ms

If I had only timed these, I would have kept the association joins. The plan explains why that would have been a mistake:

Gather
  Workers Planned: 2
  Workers Launched: 2
  ->  Parallel Hash Join
        ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders
        ->  Parallel Hash
              ->  Parallel Hash Join
                    ->  Parallel Seq Scan on users "User"  (... rows=1666667 loops=3)

PostgreSQL ran the association-join query on three CPU cores: the main process plus two workers. The other two queries each ran on one core. It is the same effect I found in the last article, and this time GORM wrote the query.

Round 2: a single CPU core for each query

With every query limited to one core, association joins took about twice as long as the other two: between 1.9 and 2.4 times, for the same rows. I ran this round twice, the second time on a fresh load of the data.

1. Association joins 2. Hand-written join 3. Subquery
Default settings, median of 4 1,478 ms 1,960 ms 1,985 ms
Single CPU core, run 1 4,271 ms 1,817 ms 1,866 ms
Single CPU core, run 2 3,740 ms 1,921 ms 1,906 ms

The plan shows where the time went:

->  Hash Join  (... actual time=478.503..2175.753 rows=1000000 loops=1)
      Hash Cond: ("User".id = "User__Address".user_id)
      ->  Seq Scan on users "User"  (... rows=5000000 loops=1)

PostgreSQL read all 5 million users and joined them to the Pune addresses before it matched a single order. That stage was not ready until 2.0 to 2.3 seconds in. In the hand-written join, the Pune addresses were ready at about 0.3 seconds.

A busy production server may not have spare cores to hand out, so I treat the single-core figure as the more realistic one.

What the plans show, whatever the clock says

The run times moved around between rounds. The amount of work did not. BUFFERS reports how many pages each query touched, and those figures were almost identical in every run.

1. Association joins 2. Hand-written join 3. Subquery
Reads all of users Yes, 5 million rows No No
Table pages read About 102,400 70,504 70,504
Temp file pages read 63,000 to 68,500 30,760 30,760
Row width in the plan 73 bytes 30 bytes 30 bytes

Three things stand out.

  • Association joins read 45% more table pages and about twice the temp file data. The extra pages are the users table, which the result did not need for filtering.
  • Each row is about 2.4 times as wide. GORM selects the user and address columns for every order so it can fill in order.User and order.User.Address. EXPLAIN does not count the cost of sending those rows to the application or building the structs, so the real gap is larger than these timings show.
  • The hand-written join and the subquery are the same query to PostgreSQL. Their plans match line for line. PostgreSQL turned IN (SELECT ...) into the same hash join.

One more detail is worth knowing. GORM writes LEFT JOIN, but the plan shows plain hash joins. The WHERE clause filters on the address, which discards any order without a matching address, so PostgreSQL treats both joins as inner joins.

When association joins are the right choice

Association joins are not wrong. They do more because they return more: every order comes back with its user and that user's address already filled in.

If an endpoint needs to show the customer's name and city next to each order, that extra work buys something, and one joined query is a reasonable way to get it.

The problem is using them only to filter. I wanted orders, I needed the city just to decide which orders, and the query paid for 5 million user rows and extra columns on every order that nothing used.

What I do differently now

In the last article I was afraid that raw SQL would let me write a wasteful join without noticing. The same join was already in my GORM code, written by the feature I trusted most.

Three habits came out of this.

  • Filter with a subquery or a hand-written join. If I only need a related table to decide which rows to return, I no longer use association joins for it.
  • Load related data on purpose. If I need a couple of fields from a related table, I select those fields, instead of letting GORM load whole nested structs by default.
  • Read the SQL before shipping. For list and reporting endpoints I print the statement with ToSQL or Debug() and run it through EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). The page counts tell me more than the run time does.

Limits of this test

  • It ran on one machine, with PostgreSQL 16 in Docker Desktop and the default configuration.
  • The single-core figures are from two runs, the second on a fresh load of the data. The default-settings figures are medians of four runs.
  • The timings come from EXPLAIN ANALYZE, so they cover the database only. They leave out sending rows to the application and GORM building the structs.
  • It covers one query shape on one dataset, with about one order per user. Other data could behave differently.
  • I tested three ways of writing the query. GORM has others, such as Preload and InnerJoins, that I have not measured.
  • The GORM version is whatever go mod tidy fetched on the day. The exact version is in go.mod in the repository.

title: Fraud Detection with Feast and MongoDB
description:
When building ML systems, you may need the exact same feature definitions, such as a user's recent transaction patterns computed in two very different contexts. At training time, you need historical features assembled correctly, without accidentally mixing past and future data (point-in-time correctness). At serving time, when a transaction happens, you need the current value of those same features computed and returned in milliseconds, not seconds.

Most teams achieve this by running three separate databases: the application's primary database, a dedicated low-latency online store for serving, and a separate data warehouse for offline training retrieval. Feast, combined with MongoDB, solves this by defining features once and serving them consistently in both contexts. MongoDB can act as both Feast’s online and offline store, removing the need for separate systems.

Feast is the leading open-source feature store for machine learning, which MongoDB supports as an online and offline store. This enables machine learning teams to serve features at low latency and generate point-in-time-correct training datasets directly against MongoDB.

This tutorial only configures MongoDB as Feast's online store; the offline store uses a local Parquet file (offline_store: type: file in feature_store.yaml). MongoDB can also serve as Feast's offline store to fully realize the single-cluster, ETL-free architecture described above.

In this tutorial, we will build a fraud detection pipeline using MongoDB as Feast’s online store with the Django MongoDB Backend.
Specifically, you will learn:

  • How to use the Django MongoDB backend to model and persist transactions in MongoDB
  • How to use Feast as a feature store, with a local Parquet file as the offline store
  • How to use MongoDB as Feast's online store for low-latency lookups
  • How to build a statistical model (a z-score on transaction amount) to identify potentially fraudulent transactions in real time

In the end, you will use user_id to fetch a user's most recent materialized features from MongoDB (online store) using Feast and return whether that transaction looks fraudulent or not.

There are two ways to follow this tutorial.

  • Option A: Clone the GitHub repo containing the finished code from this tutorial, set it up using the repo's README, and explore it on your own.
  • Option B: Start the project from scratch by following the steps below.

Outline

  • Prerequisites
  • Create a project folder and virtual environment
  • Create the Django project and Django app
  • Generate synthetic financial data
  • Define the Transaction model
  • Load the synthetic data into MongoDB
  • Scaffold the feature repository with Feast
  • Define the Transaction features
  • Configure Feast to use MongoDB
  • Train a fraud model
  • Materialize features into MongoDB
  • View the materialized features in MongoDB Atlas
  • Produce real-time predictions
  • Conclusion and next steps

Prerequisites

Before starting, make sure you have:

  • Python 3.12+
  • A MongoDB Atlas cluster; a local Atlas deployment (connection string mongodb://localhost:27017/?directConnection=true) also works.

Once these prerequisites are complete, the next step is to create your project folder.

Create a project and virtual environment

Create an empty folder for your project and cd into it.

mkdir fraud_detection
cd fraud_detection

From the project root, create a virtual environment:

python3 -m venv .venv

Then activate it.

On macOS/Linux:

Run source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows:

Run .venv\Scripts\activate

Install dependencies

Create a requirements.txt file at the root of the project with the following contents:

# requirements.txt
django-mongodb-backend==6.0.4
python-dotenv==1.2.4
feast==0.67.0
pymongo==4.19.0
pandas==2.3.3
numpy==2.5.4
pyarrow==26.0.0

django-mongodb-backend 6.0.x installs Django 6.0, which matches the 6.0.x project template used in the next step.

Then install everything:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Create Django Project and Django App

From your project's root directory, run the following command to create a new Django project from the MongoDB project template. The . after the project name tells Django to create the project in the current directory instead of a new nested folder.

django-admin startproject fraud_detection . --template https://github.com/mongodb-labs/django-mongodb-project/archive/refs/heads/6.0.x.zip

The template adds a README.md, but it doesn’t overwrite your requirements.txt.

Create the transactions app 

python manage.py startapp transactions

Register the app in fraud_detection/settings.py by adding transactions to the end of the existing INSTALLED_APPS list. The template already has the other entries:

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'fraud_detection.apps.MongoAdminConfig',
    'fraud_detection.apps.MongoAuthConfig',
    'fraud_detection.apps.MongoContentTypesConfig',
    'django.contrib.sessions',
    'django.contrib.messages',
    'django.contrib.staticfiles',
    'django_mongodb_backend',
    'transactions',
]

Configure environment variables

Create a .gitignore file at the root of the project so that secrets and generated files are not added when you push.

#.gitignore
.env
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
data/transactions.parquet
training/model_params.json
feature_repo/feature_repo/data/registry.db

Then create a .env file at the root of the project with your own values.

# .env
SECRET_KEY='<your-secret-key>'
MONGODB_URI='mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<cluster>.mongodb.net/?retryWrites=true&w=majority'
DB_NAME='fraud_detection'

NB: Keep the single quotes.

For SECRET_KEY, copy the value Django generated in settings.py when you ran startproject, or generate a new one:

python -c "from django.core.management.utils import get_random_secret_key; print(get_random_secret_key())"

Django hardcodes the secret key in settings.py by default, but we move it into .env to keep it out of version control, since it's used to sign session cookies, CSRF tokens, and other security-sensitive data.

Now, update fraud_detection/settings.py to read the secret key and the database configuration from the environment instead of hardcoding them. Make the following changes and leave the rest of the file as is.

At the top of the file, add the imports and the load_dotenv() call:

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

Replace the hardcoded SECRET_KEY = '...' line with:

SECRET_KEY = os.getenv('SECRET_KEY')

In the existing DATABASES setting, replace the HOST and NAME values:

DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': 'django_mongodb_backend',
        'HOST': os.getenv("MONGODB_URI"),
        'NAME': os.getenv("DB_NAME"),
    },
}

Generate synthetic financial data

Since we don't have a real transaction feed, we'll generate a small synthetic dataset with a handful of users, categories, and locations, plus a small percentage of inflated-amount "fraudulent" transactions.

First, create a data/ directory at the root of the project (alongside manage.py) to hold this script and the generated file:

mkdir data

Then create data/generate_transactions.py with the following contents:

"""Generates random transactions data for the Feast + MongoDB tutorial."""

from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

TRANSACTIONS_PARQUET_FILE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "transactions.parquet"

random_generator = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
N, FRAUD_RATE = 50, 0.02

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "user_id": random_generator.integers(1, 9, N),
    "transaction_id": [f"txn_{i:04d}" for i in range(N)],
    "amount": random_generator.lognormal(mean=3.5, sigma=0.6, size=N).round(2),
    "category": random_generator.choice(["food", "utilities", "entertainment", "travel", "shopping"], size=N),
    "location": random_generator.choice(["Accra", "Lagos", "New York", "London", "Paris"], size=N),
    # Timezone-aware: Django runs with USE_TZ = True, and Feast expects UTC.
    "event_timestamp": pd.Timestamp("2026-07-01", tz="UTC") + pd.to_timedelta(random_generator.integers(0, 30 * 24 * 60, N), unit="m"),
}).sort_values("event_timestamp").reset_index(drop=True)

# Choose a fraud row from each user's most recent transactions
latest_per_user = df.groupby("user_id").tail(1)
fraud_indices = latest_per_user.sample(n=max(1, round(N * FRAUD_RATE)), random_state=42).index
df["is_fraudulent"] = False
df.loc[fraud_indices, "is_fraudulent"] = True
# Inflate the amount for fraudulent transactions
df.loc[fraud_indices, "amount"] *= random_generator.uniform(5, 10, len(fraud_indices))   

df["created_timestamp"] = df["event_timestamp"]

df.to_parquet(TRANSACTIONS_PARQUET_FILE, index=False)
print(f"Wrote {len(df)} transactions to parquet file, {df['is_fraudulent'].sum()} of which are fraudulent.")

Feast requires an event_timestamp column (when the fact occurred) and, since we're using a FileSource, a created_timestamp column (when the row was written) for tie-breaking. The timestamps are timezone-aware (UTC) because Django runs with USE_TZ = True and Feast works in UTC.

Run the script from the project root:

python data/generate_transactions.py

The expected output should be Wrote 50 transactions to parquet file, 1 of which are fraudulent.

This writes data/transactions.parquet, which is used both to load data into MongoDB via the Django ORM and as Feast's offline store for training.

Define the Transaction model

transactions/models.py defines the Django model that maps to the transactions collection in MongoDB:

from django.db import models

class Transaction(models.Model):
    transaction_id = models.CharField(max_length=64, unique=True)
    user_id = models.IntegerField()
    amount = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)
    category = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    location = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    timestamp = models.DateTimeField()
    is_fraudulent = models.BooleanField(default=False)

    class Meta:
        db_table = 'transactions'
        indexes = [
            models.Index(fields=['user_id']),
            models.Index(fields=['timestamp']),
        ]

    def __str__(self):
        return f"Transaction {self.transaction_id} - Amount: {self.amount} - Fraudulent: {self.is_fraudulent}"

user_id is an IntegerField so that it matches the Feast entity's INT64 type and the <int:user_id> URL parameter we will define later. It is also indexed because the app looks up transactions by user.

Generate and run the migration 

python manage.py makemigrations transactions
python manage.py migrate

Load the synthetic data into MongoDB

Create the folders for the custom management command:

mkdir -p transactions/management/commands
touch transactions/management/__init__.py
touch transactions/management/commands/__init__.py

transactions/management/commands/load_transactions.py is a custom management command that reads data/transactions.parquet and bulk-inserts the rows into MongoDB through the Django ORM:

from decimal import Decimal

import pandas as pd
from django.conf import settings
from django.core.management.base import BaseCommand
from transactions.models import Transaction

class Command(BaseCommand):
    help = "Loading transaction data from data/transactions.parquet into the database via Django ORM"

    def add_arguments(self, parser):
        parser.add_argument(
            "--path",
            default=settings.BASE_DIR/"data"/"transactions.parquet",
            help="Path to the Parquet file containing transaction data",
        )

    def handle(self, *args, **options):
        df = pd.read_parquet(options["path"])
        transactions = [
            Transaction(
                user_id=int(row["user_id"]),
                transaction_id=row["transaction_id"],
                amount=Decimal(f"{row['amount']:.2f}"),
                category=row["category"],
                location=row["location"],
                timestamp=row["event_timestamp"],
        is_fraudulent=bool(row["is_fraudulent"]),
            )
            for row in df.to_dict("records")
        ]

        Transaction.objects.all().delete()
        Transaction.objects.bulk_create(transactions)

        self.stdout.write(
            self.style.SUCCESS(
                f" Loaded {len(transactions)} transactions into MDB database."
            )
        )

A few details to note:

  • amount is converted to a Decimal with two decimal places to match the DecimalField.
  • Existing transactions are deleted before inserting, so you can re-run the command after regenerating the data without hitting the unique constraint on transaction_id.
  • The default --path is built from settings.BASE_DIR so that the command will find the Parquet file no matter which directory you run it from.

Then run it:

python manage.py load_transactions

Scaffold the feature repository with Feast

Before we go ahead to define features, we need to initialize a Feast project. From the root of your directory, run:

feast init feature_repo

This generates a demo Feast project in feature_repo/feature_repo/. Alongside the feature_store.yaml configuration file, it includes three things you won't need for this tutorial:

  • feature_definitions.py: example feature definitions for the demo dataset
  • test_workflow.py: a script that runs through the demo end to end
  • data/driver_stats.parquet and data/driver_quality_labels.parquet: sample data for the demo

Delete these files, but keep the data/ folder, since Feast stores its registry there. You'll replace the demo definitions with your own features.py (below) and update feature_store.yaml as shown in "Configure Feast to use MongoDB".
feast init also creates feature_repo/README.md and feature_repo/.gitignore. You can delete them or leave them; they don’t affect anything.

Define the Transaction features

Feast needs its own definitions of the entity and features, independent of the Django model, because it reads directly from the Parquet file rather than through the Django ORM. These live in feature_repo/feature_repo/features.py:

from datetime import timedelta
from pathlib import Path
from feast import Entity, FeatureView, Field, FileSource
from feast.types import Float32, String
from feast.value_type import ValueType

# An entity is the key used to look up features; here, it is the user_id
user = Entity(
    name="user_id",
    join_keys=["user_id"],
    value_type=ValueType.INT64,
)

# Feast reads the Parquet file directly; it does not go through the Django ORM.
TRANSACTIONS_PARQUET_FILE = (
    Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data" / "transactions.parquet"
)

transaction_source = FileSource(
    name="transaction_source",
    path=str(TRANSACTIONS_PARQUET_FILE),
    timestamp_field="event_timestamp",
    created_timestamp_column="created_timestamp",
)

transaction_features = FeatureView(
    name="transaction_features",
    entities=[user],
    ttl=timedelta(days=365),
    schema=[
        Field(name="amount", dtype=Float32),
        Field(name="category", dtype=String),
        Field(name="location", dtype=String),
    ],
    source=transaction_source,
)
  • user is the entity: the key (user_id) that features are looked up by.
  • transaction_source points Feast to the generated Parquet file. timestamp_field tells Feast which column holds the event time used for point-in-time joins, and created_timestamp_column breaks ties when two rows share the same event time.
  • transaction_features is the feature view that ties the entity, the source, and the individual fields (amount, category, location) together.

Configure Feast to use MongoDB

Feast's project configuration lives in feature_repo/feature_repo/feature_store.yaml:

project: fraud_detection
registry: data/registry.db
provider: local

offline_store:
  type: file

online_store:
  type: mongodb
  connection_string: ${MONGODB_URI}
  database_name: ${DB_NAME}

entity_key_serialization_version: 3
  • offline_store.type: file tells Feast to use the local Parquet file for historical/training queries.
  • online_store.type: mongodb tells Feast to use MongoDB for low-latency online lookups, using the same MONGODB_URI connection string and DB_NAME database as Django.

Feast substitutes ${MONGODB_URI} and ${DB_NAME} from the process environment. Unlike Django, the feast CLI does not read your .env file (it never imports settings.py), so export the variables into your shell first.

On macOS/Linux, from the project root:

set -a; source .env; set +a

If you skip this, Feast won’t raise an error about missing variables. It leaves ${MONGODB_URI} and ${DB_NAME} as literal text, and the next command fails with a confusing error such as pymongo.errors.InvalidName: database names cannot contain the character '$'.

On Windows, set them in your shell instead, for example $env:MONGODB_URI="..." and $env:DB_NAME="..." in PowerShell. Run all of the following feast and Python commands from this same shell.

From the project root, register the entity and feature view with Feast:

cd feature_repo/feature_repo
feast apply

This creates or updates data/registry.db with your entity and feature view definitions.

Train a fraud model

Return to the root after feast apply.

cd ../..

From the project root, create a training/ folder to contain the training script and the model parameters it produces:

mkdir training

training/train_model.py pulls point-in-time-correct historical features from Feast's offline store and derives the parameters for a simple z-score model:

A z-score measures how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean. Transaction amounts are right-skewed (a few large purchases, many small ones), so we compute the z-score on log(amount), which is roughly normally distributed. The mean and standard deviation are fit on legitimate transactions only and transactions with log-amounts more than 2 standard deviations above the mean are flagged as potentially fraudulent.

For each row in entity_df, get_historical_features() looks backward from that row's timestamp and finds the most recent feature value available at that point in time, which is what makes the result point-in-time-correct.

If no feature value exists within the ttl window before a given timestamp, that row comes back with nulls instead of a stale, overly-old value. Shortening the ttl makes the lookup stricter, as only recent data will be added; lengthening it allows older values to still be considered valid.

"""
Retrieves point-in-time training data from Feast’s offline store, then
“trains” a z-score model on it.
The model parameters are written to training/model_params.json so that the
Django view reads them instead of having to copy them in by hand.
"""
import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from feast import FeatureStore

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
TRANSACTIONS_PARQUET_FILE = BASE_DIR / "data" / "transactions.parquet"
PARAMS_PATH = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "model_params.json"
store = FeatureStore(repo_path=str(BASE_DIR / "feature_repo" / "feature_repo"))
transactions_df = pd.read_parquet(TRANSACTIONS_PARQUET_FILE)


# Extra entity_df columns (here, the is_fraudulent label) are passed through to the result unchanged.
entity_df = transactions_df[["user_id", "event_timestamp", "is_fraudulent"]].copy()
training_df = store.get_historical_features(
    entity_df=entity_df,
    features=[
        "transaction_features:amount",
        "transaction_features:category",
        "transaction_features:location",
    ],
).to_df()
print(training_df.head(10))
print(f"\nPulled {len(training_df)} rows of training data.")

# --- The “model”: mean and standard deviation of log(amount) ---
# Amounts are right-skewed (lognormal), so the z-score is computed on 
# log(amount), which is roughly normal. The baseline is fit on legitimate
# transactions only, so fraud doesn’t inflate its own threshold.
# A transaction is flagged if its log-amount is more than 2 standard
# deviations ABOVE the mean (one-sided: unusually small amounts aren’t flagged).


legit_log_amounts = np.log(training_df.loc[~training_df["is_fraudulent"], "amount"])
TRAIN_MEAN_LOG_AMOUNT = float(legit_log_amounts.mean())
TRAIN_STD_LOG_AMOUNT = float(legit_log_amounts.std())
PARAMS_PATH.write_text(
    json.dumps(
        {
            "mean_log_amount": TRAIN_MEAN_LOG_AMOUNT,
            "std_log_amount": TRAIN_STD_LOG_AMOUNT,
            "z_score_threshold": 2.0,
        },
        indent=2,
    )
    + "\n"
)
print(f"\nFit on {len(legit_log_amounts)} legitimate transactions.")
print("Trained model parameters:")
print(f"TRAIN_MEAN_LOG_AMOUNT = {TRAIN_MEAN_LOG_AMOUNT}")
print(f"TRAIN_STD_LOG_AMOUNT = {TRAIN_STD_LOG_AMOUNT}")
print(f"\nWrote parameters to {PARAMS_PATH}")

From the project root, run:

python training/train_model.py

With the seeded data, you should see Fit on 49 legitimate transactions. , TRAIN_MEAN_LOG_AMOUNT = 3.5326…, and TRAIN_STD_LOG_AMOUNT = 0.4687….
The script writes these values to training/model_params.json, which the Django view reads at request time. training/model_params.json is already in your .gitignore; it's regenerated each time you train.

Materialize features into MongoDB

"Materializing" pushes the latest feature values for each entity from the offline store to the online store (MongoDB), which is what serves low-latency lookups at request time.

From the project root, run:

cd feature_repo/feature_repo
feast materialize 2020-01-01T00:00:00 2026-09-01T00:00:00

The end date must be after the most recent event_timestamp in your data (30 July 2026 for seeded data).
You should see output similar to the following along with a progress bar:

Materializing 1 feature view from 2020-01-01 00:00:00+00:00 to 2026-09-01 00:00:00+00:00 into the mongodb online store.

transaction_features:

You can confirm the features landed in MongoDB by using Feast to read them back.

Create feature_repo/feature_repo/test_online_features.py:

"""
Confirms Feast can read materialized features back out of MongoDB
via get_online_features()
"""

from pathlib import Path

from feast import FeatureStore


def main():
    store = FeatureStore(repo_path=str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent))

    entity_rows = [{"user_id": 2}]

    online_features = store.get_online_features(
        features=[
            "transaction_features:amount",
            "transaction_features:category",
            "transaction_features:location",
        ],
        entity_rows=entity_rows,
    ).to_dict()

    print(online_features)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The work is wrapped in main() behind an if __name__ == "__main__": guard because feast apply imports every Python file in the feature repository. Without the guard, this script would query the online store every time you run feast apply.

You are still in feature_repo/feature_repo, so run the following command and return to the project root:

python test_online_features.py
cd ../..

You should see something like this:
{'user_id': [2], 'amount': [28.079999923706055], 'category': ['entertainment'], 'location': ['London']}

The online store holds each entity's latest value only, not full history, so a flagged transaction won't necessarily surface if newer transactions have since materialized over it. Re-run feast materialize whenever new transactions are generated and loaded.

View the materialized features in MongoDB Atlas

After connecting to your MongoDB Atlas cluster, open your cluster and browse collections.
Select the database you set as DB_NAME in .env (the same database used by Django and by database_name in feature_store.yaml).
Open the fraud_detection_latest collection. Feast names it <project>_latest, and its MongoDB online store keeps one document per entity holding only the most recent materialized feature values.

Materialized features in the fraud_detection_latest collection, one document per user. User 6’s document holds the fraudulent amount (143.044…).

Produce real-time predictions

Back in the Django app, transactions/feast_client.py wraps the Feast online lookup:

from django.conf import settings
from feast import FeatureStore

FEATURE_REPO_PATH = settings.BASE_DIR / "feature_repo" / "feature_repo"
_store = FeatureStore(repo_path=str(FEATURE_REPO_PATH))


def get_latest_transaction_features(user_id: int) -> dict:
    """
    Looks up the most recent materialized transaction features for a
    user_id from MongoDB (the online store) via Feast.
    """
    result = _store.get_online_features(
        features=[
            "transaction_features:amount",
            "transaction_features:category",
            "transaction_features:location",
        ],
        entity_rows=[{"user_id": user_id}],
    ).to_dict()

    return {key: values[0] for key, values in result.items()}

transactions/views.py uses it to apply the z-score model trained in "Train a fraud model" section and flag potentially fraudulent transactions. It reads the model parameters from training/model_params.json:

import json
import math

from django.conf import settings
from django.http import JsonResponse

from transactions.feast_client import get_latest_transaction_features

PARAMS_PATH = settings.BASE_DIR / "training" / "model_params.json"
def _load_model_params():
    with open(PARAMS_PATH) as f:
        return json.load(f)


def score_transaction(request, user_id: int):
    try:
        params = _load_model_params()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return JsonResponse(
            {"error": "Model parameters not found. Run training/train_model.py first."},
            status=503,
        )


    features = get_latest_transaction_features(user_id)
    amount = features.get("amount")
    if amount is None:
        return JsonResponse(
            {"error": f"No features found for user_id {user_id}"}, status=404
        )


    z_score = (math.log(amount) - params["mean_log_amount"]) / params["std_log_amount"]
    is_potentially_fraudulent = z_score > params["z_score_threshold"]
    return JsonResponse({
        "user_id": user_id,
        "amount": amount,
        "category": features.get("category"),
        "location": features.get("location"),
        "z_score": round(z_score, 3),
        "is_potentially_fraudulent": is_potentially_fraudulent,
    })

From the project root, start the development server:

python manage.py runserver

In a second terminal, request a score for a given user:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/score/2/

You should get a JSON response like:

{
  "user_id": 2,
  "amount": 28.079999923706055,
  "category": "entertainment",
  "location": "London",
  "z_score": -0.422,
  "is_potentially_fraudulent": false
}

User 2’s latest transaction is normal. The seeded data’s fraudulent transaction is user 6’s latest so we can request that by running:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/score/6/

Results:

{
  "user_id": 6,
  "amount": 143.04425048828125,
  "category": "utilities",
  "location": "London",
  "z_score": 3.052,
  "is_potentially_fraudulent": true
}

The online store holds only each user’s latest values, so an older fraudulent transaction would be overwritten by newer ones. The generator deliberately makes the fraud a user’s most recent transaction so you can see a positive result.

NB: the z-score is a baseline; it uses one baseline for all users rather than each user’s spending pattern and it’s evaluated in the same data it was trained on with no test set.

Conclusion and next steps

Great job on making it to this point 🎉. You've built an end-to-end pipeline that generates transaction data, stores it in MongoDB through Django, defines and registers features with Feast, trains a statistical model on historical features, materializes the latest feature values into MongoDB as an online store, and serves real-time fraud scores from a Django view.

From here, you could explore:

  • Replace the z-score model with a trained scikit-learn classifier (pip install scikit-learn).
  • Add more features such as the average spend per user to transaction_features.
  • Schedule feast materialize-incremental to run on a cron job so the online store stays up to date as new transactions are loaded.
  • Add authentication and input validation to the score_transaction endpoint.

References

  • Feast-Powered AI Agent
  • MongoDB Support in Feast Framework
  • Integrate MongoDB with Feast
  • Get Started with Django MongoDB Backend

title: How to make a pivot table in Excel in five steps (no formulas)
description:
To make a pivot table in Excel, click any cell inside your data, open Insert, choose PivotTable, and drag one text field into Rows and one number field into Values. The summary appears in seconds, and you never write a formula to get it.

When a pivot misbehaves, the source data is almost always the culprit. The steps below assume one header row, no blank rows and one kind of value per column. Menu names come from the Microsoft 365 desktop app on Windows, so expect small differences in other versions. Work on a copy of the workbook while you learn, so a misplaced drag never touches the original file.

Clean the source before you click anything

A pivot wants a database-style layout. Every column needs a unique, non-blank header, every row is one record, and every column holds one type of value. Merged cells are the classic trap. A region typed once with empty cells beneath it breaks the grouping, and dollar amounts pasted from an email often arrive as text, which Excel quietly skips in a sum.

Next, select the data and press Ctrl+T to turn it into an Excel Table. A pivot built on a plain range remembers the exact cells you selected, so rows pasted underneath later get ignored. A Table grows with the data, and the pivot can follow it.

Build the first pivot in five steps

Imagine a small sales table with six rows and the columns date, region, rep, product, units and sales. Click one cell, go to Insert, click PivotTable, confirm the range, and choose New Worksheet. Then drag Region into Rows and Sales into Values.

The result should read East at 3,900 dollars, South at 1,200 and West at 3,300, with a grand total of 8,400. Right-click a value, apply a currency format, and the sheet starts to look like a report someone would actually read.

Now drag Product into Columns. Laptops come to 6,000 and monitors to 2,400, and those two add back up to the same 8,400. Two different cuts agreeing on the grand total is the cheapest check you have, so run it every time.

Good to read before you audit totals:

Change the math and group the dates

Click a value field and open Value Field Settings to change the calculation. The same Sales column answers three questions. Sum tells you revenue, Count tells you how many orders, and Average tells you how large a typical order is. In the sample, East leads on revenue while West has the bigger average order, which you would miss if you only looked at totals.

Dates need extra care. Right-click any date in the pivot, choose Group, and pick Months, Quarters or Years. If your data spans more than one year, select Years along with Months, or January 2026 and January 2027 collapse into a single January row. If Group is greyed out, the date column still contains text or blanks.

When something breaks along the way, the symptom fix table in the original post lists the common errors with a cause and a fix for each one. I would bookmark that part before anything else.

Refresh, slice and trust the numbers

A pivot is a snapshot. Editing the source changes nothing until you choose PivotTable Analyze and then Refresh, or Refresh All when a workbook holds several pivots. If you want fresh numbers every time the file opens, switch that on under PivotTable Options.

Slicers replace dropdowns with buttons that anyone can click. Insert one from PivotTable Analyze, and if a second pivot should respond to the same buttons, open Report Connections and tick it. That single step is what turns a pivot into a tool a manager will actually use.

Pivots never alter the underlying numbers, so experimenting is safe. Drag fields around until the report answers your question, then check the grand total once more against a plain SUM of the source column. If the two disagree, the source is the place to look first.

One habit saves a lot of confusion. Name the pivot sheet something clear, such as Sales by Region, and keep the source on its own tab. A pivot pointing at a moving target is hard to debug, while a clean layout makes refreshes predictable.

The original post lists seven symptoms, each with a fix and its cause:

See the symptom fix table on daylongs.com
