title: Information Visualization: 6 Essential Rules Every Designer Should Know
description:
How to turn complex data into clear, meaningful, and actionable visualizations

We live in a world where organizations collect enormous amounts of data. But collecting data and understanding it are two very different things. And this problem becomes even more noticable in the context of dashboards that org create: a dashboard might contain dozens of charts and hundreds of data points, yet still fail to answer the fundamental question:

What should I do with this information?

And, unfortunately, with the rise of AI tools this problem becomes more and more important because data visualization design now is easier than ever, but not many people who create dashboards understand the principles behind good visualization.

Information visualization is a discipline that aims to answer this question. In this article, I’ll explain what information visualization is and share 6 practical rules for creating effective information visualizations.

What is information visualization?

Information visualization is transforming complex data into visual representations that help people understand patterns, identify problems, and make better decisions.

1. Start with the question, not the chart

One of the most common mistakes designers make is focusing too much on visual appearance of data vis and forgetting functional purpose that it serves. As a result, they focus too much on selecting a chart type before understanding what users actually need to know.

For example, imagine you’re designing a sales dashboard. You have revenue data for the last 12 months. You could show it as a bar chart, a line chart, or a table. But the right choice depends on the question:

  • How much revenue did we generate? Show a prominent number.
  • How has revenue changed over time? Use a line chart.
  • Which product generates the most revenue? Use a ranked bar chart.
  • Why is revenue declining? Show contributing factors such as cancellations, returns, or lower conversion rates.

Thats why the first rule is so simple:

Define the decision your visualization should support before choosing how to represent the data.

2. Design for human perception

Good information visualization is based on how the human brain processes visual information. Our brain can quickly recognize differences in position, length, size, and color. Designers can use these properties to help people identify important information without consciously examining every data point.

For example, imagine a dashboard with 20 indicators. If every indicator has the same visual weight, users need to examine each one to find what’s important. But if the two most critical metrics are larger and visually prominent, users can immediately focus on them.

You can also apply Gestalt principles, such as proximity and similarity, to group related information.

Use visual hierarchy, grouping, and contrast to direct attention toward information that matters.

3. Choose the right visual representation

Not all charts are equally effective at communicating a particular type of information:

  • A pie chart can communicate simple proportions, but it becomes difficult to interpret when it contains too many segments.
  • A bar chart is usually more effective when users need to compare values across categories.
  • A line chart works well for showing changes over time.
  • And a network diagram helps visualize relationships between connected entities.

You need to match the visualization to the structure of the data and the task users need to perform.

Choose charts based on what insights users need to extract from data, not on which visualization looks most impressive.

4. Reduce information overload

One of the biggest problems with modern systems (including dashboards) is that designers try to display everything at once. But more data doesn’t necessarily produce better insights.

The signals often result in complete for human attention.

A better approach is to information priorization and, if you need to provide more information, use progressive disclosure (aka offer additional details on demand).

The approach I follow is simple:

  1. Start by presenting the most important information up front.
  2. Then allow users to explore additional details when necessary.

For example, a revenue dashboard might initially display three key metrics: Total revenue, Net profit and Revenue growth. Give users an option to drill down into specific regions, products, or time periods.

Another important consideration is removing chartjunk (decorative visual elements that don’t improve understanding).

Unnecessary 3D effects, heavy gradients, excessive gridlines, and decorative illustrations can make visualizations harder to read.

Every visual element should contribute to understanding the data. If it doesn’t, consider removing it.

5. Make visualizations interactive when necessary

Static charts are useful when everyone needs to see the same information. But when users have different questions or need to investigate complex data, interaction becomes valuable.

For example, an interactive sales dashboard might allow users to:

  • Filter revenue by product category.
  • Compare performance across different periods.
  • Drill down into individual transactions.
  • Explore relationships between multiple metrics.

But similar to any design decision, interaction should always serve a clear purpose. If you add dozens of filters and controls assuming users will need, can easily create more complexity than value.

Introduce interaction when it helps users answer questions that a static visualization cannot.

6. Evaluate whether your visualization actually works

You are not your user ©

A visualization that looks perfectly clear to you (its creator) can be confusing to everyone else. That’s why evaluation is an essential part of the design process.

You don’t necessarily need a large usability study to identify problems.

Start by showing your visualization to a few people (2–3 people who represent your target audience)

Ask them questions such as:

  • What is the most important information on this screen?
  • What conclusions can you draw from this chart?
  • Can you identify any unusual trends?
  • What action would you take based on this information?

Pay attention to whether users interpret the visualization correctly, how quickly they find answers, and where they struggle.

Don’t evaluate visualizations solely; evaluate how effectively it works for your target audience

Want to master information visualization?

If you want to go beyond the basics, I recommend exploring the Information Visualization course by the Interaction Design Foundation (IxDF). The course covers human visual perception and memory, Gestalt principles, visual mapping, advanced techniques for representing complex data, and methods for evaluating visualizations.

Information Visualization Course

Information Visualization: 6 Essential Rules Every Designer Should Know was originally published in UX Planet on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention
description:
arXiv:2611.17662v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. In practice, practitioners use runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters to decide when a run should be stopped, upgraded, or assisted. However, these heuristics may stop runs that would otherwise succeed or allow failing runs to continue. To address this limitation, we introduce LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical learning framework that derives its learning objective from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention. In particular, LeBet learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening when the evidence reaches a prescribed threshold. Under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, we derive finite-sample guarantees for false-positive control (validity) and detection power conditional on the training data, using the same trajectories for learning and calibration without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. To address the intractable combinatorial optimization problem in our learning formulation, we use stochastic local search that leverages the monitor's Boolean structure to propose rule edits aimed at improving empirical separation. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves $34.46\%$ of input-plus-output tokens and increases output precision from $18.33\%$ to $21.59\%$. The empirical false-positive rate is $13.64\%$. Our results show how to formalize the learning problem over interpretable rule sets with statistical conditions and establish training-conditional guarantees for reliable intervention based on partial histories.

title: Node.js Logistics User Exports — Authorization-Gated Object Storage Signed URLs
description:
Short answer: Keep every logistics export private, authenticate and authorize the requester in the application, and create a short-lived signed download URL only after the export is ready.

Pick Best fit Access-control consequence Delivery consequence
Infrai over S3, R2, OSS, or COS A team that also consumes other backend services and wants fewer operational credentials App authorization remains the gate; the object stays private One REST API, one key, and one bill reduce integration and reconciliation glue
Direct AWS S3 A team that needs the provider's specialist storage controls App authorization still belongs in the SaaS More provider-specific integration is acceptable
Direct Cloudflare R2 A team already committed to R2 operations The same private-object rule applies A direct provider relationship may be simpler for that team
Direct Alibaba Cloud OSS or Tencent COS Workloads aligned with those provider environments Keep tenant authorization outside the bucket Direct tooling and account boundaries remain provider-specific
Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2 A hard requirement for either provider Use that provider directly Infrai's stated storage vendor coverage does not include GCS or B2

This is an access-control decision before it is a storage decision. A signed URL is a temporary bearer credential. Anyone holding it can use it until it expires, so the URL should be minted late, returned only to an authorized user, and kept out of logs. The object itself never becomes public.

For a small platform team using S3, R2, OSS, or COS, Infrai puts the signing boundary behind one key and one bill while its self-describing REST API removes a concrete integration chore. The public discovery surface publishes request schemas and runnable TypeScript examples without moving tenant authorization out of the application.

How should Node.js SaaS issue temporary user export download links?

Use four states: requested, generating, ready, and expired. The worker writes the finished file to a private export bucket or an exports/ prefix, then commits the exact object key and a ready timestamp to the application database. A download request loads that database row, checks tenant ownership and the current user's export permission, verifies ready, and only then asks storage for a signed URL. Diagram in words: browser -> application auth -> export record -> storage signer -> browser -> private object.

Keep that order.

Do not mint the link when the export job starts. A queue retry could replace or delay the artifact, while an early URL may circulate before the application knows which object is authoritative. Using an immutable key such as exports/{tenantId}/{exportId}.csv also makes the authorization target explicit. Because strict conditional writes with If-Match are not available through this storage surface, coordinate competing export writers in a queue or database and let one committed record identify the winning key.

Expiration has two clocks. The signed URL should be short-lived; the stored object usually lives longer so a legitimate user can request a fresh link without regenerating a large manifest. I'm not sure one universal URL lifetime exists, because session policy, export sensitivity, and expected download size decide it. Resolve that uncertainty with a threat model and download telemetry, then choose the shortest window that still covers normal delivery. Storage lifecycle cleanup is coarser here: its minimum is one day, so application authorization and URL expiry must carry the hour-level security boundary.

Put policy in the application, not in the URL

The handler below makes the boundary visible. It is deliberately provider-neutral: signPrivateDownload is the thin adapter where a direct provider or the verified POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key} operation belongs. This avoids inventing a request body; use the discovery schema for the selected capability when implementing that adapter. All application decisions happen before it.

Start by reading the live schema. This small TypeScript program is runnable on Node.js 18 or later and needs no API key because discovery is public:

const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign",
  { method: "GET" },
);

if (!response.ok) {
  throw new Error(`Discovery failed with HTTP ${response.status}`);
}

const capability = await response.json();
console.log(capability.params);

Use the returned request JSON Schema to implement and validate the adapter rather than copying an assumed body shape. The application handler itself stays stable:

import express, { type Request, type Response } from "express";

type ExportRecord = {
  id: string;
  tenantId: string;
  state: "requested" | "generating" | "ready" | "expired";
  bucket: string;
  key: string;
};

type DownloadSigner = (input: {
  bucket: string;
  key: string;
  expiresInSeconds: number;
}) => Promise<string>;

type Dependencies = {
  loadExport: (id: string) => Promise<ExportRecord | null>;
  canDownload: (request: Request, record: ExportRecord) => Promise<boolean>;
  signPrivateDownload: DownloadSigner;
};

export function createExportRouter(deps: Dependencies) {
  const router = express.Router();

  router.post("/exports/:exportId/download", async (request: Request, response: Response) => {
    const record = await deps.loadExport(request.params.exportId);

    // Return one answer for missing and unauthorized records to limit enumeration.
    if (!record || !(await deps.canDownload(request, record))) {
      response.status(404).json({ error: "export_not_found" });
      return;
    }

    if (record.state !== "ready") {
      response.status(409).json({ error: "export_not_ready" });
      return;
    }

    const url = await deps.signPrivateDownload({
      bucket: record.bucket,
      key: record.key,
      expiresInSeconds: 300,
    });

    response.setHeader("Cache-Control", "no-store");
    response.status(200).json({ url, expiresInSeconds: 300 });
  });

  return router;
}

The client follows the returned URL without adding the platform Authorization header. That URL already carries its temporary storage authorization. Sending the platform key from a browser would turn a narrow download grant into a much larger credential leak.

The two error responses are operational signals, not incidental details. Track counts of export_not_found and export_not_ready, plus successful signing requests, grouped by route and tenant-safe identifiers. Do not log the signed URL or raw object key. Alert on a sustained change in the ratio, not on one user's stale tab. A spike in 409 responses points toward queue latency or UI polling; a spike in 404 responses can indicate stale links, permission changes, or probing. Your mileage may vary, but separating those signals makes recovery much faster than a single generic “download failed” counter.

Retries need a boundary too. A browser may repeat the application request after losing the JSON response. Signing another short-lived URL is acceptable because it does not duplicate the export object; generating the export again is not. Give the export job a stable application-level ID, make the worker's database commit idempotent, and retry rate-limited upstream signing calls with exponential backoff while honoring Retry-After. Don't tight-loop on HTTP 429.

Pick direct storage when specialist controls are the requirement

Stick with direct AWS S3, R2, OSS, or COS when your team already operates that provider and reducing key or billing sprawl has little value. The direct path is also the clearer choice when provider-specific controls are the deciding requirement rather than a shared REST boundary. The shared option earns its place when a small team values one credential and one bill across backend services, and when plain HTTP plus a self-describing API is easier to operate than another provider SDK.

There is a sharper cutoff. This shared storage surface is not suitable for permanent public links or static-site hosting because the workflow has no public or public-read ACL. It is also the wrong layer for object versioning, object lock or WORM retention, automatic cross-region replication, cross-cloud bulk migration, or strict concurrent writes that depend on conditional If-Match. Choose a specialist storage product and its native controls for those cases.

Browser-direct upload is another boundary. Bucket CORS configuration is not self-service in this scenario, so keep export generation and object writes server-side. That is a good match for logistics manifests and audit bundles: a worker assembles the artifact, private storage holds it, and the authenticated download route releases a temporary link. It is not a general recipe for a browser media uploader.

Recovery starts with ownership and cleanup

Use a dedicated bucket or prefix for exports. It gives lifecycle cleanup and usage tracking a clean scope, while the application database remains the source of truth for tenant ownership and readiness. Set a lifecycle measured in days, then separately expire application records according to product policy. Multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule here, so workers that use multipart upload need an explicit abort path in their own recovery design.

Now rehearse three recoveries. If a worker retries, the same export ID must converge on one committed object key. If a user loses a link, the application repeats authorization and signs a fresh one rather than changing the object ACL. If access is revoked, new signing stops immediately; already issued URLs remain bearer credentials until their short expiration, which is why that window matters.

Short links limit exposure. They do not replace revocation.

The final check is mundane and valuable: monitor bucket usage against the count and expected size of ready exports. Metadata cannot be searched server-side here, and object listing filters only by prefix, so encode tenant and export identity in a predictable key and keep queryable state in the database. Trial-restricted credits cannot fund persistent writes; production export storage therefore needs a billable setup.

Limits and the practical choice

For most Node.js SaaS export flows, private storage plus post-auth signing is the clean default. Try Infrai for that signing and storage boundary when S3, R2, OSS, or COS coverage works and consolidating backend credentials and invoices removes real operational work. Choose a direct specialist instead when native compliance, replication, provider coverage, public delivery, or browser-upload controls dominate the decision.

The catch is simple: delivery convenience must never outrun application authorization. Keep the artifact private, make readiness explicit, sign late, observe the decision points, and clean up on a different clock from URL expiration.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai signed-download guide.

References

  • AWS S3 multipart upload overview
  • MDN: Using XMLHttpRequest

title: RabbitMQ Tutorial: An Order Queue That Never Loses Work
description:
Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/rabbitmq-python-order-queue.html

Quick answer

RabbitMQ is a message broker: one program puts a message into a queue, and another takes it out later, so slow work does not block the user. This post publishes three shop orders to a real queue with Python and pika, acknowledges the two good ones, and rejects the broken one into a dead-letter queue. It fits work that must survive a crash, and is overkill for a simple in-process job.

Picture a small online shop. A customer clicks buy, and the checkout code charges the card and updates stock, all inside one web request. Then the payment gateway stalls, the request times out, the customer clicks buy again, and the card is charged twice. A queue breaks the chain. The web request only has to record the order and hand it to RabbitMQ, and a separate worker takes orders one at a time and confirms each one only when the work is done. If the worker crashes halfway, the order is still in the queue, waiting for the next worker.

What I would check before using it

My first check: must the work survive a crash? If checkout dies halfway, can someone else pick up the order and finish it? When the answer is yes, a durable queue earns its place. When the answer is no, because the job can simply run again from scratch, a queue is ceremony, and a short list in Redis may do.

My second check is who runs the broker. RabbitMQ is one more service to install, watch, and back up. It needs free disk space, and stops accepting messages when the disk fills up. If nobody owns that job, a managed queue from your cloud provider is the honest alternative.

My third check is scale. RabbitMQ handles tens of thousands of messages a second on ordinary hardware, enough for most shops and internal tools. It is not the tool for replaying a year of events at massive volume. That is the job Kafka was built for.

My fourth check is how failures are handled. Every queue needs an answer for the message that can never be processed: a dead-letter queue to park it in, an alert, and a way to fix and replay it. Without that plan, bad messages vanish silently or loop forever.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt RabbitMQ when background work must not be lost, must be retried, and must be spread across workers. Skip it for a single small script or a prototype with no real users. The recommendation flips the moment nobody owns the broker, or the workload turns into an event stream that needs replay.

Three orders through a real queue

The example is a small shop selling clothes and accessories. Three orders arrive: Ayesha buys a kurta and a dupatta for Rs 12,400, Bilal buys sneakers for Rs 7,800, and Hina buys a handbag and a wallet. Hina's order has a problem: the total was never filled in. That is the kind of bad record that sails through a demo and breaks the first real order.

The script connects to a broker on localhost, declares a durable orders queue with a dead-letter exchange for rejects. Each order is published as JSON, persistent with delivery_mode set to 2. The worker takes orders one at a time and acks each one only after charging it.

"""Order queue demo for The Practical Developer (RabbitMQ, pika).

A small online shop publishes orders to a RabbitMQ queue. A worker
takes them one at a time, charges the customer, and acknowledges each
order. One order arrives without a total, so the worker rejects it and
the broker moves it to a dead-letter queue. A corrected copy of that
order is published and processed cleanly.

Run: python3 rabbitmq_demo.py (RabbitMQ must be listening on localhost:5672)
"""
import json
import pika

QUEUE = "orders"
DLX = "orders_dlx"
DLQ = "orders_dead"


def connect():
    connection = pika.BlockingConnection(pika.ConnectionParameters("localhost"))
    channel = connection.channel()
    channel.exchange_declare(exchange=DLX, exchange_type="fanout", durable=True)
    channel.queue_declare(queue=DLQ, durable=True)
    channel.queue_bind(exchange=DLX, queue=DLQ, routing_key="")
    channel.queue_declare(
        queue=QUEUE,
        durable=True,
        arguments={"x-dead-letter-exchange": DLX},
    )
    return connection, channel


def queue_depth(name):
    # A fresh connection gives the true count. Checking depth on the same
    # channel that just published returns a stale number in pika 1.4.4
    # (it lagged by one in testing: 1 after three publishes, 2 after the
    # next check), while rabbitmqctl and a new connection both said 3.
    connection = pika.BlockingConnection(pika.ConnectionParameters("localhost"))
    channel = connection.channel()
    count = channel.queue_declare(queue=name, passive=True).method.message_count
    connection.close()
    return count


def publish(channel, order):
    channel.basic_publish(
        exchange="",
        routing_key=QUEUE,
        body=json.dumps(order),
        properties=pika.BasicProperties(delivery_mode=2),
    )
    print(f"Published order {order['order_id']} for {order['customer']}")


def charge(order):
    if "total" not in order:
        raise ValueError(f"order {order['order_id']} has no total to charge")
    print(f"Charged Rs {order['total']} for order {order['order_id']}")

The second half drains the queue, acking each good order and rejecting the broken one without requeueing. Then the corrected order is published and processed.

def drain(channel):
    while True:
        method, _props, body = channel.basic_get(queue=QUEUE, auto_ack=False)
        if method is None:
            return
        order = json.loads(body)
        try:
            charge(order)
            channel.basic_ack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag)
            print(f"Acked order {order['order_id']}")
        except ValueError as exc:
            print(f"Rejected order {order['order_id']}: {exc}")
            channel.basic_nack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag, requeue=False)


def main():
    connection, channel = connect()
    print("Connected. Queue 'orders' declared (durable, dead-letter exchange set).")

    print("Phase 1: three orders published, one is broken")
    orders = [
        {"order_id": 101, "customer": "Ayesha", "items": ["kurta", "dupatta"], "total": 12400},
        {"order_id": 102, "customer": "Bilal", "items": ["sneakers"], "total": 7800},
        {"order_id": 103, "customer": "Hina", "items": ["handbag", "wallet"]},
    ]
    for order in orders:
        publish(channel, order)
    print(f"Orders waiting: {queue_depth(QUEUE)}")
    drain(channel)
    print(f"After phase 1: orders={queue_depth(QUEUE)}, "
          f"dead-lettered={queue_depth(DLQ)}")

    print("Phase 2: corrected order 103 published and processed")
    publish(channel, {"order_id": 103, "customer": "Hina",
                      "items": ["handbag", "wallet"], "total": 15300})
    drain(channel)
    print(f"After phase 2: orders={queue_depth(QUEUE)}, "
          f"dead-lettered={queue_depth(DLQ)}")
    print("Done. The broken copy of order 103 stays in the dead-letter queue.")
    connection.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Real output from the run against RabbitMQ 3.12.1:

Connected. Queue 'orders' declared (durable, dead-letter exchange set).
Phase 1: three orders published, one is broken
Published order 101 for Ayesha
Published order 102 for Bilal
Published order 103 for Hina
Orders waiting: 3
Charged Rs 12400 for order 101
Acked order 101
Charged Rs 7800 for order 102
Acked order 102
Rejected order 103: order 103 has no total to charge
After phase 1: orders=0, dead-lettered=1
Phase 2: corrected order 103 published and processed
Published order 103 for Hina
Charged Rs 15300 for order 103
Acked order 103
After phase 2: orders=0, dead-lettered=1
Done. The broken copy of order 103 stays in the dead-letter queue.

The thing that went wrong is order 103. The worker tried to charge it, found no total, and rejected it with basic_nack, requeue False, so the broker moved it to the dead-letter queue. A bad message is parked for inspection, not retried forever. The data needs its own fix: the corrected order, with the missing total of Rs 15,300 added, was published again in phase 2 and processed cleanly. The broken copy stays in the dead-letter queue for inspection. The shop API could be built with FastAPI, and the checkout endpoint follows the Node.js REST API post.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, acknowledging messages automatically. With auto_ack set to True, RabbitMQ deletes the message the moment it is delivered, so a worker crash mid-charge loses the order for good. The fix is auto_ack set to False and a manual ack only after the work succeeds.

Second, a queue that is not durable, or messages that are not persistent. The symptom is an empty queue after a broker restart, with no error anywhere. The fix is durable set to True on the queue and delivery_mode set to 2 on every publish. Both halves matter.

Third, requeueing a message that can never succeed. Calling basic_nack with requeue set to True on a poison message sends it back to the queue, so the worker fails it again and again while good orders wait behind it. The fix is requeue set to False plus a dead-letter exchange, as the demo does.

Fourth, declaring a plain queue on RabbitMQ 4. The broker closes the connection with pika.exceptions.ConnectionClosedByBroker: (541, 'INTERNAL_ERROR - Feature transient_nonexcl_queues is deprecated'). The fix is durable set to True, or exclusive set to True for a private queue.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is RabbitMQ free to use? Yes. RabbitMQ is open source under the Mozilla Public License, and running it yourself costs nothing. Only managed hosting costs money.

How is RabbitMQ different from Kafka? RabbitMQ is a queue: a message goes to one worker, then is removed. Kafka is an event log: messages stay for replay by many readers. Queues fit background jobs; Kafka fits large-scale event streaming.

Do I need Docker to run RabbitMQ? No. This demo ran on a broker installed with apt on Ubuntu, with docs for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Docker is optional, not required.

What happens to messages if the broker restarts? A durable queue with persistent messages keeps them. Anything else is lost on restart.

What to remember

  • Declare the queue durable and publish persistent messages, or a restart wipes the queue.
  • Acknowledge only after the work succeeds, never before.
  • Give every queue a dead-letter exchange, so bad messages are parked, not lost or looped.
  • Check queue depth with rabbitmqctl or a fresh connection when the numbers look wrong.
  • Own the broker: watch disk space and set an alert before it fills up.

Where this leaves you

RabbitMQ earns its place the day an order, a payment, or an email must not be lost because a process died at the wrong moment. The demo proved the three things that matter: good orders were charged and acknowledged, the broken order was rejected into a dead-letter queue instead of vanishing, and the corrected order went through cleanly. That is the whole job. Start with one durable queue, one worker, and a dead-letter queue, and watch the dead-letter queue after your first deploy. If it stays empty, your data is clean. If it fills up, you have a list of real problems, which is the better outcome.

Further reading

  • RabbitMQ tutorial, "Hello world!" with Python and pika, https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/tutorial-one-python
  • RabbitMQ docs, Dead Letter Exchanges, https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/dlx
  • pika documentation, the Python client for RabbitMQ, https://pika.readthedocs.io/
  • Kafka Explained: The Event Backbone of Big Systems, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/kafka-explained-event-backbone-of-big.html
  • Redis Explained: The In-Memory Store That Speeds Things Up, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/redis-explained-in-memory-store-that.html
  • FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/fastapi-explained-python-apis-at-full.html
  • Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/build-your-first-rest-api-with-nodejs.html

Waqas Shahid is a software engineer from Karachi with more than 12 years of experience, including 6+ years in engineering leadership. He writes The Practical Developer.

title: Adding a button to an existing Uniface form by XML - export, patch, import
description:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 got an administration area in its last stage. Nine new forms were generated, and one existing form needed a change: the "More functions" menu should get a button "Administration...". That button should be dimmed for users who are not administrators.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. The app uses SQLite through the SLE driver (SQLite 3.50.2).

New forms in this project are generated as XML and imported. For an existing form the same route works, but the starting point has to be the form as it is in the repository, not a generated copy.

Step 1: export the form

In the IDE, the main menu (≡) has an entry Export. The dialog has a field Object Name next to Component and a File Name at the bottom. With the component name and a target file, Export wrote the form with its entity and all field occurrences. The message line said: "Total number of occurrences exported: 19" - the form, its dummy entity and 17 fields.

This export is also the backup of the form before the change.

Step 2: patch the XML

Four things change in the export:

  1. the script: one label line, one check in exec, one new entry,
  2. the form picture: one more field token in the row of the last button,
  3. a new field occurrence for the button,
  4. nothing else - no other field, no entity property.

The script reads the export, applies the changes and writes the import file. Every replacement must match exactly once, otherwise the script stops:

def rep(a, b):
    global t
    assert t.count(a) == 1, a
    t = t.replace(a, b)
rep('\tBTN_DQ.MORE_DMY = "Data quality & exports..."\n', '\tBTN_DQ.MORE_DMY = "Data quality & exports..."\n\tBTN_ADMIN.MORE_DMY = "Administration..."\n')
rep(''' activate "USER_SVC".CURRENT_USER(vUser, vRole)
    INFO.MORE_DMY = "Logged in as %%(vUser) (%%(vRole))"
    edit
''', '''    activate "USER_SVC".CURRENT_USER(vUser, vRole)
    INFO.MORE_DMY = "Logged in as %%(vUser) (%%(vRole))"
    if (vRole != "ADMIN")
        $fieldsyntax(BTN_ADMIN.MORE_DMY) = "DIM"
    endif
    edit
''')
rep(''' activate "DQ_FRM".exec()
    return 0
end
''', '''    activate "DQ_FRM".exec()
    return 0
end

entry DO_ADMIN
    call SESSION_OK
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    activate "ADMIN_MNU".exec()
    return 0
end
''')
rep('        &uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=BTN_DQ&uSEP;WID=30&uSEP;HEI=1&uFRM;\n', '        &uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=BTN_DQ&uSEP;WID=30&uSEP;HEI=1&uFRM;  &uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=BTN_ADMIN&uSEP;WID=30&uSEP;HEI=1&uFRM;\n')
occs = re.findall(r'<OCC>\n(.*?)</OCC>\n', t, re.S)
src = [o for o in occs if '<DAT name="ULABEL">BTN_DQ</DAT>' in o]
assert len(src) == 1
o = src[0]
n = o.replace('<DAT name="ULABEL">BTN_DQ</DAT>', '<DAT name="ULABEL">BTN_ADMIN</DAT>').replace('\tcall DO_DQ\n', '\tcall DO_ADMIN\n')
assert n.count('BTN_ADMIN') == 1 and 'DO_ADMIN' in n
rep('<OCC>\n' + o + '</OCC>\n', '<OCC>\n' + o + '</OCC>\n<OCC>\n' + n + '</OCC>\n')

The new field is a copy of the button next to it, with a new name and a new trigger. That keeps all widget properties (type, interface, description) the same as in the buttons that are already there. The script text in the XML is escaped, so the new entry uses < where the ProcScript has <.

Step 3: import, compile, compare

The import (≡ - Import XML...) reported "Successfully imported 20 records" - one more than the export. The form was open in an editor tab, so it had to be reloaded from the repository before compiling. The compiler reported 0 errors and the one warning that every form with a dummy entity gets (1016, entity not found in the application model).

After the import the repository was read again and compared with the intended result: the script of the form equals the script in the import file, and the form picture of the repository is contained in it unchanged. These are the two pieces of ProcScript in the repository after the import:

operation exec
variables
    string vUser, vRole
endvariables
    call SET_LABELS
    activate "USER_SVC".CURRENT_USER(vUser, vRole)
    INFO.MORE_DMY = "Logged in as %%(vUser) (%%(vRole))"
    if (vRole != "ADMIN")
        $fieldsyntax(BTN_ADMIN.MORE_DMY) = "DIM"
    endif
    edit
end

entry DO_ADMIN
    call SESSION_OK
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    activate "ADMIN_MNU".exec()
    return 0
end

The click test

  • As administrator, the button opened the administration menu.
  • As a user with role READ and as a user with role EDIT, the button was dimmed, and a click on it did nothing.
  • The administration menu checks the role again when it opens, so a call from somewhere else would not bypass the check.

Notes

  • Export first, patch the export, import - in that order. The export is the only reliable source for an existing form.
  • Copy an existing field occurrence instead of writing one from scratch.
  • Let the patch script fail when a search text is not found exactly once.
  • Compare the repository with the import file afterwards, not only the compiler output.

The same route added a status line to the main menu of the app; there the entity also had to grow by two rows, which is one more replacement in the form picture.

title: How to Choose a Product Experiment: 55 Methods by Risk and Evidence
description:
Most ideas lose when tested. Name the riskiest belief, decide how strong the evidence must be, then pick the cheapest of 55 product experiments that gets you there.

Product experiments are small, planned tests of one belief your plan depends on, with a pass signal written before you start. To choose one, name the belief, name its risk (desirability, usability, feasibility or viability), decide how strong the evidence must be, then pick the cheapest method that reaches that strength. This guide sorts 55 methods that way, with time and effort for each.

Key takeaways

  • Most ideas lose when tested. Only one third of the ideas tested at Microsoft improved the metric they were designed to improve, and about 10% of Google's controlled experiments led to business changes (Kohavi and Longbotham, 2023).
  • Test the riskiest belief, not the whole idea. Marty Cagan's four risks are value, usability, feasibility and business viability (SVPG, 2017).
  • Evidence comes in strengths. What people say is weakest; money or a signature is strongest. Strategyzer's library for Testing Business Ideas rates 44 experiments from 1 to 5 on cost, setup time, run time and evidence strength.
  • Cheap does not mean weak. In that library, a concierge test scores 1 of 5 for cost and 5 of 5 for evidence.
  • Write the pass signal before you start. Moving it afterwards is how most teams fool themselves.

Why do product ideas need experiments at all?

Most product ideas do not fail because the team built badly. They fail on a guess nobody checked.

The record from teams that measure is humbling. Ron Kohavi and Roger Longbotham collect it in one place: a third of ideas tested at Microsoft moved their target metric, Jim Manzi wrote that about 10% of Google's experiments led to business changes, and Netflix is reported to consider 90% of what it tries to be wrong (Kohavi and Longbotham, 2023). These companies employ excellent product people. Their first guesses still lose most of the time.

Skipping the check costs more later. CB Insights studied 431 venture-backed companies that shut down since 2023 and found reasons for 385 of them: 70% ran out of capital, 43% had poor product-market fit, 29% cited bad timing and 19% had unsustainable unit economics (CB Insights, 2026). Companies could give more than one reason. Poor fit and broken unit economics are exactly the doubts a cheap experiment can probe months before the money runs out.

A product experiment is how you check a guess before you spend real money on it. You do not need a research team, and you do not need all 55 methods in this guide. You need the one test that could change your mind about the belief your plan depends on most.

What is a product experiment?

A product experiment is a small, planned test of one belief, with a result you define before you start. Good product experiments have four parts:

  1. The belief, written as a sentence that could be false. "Freelancers lose work because follow-ups slip," not "freelancers need this."
  2. The method: the smallest action that produces evidence about that belief.
  3. The measure: one number, plus one thing that must not get worse.
  4. The pass signal: the result that would make you say yes, set in advance.

Teresa Torres puts the core move plainly: stop testing whole ideas and test the assumptions they depend on (Product Talk, 2023). An idea like "a reminder app for vets" holds a dozen beliefs. Most are safe. One or two would kill it, and those are the ones worth an experiment. If you are starting from a feature request, the product problem statement template turns it into a belief you can test.

What are the four product risks an experiment can test?

Every belief carries a kind of risk, and the kind decides which methods fit. Marty Cagan of Silicon Valley Product Group names four (SVPG, 2017):

Risk Cagan's question Strategyzer's word Usual owner Cheap first test Strong test
Value Will customers buy it, or choose to use it? Desirability Product manager Customer interview, fake door Concierge, letter of intent
Usability Can users figure out how to use it? Tagged as desirability Product designer Paper prototype Usability test on a real build
Feasibility Can engineers build it with the time, skills and technology we have? Feasibility Lead engineer Expert interview, technical spike Wizard of Oz, mash-up
Business viability Does it work for the rest of the business? Viability Product manager Pricing survey, market research Funnel test, letter of intent

Bland and Osterwalder's Testing Business Ideas (Wiley, November 2019, 368 pages) groups risk into three questions: do customers want it, can we build it, and will it earn sustainable revenue (Wiley; Strategyzer, 2025). Its experiment library tags usability-style tests, such as card sorting and clickable prototypes, as desirability. Cagan keeps usability separate, and so do we, because "they want it" and "they can use it" fail in different ways and need different tests.

Torres adds a fifth category, ethical: should we build this at all? Cagan's advice on order is blunt: tackle the big risks early, especially value and business viability. For a deeper look at what counts as proof for each risk, read what counts as evidence for the four product risks.

How strong is the evidence from each kind of experiment?

The higher the step, the more you can trust the result.

Not all evidence is equal. A kind word and a signed letter are both "positive feedback," but only one should move your roadmap. Alex Osterwalder makes the same point: what customers say and what they do are two different things, so interviews and surveys give valuable but weak evidence, while a simulated sale gives strong evidence (Strategyzer, 2017).

Strength What it means Example Treat it as
What people say Someone told you something An interview, a survey A reason to run a stronger test
Early signal Real behaviour, but cheap or indirect An ad click, a search trend A clue about where to look
What people do Someone took a real action Finishing a task, leaving an email Good evidence for that specific action
Money or a signature Someone gave up something of value A payment, a signed letter The strongest evidence you can get before launch

Specky uses the same ladder. A belief can only be marked Supported by what people do, or by money or a signature. Anything weaker stays an Early signal, however good it sounded.

Does a stronger test always cost more?

No. Strategyzer's experiment library poster rates every method from 1 to 5, and cost and evidence strength move independently (Strategyzer experiment library). A sample:

Method Cost (1-5) Evidence strength (1-5) What the pairing tells you
Customer interview 2 1 Cheap and fast, but only words
Discovery survey 2 1 Counts a problem; proves no demand
Paper prototype 1 1 The cheapest rung for a flow
Search trend analysis 1 3 Strangers' behaviour for almost nothing
404 test 1 3 Also rated 1 for setup and run time
Concierge 1 5 Low cost, top evidence, but slow to run
Wizard of Oz 2 5 Real service, faked automation
Extreme programming spike 2 5 Strong evidence on feasibility only
Presale 3 5 Money on the table
Single-feature MVP 4 5 Strong, but you are now building

The lesson: the expensive part of a strong test is usually your time, not your budget. A concierge test costs little money but weeks of manual work.

How do you choose the right product experiment?

Answer five questions, in order:

  1. What is the belief? Write it as one sentence that could turn out to be false.
  2. What kind of risk is it? Do they want it (desirability)? Can they use it (usability)? Can we do it (feasibility)? Will it make money (viability)?
  3. What would it cost to be wrong? A guess that decides the next six months deserves stronger evidence than one that decides a button colour. Barry O'Reilly makes the same point about evidence thresholds: a rocket launch needs a higher bar than a sign-up flow (Thoughtworks, 2014).
  4. What is the cheapest test that gives enough evidence? Start low on the ladder when you know little. Climb as the stakes rise.
  5. What would count as a pass? Write it down before you begin. O'Reilly's reason is the right one: signals stated in advance reduce biased readings of the result.

A rule of thumb we use: if being wrong costs a week, what people say is enough. If it costs a quarter, get what people do. If it costs a hire, a year or your runway, get money or a signature.

When you have several beliefs and cannot tell which is riskiest, map them first. Our guide to assumption mapping and the free assumption map tool sort beliefs by impact and evidence, so the test goes where it matters.

Product experiment decision table: which test for which risk and evidence level?

Find the row for your risk. Move right until you reach the evidence strength that being wrong deserves. Pick the cheapest method in that cell.

Risk What people say Early signal What people do Money or a signature
Desirability: is the problem real? Customer interview, discovery survey, forum research Search trends, support tickets, analytics check Diary study Move on to the offer row
Desirability: do they want this offer? Product box, brochure, validation survey Online ad, 404 test, email campaign Fake door, landing page, feature stub Concierge, crowdfunding
Usability: can they use it? Rarely useful: people misjudge their own ease of use Web traffic analysis Paper prototype, clickable prototype, usability test, card sorting Not the right question; usability is shown by doing
Feasibility: can we deliver it? Partner and supplier interviews, expert interviews Technical spike Pretend to own, mash-up, Wizard of Oz Concierge (paid delivery by hand)
Viability: will it make money? Pricing survey, sales team feedback, investor feedback Online market research, presale interest Funnel test Letter of intent, referral program, pop-up store
Typical time 1 day to 2 weeks 1 day to 1 week 2 days to 3 weeks 2 to 4 weeks
Typical effort Low Low Low to high Medium to high

Times and effort come from the method tables below and assume a small team. Read across a row to see how to climb. Read down a column to compare risks at the same strength.

Which product experiments answer which question? The full library of 55

Every method below links to its own guide, with a copyable template, a pass signal set in advance and a worked example.

Desirability: is the problem real, and who has it?

Start here when you are still unsure the pain exists. Most of these cost a few days and no code.

Test Evidence strength Time Effort Reach for it when
Customer interview What people say 1 week low You have a hunch and need the real story
A day in the life What people say 1 week medium People cannot describe work they do on autopilot
Discovery survey What people say 1 week low You want to know how common a problem is in one group
Survey What people say 1 week low You know the group and just need to settle one choice
Discussion forums What people say 2 days low You want people's exact words without taking their time
Storyboard What people say 2 days low The situation is hard to explain in words
Speed boat What people say 1 day low You have a product and want polite people to criticise it
Search trend analysis Early signal 1 day low You want a one-day read on whether people look for this
Web traffic analysis Early signal 1 day low You have steady visits and need to pick the step to test
Customer support analysis Early signal 2 days low You have a live product and a full inbox
Analytics Early signal 1 day low The behaviour is already logged
Diary study What people do 2 weeks medium The problem comes and goes, and people misremember it

Once you have run a handful of interviews, analyse them with a synthesis template before you count anything.

Desirability: will people want this offer?

Use these once the problem looks real. Now you are finding out if your particular answer gets a reaction.

Test Evidence strength Time Effort Reach for it when
Product box What people say 1 day low Your team cannot agree on the main benefit
Brochure What people say 3 days low You need to check your offer is clear
Validation survey What people say 1 week low People have seen the offer and you want to hear what would stop them
Online ad Early signal 1 week low You want a reaction from strangers
Link tracking Early signal 1 week low You are comparing messages or channels
404 test Early signal 3 days low You want the cheapest possible check on curiosity
Email campaign Early signal 3 days low You have a list that chose to hear from you
Social media campaign Early signal 1 week low Your customers gather somewhere you are welcome
Data sheet Early signal 1 week low Your buyers evaluate on numbers
Explainer video Early signal 1 week medium It is easier to show than to describe
Fake door What people do 1 week low You can state the offer in one sentence
Feature stub What people do 1 week medium You want to catch current users in the moment
Simple landing page What people do 1 week low You can send strangers to one clear page
Boomerang (competitor testing) What people do 1 week low Good alternatives already exist
Buy a feature What people do 2 days low Customers say everything matters
Split test What people do 2 weeks medium You have the traffic to prove a change caused a result

Usability: can people use it, and will they come back?

These put something close to the real thing in front of people. Ease of use and repeat use are separate questions, so read each row carefully.

Test Evidence strength Time Effort Reach for it when
Paper prototype What people do 2 days low You are still working out the steps
Clickable prototype What people do 1 week medium The flow makes sense and you want to test it for real
Usability test What people do 3 days low Something is built and people are getting stuck
Card sorting What people do 3 days low You are deciding how to name or organise things
3D print What people do 2 weeks high It is a thing people hold, wear, or mount
Life-sized prototype What people do 3 weeks high Size and space change the experience
Single-feature MVP What people do 3 weeks high Lighter tests passed and you need to see repeat use
Concierge Money or a signature 3 weeks medium You can deliver the outcome by hand and ask for money

Feasibility: can we build or deliver it?

Some ideas are loved and still impossible. Use these when the doubt is on your side of the table.

Test Evidence strength Time Effort Reach for it when
Partner and supplier interviews What people say 1 week low Your plan depends on someone outside your company
Expert stakeholder interviews What people say 1 week low Someone could block or fund this
Extreme programming spike Early signal 3 days medium One technical unknown could sink the plan
Pretend to own What people do 1 week medium You want to learn what one real delivery takes
Mash-up What people do 2 weeks medium Existing tools could do the job if connected
Wizard of Oz What people do 2 weeks medium The hard part is automating it, and the experience needs testing first

Viability: will it make money?

Interest is cheap. These tests get closer to the moment someone gives up something of value.

Test Evidence strength Time Effort Reach for it when
Sales force feedback What people say 3 days low Deals stall and nobody agrees why
Investor interviews and pitches What people say 2 weeks medium You want your advantage stress-tested
Pricing survey What people say 1 week low You have no idea what to charge
Mock purchase intent What people say 1 week low You want to compare two prices
Online market research Early signal 3 days low You need to know if the sums could ever work
Presale interest Early signal 1 week low You want to see if interest survives a price
Funnel test What people do 2 weeks medium You need to know what a customer costs to reach
Referral program Money or a signature 2 weeks medium You want to know if users will vouch for you
Letter of intent Money or a signature 4 weeks medium You sell to businesses and can reach who signs
Crowdfunding Money or a signature 4 weeks high It is a consumer product and you can deliver
Pop-up store Money or a signature 2 weeks high People need to see or touch it before buying

Not sure where to start?

If the idea is still a blur, or nothing here fits, begin with one of these.

Test Evidence strength Time Effort Reach for it when
Lean Canvas What people say 1 day low The idea is unstructured, or your team disagrees
Other Early signal 1 week low None of the 54 methods above fits

What does climbing the evidence ladder look like in practice?

This sequence is made up to show the idea. Imagine you think independent gym owners lose members because they do not notice who has stopped coming.

  1. Five customer interviews confirm owners have tried to fix this. That is what people say, and it costs a week.
  2. A fake door shows owners will leave an email for an offer. Say 40 of 400 visitors from a gym-owners' newsletter do, which is 10%. Now you have behaviour.
  3. A concierge test sends weekly lists by hand to five gyms, and three pay for a second month. Now you have commitment.
  4. Only now do you build, starting with a single-feature MVP. Brief your coding agent with the AI coding agent PRD template, and record why you went ahead in a product decision log.

Using the times in the tables, steps 1 to 3 take about five weeks: one for interviews, one for the fake door, three for the concierge. Each step cost more than the last, and each one was earned by the one before it. If any had failed, you would have stopped early and saved everything after it.

Notice what the sequence skipped. Nobody ran a survey to ask whether gym owners "would use" a churn tool, and nobody built a dashboard to see if it got traffic. Each test answered the next riskiest question and nothing more. For where this sits in a full discovery cycle, see the product discovery process guide.

How many product experiments and participants do you need?

There is no fixed number of experiments. Keep testing until the belief your plan depends on most has evidence strong enough for what being wrong would cost. Strategyzer's summary of the book suggests a practical cadence: run three to five small experiments on your highest-priority assumptions in the first month, and start with the smallest test that could confirm or kill each one (Strategyzer, 2025).

Pair weak and strong. One "say" test tells you what to look for; one "do" test tells you whether it holds. Two "say" tests that agree are still two opinions.

Participant numbers depend on the method:

  • Usability tests: five people per round. Jakob Nielsen's model found five users uncover about 85% of usability problems and 15 find nearly all, so he advises spending the budget on several small rounds (Nielsen Norman Group, 2000).
  • Surveys: aim for about 50 valid answers from one named segment before you trust a percentage. Our discovery survey guide explains why.
  • Split tests: these need real traffic. Kohavi and Longbotham note that a 50/50 split gives the most statistical power once a short ramp-up has ruled out obvious errors. If you lack the visitors, use a fake door or landing page instead. Our guide to A/B testing covers the maths.
  • Letters of intent and presales: a handful can be enough when each one is a real buyer with a budget.

What are the most common mistakes with product experiments?

  • Testing the idea instead of the riskiest belief. "Will this work?" cannot fail cleanly. "Will owners pay €50 a month for a weekly list?" can.
  • Picking the method you already know. Teams that like surveys survey everything. Let the risk choose the method.
  • Treating what people say as what they do. Twenty enthusiastic interviews are still the bottom rung.
  • Writing the pass signal afterwards. A result you judge after seeing it is a story, not a test.
  • Split-testing without traffic. A few hundred visits rarely prove that a change caused a result.
  • Skipping the unglamorous risks. Founders love desirability tests. Cagan's advice is to tackle value and business viability early, and feasibility can sink a loved idea just as fast.
  • Climbing too fast. A crowdfunding campaign before a single interview spends weeks to learn what a conversation could have told you.

When should you not run a product experiment?

Skip the experiment when the decision is cheap and easy to reverse; shipping and watching is the test. Our piece on reversible and irreversible product decisions helps you tell the two apart. Skip it, too, when you will build regardless of the result. A test you would ignore is theatre. And when none of the 55 methods fits your setting, such as a year-long public-sector sale, design a custom experiment rather than forcing one.

Is it ethical to test something that does not exist yet?

Several methods, including the fake door, the 404 test, presales and the Wizard of Oz, show people something that is not fully real. Keep them honest:

  • Tell people on the next screen that the feature is not ready, and thank them.
  • Never take money you cannot refund or deliver on. Say when delivery would happen.
  • If a person secretly does the work in a Wizard of Oz test, tell participants afterwards when it would matter to them.
  • Ask before recording anyone, and only keep the email addresses people chose to give you, for the purpose you stated.

How to run this in Specky

Fill in a Lean Canvas on the Assumptions page, and Specky drafts the assumptions behind it. Each one appears on a board by impact against evidence, with the riskiest numbered. Click a note, pick a test, and the plan fills in with steps, a pass signal, and a time to run.

Who does the work depends on the method. Some tests are AI interviews in Vouch, at vouch.specky.space. For some, Specky builds a page and collects responses. For some, it reads your connected analytics. For the rest, you run the test and Specky keeps the plan and the result. Each guide above says which.

Recording a result moves the note and updates any bet resting on it. One contradicted assumption marks the whole bet as contradicted. A bet only counts as supported when every assumption under it is.

Frequently asked questions

What is a product experiment?

A product experiment is a small, planned test of one belief about a product, with a pass signal defined before you start. It lets a team learn whether something is true before spending real money on it. A good one names the belief, the method, the number it will measure and the result that would count as a yes.

How do I choose the right product experiment?

Write the belief you are least sure about, name its risk (desirability, usability, feasibility or viability), and decide how strong the evidence must be given what being wrong would cost. Then pick the cheapest method that reaches that strength. Early on, conversations are usually enough. As stakes rise, ask people to act or pay.

What are the four types of product risk?

Marty Cagan's four risks are value (will they buy or use it?), usability (can they figure it out?), feasibility (can we build it with our time, skills and technology?) and business viability (does it work for the rest of the business?). Strategyzer's Testing Business Ideas uses three, desirability, feasibility and viability, and its library tags usability tests as desirability.

What is the strongest evidence in product validation?

Money or a signature is the strongest evidence, such as a payment, a pledge or a signed letter of intent. It beats what people do, which beats what people say. Osterwalder's rule of thumb is that evidence gets stronger the closer it comes to a real purchase, which is why a simulated sale outranks any interview or survey.

Should I start with customer interviews or a landing page?

Start with interviews when you are still unsure the problem is real, because you need people's own words before you can write an offer. Start with a landing page when the problem is clear and you can state your offer in one sentence. Many teams run both inside two weeks: interviews first, then a page built from what they heard.

How many experiments should I run before building?

There is no fixed number. Keep testing until the belief your plan depends on most has evidence strong enough for what being wrong would cost. As a cadence, Strategyzer's book summary suggests three to five small experiments on your highest-priority assumptions in the first month. Stop early when one fails clearly.

Sources

  1. Silicon Valley Product Group — The Four Big Risks (Marty Cagan, 2017)
  2. Strategyzer — Testing Business Ideas Experiment Library (poster)
  3. Wiley — Testing Business Ideas: A Field Guide for Rapid Experimentation (Bland and Osterwalder, 2019)
  4. Strategyzer — Testing Business Ideas: Book Summary and Key Takeaways (2025)
  5. Strategyzer — How Strong Is Your Innovation Evidence? (Alex Osterwalder, 2017)
  6. Kohavi and Longbotham — Online Controlled Experiments and A/B Tests, Encyclopedia of Machine Learning and Data Science (2023)
  7. CB Insights — Top reasons startups fail (report, March 2026)
  8. Product Talk — Assumption Testing: Everything You Need to Know to Get Started (Teresa Torres, 2023)
  9. Thoughtworks — How to Implement Hypothesis-Driven Development (Barry O'Reilly, 2014)
