title: Deploying a Containerized Web Application on AWS ECS Fargate using Terraform and AWS CodeBuild
description:
Table of Contents

Introduction
Business Requirements
Architecture
Pre-requisites
Implementation Steps in Words
Technical Implementation Steps
Pipeline Configuration
Key Benefits
Conclusion

1. Introduction

Modern application delivery demands speed, scalability, and reliability. Running workloads on traditional servers often introduces overhead — managing OS patches, scaling infrastructure manually, and dealing with environment inconsistencies between development and production.
This blog walks you through a fully automated, Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) driven deployment of a containerized web application on AWS ECS Fargate using Terraform and AWS CodeBuild. The entire infrastructure — from container registry to load balancer — is provisioned and torn down through automated pipelines, eliminating manual intervention and enabling repeatable deployments.
By the end of this guide, you will understand:

How to containerize a simple Apache web server using Docker
How to provision AWS ECS Fargate infrastructure using Terraform
How to automate the full deploy and destroy lifecycle using AWS CodeBuild buildspec files.

2. Business Requirements

Organizations moving to the cloud typically have the following non-negotiable requirements:

Requirement How This Project Addresses It
Zero server management AWS Fargate removes the need to provision or manage EC2 instances
Automated deployments AWS CodeBuild pipelines handle build, push, and deploy automatically
Cost control Infrastructure can be destroyed on demand using the destroy pipeline
High availability ECS service runs 2 task replicas across multiple private subnets
Security Containers run in private subnets; only the ALB is internet-facing
Centralized logging All container logs are shipped to AWS CloudWatch with KMS encryption
State management Terraform remote state is stored in S3 for team collaboration

3. Architecture

                        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                        │                        AWS Cloud (us-east-1)                 │
                        │                                                               │
   User Request         │   ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────────┐  │
 ──────────────────────►│   │  Application  │        │        VPC (custom-vpc)       │  │
        Port 80         │   │ Load Balancer │        │                               │  │
                        │   │  (internet-  │        │  Public Subnets               │  │
                        │   │   facing)    │        │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │  │
                        │   │              │◄───────┤  │ public-1 │ │ public-2 │   │  │
                        │   │  SG: SG_LB   │        │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘   │  │
                        │   └──────┬───────┘        │                               │  │
                        │          │ Port 8080       │  Private Subnets              │  │
                        │          ▼                 │  ┌──────────────────────┐    │  │
                        │   ┌──────────────┐        │  │  ECS Fargate Service │    │  │
                        │   │  Target Group │        │  │  (desired count: 2)  │    │  │
                        │   │  (Ubuntu-tg)  │───────►│  │                      │    │  │
                        │   │  Health: /    │        │  │ ┌────────┐ ┌───────┐ │    │  │
                        │   └──────────────┘        │  │ │Task 1  │ │Task 2 │ │    │  │
                        │                            │  │ │Ubuntu  │ │Ubuntu │ │    │  │
                        │   ┌──────────────┐        │  │ │:8080   │ │:8080  │ │    │  │
                        │   │  Amazon ECR  │        │  │ └────────┘ └───────┘ │    │  │
                        │   │ (ubuntu-repo)│        │  │  SG: sg_ecs          │    │  │
                        │   └──────────────┘        │  └──────────────────────┘    │  │
                        │                            └──────────────────────────────┘  │
                        │   ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐  │
                        │   │  CloudWatch  │   │   KMS Key    │   │   S3 (State)  │  │
                        │   │  Log Group   │   │ (Encryption) │   │  terraform-   │  │
                        │   └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘   │  state-files  │  │
                        │                                           └───────────────┘  │
                        └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Traffic Flow:

  • User sends an HTTP request to the ALB on port 80.

  • ALB listener forwards the request to the Target Group on port 8080.

  • Target Group routes traffic to one of the two ECS Fargate tasks running in private subnets.

  • The Ubuntu container responds with a dynamic hostname-based message
    Container logs are streamed to CloudWatch Logs, encrypted with KMS.

4. Pre-requisites

Before you can run this project, ensure the following AWS resources are already created in your account:

  • VPC named custom-vpc with public and private subnets tagged public-* and private-*.

  • Security Groups: SG_LB (for the load balancer) and sg_ecs (for ECS tasks).

  • IAM Roles: ecsTaskExecutionRole and ecsTaskRole with appropriate ECS permissions.

  • S3 Bucket: terraform-state-files-8759855 for Terraform remote state storage.

  • AWS CodeBuild Projects: One for deploy (deploybuildspec.yaml) and one for destroy (destroybuildspec.yaml)
    Docker must be enabled in the CodeBuild environment (use a build image that supports Docker)

5. Implementation Steps in Words

Here is the high-level journey from code commit to a live application:

Step 1 — Dockerize the Application
A simple Ubuntu-based Apache web server is containerized. The Dockerfile installs Apache, reconfigures it to listen on port 8080 (instead of the default 80), and serves a dynamic HTML page showing the container's hostname.

Step 2 — Define Infrastructure as Code
All AWS infrastructure is defined using Terraform across modular .tf files. Variables are cleanly separated from resource definitions, and all sensitive configuration lives in terraform.tfvars.

Step 3 — Provision ECR and Push Docker Image
The deploy pipeline first creates the ECR repository using a targeted Terraform apply, then builds the Docker image locally, authenticates to ECR, and pushes the image with the latest tag.

Step 4 — Provision Full AWS Infrastructure
With the image available in ECR, Terraform provisions the full stack: CloudWatch log group, KMS key, ECS cluster, task definition referencing the pushed image, ECS Fargate service, ALB, target group, and listener.

Step 5 — Application Goes Live
ECS pulls the container image from ECR and starts 2 task replicas in private subnets. The ALB distributes traffic across them. The application is accessible via the ALB DNS name.

Step 6 — Teardown on Demand
The destroy pipeline runs terraform destroy to cleanly remove all provisioned resources, ensuring no lingering costs.

6. Technical Implementation Steps

6.1 Dockerfile

FROM public.ecr.aws/docker/library/ubuntu:24.04

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y apache2 && apt-get clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN sed -i 's/80/8080/g' /etc/apache2/ports.conf

RUN sed -i 's/<VirtualHost \*:80>/<VirtualHost *:8080>/' /etc/apache2/sites-available/000-default.conf

RUN echo "ServerName localhost" >> /etc/apache2/apache2.conf

CMD ["/bin/bash","-c","echo \"This is web server $(hostname)\" > /var/www/html/index.html && exec apache2ctl -D FOREGROUND"]

EXPOSE 8080

The Dockerfile starts from the official Ubuntu 24.04 image pulled from the public ECR gallery. It installs Apache2, then uses sed to reconfigure Apache's listening port from the default 80 to 8080 — both in ports.conf and the default virtual host config. At container startup, it dynamically writes the container's hostname into index.html, making it easy to verify load balancing by seeing different hostnames on page refresh. Apache runs in the foreground as the main container process.

6.2 Terraform/provider.tf — Backend & Provider Configuration

terraform {
    backend "s3" {
        bucket = "terraform-state-files-8759855"
        key    = "ecs.tfstate"
        region = "us-east-1"
    }
    required_providers {
        aws = {
            source  = "hashicorp/aws"
            version = "6.51.0"
        }
    }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.aws_region
}

This file does two critical things. First, it configures an S3 remote backend to store the Terraform state file (ecs.tfstate), which is essential for team collaboration and pipeline-based deployments — the state is never stored locally. Second, it pins the AWS provider to version 6.51.0, preventing unexpected breaking changes from provider upgrades. The region is kept dynamic via a variable.

6.3 Terraform/data.tf — Reading Existing AWS Resources

data "aws_vpc" "custom-vpc" {
  filter { name = "tag:Name"  values = ["custom-vpc"] }
}

data "aws_subnets" "public" {
  filter { name = "tag:Name"  values = ["public-*"] }
}

data "aws_subnets" "private" {
  filter { name = "tag:Name"  values = ["private-*"] }
}

data "aws_security_group" "sg_lb"  { name = "SG_LB" }
data "aws_security_group" "sg_ecs" { name = "sg_ecs" }

data "aws_iam_role" "task_exec" { name = "ecsTaskExecutionRole" }
data "aws_iam_role" "task_role" { name = "ecsTaskRole" }

Rather than recreating foundational resources like VPC, subnets, security groups, and IAM roles, this file uses Terraform data sources to reference resources that already exist in the AWS account. This follows the principle of separation of concerns — the networking layer is managed independently, and this project simply reads its outputs. Subnets are looked up by tag name pattern (public-, private-), making the code flexible across multi-AZ setups.

6.4 Terraform/ecr.tf — Amazon ECR Repository

resource "aws_ecr_repository" "ecr" {
  name                 = var.ecr_repo_name
  image_tag_mutability = "MUTABLE"

  image_scanning_configuration {
    scan_on_push = true
  }
}

This creates the Amazon Elastic Container Registry repository where the Docker image is stored. image_tag_mutability = "MUTABLE" allows the latest tag to be overwritten on each pipeline run, enabling a simple continuous deployment pattern. scan_on_push = true enables automatic vulnerability scanning every time an image is pushed, providing a built-in security gate without any additional tooling.

6.5 Terraform/ecs.tf — ECS Cluster, Task Definition & Service

# CloudWatch Log Group
resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "cw_log" {
  name = var.cloudwatch_log_group
}

# KMS Key for encryption
resource "aws_kms_key" "kms" {
  description             = "kms key required for encryption"
  deletion_window_in_days = 7
}

# ECS Cluster with encrypted exec logging
resource "aws_ecs_cluster" "ecs" {
  name = var.ecs_name
  configuration {
    execute_command_configuration {
      kms_key_id = aws_kms_key.kms.arn
      logging    = "OVERRIDE"
      log_configuration {
        cloud_watch_encryption_enabled = true
        cloud_watch_log_group_name     = aws_cloudwatch_log_group.cw_log.name
      }
    }
  }
}

# Task Definition
resource "aws_ecs_task_definition" "task_def" {
  family                   = var.ecs_task_definition.family
  requires_compatibilities = var.ecs_task_definition.requires_compatibilities
  network_mode             = var.ecs_task_definition.network_mode
  cpu                      = var.ecs_task_definition.cpu
  memory                   = var.ecs_task_definition.memory
  task_role_arn            = data.aws_iam_role.task_role.arn
  execution_role_arn       = data.aws_iam_role.task_exec.arn
  container_definitions    = jsonencode([...])
}

# ECS Fargate Service
resource "aws_ecs_service" "ecs_service" {
  name            = "susseta"
  cluster         = aws_ecs_cluster.ecs.id
  task_definition = aws_ecs_task_definition.task_def.arn
  desired_count   = 2
  launch_type     = "FARGATE"
  load_balancer { ... }
  network_configuration {
    assign_public_ip = false
    security_groups  = [data.aws_security_group.sg_ecs.id]
    subnets          = data.aws_subnets.private.ids
  }
}

This is the core of the infrastructure. It creates four interconnected resources:

CloudWatch Log Group — captures all stdout/stderr from running containers
KMS Key — encrypts ECS Exec session logs and CloudWatch logs for security compliance
ECS Cluster — the logical boundary for your containerized workloads, configured with encrypted exec command logging
Task Definition — the blueprint for the container: 1 vCPU, 2 GB RAM at the task level (800 CPU units and 1500 MB reserved for the container), pointing to the ECR image URL, with awslogs log driver configured
ECS Service — maintains 2 running replicas of the task using the Fargate launch type, placed in private subnets with no public IP, wired to the ALB target group.

6.6 Terraform/alb.tf — Application Load Balancer

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "tg" {
  name        = var.target_group.name
  port        = var.target_group.port
  protocol    = var.target_group.protocol
  target_type = var.target_group.target_type
  vpc_id      = data.aws_vpc.custom-vpc.id
  health_check {
    enabled           = var.target_group.health_check_enable
    healthy_threshold = var.target_group.healthy_threshold
    interval          = var.target_group.interval
    path              = var.target_group.path
  }
}

resource "aws_lb" "alb" {
  name               = var.lb.name
  load_balancer_type = var.lb.load_balancer_type
  internal           = var.lb.internal
  ip_address_type    = var.lb.ip_address_type
  security_groups    = [data.aws_security_group.sg_lb.id]
  subnets            = data.aws_subnets.public.ids
}

resource "aws_lb_listener" "listener" {
  count             = length(data.aws_subnets.public.ids)
  load_balancer_arn = aws_lb.alb.arn
  port              = var.lb_listener.port
  protocol          = var.lb_listener.protocol
  default_action {
    type             = var.lb_listener.type
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.tg.arn
  }
}

Three resources work together to expose the application to the internet. The Target Group (Ubuntu-tg) uses ip as the target type — required for Fargate — and performs health checks against the root path / every 30 seconds, requiring 5 consecutive successes to mark a target healthy. The ALB (frontend-lb) is internet-facing, deployed across public subnets, and protected by the SG_LB security group. The Listener watches on port 80 and forwards all HTTP traffic to the target group, with one listener created per public subnet.

6.7 Terraform/var.tf & terraform.tfvars — Variables

# var.tf — type definitions and descriptions
variable "ecs_task_definition" {
  type = object({
    family                   = string
    network_mode             = string
    requires_compatibilities = list(string)
    cpu                      = number
    memory                   = number
    cpu_allocations          = number
    memory_allocations       = number
    container_name           = string
    container_port           = number
    log_driver               = string
  })
}

# terraform.tfvars — actual values
ecr_repo_name        = "ubuntu-repo"
cloudwatch_log_group = "aws-cloudwatch-group-ubuntu"
ecs_name             = "Ubuntu-cluster"
ecs_task_definition = {
  family                   = "Ubuntu-td"
  network_mode             = "awsvpc"
  log_driver               = "awslogs"
  requires_compatibilities = ["FARGATE"]
  cpu                      = 1024
  memory                   = 2048
  cpu_allocations          = 800
  memory_allocations       = 1500
  container_name           = "Ubuntu"
  container_port           = 8080
}
aws_region = "us-east-1"

The variable strategy cleanly separates type safety (var.tf) from runtime values (terraform.tfvars). Using object() types for complex variables like ecs_task_definition, target_group, lb, and lb_listener groups related settings together, avoids variable sprawl, and lets Terraform validate the entire object shape at plan time. To deploy to a different environment, only the .tfvars file needs to change — the resource definitions remain untouched.

6.8 Terraform/output.tf — Outputs

output "public_subnet_ids" {
  value = data.aws_subnets.public.ids
}

output "private_subnet_ids" {
  value = data.aws_subnets.private.ids
}

Outputs make key infrastructure values accessible after terraform apply, useful for debugging, downstream automation, or cross-stack references. Here, the resolved public and private subnet IDs are exported — helpful for verifying that the correct subnets were selected by the tag-based data source filters.

7. Pipeline Configuration

The CI/CD automation is powered by two AWS CodeBuild buildspec files that handle the complete infrastructure lifecycle.

7.1 Deploy Pipeline — deploybuildspec.yaml

version: 0.2

env:
  variables:
    TF_VERSION: "1.8.5"
    TERRAFORM_DIR: "Terraform"
    URL: "009846316881.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/"
    REPO: "ubuntu-repo"
    TAG: "latest"

phases:
  install:
    commands:
      - curl -fsSLo terraform.zip "https://releases.hashicorp.com/terraform/${TF_VERSION}/..."
      - unzip -q terraform.zip -d /usr/local/bin/

  pre_build:
    commands:
      - terraform init && terraform validate
      - terraform plan -target=aws_ecr_repository.ecr -out=tfplanecr
      - terraform apply -target=aws_ecr_repository.ecr tfplanecr
      - docker buildx build -t $URL$REPO:$TAG .
      - aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $URL
      - docker push $URL$REPO:$TAG

  build:
    commands:
      - terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan
      - terraform apply -input=false tfplan

The deploy pipeline is split into three phases:

Install Phase: Downloads and installs the pinned Terraform version (1.8.5) directly from HashiCorp releases into /usr/local/bin, ensuring a consistent toolchain regardless of the CodeBuild base image.

Pre-Build Phase: This is the most critical phase. It first creates only the ECR repository using a targeted apply (-target=aws_ecr_repository.ecr). This is necessary because the ECS task definition references the ECR image URL — the repository must exist before the full plan can succeed. Then it builds the Docker image using buildx, authenticates to ECR using the AWS CLI's temporary credential mechanism (get-login-password), and pushes the image. A 60-second sleep is included to allow ECR to fully register the pushed image.

Build Phase: With the image safely in ECR, a full Terraform plan and apply provisions the remaining infrastructure — ECS cluster, task definition, service, ALB, target group, and listener.

7.2 Destroy Pipeline — destroybuildspec.yaml

version: 0.2

env:
  variables:
    TF_VERSION: "1.8.5"
    TERRAFORM_DIR: "Terraform"

phases:
  install:
    commands:
      - curl -fsSLo terraform.zip "https://releases.hashicorp.com/terraform/${TF_VERSION}/..."
      - unzip -q terraform.zip -d /usr/local/bin/

  pre_build:
    commands:
      - terraform init -input=false

  build:
    commands:
      - terraform plan -destroy -input=false -out=destroy.tfplan
      - terraform apply -input=false destroy.tfplan

The destroy pipeline is intentionally lean. It installs the same Terraform version, initializes the backend to load the existing state, generates a destroy plan (-destroy flag), and applies it. Using a plan file (destroy.tfplan) before the apply adds an extra layer of safety — you can inspect what will be destroyed before it happens. This pipeline is typically triggered manually to tear down the environment and stop incurring costs.

7.3 Pipeline Flow Diagram

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    DEPLOY PIPELINE                               │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌───────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ INSTALL  │──►│    PRE_BUILD      │──►│       BUILD        │ │
  │  │          │   │                   │   │                    │ │
  │  │ Download │   │ terraform init    │   │ terraform plan     │ │
  │  │ Terraform│   │ terraform validate│   │ terraform apply    │ │
  │  │ v1.8.5   │   │ Apply ECR only    │   │ (full infra)       │ │
  │  └──────────┘   │ docker build      │   └────────────────────┘ │
  │                  │ docker push       │                           │
  │                  └───────────────────┘                           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    DESTROY PIPELINE                              │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌───────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ INSTALL  │──►│    PRE_BUILD      │──►│       BUILD        │ │
  │  │          │   │                   │   │                    │ │
  │  │ Download │   │ terraform init    │   │ terraform plan     │ │
  │  │ Terraform│   │ (loads S3 state)  │   │ -destroy           │ │
  │  │ v1.8.5   │   └───────────────────┘   │ terraform apply    │ │
  │  └──────────┘                            │ (destroys all)     │ │
  │                                          └────────────────────┘ │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

8. Key Benefits

No Server Management ECS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers. There are no EC2 instances to patch, resize, or monitor. AWS manages the underlying infrastructure entirely.

Immutable Infrastructure Every deployment produces a fresh infrastructure state from code. There is no configuration drift because resources are never modified in place — they are planned, applied, and optionally destroyed.

Security by Default

  • Containers run in private subnets with no public IPs.

  • Only the ALB is exposed to the internet.

  • Container logs are encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key.

  • ECR scans every pushed image for vulnerabilities automatically.

  • IAM roles follow least privilege — the task execution role and task role are separate.

Cost Efficiency Fargate charges only for the vCPU and memory reserved per running task. The destroy pipeline ensures you can completely eliminate costs when the environment is not needed, such as in a dev or demo setup.

Repeatable and Portable The entire stack is defined in code. Deploying to a new AWS region or account requires changing a handful of values in terraform.tfvars and re-running the pipeline

Observability Built In Every container's stdout and stderr are automatically captured by CloudWatch Logs under the aws-cloudwatch-group-ubuntu log group, with stream prefix app. No additional logging agents are needed inside the container.

9. Conclusion

This project demonstrates a production-aligned pattern for containerized application deployment on AWS. By combining Docker for application packaging, Terraform for infrastructure provisioning, and AWS CodeBuild for CI/CD automation, the entire lifecycle — from code to running container to teardown — is managed as code with no manual steps.
The architecture enforces security best practices by keeping workloads in private subnets, using encrypted logging, and leveraging IAM roles for all AWS API access. The modular Terraform structure makes it straightforward to extend — adding auto-scaling policies, HTTPS listeners, or additional services requires minimal changes to the existing files.
Whether you are building a proof of concept or a foundation for a production microservice, this approach gives you a reliable, auditable, and cost-controlled deployment platform on AWS.

Repository Structure

aws-app-deployment-ecs/
├── Dockerfile                  # Container image definition
├── deploybuildspec.yaml        # CodeBuild spec for deploy pipeline
├── destroybuildspec.yaml       # CodeBuild spec for destroy pipeline
└── Terraform/
    ├── provider.tf             # AWS provider & S3 backend config
    ├── data.tf                 # Data sources for existing AWS resources
    ├── ecr.tf                  # ECR repository resource
    ├── ecs.tf                  # ECS cluster, task definition & service
    ├── alb.tf                  # ALB, target group & listener
    ├── var.tf                  # Variable type definitions
    ├── terraform.tfvars        # Variable values
    └── output.tf               # Stack outputs

Built with ❤️ using AWS ECS Fargate, Terraform, and AWS CodeBuild

title: OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination
description:
arXiv:2611.17933v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In many long-horizon settings, an agent's own choices create future constraints: committing finite capacity establishes future obligations and forecloses later opportunities. Sustaining performance therefore requires both keeping evolving plans feasible and comparing the value of resource allocations with the alternatives they displace. Recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate LLM agents in continuing operations, but give less attention to how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing resource allocations as opportunities change. We introduce OutfitterBench, where agents manage an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, purchasing from a 46-product catalog and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests. Under a fixed capital ceiling, reservations and uncertain walk-in demand compete for reusable equipment whose availability changes over time. Experiments with seven frontier LLMs show that several agents underperform a simple rule-based baseline, while only the leading agent consistently surpasses it. Trajectory analysis shows that some agents apply known constraints inconsistently and make new decisions that conflict with existing commitments. Agents with more reliable fulfillment can still secure low returns from comparable commitments or delay resource reallocation. The leading agent better connects preparation with economic choices but also misses opportunities for more profitable asset use. These findings highlight limitations in sustaining coherent resource plans and reassessing their value over time. The benchmark code is publicly available at https://github.com/adminblackjack/OutfitterBench.

title: Where to Predict in Retinal OCT? Anatomy-Guided Target Selection for I-JEPA
description:
arXiv:2611.17586v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised learning aims to learn meaningful representations from unlabeled data, potentially allowing models to capture subtle anatomical variations across patients and reduce the amount of labeled data needed. Image-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA) learns by predicting target-region representations from visible context rather than reconstructing pixels. However, its uniform target placement does not account for the anatomical structure of retinal OCT, where retinal tissue occupies only part of each B-scan. We investigate anatomy-guided target selection using image intensity and predicted retinal segmentation while retaining the I-JEPA architecture and latent prediction objective. We compare anatomy-guided rectangular targets, anatomy-shaped targets and coverage-constrained placement with uniform masking, and evaluate the learned representations using linear probing for glaucoma classification on FairVision. We found that rectangular targets guided by image intensity achieved the highest linear-probe AUC in our comparisons. We show that anatomically meaningful target selection is promising for retinal OCT representation learning, while greater anatomical specificity did not consistently improve performance.

title: A four-eyes approval in a Uniface service - one table, two rules, and the gaps it leaves
description:
Some actions in the customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 should not be done by one person alone: writing off an open invoice, changing a price by more than a few percent, moving a customer to another account owner, paying a large supplier bill. The app got a four-eyes approval for these four cases.

It is a small service - one table, five operations - but the details decide whether it actually helps. This article walks through them, including the parts it does not cover.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition and SQLite 3.50.2, October 2026.

The table 

CREATE TABLE APPROVAL (
  APPROVAL_ID    INTEGER NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  APPROVAL_TYPE  VARCHAR(12) NOT NULL,   -- WRITEOFF, PRICE, TRANSFER, BILL
  REF_ID         INTEGER NOT NULL,       -- invoice, product, customer or bill
  AMOUNT_CENTS   INTEGER,                -- amount or new price
  NEW_VALUE      VARCHAR(100),           -- new owner for TRANSFER
  REQUEST_NOTE   VARCHAR(200),
  STATUS         VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,   -- PENDING, APPROVED, REJECTED
  REQUESTED_AT   DATETIME NOT NULL,
  REQUESTED_BY   VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  DECIDED_AT     DATETIME,
  DECIDED_BY     VARCHAR(30),
  DECISION_NOTE  VARCHAR(200)
);
CREATE INDEX IX_APPROVAL_STATUS ON APPROVAL (STATUS, REQUESTED_AT);

One generic table instead of one per action type. The reference is a plain ID whose meaning depends on the type; the payload is either an amount or a short text. That is less strict than four specific tables, but the list of open requests is one query and the history of all decisions is one table.

When is an approval needed?

The thresholds are settings, so they can change without a release:

Type Needs approval when Setting (default)
WRITEOFF amount above the limit APPROVAL_WRITEOFF_CENTS (5000)
PRICE change above a percentage of the old price APPROVAL_PRICE_PCT (10)
BILL gross amount above the limit APPROVAL_BILL_CENTS (100000)
TRANSFER always -

The check is its own read-only operation, so the user interface can ask before it offers the button:

    call SETTING_NUM("APPROVAL_PRICE_PCT", "10", vLimit)
    if (vOld = 0)
        if (vAmount > 0)
            pNeeded = 1
        endif
        return 0
    endif
    call COUNT_SQL("SELECT ABS(%%(vAmount) - %%(vOld)) * 100.0 / %%(vOld) FROM (SELECT 1 AS X)", vPct)
    if (vPct > vLimit)
        pNeeded = 1
    endif

The special case vOld = 0 is not cosmetic: a product without a price would otherwise divide by zero, and any first price is a 100 % change anyway.

The request validates everything up front

REQUEST checks that the action could be executed right now: the invoice exists and is still open, the product exists, the new owner is an active user, the bill is still open. A write-off also needs a reason.

    if (vType = "WRITEOFF")
        call GET_TEXT("SELECT STATUS FROM SALES_DOC WHERE DOC_ID = %%(pRefId) AND DOC_TYPE = 'INVOICE'", vStatus)
        if (vStatus != "ISSUED" & vStatus != "PARTLY_PAID")
            pError = "The invoice %%(pRefId) does not exist or is not open."
            return -1
        endif
        ...
        if (vNote = "" | $length(vNote) > 60)
            pError = "A write-off needs a reason with at most 60 characters."
            return -1
        endif

And there can only be one open request per object and type:

    call COUNT_SQL("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM APPROVAL WHERE APPROVAL_TYPE = '%%(vType)' AND REF_ID = %%(pRefId) AND STATUS = 'PENDING'", vCount)
    if (vCount > 0)
        pError = "There is already a pending request for this object."
        return -1
    endif

Without that rule, two people can request two different write-offs for the same invoice, and the approver sees two plausible requests without knowing they compete.

Rule 1: someone else decides

Approving and rejecting require the administrator role - and the decider must not be the person who asked:

entry OTHER_ADMIN
params
    string pRequestedBy : IN
    string pUser : OUT
    string pError : OUT
endparams
variables
    string vRole
endvariables
    pError = ""
    activate "USER_SVC".CURRENT_USER(pUser, vRole)
    if (pUser = pRequestedBy)
        pError = "A request must be decided by another administrator."
        return -1
    endif
    return 0
end

This is checked on the server side, in the service, not by hiding a button. A test logs in as the requesting administrator, tries to decide the request and expects this error.

Rule 2: the approver executes

The approval is not a flag that the requester checks later. The APPROVE operation performs the action itself, by calling the same service operation that would otherwise be called directly:

    if (vType = "WRITEOFF")
        activate "SETTLE_SVC".WRITE_OFF(vRefId, vAmountText, vNote, vPaymentId, pError)
    elseif (vType = "PRICE")
        activate "PRODUCT_SVC".UPDATE_PRODUCT(vRefId, "", "", vAmountText, -1, 0, pError)
    elseif (vType = "TRANSFER")
        activate "OWNER_SVC".SET_OWNER(vRefId, vValue, pError)
    else
        activate "PAYABLE_SVC".PAY_BILL(vRefId, "", pError)
    endif
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    ...
    sql "UPDATE APPROVAL SET STATUS = 'APPROVED', DECIDED_AT = datetime('now', 'localtime'), DECIDED_BY = %%(vUserLit), DECISION_NOTE = %%(vDecisionLit) WHERE APPROVAL_ID = %%(pApprovalId)", "CUSTOMERS"

Two reasons for this order:

  • What was approved is what happens. The amount and the new price come from the request row, not from a second input. Nobody can approve 40.00 and then book 400.00.
  • The existing rules still apply. The write-off goes through the settlement service with all its checks and its own audit trail. If the invoice was paid in the meantime, the write-off fails, the operation returns the error, and the request stays PENDING for a decision.

The status is only set after the action succeeded. Action and status update run in the same transaction, so a failure in between doesn't leave an executed action with a pending request - as long as the caller rolls back on an error.

Rejecting needs a reason (1 to 200 characters) and only sets the status.

What this does not protect against

This is the part readers will ask about, so here it is up front.

The direct path still exists. SETTLE_SVC.WRITE_OFF and the other operations were there before the approval service, and they still work when called directly by a user with the right role. The four-eyes rule holds only as long as the user interface routes these actions through REQUEST. A hard guarantee would need each of the four operations to check for an approved request itself - and then the approver would need a way past that check. I chose the softer version and wrote it down.

One person with two accounts. The check compares user names. An administrator who can create users can create a second administrator account. The usual answer is organisational: user administration in different hands.

Time between request and decision. The request validates the state at request time; the approval re-validates by executing the action. A price change requested at 10 % but approved after someone else changed the price will apply the requested new price anyway. Whether that is right depends on the business; here it is accepted.

What the tests cover

  • The limits per type, including the price of 0.
  • Requests of all four types are stored as pending; a second request for the same object is refused; requests for objects that don't exist or aren't open are refused.
  • Approving executes the price change, the write-off and the customer transfer.
  • Rejecting without a reason fails and leaves the object unchanged.
  • The requester cannot decide their own request.
  • A user with only the edit role can request and list, but not decide.

One case is not automated yet: an action that fails at approval time (for example an invoice paid in the meantime) must leave the request pending. It is the next test I would add.

Takeaways

Check "who decides" in the service, not in the user interface.

Let the approval execute the action with the stored values, through the existing operations.

Validate on request and again on execution; set the status only after the action succeeded.

One pending request per object.

Write down what the design doesn't cover. Someone will ask.

title: Adversarially Batched Online Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.17500v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce adversarially batched online learning, where the learner may update its decision rule only at a restricted set of time steps. Equivalently, the time horizon is partitioned into batches, within which the learner must use a fixed policy. We study this model for four canonical problems: stochastic bandits, online convex optimization, prediction with expert advice, and adversarial bandits. For stochastic bandits, we identify a universal complexity measure based on relative batch growth and establish both gap-dependent and gap-independent regret bounds. We show that the multiplicative penalty relative to the standard gap-dependent complexity can grow superlinearly in batch hardness. For the remaining three, we show that the optimal regret is tightly characterized by the 2-norm of the batch-length sequence. The upper bound is achieved by a batch-oblivious learner who does not know the batch structure, via a generic adaptive doubling trick tailored to this complexity measure. In contrast, the lower bound holds even for batch-aware learners.

title: Reasoning Models Confabulate to Defend Injected Beliefs About Their Own Requests
description:
arXiv:2611.17958v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring and self-report are proposed as levers for AI oversight, on the assumption that a model's account of what it is doing is anchored to what it was asked. We show this anchor can be cut. An activation edit invisible in the prompt text, the injected forming-trace of an off-topic concept, overwrites a reasoning model's belief about its own request: across six models spanning scale, architecture, and recipe, the injected topic becomes the task it reasons about, reports back, and answers: the forced quote-back returns the injected topic in 47 of 48 model-concept cells, and on the four models with clean final haiku the injected answer follows in 99% of generations. Warnings barely move it: even one naming the true topic yields under 5% true-topic answers. Handed the truth in clean tokens, the model confabulates a story about the user ("maybe they got confused and corrected themselves") and answers with the injection anyway, its behavior and chain-of-thought corrupted together: a concrete limit on CoT monitorability. Opening the model up offers no reprieve: it attends to the true request even harder after edits, yet that attention is causally inert, and the injected content rides intact task circuits, so attention maps and circuit attributions read as on-task too; the same edit redirects the request's language and format, not only its topic. What the injection reaches is the model's reference to its own input; what it elicits is its defense of it.

title: YouTube transcript APIs: existing captions or speech-to-text
description:
Choose an existing-caption API when you need the text and timestamps already published on YouTube. Choose a service with documented speech-to-text fallback when videos without captions must still yield text, and budget for minutes rather than assuming one cheap request. Official YouTube captions require video-management permission; a self-hosted library shifts operations to you. The hosted APIs below differ in both missing-track behavior and billing.

Provider Text source and timestamps Entry price and unit Free or trial When to choose it
YouTube Data API captions (official) Authorized caption-track download; the caller must be allowed to edit the video. Timed subtitle formats, not arbitrary public-video access or STT. 200 quota units per captions.download call; not a USD-per-1,000 tariff. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC Uses the project’s API quota; not a transcript trial package. Owners or authorized managers downloading their own caption tracks.
youtube-transcript-api (jdepoix) Self-hosted Python library reading existing manual or YouTube-generated tracks; timed snippets. No hosted STT fallback. Open-source software: $0 license fee; your compute and any proxy costs are separate. Not directly comparable to hosted requests. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC No SaaS trial; run it yourself. Teams comfortable operating extraction and handling blocked cloud IPs.
Supadata Existing transcripts with timestamps; AI speech recognition fallback when captions are absent. Basic: $5/month equivalent, billed $60/year, 300 credits/month. Existing transcript: 1 credit; generated: 2 credits/video minute. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC Free: 100 credits/month; generated minutes consume that budget faster than existing-track requests. Applications that need text even when no caption track exists and can budget for STT.
TranscriptAPI Transcript JSON with or without timestamps. Public pages checked do not establish whether missing captions trigger STT. Monthly: $5 for 1,000 credits; 1 transcript = 1 successful request = 1 credit. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC 100 free trial credits, no card required. A simple successful-request allowance; confirm missing-caption behavior if it is essential.
Captapi Existing captions: its FAQ says missing tracks return 404 no_captions, charged 0 credits. Transcript timestamp fields were not established by the public pages checked. Starter: $9/month for 2,000 credits. Transcript-specific credits/request not verified; do not read this as 2,000 transcripts. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC 100 lifetime credits after email verification; not a monthly refill. Teams using its wider API catalog and accepting an explicit no-captions failure.
FlashData YouTube Data Transcript defaults to YouTube automatic captions; Captions defaults to uploader tracks. Both return timed text. No generated transcription, translation or source fallback. PAYG: $0.50/1,000 standard requests; no monthly fee. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC Shared new-account trial credits; failed requests are not billed. Applications needing existing tracks with explicit source selection and timestamp segments.

FlashData’s Google Search and YouTube Download are separate products sharing the account key. Download bytes are not the billing unit for the YouTube Data row above.

An automatic YouTube caption is still an existing track

“Automatic” can describe text YouTube has already generated, or a provider generating new text from audio now. These are different operations. The jdepoix library reads available manual or generated tracks and supports YouTube-provided translations. Google’s authorized captions.download also has a translation parameter. Neither fact means FlashData translates or generates a missing track.

For FlashData, Transcript selects automatic captions by default and Captions selects uploader captions by default. The auto parameter explicitly selects the source; the API does not silently switch sources. Both return timestamp segments and full text. If the requested track or language does not exist, there is no STT fallback.

When missing captions must still produce text

Supadata explicitly documents AI speech recognition through the same endpoint when captions are absent. Its generated-transcript unit is video minutes, while existing-transcript retrieval uses credits per request. Its pricing page gives a 100-credit monthly free budget; a product-page phrase of “100 requests/month” should not be read as 100 arbitrarily long generated transcripts.

Captapi documents a no_captions error rather than an automatic transcription fallback. TranscriptAPI’s public pricing and examples establish timestamps and one-credit successful requests, but did not establish its no-caption policy in this review. If this behavior determines your choice, ask for the endpoint’s documented behavior instead of inferring it from “transcript API.”

Keep quota, request fees and usage rights separate

The official YouTube captions API requires OAuth authorization and permission to edit the video. Its 200 quota units are not a dollar rate and cannot be converted into a hosted API’s price per 1,000 requests without inventing an exchange rate. For self-hosted youtube-transcript-api, operating costs and cloud-IP blocks belong to the caller.

FlashData Extended Search has a different rate from standard YouTube Data requests and is unrelated to retrieving a transcript. A license check reports whether a video is labeled Creative Commons; it does not grant training rights. Trial credits are shared across the account. A job marked failed is not billed; a client timeout alone does not prove that the job failed.

Implementation after selection

For FlashData, read the Supadata comparison, JavaScript transcript tutorial, caption-language guide, Transcript reference and Captions reference.

Where the numbers come from

All prices are in USD. Official pages were checked on 2026-11-15 UTC. This is a vendor-document comparison published by FlashData, not an independent performance benchmark.

  • YouTube captions.download: authorization, edit permission, subtitle formats and 200 quota units.
  • youtube-transcript-api README: open-source library, existing tracks, translation and IP-blocking behavior.
  • Supadata pricing and YouTube transcript product: annual-billed Basic allowance, existing-track credits and generated minutes.
  • TranscriptAPI: monthly credits, trial and timestamp example; no verified STT price.
  • Captapi pricing and FAQ: credits, lifetime trial and no_captions behavior; transcript-specific credit cost not verified.
  • FlashData pricing, Transcript and Captions: standard data requests and existing timed tracks only.

Originally published at FlashData.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Scientific Paper Search: Retrieval Success and Inference Latency on Mac Studio and NVIDIA A100
description:
arXiv:2611.17929v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific literature search can benefit from locally deployed LLM assistants, which reduce reliance on hosted model providers while giving research teams greater control over their data and infrastructure. This work investigates whether open-weight models can support web-assisted paper retrieval under practical computing constraints. We first characterize inference latency as the input context grows from 512 to 128k tokens on a Mac Studio and a server equipped with two NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We then evaluate eight models on the retrieval of 70 papers from seven scientific repositories, using queries that represent three levels of domain knowledge. The results show that retrieval success depends strongly on the selected model and the specificity of the query. And that A100 GPUs are generally faster than the Mac Studio, but its unified memory allows larger models that could not be loaded in the tested GPU configuration.
