title: What Is Web Development? A Complete Beginner's Guide
description:
You typed "what is web development" into a search box, and every answer was either a dictionary definition or an advert for a course. Today I'll give you the real map: what web development is, the three languages behind every page, what the browser does and what the server does, how a page reaches your screen, and how to start without drowning. Every piece of code here runs, and some of it you'll click yourself.

Web development, in plain words

Web development is building the things that run in a web browser, and the machines behind them that make those things work. The page you're reading now, your online banking, the form where you book a dentist appointment, the admin screen behind a web shop: someone wrote all of that, and writing it is web development. That's the whole definition. Everything else in this article is detail.

Here's a comparison I'll keep coming back to. A website is a restaurant. The dining room is what you see: the tables, the menu, the look of the place. That's the front end, the part that runs in your browser. The kitchen is where the real work happens, out of sight: the orders, the stock, the recipes. That's the back end, the server. And the waiter who carries your order in and your food out is the connection between the two. We'll meet all three today, and we'll build a tiny version of each.

How to read this. If you're starting from zero, read top to bottom, and don't skip the code, because the code is the point. If you've built a page or two and the part that confuses you is "what does the server actually do", jump to the section where we build one. If you already work as a developer and you're here to send this to someone, the parts marked "for advanced readers" are the bits I'd want a junior to hear from you.

Why this feels so confusing when you start

I wanted to do this since I was about twelve. An older cousin of mine went to a technical school, and watching him was enough to know what I wanted. So I went looking for material, and there's an ocean of it. Videos, courses, roadmaps with two hundred boxes. And almost nobody is direct. Nobody sits you down and says: here's what this is, here's how the pieces connect, here's where you start.

Courses were the worst for this. I finished them and still felt I knew nothing. They taught me to find prime numbers in a loop and pull a name out of an array, and never once showed me where that turns up in a real website. I wrote about that whole problem in why courses leave you feeling like you know nothing, so I won't repeat it here. The short version: you get the pieces, and nobody connects them.

Why does the confusion exist at all? Because the web wasn't designed in one go. It grew. The first web pages, in the early nineties, were documents with links between them. Then people wanted them to look nice, so a language for styling was added. Then they wanted pages that react when you click, so a programming language was put into the browser. Then they wanted logins and shopping carts, so servers and databases got involved. Each layer landed on top of the last one, over thirty years, built by different people solving different problems.

When you learn it the way most tutorials teach it, layer by layer, you get each piece without the reason it exists. That's the confusion. It isn't you. So let's do it the other way round: first the map, then the pieces.

The basics of web development: three languages, two places, one conversation

That's the whole map, and I want you to hold on to it, because every tool you'll ever hear about fits somewhere on it.

  • Three languages. HTML gives a page its structure: this is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is a link. CSS gives it its look: colours, spacing, fonts, where things sit. JavaScript gives it behaviour: what happens when you click, type or scroll.
  • Two places. The browser, on the visitor's phone or laptop, is where the front end runs. The server, a computer somewhere that's always on, is where the back end runs: it keeps the data and decides what the visitor is allowed to do.
  • One conversation. The browser asks for something, the server answers. A request, a response. Every page load, every "add to cart", every login is one of those conversations.

Look, that's all it is. Three languages, two places, one conversation. When a new tool shows up, and one shows up every month, ask which part of the map it belongs to, and it stops being scary. React is a JavaScript tool for the browser. PostgreSQL is a place to keep data, next to the server. Next.js is a tool that works on both sides. Nothing escapes the map.

Now let's build each piece, small enough to understand and real enough to run.

Step 1: HTML, the structure. A website is a folder of files

Here's something that surprised me early on: a website is a file. A few files, in a folder. Your browser opens them the way a music player opens a song. So let's make one. Create a folder called my-site, and inside it a file called index.html. Open it in any text editor and type this in.

my-site/index.html

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
    <title>Emily's page</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css" />
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hi, I'm Emily</h1>
    <p>I'm learning web development, one page at a time.</p>
    <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/">The site I read most</a>
    <script src="script.js"></script>
  </body>
</html>

Every line here does a job, so let's go through them.

  • The first line, doctype html, tells the browser "this is modern HTML, use the current rules". Leave it out and browsers fall back to an old compatibility mode where some CSS behaves strangely. It costs you nothing to keep it.
  • html lang="en" is the root element, the box that holds everything. The lang part tells screen readers how to pronounce the text and tells search engines what language the page is in.
  • head holds information about the page. None of it is drawn on screen. The charset line makes sure letters like é display correctly. The viewport line stops phones from zooming the page out to desktop size. The title is what you see in the browser tab, and what Google shows as the headline of a search result. The link line loads our stylesheet, which we'll write next.
  • body holds what you see. h1 is the main heading; a page should have exactly one. p is a paragraph. a is a link, and href is where it goes.
  • The script line at the bottom loads our JavaScript. It sits at the end on purpose: by the time it runs, the heading and paragraph already exist. We'll see what breaks if you move it.

A word on words. Those things in angle brackets are tags, and a tag with its content is an element. HTML is the bones of every page. If you stripped a beautiful website of all its styling and all its interactivity, what would be left is the HTML, like the framing of a house before the paint and the furniture arrive.

Save the file and double-click it. Your browser opens it and shows a heading, a sentence and a link. It looks plain. That's correct. You've made a website. No, really: that file is a website. Put it on a server and anyone on earth can open it. Everything from here on is making it look better, do more, and talk to other computers.

Step 2: CSS, the look

Now create styles.css in the same folder. A CSS file is a list of rules, and each rule says the same thing: find these elements, and make them look like this.

my-site/styles.css

body {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  max-width: 40rem;
  margin: 3rem auto;
  padding: 0 1rem;
  color: #1f2937;
}

h1 {
  color: #0f766e;
}

a {
  color: #0f766e;
  text-decoration: underline;
}
  • body { ... } is a rule. The word before the curly braces is the selector, the thing to find; here it's the body element, so these settings apply to the whole page. Inside the braces are declarations: a property, a colon, a value, a semicolon.
  • font-family: system-ui, sans-serif tells the browser to use the operating system's own font, and if it can't, any font without serifs. Lists like this are fallbacks, read left to right.
  • max-width: 40rem stops lines of text from growing wider than about 640 pixels. A rem is a unit relative to the default text size, which is 16 pixels unless the visitor changed their browser settings, so 40rem is usually 640. Long lines are hard to read; this is the single cheapest thing you can do for readability.
  • margin: 3rem auto puts space above and below the page, and auto on the left and right splits the leftover space evenly, which centres the box. Yes, centring in CSS can be this easy. Not always, but here.
  • padding: 0 1rem keeps the text off the screen edge on a phone. Remove it and your words will touch the glass.
  • The h1 and a rules give the heading and the link a teal colour. The link keeps its underline on purpose: an underline is how people know something is clickable.

What breaks if you delete the link line from the head of index.html? Nothing errors. The page goes back to the browser's defaults: black text, the default serif font, full width. CSS never breaks a page. It just stops dressing it. That's the whole relationship: HTML is the person, CSS is the clothes. Same person, different outfit.

If you want to build a complete page this way, with a proper layout and the box model explained, the HTML and CSS beginner guide walks you through a real one from an empty folder, and flexbox versus grid shows you how to arrange things once you've got more than a few on the page.

Step 3: JavaScript, the behaviour

Now the third file, script.js. HTML and CSS describe a page. JavaScript lets the page do something. Here's the smallest useful example I know: a heading that counts how often you click it.

my-site/script.js

const heading = document.querySelector("h1");
let clicks = 0;

heading.addEventListener("click", () => {
  clicks = clicks + 1;
  heading.textContent = "You clicked me " + clicks + " times";
});
  • document.querySelector("h1") searches the page for the first h1 element and hands it back. We store it in a constant called heading, so we've got a handle on that element, like a remote control for it.
  • let clicks = 0 creates a variable: a named box that holds a value, starting at zero. let means the value can change later. const, on the line above, means it can't.
  • heading.addEventListener("click", ...) says: when a click happens on this heading, run the function that follows. An event is anything that happens on the page: a click, a key press, the page finishing loading. Listening for events is most of what front-end JavaScript does.
  • The part in parentheses with the arrow is the function: a block of code waiting to be run. It adds one to clicks, then replaces the text inside the heading with a new sentence. textContent is the text between the tags, and setting it changes the page immediately.

Reload the page and click the heading. "You clicked me 1 times". Click again: 2. Nothing reloaded. The page changed itself. That's what JavaScript is for, and that's the feeling you're chasing for the first few weeks: a page that reacts.

Yes, "1 times" is bad grammar. Leave it in. It's a good first bug to fix on your own, and the fix is an if statement, which you'll learn in your first week.

Now the promised breakage. Move the script line from the bottom of the body up into the head, reload, and click the heading. Nothing happens. Open the browser's console (press F12) and you'll see an error that every web developer has met: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'addEventListener'). The browser reads your file from top to bottom. In the head, the script ran before the heading existed, so querySelector found nothing and returned null, and you can't add a listener to nothing. Order matters, and now you know why.

All three together, live

Here's a small page you can use right now, inside this article. Type a name and press the button. Click the counter. Then open the HTML, CSS and JavaScript tabs and read the source: it's the same three languages doing the same three jobs as in our folder, just on one page.

Live demo: All three languages on one page. It runs right in the page, so try it in the original article.

A few things in there are worth a closer look, because they come up in every real form you'll ever build.

  • In the HTML, the label has for="name" and the input has id="name". That pairs them: clicking the label focuses the input, and a screen reader announces "Your name" when the input is selected. The button has type="submit", so pressing Enter in the input submits the form too. The counter button has type="button", so it doesn't.
  • The answer paragraph has aria-live="polite". That asks screen readers to read out the greeting when it appears, without interrupting. One attribute, and the page works for people who can't see it.
  • In the CSS, display: flex on the form puts the label, input and button in one row, gap is the space between them, and flex-wrap lets them drop onto a second row on a narrow phone. The rest is colour and padding.
  • In the JavaScript, the form listens for the submit event. The first line inside it, event.preventDefault(), stops the browser from doing its default thing, which is to send the form to a server and reload the page. We've got no server yet, so we handle it ourselves. trim() removes spaces from both ends of what was typed, and if nothing is left, we show a message and stop with return. Otherwise we build the greeting.

Take preventDefault out in your head: the page would reload and the greeting would vanish before you could read it. That one line is the difference between "the page reacts" and "the page restarts". You'll write it in every form you ever make.

One honest note. This demo checks the name in your browser only. In a real app, anything that matters is checked again on the server, because the browser belongs to the visitor, not to you, and anyone can change what it sends. That idea is big enough to get its own article: why you check a login form twice. For now, just remember: the browser is the dining room. You don't let guests into the kitchen.

How a page reaches your screen

Now the conversation. You type codefromscratch.org into the address bar and press Enter. In the half second before the page appears, this happens.

  • Address lookup. Your browser asks the Domain Name System, DNS, for the numeric address of codefromscratch.org. DNS is a phone book: you know the name, it gives you the number. Computers talk to numbers, not names.
  • Connection. The browser opens a connection to that number. With https, the connection is encrypted first, which is what the padlock in the address bar means: nobody between you and the server can read what passes through.
  • Request. The browser sends a short message in a format called HTTP: "GET /blog/what-is-web-development-beginners-guide". GET means "give me", and the path says which page.
  • Response. The server reads the request, maybe asks a database for the article, builds the HTML and sends it back with a status code. 200 means "here you go".
  • Rendering. The browser reads the HTML, notices it references a stylesheet and some scripts, asks for those too, and then draws the page. JavaScript runs, and the page becomes interactive.

Those five steps are the version MDN teaches in How the web works, with a few more details if you want them. Steps one to three are plumbing; you'll learn enough to understand them, and you don't need to become a network engineer. Step four is the back end. Step five is the front end. The whole industry lives in those two.

You can watch two of these steps yourself. Open a terminal, the black window with text, and type this.

terminal

nslookup codefromscratch.org

The answer looks something like "Addresses: 64.29.17.1, 216.198.79.1". Two numbers, because hosting companies answer from more than one machine, and the numbers can change over time. That's step one, done by hand. Now step three and four.

terminal

curl -I https://codefromscratch.org/

output (shortened)

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Server: Vercel

curl is a tool that sends requests without a browser, and -I asks for the headers only: the envelope, not the letter. The first line is the status, 200 OK. Content-Type tells the browser what kind of thing it's getting, here an HTML page. Server tells you who answered. Try the same command with a page that doesn't exist, like codefromscratch.org/nothing-here, and the first line becomes 404 Not Found. Status codes are the server's one-word answers: 200 fine, 404 no such page, 500 I broke something. You'll meet all three.

When you buy your own domain one day and wonder why it doesn't point at your site yet, that's step one again, and the domain, SSL and DNS guide walks through it.

Step 4: the server, a kitchen you can build in twelve lines

Time for the other side. A server sounds like a big machine in a cold room, and sometimes it is, but the word also means something simpler: a program that waits for requests and answers them. It runs on a computer that's always on. On your laptop it works exactly the same way, except only you can reach it.

We'll write it in JavaScript, which needs one more piece. JavaScript was born inside the browser. Node.js is JavaScript running outside the browser, as an ordinary program on your computer. That's why most beginner paths use it for the server: one language on both sides, nothing new to learn except the server idea itself.

Install it from nodejs.org and take the version marked LTS, which stands for long-term support: the one that gets fixes for years. As I write this, at the end of October 2026, Node 26 has just become the newest LTS line, and the Node team's own advice on that page is that production applications use only LTS releases. The examples here were run on Node 24, the previous LTS, and nothing in them is version-specific.

Now, in a new folder, create server.mjs. The .mjs ending tells Node the file uses the modern import syntax; name it .js and Node still runs it, but prints a warning about guessing.

server.mjs

import { createServer } from "node:http";

const server = createServer((request, response) => {
  if (request.url === "/api/greeting") {
    response.setHeader("Content-Type", "application/json");
    response.end(JSON.stringify({ message: "Hello from the server" }));
    return;
  }
  response.statusCode = 404;
  response.end("Not found");
});

server.listen(4321, () => {
  console.log("Listening on http://localhost:4321");
});
  • import { createServer } from "node:http" pulls in the function we need from a module that ships with Node. Nothing to install. The node: prefix says it's a built-in.
  • createServer takes a function and runs it once for every request that arrives. The function gets two objects: request, which holds what the browser asked for, and response, which we fill in with our answer.
  • if (request.url === "/api/greeting") checks which path was asked for. For that one path, we set a header saying "the body is JSON", write the body with response.end, and return so the code below doesn't run as well.
  • For any other path, we set the status to 404 and answer "Not found". Every server needs an answer for the unexpected; this is yours.
  • server.listen(4321, ...) starts waiting for requests on port 4321. A port is a numbered door on your computer. The browser knocks on door 4321, and this program answers. The function after it runs once, when the door is open, and prints the address.

Start it and ask it something. Two terminals: one to run the server, one to be the browser.

terminal 1

node server.mjs
# Listening on http://localhost:4321

terminal 2

curl -i http://localhost:4321/api/greeting

output

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"message":"Hello from the server"}

localhost means "this computer". The -i flag shows the headers and the body together. And the body is JSON: a text format for data that both sides understand, which looks like a JavaScript object with quotes around the names. It's how the kitchen passes plates to the waiter. Almost every server you'll ever talk to speaks it.

Now the browser side of the same conversation. Three lines.

client.mjs

const response = await fetch("http://localhost:4321/api/greeting");
const data = await response.json();
console.log(data.message);
  • fetch(...) sends a request to that address, the same GET our browser sent earlier. It returns a promise, a placeholder for an answer that isn't here yet, and await pauses this code until the answer arrives. Like ordering and sitting down, instead of standing at the counter frozen.
  • response.json() reads the body and turns the JSON text into a real object. It also takes a moment, so it also gets an await.
  • data.message is the value we put in on the server. Printed, it says "Hello from the server". Same words, other side of the counter.

Run it with node client.mjs while the server is up, and you'll see the greeting. The same three lines work inside a web page, in the browser, as long as the page came from the same server; a page from one site asking another site's server gets blocked by the browser unless that server allows it, a rule called CORS that you'll meet later and curse once.

So that's all it is. A server is a program that answers questions. The browser never walks into the kitchen; it asks the waiter, and a plate comes back. Everything you'll ever build on the back end, logins, carts, dashboards, is this loop with more rules about who may ask for what.

Note: For advanced readers: a real back end is a framework on top of this same idea (Express, Hono, or Next.js route handlers) with a database behind it. The shape never changes: request in, response out. What changes is the part that matters in production: who is allowed to ask (authentication), what they're allowed to get (authorization), how often (rate limits), and what happens when the database is down. Beginners can ignore all of that today. Nobody shipping to real users can.

And the database? It's the storeroom behind the kitchen: the place where accounts, orders and articles live so they survive the server restarting. PostgreSQL is the safe default for most new projects. How you talk to one from JavaScript is a topic of its own, covered in Prisma from zero to production, and the full picture of how every layer of a modern app fits together is in modern full-stack development, explained end to end. Read those later, not now.

Front end, back end, full stack: what the job titles mean

You'll see job adverts for front-end developers, back-end developers and full-stack developers. Now you can translate them.

Front-end developers work in the browser. They care about layout, how a button feels under a thumb on a cheap phone, whether the page works for someone using a screen reader, and whether it loads fast on a bad connection. Back-end developers work on the server. They care about data, correctness and security, and about what happens when ten thousand people press the same button in the same second. Full-stack developers do both to a usable level. Most freelancers and people on small teams end up there out of necessity: when a local shop asks you for a website, it has to work end to end, not just look nice.

You'll also hear names of tools, so here's where they sit on the map. React is a JavaScript library for building the browser side out of reusable pieces called components. Next.js is a framework around React that also runs on the server; this site is built with it. Vue and Svelte do the same job as React with different ideas about how. On the server side, JavaScript with Node is one option. Python, with frameworks like Django or FastAPI, is another. PHP still runs a huge slice of the web through WordPress, which the statistics company W3Techs counted on about 39.5 percent of all websites in October 2026. Go and Ruby are there too. All of them fit the map. None of them need picking today.

Source for the WordPress figure: W3Techs, usage of content management systems. Treat it as a survey, not a law of nature.

Where this blog stands: most of what I write uses JavaScript on both sides, with Next.js, because it's what I work with as a web developer, and because one language first is kinder to a beginner than two. That's a preference, not a verdict. The map is the same in every language.

Tools you'll meet in the first month

You don't need a powerful computer, a paid program or a particular brand of laptop. Here's what shows up on day one and stays with you for the rest of your career.

  • A code editor. VS Code is free and is what most working developers use. It colours your code, points out typos, and has an extension for everything.
  • A browser with developer tools. Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari, they all have them. Press F12 (or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac) and a panel opens that lets you inspect any page on earth, see its HTML, change its CSS live, and read the errors your JavaScript throws. You'll live in it.
  • Git and GitHub. Git keeps every version of your files so you can undo anything; GitHub is where you store and share them. Learn the five basic commands in week one. Future you will be grateful.
  • Node.js and npm. Node runs JavaScript outside the browser, as you saw. npm, which comes with it, installs code other people wrote so you don't have to write it yourself.
  • A terminal. The text window. Scary for a week, useful forever. About ten commands cover the first year.

Total cost to start: zero. Any laptop from the last several years is fine.

And then there's AI. You'll be tempted to let an AI tool write all of it, and you'll see people online who build whole apps that way without understanding a line. I use AI tools a lot in my work, and I check what they write as far as I can, because they make mistakes without meaning to, and they assume things they shouldn't. Here's the honest rule: AI is good at typing code and bad at knowing what should be typed. If you don't understand the three languages and the conversation, you can't tell when it's wrong, and it will be wrong, and the first bug you can't read will stop you cold. Learn the map first. Then AI becomes a fast colleague instead of a mystery box, and you become the person who directs it, which is where this job is going.

Beginning web development: what to learn, in what order

I'm not going to give you "become a developer in 30 days". I don't have an honest number, and anyone who gives you one is selling something. What I can give you is the order, because the order is where most people go wrong.

  • First, HTML and CSS, on a page that is yours. About you, your dog, your football team, your favourite recipes. Then find a simple page you like online and rebuild it by hand, without a template. You'll be slow and you won't always know why something works. Repetition is the teacher here.
  • Second, JavaScript, by making your page react. A dark-mode toggle. A counter. A list you can add things to. Expect to relearn functions, events and the difference between an array and an object three or four times before they stick. That is normal. People who are good at this now were confused at this exact point.
  • Third, one real small project, finished. Not five started. Pick something you'd use yourself and take it to done, ugly if necessary. Finishing is a skill, and it's the one that courses never train.
  • Fourth, the conversation. A tiny server like the one above, a form that sends to it, and data that survives a restart. The day a form on your page writes a row into a database is the day it all clicks.
  • Fifth, and only now, a framework such as React or Next.js. People who jump to React in week two get lost, because a framework hides the JavaScript under it and they never learned what's being hidden.
  • Sixth, put something online with a real address and show it to a real person. That's when it stops being an exercise.

When you reach step six, shipping a Next.js app to production covers the whole move from your laptop to a real URL. Bookmark it, don't read it yet.

On pace. You'll read "study two or three hours every day". I think that's bad advice for a beginner. Some days code goes in and some days it doesn't. You get sick, you have moods, life happens. Take a day or two off rather than get sick of the whole thing. But don't take long breaks or frequent ones either, because then no habit forms and you forget what you learned. A little, most days. One percent a day over a year beats a heroic weekend followed by a month off.

And if you're starting late, or starting over: I had to restart my education from the beginning in a new country, in a language I didn't speak yet. It was a detour, and detours are fine. If you love this enough to come back to it on evenings and weekends, you'll get there. That's not advice to overwork, and I'll keep saying so. It's advice to keep going.

Myths, corrected

  • "You need to be good at maths." You need to be good at logical thinking. The maths behind most of the web is adding, multiplying and percentages. Game engines and 3D graphics are the exception, and you're not starting there.
  • "It's too late to start at 30 or 40 or 50." Your previous career is an advantage. People who can talk to clients, write clearly and run a project are rarer in this field than people who can code.
  • "AI will replace developers." AI changes how the work is done, less typing and debugging, more directing and checking. The people who fall behind are the ones who never learn to check. Whoever lags falls behind fast, because AI moves fast. Learn the map and you're ahead of most of the room.
  • "You need to learn everything before you start." You need to learn enough to build one small thing, then the next thing as you build the next small thing. Nobody knows the whole field, and many people working in companies don't know everything and need help every week. That's normal. Not knowing yet is fine.
  • "You need a degree." You need a browser, an editor and the patience to ship things that look bad before they look good. Study if you can, it helps. It isn't the gate.

What to be careful about, and the Plan B

Here's what I'd tell myself at the start, because I got every one of these wrong. For a long time I built things from my head until I liked how they looked. No plan, no sketch, no thought about which tags I was using, whether anyone would ever find the site, or whether the people using it were safe. All of that caught up with me later.

  • Plan before you type. Even a sketch on paper. Decide what the page is for and what's on it, then build. "From my head until it looks good" works right up until it doesn't.
  • Use the right tags, not just div for everything. Screen readers and search engines read your HTML, not your screen. A heading should be an h1, a list a ul, a button a button.
  • Think about being found. The best content on earth is invisible if a search engine never shows it. I didn't think SEO mattered. It does, and it starts with a good title and clean HTML, which you now have.
  • Never trust the browser. Anything that matters, prices, permissions, passwords, is checked on the server. The front end is the dining room; the rules live in the kitchen.
  • Don't just watch. Tutorials you only watch leave nothing behind. Type every example, break it on purpose, fix it.
  • Don't ship what you can't explain. If an AI wrote it and you can't say what each line does, you don't own it yet. Ask it to explain, then check the explanation. I wrote a separate piece on learning web development with AI: what to learn yourself and what to hand off.

And the Plan B for when you're stuck, because you will be. First, read the error message out loud, word by word. It's usually telling the truth, like our null error above. Second, make the smallest possible page that still shows the problem; half the time the bug reveals itself while you shrink it. Third, search the exact text of the error. Fourth, ask someone. Write to me if you like. I mean that. Being stuck for an hour is learning. Being stuck for a week alone is how people quit.

Warning: For advanced readers who mentor beginners: the most useful thing you can give someone is the map above and one real project, not a list of technologies to learn. The list is what made them feel they knew nothing in the first place. And when you review their code, explain why, every time. The why is what they can't get from a tutorial.

So that's all it is

Three languages: HTML for structure, CSS for the look, JavaScript for behaviour. Two places: the browser and the server. One conversation: request, response. You built a page, styled it, made it react, watched a request with your own eyes, and wrote a server that answered one. That's not an introduction to web development. That's web development, small.

What next, in order. Build your first real page with the HTML and CSS beginner guide. When you've got more than a few things to arrange, read flexbox versus grid on real layouts. When your first form is ready, read why you check a login form twice and you'll see the conversation from both sides. Much later, when something of yours has real users, the production-grade code checklist is the list of habits that keep them safe.

You can do this, and you have to. If you weren't capable, I wouldn't spend my time on you. Just don't give up, and you'll always have me on your side.

This article first appeared on CodeFromScratch, where the live demos run right in the page.

title: Programmatic Location Pages in Next.js Without Creating Thin Content
description:
If you build sites for local service businesses, sooner or later someone asks for city pages. A plumbing company serves twelve suburbs, a law firm takes clients across three counties, an HVAC contractor wants to show up for "AC repair" in every town on its route. The obvious engineering answer is a dynamic route, a list of cities and a template. The obvious SEO risk is that you ship forty near-identical pages that search engines treat as thin or duplicate content and quietly ignore.

This post covers how to build location pages in the Next.js App Router so they are fast, crawlable and genuinely different from each other. The code is simple. The harder part is the data model, because the data is what makes each page worth indexing.

Start with the data, not the template

Most thin location pages come from a template that swaps one word. "We offer plumbing in {city}" repeated forty times is not forty pages of content, it is one page with a find and replace.

Before writing any routes, define what actually differs between locations. For a real service business, that usually includes:

  • The neighborhoods or zip codes actually served from that area
  • Which services are offered there (not every crew covers every service everywhere)
  • Typical response time or scheduling notes for that area
  • Local conditions that change the work, such as older housing stock, hard water, climate or permit rules
  • Projects or job types that are common in that area
  • Answers to questions customers in that area actually ask

If you cannot fill those fields with something true for a city, that city probably should not have its own page yet. That rule alone prevents most thin content.

Here is a typed shape for that data:

// lib/locations.ts
export type Location = {
  slug: string;
  city: string;
  region: string;
  areasServed: string[];
  services: string[];
  intro: string;
  localNotes: string[];
  faqs: { q: string; a: string }[];
  indexable: boolean;
};

export const locations: Location[] = [
  {
    slug: "houston",
    city: "Houston",
    region: "TX",
    areasServed: ["Heights", "Montrose", "Bellaire", "Spring Branch"],
    services: ["website-design", "local-seo", "google-ads"],
    intro: "Written specifically for this market, not generated.",
    localNotes: ["Notes that only make sense for this city."],
    faqs: [{ q: "A real local question", a: "A real answer." }],
    indexable: true,
  },
];

export function getLocation(slug: string) {
  return locations.find((l) => l.slug === slug);
}

The indexable flag matters. It lets you keep a draft location in the data without exposing it to search engines until it has real content.

Whether this lives in a TypeScript file, a CMS or a database does not change the approach. A typed file is fine for a few dozen locations and keeps everything in version control.

The dynamic route

With the App Router, one folder handles every location:

app/
  locations/
    page.tsx
    [slug]/
      page.tsx

Generate the static paths at build time so every page is pre-rendered HTML:

// app/locations/[slug]/page.tsx
import { notFound } from "next/navigation";
import { locations, getLocation } from "@/lib/locations";

export const dynamicParams = false;

export function generateStaticParams() {
  return locations.map((l) => ({ slug: l.slug }));
}

export default async function LocationPage({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>;
}) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  const loc = getLocation(slug);
  if (!loc) notFound();

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Web Design and Local SEO in {loc.city}, {loc.region}</h1>
      <p>{loc.intro}</p>

      <section>
        <h2>Areas we serve around {loc.city}</h2>
        <ul>
          {loc.areasServed.map((a) => (
            <li key={a}>{a}</li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      </section>

      <section>
        <h2>What is different about {loc.city}</h2>
        {loc.localNotes.map((n, i) => (
          <p key={i}>{n}</p>
        ))}
      </section>
    </main>
  );
}

Setting dynamicParams = false means any slug not returned by generateStaticParams gets a real 404 instead of rendering an empty template. That prevents a whole class of accidental junk URLs, such as typos in links that would otherwise produce a soft 404.

Note that in recent Next.js versions params is a Promise, so it is awaited. If you are on an older version you will see it as a plain object.

Unique metadata per page

Every location page needs its own title, description and canonical URL. generateMetadata runs on the server alongside the page:

import type { Metadata } from "next";

export async function generateMetadata({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>;
}): Promise<Metadata> {
  const { slug } = await params;
  const loc = getLocation(slug);
  if (!loc) return {};

  const url = `https://www.example.com/locations/${loc.slug}`;
  return {
    title: `Web Design and Local SEO in ${loc.city}, ${loc.region}`,
    description: `Websites and local search for ${loc.city} businesses, serving ${loc.areasServed.slice(0, 3).join(", ")} and nearby areas.`,
    alternates: { canonical: url },
    robots: loc.indexable ? undefined : { index: false, follow: true },
  };
}

Two details are worth calling out. The canonical is always self-referencing and always uses the same host, so you never end up with example.com and www.example.com versions competing. And the robots field reads the indexable flag, so drafts render for review but carry a noindex tag.

Keep the sitemap in sync

The sitemap should come from the same data, filtered by the same flag, so it can never list a page you have marked noindex:

// app/sitemap.ts
import type { MetadataRoute } from "next";
import { locations } from "@/lib/locations";

export default function sitemap(): MetadataRoute.Sitemap {
  const base = "https://www.example.com";
  return [
    { url: `${base}/locations` },
    ...locations
      .filter((l) => l.indexable)
      .map((l) => ({ url: `${base}/locations/${l.slug}` })),
  ];
}

One source of truth for routes, metadata and sitemap removes the most common drift problem, where a page gets deleted but the sitemap keeps advertising it for months.

Internal linking is part of the feature

Location pages that are only reachable through the sitemap are orphans. Search engines find them but have little reason to treat them as important. Build links into the structure:

  • A hub page at /locations that lists every indexable city with a short line about each
  • Links from each location page to the relevant service pages
  • Links from service pages back to the locations where that service is offered
  • A small "nearby areas" block on each city page linking to neighboring cities

For a working example of the hub and spoke pattern, the CodeHunterz locations hub lists each city page and links into the matching service pages, so every location is two clicks from the homepage.

The nearby block is easy to derive if you store coordinates or a manual neighbor list. A manual list is usually better, because "nearby" for a service business means "on the same route," not straight-line distance.

Add LocalBusiness schema with areaServed

Structured data helps search engines connect each page to the business and the area it covers. For a service area business without a storefront in every city, use areaServed rather than inventing addresses:

function LocationSchema({ loc }: { loc: Location }) {
  const data = {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "ProfessionalService",
    name: "Example Co",
    url: `https://www.example.com/locations/${loc.slug}`,
    areaServed: loc.areasServed.map((name) => ({
      "@type": "Place",
      name: `${name}, ${loc.city}`,
    })),
  };
  return (
    <script
      type="application/ld+json"
      dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(data) }}
    />
  );
}

Never put a fake street address on a city page to look local. It misleads users, and it conflicts with the business information search engines already have.

A build-time guard against thin pages

Rules in a document get ignored. Rules in the build do not. A small check can fail the build if an indexable location is missing real content:

// scripts/check-locations.ts
import { locations } from "../lib/locations";

const problems: string[] = [];
const intros = new Set<string>();

for (const l of locations.filter((x) => x.indexable)) {
  if (l.intro.split(" ").length < 60) problems.push(`${l.slug}: intro too short`);
  if (l.faqs.length < 3) problems.push(`${l.slug}: fewer than 3 FAQs`);
  if (l.localNotes.length < 2) problems.push(`${l.slug}: needs local notes`);
  if (intros.has(l.intro)) problems.push(`${l.slug}: duplicate intro`);
  intros.add(l.intro);
}

if (problems.length) {
  console.error(problems.join("\n"));
  process.exit(1);
}

Run it in prebuild in package.json. The thresholds are arbitrary and you should tune them, but having any automated floor changes behavior. Nobody can quietly add twenty cities with copied intros.

You can go further by comparing text similarity between pages, but in practice the duplicate check plus required fields catches the worst cases.

Performance still counts

Location pages often get traffic from mobile searches by people who need help now. Since every page here is statically generated, the HTML is fast by default. The usual things still slow pages down:

  • A large hero image on every city page. Use next/image with explicit sizes and only mark the first visible image as priority.
  • Embedding a map iframe at the top of the page. Lazy load it below the fold, or use a static image linked to the map.
  • Loading a chat widget or tracking scripts eagerly. Use next/script with lazyOnload for anything not needed on first paint.

A click-to-call link near the top of the page is often more useful to a local visitor than any of those heavy elements.

When not to build location pages

Sometimes the right engineering decision is to push back on the request. If the business genuinely serves one metro area with no meaningful differences between suburbs, one strong service area page will usually do better than fifteen weak ones. Good local SEO is about relevance and trust, not page count.

A reasonable rule: add a location page when you have something true and specific to say about that location, and the business actually wants calls from there. Otherwise list the area on a single service area page and move on. The CodeHunterz guide on SEO for service area businesses covers that decision from the marketing side, which is useful context to share with the client.

Summary

  • Model the data that actually differs between locations before writing a template.
  • Use generateStaticParams with dynamicParams = false so only real locations exist.
  • Generate unique metadata and self-referencing canonicals per page.
  • Drive the sitemap and robots rules from the same indexable flag.
  • Link locations into a hub and into service pages so none are orphaned.
  • Use areaServed in schema instead of invented addresses.
  • Add a prebuild check so thin pages cannot ship.

If you want to see how this structure looks on a production site, or you need help planning one, the team behind these notes builds Next.js sites for local businesses using this same pattern.

CodeHunterz Team

title: ERGo: Energy-Efficient Hybrid Graph Neural Network Training on Processing-In-Memory Architectures
description:
arXiv:2611.17478v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Processing-in-memory (PIM) has been proposed as an alternative computing paradigm for training Deep Neural Networks, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Despite these advancements, training GNN workloads on PIM devices necessitates off-chip memory access. This off-chip access is expensive in terms of performance and energy, thereby impacting the overall energy efficiency of the training process on PIM platforms. In this paper, we propose a novel hybrid training framework called ERGo that automatically switches from a full-parameter phase to a parameter-efficient phase during the training process with negligible loss in predictive accuracy. The parameter-efficient phase employs low-rank representations of GNN weights, effectively reducing the number of trainable parameters. This helps in reducing the off-chip access during the end-to-end training process on PIM architectures, leading to notable improvements in both performance and energy efficiency. ERGo outperforms the conventional full-parameter GNN training on a PIM-based platform by up to 3.15x in speedup and enhances energy efficiency by 10.5x. Furthermore, ERGo offers additional advantages when utilized on heterogeneous architectures incorporating non-volatile memory (NVM) and static random-access memory (SRAM). Training on the heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture typically utilizes NVM for the forward-pass and SRAM for the backward-pass. However, NVM cells suffer from low device endurance and repeated write operations due to weight updates can lead to poor lifetime. ERGo improves the lifetime of NVM devices by freezing the weights and preventing weight updates in the parameter-efficient phase. Experimental results demonstrate that ERGo improves the lifetime of heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture by up to 33x in comparison to full-parameter implementation.

title: Engineering Sub-Second WordPress Architectures: How Custom Containers Achieve 95+ PageSpeed
description:
Engineering Sub-Second Web Platforms: How Custom WordPress Containers Achieve 95+ Google PageSpeed

In modern web development, speed is not merely an engineering metric — it is the single most critical factor determining user retention, search engine rankings, and conversion rates. Yet, the vast majority of WordPress and Elementor websites suffer from catastrophic page builder bloat: massive DOM trees exceeding 2,500 nodes, dozens of unminified CSS/JS requests, and sluggish Core Web Vitals (INP, LCP, CLS).

At UCDREAMS, our engineering philosophy is straightforward: WordPress can and should load in sub-second times with 95+ scores on Google PageSpeed Insights.

Here is an architectural breakdown of how our senior engineering team designs, develops, and delivers ultra-fast, zero-bloat web platforms for international clients, startups, and agencies.

1. Eradicating Page Builder Bloat: The Container Revolution

Traditional WordPress page builders wrap every section, row, column, and widget in 4 to 7 layers of nested <div> tags. A standard 5-section homepage frequently generates over 2,200 DOM nodes.

Google's Lighthouse and Chrome UX Report (CrUX) penalize deep DOM hierarchies because every layout reflow consumes main thread compute time, spiking Interaction to Next Paint (INP).

The Container Approach:

By enforcing modern CSS Flexbox and CSS Grid containers:

  • Nested DOM depth is reduced from 7+ layers down to a lean 2-layer structure.
  • DOM node count is slashed by 65% to 75% (often below 550 total nodes).
  • Layout shifts (CLS) are eliminated by strictly defining explicit aspect ratios on all image containers and media blocks. 
<!-- Clean Semantic Container Pattern -->
<section class="hero-container" aria-label="Hero Section">
  <div class="hero-grid">
    <div class="hero-content">
      <h1>Engineering High-Performance Web Architectures</h1>
      <p>Sub-second speeds, zero bloat, and guaranteed 95+ PageSpeed scores.</p>
      <a href="https://ucdreams.com/contact-us/" class="cta-btn">Discuss Your Project</a>
    </div>
    <div class="hero-media">
      <img src="/assets/hero-architecture.webp" width="640" height="480" fetchpriority="high" alt="Web Architecture">
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

2. Granular Asset Unloading & Critical CSS Inlining

A standard WordPress theme loads all scripts and stylesheets globally across every URL, regardless of whether a page actually uses them. Contact Form 7, WooCommerce styles, slider scripts, and icon fonts bloat pages that do not need them.

Our Optimization Protocol:

  1. Conditional Asset Loading: Unregister scripts and styles for plugins that are not instantiated on the active template.
  2. Critical CSS Extraction: Inline above-the-fold critical CSS directly into the <head> while deferring non-critical styles asynchronously via media="print" onload="this.media='all'".
  3. Local Self-Hosted Typography: Google Fonts DNS lookups and external CSS roundtrips add 150-300ms of latency. We subset font glyphs to Latin-only WOFF2 and preload primary heading/body weights directly from the root domain with font-display: swap.

3. High-Converting Engineering CTAs & Dynamic CMS

Speed without maintainability is useless. We bind custom frontends directly to Advanced Custom Fields Pro (ACF Pro) or bespoke Custom Post Types. This allows marketing teams to edit copy, update images, and manage testimonials seamlessly in WordPress without ever breaking layout styling or degrading performance.

Every page is engineered as a conversion engine with clean, professional CTAs directing business inquiries to our dedicated discovery funnel: UCDREAMS Contact & Project Discovery.

4. Living Proof-of-Work: The UCDREAMS Ecosystem

Our engineering standards are demonstrated live across the entire UCDREAMS ecosystem:

  • UCDREAMS Tools Hub: A suite of 100% free, client-side, zero-server utilities running WebAssembly, WebRTC P2P streaming, and client-side ONNX models (such as our Free In-Browser Background Remover and 50GB P2P FileShareOnline).

  • ApplyPilot: A 100% free job application autofill Chrome extension engineered for tech professionals and job seekers.

title: Designing Circuit Breaker Fallbacks to Prevent Thread Exhaustion from Slow External APIs
description:
Designing Circuit Breaker Fallbacks to Prevent Thread Exhaustion from Slow External APIs

1. Anatomy of the Failure: Why Threads Get Exhausted

When an external API experiences high latency, it can trigger a cascading failure that brings down your entire system. The process unfolds as follows:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as "Client"
    participant Server as "Internal API Server"
    participant External as "External API (High Latency)"

    Client->>Server: Send Request
    Server->>External: Call External API (Establish Connection)
    Note over External: No response returned (Delayed)
    Note over Server: Worker threads remain blocked
    Client->>Server: Send Additional Requests
    Note over Server: Connection pool completely exhausted
    Server-->>Client: 504 Gateway Timeout / Connection Refused

A degradation in a single external dependency can effectively halt every endpoint in your service. To decouple this dependency and prevent cascading failures, we introduce the Circuit Breaker pattern, which operates across three distinct states: CLOSED, OPEN, and HALF-OPEN.

2. Design and Architecture

The circuit breaker implementation must satisfy the following core requirements:

  1. Threshold-Based Tripping (OPEN): Upon detecting a predefined number of consecutive failures or timeouts, immediately halt all outgoing calls to the external API.
  2. Fast Fallback (FALLBACK): While in the OPEN state, bypass the external API entirely and return cached data or safe default values, thereby protecting internal server resources and thread pools.
  3. Probing Recovery (HALF-OPEN): After a specified duration (the recovery timeout) has elapsed, allow a limited number of test requests through to verify whether the external dependency has recovered.

The following state diagram illustrates the complete lifecycle of these state transitions:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CLOSED
    CLOSED --> OPEN: Consecutive failures reach threshold
    OPEN --> HALF-OPEN: Recovery timeout elapsed
    HALF-OPEN --> CLOSED: Test request succeeds
    HALF-OPEN --> OPEN: Test request fails

3. Implementation: A Robust Validation Script with Pydantic and orjson

For input and output validation, we use Pydantic, paired with orjson for high-performance JSON serialization. This combination ensures strict type safety while keeping serialization overhead minimal under heavy load.

The following standalone script simulates the complete behavior of the circuit breaker—from detecting external API timeouts, to tripping the circuit, and finally recovering to normal operation.

import time
import orjson
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class APIRequest(BaseModel):
    user_id: str = Field(..., description="Target user ID for the request")
    action: str = Field(..., description="Action to execute")


class APIResponse(BaseModel):
    status: str = Field(..., description="Processing status (success, fallback, error)")
    data: dict = Field(..., description="Response payload or fallback values")
    latency_ms: float = Field(..., description="Response latency in milliseconds")


class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold: int = 3, recovery_timeout: float = 2.0, timeout: float = 1.0):
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.recovery_timeout = recovery_timeout
        self.timeout = timeout

        self.state = "CLOSED"  # CLOSED, OPEN, HALF-OPEN
        self.consecutive_failures = 0
        self.state_changed_at = time.time()

    def _update_state(self):
        now = time.time()
        if self.state == "OPEN":
            if now - self.state_changed_at > self.recovery_timeout:
                self.state = "HALF-OPEN"
                self.state_changed_at = now
                print("[CircuitBreaker] State Transition: OPEN -> HALF-OPEN (Allowing probe traffic)")

    def execute(self, request_func, request_payload: APIRequest) -> APIResponse:
        self._update_state()

        if self.state == "OPEN":
            print("[CircuitBreaker] State: OPEN - Skipping external API call and executing fallback.")
            return self._fallback_response("Circuit breaker is OPEN")

        start_time = time.time()
        try:
            # Simulate external API call (including timeout evaluation)
            success, latency = request_func(request_payload, self.timeout)

            if not success:
                raise TimeoutError("External API timed out or failed.")

            # Handle successful execution
            elapsed = (time.time() - start_time) * 1000
            self._on_success()
            return APIResponse(
                status="success",
                data={"message": "Normal response from external API", "user_id": request_payload.user_id},
                latency_ms=round(elapsed, 2)
            )

        except Exception as e:
            elapsed = (time.time() - start_time) * 1000
            self._on_failure()
            print(f"[CircuitBreaker] Failure Detected: {e}")
            return self._fallback_response(str(e))

    def _on_success(self):
        self.consecutive_failures = 0
        if self.state == "HALF-OPEN":
            self.state = "CLOSED"
            self.state_changed_at = time.time()
            print("[CircuitBreaker] State Transition: HALF-OPEN -> CLOSED (Normal operation restored)")

    def _on_failure(self):
        self.consecutive_failures += 1
        if self.state == "HALF-OPEN" or self.consecutive_failures >= self.failure_threshold:
            self.state = "OPEN"
            self.state_changed_at = time.time()
            print(f"[CircuitBreaker] State Transition: -> OPEN (Consecutive failures: {self.consecutive_failures})")

    def _fallback_response(self, reason: str) -> APIResponse:
        # Return safe default values (cached or static fallback)
        fallback_data = {
            "message": "Fallback data (using cached/default values)",
            "reason": reason,
            "default_permissions": ["read_only"]
        }
        return APIResponse(status="fallback", data=fallback_data, latency_ms=0.0)


# Mock external API for simulation (reproduces latency and failures)
def mock_external_api(payload: APIRequest, timeout: float):
    # Intentionally trigger a timeout for user_id "timeout_user"
    if payload.user_id == "timeout_user":
        time.sleep(timeout + 0.5)  # Delay exceeding the configured timeout
        return False, timeout + 0.5

    time.sleep(0.1)  # Normal fast response
    return True, 0.1


def main():
    breaker = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=2, recovery_timeout=1.5, timeout=0.5)

    print("=== Starting Circuit Breaker Verification Scenario ===")

    requests_sequence = [
        APIRequest(user_id="normal_user_1", action="fetch_profile"),
        APIRequest(user_id="timeout_user", action="fetch_profile"),  # 1st failure
        APIRequest(user_id="timeout_user", action="fetch_profile"),  # 2nd failure (Threshold reached -> Transitions to OPEN)
        APIRequest(user_id="normal_user_2", action="fetch_profile"),  # Immediate fallback due to OPEN state
    ]

    for i, req in enumerate(requests_sequence, 1):
        print(f"\n--- Request #{i} (User: {req.user_id}) ---")

        response = breaker.execute(mock_external_api, req)
        json_output = orjson.dumps(response.model_dump(), option=orjson.OPT_INDENT_2)
        print(json_output.decode("utf-8"))

    print("\n=== Waiting for recovery timeout (1.6s) ===")
    time.sleep(1.6)

    print("\n--- Request #5 (Testing HALF-OPEN state) ---")
    recovery_req = APIRequest(user_id="normal_user_3", action="fetch_profile")
    response = breaker.execute(mock_external_api, recovery_req)
    json_output = orjson.dumps(response.model_dump(), option=orjson.OPT_INDENT_2)
    print(json_output.decode("utf-8"))

    print("\n=== Circuit Breaker Verification Scenario Completed ===")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

💡 For immediate deployment: The complete source code suite (ZIP) for this architecture is available on Gumroad for $0+ (Pay What You Want).

4. Execution Results and Verification

Running the script above outputs the complete sequence of events—from failure detection and circuit tripping to recovery—directly to the console:

=== Starting Circuit Breaker Verification Scenario ===

--- Request #1 (User: normal_user_1) ---
{
  "data": {
    "message": "Normal response from external API",
    "user_id": "normal_user_1"
  },
  "latency_ms": 100.85,
  "status": "success"
}

--- Request #2 (User: timeout_user) ---
[CircuitBreaker] Failure Detected: External API timed out or failed.
[CircuitBreaker] State Transition: -> OPEN (Consecutive failures: 1)

    "default_permissions": [
      "read_only"
    ],
    "message": "Fallback data (using cached/default values)",
    "reason": "External API timed out or failed."
  },

--- Request #3 (User: timeout_user) ---
[CircuitBreaker] Failure Detected: External API timed out or failed.
[CircuitBreaker] State Transition: -> OPEN (Consecutive failures: 2)

As soon as consecutive failures reach the configured threshold (2), the state locks into OPEN. Subsequent requests immediately return the fallback payload without making any network calls to the external API.

Conclusion

In systems with external dependencies, failures are not a matter of if, but when. By combining strict timeouts with a circuit breaker that enforces fast fallbacks, you can isolate faults, prevent cascading thread exhaustion, and maintain overall system resilience. title: How to redesign a website without losing Google rankings
description:
A website redesign is exciting for any business. You get clean visuals, faster page loads, and updated messaging that reflects where your company is heading. But redesigns also come with a common worry: losing the search traffic you spent years building.

It is common to see traffic drop after a relaunch simply because technical details were missed during the handover. Search engine crawlers do not automatically know that a newly designed page at a fresh web address is the exact same resource that held a top ranking last week.

Whether you are freshening up an existing template or handling a full WordPress to Next.js migration, search visibility does not have to take a hit. Here is the process to keep your rankings intact before, during, and after a website redesign.

Crawl and document your current site architecture

Before your designer opens a canvas or your developer writes code, you need a complete record of your existing website. You cannot protect pages you have not cataloged.

Use a website crawler to export a complete list of every live URL, HTTP status code, title tag, and meta description. Next, open Google Search Console and your analytics dashboard to identify which specific URLs generate organic impressions, clicks, and incoming leads.

Every site has pages that look outdated to an internal team but quietly bring in valuable search queries. Categorizing your pages before touching any code ensures you do not accidentally discard top-performing content during a visual refresh.

  • High-priority URLs: Core service pages, case studies, and informational articles that already rank on page one.
  • Secondary URLs: Company details, legal notices, and utility pages that need clean metadata parity.
  • Prunable URLs: Thin or duplicate pages you deliberately plan to retire and consolidate into broader guides.

Retain core content and heading hierarchy

Designers often look to simplify page copy during a redesign. While trimming repetitive sentences makes an interface cleaner, cutting out substantive explanations can confuse search engines.

Google evaluates pages based on how well their text answers a user search query. If an existing service page ranks well because it clearly answers five specific customer questions, replacing that detailed copy with a vague three-sentence marketing slogan often hurts your visibility.

Heading structure matters just as much. Keep your primary target terms in the main H1 tag, and ensure subheadings follow a logical order from H2 down through H3. In my projects, when structuring content into custom components, I make sure the semantic hierarchy remains sound even when the visual layout looks completely new.

Match title tags, metadata, and structured data

Page titles and descriptions are among the easiest elements to lose during a platform switch. New templates and content management systems frequently ship with generic default tags, which overwrite years of deliberate search engine optimization.

Your title tags and meta descriptions should be migrated deliberately. If a page already enjoys a strong click-through rate in search results, keep that title tag identical on the new design. Changing titles at the same time as changing layouts makes it impossible to pinpoint what caused a shift if rankings fluctuate later.

Structured data also requires close attention. If your current website includes schema markup to tell search engines about your organization, local address, frequently asked questions, or reviews, that structured data must be added to the new code. Modern frameworks allow you to write clean JSON-LD structured data directly into the page header without relying on fragile third-party plugins.

Map every redirect before writing production code

Unplanned URL changes are the single largest reason websites lose traffic after a redesign. Whenever possible, keep your existing URL paths exactly as they are. If your blog posts currently sit under a specific folder path, leave them there unless you have an unavoidable strategic reason to move them.

When an address change is necessary, a permanent 301 redirect is mandatory. A 301 status code tells search crawlers that a page has moved permanently to a new location, transferring established ranking signals to the new URL.

Build a comprehensive redirect spreadsheet well before launch day. Every old URL should point directly to its closest relevant match. Pointing dozens of retired pages directly to the home page frustrates visitors who clicked looking for specific information and gives search engines poor context about where your content went.

Check Core Web Vitals and technical health

A redesign is not merely about aesthetic updates; it is your chance to eliminate the technical overhead dragging down your old site. Search engines prioritize fast, stable, and responsive user experiences through Core Web Vitals.

Google defines Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) under 2.5 seconds, Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) under 0.1, and Interaction to Next Paint (INP) under 200 milliseconds as the thresholds for a good user experience. If a new design loads heavy script libraries, uncompressed graphics, or shifting banners, your rankings can suffer regardless of how good your content is.

If speed was an issue on your previous site, run a dedicated speed and Core Web Vitals fix audit on a staging environment before public launch. Test real mobile speeds and ensure image dimensions are explicitly declared so page layouts remain stable while loading.

Verify search settings on launch day

Flipping the switch to go live is only the midpoint of a redesign project. Carrying out immediate technical checks right after DNS changes propagate prevents small oversights from turning into indexation problems.

First, inspect your robots.txt file to ensure search engines are not blocked. It is common for staging environments to use disallow rules to prevent search engines from finding test pages; leaving that directive active on your live site will cause pages to drop out of search results quickly.

Next, submit your fresh XML sitemap inside Google Search Console. Monitor the coverage and indexing reports daily for the first two weeks. Keep a close eye on your server 404 error logs so you can catch broken links and resolve missing redirects before your visitors run into dead ends.

Practical takeaways for your redesign

Redesigning your website does not have to mean risking your organic reach. By treating technical search requirements as an integral part of development rather than an afterthought, you protect the search presence your business depends on.

  • Crawl and document all existing URLs, title tags, and meta descriptions before designing new templates.
  • Keep existing URL structures unchanged wherever possible, and build 1:1 permanent 301 redirects for any paths that must move.
  • Retain the depth of your best-performing copy and maintain a logical heading structure.
  • Verify your robots.txt file and submit updated XML sitemaps immediately after changing DNS records.

Want help with this? See my WordPress → Next.js + Sanity migration service, or send me your site for a free review.

Originally published at sagarbharvadiya.com.

title: Do Mixture-of-Experts Routers Benefit from Ensembling?
description:
arXiv:2611.17472v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.
