title: A estrela andou 10 segundos de arco por ano, e a parte difícil foi dizer quando não confiar na imagem
description:
Como dois devs de Cuiabá transformaram imagens do SPHEREx em um time-lapse do céu e mediram o movimento de estrelas próximas contra o Gaia.

Piscar duas fotos

Em 1930, Clyde Tombaugh achou Plutão alternando duas fotos da mesma região do céu, tiradas com dias de diferença. As estrelas ficavam paradas; um pontinho pulava. A técnica tem nome até hoje: blink comparison.

No fim de semana de 14 e 15 de novembro, eu e o Francisco fizemos a mesma coisa, só que com imagens infravermelhas do SPHEREx, telescópio da NASA lançado em 2025. O resultado é o SkyBlink: você escolhe um ponto do céu e ele toca as imagens reais daquela região, temporada por temporada, como um pequeno vídeo.

Na demo, a Estrela de Barnard desliza diante de um fundo parado. O SkyBlink mediu 10,47 ± 0,34 segundos de arco por ano; o catálogo, com dados do Gaia, prevê 10,65 para as mesmas datas. Uma diferença de 1,7%, dentro da barra de erro.

Mas o número não é a parte de que mais me orgulho. A parte difícil foi fazer a ferramenta dizer quando a imagem não merece confiança. É disso que este post trata.

Ferramenta: https://skyblink-swart.vercel.app
Repositório: https://github.com/carvalhocaio/skyblink

O desafio e o dado

O desafio Planet X and SPHEREx, do NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, pedia uma ferramenta web pública para explorar imagens do SPHEREx e perceber como o céu muda ao longo do tempo. A inspiração declarada era o WiseView, que faz o mesmo com o telescópio WISE.

O SPHEREx mapeia o céu inteiro em 102 faixas de comprimento de onda no infravermelho, a cada seis meses. Isso significa muita imagem, e cada uma chega como um arquivo FITS com várias camadas:

Extensão O que guarda Por que importa
IMAGE o brilho medido em cada pixel é a foto em si
VARIANCE a incerteza de cada pixel define o peso de cada exposição no empilhamento
FLAGS bits de problema por pixel (quente, saturado, satélite…) separa defeito do instrumento de sinal real
ZODI o brilho estimado da luz zodiacal uma "névoa" do Sistema Solar que precisa sair antes de comparar
PSF o formato de uma estrela pontual útil para modelar fontes

Como engenheiro de dados, a primeira coisa que me chamou atenção foi que a imagem sozinha não é o dado. Sem a variância e as flags, um pixel quente vira estrela e uma diferença de filtro vira "variação". É como avaliar a qualidade de um fardo de algodão olhando só a cor: sem o laudo de HVI, você não sabe o que está vendo.

O pipeline, visto por um engenheiro de dados

O backend é FastAPI com Python 3.12, separado em domínio, adaptadores e serviços. São cerca de 3 mil linhas e 117 testes. O caminho de um pedido é este:

  1. Descoberta: consulta o serviço SIA2 do arquivo IRSA nas duas coleções do SPHEREx e junta os resultados.
  2. Temporadas: agrupa as exposições onde houver um intervalo de mais de 30 dias.
  3. Recortes: baixa só um pedaço pequeno em volta do alvo de cada exposição, com retry para os 503 frequentes do arquivo, e guarda em cache compacto (~4 MB viram ~0,19 MB).
  4. Limpeza: subtrai a luz zodiacal, remove o fundo local e mascara pixels ruins.
  5. Empilhamento: reprojeta tudo numa grade comum de 6,15" por pixel e combina com média ponderada pela variância.
  6. Renderização: uma escala de brilho por detector, fixada no primeiro quadro, para os quadros serem comparáveis.
  7. Alertas e movimento: mede a posição do alvo em cada temporada e compara com o catálogo.

A temporada funciona como a safra: o SPHEREx passa pela mesma região algumas vezes em poucas semanas e depois só volta meses depois. O agrupamento é simples de propósito:

SEASON_GAP_DAYS = 30.0


def group_into_seasons(exposures: Iterable[Exposure], gap_days: float = SEASON_GAP_DAYS) -> list[Season]:
    ordered = sorted(exposures, key=lambda e: e.mjd)
    groups: list[list[Exposure]] = []
    for exposure in ordered:
        if groups and exposure.mjd - groups[-1][-1].mjd <= gap_days:
            groups[-1].append(exposure)
        else:
            groups.append([exposure])
    return [Season(id=index, exposures=tuple(group)) for index, group in enumerate(groups)]

Uma decisão que me poupou horas: não fixar os bits das flags no código. Cada arquivo FITS descreve os próprios bits no cabeçalho, em pares de cartões MSKNnnnn (nome) e MSKMnnnn (máscara). O código lê essa tabela a cada arquivo:

_NAME_CARD = re.compile(r"^MSKN(\d{4})$")


def parse_flag_bits(header: Mapping[str, object]) -> dict[str, int]:
    bits: dict[str, int] = {}
    for key in header:
        match = _NAME_CARD.match(key)
        if match:
            plane = match.group(1)
            bits[str(header[key]).strip()] = int(header.get(f"MSKM{plane}", 1 << int(plane)))
    return bits

O empilhamento é onde o ruído cai. Cada exposição pesa pelo inverso da variância, e, com pelo menos 5 exposições, valores a mais de 4 desvios robustos (MAD) são rejeitados antes da média. É isso que apaga raios cósmicos e satélites.

O resto é engenharia de dados de sempre: cache de descobertas com validade de 24 h, resultados persistidos por versão do pipeline, um semáforo global de downloads e um teto de 8 GB no cache de recortes. Isso salvou a demo: com o IRSA fora do ar, os cinco alvos do desafio continuavam abrindo em menos de um segundo.

Conferindo com o Gaia

Uma animação bonita não prova nada. Para cada alvo, o SkyBlink mede o centro da estrela em cada temporada, corrige a posição usando estrelas de referência do fundo e compara com a previsão do catálogo (SIMBAD, com astrometria do Gaia) nas mesmas datas, incluindo a paralaxe anual.

Os cinco alvos do desafio, no detector D6 (4,41-5,01 µm):

Alvo Medido (″/ano) Previsto (″/ano) Diferença
Estrela de Barnard 10,47 ± 0,34 10,65 −0,53σ
Epsilon Indi B 4,67 ± 0,38 4,10 +1,52σ
RW Aurigae 0,49 ± 0,62 0,03 +0,75σ
WISE 0855−0714 não reportado (sinal fraco demais) – –
R Draconis não reportado (núcleo saturado) – –

Três detalhes fizeram diferença:

  • A paralaxe muda a resposta. Para Epsilon Indi B, o movimento próprio sozinho daria 4,68"/ano; nas datas observadas, a previsão correta é 4,10. Comparar com o número "de tabela" faria nosso resultado parecer perfeito (4,67 contra 4,68), por pura coincidência.
  • A barra de erro tem duas partes. Um bootstrap com 200 reamostragens das exposições dá o erro estatístico; as estrelas de referência dão o erro de alinhamento. Os dois entram em quadratura.
  • O resultado não depende do recorte. Barnard medido com campos de 6', 15' e 30' deu 10,47, 10,53 e 10,45"/ano, todos dentro de 1σ entre si.

E nem tudo saiu certo de primeira. A primeira versão usava o meio do intervalo da temporada como data, em vez da média das datas das exposições empilhadas, o que enviesava a taxa. Epsilon Indi B chegou a sair longe do previsto, porque uma estrela de referência ruim puxava o alinhamento e o erro estava subestimado. A correção foi rejeitar referências discrepantes com um critério robusto e somar o erro de alinhamento. Foram cinco versões de pipeline até aqui.

O que a ferramenta se recusa a afirmar

Esta é a parte de que mais gosto. Uma diferença entre duas imagens não explica a própria causa, então o SkyBlink mostra alertas ao lado do vídeo, sem cobri-lo:

Alerta Quando aparece
NO_COVERAGE o SPHEREx ainda não tem imagens da região
SINGLE_SEASON só há uma temporada, então não há movimento para mostrar
FEW_EXPOSURES o quadro combina poucas exposições e pode parecer ruidoso
SATURATED_CORE a estrela é brilhante demais: a posição é visível, o brilho não é medido
ALIGNMENT_DRIFT as estrelas de fundo se deslocam mais de 0,2 pixel: a mudança pode ser de alinhamento

O alerta de saturação é um bom exemplo de como uma regra ingênua engana. A primeira versão marcava saturação se qualquer exposição saturasse perto do alvo, e disparava em 8,5% a 12,5% dos quadros sem estrela brilhante nenhuma. Pixels isolados marcados como saturados aparecem em cerca de 1 a cada 2.000 pixels; com dezenas de exposições, algum sempre cai no centro. A regra atual exige repetição:

SATURATED_CORE_MIN_FRACTION = 0.25
SATURATED_CORE_MIN_EXPOSURES = 2


def is_saturated_core(saturated_exposures: int, n_exposures: int) -> bool:
    return (
        saturated_exposures >= SATURATED_CORE_MIN_EXPOSURES
        and saturated_exposures >= SATURATED_CORE_MIN_FRACTION * n_exposures
    )

Com ela, os falsos alarmes ficam abaixo de 0,06%, e estrelas realmente saturadas continuam saturando em 100% das exposições.

O movimento também é recusado quando a medida é fraca: sinal/ruído abaixo de 10, poucas exposições, menos de duas temporadas ou menos de três estrelas de referência consistentes. A resposta diz o motivo. Para WISE 0855, a anã marrom mais fria conhecida, o sinal/ruído na primeira temporada foi 3. "Dados insuficientes" é uma resposta legítima.

Três limites ficaram documentados no README:

  • Brilho não é variabilidade. O SPHEREx usa filtros lineares variáveis: dentro de uma faixa, cada exposição vê um comprimento de onda um pouco diferente, e cada temporada mistura essas exposições em proporções diferentes. Uma estrela pode "mudar de brilho" só por isso.
  • A barra de erro cobre ruído e alinhamento, mas não deslocamentos de centro causados por cor.
  • Objetos rápidos somem. Cada quadro empilha semanas de exposições; asteroides e cometas se movem durante o empilhamento e são rejeitados como valores discrepantes.

E o Planet X? Pela mesma razão, um planeta distante não apareceria como um pontinho deslizando. A uma distância d em UA, a paralaxe da órbita da Terra o desloca cerca de 3.550/d segundos de arco por dia, e entre temporadas opostas ele salta cerca de 2/d radianos: uns 14 minutos de arco a 500 UA, bem fora de um recorte de 6′. O SkyBlink foi feito para movimentos lentos, como estrelas próximas e anãs marrons. Dizer isso com clareza também faz parte da ferramenta.

Como trabalhamos

Somos dois, o time Capivaláxias, de Cuiabá. Eu fiquei com o backend e os dados; o Francisco, com a interface em Next.js, incluindo o player, o modo em português e um modelo 3D do telescópio. Em ~54 commits, de sábado de manhã a domingo à noite, o contrato da API foi a fronteira entre nós: ele desenvolveu contra um mock enquanto o pipeline ficava pronto.

Três decisões de escopo seguraram o projeto:

  • Escopo em níveis. O nível 1 era um detector, três quadros de Barnard e um link compartilhável. Os demais detectores, o movimento medido e os alertas de alinhamento só vieram depois que o nível 1 estava no ar.
  • Dado real antes de código. Nenhum formato foi assumido a partir da documentação: cada decisão sobre cabeçalhos e extensões foi conferida contra respostas reais do IRSA antes de virar código.
  • Submissão de segurança. Enviamos uma versão funcional no domingo à tarde e só depois partimos para o vídeo.

Sobre IA, com a mesma transparência do README: o código do backend e da interface foi escrito com o Claude Code, a partir das nossas especificações e com revisão nossa, e a narração do vídeo foi gerada com o ElevenLabs. A IA acelerou muito a escrita de código. Não decidiu o que medir, não escolheu os critérios dos alertas e não aceitou um resultado sem a comparação com o Gaia. Esse papel continuou sendo nosso.

Fechando

Plutão foi achado piscando duas fotos de vidro. Quase cem anos depois, piscar imagens continua sendo uma ótima forma de ver o céu mudar. A diferença é que agora dá para dizer, com números, quando o que o olho vê é movimento e quando é o instrumento.

Se quiser testar, abra a Estrela de Barnard, aperte play e veja ela andar. Depois troque para qualquer coordenada.

  • Ferramenta: https://skyblink-swart.vercel.app/
  • Código: https://github.com/carvalhocaio/skyblink
  • Desafio: https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/challenges/planet-x-and-spherex/

Dados do SPHEREx: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). Astrometria: SIMBAD (CDS) e Gaia (ESA).

title: When AI Can Code, What Is Left for Programmers to Do?
description: AI is in such widespread use for programming that project maintainers (particularly for free and open source software) are complaining about the burden of reviewing mounds of low-quality code. In fact, AI can help with every stage of code development: writing the specification, coding, uncovering bugs, and repairing the code. This article describes human-AI collaboration […]

title: DoubleTake: Focused Verification of Visual Evidence for Long-Document Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.17853v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In long-document question answering, a vision-language model can answer incorrectly even when the retrieved pages contain sufficient evidence. Rereading those pages with the original question gives the model little guidance about which fact to check. We introduce DoubleTake, a training-free framework for focused verification of visual evidence. An initial reading produces a candidate answer and a separate evidence record that guides retrieval for a second reading. A planner compares the two candidates and their supporting evidence to formulate a factual question. A verifier answers it from the source images without seeing either candidate or evidence record, and a reasoner uses this observation to resolve the original question. With a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone, DoubleTake achieves the highest overall accuracy among the evaluated methods on each of four benchmarks. With the same pages and number of model calls, asking a focused factual question yields higher accuracy on all four benchmarks than asking the original question again. Our code is available at https://github.com/small-code-cat/double_take.

title: Does the Ranking Hold? A Practitioner-Facing Audit of Hallucination Detectors on Small, Quantized, On-Device LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.17339v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. Cross-model ranking transfer is poor: Spearman rho is -0.80 and Kendall tau-b is -0.667, meaning the detector ranking actively inverts between the two models, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency detectors on both models under bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals. As a second, methodological contribution, we show that the standard token-overlap-to-multiple-choice correctness labeler for TruthfulQA-Generation produces near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for all four detectors on both models, a labeler failure, not a detector failure, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89 AUROC on TriviaQA under the identical pipeline. We release the harness, prompts, and per-item scores and frame the detector choice explicitly as a fairness-of-error-rates allocation problem for practitioners deploying on resource-constrained, on-device hardware.

title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Target-Centric Causal Discovery in Industrial Processes
description:
arXiv:2611.17556v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Causal discovery promises to find which recorded variables drive a process target such as product quality, yield or energy use. Process data with known causes are rare, and in existing benchmarks the difficulty of identifying the causes of a target is either fixed by the recorded data or set for the whole graph. We present a synthetic benchmark for target-centric causal discovery in industrial processes. Its generator is a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon of process data, such as a control loop or a delayed effect. The graph is built around the target: without sensor error, every non-cause can be distinguished from the direct causes by conditioning on them or by time order. Each component is set independently, so the difficulty can be varied one condition at a time. We evaluate eight methods, from association measures to effect estimation, with an error analysis by the role of the selected candidate; all degrade as the difficulties combine, each in a way consistent with its assumptions.

title: NestJS Core Architecture and How We Used It in a Real Project
description:
※ The code examples in this article are based on a real product, but project names, service names, variable names, and anything else that could identify a specific product have been changed or generalized.

(I didn't write all of this from scratch. I took AI-generated content and fixed it up, so I could use it as a kind of dictionary for the project.)

NestJS is a server-side framework built with TypeScript, known for its module-oriented architecture inspired by Angular. In this article, I'll explain the core concepts of NestJS and show how we used them in a real SaaS product (GraphQL API / multi-tenant setup).

(*Update) ↑ I made that sound impressive, but I didn't actually work on that project much, so honestly most of this article isn't in my head lol

Table of contents

  1. Module
  2. Controller / Resolver
  3. Service / UseCase
  4. DI (Dependency Injection)
  5. Guard (Authentication and Authorization)
  6. Layered Entity Definitions
  7. Prisma Integration (Repository + Mapper)
  8. How the Auth Context Flows
  9. Summary: Standard NestJS vs. a Real Project

1. Module

NestJS basics

A NestJS application is organized in units called Modules. With the @Module() decorator, you define providers (services it provides), imports (modules it depends on), and exports (services it exposes to others), which together configure the DI container.

@Module({
  providers: [CatService],
  imports: [DatabaseModule],
  exports: [CatService],
})
export class CatModule {}

In the real project

In this project, modules are split into three layers following a layered architecture.

app.module.ts
  ├─ ResolverModules (interface/di/)        ← presentation layer
  ├─ UseCaseModules (app/di/)               ← application layer
  └─ RepositoryModules (infra/prisma/di/)   ← infrastructure layer

The directory structure looks like this:

packages/api/src/
├── app/                      # Application layer
│   ├── di/                   # UseCase module definitions
│   └── useCases/             # UseCase implementations
├── domain/                   # Domain layer
│   ├── entities/             # Domain entities and type definitions
│   ├── restrictFilters/      # Permission filters
│   └── common/               # Shared types and utilities
├── interface/                # Interface layer
│   ├── di/                   # Resolver module definitions
│   ├── resolvers/            # GraphQL resolvers
│   ├── schema/               # Request/response types
│   └── auth/                 # Auth guards
├── infra/                    # Infrastructure layer
│   ├── prisma/               # Repositories and mappers
│   └── ...                   # External service integrations
└── entities/                 # GraphQL ObjectType definitions

A ResolverModule resolves its dependencies by imports-ing UseCaseModules.

@Module({
  providers: [CommentResolver],
  imports: [
    CommentUseCaseModule,
    UserUseCaseModule,
  ],
})
export class CommentResolverModule {}

A UseCaseModule imports RepositoryModules and other ServiceModules.

@Module({
  providers: [CommentUseCase],
  exports: [CommentUseCase],
  imports: [
    PrismaCommentRepositoryModule,
    PrismaRoomRepositoryModule,
    NotificationServiceModule,
  ],
})
export class CommentUseCaseModule {}

Key point: We use NestJS's module system to enforce a clean-architecture-style dependency direction (interface → app → domain ← infra).

2. Controller / Resolver

NestJS basics

For a REST API, you use decorators like @Get() / @Post() on a @Controller().

@Controller('cats')
export class CatController {
  @Get()
  findAll() { return 'All cats'; }

  @Post()
  create(@Body() dto: CreateCatDto) { ... }
}

For GraphQL, you use @Query() / @Mutation() / @ResolveField() on a @Resolver().

In the real project

This project uses GraphQL with a code-first approach, generating the schema automatically.

// app.module.ts
GraphQLModule.forRoot<ApolloDriverConfig>({
  driver: ApolloDriver,
  autoSchemaFile: join(process.cwd(), 'src/schema.gql'), // generated from TypeScript
  fieldResolverEnhancers: ['guards'],
}),

A resolver example:

@Resolver(() => GqlComment)
export class CommentResolver {
  constructor(private readonly commentUseCase: CommentUseCase) {}

  // Query: fetch data
  @UseGuards(AuthGuard)
  @Query(() => [GqlComment])
  async commentList(
    @Args('input') input: GetCommentListInput,
    @Context() context: OperationContext,
  ) {
    return this.commentUseCase.getCommentList(input, context);
  }

  // Mutation: change data
  @UseGuards(AuthGuard)
  @Mutation(() => GqlComment)
  async createComment(
    @Args('input') input: CreateCommentInput,
    @Context() context: OperationContext,
  ) {
    return this.commentUseCase.createComment(input, context);
  }

  // ResolveField: resolve a nested field
  @ResolveField('author', () => GqlUser)
  async getAuthor(@Parent() comment: Comment) {
    return this.userUseCase.findOne({ id: comment.userId });
  }
}

Main decorators

Decorator Purpose
@Resolver(() => Type) Declares the class as a resolver
@Query(() => Type) Defines a GraphQL query
@Mutation(() => Type) Defines a GraphQL mutation
@ResolveField('name', () => Type) Resolves a nested field
@Args('input') Binds input arguments
@Parent() Accesses the parent object
@Context() Gets the GraphQL context (auth info, etc.)

InputType (request type)

GraphQL input types are also defined with decorators.

@InputType()
export class CreateCommentInput {
  @Field(() => GraphQLJSON)
  content: Prisma.JsonObject;

  @Field()
  roomId: string;

  @Field(() => [Int], { nullable: true })
  imageIds?: number[];
}

This automatically generates the following GraphQL schema:

input CreateCommentInput {
  content: JSON!
  roomId: ID!
  imageIds: [Int!]
}

3. Service / UseCase

NestJS basics

You use a class with the @Injectable() decorator as a service, and gather business logic there.

@Injectable()
export class CatService {
  constructor(private readonly catRepository: CatRepository) {}

  findAll() {
    return this.catRepository.findAll();
  }
}

In the real project

In this project, we name these "UseCase" instead of "Service", and split classes by use case.

@Injectable()
export class CommentUseCase {
  constructor(
    private readonly commentRepository: PrismaCommentRepository,
    private readonly roomRepository: PrismaRoomRepository,
    private readonly notificationService: NotificationService,
  ) {}

  async createComment(input, context: OperationContext) {
    // 1. Domain validation
    const room = CoreAssert.isNotEmpty(
      await this.roomRepository.findOneById({ id: input.roomId }, context),
    );

    // 2. Create the domain entity
    const comment = createCommentSeed({
      ...input,
      userId: context.executor.userId,
    });

    // 3. Save to the DB
    const created = await this.commentRepository.create(comment);

    // 4. Notifications and external integrations
    await this.notificationService.send({ ... });

    return created;
  }
}

Key point: Inside a UseCase, the flow is domain validation → DB save → side effects (notifications, external integrations). Repositories and external services are all injected through the constructor, which makes it very testable.

4. DI (Dependency Injection)

NestJS basics

NestJS's DI automatically resolves providers from TypeScript type information. You register an @Injectable() class in a module's providers, and it's injected automatically based on the constructor's types.

In the real project

Dependencies that cross layers are controlled with imports / exports.

Resolver → constructor(useCase: CommentUseCase)     // resolved by type
UseCase  → constructor(repo: PrismaCommentRepository) // resolved by type

On the module side:

// UseCaseModule: expose CommentUseCase to the outside
@Module({
  providers: [CommentUseCase],
  exports: [CommentUseCase],          // usable from other modules
  imports: [PrismaCommentRepositoryModule],
})
export class CommentUseCaseModule {}

// ResolverModule: import the UseCaseModule to use it
@Module({
  providers: [CommentResolver],
  imports: [CommentUseCaseModule],    // CommentUseCase becomes available
})
export class CommentResolverModule {}

When you hit a circular dependency, you work around it with forwardRef().

@Module({
  imports: [forwardRef(() => RelatedModule)],
})
export class SomeModule {}

5. Guard (Authentication and Authorization)

NestJS basics

You create a guard class that implements the CanActivate interface and apply it with the @UseGuards() decorator.

@Injectable()
export class AuthGuard implements CanActivate {
  canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const request = context.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    return validateToken(request.headers.authorization);
  }
}

In the real project

Because this project is a multi-user SaaS, we use a pattern that routes to different auth guards depending on the user type (admin / guest).

@Injectable()
export class MultiUserAuthGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(
    private readonly adminAuthGuard: AdminAuthGuard,
    private readonly guestAuthGuard: GuestAuthGuard,
  ) {}

  async canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const ctx = GqlExecutionContext.create(context);
    const request = ctx.getContext().req;
    const userType = request.headers['x-user-type'];

    if (userType === 'Admin') {
      // JWT verification (external auth service)
      return this.adminAuthGuard.canActivate(context);
    } else if (userType === 'Guest') {
      // Session token verification
      return this.guestAuthGuard.canActivate(context);
    }

    throw new UnauthorizedException();
  }
}

We also implement fine-grained permission control at the @ResolveField level.

@ResolveField('author', () => GqlUser)
@UseGuards(UserTypesGuard)
@RequiredUserTypes('ADMIN')  // metadata set via a custom decorator
async getAuthor(@Parent() comment: Comment) {
  return this.userUseCase.findOne({ id: comment.userId });
}

UserTypesGuard reads that metadata with Reflector and checks permissions.

@Injectable()
export class UserTypesGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private reflector: Reflector) {}

  canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const requiredTypes = this.reflector.get<string[]>(
      'requiredUserTypes',
      context.getHandler(),
    );
    if (!requiredTypes) return true;

    const gqlContext = GqlExecutionContext.create(context);
    const user = gqlContext.getContext().req.user;
    return requiredTypes.includes(user.executor.userType);
  }
}

6. Layered Entity Definitions

NestJS basics

In a typical NestJS application, a single entity class often serves as both the DB definition and the API definition.

In the real project

This project uses three layers of entity definitions.

Layer Example file Purpose
GraphQL Entity entities/Comment.entity.ts Defines the API output type with @ObjectType()
Domain Entity domain/entities/Comment/index.ts Type-safe business model using brand types
Prisma Model prisma/schema.prisma DB schema definition

GraphQL Entity (API layer) 

@ObjectType()
export class Comment {
  @Field(() => Int)
  id: number;

  @Field(() => GraphQLJSON)
  content: Prisma.JsonObject;

  @Field()
  createdAt: Date;

  @Field(() => [CommentImage])
  commentImages: CommentImage[];  // nested field
}

Domain Entity (domain layer)

Brand types let you tell different kinds of IDs apart, even though they're all number.

// Brand type definition
type Brand<T, U> = T & { __brand: U };

// Distinguish IDs at the type level
export type CommentId = Brand<number, 'CommentId'>;
export type UserId = Brand<number, 'UserId'>;

// Type error: CommentId and UserId are not compatible
const commentId: CommentId = 1 as CommentId;
const userId: UserId = commentId; // compile error!

The domain entity definition:

export type Comment = {
  id: CommentId;
  content: Prisma.JsonObject;
  roomId: RoomId;
  userId: UserId;
  tenantId: TenantId;
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
};

// Factory function
export const createCommentSeed = (payload: CommentSeed): CommentSeed => {
  return { ...payload };
};

Prisma Model (DB layer) 

model Comment {
  id        Int       @id @default(autoincrement())
  content   Json?
  roomId    String
  Room      Room      @relation(fields: [roomId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  userId    Int
  createdAt DateTime  @default(now())
  updatedAt DateTime  @default(now()) @updatedAt
}

Key point: Splitting into three layers means API spec changes don't affect domain logic, and DB schema changes don't leak into the API layer.

7. Prisma Integration (Repository + Mapper)

NestJS basics

In NestJS, it's common to use TypeORM or Prisma directly from services.

In the real project

This project uses a Repository + Mapper pattern to convert Prisma types into domain types.

Repository 

@Injectable()
export class PrismaCommentRepository {
  async create(input: CommentSeed, db = client): Promise<Comment> {
    const prismaComment = await db.comment.create({
      data: {
        contentJson: input.content,
        roomId: input.roomId,
      },
      include: { Room: true },
    });

    // Convert Prisma type → domain type
    return PrismaCommentMapper.toDomainComment(prismaComment);
  }

  async findList(input, context, db = client): Promise<Comment[]> {
    const results = await db.comment.findMany({
      where: {
        roomId: input.roomId,
        Room: { tenantId: context.tenantId }, // tenant isolation
      },
      orderBy: { createdAt: 'asc' },
    });
    return results.map(PrismaCommentMapper.toDomainComment);
  }
}

Mapper 

export class PrismaCommentMapper {
  static toDomainComment(prismaComment): Comment {
    return {
      id: prismaComment.id as CommentId,
      content: prismaComment.contentJson as Prisma.JsonObject,
      roomId: prismaComment.roomId as RoomId,
      userId: prismaComment.userId as UserId,
      tenantId: prismaComment.Room.tenantId as TenantId,
      createdAt: prismaComment.createdAt,
      updatedAt: prismaComment.updatedAt,
    };
  }
}

Transactions

Operations that span multiple tables use prisma.$transaction() to guarantee atomicity.

const result = await prisma.$transaction(async (db) => {
  const room = await this.roomRepository.create(roomData, context, db);
  await this.memberRepository.create(memberData, db);
  return room;
});

Key point: Repository methods take an optional db argument, so they're designed to work both inside a transaction and standalone.

8. How the Auth Context Flows

This is how auth information propagates in a multi-tenant SaaS.

1. GraphQL request
   ├─ Header: Authorization: "Bearer <JWT>"
   └─ Header: x-user-type: "Admin" or "Guest"

2. Guard (authentication)
   ├─ Admin → verify JWT → build OperationContext
   └─ Guest → verify session → build OperationContext
   └─ set request.user = OperationContext

3. Resolver
   └─ get it via @Context() context: OperationContext

4. UseCase / Repository
   └─ use the context for permission control and tenant isolation

OperationContext is defined type-safely with a Zod schema.

export const operationContextSchema = z.object({
  tenantId: tenantIdSchema,
  executor: z.union([
    z.object({
      userType: z.literal('ADMIN'),
      userId: userIdSchema,
      role: roleSchema,
    }),
    z.object({
      userType: z.literal('GUEST'),
      userId: userIdSchema,
    }),
  ]),
});

export type OperationContext = z.infer<typeof operationContextSchema>;

It's injected into resolvers with the custom @Context() decorator.

export const Context = createParamDecorator(
  (data: unknown, context: ExecutionContext) => {
    const ctx = GqlExecutionContext.create(context);
    return ctx.getContext().req.user as OperationContext;
  },
);

Permission filters handle tenant isolation in DB operations.

export const commentRestrictFilter = (
  context: OperationContext,
): Prisma.CommentWhereInput[] => {
  return [{ Room: { tenantId: context.tenantId } }];
};

// Usage
const comments = await prisma.comment.findMany({
  where: { AND: commentRestrictFilter(context) },
});

9. Summary: Standard NestJS vs. a Real Project

Aspect Standard NestJS Real project
API style REST (@Controller) GraphQL code-first (@Resolver)
Business logic Service UseCase (split by use case)
Data access ORM used directly Repository + Mapper pattern
Auth Single guard Guard that routes by user type
Type safety Standard TypeScript Brand types + Zod validation
Tenant isolation None OperationContext + RestrictFilter
Entity Single definition 3 layers (GraphQL / Domain / Prisma)
Module structure By feature By layer (Resolver / UseCase / Repository)

Wrapping up

NestJS is powerful enough out of the box, but it's also flexible enough to customize the architecture to fit a project's size and requirements.

In this project, we built on NestJS's DI system and added a few things:

  • Layered architecture: separate layers by module and control the dependency direction
  • Code-first GraphQL: generate the schema automatically from TypeScript decorators
  • Brand types: catch mixed-up IDs at compile time
  • RestrictFilter: turn multi-tenant data isolation into a reusable pattern

Once you understand the core NestJS concepts (Module / DI / Guard / Decorator), extending it to fit your project's needs is easy. I hope this helps.

title: Notification Preferences Testing: Follow the Setting Into the Next Product Event
description:
Notification preferences testing should follow a saved setting into a newly triggered product event and its intended delivery channels. A toggle changing color is only the beginning. The useful question is whether the next relevant event follows the preference the interface promised.

That makes a good public SaaS demo task. A founder peer can trace an event, a recipient and a setting, then report the mismatch they actually observed. You get more useful feedback than a screenshot of a polished preferences page.

This walkthrough uses a fictional document-review app with synthetic accounts and a test inbox. It proposes a test design, not findings from a real product. Keep real customers, production recipients and private messages out of any public demonstration you prepare.

Write the notification promise before testing the switch

Imagine that the app offers a setting called email me when a review is assigned. The label implies a particular event, a delivery channel and a recipient. Write those three parts down before asking someone to assess the feature.

Then clarify scope. Is this a personal preference for the signed-in reviewer, a workspace default or a setting controlled by an administrator? If the interface does not make the distinction clear, that is already useful feedback about the design.

Real products can offer several notification routes. GitHub's notification documentation describes choices about activity and delivery through its web interface, mobile app and email. Those are GitHub's documented options, not a universal model every SaaS must copy.

For the fictional review app, keep the first task smaller: one assignment event, an email channel and an in-app inbox. Define what should happen on each route. Do not assume that turning off email should also remove the in-app notification unless that is the promise you have chosen.

Prepare a safe baseline that another person can understand

Use two fictional members: a requester who creates the assignment and a reviewer who receives it. Keep their roles distinct so the person triggering the event does not accidentally become the person whose preference you are evaluating.

Prepare a uniquely named sample document for the task. The reviewer should be able to distinguish this event from earlier tests without exposing a real customer name or message. Note when the event was triggered so old inbox items do not masquerade as new deliveries.

Before changing the preference, demonstrate the baseline you intend to compare against. If the setting is on, trigger a new assignment and inspect the agreed channels. Record any uncertainty, including a test inbox that is unavailable or an event that did not finish creating.

A missing message is not automatically evidence that preferences work. The assignment may have failed, the recipient may be wrong or the notification service may be unavailable. Establish that you can observe the relevant event and channel before interpreting absence as success.

Change one preference and reopen the saved view

Ask the reviewer to turn assignment emails off, save if required, then leave and reopen the settings page. Check that the displayed preference persists. That establishes what the saved interface says; delivery behavior still needs its own check.

Now create a new assignment with a different synthetic document name. Inspect the test inbox and the in-app inbox according to the promise you wrote. Keep the new event separate from any message already in transit before the preference changed.

Define a reasonable observation window for your own system and explain it in the test notes. Do not invent a universal email-delivery deadline. If the system has known delays or the test cannot establish whether a queue finished, record the outcome as unresolved rather than declaring that nothing will arrive.

Finally, turn the setting on again and repeat with another new event. A setting that suppresses everything regardless of its state might appear to pass the off case. The return to an expected delivery helps expose that possibility.

Test the boundary between event type, channel and account

After the basic case works, change one dimension at a time. Keep assignment emails off while triggering a different event whose preference remains on. The expected outcome should follow the product's actual labels and documented distinctions.

Then inspect the second channel. If the interface says the setting controls email only, an in-app assignment may still be correct. The test report should identify the channel rather than broadly saying that notifications were disabled.

Use a second synthetic reviewer to check personal scope. Changing one person's preference should not silently change another person's setting unless the control explicitly manages a shared default. Reopen both views and record which account is active before drawing that conclusion.

If the app has workspace overrides, make those visible in a separate test. Do not bury several possible rules in the first demo task. A useful review starts with a clear expectation and expands when the product's actual behavior requires more context.

Investigate a mismatch without guessing its cause

Suppose the reviewer receives an assignment email after turning the setting off. Preserve the event name, recipient account, visible saved preference, trigger time and channel where the message appeared. Avoid publishing inbox headers or identifiers that contain private information.

Check whether the event was created before or after the change. If it was already queued, the observation may concern how in-flight messages are handled rather than how newly created events read the saved preference.

Also distinguish message creation from final delivery. A public demo may expose only the recipient's view. That can reveal an experience problem without proving which internal service caused it. Investigate logs privately through the product's authorized development workflow when needed.

The same discipline applies to missing messages. Record what you can observe, what you expected and what remains unknown. A precise report gives another developer a path to reproduce the issue without turning one attempt into an unsupported technical diagnosis.

Give founder peers a task they can safely repeat

Buildside gives founders a context for sharing work, questions and lessons. A public-building post can invite peers to review a safe notification flow using the task, sample data and boundaries you prepared.

Include a short sequence: confirm the synthetic recipient, inspect the baseline preference, change the setting, reopen it and trigger a new sample event. State which channel the reviewer should inspect and what they should do if the expected delivery cannot be observed.

Keep the invitation focused on a product question. For example: does the wording make it clear that this control affects assignment email for this reviewer, while in-app assignments remain available? A peer can assess that explanation even if you cannot give them access to delivery infrastructure.

Do not ask reviewers to send messages to real customers or alter their own production notification preferences. The task should stay inside the safe environment you described. If you cannot provide one, share a clearly labelled walkthrough and ask about the interaction design instead of claiming end-to-end testing.

Report the behavior you verified

A useful release update names the event, preference, scope and channel you checked. It might explain that a personal assignment-email setting now survives reopening and is respected by newly created synthetic assignments. Publish that wording only after those checks actually happen.

Keep broader conclusions separate. Passing one assignment task does not establish that every event type, workspace override or delivery route is correct. List the important untested boundaries when they affect what someone can rely on.

That level of detail makes visible development more useful to both peers and early users. The update explains a promise the product makes and the evidence behind it. The preferences screen becomes a starting point for understanding behavior, rather than the entire proof that the behavior works.

title: TRON Out of Energy Error: Check a Failed USDT Transfer
description:
Disclosure: I work on EnergyPriceBoard, the price board referenced in this article. The same team runs tronfor.me, an energy shop listed on the board.

Quick fix in 3 steps

  1. Find the TXID (your transfer's tracking number) in your wallet. Look it up in a TRON transaction explorer.
  2. Read the result and the TRX fee. Check how much Energy (the resource TRON uses to run a USDT transfer) the attempt used.
  3. Check the sending address and your wallet's fee preview. Then decide whether to try again.

A confirmed OUT_OF_ENERGY result for a USDT contract call means that attempted transfer did not finish. The attempt can still use resources and cost TRX. Sending the same transfer again without checking the cause can cost more TRX. TRON's resource guide, accessed 16 Nov 2026.

Start with the failed transfer's record, or receipt. It shows the result and the cost.

Find the failed transfer first

Copy the TXID from your wallet and search for it in a TRON explorer such as TRONSCAN. Check the addresses, result and fee. If no confirmed transaction appears, check your wallet's pending status and address history. A wallet error alone does not prove a network charge.

Two TRON resources can appear in this check. Energy runs the USDT contract, the program that carries out the transfer. Bandwidth (the resource used for the transaction's data) is separate. Having Bandwidth does not mean you had enough Energy. TRON's resource guide, accessed 16 Nov 2026.

Read one real failed USDT transfer

This public failed transfer happened on 25 Apr 2026 at 13:20:21 UTC. It called the TetherToken contract. TronGrid's receipt, transaction record and contract record were checked on 16 Nov 2026 at 21:58 UTC. These API links identify methods, not the transaction itself.

SUN is a small unit of TRX: 1 TRX equals 1,000,000 SUN (TRON's resource guide, accessed 16 Nov 2026). In the table, fee_limit means the maximum resource-cost allowance set for the caller's part of this contract call. It is not the fee actually charged.

For a first check, focus on Result and TRX fee. The other rows explain the technical details.

What the receipt says Value In plain words
Result OUT_OF_ENERGY The USDT transfer did not finish.
Total Energy used 92,200 Energy What this failed attempt used in all.
Sender-side resource use 65,045 Energy Energy used from the caller's resources, recorded apart from the TRX charge.
TRX fee 2,715,500 SUN (2.7155 TRX) What this attempt actually cost in TRX. The Energy fee and the total TRX fee were the same.
fee_limit 9,220,000 SUN (9.22 TRX) What the caller's part of the call was allowed to use, not what was charged.

The table describes that 25 Apr 2026 transfer, rechecked on 16 Nov 2026 at 21:58 UTC. The receipt also shows 345 Bandwidth and 25,905 Energy already included in the total, not an extra charge. Its error message says there was not enough Energy for a storage-write operation in the USDT contract. Receipt field guide, accessed 16 Nov 2026.

The difference between the total and sender-side resource use is 27,155 Energy. At the network rate of 100 SUN per Energy queried on 16 Nov 2026 at 21:58 UTC, 27,155 × 100 = 2,715,500 SUN. That agrees with the fee in this receipt.

What can cause a TRON out of energy error?

Check both the Energy available to the sending address and the limit set on the call. Energy may come from the sender's staked or delegated resources. If those are short, TRON can burn the caller's TRX for Energy. The caller can use resources or burn TRX within the call's limits; a contract developer may contribute Energy separately. So fee_limit is not the fee actually paid or a cap on every participant's Energy, and an address showing some Energy can still hit its limit. TRON's resource guide, accessed 16 Nov 2026.

The TRX charge was below the configured limit, yet the call stopped. The error reports a 92,200 Energy execution limit, matching 9,220,000 SUN divided by the checked rate of 100 SUN per Energy. That match does not reveal the sender's TRX balance or Energy available at the time.

What should you check before trying again?

Check the sending address. If you arranged delegated or rented Energy, check that it reached that address and is still there. Check the recipient too. According to EPB's error guide, its approximate estimates depend on the recipient's USDT balance. Review your wallet's preview for this transfer.

If Energy is missing, check the sender's TRX balance or delegated Energy. The EPB price board lists rental offers. If your wallet exposes fee_limit, review it before signing. Raising it allows a larger caller contribution. For fee details, see EPB's USDT transfer cost explanation.

What this check cannot establish

This old receipt is not a limit to copy. It cannot reconstruct the sender's past balance, available resources or other wallet settings; today's balance does not show them. Nor can it tell you how much Energy another transfer needs. The later rate query alone does not prove the rate on the transfer date. We checked API data but could not open this TXID's TRONSCAN page, so the table does not describe that site's layout. This article does not inspect your wallet, verify rental delivery or speed, give live rental prices, or promise success or savings. Prices in the linked cost article are historical. Never share a seed phrase or private key.

FAQ

Why did my failed transfer still cost TRX?

The contract used resources before it stopped. The 25 Apr 2026 receipt, checked on 16 Nov 2026 at 21:58 UTC, shows a failed result and a fee (receipt method). A retry does not undo that charge.

Did my USDT leave the wallet?

An OUT_OF_ENERGY result means that attempted transfer did not complete. Check your address history for any other successful transfer before you send again (TRON's resource guide, accessed 16 Nov 2026).

Why did it fail even though I had Energy?

Your address may have had some Energy, but not enough for the call within its allowed limit. Look at the failed receipt, the sender's available resources and the wallet's limit setting separately (TRON's resource guide, accessed 16 Nov 2026).

Can I recover the Energy or TRX spent on the failed attempt?

Burned TRX is not refunded. Used staked or delegated Energy gradually recovers over 24 hours (TRON's resource guide, accessed 16 Nov 2026). If your wallet shows a different fee from the on-chain receipt, ask its provider about the difference and give them the TXID, not your secret keys.

In short

Find the failed transaction and read its result and fee. Check the sending address, available Energy and wallet limit before deciding whether to retry.

What did your wallet show when your USDT transfer failed?

title: Fixing Java's 'PKIX path building failed: unable to find valid certification path'
description:
You call an HTTPS URL from Java and get this:

javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: PKIX path building failed:
sun.security.provider.certpath.SunCertPathBuilderException:
unable to find valid certification path to requested target

This post explains what it means and how to fix it properly. I reproduced it on a local test server so every command and output below is real (JDK 21, OpenSSL 3.5, Windows 11). Hostnames and paths on your system will differ.

What the error means

When Java opens a TLS connection, the server sends its certificate chain. Java then tries to build a path from that chain to a certificate it trusts. The trusted certificates live in a truststore. If no path ends at something in the truststore, you get unable to find valid certification path to requested target.

So the message is not about the server being down or the certificate being expired. It says the CA that signed this certificate is not in the truststore your JVM is using. The usual causes:

  1. A corporate TLS-inspection proxy. The proxy re-signs traffic with a company CA. Browsers trust it because IT installed it in the OS store. Java uses its own store and does not.
  2. A self-signed or internal CA. Test servers, staging environments, internal services.
  3. A missing intermediate certificate on the server. The server sends only its own certificate, not the CA in between.

The lab setup

To get a real error without touching a real site, I made a tiny CA and a server certificate for localhost, and served HTTPS from Python on 127.0.0.1:8443.

# Git Bash
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout ca.key -out ca.crt -days 30 \
  -subj "/CN=Lab Root CA" \
  -addext "basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE" -addext "keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign"

openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout server.key -out server.csr -subj "/CN=localhost"
printf "subjectAltName=DNS:localhost,IP:127.0.0.1\nbasicConstraints=CA:FALSE\n" > server.ext
openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out server.crt -days 30 -extfile server.ext

server.py:

import http.server, ssl, sys
cert, key, port = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3])
ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
ctx.load_cert_chain(cert, key)
srv = http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), http.server.SimpleHTTPRequestHandler)
srv.socket = ctx.wrap_socket(srv.socket, server_side=True)
srv.serve_forever()

Start it with python server.py server.crt server.key 8443.

The Java client, Client.java, is a single file that prints the exception chain:

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;

public class Client {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        HttpClient c = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
        HttpRequest r = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(args[0])).build();
        try {
            HttpResponse<String> resp = c.send(r, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
            System.out.println("HTTP " + resp.statusCode());
        } catch (Exception e) {
            Throwable t = e; System.out.println(e);
            while (t.getCause() != null) { t = t.getCause(); System.out.println("caused by: " + t); }
        }
    }
}

Run it:

$ java Client.java https://localhost:8443/
javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: (certificate_unknown) PKIX path building failed: sun.security.provider.certpath.SunCertPathBuilderException: unable to find valid certification path to requested target
caused by: sun.security.validator.ValidatorException: PKIX path building failed: ...
caused by: sun.security.provider.certpath.SunCertPathBuilderException: unable to find valid certification path to requested target

That is the error.

Step 1: See what the server sends 

openssl s_client -connect localhost:8443 -showcerts </dev/null

The full output is long. The lines that matter:

Certificate chain
 0 s:CN=localhost
   i:CN=Lab Root CA
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...
Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)

s: is the subject, i: is the issuer. Here the server certificate was issued by Lab Root CA. On a real site behind an inspection proxy, you would see your company's CA as the issuer instead of the public CA you expect. That alone tells you the cause.

Each -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- block is a certificate you can copy into a .pem file. Pass the CA's certificate to -CAfile to check that it is the right one:

$ echo | openssl s_client -connect localhost:8443 -CAfile ca.crt
...
Verify return code: 0 (ok)

I ran the same s_client command from WSL Ubuntu against the Windows-hosted server on 127.0.0.1 and it showed the same chain.

Do not install a certificate just because it makes the error go away. Make sure you know who issued it and that you trust that issuer. For a corporate proxy, ask IT for the root certificate.

Step 2: Find which truststore Java uses

By default Java uses cacerts in the JDK, at $JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts on current JDKs (older layouts differ; the debug flag below prints the exact path for yours). The default password is changeit. You can override the store with -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=<path> and -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=<password>.

To check which one a run actually used, turn on trust manager debugging:

$ java -Djavax.net.debug=ssl:trustmanager Client.java https://localhost:8443/
... TrustStoreManager.java:162|Inaccessible trust store: C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-21.0.11.10-hotspot\lib\security\jssecacerts
... TrustStoreManager.java:113|trustStore is: C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-21.0.11.10-hotspot\lib\security\cacerts
trustStore type is: pkcs12

Java looks for jssecacerts first and falls back to cacerts, which is what those two lines show. Your application server, Gradle daemon or IDE may run a different JDK than the one on your PATH, so check the JDK that actually runs the failing code.

Step 3: Import the CA into a copy of cacerts

Do not edit the JDK's cacerts in place. JDK updates replace it, it often needs admin rights, and every Java program on the machine would trust your change. Copy it and edit the copy.

# Git Bash. Adjust the JDK path for your machine.
cp "/c/Program Files/Eclipse Adoptium/jdk-21.0.11.10-hotspot/lib/security/cacerts" my-cacerts

keytool -importcert -alias lab-root-ca -file ca.crt -keystore my-cacerts -storepass changeit -noprompt

Certificate was added to keystore

Check the entry:

$ keytool -list -keystore my-cacerts -storepass changeit -alias lab-root-ca
lab-root-ca, Nov 16, 2026, trustedCertEntry,
Certificate fingerprint (SHA-256): 91:4A:28:2F:98:E9:1A:69:91:F9:24:97:87:DF:71:DD:AF:8A:8C:3D:6E:B3:99:11:66:24:ED:94:0C:0D:D9:73

Without -noprompt, keytool shows the certificate and asks Trust this certificate? [no]:. Read it before answering yes.

Now point the program at the copy:

$ java -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=my-cacerts -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit Client.java https://localhost:8443/
HTTP 200

It works. The same command also worked from PowerShell. Because the copy still contains all the original public CAs, other HTTPS calls from that program keep working. If you set trustStore to a file that holds only your CA, every other HTTPS call will fail with the same PKIX error.

Import the CA certificate (the issuer), not just the server's own certificate. A server certificate is replaced every few months, and the CA certificate lasts years.

If you can't change the command line, the JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS environment variable passes the same flags to any JVM started from that shell:

$ JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=my-cacerts -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit" java Client.java https://localhost:8443/
Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=my-cacerts -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit
HTTP 200

The Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS line is printed to stderr every time; it is a notice, not an error (PowerShell shows it in red). App servers, build tools and IDE run configurations each have their own JVM-options setting for the same two flags.

Why not disable verification?

Many answers on the web give you a TrustManager that accepts everything, or a HostnameVerifier that returns true. That makes the error go away by removing the check. Anyone on the network path can then impersonate the server and read or change the traffic, and these hacks tend to stay in code long after "just for testing". Importing one CA into a copy of the truststore fixes the actual problem and keeps verification on.

The missing intermediate case

Public sites are usually signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root. The server is supposed to send the leaf and the intermediate. If it sends only the leaf, browsers can often fetch the intermediate themselves, but Java generally will not. So you get the same PKIX error even though the root is trusted.

I tested it: root, then Lab Intermediate CA, then a localhost leaf. One server (port 8444) sends only the leaf, another (port 8445) sends leaf plus intermediate.

openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout int.key -out int.csr -subj "/CN=Lab Intermediate CA"
printf "basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE,pathlen:0\nkeyUsage=critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign\n" > int.ext
openssl x509 -req -in int.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out int.crt -days 30 -extfile int.ext
openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout leaf.key -out leaf.csr -subj "/CN=localhost"
openssl x509 -req -in leaf.csr -CA int.crt -CAkey int.key -CAcreateserial -out leaf.crt -days 30 -extfile server.ext
cat leaf.crt int.crt > leaf-fullchain.crt
python server.py leaf.crt leaf.key 8444            # leaf only
python server.py leaf-fullchain.crt leaf.key 8445  # leaf + intermediate

s_client shows the difference right away. Leaf only:

Certificate chain
 0 s:CN=localhost
   i:CN=Lab Intermediate CA

Leaf plus intermediate:

Certificate chain
 0 s:CN=localhost
   i:CN=Lab Intermediate CA
 1 s:CN=Lab Intermediate CA
   i:CN=Lab Root CA

With a truststore that holds only the root (root-only.p12, created with keytool -importcert -alias lab-root-only -file ca.crt -keystore root-only.p12 -storetype PKCS12 -storepass changeit -noprompt):

$ java -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=root-only.p12 -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit Client.java https://localhost:8444/
javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: (certificate_unknown) PKIX path building failed: ...

$ java -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=root-only.p12 -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit Client.java https://localhost:8445/
HTTP 200

There are two fixes. The better one is on the server: configure it to send the full chain (with Let's Encrypt that is fullchain.pem). If you cannot change the server, import the intermediate into the truststore:

$ keytool -importcert -alias lab-intermediate -file int.crt -keystore root-only.p12 -storepass changeit -noprompt
Certificate was added to keystore

$ java -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=root-only.p12 -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword=changeit Client.java https://localhost:8444/
HTTP 200

The tell-tale sign of this case is in s_client: the chain has one certificate and its issuer is not a root you recognize.

The same fix inside IntelliJ with Keystore Workbench

Disclosure: I built this plugin. Keystore Workbench is a JetBrains IDE plugin from Datawharf Tools for viewing and editing Java keystores. The keytool fix above works fine on its own. This section is for people who would rather do it in the IDE.

Free:

  • Tools | Open JDK cacerts opens the JDK truststore read-only (password changeit), so you can check whether a CA is already in there.
  • Open keystores, see certificate details, expiry and the chain, and export public certificates.

Pro (US$19 per year for individuals, 30-day trial). Importing is Pro:

  • Open the truststore, choose Allow editing, click Import, pick the .pem file, then Save.
  • Analyze | Verify Chain says when the chain is incomplete and names the missing issuer, which is the intermediate case above.

Two practical notes. The plugin makes no network connections, so you still get the certificates yourself with openssl s_client -connect host:443 -showcerts or by exporting them from the browser. And if the JDK folder is protected, copy cacerts to your project, edit the copy and start the program with the two -D flags, exactly as in step 3.

The lab above uses only OpenSSL, keytool and Java, so you don't need the plugin to follow it. The plugin is at https://plugins.jetbrains.com/plugin/36134-keystore-workbench.

Summary

  1. The error means the issuing CA is not in the truststore the JVM uses.
  2. openssl s_client -connect host:443 -showcerts shows who issued the server certificate and whether an intermediate is missing.
  3. -Djavax.net.debug=ssl:trustmanager shows which truststore was used.
  4. Copy cacerts, run keytool -importcert on the copy, and start the app with -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore and -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStorePassword.
  5. Do not disable verification. If an intermediate is missing, fix the server or import the intermediate.

title: You Awaited Every Save Inside forEach and the Import Said Done Before Any Had Finished
description:
The import endpoint
took a file of price changes,
saved each row,
and replied with a count.

rows.forEach(async (row) => {
await savePrice(row);
});

return { saved: rows.length };

It read well.

There was an await
on every save.

It passed review.

It passed the tests,
mostly.

Then the support desk
started hearing a strange story.

The screen said
two hundred prices updated.

The shop still showed
the old ones.

Ten seconds later,
some of them had changed.

And now and then
the whole Node process
fell over in the night
with an unhandled rejection
nobody could tie to a request.

Here is the mechanism.

An async function
returns a promise
the moment it reaches its first await.

forEach calls your function
once per row
and throws the return value away.

It does not wait for it.

It cannot.

It was written
before promises existed,
and it was never taught
what one is.

So the loop started
two hundred saves,
finished in a millisecond,
and the endpoint replied
while every one of them
was still in flight.

The await was real.

It just paused
the little function inside,
not the code around it.

And when a save failed,
its rejection had nobody waiting for it.

Since Node 15
an unhandled rejection
ends the process by default.

That was the crash in the night.

The fix is to choose,
on purpose,
how the saves should run.

One after another:

for (const row of rows) {
await savePrice(row);
}

All at once,
and wait for every one:

await Promise.all(rows.map(savePrice));

The first is slower
and keeps the order.

The second is faster
and can flood the database,
so cap it
if the list can be long.

Either way,
the reply now comes
after the work,
and a failure
comes back to the caller
instead of to the process.

Most linters can catch this.

Turn on the rule
that flags a promise nobody handles.

The lesson is bigger than one method.

An await only waits
inside the function it is written in.

If the caller
does not wait for that function,
nothing waited at all.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: Edtech Cost Attribution: Go Failure Alerting via Metrics API Poll Queries
description:
A one-minute polling interval creates a one-minute detection floor before retries, scheduler drift, and notification delivery even enter the picture. TL;DR: for a small edtech AI agent, use a metrics or error API poller only when cost attribution matters enough to justify owning the scheduler, deduplication, and notification path; choose built-in alerting when the page itself is the product requirement. A unified backend API can be reasonable for the DIY branch because one key and one bill cover backend services, while per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata support attribution, but this option lacks threshold rules and notification routing.

Consider a bounded production exercise, not a claimed incident: a tutoring agent makes several model calls for one student turn, and the team needs to detect a failed loop while assigning its cost to the course or workflow that initiated it. I would start with a 60-second polling objective, three consecutive failed loops as an example page threshold, and a separate dead-man check for the poller. Those are policy inputs, not measured performance. A course-level cost label must be attached before aggregation; trying to infer it later from a blended total makes both the budget review and the incident review weaker. The invariant is stricter than "the query returned data": every alerting interval needs evidence that collection ran, attribution survived, and notification either succeeded or remained retryable. A duplicate invocation must be harmless, while a skipped invocation must become visible through a second path.

Should a metrics API poll query own failure alerting?

The obvious failure is an unhealthy agent loop. The dangerous failure is silence: the scheduled job does not run, its credential expires, the query cannot complete, or the webhook times out, so a quiet dashboard is mistaken for health. A metrics API cannot prove the poller that calls it is alive. Healthchecks.io is the clean complement for that "task should have run" signal, because its model is built around expected check-ins; it does not replace agent metrics or their cost dimensions.

Silence is ambiguous.

The poller also needs durable state. At minimum, store the last successful poll time, the last closed window, and an idempotency key for each notification. Query overlapping windows so a delayed invocation does not open a gap, then deduplicate by stable event identity or by a deterministic tuple such as service, window, and policy version. Do not page directly on a single transient sample unless the SLO calls for it. Three words matter: count the budget.

For the tutoring loop, attribution should be decided before aggregation. A useful internal record associates a loop ID with a course or workflow, model vendor, latency, and cost; Infrai specifies per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata on its AI surfaces, while one key and one bill cover its backend services. A separate advantage is Infrai's single REST API with no required SDK: the Go Lambda and Node.js application can call the same HTTP contract without coordinating client-library releases. Its public, self-describing discovery surface needs no key and exposes the full request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples, which lets the poller validate that contract before deployment. Every documented capability has examples in ten languages. That combination removes a specific source of friction here: two runtimes can share schema-derived fixtures while keeping their deployment schedules independent.

One REST API also puts 295 routes across 20 modules behind consistent conventions and the same credential. That breadth is useful only if the team already wants other backend capabilities under the same operational boundary; it is not a reason to replace a focused alerting product. The observability query filters are not declared, so I would design the adapter around the discovered contract rather than inventing URL parameters. Logs can carry trace and span identifiers for correlation, but this option does not support distributed trace queries or span trees. That boundary changes what can be debugged after a page.

The preventative path in Go

This runnable query deliberately sends no filters because none are declared. It uses one documented route, checks every status, applies exponential backoff on HTTP 429, honors Retry-After when it is an integer number of seconds, and prints the response for an adapter to validate against the current discovery schema. It makes a read-only request, so write idempotency does not apply.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("METRICS_API_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        panic("METRICS_API_BASE_URL is required")
    }

    delay := time.Second
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/v1/metrics/query", nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            delay *= 2
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("query returned %s: %s", res.Status, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("query remained rate limited after five attempts")
}

The polling wrapper still needs a lease so concurrent invocations do not evaluate the same window, persistent notification deduplication, and a stored last-success timestamp. A failed send stays retryable. The code stops at the query boundary because pretending to know an undeclared response field would teach a brittle integration; the adapter should validate the live response and map only fields actually present.

Which alerting owner fits the service?

The decision is about who owns failure semantics, not a feature-count contest. I use this buy-versus-build table at roadmap review, then validate the shortlisted product against the actual escalation policy.

Option Best fit Team owns Boundary that matters here
PagerDuty Human escalation and incident-response workflows are primary Instrumentation and event quality More operational machinery than a tiny app may need; cost attribution still originates upstream
Better Stack Uptime checks and managed alerting should arrive together Service-specific instrumentation Agent-loop cost dimensions still need an application or telemetry source
Grafana Alerting Metrics already live in a supported data source and rules should stay near dashboards Data-source operation, rule quality, and contact points Self-managed components increase on-call surface; managed deployment shifts that burden
Healthchecks.io The central risk is a scheduled poller or job that does not run Agent-failure query and downstream escalation Dead-man monitoring does not analyze agent-loop failures by itself
Unified API poller One REST integration, one credential, and consolidated billing matter, and custom delivery is acceptable Scheduling, thresholds, state, deduplication, retries, and routing No built-in threshold engine, webhook push, phone, or SMS alert routing

PagerDuty is the conservative choice when missed or misrouted pages threaten an SLO and the team needs an incident-response system. Better Stack fits a small service whose first question is external availability. Grafana Alerting makes sense when the organization already operates Grafana and its supported data sources, because moving the rule elsewhere creates another control plane. Healthchecks.io should remain narrow: it watches the watcher.

The DIY row wins under a different constraint. If the platform already runs reliable scheduled work and a notification adapter, adding one small policy may be less organizational weight than adopting another alerting control plane, particularly when the same credential and bill already cover other backend capabilities. Yet the apparent simplicity disappears as soon as escalation schedules, acknowledgement, suppression, grouping, or audit requirements arrive.

Then buy.

Capacity planning before the first page

A one-minute cadence means 1,440 poll attempts per day for each independently scheduled target. Ten targets mean 14,400 attempts. Those are arithmetic consequences of configuration, not vendor throughput claims, and they belong beside query quotas, scheduler concurrency, storage writes, and notification retry limits before deployment. The sample's five attempts can sleep for 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 seconds before scheduler overhead if no usable Retry-After value arrives; that retry envelope must fit the job timeout. Polling every ten seconds multiplies the attempt volume by six while improving only the best-case observation delay. It does nothing for a dead scheduler.

Set two objectives. The detection SLO measures how quickly qualifying agent-loop failures become an alert. The alert-pipeline SLO measures successful poll completion and notification handoff. Track both with separate signals, because combining them lets the monitoring system hide its own outage. For cost attribution, also track the fraction of loop records carrying the required course or workflow dimension; a total cost without an owner is an accounting failure even if every request completed.

This design is not suitable for browser crash investigation, source-map decoding, Electron minidumps, session replay, or full trace-tree analysis. It also does not solve GDPR deletion by user, bulk log export, configurable retention, or feature-flag audit and evaluation analysis. If any of those are acceptance criteria, select a system that explicitly provides them instead of stretching a polling loop across the gap.

The decision rule

Choose the poller when there is one small team, a small number of stable policies, an existing scheduler and notification path, and a real need to join failure evidence with per-loop AI cost attribution. Require overlapping windows, durable deduplication, a dead-man check, and an owner for every page. The query endpoint is a data source, not an alerting system.

Choose managed alerting when routing, acknowledgement, schedules, suppression, external probes, or auditability are requirements rather than future ideas. A platform lead should charge the DIY option for engineering time and on-call exposure, not merely API usage. The fair comparison is the total operational obligation over an SLO period.

References

  • Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
  • PagerDuty developer documentation: Events API
  • Better Stack documentation: Uptime monitoring
  • Grafana documentation: Alerting
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • Logback manual: Appenders

title: AI Reviews Are Biased Towards the Appendix
description:
arXiv:2611.17811v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by reviewers to highlight weaknesses during the reviewing process, and their outputs often shape the reviews that humans submit. Prior work studies how LLM reviews align with human ones, yet we know little about which parts of a paper these models actually criticize. In this work, we investigate 2,000 papers from ACL, EMNLP, COLM, and ICLR, and show that the latest GPT and Claude models draw about 50% or more of their review weaknesses from the appendix. This behavior holds across the API, coding-agent, and web access methods for using LLMs to review a paper. In contrast, we find that humans draw only 8.4% of their weaknesses from the appendix, and these weaknesses primarily revolve around a paper's presentation and content related to its core idea. Meanwhile, LLMs draw weaknesses from deep in the appendix that concern fine-grained technical details not central to the paper's contributions. We anticipate that our analysis will contribute to the scholarly discourse on AI reviews. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/cincynlp/review_appendix.
