title: Can Agents Keep Up with Time? An Empirical Analysis of Temporal Adaptation After a Conversational Hiatus
description:
arXiv:2611.17806v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon agents increasingly serve as persistent personal assistants across modern web platforms, managing schedules, applications, and multi-step plans over weeks or months. Users often return to an ongoing conversation after a long conversational hiatus, while earlier bookings and preparation notes stay on record. During this hiatus, scheduled dates may pass even though the retained records remain unchanged and event outcomes go unrecorded. Existing evaluations of long-horizon agents focus on fact retention and explicit state updates. Whether agents perceive the passage of time and adapt their advice accordingly therefore remains unknown. We frame this ability as temporal state perception and use, which means perceiving the current time and applying it when interpreting dated records. To study it, we design session-rekindling tasks that keep the earlier conversation fixed and vary only the follow-up date and the way temporal information reaches the agent. Experiments across five model routes and five temporal-information conditions show that agents can obtain the current time but often fail to use it. They reliably query the clock and even note in their reasoning that the scheduled date has passed, yet many still tell users to prepare for the expired event. Supplying explicit temporal context reduces this error, and providing the computed date relation removes it entirely. Keeping up with time therefore depends on turning perceived time into updated plans. Based on these findings, we design a session-rekindling benchmark that provides temporal-awareness guidance for designing long-horizon agents. The code can be found at https://github.com/Adoreu2/session-rekindling-benchmark.

title: FEND: Far-End Detection in Outbound Voice AI Calls
description:
arXiv:2611.18050v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a conversational Voice AI agent places an outbound call, the far end may be a live person, a voicemail greeting, an interactive voice response (IVR) system, or increasingly another AI system answering on the callee's behalf. Standard Answering Machine Detection (AMD) reports only whether a human or a machine picked up, a design meant for human call centres, where one machine is as uninteresting as another. That single bit does not tell a Voice AI agent what to do, since leaving a voicemail message, navigating an IVR and holding a short exchange with another AI are three different actions and a two-valued label cannot distinguish them. In 1,000 randomly sampled calls from our own outbound deployment, a live person answered 48.1%, a voicemail system 44.6%, an AI 6.9% and an IVR 0.4%. Our proposed framework, FEND, reads the far end's audio and its streaming transcript and runs one detector for each automated class (voicemail, IVR, AI callee), with human the default when nothing fires, returning a single label within 20 seconds. On a public benchmark the voicemail components reach 100% accuracy without ever misclassifying a live human, where Asterisk's AMD misclassifies 30 to 66% of them. For the AI callee, acoustic features do not transfer across recording conditions, but speech timing does, separating AI from human at 0.952 ROC-AUC, because synthesised speech leaves far shorter gaps between words. On production traffic, separating a live person from any automated far end reaches F1 0.979, and only 2.9% of live people are given an automated label, the error that matters most for an agent acting on the result.

title: Test data that skips the number range - an error in a Uniface click test that was not a bug
description:
Follow-ups in the app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 can repeat: every n days, weeks or months. When a repeating follow-up is completed, the service creates the next one. Stage 28 added a form for that, and the click test failed at exactly this step.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. The app uses SQLite through the SLE driver (SQLite 3.50.2).

The form 

entry DO_COMPLETE
variables
    numeric vNextId
    string vNextDue, vUser, vRole, vError
endvariables
    call NEED_FID
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    askmess/question "Mark follow-up %%(F_ID.FU3_DMY) as done?~Complete", "Yes,No"
    if ($status != 1)
        return 0
    endif
    activate "USER_SVC".CURRENT_USER(vUser, vRole)
    activate "FOLLOWUP3_SVC".COMPLETE(F_ID.FU3_DMY, vUser, vNextId, vNextDue, vError)
    if ($status < 0)
        rollback
        INFO.FU3_DMY = vError
        return -1
    endif
    commit
    if ($cCust$ > 0)
        call DO_FUPS
    endif
    if (vNextId > 0)
        INFO.FU3_DMY = "Follow-up %%(F_ID.FU3_DMY) done; next follow-up %%(vNextId) on %%(vNextDue)."
    else
        INFO.FU3_DMY = "Follow-up %%(F_ID.FU3_DMY) done."
    endif
    return 0
end

The message in the info line was: "The follow-up could not be saved (error -3)." The follow-up itself was still open after the message, because the form rolled back.

Where the message came from

Completing calls the service that marks the follow-up as done, computes the next due date and adds the new follow-up. Adding it gets a new id from a number range:

    activate "CUSTOMER_SVC".NEXT_RANGE_ID("FOLLOWUP", pId, pError)
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif

The number ranges live in a small table, one row per range, and NEXT_RANGE_ID increments the row for "FOLLOWUP".

The cause: the test data

For the test the database copy got two follow-ups with ids 1 and 2, inserted with SQL before the app was started. The counter for "FOLLOWUP" stayed at 0. So the service handed out id 1 for the new follow-up, the insert failed because id 1 already existed, and the service returned the message with the error code from the database layer.

The fix was in the test data, not in the code. With the app closed, the test database got:

PRAGMA journal_mode=OFF;
UPDATE CUSTOMER_SEQ SET LAST_ID = 2 WHERE SEQ_NAME IN ('FOLLOWUP', 'ACTIVITY');

After that, the same click produced: "Follow-up 2 done; next follow-up 3 on 2026-11-10."

What the failure showed

  • The rollback worked. One service call had already marked follow-up 2 as done when the next one failed; after the message, follow-up 2 was still open. The commit happens only after the whole operation succeeded.
  • The error text named the operation that failed ("could not be saved") and the code. That was enough to look at the insert and then at the id.

Notes

  • If test data goes in through SQL, it must also update everything the application keeps next to the rows: counters, sequences, version numbers.
  • Alternatively, create test data through the application's own services, then the counters are right by construction.
  • Before calling a failure a bug, check whether the test data could have been created by the application at all.

title: Vessel2Brain: Edge-Aware Multi-Scale Flow Matching for 3D Brain Image Generation from Vessel Masks
description:
arXiv:2611.17919v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating realistic 3D brain MRI volumes from sparse anatomical priors is a highly ill-posed yet clinically valuable problem, with important applications in data augmentation, simulation, and downstream neuroimaging analysis. In this work, we investigate the challenging task of synthesising full 3D brain MRI volumes conditioned solely on vascular label maps. While vascular structures provide strong anatomical and topological cues, they occupy only a small fraction of the brain volume and offer no direct information about surrounding tissue appearance. To address this challenge, we propose Vessel2Brain, an edge-aware multi-scale conditional flow matching framework that explicitly incorporates vascular structure information into the generative process. Our approach formulates vessel-guided brain image synthesis as a conditional continuous flow, enabling stable training and flexible generation while preserving structural correspondence. A multi-scale flow matching strategy is introduced to jointly model global anatomical coherence and fine-grained local details, with auxiliary velocity predictions providing additional supervision across spatial resolutions. Furthermore, we design an edge-aware objective that emphasises vascular boundaries during training, encouraging anatomically faithful tissue synthesis around vessel structures. We evaluate Vessel2Brain on two public 3D brain MRI datasets with paired vascular annotations. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art generative models in terms of reconstruction accuracy, structural consistency, and distributional realism.

title: RAG-FGO: Dynamic Optimization of Query-Rewriting Agents for Generative RAG
description:
arXiv:2611.17788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), query rewriting serves as a core interface that aligns user intent with external knowledge bases, and its effectiveness directly determines overall system performance. However, generative retrieval faces three critical challenges in real-world deployment: noisy retrieval feedback, the difficulty of jointly optimizing discrete prompt templates and continuous decoding-control parameters, and the limited generalization of static rewriting strategies under semantically complex scenarios. To address these issues, we propose RAG-FGO, a dynamic optimization framework for generative retrieval strategies. RAG-FGO formulates query rewriting as a non-differentiable black-box optimization problem in a mixed discrete-continuous space, and represents prompt templates and decoding parameters as adaptively optimizable query-rewriting agents. The framework performs global search to enable semantic jumps and structural reorganization that escape local optima, while applying local perturbations for fine-grained alignment and precise refinement. In addition, RAG-FGO introduces an elite-preserving memory pool that accumulates high-quality strategies across iterations, thereby mitigating the impact of stochasticity and noisy feedback on optimization stability. Experimental results on a diverse suite of benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method, supporting its applicability to complex semantic retrieval tasks.

title: CO-197 Denial Code: Missing Prior Authorization
description:
The Medicare Advantage prior authorisation data contains a number that should alter the way your practice interprets this code. not the rate of denial. rate of overturns.

An authorisation denial is often seen as final. According to the data, it's usually not.

What does the CO 197 denial code mean?
Code 197, which was last updated on May 1, 2018, is defined by X12 as "Precertification/authorization/notification/pre-treatment absent," with effect from October 31, 2006.

There is no mention of "doing the work." The payer does not claim that the service was unneeded or uncovered. It indicates that a necessary permission step was not completed prior to the provision of the service.

What is authorisation in advance? A service must be approved by the payer before it is rendered. Regardless of whether the service was appropriate, the payer refuses payment in the absence of approval.

Pre-certification, authorisation, notification, and pre-treatment are the four different topics covered by the term. A payer who demands notification within 48 hours is enforcing something very different from one who demands clearance before to the first session. These are distinct requirements with separate regulations. Examine your contracts to see if they apply.

Since the group code is CO, the amount is not the patient's responsibility but rather a contractual obligation. Generally speaking, you cannot bill the patient for a service you did not obtain authorisation for, and trying to do so would likely result in a complaint.

How often is this actually denied, and how often is it overturned?
This is the real-world application of the data. Medicare Advantage insurers "fully or partially denied 4.1 million prior authorisation requests, which is a somewhat larger share (7.7%) of all requests" (KFF) of the roughly 53 million prior authorisation requests that were filed to them in 2024.

"Just 11.5% of denied prior authorisation requests were appealed to Medicare Advantage insurers in 2024," and "80.7" of those appeals were partially or totally reversed (KFF). This is the bit that counts for your workflow.

Together, read those two numbers. Approximately one in nine denials are contested, and four out of five challenges are successful. It is evident that a significant number of appealable denials are being accepted without any testing.

Commercial coverage follows the same trend. KFF discovered that "8% due to lack of preauthorization or referral" was one of the stated reasons for denials in HealthCare.gov marketplace plans in 2021, while customers appealed "less than two-tenths of 1." of in-network denials.

Just to be clear, the Medicare Advantage numbers include denials of prior authorisation requests, which are a slightly different demographic than claims that are denied with CO 197 after the fact. It is nevertheless difficult to dispute the findings' direction.

What do you do when a CO 197 arrives?
Work in this sequence. Neither the appeal nor the write-off should be used first.

Verify the existence of the authorisation. It did, surprisingly frequently, and the number was just not sent on the claim. It settles in a single cycle and is a rectified claim rather than an appeal. This is similar to CO 16, where the stated cause is incomplete information.

Make a request for retroactive approval. In situations where the service was urgent or eligibility was questionable at the time, many payers allow it within a specified window. This is the most frequently omitted phase.

Verify if authorisation was indeed necessary. Requirements are subject to change more frequently than most practices keep track of. It is worthwhile to contest a denial that claims there was no authorisation for a service that no longer needs one.

Make an appeal using clinical records. The appeal focuses on medical necessity and the accompanying documentation if the service was required and provided.

After the foregoing, merely write off. Writing off at step one is leaving money behind due to the overturn rates.

Why is behavioral health hit harder by this?
Because authorisation requirements in the field of behavioural health are more specific, more inconsistent between payers, and more likely to be associated with session counts as opposed to a single authorised episode.

Usually, one authorisation is required for a medical operation. An initial authorisation, a concurrent review at a predetermined number of sessions, and then another may be required for a course of therapy. Each of those represents a distinct chance to miss a deadline, and failing to meet the second one eliminates all subsequent sessions.

This arrangement creates a particular failure mode that is worth keeping an eye out for. Because it belongs to someone, the initial authorisation is sought with caution. The refusal for sessions eleven through eighteen appears all at once, and the concurrent review is overlooked since no one was monitoring session counts against the authorised number.

A tracked session count against each active authorisation, with a trigger prior to the limit instead of after it, is the solution. That is a tracking issue, and tracking issues can be resolved.

Where automation actually helps with CO 197
This is the code where automation pays off the most on both sides. Routing recovers a significant portion of the remaining volume after prevention eliminates the majority of it.

At scheduling, requirements are checked. At the time of booking, it is known whether this payer needs authorisation for this service. The intervention that completely stops the denial is checking it at each appointment.

monitoring the session count in relation to authorisation. There is only a counting issue with the concurrent review failure. Instead of raising the flag after the limit, a system that has the authorised number and the sessions provided can do it before.

Sending denials in the proper direction. A rectified claim is a CO 197 where the authorisation was present. An appeal or a retroactive request can be one in which it didn't. Separating those distinct operations prevents everything from defaulting to write-off.

In order to close the gap that the KFF figures highlight—denials that were appealable but were never appealed—Supabill automates benefits verification across payers and handles denials with routing and appeals.

It's worth specifying the actual limit. Automation cannot create medical necessity or get an authorisation that a payer declines to provide. The write-off is appropriate when a service was actually not authorised and the payer refuses to grant it retroactively. The difference with automation is that you come to that decision after testing it, as opposed to before.

title: Node.js Media Renewal Jobs: At-Least-Once Replay Governance for Duplicate Processing
description:
A media subscription renewal reminder has a deadline, and the queue does not know about it. The queue only knows delivery. With an at-least-once background job queue, retries and duplicate jobs are normal; the engineering decision is how replay is governed so one renewal cycle creates one reminder intent.

Short answer: make replay a recorded business decision. Derive one idempotency key from the renewal cycle, store the decision and outbound intent together, and route every later delivery through that record. Acknowledging a message is not evidence that the reminder happened.

This framing matters during incidents. A consumer can disappear after committing storage but before acknowledging its delivery. The next consumer must be able to say “already decided” without calling the mail provider again.

Define the replay subject before tuning the queue

For a renewal due at 2026-09-01T09:00:00Z, the reminder subject is one subscription, one renewal cycle, and one reminder kind. That tuple is the replay subject. A delivery ID, worker ID, or attempt number is not; each changes when the transport retries.

The producer calculates remindAt once and publishes it with the business data. It also canonicalizes the cycle string. 2026-09 and September-2026 must not become two identities for the same event.

One key. One intent.

type RenewalReminder = {
  subscriptionId: string;
  renewalCycle: string;
  remindAt: string;
  recipient: string;
};

function idempotencyKey(job: RenewalReminder): string {
  return ["renewal-reminder", job.subscriptionId, job.renewalCycle].join(":");
}

I start with this key in design review because it makes the later audit trail legible. “Duplicate suppressed” should answer which renewal was protected, not which opaque queue message happened to arrive first.

When is a replay safe for a deadline-bound reminder?

The worker needs a small durable ledger. Its states can be claimed, queued, and sent, with an outbox ID attached to the business key. The exact labels are less important than the invariant: a second delivery reads the first decision and returns the same intent.

type Claim = { key: string; outboxId: string | null; state: "claimed" | "queued" | "sent" };

interface Tx {
  lockClaim(key: string): Promise<Claim | null>;
  insertClaim(key: string): Promise<Claim>;
  insertOutbox(job: RenewalReminder): Promise<{ id: string }>;
  markQueued(key: string, outboxId: string): Promise<void>;
}

interface Db {
  transaction<T>(fn: (tx: Tx) => Promise<T>): Promise<T>;
}

async function accept(db: Db, job: RenewalReminder) {
  const key = idempotencyKey(job);

  return db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    let claim = await tx.lockClaim(key);
    if (!claim) claim = await tx.insertClaim(key);

    if (claim.outboxId) {
      return { outboxId: claim.outboxId, duplicate: true };
    }

    const outbox = await tx.insertOutbox(job);
    await tx.markQueued(key, outbox.id);
    return { outboxId: outbox.id, duplicate: false };
  });
}

The database supplies the guarantee here: a unique constraint on the business key, a unique constraint on the outbox representation, and a transaction that locks the claim. TypeScript describes the contract; it does not serialize two workers. The outbox sender can retry independently while preserving the same outbox ID.

Picture the failure window in detail. Worker A claims renewal-reminder:sub_418:2026-09, writes outbox row out_91, and commits at 08:59:59. It dies before the queue acknowledgment reaches the broker. Worker B receives the redelivery at 09:00:01, waits for the claim lock, sees out_91, and acknowledges without sending. If the key had included A's delivery ID, B would have created a second row even though the business event had not changed. That is the distinction an incident review needs to capture: transport repetition was expected; the ledger made the business effect singular.

How should a Node.js background job queue handle at-least-once retries and duplicate processing?

Treat retry as a policy with four explicit outcomes: retry now, retry later, quarantine, or acknowledge as a duplicate. That vocabulary is useful in dashboards and runbooks because it separates transport behavior from business state.

When a downstream HTTP service returns 429 Too Many Requests, MDN documents Retry-After as the signal for when to try again. Parse either delay seconds or an HTTP date, add bounded jitter, and keep the original idempotency key. If the header is absent, use a documented local ceiling rather than an unbounded loop.

function retryAt(response: Response, now: Date): Date | null {
  if (response.status !== 429) return null;
  const value = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (!value) return null;

  const seconds = Number(value);
  if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) {
    return new Date(now.getTime() + seconds * 1000);
  }

  const date = new Date(value);
  return Number.isNaN(date.getTime()) ? null : date;
}

Run the sender from the outbox, not from the queue callback. If the callback sends first and records later, a crash can leave an unrecorded email. If it records first and the sender retries by creating a new key, the ledger loses its purpose.

The ledger is the incident artifact

AWS describes a dead-letter queue as a destination for messages that could not be processed successfully after repeated attempts. For renewal reminders, that destination is a review boundary, not a delete button. Preserve the stable business key, original remindAt, attempt count, and a bounded error summary. A replay should re-enter the same claim check.

The useful metrics are decision metrics: duplicate acknowledgments, claim-to-outbox latency, outbox-to-send latency, deadline misses, and dead-letter count. Keep subscription IDs out of metric labels. High-cardinality labels turn a useful incident graph into expensive noise.

Outcome Durable record Next action
Duplicate delivery Existing outbox ID Acknowledge without sending
Temporary rate limit Same outbox ID and notBefore Retry after the server signal
Repeated processing failure Original key and bounded error Quarantine for review

I benchmark the ugly path first: two consumers racing on one key, a worker stopping after the transaction commits, and a provider returning both forms of Retry-After. Clean throughput is a weak proxy for this system's risk.

Set retention from the replay horizon

Storage forgets. If the claim disappears before the maximum dead-letter replay or dispute window, an old delivery can create a second reminder. Keep the key at least as long as that horizon, then test backup restoration against it. Your mileage may vary because the horizon comes from policy and customer support, not queue defaults.

The catch is operational weight. A ledger and outbox require a poller, retention jobs, replay permissions, and an audit view. They are not suitable for a harmless internal update where repeating the write has no effect. Stick with a single idempotent database update in that case. For a customer-facing renewal reminder, the extra machinery buys a clear, inspectable rule: one business intent per cycle.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429

title: This isn't Three.js. This world is code. Meet Wallhammer Web.
description:
This isn't Three.js. Wallhammer Web has its own WebGL2 renderer, and everything in this village comes from code. No imported models. No texture files.

Houses, cobblestones, trees, villagers and flowing water, generated in the browser. Watch the sunlight fade and the windows and lanterns come on:

Graphics made with code

The world is a set of generators. A roof, a tree and a villager are geometry produced by TypeScript. Change the recipe and the world changes. A seed controls repeatable variation.

Wallhammer Web brings the renderer, cameras, environment, world streaming and simulation into one engine. The sun, sky and time of day work together, so the village can move from afternoon into evening as one scene.

Agent-first, from the start

An AI agent can work directly on the world because the world is code. It can build a scene, inspect the result and revise the generators.

The workflow pairs planning and review with implementation. Architecture checks enforce module boundaries. Generator checks, screenshots and performance tools help verify what the agent built. The rendered scene matters as much as the code.

That's what I mean by an agent-first engine: the tools to create a world and check it belong in the same workflow.

The village is one example

The same core also powers a planet with a continuous surface-to-orbit flight, a solar system, building destruction and endlessly streamed terrain. There is a character controller for exploring the world on foot, too.

Simulation runs at a fixed step and can run in Node without a browser or GPU. Rendering stays separate from world logic.

This video is the latest fantasy village running in Wallhammer Web. Graphics made with code. Worlds built by agents.

title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
description:
arXiv:2611.17501v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture.
  To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.

title: How Modern CSS Anchor Positioning Replaces Popper.js (Zero JavaScript)
description:
For years, whenever you needed a tooltip or dropdown that dynamically stays attached to a button and flips when hitting the screen edge, you reached for getBoundingClientRect(), scroll listeners, or libraries like Popper.js / Floating UI.

With CSS Anchor Positioning (Chrome/Edge 125+, Safari 26+), this entire problem is solved in pure CSS.

The Mental Model: Boat & Dock

Think of the button as a Dock and the floating tooltip as a Boat:

  • anchor-name: --dock-btn; (assigns an anchor identifier to the target)
  • position-anchor: --dock-btn; (tethers the floating element)
  • top: anchor(bottom); (positions it relative to the dock edges)
  • position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline; (the browser automatically calculates viewport collisions and flips the element to open space!)

4 Real UI Patterns You Can Build Without JavaScript:

  1. Self-Centered Tooltips across separate DOM containers: Using justify-self: anchor-center.
  2. Collision Auto-Flipping: Using @position-try or keyword presets like flip-block.
  3. Dynamic Width Matching: Setting width: anchor-size(width) so a dropdown automatically resizes to match the search bar above it.
  4. Zero-JS Click Menus: Pairing the native HTML popover and popovertarget attributes with inset: auto.

I put together an animated visual explainer breaking down these 4 patterns with live DOM inspection and code walkthroughs:

If you want to practice, I also created an open-source 60-second coding challenge with starter HTML and tests on GitHub:
https://github.com/muneebali500/cascadedev-code-vault/tree/main/01-CSS/03-anchor-positioning

How are you approaching browser support today? Are you using the OddBird polyfill or progressively enhancing with @supports (anchor-name: --a)?

title: Learned Indexes vs B-Trees in Storage Engines
description:
An index is a bet that the next lookup is close to the last one. B-tree indexes keep that bet in sorted pages, one pointer per key, and pay a page fault or two to find it. Learned index structures replace the pages with a model that predicts a key's position from its value, so the index stores a function instead of a list. The pitch is an order of magnitude less memory and one cache miss instead of three. The catch is that a function fitted to yesterday's data is a liability the moment the distribution moves.

A B-tree spends 16 to 32 bytes per key and three or four cache misses per lookup, while a learned index stores a few bytes per key and predicts the position in one step.

Part One: What is being compared

The headline number is the wrong unit: a budget records cost before the first result, per operation, and on bad days.

Both map a key to a location, both handle duplicates and variable-length keys, and both sit under the same buffer pool and write-ahead log.

Part Two: The arithmetic

The arithmetic is about bytes per key. A B-tree entry costs a key plus a pointer plus fill-factor slack, commonly 16 to 32 bytes, and a lookup walks three or four levels, each a potential cache miss. A learned index stores a small model plus a bounded error, often a few bytes per key, predicts the position in one step, then scans a short range to find the exact entry. On read-heavy keys the memory saving can be tenfold.

The mechanism is about information: one design makes part of the problem observable, and someone must still calibrate the instrument.

Part Three: Where the model breaks

Writes are where the model breaks. B-tree indexes absorb an insert by splitting a page, a local operation with bounded cost. Learned index structures assume a distribution, so an insert outside the fitted range forces a retrain or lands in a delta buffer searched separately. Skewed or adversarial keys, the ones a multi-tenant system sees every day, are exactly where the error bound stops holding and the lookup degrades to a scan.

Inserts outside the fitted distribution force a retrain or a delta buffer, which is why learned indexes win on append-only data and struggle with multi-tenant skew.

Part Four: The later cost

The constant factors are unglamorous. Model inference costs a few SIMD operations, cheap next to a cache miss and expensive next to two comparisons in a hot node. That is why learned indexes win on large, cold indexes and lose on small, hot ones, and why the results cluster around read-only datasets. The engine must also keep the model consistent across compaction, replication and crash recovery.

Expect a split by scale: large operators amortise the fixed side, smaller ones stay because their load is spiky.

Part Five: Outside the team

For the team running a multi-tenant database, the difference is whether one tenant's key pattern can blow up everyone's tail latency. For the user, it is a query that returns in ten milliseconds or two hundred. The daily-life version is a librarian who memorised the shelving plan versus one who reads the labels.

Outside engineering the consequence is access: a system that needs less of the scarce resource can be replicated more widely.

A fair comparison fixes the workload mix, including insert rate and key skew, and prices memory, cache misses and retraining. A lookup benchmark on a static dataset measures the easy half of the problem.

Market sizing check

If learned indexes stay inside specialised engines rather than general databases by 2030, the addressable market is small, perhaps $300M to $1.5B a year embedded in storage products. The deciding factor is write-heavy multi-tenant workloads, not read benchmarks.

All figures are a synthesis of published ranges and a stated model, not a measurement of a shipped system.

The comparison that matters

The comparison that matters is between an index that stores a function and one that stores a sorted list. Learned indexes win on memory and cold-read latency for stable, large keyspaces; B-trees win on inserts, skew, recovery and predictability. Adopt the model where data is append-only.

The ranking assumes the workload keeps its shape; shift the mix and the result changes with no technology changing.

Use a learned index for large, cold, read-mostly keyspaces and keep the B-tree wherever writes, recovery and worst-case bounds are part of the contract.

Security

The Cloud Profiler Java agent is updated with a new Certification Authority (CA) certificate bundle, in response to security bulletin GCP-2026-071. Google Cloud infrastructure and the Cloud Profiler backend service are not affected.

If you use the Cloud Profiler Java agent, take one of the following actions:

  • Upgrade the Java agent to cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00 (GitHub release v0.5.0) or later, and then rebuild and redeploy your applications. Download the updated archive, https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud-profiler/java/cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00.tar.gz, or, for musl-based Alpine Linux containers, https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud-profiler/java/cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00_alpine.tar.gz.
  • If you can't immediately upgrade or rebuild, update your host or container operating system's CA certificate store as described in GCP-2026-071, and then set the GRPC_DEFAULT_SSL_ROOTS_FILE_PATH environment variable to point to the updated PEM bundle.

For more information about installing the agent, see Profiling Java applications.

For more information, see Set the latency tier.
  • Autoscaling schedules: You can configure recurring autoscaling schedules to automatically apply parameter overrides—such as minimum and maximum workers, worker utilization hints, or latency tiers—during specific time windows. For more information, see Schedule autoscaling changes.

You can configure these features when you create a job or update them while the job is running.

title: What Do Multilingual Self-Supervised Speech Encoders Know About Sentence Meaning?
description:
arXiv:2611.17686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) have been scaled up to thousands of languages and millions of hours of audio, yet little is known about how these models structure semantic knowledge across languages. In this work, we probe sentence-level semantics in massively multilingual S3Ms across 76 languages, using linear maps from frozen speech representations into a frozen text embedding space, evaluated by cross-modal retrieval. Sentence meaning is linearly accessible but highly uneven across languages and resource tiers. Cross-lingual probes can match language-specific probes on languages never seen in probe training, but per-model monolingual decodability does not predict transfer. Within the OmniASR wav2vec family, scaling from 300M--7B disproportionately benefits high-resource languages, and ASR tuning sharply improves semantic decodability while making representations more language-specific. However, semantic content is entangled with acoustics, inflating apparent performance on single-speaker corpora.

title: Antidistillation is Cheap: Lightweight Distillation-Resistance via Stylistic Corruption
description:
arXiv:2611.17772v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly effective paradigm for transferring capabilities from large language models (LLMs) to smaller, more specialized student models. In commercial deployment where frontier models are restricted behind black-box APIs, sequence-level distillation remains a potent vector for competitors to clone proprietary capabilities at a fraction of the development cost. Existing defenses mostly rely on surrogate models to manipulate next-token sampling, which increases computational overhead and real-time inference latency. In this work, we propose a lightweight defense that dynamically injects style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations upon malicious queries. This framework offers exceptional flexibility, allowing hosts to customize target defensive styles and dynamically blend them to maximize stylistic variance. Crucially, this inference-time intervention preserves semantic utility and fluency during malicious queries, misleading adversaries into believing that they are extracting pristine teacher outputs, while standard consumers continue to receive original, unmodified responses. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework successfully disrupts student learning, achieving substantial anti-distillation performance while incurring negligible overhead and preserving text naturalness. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/distill-resist-38C6/.

title: Enrichment-Oriented Virtual Screening of Perovskite Solar Cells through Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.18043v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Experimental optimization of perovskite solar cells is constrained by combinatorial diversity in absorber compositions, device layers, and processing, which makes virtual screening attractive for prioritizing recipes before fabrication. We develop a surrogate-guided reinforcement-learning framework that casts recipe generation as virtual screening, enriching candidate shortlists near high-performing experimental neighbors. A frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) guides recipe generation, while a reference pool of 890 measured devices enables neighborhood-based assessment. Five-fold evaluation on 1,846 devices shows top-ten selection raises mean power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 19.68\% to 23.74\%. Three learned policies are compared with six baselines under 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run. In top-100 shortlists, Proximal policy optimization (PPO) and recurrent PPO (RPPO) achieve neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23\% and 24\% (7.9- and 8.3-fold Pure Random's 2.9\%), versus 10\% (3.4-fold) for the baselines with the highest supported hit rate (L-SHADE and Ax BO, tied) at $K = 100$. Gains coexist with weak-support fractions. Of 9,000 recipes, 65.4\% match a composition family at similarity 0.80, falling to 11.7\% at 0.90. Results support enrichment-oriented prioritization but not experimental performance, seed robustness, or matched-budget advantage.

title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks
description:
arXiv:2611.17766v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom. We release the evaluation harness and three public tasks; the other 67 are held out to protect the leaderboard from contamination.

title: Building an Async Java REST Client with CompletableFuture, Concurrent Requests, and Virtual Threads
description:
Synchronous HTTP code is simple.

But sometimes your application needs to call several APIs at once, reduce waiting time, or avoid tying up threads while requests are in flight.

That is where asynchronous programming becomes useful.

In this tutorial, we'll build on Java's built-in HttpClient and explore:

  • sendAsync()
  • CompletableFuture
  • Running multiple HTTP requests concurrently
  • Combining several API responses
  • Handling async errors
  • Applying timeouts
  • Using Jackson with asynchronous responses
  • Comparing CompletableFuture with virtual threads
  • Understanding when async code is actually worth using

By the end, you'll have several practical patterns for building concurrent REST clients in modern Java.

1. Synchronous vs Asynchronous HTTP

A normal synchronous request looks like this:

HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(
        request,
        HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
);

The current thread waits until the response arrives.

Conceptually:

Send request
    ↓
Wait
    ↓
Wait
    ↓
Receive response
    ↓
Continue

This is easy to understand.

But if you need to call three independent APIs:

API A → 2 seconds
API B → 3 seconds
API C → 1 second

and you call them one after another, the total time can be roughly:

2 + 3 + 1 = 6 seconds

That is where concurrency can help.

2. HttpClient.sendAsync()

Java's HttpClient has an asynchronous method:

sendAsync()

Instead of returning:

HttpResponse<String>

it returns:

CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>

Example:

CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>> future =
        client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        );

The request starts, but the current thread does not block waiting for the result.

3. Your First Async Request

Let's create a simple example.

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

public class AsyncExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        HttpClient client =
                HttpClient.newHttpClient();

        HttpRequest request =
                HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                        .uri(URI.create(
                                "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1"
                        ))
                        .GET()
                        .build();

        CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>> future =
                client.sendAsync(
                        request,
                        HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
                );

        future.thenAccept(response -> {
            System.out.println(
                    response.statusCode()
            );

            System.out.println(
                    response.body()
            );
        });

        future.join();
    }
}

The important line is:

future.thenAccept(...)

This says:

When the response arrives, run this code.

4. What Does join() Do?

In the previous example, we used:

future.join();

Why?

Because this is a small console application.

Without it, the main method could finish before the asynchronous response is processed.

join() waits for the CompletableFuture to complete.

So although the HTTP operation is asynchronous, our demo waits at the end so the application stays alive.

In larger applications, you often won't call join() immediately.

5. thenApply() vs thenAccept()

These two methods are commonly used with CompletableFuture.

thenAccept()

Use it when you want to consume a result but not return another value.

future.thenAccept(response -> {
    System.out.println(
            response.body()
    );
});

thenApply()

Use it when you want to transform the result.

CompletableFuture<String> bodyFuture =
        future.thenApply(
                HttpResponse::body
        );

Now:

bodyFuture

is:

CompletableFuture<String>

rather than:

CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>

6. Transforming an HTTP Response

A common pattern is:

CompletableFuture<String> result =
        client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        )
        .thenApply(
                HttpResponse::body
        );

Then:

String body = result.join();

This is much cleaner if you only care about the body.

But in production code, you should usually check the status code first.

7. Validate the Status Code

Let's create a helper:

private static HttpResponse<String> validate(
        HttpResponse<String> response
) {

    int status =
            response.statusCode();

    if (status >= 200 &&
        status < 300) {

        return response;
    }

    throw new RuntimeException(
            "HTTP " +
            status +
            ": " +
            response.body()
    );
}

Now:

CompletableFuture<String> bodyFuture =
        client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        )
        .thenApply(
                AsyncExample::validate
        )
        .thenApply(
                HttpResponse::body
        );

The flow becomes:

sendAsync()
    ↓
validate()
    ↓
extract body

8. Add Jackson

Now let's combine async HTTP with Jackson.

Suppose an API returns:

{
  "id": 1,
  "title": "Hello",
  "body": "Example",
  "userId": 1
}

Create a record:

public record Post(
        int id,

}

Then use Jackson:

ObjectMapper mapper =

9. Async JSON Deserialization

Example:

CompletableFuture<Post> postFuture =
        client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        )
        .thenApply(
                AsyncExample::validate
        )
        .thenApply(
                HttpResponse::body
        )
        .thenApply(body -> {

                return mapper.readValue(
                        body,

Now:

is:

Post post =
        postFuture.join();

System.out.println(
        post.title()
);

10. Create a Reusable Async GET Method

Let's make the pattern reusable.

public <T> CompletableFuture<T> getAsync(
        String url,
        Class<T> responseType
) {

    HttpRequest request =
            HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                    .uri(URI.create(url))
                    .header(
                            "Accept",
                            "application/json"
                    )
                    .GET()
                    .build();

    return client.sendAsync(
            request,
            HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
    )
    .thenApply(this::validate)
    .thenApply(response -> {

        try {

            return mapper.readValue(
                    response.body(),
                    responseType
            );

        } catch (IOException e) {

            throw new CompletionException(e);
        }
    });
}

Now calling an API becomes:

CompletableFuture<User> future =
        restClient.getAsync(
                "https://example.com/users/1",
                User.class
        );

11. Why CompletionException?

Inside a CompletableFuture pipeline, checked exceptions are awkward.

Jackson can throw:

IOException

but a lambda passed to thenApply() cannot simply throw it.

A common pattern is:

throw new CompletionException(e);

This wraps the checked exception inside an unchecked exception that works naturally with CompletableFuture.

12. Run Multiple Requests Concurrently

This is where async becomes especially useful.

Suppose we want:

/users/1
/posts/1
/todos/1

We can start all three requests immediately:

CompletableFuture<User> userFuture =
        client.getAsync(
                userUrl,
                User.class
        );

CompletableFuture<Post> postFuture =
        client.getAsync(
                postUrl,
                Post.class
        );

CompletableFuture<Todo> todoFuture =
        client.getAsync(
                todoUrl,
                Todo.class
        );

At this point, all three requests can be in flight at the same time.

13. Sequential vs Concurrent Timing

Sequential:

Request A
    ↓
wait
    ↓
Request B
    ↓
wait
    ↓
Request C

Concurrent:

Request A ──────────────┐
Request B ──────────┐   │
Request C ───────┐  │   │
                 ↓  ↓   ↓
               results arrive

If the requests are independent, concurrent execution can reduce total waiting time significantly.

14. Combine Two Futures with thenCombine()

Suppose we want to combine:

CompletableFuture<User>

and:

CompletableFuture<List<Post>>

We can use:

thenCombine()

Example:

CompletableFuture<UserProfile> profileFuture =
        userFuture.thenCombine(
                postsFuture,
                (user, posts) ->
                        new UserProfile(
                                user,
                                posts
                        )
        );

Now:

profileFuture

contains both results.

15. Example UserProfile 

public record UserProfile(
        User user,
        List<Post> posts
) {
}

Then:

UserProfile profile =
        profileFuture.join();

This is useful when several endpoints contribute to one final result.

16. Combine Many Futures with allOf()

thenCombine() works well for two futures.

For many futures, use:

CompletableFuture.allOf(...)

Example:

CompletableFuture<User> userFuture =
        getUser();

CompletableFuture<List<Post>> postsFuture =
        getPosts();

CompletableFuture<List<Todo>> todosFuture =
        getTodos();

Then:

CompletableFuture<Void> all =
        CompletableFuture.allOf(
                userFuture,
                postsFuture,
                todosFuture
        );

Wait for all:

all.join();

Then retrieve:

User user =
        userFuture.join();

List<Post> posts =
        postsFuture.join();

List<Todo> todos =
        todosFuture.join();

17. Build the Final Object After allOf()

A cleaner approach:

CompletableFuture<Dashboard> dashboardFuture =
        CompletableFuture.allOf(
                userFuture,
                postsFuture,
                todosFuture
        )
        .thenApply(ignored ->
                new Dashboard(
                        userFuture.join(),
                        postsFuture.join(),
                        todosFuture.join()
                )
        );

Now:

Dashboard dashboard =
        dashboardFuture.join();

18. A Helper for Lists of Futures

Suppose we have:

List<CompletableFuture<User>>

and want:

CompletableFuture<List<User>>

We can create:

public static <T>
CompletableFuture<List<T>> sequence(
        List<CompletableFuture<T>> futures
) {

    CompletableFuture<Void> all =
            CompletableFuture.allOf(
                    futures.toArray(
                            CompletableFuture[]::new
                    )
            );

    return all.thenApply(
            ignored ->
                    futures.stream()
                            .map(
                                    CompletableFuture::join
                            )
                            .toList()
    );
}

Usage:

List<CompletableFuture<User>> futures =
        ids.stream()
                .map(
                        id ->
                                client.getAsync(
                                        "/users/" + id,
                                        User.class
                                )
                )
                .toList();

CompletableFuture<List<User>> usersFuture =
        sequence(futures);

This is a very useful pattern.

19. But Don't Launch Unlimited Requests

There is an important danger.

Imagine:

10,000 user IDs

and you do:

ids.stream()
        .map(id -> getAsync(...))
        .toList();

You might launch thousands of HTTP requests at once.

That can:

  • Overload the remote API
  • Hit rate limits
  • Exhaust resources
  • Create huge memory pressure

Concurrency still needs limits.

20. Limit Concurrency

One simple approach is batching.

Instead of:

10,000 concurrent requests

do:

50 at a time

For example:

int batchSize = 50;

Then process IDs in batches.

Conceptually:

Batch 1
    → 50 requests
    → wait

Batch 2
    → 50 requests
    → wait

Batch 3
    → 50 requests

This is often safer than unlimited concurrency.

21. Async Error Handling with exceptionally()

Suppose a request fails.

You can handle it using:

exceptionally()

Example:

CompletableFuture<User> future =
        client.getAsync(
                url,
                User.class
        )
        .exceptionally(error -> {

            System.err.println(
                    error.getMessage()
            );

            return null;
        });

This converts the failed future into a successful future containing:

null

That can be useful, but be careful.

Returning null can hide failures.

22. Use handle() When You Need Both Cases

handle() receives both:

result
error

Example:

future.handle(
        (user, error) -> {

            if (error != null) {

                System.err.println(
                        "Request failed: " +
                        error.getMessage()
                );

                return fallbackUser();
            }

            return user;
        }
);

This is useful for fallback logic.

23. Use whenComplete() for Logging

Sometimes you don't want to change the result.

You just want to observe it.

Use:

whenComplete()

Example:

future.whenComplete(
        (result, error) -> {

            if (error != null) {

                System.err.println(
                        "Failed: " +
                        error.getMessage()
                );

            } else {

                System.out.println(
                        "Request completed"
                );
            }
        }
);

The original future result continues unchanged.

24. exceptionally() vs handle() vs whenComplete()

A useful rule:

exceptionally()
    → recover only from failure

handle()
    → transform success or failure

whenComplete()
    → observe success or failure

25. Add Async Timeouts

CompletableFuture provides timeout helpers.

Fail after a timeout 

future.orTimeout(
        5,
        TimeUnit.SECONDS
);

If the future does not complete in time, it fails.

Return a fallback value 

future.completeOnTimeout(
        fallbackUser,
        5,
        TimeUnit.SECONDS
);

This can be useful in applications where partial results are acceptable.

26. HTTP Timeout vs Future Timeout

These are different.

HttpRequest.timeout(...)

Controls the HTTP request.

HttpRequest.newBuilder()
        .timeout(
                Duration.ofSeconds(10)
        )

CompletableFuture.orTimeout(...)

Controls the future pipeline.

future.orTimeout(
        12,
        TimeUnit.SECONDS
);

Using both can provide stronger protection.

27. Async POST Requests

POST can also be asynchronous.

Example:

public <T, R>
CompletableFuture<R> postAsync(
        String url,
        T requestBody,
        Class<R> responseType
) {

    try {

        String json =
                mapper.writeValueAsString(
                        requestBody
                );

        HttpRequest request =
                HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                        .uri(URI.create(url))
                        .header(
                                "Content-Type",
                                "application/json"
                        )
                        .POST(
                                HttpRequest.BodyPublishers
                                        .ofString(json)
                        )
                        .build();

        return client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        )
        .thenApply(this::validate)
        .thenApply(response -> {

            try {

                return mapper.readValue(
                        response.body(),
                        responseType
                );

            } catch (IOException e) {

                throw new CompletionException(e);
            }
        });

    } catch (IOException e) {

        return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(
                e
        );
    }
}

28. Why failedFuture() Is Useful

Suppose serialization fails before the HTTP request starts.

We still want to return:

CompletableFuture<R>

instead of throwing immediately.

Java provides:

CompletableFuture.failedFuture(error)

So the caller sees the failure through the same async API.

29. Build an Async RestClient

Let's create a more complete version.

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.DeserializationFeature;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException;

public class AsyncRestClient {

    private final HttpClient client;
    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    public AsyncRestClient() {

        this.client =
                HttpClient.newBuilder()
                        .connectTimeout(
                                Duration.ofSeconds(10)
                        )
                        .build();

        this.mapper =
                new ObjectMapper()
                        .configure(
                                DeserializationFeature
                                        .FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES,
                                false
                        );
    }

    public <T> CompletableFuture<T> getAsync(
            String url,
            Class<T> responseType
    ) {

        HttpRequest request =
                HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                        .uri(
                                URI.create(url)
                        )
                        .timeout(
                                Duration.ofSeconds(20)
                        )
                        .header(
                                "Accept",
                                "application/json"
                        )
                        .GET()
                        .build();

        return client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        )
        .thenApply(this::validate)
        .thenApply(
                response ->
                        deserialize(
                                response.body(),
                                responseType
                        )
        );
    }

    private HttpResponse<String> validate(
            HttpResponse<String> response
    ) {

        int status =
                response.statusCode();

        if (status >= 200 &&
            status < 300) {

            return response;
        }

        throw new ApiException(
                status,
                response.body()
        );
    }

    private <T> T deserialize(
            String body,
            Class<T> responseType
    ) {

        try {

            return mapper.readValue(
                    body,
                    responseType
            );

        } catch (IOException e) {

            throw new CompletionException(e);
        }
    }
}

30. Add Authentication

We can add a bearer token:

private final String token;

Constructor:

public AsyncRestClient(
        String token
) {

    this.token = token;

    // initialize client and mapper
}

Then create a shared builder:

private HttpRequest.Builder requestBuilder(
        String url
) {

    HttpRequest.Builder builder =
            HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                    .uri(
                            URI.create(url)
                    )
                    .timeout(
                            Duration.ofSeconds(20)
                    )
                    .header(
                            "Accept",
                            "application/json"
                    );

    if (token != null &&
        !token.isBlank()) {

        builder.header(
                "Authorization",
                "Bearer " + token
        );
    }

    return builder;
}

Then:

HttpRequest request =
        requestBuilder(url)
                .GET()
                .build();

31. Async Retries

Retries can also work with async requests.

A simple recursive pattern:

private CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>
sendWithRetry(
        HttpRequest request,
        int attempt
) {

    return client.sendAsync(
            request,
            HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
    )
    .thenCompose(response -> {

        if (!isRetryableStatus(
                response.statusCode()
        )) {

            return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(
                    response
            );
        }

        if (attempt >= 3) {

            return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(
                    response
            );
        }

        return delay(
                Duration.ofSeconds(attempt)
        )
        .thenCompose(
                ignored ->
                        sendWithRetry(
                                request,
                                attempt + 1
                        )
        );
    });
}

Now we need an async delay.

32. Async Delay Without Thread.sleep()

Blocking with:

Thread.sleep(...)

inside async code defeats part of the purpose.

A better option is:

CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(...)

Example:

private CompletableFuture<Void> delay(
        Duration duration
) {

    return CompletableFuture.runAsync(
            () -> {},
            CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(
                    duration.toMillis(),
                    TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS
            )
    );
}

Now the retry delay itself does not block the request-handling thread.

33. Async Retry with Exponential Backoff

We can calculate:

private Duration retryDelay(
        int attempt
) {

    long millis =
            1000L *
            (1L << (attempt - 1));

    return Duration.ofMillis(
            millis
    );
}

Then:

return delay(
        retryDelay(attempt)
)
.thenCompose(
        ignored ->
                sendWithRetry(
                        request,
                        attempt + 1
                )
);

This produces:

1 second
2 seconds
4 seconds

34. Async Code Can Become Hard to Read

This is the main downside.

Simple synchronous code:

User user =
        client.getUser();

List<Post> posts =
        client.getPosts();

Async code:

CompletableFuture<User> userFuture =
        client.getUserAsync();

CompletableFuture<List<Post>> postsFuture =
        client.getPostsAsync();

CompletableFuture<UserProfile> profile =
        userFuture.thenCombine(
                postsFuture,
                UserProfile::new
        );

The async version can be faster for independent requests.

But it is also more complex.

So don't use async just because it looks more advanced.

35. Enter Virtual Threads

Modern Java gives us another option:

virtual threads

Virtual threads make blocking code much cheaper than traditional platform threads.

This changes how we think about HTTP concurrency.

Instead of writing async pipelines, we can often write normal blocking code while still achieving high concurrency.

36. Traditional Threads vs Virtual Threads

Traditional threads are relatively expensive.

You generally don't want:

10,000 platform threads

Virtual threads are much lighter.

So this style becomes practical:

try (var executor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

    // submit many blocking tasks
}

Each task can call:

client.send(...)

normally.

37. Virtual Thread Example

Suppose we want three HTTP calls.

try (var executor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

    Future<User> userFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getUser()
            );

    Future<List<Post>> postsFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getPosts()
            );

    Future<List<Todo>> todosFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getTodos()
            );

    User user =
            userFuture.get();

    List<Post> posts =
            postsFuture.get();

    List<Todo> todos =
            todosFuture.get();
}

These calls run concurrently.

But each method can remain synchronous internally.

38. Why Virtual Threads Are Attractive

Compare these two approaches.

CompletableFuture 

userFuture
        .thenCombine(
                postsFuture,
                UserProfile::new
        )
        .thenApply(...)
        .exceptionally(...)

Virtual threads 

User user =
        userFuture.get();

List<Post> posts =
        postsFuture.get();

return new UserProfile(
        user,
        posts
);

Virtual threads often let you keep simpler control flow.

39. Does HttpClient Work with Virtual Threads?

Yes.

You can use regular blocking:

client.send(...)

inside a virtual thread.

That is often a very clean design for applications that need high concurrency but prefer straightforward imperative code.

40. CompletableFuture vs Virtual Threads

A rough comparison:

Feature CompletableFuture Virtual Threads
Non-blocking style Yes No, logically blocking
Readability Can become complex Usually simpler
Composition Excellent Straightforward
High concurrency Yes Yes
Best for pipelines Excellent Good
Best for imperative code Okay Excellent
Error handling Functional style Traditional try/catch

Neither approach is always better.

41. When CompletableFuture Is a Good Fit

Use it when:

  • You already have an asynchronous API
  • You need to compose several asynchronous stages
  • You want non-blocking pipelines
  • You need thenCombine(), allOf(), or async transformations
  • Your framework already works heavily with futures

Example:

HTTP request
    ↓
parse response
    ↓
fetch another resource
    ↓
combine results
    ↓
transform

42. When Virtual Threads Are a Good Fit

Virtual threads are often excellent when:

  • Your code is naturally synchronous
  • You want many concurrent blocking operations
  • You want simple try/catch control flow
  • You don't want deeply nested future chains
  • Your application uses lots of I/O

Example:

User user =
        userApi.getUser(id);

List<Post> posts =
        postApi.getPosts(id);

return new Profile(
        user,
        posts
);

This style is easier to debug and understand.

43. Avoid Mixing Styles Without a Reason

You can technically combine:

CompletableFuture
virtual threads
reactive code
blocking code

in one application.

But complexity grows quickly.

Choose the simplest model that fits your needs.

A useful rule:

Simple request
    → synchronous

Many concurrent blocking tasks
    → consider virtual threads

Async pipeline composition
    → consider CompletableFuture

44. Example: Fetch 100 Users Concurrently with CompletableFuture 

List<Integer> ids =
        IntStream.rangeClosed(
                1,

        )
        .boxed()
        .toList();

List<CompletableFuture<User>> futures =
        ids.stream()
                .map(
                        id ->
                                client.getAsync(

                                        "/users/" +

List<User> users =
        sequence(futures)

This works well.

But remember: concurrency should still be bounded for large workloads.

45. Example: Fetch 100 Users with Virtual Threads 

try (var executor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

    List<Future<User>> futures =
            ids.stream()
                    .map(
                            id ->
                                    executor.submit(
                                            () ->
                                                    client.get(
                                                            "/users/" +
                                                            id,

46. Partial Failure

Suppose you request:

100 users

and one request fails.

Should the entire operation fail?

Maybe.

Maybe not.

This depends on your application.

All-or-nothing 

One failure
    → entire operation fails

Best effort 

Successful responses
    → keep them

Failed responses
    → log and continue

You should decide this explicitly.

47. Best-Effort Async Example 

CompletableFuture<User> future =
        client.getAsync(
                url,
                User.class
        )
        .handle(
                (user, error) -> {

                    if (error != null) {

                        System.err.println(
                                "Failed: " +
                                url
                        );

                        return null;
                    }

                    return user;
                }
        );

Then filter:

List<User> users =
        sequence(futures)
                .join()
                .stream()
                .filter(
                        Objects::nonNull
                )
                .toList();

48. Preserve Error Information

Returning null loses useful information.

A cleaner approach is a result wrapper.

public record Result<T>(
        T value,
        Throwable error
) {

    public boolean isSuccess() {
        return error == null;
    }
}

Then:

CompletableFuture<Result<User>> future =
        client.getAsync(
                url,
                User.class
        )
        .handle(
                (user, error) ->
                        new Result<>(
                                user,
                                error
                        )
        );

Now every operation produces a result.

49. Use Cases for Concurrent REST Calls

Concurrency is especially useful when:

  • Building dashboards from several APIs
  • Aggregating microservice responses
  • Calling independent third-party services
  • Fetching multiple pages
  • Processing many independent resources
  • Enriching data from several endpoints

For example:

Customer profile
    ↓
Customer API
Orders API
Payments API
Shipping API

If those requests are independent, they can often run concurrently.

50. Don't Parallelize Dependent Requests

Suppose:

Request B needs data from Request A

Then you cannot simply run them together.

Example:

GET /users/10
    ↓
extract accountId
    ↓
GET /accounts/{accountId}

That is a dependency chain.

With CompletableFuture:

CompletableFuture<Account> accountFuture =
        getUserAsync(10)
                .thenCompose(
                        user ->
                                getAccountAsync(
                                        user.accountId()
                                )
                );

Notice:

thenCompose()

not:

thenApply()

51. thenApply() vs thenCompose()

This distinction is important.

Suppose:

getUserAsync()

returns:

CompletableFuture<User>

and:

getAccountAsync(...)

returns:

CompletableFuture<Account>

If you use:

thenApply(...)

you may get:

CompletableFuture<
    CompletableFuture<Account>
>

That's usually not what you want.

Use:

thenCompose(...)

to flatten it into:

CompletableFuture<Account>

52. The Mental Model

A useful rule:

thenApply
    → T becomes R

thenCompose
    → T becomes CompletableFuture<R>
      and Java flattens it

Example:

future.thenApply(
        user ->
                user.name()
);

versus:

future.thenCompose(
        user ->
                getPostsAsync(
                        user.id()
                )
);

53. Full Example: Async User Dashboard

Suppose we have:

public record User(
        int id,
        String name
) {
}

public record Post(
        int id,
        int userId,
        String title
) {
}

public record Todo(
        int id,
        int userId,
        String title,
        boolean completed
) {
}

And:

public record Dashboard(
        User user,
        List<Post> posts,
        List<Todo> todos
) {
}

Then:

CompletableFuture<User> userFuture =
        getUserAsync(userId);

CompletableFuture<List<Post>> postsFuture =
        getPostsAsync(userId);

CompletableFuture<List<Todo>> todosFuture =
        getTodosAsync(userId);

CompletableFuture<Dashboard> dashboardFuture =
        CompletableFuture.allOf(
                userFuture,
                postsFuture,
                todosFuture
        )
        .thenApply(
                ignored ->
                        new Dashboard(
                                userFuture.join(),
                                postsFuture.join(),
                                todosFuture.join()
                        )
        );

Now:

Dashboard dashboard =
        dashboardFuture.join();

54. The Same Idea with Virtual Threads 

try (var executor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

    Future<User> userFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getUser(userId)
            );

    Future<List<Post>> postsFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getPosts(userId)
            );

    Future<List<Todo>> todosFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getTodos(userId)
            );

    Dashboard dashboard =
            new Dashboard(
                    userFuture.get(),
                    postsFuture.get(),
                    todosFuture.get()
            );
}

Same concurrency.

Different programming model.

55. Which Version Would I Choose?

For this particular example, virtual threads are arguably easier to read.

The control flow is straightforward.

But if the rest of your system already uses asynchronous APIs and futures, CompletableFuture may fit better.

The important thing is not to choose the most complicated option.

Choose the model that makes the code easiest to understand and maintain.

56. Quick CompletableFuture Cheat Sheet

Start an async HTTP request 

client.sendAsync(
        request,
        HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
);

Transform result 

future.thenApply(...)

Chain another async operation 

future.thenCompose(...)

Consume result 

future.thenAccept(...)

Combine two futures 

future1.thenCombine(
        future2,
        (a, b) -> ...
);

Wait for many 

CompletableFuture.allOf(
        futures...
);

Recover from error 

future.exceptionally(...)

Handle success or failure 

future.handle(...)

Observe completion 

future.whenComplete(...)

Wait for result 

future.join()

57. Quick Virtual Thread Cheat Sheet

Create an executor:

try (var executor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

}

Submit a blocking task:

Future<User> future =
        executor.submit(
                () ->
                        getUser()
        );

Get the result:

User user =
        future.get();

This lets you keep synchronous APIs while still achieving a high degree of concurrency.

58. Production Checklist

Before shipping concurrent HTTP code, ask:

  • Are requests independent?
  • Is concurrency bounded?
  • Are timeouts configured?
  • Are rate limits respected?
  • Are retries bounded?
  • Are errors preserved?
  • Is partial failure acceptable?
  • Are async exceptions handled?
  • Are POST retries safe?
  • Are large batches controlled?
  • Is the code still readable?
  • Would virtual threads make it simpler?

Concurrency can improve performance, but uncontrolled concurrency can create new problems.

Final Thoughts

Java now gives us several strong options for HTTP concurrency.

You can use:

HttpClient.sendAsync()
        +
CompletableFuture

for asynchronous pipelines.

Or:

virtual threads
        +
blocking HttpClient.send()

for high-concurrency code that still looks synchronous.

The key is understanding the tradeoff.

CompletableFuture is excellent when your workflow is naturally asynchronous and composed from multiple stages.

Virtual threads are excellent when you want simple blocking code but still need lots of concurrent I/O.

A useful progression is:

Simple request
    ↓
Synchronous HttpClient

Several independent requests
    ↓
CompletableFuture or virtual threads

Large-scale concurrent I/O
    ↓
Bounded concurrency + timeouts + retries + rate limits

The goal is not to make your code "more asynchronous."

The goal is to make it faster where concurrency helps, while keeping the code understandable.

title: Fuse-All MoE Inference Kernel with Load Balancing on TPUs
description:
arXiv:2611.17857v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures activate only a subset of experts for each token, allowing large language models (LLMs) to scale parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation per token. However, intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads limit the efficiency of MoE inference on TPUs. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce Fuse-All MoE, a TPU kernel design that jointly optimizes expert computation, output communication, and load balancing. The kernel fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes, retaining expert computation intermediates on chip. Fixed token-slot destinations allow scheduling and expert placement to change while preserving routing semantics. In prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving, Fuse-All MoE balances EP16 prefill workloads through scheduling and expert redistribution, while symmetric EP8TP2 shares active expert computation between the two TensorCore devices within each chip during decode. Our experiments show that Fuse-All MoE reduces kernel runtime for a measured skewed EP16 prefill workload from 2.3x to 1.09x the same fixed reference time for a balanced workload. Across 32-512 decode tokens, symmetric EP8TP2 reduces kernel latency by up to 21.3% relative to fused EP16. With accompanying serving stack optimizations, the integrated system improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.
