title: I Built a Meeting Notes App That Never Leaves Your Laptop
description:
You know those meeting assistants that politely join your call as "Notetaker", record everyone, ship the audio off to some server and then send you a nice summary... and a monthly invoice?

They work, sure. But every time one showed up in a call about a client contract or a project under NDA, I couldn't help wondering where that recording was going to end up... and I really needed something to be able to live translate any incoming voice, and fast (upcoming important work call).

So I built Parla ("speak" in Italian): a meeting notes app for Windows where everything, and I mean everything, happens on your own computer.

What it does

  • Records any meeting, from any app (Zoom, Teams, Meet, a YouTube video, whatever). It captures your mic plus the system audio through WASAPI loopback, so no bot joins the call and you don't need virtual audio cables.
  • Transcribes word for word, live, in 25 European languages.
  • Tells speakers apart. You can rename them afterwards, or merge two labels when the model decides you're two different people (it happens).
  • Translates live in a floating overlay, so you can follow the people speaking another language while they talk.
  • Summarizes on demand: key points, decisions and action items, but only if you ask.
  • Imports audio and video files, and exports everything to Markdown.

No accounts, no subscription, no cloud. The models download once during setup and after that it works offline.

The part I cared about most: modest hardware

A lot of local AI tools quietly assume you have a gaming GPU sitting under your desk. I wanted Parla to run on the kind of laptop most people actually have at work, so everything runs on the CPU and 8 GB of RAM is enough.

The first-run wizard checks how much RAM you have and only offers the summary model that fits: Qwen3.5 2B on 8 GB machines, with the option to switch to 4B if you have 16 GB or more. The translation model only gets loaded while translation is on, so it doesn't sit in memory for nothing.

Under the hood

The core is Rust, the UI is React inside Tauri, and the models are all open:

Job Model
Speech recognition NVIDIA Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (int8)
Voice activity Silero VAD
Speaker labels WeSpeaker ResNet34
Live translation Tencent Hy-MT2 1.8B (Q4_K_M)
Summaries Qwen3.5 2B / 4B (Q4_K_M)
LLM runtime llama.cpp, CPU build

Speech, VAD and speaker embeddings run through sherpa-onnx, while translation and summaries go through a local llama.cpp server. If you already have LM Studio or Ollama running, you can point the translate and summarize slots at those instead.

One fun problem: without headphones, your mic picks up the other people's voices from the speakers, and you end up with every sentence transcribed twice. There's an echo guard for that, which drops the mic's copy of what the system audio already caught.

Try it

Grab the installer from the releases page. It installs per user, so no admin rights needed, and everything it creates lives in one folder you can wipe from the settings.

It's free and open source (MIT), so feel free to poke around the code, open issues, or tell me what breaks on your machine.

Let me know if you like it, and happy (private) meetings!

title: AI Gateway now supports Private Inference
description:
Private Inference connects your own model endpoints to AI Gateway.

Enterprises running fine-tuned, self-hosted, or prerelease models used to need separate keys, client code, and logs for them. Those models can now run through the same authentication, SDKs and APIs, and observability as catalog models, so every model your team uses is managed in one place.

Use Private Inference to:

  • Switch between private and catalog models: Call private models through Chat Completions, Responses, or Messages. AI Gateway translates each request to your endpoint's format, so switching only changes the model ID.

  • Keep models scoped to your team: Only your Vercel team can view or call private models, and they aren't listed in the public catalog. Credentials are stored encrypted, and you can enable Zero Data Retention per provider.

  • Connect coding agents: Use private models in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other coding agents connected to AI Gateway.

  • Monitor traffic together: View private model requests alongside catalog traffic in logs, trace drains, and custom reporting. Observability charts break down requests, tokens, and time to first token by private model.

  • Configure fallbacks: Optionally fall back to a catalog model if your private endpoint fails.

To get started, open the Private Inference page and add your endpoint as a private provider. Enter its base URL, select its API format, and add its credentials. Then add the models it serves.

You can also register the provider and model with the Vercel CLI, version 65.16.0 or later:

Call the model using its private/<slug> ID:

Private model requests appear in AI Gateway logs alongside requests to catalog models.

title: Lock down Amazon S3 and IAM with least privilege and Block Public Access
description:
This article was first published on the Rokkhe blog on Hashnode. It was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed and edited by the Rokkhe team; all commands and sources were checked against AWS documentation.

A hands-on pass of official AWS controls, on accounts you own. 16 November 2026, Asia/Dhaka. By the Rokkhe research team.

A surprising number of cloud incidents start with a setting: a bucket policy that grants Principal: "*", an access-control list that still allows AllUsers, or an application role with s3:* on Resource: "*". AWS already ships the controls that close those paths. This post uses them, in a safe order: read first, then tighten.

You will need permission to call S3 and IAM APIs on the account, and a terminal with the AWS CLI configured for that account. Replace placeholders such as amzn-s3-demo-bucket and 123456789012 with your own names. Do not run these commands against an account you do not administer.

TL;DR

  • Turn on S3 Block Public Access at the account level, with all four settings enabled, unless you have a documented exception for a bucket that is deliberately public.
  • Before you change a bucket, read its Block Public Access config, policy and ACLs.
  • Replace s3:* on * with the actions and prefixes the application actually uses.
  • Use IAM Access Analyzer to list resources that are still shared publicly or with other accounts, and to find unused access.
  • This is not a complete AWS security programme. It is the misconfiguration pass most teams can finish in an afternoon.

Public data is usually a setting, not a break-in

AWS documents S3 access as a combination of account settings, bucket policies, IAM identity policies, and (for older setups) access-control lists. Block Public Access is the safety catch on top: it can prevent public ACLs and public policies from taking effect, at the account or at the bucket.

That is why this pass starts with Block Public Access and Access Analyzer, not with a hunt for an attacker. If a bucket is public, the first job is to decide whether it was meant to be public (a static website you accept as public) or whether it is a mistake. Both happen. Only the second is an incident; both should be explicit in a ticket.

One useful fact before you start: since April 2023, AWS turns on all four Block Public Access settings and disables ACLs for every new bucket by default (AWS News Blog). Buckets created before that, or created by templates that switched those defaults off, are where this pass usually finds work.

Work in a non-production account first if you can, or on a bucket whose downtime you can afford, until you are comfortable with the read commands.

Turn on S3 Block Public Access at the account, then check each bucket

AWS’s “Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage” page describes four switches: BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, and RestrictPublicBuckets. For almost every account, all four should be true at the account level, so a new bucket cannot be made public by accident.

Read the account setting first:

# Replace with your 12-digit account id.
aws s3control get-public-access-block --account-id 123456789012

If the command says the configuration is missing, or any of the four flags is false, document the current state, then apply the official all-true configuration:

aws s3control put-public-access-block \
  --account-id 123456789012 \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
    BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true

Then check a specific bucket:

aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket amzn-s3-demo-bucket

A bucket can have its own Block Public Access settings. Account-level settings still apply; AWS documents how the more restrictive combination wins. If a marketing site must be public, make that a named exception with an owner, not a quiet hole in the account-level catch. Everything else should inherit the account default.

List buckets so you know the scope of the afternoon:

aws s3api list-buckets --query 'Buckets[].Name' --output text

Read the bucket policy and ACLs without changing them first

For each bucket that matters (internet-adjacent, customer data, backups, logs), take a snapshot of how it is currently shared:

BUCKET=amzn-s3-demo-bucket

aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket "$BUCKET" --output text > /tmp/${BUCKET}-policy.json
aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket "$BUCKET" > /tmp/${BUCKET}-acl.json
aws s3api get-bucket-policy-status --bucket "$BUCKET"
aws s3api get-bucket-ownership-controls --bucket "$BUCKET"

get-bucket-policy-status tells you whether AWS currently considers the policy public. Read the saved policy before you edit it. Look for "Principal": "*" combined with Allow, for s3:GetObject on the whole bucket, and for any statement you cannot explain.

ACLs that grant AllUsers or AuthenticatedUsers are a second path to public or overly broad access. Newer buckets often use “bucket owner enforced” ownership, which disables ACLs; that is the direction AWS has been steering accounts toward. If you still have ACL-based sharing, record it and plan to replace it with a bucket policy you can read.

Do not delete a policy until you know what still needs legitimate access (a CloudFront distribution, a partner account, a log-delivery service). Taking the bucket private is easy. Recreating a working partner integration at 2 a.m. is not.

Write a least-privilege IAM policy for one application role

Pick one application role that can read or write a bucket, and tighten that role rather than boiling the ocean. A policy that is too broad usually looks like this:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}

Version here is the IAM policy-language version, which AWS documents as 2012-10-17. It is not a date you made up, and it is not “the policy is from 2012.”

A narrower starting point, which you must still edit to your prefix and account, is:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "ListOnlyOnePrefix",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket",
      "Condition": {
        "StringLike": {
          "s3:prefix": ["app-name/*"]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ReadWriteOnlyOnePrefix",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/app-name/*"
    }
  ]
}

Anything you do not list is denied by default, so leave out what the application does not call. Add s3:PutObjectAcl only if the application truly needs it; many public-bucket accidents start with an object ACL change. Prefer the application role over a long-lived access key on a human IAM user. If a human still has an access key, list and age those keys:

aws iam list-access-keys --user-name A_HUMAN_USER
aws iam get-access-key-last-used --access-key-id AKIA_EXAMPLE

Rotate unused keys; do not leave a spare key “for emergencies” in a ticket or a git repo (see post 3: find leaked secrets in Git and rotate them).

Test the new policy on a staging role with IAM policy simulator or a canary request, then attach it. Watch the application’s error logs for AccessDenied on a path you intended to allow, and widen that path only.

Let IAM Access Analyzer show you what is still shared

IAM Access Analyzer is the official way to list resources shared outside the account, and, with a separate unused-access analyzer, to find unused roles, keys and permissions.

Create or reuse an external access analyzer in the region you care about, then list findings for S3:

# After an analyzer exists in the account:
aws accessanalyzer list-analyzers --region us-east-1
aws accessanalyzer list-findings --analyzer-arn arn:aws:access-analyzer:us-east-1:123456789012:analyzer/CONSOLE_OR_NAME \
  --filter '{"resourceType":{"eq":["AWS::S3::Bucket"]}}'

AWS also documents Access Analyzer for S3 in the S3 console, which highlights buckets that are public or shared with other accounts. Walk that list. Every public bucket should have a ticket: “intended and covered by Block Public Access exceptions” or “close it.”

If you enable an unused access analyzer, use it for IAM users and roles, not as an S3 public-access tool. AWS documents that unused-access analysis covers IAM users and roles (keys, passwords, unused permissions) over a tracking period you choose. It is a good weekly companion to the least-privilege work above, not a substitute for Block Public Access.

Checklist

  • [ ] Account-level S3 Block Public Access is on, all four flags true, or exceptions are named and owned.
  • [ ] Every production bucket has a recorded policy, ACL, ownership setting and policy-status snapshot.
  • [ ] No unexplained Principal: "*" Allow remains on a private bucket.
  • [ ] At least one application role no longer uses s3:* on Resource: "*".
  • [ ] Human access keys are inventoried; unused keys are disabled.
  • [ ] IAM Access Analyzer (external access) has been reviewed for S3 findings.
  • [ ] Deliberately public buckets are documented, monitored, and contain only what you intend to publish.
  • [ ] Changes were made in a ticket, with a rollback (the saved policy files).

FAQ

Will account-level Block Public Access break a static website?
It will block public access, so a public website hosted directly from a bucket will stop working until you give that bucket a documented exception or you put a CDN/signed-URL design in front of a private bucket. Discover that in staging, not in production.

Is a bucket policy enough without Block Public Access?
A policy can be edited later, including by a too-broad role. Block Public Access is the backstop. Use both.

Does this cover encryption, logging and malware in objects?
No. Turn on default encryption, access logging or CloudTrail data events, and object inspection as separate work. This post is about who can reach the data.

Can we do the same thing in Terraform or CloudFormation?
Yes. The same four Block Public Access flags and the same IAM statements belong in infrastructure as code, reviewed in a pull request. The CLI commands here are for discovery and for accounts that are not fully in code yet.

Sources

  • AWS Docs, Blocking public access to your Amazon S3 storage
  • AWS Docs, Identity-based policies for Amazon S3
  • AWS Docs, IAM Access Analyzer
  • AWS Docs, Reviewing bucket access using IAM Access Analyzer for S3
  • AWS Docs, Controlling ownership of objects and disabling ACLs
  • AWS News Blog, Amazon S3 security changes in April 2023

Next in the series

Test your API against the OWASP API Security Top 10 2023. Previous: Build a weekly CVE triage workflow with CISA KEV, EPSS and CVSS. If a public bucket shows up in that triage, this post is the fix list. Start of the series: Pin your GitHub Actions by commit SHA.

Rokkhe is an AI pentesting and security-operations workspace. Learn more at rokkhe.com.

title: How I Fixed Two Hidden Bugs in wreq While Updating My Search Engine
description:
Recently I contributed to wreq, a fast Rust HTTP library. It started while I was updating my open source Rust search engine SearchWala and testing some of its core libraries. Since SearchWala relies on wreq to fetch web pages, I decided to check the library from a security and reliability angle. The main engine for browser profiles and network requests worked great, but when I looked closely at the cookie and connection layers, I found two real problems.

  • Cookie security and memory cleanup. Websites should not be allowed to set cookies for broad public domains like .com or .co.uk because that can leak data across unrelated sites. I added checks to block these broad cookies. Also, in a long running app like a search engine, expired cookies were piling up in RAM and every request scanned the full cookie list. Now expired cookies get cleared automatically to free memory, and lookups only check relevant domains instead of scanning everything.
  • Reusing connections on redirects. When an HTTP/1.1 server sends a redirect with extra response data, dropping it right away leaves leftover data on the connection and forces the client to close it. I updated wreq to clear up to 256 KB of that leftover data before following the redirect so the same connection stays clean and can be reused for the next request.

I originally sent both fixes together, and at the maintainer's request, I split them into two separate pull requests with proper tests. The cookie security and memory cleanup fix is now merged and pushed as the latest commit aa9644f on the main branch, while the redirect connection reuse fix is still open for review.

  • Merged cookie security and memory cleanup fix https://github.com/0x676e67/wreq/pull/1389
  • Open redirect connection reuse fix https://github.com/0x676e67/wreq/pull/1390

Checking the libraries you depend on in your own projects is a practical way to catch real issues and make open source software safer and faster for everyone. Both pull request links are included here if you work with Rust or HTTP clients and want to check out the code.

title: Mockeamos la API de un proveedor para salvar el CI, y el mock nos mintió
description:
Era martes. La ejecución de GitHub Actions llevaba unos 40 minutos cuando la suite de integración murió con el mismo error por tercera vez esa mañana:

FetchError: request to https://sandbox.<proveedor>.com/v1/rates failed
  status: 429 Too Many Requests
  retry-after: 3600

Nuestro proveedor de tarifas de envío limita su sandbox a 1.000 llamadas al día por clave. Éramos cuatro desarrolladores, una clave compartida y una suite que hacía unas 180 llamadas por ejecución. Con seis pushes y un par de reintentos, la cuota se acababa antes de comer.

Esa semana perdimos casi dos días de sprint con un pipeline en rojo que nadie podía arreglar, porque en realidad no había nada roto. Al mes siguiente descubrimos que el proveedor también cobra el exceso de llamadas al sandbox. Unos 340 dólares por el privilegio de fallar nuestros propios tests.

Así que montamos un mock server. Arregló el pipeline. Y cinco semanas después dejó pasar un bug real hasta producción. Las dos mitades de la historia merecen contarse.

Lo que necesitábamos de verdad

No quería una librería de mocks repartida por los archivos de test. Ya lo habíamos hecho en un proyecto anterior con nock y cada test acabó con su propia versión, ligeramente distinta, de lo que devolvía el proveedor. Cambiar un endpoint significaba tocar 30 archivos.

Quería algo aburrido: un servidor HTTP local con las mismas rutas que el proveedor, que devuelva JSON grabado y que se active con una sola variable de entorno. El código de la aplicación no debería enterarse.

Si alguien de tu equipo no tiene claro el concepto, yo pasé por el canal interno la guía de Keploy sobre mock servers. Explica la diferencia entre hacer stubs dentro de un test y levantar un servidor aparte, que era justo la discusión que teníamos cada semana.

Son unas 30 líneas

Sin framework. El módulo http de Node es suficiente.

// mock-server.js
const http = require('node:http');
const fs = require('node:fs');
const path = require('node:path');

const fixtures = {
  'POST /v1/rates': 'rates-ok.json',
  'GET /v1/shipments/shp_123': 'shipment.json',
};

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  const url = new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost');
  const key = `${req.method} ${url.pathname}`;
  const file = fixtures[key];

  if (!file) {
    res.writeHead(404, { 'content-type': 'application/json' });
    return res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: `no fixture for ${key}` }));
  }

  const body = fs.readFileSync(path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures', file));
  res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': 'application/json' });
  res.end(body);
});

server.listen(process.env.MOCK_PORT || 4010, () => {
  console.log(`mock listening on ${server.address().port}`);
});

Los fixtures eran respuestas reales que capturé del sandbox con curl. En CI, el workflow arranca el mock en segundo plano y apunta la aplicación hacia él:

node mock-server.js &
VENDOR_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4010 npm test

El 404 con el nombre de la ruta resultó ser la línea más útil del archivo. Cuando alguien añade una llamada nueva y se olvida del fixture, el fallo le dice exactamente qué falta en lugar de quedarse colgado hasta el timeout.

Esa suite pasó de unos 40 minutos (casi todo reintentos y esperas) a menos de uno. Las llamadas al sandbox desde CI bajaron a cero y el cargo extra desapareció de la factura.

Durante cinco semanas pensé que habíamos terminado.

Dónde me equivoqué

El proveedor cambió su endpoint de tarifas. El campo amount, un decimal en euros, pasó a ser amount_cents, un entero. Lo anunciaron en un correo de novedades que llegó a un buzón compartido que nadie lee.

Nuestros fixtures seguían teniendo amount. Nuestros tests seguían pasando. Claro que pasaban: estaban probando contra una foto de la API de hacía mes y medio.

En producción, rate.amount llegó como undefined. El checkout mostró el envío como "NaN €" durante unas tres horas de un día laborable, hasta que nos llegó un ticket de soporte.

Eso fue culpa mía. Traté los fixtures como algo terminado cuando en realidad son una caché, y las cachés caducan. Un mock te dice que tu código maneja bien una respuesta concreta. No te dice nada sobre si esa respuesta sigue existiendo.

La comprobación nocturna

La solución no fue tirar el mock. Fue añadir un job pequeño que, una vez cada noche, compara la forma del fixture con lo que devuelve el sandbox en ese momento. Gasta un puñado de llamadas, no 180 por push.

// check-drift.js (Node 18+, usa fetch global)
const fixture = require('./fixtures/rates-ok.json');

function keys(obj, prefix = '') {
  return Object.entries(obj).flatMap(([k, v]) =>
    v && typeof v === 'object' && !Array.isArray(v)
      ? keys(v, `${prefix}${k}.`)
      : [`${prefix}${k}`]
  );
}

(async () => {
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.SANDBOX_URL}/v1/rates`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANDBOX_KEY}`,
      'content-type': 'application/json',
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ from: '28001', to: '08001', weight_g: 500 }),
  });

  const liveKeys = keys(await res.json());
  const missing = keys(fixture).filter((k) => !liveKeys.includes(k));

  if (missing.length) {
    console.error('el fixture tiene campos que la API ya no devuelve:', missing);
    process.exit(1);
  }
  console.log('el fixture coincide con la API real');
})();

Es tosco. Solo mira nombres de campos, no tipos, y trata los arrays como hojas. Pero habría detectado el cambio de amount a la mañana siguiente, y ese era el listón. Corre a las 2 de la madrugada y avisa por Slack si falla.

Lo que le diría a un compañero que empieza hoy

Graba los fixtures desde respuestas reales. No los escribas a mano a partir de la documentación. La documentación miente más que los sandboxes.

Mantén el mock tonto. En cuanto empieza a tener lógica ("si el peso supera 10 kg devuelve este otro fixture") estás manteniendo una segunda versión, peor, de la API del proveedor. Si de verdad necesitas respuestas que dependan del estado o de la petición, eso ya es simulación de APIs y conviene tratarlo como un proyecto aparte, no como un if más dentro del mock.

Yo no mockearía todo. La base de datos, por ejemplo, la sigo levantando de verdad en un contenedor, porque ahí los mocks esconden justo los fallos que más duelen.

Y ponle nombre y apellido al correo de novedades del proveedor. Ese correo fue la causa real del incidente, y ninguna herramienta arregla un buzón que nadie abre.

El mock nos dio velocidad. La comprobación nocturna nos devolvió la confianza que habíamos entregado sin darnos cuenta para conseguirla.

title: HarmonyText: Harmonious Scene Text Editing via Reverse-to-Refined Pair Synthesis and Region-Decoupled Frequency Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.17733v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Natural language-guided, mask-free scene text editing aims to modify text in real-world images using only textual instructions, yet remains challenged by unreliable pseudo-GT supervision, over-smoothed text generation, and the absence of GT-free evaluation. Existing methods often rely on imperfect pseudo-targets with background discrepancies, while standard MSE-based velocity regression tends to suppress high-frequency details, leading to blurred text boundaries and weakened local textures. To address these issues, we propose HarmonyText, a mask-free scene text editing framework with region- and frequency-aware supervision. HarmonyText introduces Region-Decoupling Optimization (RDO), which aligns edited text regions with pseudo-targets while anchoring preserved regions to the source image, and Cascaded High-Frequency Texture Guidance (CHFTG), which applies cascaded wavelet-domain constraints to preserve sharp boundaries and fine-grained textures of textual content. We further propose Reverse-to-Refined Pair Synthesis (RePair) to construct STE25K, a high-quality 25K paired dataset, and introduce a GT-free evaluation protocol with Color Distribution Divergence and a Harmony Assessment Model. Extensive experiments show that HarmonyText outperforms existing methods in text editing accuracy, background fidelity, color consistency, and perceptual harmony.

title: OmniScore-Bench: Evaluating Vision-Language Models on Musical Score Reading
description:
arXiv:2611.17870v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about musical scores, but their ability to recognise notation, recover its structure and interpret its musical meaning requires separate evaluation. Existing optical music recognition (OMR) resources establish detection and transcription measurements; a transcription score alone leaves the strengths and bottlenecks of a VLM score reader unresolved. We introduce OmniScore-Bench, an evaluation of OMR capabilities in VLMs through 3,000 questions spanning six aspects and 24 task subtypes. Each question specifies a visible scope, reference annotations and an answer schema, enabling automatic evaluation from symbol localisation to musical consistency and evidence-linked question answering. Our assessment of twelve VLMs reveals operation-specific capability profiles and different transcription leaders across excerpt, single-page and multipage tasks. Controlled analyses examine the roles of score images, auxiliary givens and additional page context. On the tested subset, image removal exposes visual dependence in pitch and repeat interpretation while measuring how much performance remains with public context alone. Separate format and content analyses distinguish answer-format violations from musical errors. OmniScore-Bench supports diagnosing which score-reading operations VLMs perform reliably and which require improvement.

title: Packing a Freelance Delivery Zip: Strip Secrets, node_modules and Editor Junk with a Small Node Script
description:
The last thing I do on a freelance web job, after the site works and the client has said it looks good, is pack the files. That sounds simple. It is not, if you pack the wrong folder.

I have almost sent a client a zip that still had a .env file in it. I have also sent zips that included node_modules, a .DS_Store, an editor folder and a debug log. None of those help the client. Some of them can cause real trouble. A secret in a delivery zip is still a secret that left your machine.

I'm a freelance full-stack developer in Karachi, and I now treat the delivery zip as its own small task, with a script I can run the same way every time. This post walks through that script: a default ignore list, a way to add your own patterns, a walk of the project folder, and a zip written in plain Node with no packages to install.

If you are new to handing work back on a marketplace, Digital Dialogue's guide on what to do after you win an Upwork job covers the human side of kickoff and delivery. The freelance client onboarding checklist is useful at the other end of the job, when you first get access. Here I'll stay with the files you actually attach.

What should not go in the zip

A delivery zip is not a backup of your working copy. It is the project the client can keep, reopen and, if they want, hand to the next developer. That means:

  • Secrets stay out. .env, .env.local, private keys, .pem files.
  • Dependencies are reinstallable. node_modules is large, machine-specific and easy to rebuild from package.json.
  • Your tools stay out. .git, .vscode, .idea, .DS_Store, log files, coverage folders, Next.js cache folders.
  • The useful files stay in. Source, package.json, a lockfile if you have one, README, assets the site needs, and any .env.example that lists variable names without values.

If the agreed delivery is a built static site, you can keep dist or build and still skip the rest. The script below does not ignore those folders by default, on purpose.

The ignore list

The script starts with a list of names I do not want to ship. A line that ends with / matches a folder anywhere in the tree. A line that starts with *. matches a suffix. Anything else matches that file name, including nested copies such as src/.env.local.

export const DEFAULT_IGNORE = [
  "node_modules/",
  ".git/",
  ".svn/",
  ".hg/",
  ".DS_Store",
  "Thumbs.db",
  ".env",
  ".env.local",
  ".env.production",
  ".env.development",
  ".env.test",
  ".vscode/",
  ".idea/",
  "coverage/",
  ".next/",
  ".cache/",
  "npm-debug.log",
  "yarn-error.log",
  "*.log",
  "*.pem",
  "id_rsa",
  "id_rsa.pub",
  "id_ed25519",
  "id_ed25519.pub",
  ".deliveryignore",
];

A project can also add a .deliveryignore file next to the source, with one pattern per line and # for comments. That is how I skip a scratch file or a local screenshot folder without editing the script.

export function isIgnored(relPath, patterns) {
  const rel = relPath.split(sep).join("/");
  const parts = rel.split("/");
  const base = parts[parts.length - 1] || "";
  for (const pat of patterns) {
    if (pat.startsWith("*.")) {
      if (base.endsWith(pat.slice(1))) return true;
      continue;
    }
    if (pat.endsWith("/")) {
      if (parts.includes(pat.slice(0, -1))) return true;
      continue;
    }
    if (base === pat || rel === pat) return true;
  }
  return false;
}

The folder test is done on path parts, so node_modules/left-pad/index.js is ignored even when it sits two levels down.

Walking the project and writing the zip

The walk is a normal recursive read. In the snippet below, fromRoot is a one-line helper that returns the path from the project folder to the current file. Each skipped path is kept on a list so I can see what was left out before I send the file.

export async function listFiles(sourceDir, patterns) {
  const kept = [];
  const skipped = [];
  async function walk(dir) {
    const entries = await readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true });
    for (const entry of entries) {
      const abs = join(dir, entry.name);
      const rel = fromRoot(sourceDir, abs);
      if (isIgnored(rel, patterns) || (entry.isDirectory() && isIgnored(rel + "/", patterns))) {
        skipped.push(rel.split(sep).join("/") + (entry.isDirectory() ? "/" : ""));
        continue;
      }
      if (entry.isDirectory()) await walk(abs);
      else if (entry.isFile()) kept.push(rel);
    }
  }
  await walk(sourceDir);
  kept.sort();
  skipped.sort();
  return { kept, skipped };
}

For the zip itself I did not want a package, and I did not want to depend on a system zip binary. Node 18 and later already ship zlib.deflateRawSync and zlib.crc32, which is enough to write a standard ZIP file: a local file header and deflated bytes for each entry, then a central directory, then an end record. Any normal unzip tool can open the result, including the one on macOS, Windows and the unzip command on Linux.

The writer is a few dozen lines of buffers and unsigned integers, so I am not going to paste every byte here. The full file is pack-delivery.mjs in the companion folder I keep with this draft. The public function is small:

export async function pack(sourceDir, outPath) {
  const patterns = loadIgnore(sourceDir);
  const { kept, skipped } = await listFiles(sourceDir, patterns);
  if (kept.length === 0) {
    throw new Error("Nothing to pack. Every file matched the ignore list.");
  }
  await writeZip(sourceDir, kept, outPath);
  return { kept, skipped, outPath };
}

Run it like this:

node pack-delivery.mjs ./my-site ./my-site-delivery.zip

It prints the path it wrote, how many files were packed, and every skipped path. That skip list is the part I actually read. If .env is not on it, I stop and find out why.

A test fixture, not a hope

I do not want to discover a leaked secret after the zip has been sent. A short test builds a fake project with a source file, package.json, a README, node_modules, .env, a nested .env.local, a .DS_Store, a log file and a scratch file named in .deliveryignore. Then it packs that folder and opens the zip back up.

On a run of that test, the zip contained:

README.md, package.json, src/index.js

and skipped:

.DS_Store, .deliveryignore, .env, debug.log, node_modules/, notes.tmp, src/.env.local

That is the result I want: the project, and nothing that belongs only on my machine. The test also checks that the bytes inside src/index.js survive the round trip, so the zip is not just a list of names.

A few habits around the script

Read the skip list every time. The script will not catch a secret with a surprising name, such as passwords.txt or firebase-adminsdk.json. If I have created a file like that, I add it to .deliveryignore or I move it out of the project folder.

Keep an example env file, not a real one. A .env.example with empty or clearly fake values is useful. The real file stays out of the zip.

Say what you sent. In the delivery message I mention that node_modules is not included and that the client can run npm install from package.json. I also mention any build step, and I attach the zip as the file I just built, not an older one sitting on the desktop.

Do not pack from the wrong folder. I run the command from a known path and pass the project folder explicitly. Packing my home directory, or packing a folder that still contains other clients' work, is a mistake the ignore list cannot fix.

Built site or source folder?

Some jobs ask for the source. Some ask for a folder the client can drop onto hosting. Those are different zips.

  • Source delivery. Keep package.json, the source, the README and a lockfile. Skip node_modules and skip any compiled output you can rebuild. Say how to install and how to start the dev server.
  • Static hosting delivery. If the client only needs files they can upload to Netlify, GitHub Pages, cPanel or a similar host, pack the built output (dist, build, out or _site) plus a short README that says "upload the contents of this folder". Skip the source if that was the agreement, or send two zips if they want both.
  • WordPress or PHP on shared hosting. Pack the theme or plugin you actually built, not the whole wp-content tree of some other project, and not wp-config.php with the database password still in it.

The script does not make this choice for you. It only stops the obvious junk from riding along. You still pick the folder you point it at.

Before you click send

I run through a short list, out loud if I am tired:

  1. I opened the zip on my own machine and confirmed the top-level folder looks right.
  2. I searched the skip list for .env and for node_modules.
  3. I searched the packed file list for anything named like a key, a password or a dump.
  4. I confirmed the README I packed is the one I meant to send, not an old scratch file.
  5. I wrote the delivery message so the client knows what to unzip, what to install and how to reach me about problems.

None of that takes long. It is much cheaper than sending the wrong file and then writing an apology.

The script will not make you a more careful freelancer on its own. It just removes a class of mistakes that are easy to make at the end of a job, when you want to close the tab and move on. I still run it, every time, because that is exactly when those mistakes happen.

Once the zip is clean, the rest of the close-out is the usual work: a short delivery note, a walkthrough of how to run the project, and anything the contract says you still owe. The script only handles the files. The message still has to be written by you.

If you want a wider view of how web work runs on the marketplace, how Upwork works for a freelance web developer is a clear starting point. Use the script as a last check, not as a substitute for reading what you are about to send.

title: Agent-as-a-Judge
description:
arXiv:2611.18067v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence has progressed from task-specific systems toward general models spanning perception, generation, reasoning, and autonomous interaction, making reliable evaluation essential for comparison, deployment, and post-training feedback. At scale, modern evaluation pipelines increasingly rely on LLM-as-a-Judge to produce scores, preferences, and critiques; in its fixed-context setting, the judge relies on the supplied evaluand and evaluation materials. Yet a reliable verdict may require evidence beyond the supplied evaluand and context---either because critical environmental states remain unrecorded in the static execution log, or because controversial factual claims require external verification. Passive judges cannot obtain that missing evidence before deciding, especially when evaluating agent trajectories, executable artifacts, or domain-specific reports. Recent work therefore develops active evaluators that seek missing evidence and update their grounds for judgment before deciding. We bring these advances together through Agent-as-a-Judge, focusing on how evaluators construct and control checking processes within the broader LLM-based judging landscape. We define the scope through evaluation-directed checks and the use of their results, covering both structured workflows and observation-driven control. We organize the design space by multi-agent collaboration, tool integration, memory, and planning, and show how these mechanisms supply the checks and evidence on which a verdict rests. We consolidate published scores and reproduce missing entries for key agentic judges; the comparison reveals uneven agentic gains and motivates dedicated agentic evaluation. We conclude by characterizing application demands and open challenges in cost, reliability, safety, and governance that condition trusted deployment of agentic judges at scale.

title: How to use AI on sensitive company data without the vendor seeing it
description:
To use AI on sensitive company data without the vendor seeing it, run the vendor's application inside confidential hardware, allow it to reach only the services you approve, and check what is running before you send it anything. Lit sets this up on Google Cloud Confidential VMs, which use Intel TDX to keep the machine's memory encrypted while it works. The application runs as a Docker container. The list of services it can reach is part of the deployment, and any change to the code or that list waits for your organization to approve it on-chain. Before your team connects, a hardware attestation shows exactly which release is running.

This is for two kinds of teams. The first is a company that wants to use an AI product on legal, financial, health, or customer data and cannot accept "trust us" from the vendor. The second is an AI vendor whose customers keep asking whether the vendor can see their data, and who wants to answer with something the customer can check.

The usual options

The first option is to trust the vendor's policy. Many AI vendors promise not to train on your data or keep it. That is a policy, and the vendor can change it. A breach at the vendor would expose the data anyway.

The second is to self-host an open model on your own servers. Nobody outside your company sees the data, but you have to run the GPUs and the application yourself, and you may give up the vendor product your team wanted.

The third is to run the vendor's product in confidential hardware. The vendor's software does the work. The hardware keeps the cloud operator and the host from reading the data while it is in use, and network rules decide where the software can send it. This is what Lit sets up.

How it works

The vendor's application runs as a Docker container in a Confidential VM on Google Cloud. The processor encrypts the machine's memory, so the host operating system and Google's operators cannot read it. For models that need a GPU, Google's A3 machines with NVIDIA H100 GPUs extend confidential computing to the GPU.

Each deployment lists the exact hostnames the container may reach, on port 443 only, with no wildcards. A proxy inside the confidential machine enforces that list. If the list is empty, the application has no network route out at all and only answers requests on its own ports. The list is part of the deployment's measured configuration, so the vendor cannot quietly add a destination. Adding one is a new release, and it does not run until your organization approves it.

Here is a typical example. An enterprise search app runs in the confidential machine with your documents. Its only allowed destination is the model provider's API. Your team searches and gets cited answers. The model API is the only outside service the app can send your data to, and the vendor cannot add another one without your approval.

What you can check

Before your team connects, you can check two things. The attestation is signed by genuine Intel hardware, and the configuration it records, including the Docker image and the network list, matches a release on your deployment's approved list on Base, where anyone can read it. The first release is recorded when the deployment is created, and every change after that needs your organization's approval. Lit gives your team a command that checks all of this using only the attestation, the deployment's address, and a public Base RPC endpoint.

Decisions to make with Lit

A few choices shape how private the setup is, and Lit works through them with you.

The first is where the model runs. If the application calls an outside model API, that provider sees what the application sends it. Many teams accept that, because it is the only outside service the application can reach. If even the model provider should not see the data, the model runs inside the confidential machine too, usually as an open model on a confidential GPU.

The second is what the application keeps and sends. The attestation proves which software is running, so review that software and its network list together. Lit can help you read both.

The third is the model weights. If the application downloads weights at startup, they should be checked against the exact version you expect.

Working with Lit

Lit sets up each deployment with your team. Send us the application or the vendor's container, describe the data it will handle and the services it needs to reach, and tell us your performance goals. We will come back with a hardware plan on Google Cloud, a network list for you to approve, and the approval setup for your organization. Then we deploy it and walk your team through the check. To start, use the Lit AI contact form.

title: Fix html2canvas 'Attempting to parse an unsupported color function "oklch"' (Tailwind CSS v4)
description:
When you call html2canvas() on a page that uses Tailwind CSS v4 — or any stylesheet that emits modern CSS color functions — the official html2canvas package may throw:

Attempting to parse an unsupported color function "oklch"

The same parser also rejects related functions, so you may instead see "oklab", "lab", "lch", "color", or "color-mix" in the message.

Why it happens

html2canvas does not take a real screenshot. It walks the DOM, reads computed styles, and paints a canvas itself. That means it has to parse CSS color values.

Tailwind CSS v4 uses the oklch() color space for its default palette. The browser is fine with that. Official html2canvas 1.4.1 (January 2022), by Niklas von Hertzen, was released before oklch() / oklab() showed up in everyday stylesheets, and its color parser throws on functions it does not know.

So a page that looks correct in the browser can still fail at html2canvas(element) time. This is a parser limitation, not a Tailwind bug.

Fixes that do not use html2canvas-lts

Try these first.

1. Switch to html2canvas-pro

html2canvas-pro is an independent maintained fork by Yorick Shan. It is built as a next-generation html2canvas and supports modern CSS colors.

Verified on npm, 2026-11-16 (Asia/Shanghai): html2canvas-pro 2.6.4.

npm uninstall html2canvas && npm install html2canvas-pro

import html2canvas from 'html2canvas-pro';

If this package already does what you need, use it. Thanks to Yorick Shan and contributors for maintaining it, and to Niklas von Hertzen for the original library.

2. Keep official html2canvas, but do not feed it oklch() styles

If you must stay on html2canvas 1.4.1, the captured DOM cannot contain those color functions in computed styles. In practice that usually means:

  • not using Tailwind v4's default oklch() palette on the nodes you capture, or
  • snapshotting a clone whose colors have been rewritten to rgb() / hex first.

This is often more work than changing the library, and it is easy to miss a theme token or a shadow. Prefer (1) unless you have a hard constraint on the official 1.4.1 package.

A maintained html2canvas fork (optional)

Another option is html2canvas-lts, a drop-in fork that teaches the original parser lab(), lch(), oklab(), oklch(), color(), and color-mix() instead of throwing. It is not the official html2canvas package, and it is a separate project from html2canvas-pro. Credit for html2canvas stays with Niklas von Hertzen and the original contributors; if the original project returns, the fork is meant to step aside.

Verified on npm, 2026-11-16 (Asia/Shanghai): html2canvas-lts 1.5.4. The package README lists 37 fixes and no new runtime dependencies, including the color-function work.

npm uninstall html2canvas && npm install html2canvas-lts

The API is the same; the module name changes:

import html2canvas from 'html2canvas-lts';

html2canvas(document.querySelector('#capture')).then((canvas) => {
  document.body.appendChild(canvas);
});

A script tag still exposes window.html2canvas:

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/html2canvas-lts@1.5.4/dist/html2canvas.min.js"></script>

The current fix list is on the project page: https://cyberpusa.org/forks/html2canvas/. The fork is kept by Cyber Pusa (赛博菩萨), an AI maintainer that adopts abandoned but still-used libraries. Issues can go to cyberpusa-ai/html2canvas.

Which option to pick

  • You want a modern, independently maintained renderer: try html2canvas-pro 2.6.4.
  • You want to stay close to the original html2canvas API and pick up the oklch fix plus the other listed rendering fixes: html2canvas-lts 1.5.4.
  • You cannot change libraries: keep 1.4.1 and make sure the captured tree does not compute to oklch() / oklab() / lab() / lch() / color() / color-mix().

In every case, the underlying library is Niklas von Hertzen's html2canvas. These packages exist because that work is still in use after the last official release.

title: HEX to Pantone is a guess: making color conversion honest in an interface
description:
Every color tool eventually ships the same sentence: closest Pantone match. It sounds authoritative, and almost every implementation behind it is an approximation. That gap between the confident label and the actual math is worth designing around, because someone will print a business card from whatever your UI claims.

Three different conversions are hiding under one button

A HEX value is an sRGB triplet with a defined transfer curve. RGB to CMYK conversion is device dependent: the real answer depends on the press, the ink set, the substrate and the ICC profile used to separate the file. Without a profile you have a formula, not a measurement. A CMYK-to-Pantone lookup is a different approximation again, because Pantone references are ink recipes and physical swatches, not RGB values.

So a converter that says "this CMYK is that Pantone" is guessing at two levels. That is fine as long as the interface says so.

Distance is the part most tools skip

If you map a color to a reference library, you have to rank candidates by something. Euclidean distance in raw RGB is convenient and visibly wrong: two colors that differ by the same RGB amount do not look equally different. Converting to CIELAB first and measuring with CIEDE2000 gets much closer to perceived difference, which matters most in the greens and blues where sRGB is coarsest.

Here is the shape of the pipeline in plain terms:

  1. Parse the input into sRGB (or take CMYK percentages as given).
  2. Convert sRGB to XYZ under a D65 white point.
  3. Convert XYZ to CIELAB.
  4. Measure CIEDE2000 against every candidate reference.
  5. Return the nearest match together with the distance, not just the name.

That last step is the honest one. A nearest neighbor with a distance of 1.2 and one with a distance of 8 are not the same answer, and the user deserves to know which they got.

Design rules that keep the UI truthful

  • Show the distance. "Nearest reference, ΔE 3.4" is information. "Exact match" is a lie unless it is one.
  • Separate coated and uncoated. They are different swatch books and they produce different nearest references. Collapsing them into one answer creates a wrong answer for half the users.
  • Keep the input reproducible. If a row in a chart shows a match, link to the converter state that produced it, so the number can be checked instead of trusted.
  • State the limits in the interface, not only in a footnote. CMYK without a profile, digital approximations of a licensed library, and the need for a physical proof all belong next to the result.

What this looks like in practice

I built HueConvert around those rules: a free converter that takes HEX, RGB, CMYK or HSL, returns the other formats, and shows the nearest Pantone coated and uncoated reference with the CIEDE2000 distance attached. The three tool pages carry printable charts of 139 references each, and every row links back to the exact input that produced it. No account, no upload, and the charts render without JavaScript.

Disclosure: I operate HueConvert. It is free, has no paid placement, and this post is a write-up of the conversion decisions, not a launch announcement.

The takeaway

Color conversion is a chain of approximations. The engineering work is not pretending otherwise; it is choosing the least misleading approximation, exposing the distance, and making the result reproducible. Users forgive an approximate answer that is labeled as approximate. They do not forgive a confident one that ruins a print run.

title: Rust Roadmap: 131 Chapters from "What Is Rust?" to Compiler Internals
description:
The problem: Rust has no shortage of tutorials, but no clear path

If you've tried to learn Rust, you know the pattern. You read The Rust Programming Language, get comfortable with ownership and borrowing, then hit a wall. What comes next? Tokio? Trait objects? Macros? Unsafe? Every source assumes you already know the prerequisite and skips the bridge. The result is a language that feels documented but unnavigable.

Rust is a systems programming language built for memory safety without a garbage collector, fearless concurrency, and zero-cost abstractions. It's used in operating system kernels, embedded firmware, network services, WebAssembly, and performance-critical infrastructure. But its learning curve isn't just steep — it's uneven. Some concepts click immediately; others, like lifetimes and variance, take months to internalize.

This roadmap breaks that curve into 131 focused chapters, each one a single concept with a real, working example.

What the roadmap covers

The series starts where every Rust journey does: what systems programming actually means, installing Rustup and Cargo, and understanding why immutability is the default. From there it moves through the language in deliberate layers.

Chapters 1–10 establish the foundation: types, functions, statements versus expressions, and control flow. These are short by design — the goal is momentum, not depth.

Chapters 11–18 tackle the concept that defines Rust: ownership. Stack versus heap, move semantics, the Copy and Clone traits, references, and the aliasing XOR mutability rule. If you've bounced off Rust before, it was probably here. This section makes the rules concrete.

Chapters 19–31 cover structs, enums, Option<T>, pattern matching, modules, and the standard collections. This is where Rust starts to feel like a usable language rather than a set of constraints.

Chapters 32–45 handle errors and abstractions: Result<T, E>, the ? operator, thiserror and anyhow, generics, traits, and lifetimes. Lifetimes get four dedicated chapters — elision rules included — because they're the single most misunderstood feature in the language.

Chapters 46–63 move into testing, closures, iterators, smart pointers, and concurrency. Box, Rc, RefCell, Arc, Mutex, and channels all get their own chapter.

Chapters 64–79 are advanced territory: trait objects, object safety, the orphan rule, operator overloading, declarative and procedural macros, and serde.

Chapters 80–89 cover async Rust from first principles — the Future trait, async/await, runtime architecture, streams — through to real applications: axum and actix-web for REST APIs, sqlx for databases, ratatui for terminals, egui and iced for GUIs, and Tauri for desktop apps.

Chapters 90–105 are unsafe Rust and low-level systems work: raw pointers, FFI, inline assembly, Pin, atomics, memory ordering, WebAssembly, no_std embedded development, and custom allocators.

Chapters 106–130 go deep: compiler internals (AST to HIR to MIR), monomorphization, variance and subtyping, async executor internals, zero-copy parsing, eBPF, kernel development, SIMD, fuzzing, and formal verification with Kani.

Chapter 131 is a cheatsheet.

Why this structure matters

Most Rust resources fall into two camps: beginner books that stop at generics, and reference material that assumes you already understand the compiler's mental model. This roadmap fills the gap between them. Each chapter is a single idea, written to be read in one sitting and tied to official documentation and current stable versions — not invented examples or imaginary features.

The progression is honest about difficulty. Chapters 1–30 are approachable for any programmer. Chapters 42–45 on lifetimes require patience. Chapters 90 onward assume you're comfortable with the language and want to understand what happens beneath it. That's not padding — it's the actual shape of mastering Rust.

Who this is for

  • Developers coming from GC languages (Python, JavaScript, Go, Java) who want to understand ownership without hand-waving.
  • C and C++ programmers curious about memory safety and what Rust's borrow checker actually prevents.
  • Intermediate Rust users who can write working code but want to understand the compiler's internals.
  • Systems engineers targeting embedded, kernel, eBPF, or WebAssembly work.
  • Anyone who has read the Book and wondered what comes next.

The full series is available at tuts.kandz.me/category/programming/languages/rust.

131 chapters. One language. Start at chapter one and don't skip the ownership section.

title: Writing Data into a File in Java | File Handling
description:
In my previous blog, I covered how to read data from a text file using Java. If you haven't read it yet, check it out here:Java File Handling: From Text File to ArrayList

In the previous section, we saw how to read employee details from a text file using FileReader and BufferedReader.

Now let's see how to write data into a file using Java.

To write data into a file, we use three important classes:

  1. File: Represents the file and its location.
  2. FileWriter: Used to write characters into a file.
  3. BufferedWriter: Helps us write data efficiently.

Complete Code 

import java.io.File;
import java.io.FileWriter;
import java.io.BufferedWriter;
import java.io.IOException;

public class EmployeeController {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        File note = new File("empData1.txt");

        try {

            FileWriter pen = new FileWriter(note, true);

            BufferedWriter writer = new BufferedWriter(pen);

            writer.write("ghi");
            writer.write("jkl");

            writer.close();

        } catch (IOException io) {

            System.out.println("IO exception");

        }
    }
}

Understanding the Code Bit by Bit

1. Creating a File Object

File note = new File("empData1.txt");

First, we create a File object and pass the file name.

This represents the location of the file where we want to write our data.

2. Using FileWriter

FileWriter pen = new FileWriter(note, true);

FileWriter is used to write characters into a file.

Here, we pass two arguments:

  • note – The File object representing the file.
  • true – Tells Java to append the data instead of overwriting the existing content.

One important thing to remember:

  • If we pass true, new data is added at the end of the existing content.
  • If we pass false or don't provide the second argument, the existing content is overwritten.

3. Using BufferedWriter

BufferedWriter writer = new BufferedWriter(pen);

BufferedWriter takes the FileWriter object as an argument.

It helps us write data efficiently by buffering the characters before writing them to the file.

4. Writing Data into the File

writer.write("ghi");
writer.write("jkl");

The write() method is used to write data into the file.

Here, we are writing two Strings: "ghi" and "jkl".

The output inside the file will be:

ghijkl

Notice that the write() method doesn't automatically move to the next line.

If we want each String on a separate line, we can use:

writer.write("ghi");
writer.newLine();
writer.write("jkl");

5. Closing the Writer

writer.close();

Once writing is completed, we close the BufferedWriter to release the resources.

Conclusion

FileWriter and BufferedWriter are used to write data into files in Java.

FileWriter handles writing characters, while BufferedWriter helps make the writing process more efficient.

Using these classes, we can easily write or append data to an existing text file.

title: CSS-only Offcanvas with Native HTML
description:
I previously wrote an article on my rewrite of PicoCSS. One of the components that I introduced in the rewrite was a CSS-only and classless offcanvas using native HTML.

On the HTML side, the component works by leveraging the native <dialog> element along with command/commandfor attributes. According to the Mozilla Developer Network, the <dialog> element has been available across browsers since March 2022 and the command/commandfor attributes since December 2025

On the CSS side, the component leverages :has pseudo-class to assert a specific markup and when the user doesn't have a preference specified for the prefers-reduced-motion setting then it uses the transform property. Again, according to MDN, the :has pseudo-class has been available across browsers since December 2023 and the transform property since September 2015.

Take for example this markup:

<button type="button" command="show-modal" commandfor="demo-offcanvas">Open offcanvas</button>
<dialog id="demo-offcanvas" closedby="any" aria-labelledby="demo-offcanvas-title">
  <aside>
    <article>
      <header>
        <button type="button" command="request-close" commandfor="demo-offcanvas" aria-label="Close"></button>
        <h2 id="demo-offcanvas-title">Offcanvas panel</h2>
      </header>
      <p>A full-height side panel.</p>
      <footer>
        <button type="button" command="request-close" commandfor="demo-offcanvas">Close panel</button>
      </footer>
    </article>
  </aside>
</dialog>

The browser will natively open a dialog without any JavaScript, so all we need to do is style the dialog to look like an offcanvas. With this specific example, the DOM is structure like this: <dialog> > <aside> > <article>. The reason behind this design decision is simple:

  • <dialog>: We need to leverage the built-in HTML behavior
  • <aside>: We are indicating that this dialog should be on the "side".
    • It is sort of a stretch on the semantics side.
    • When <aside> was introduced, there was some debate on if it represented content on the side or content tangentially related to the main document and the latter sort of won out.
    • I'm using the former interpretation in this case because I think it logically makes sense for this situation.
  • <article>: This supplies the visual container.
    • The optional <header> element shows the offcanvas title and close button
    • The optional <footer> element is pushed down to the bottom of the view area with any additional information
    • This is a carryover of PicoCSS's original implementation of the modal component

To style the dialog, you can leverage the :has pseudo-class so that you can differentiate between a regular, plain-ole, dialog and an offcanvas. For example:

:where(dialog) {
  /* regular dialog styles... */
}

:where(dialog:has(> aside)) {
  /* offcanvas styles */
}

In this situation we can differentiate the offcanvas by saying "I want to style every dialog that has an aside element as it's direct child" by combining the :has and > selectors.

If you would like to see how I styled the offcanvas in T'Pico, you can check out the source code here: https://github.com/dday9/t-pico/blob/master/src/components/offcanvas.css

And as always, here's a working demo of an offcanvas in action: blob:https://coddy.tech/673eec74-b1a0-49f2-bd0b-7c58193edc24

title: Beyond Endpoints: B\'ezier Paths for Vision Foundation Model Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2611.17825v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Frozen vision foundation models can be adapted by learning a few prompt tokens shared across all images. When prompts are updated as data shift or tasks change, the distribution of image features moves from one endpoint to another. Prior theory asks which endpoints prompts can reach; we ask whether they can travel between them along the shortest path. Because shared prompts compete with each image's own content for attention, they often cannot. We quantify this restriction as the extra transport cost that shared attention imposes over the shortest path. In an exactly solvable attention model, the reachable features form a cone; unrolling it into a plane gives the exact minimum action for every pair of endpoints and explicit optimal prompts on short arcs. The analysis reveals a sharp threshold in content normalization, which measures how much attention each image's own tokens absorb: for same-sign endpoints, at most two distinct levels allow prompts to follow the shortest path, whereas three or more force a strictly positive extra cost unless the endpoints differ only by rescaling. This gap persists with more prompts, small content perturbations, and aligned multihead outputs. On ViT-B/16 with VTAB-1k, a quadratic B\'ezier prompt path that minimizes feature action reduces held-out transport action relative to linear and cross-entropy-trained paths between the same endpoints and improves intermediate and online accuracy under unlabeled distribution shift, while cross-entropy-trained paths retain higher minimum accuracy when labeled calibration data are available. Reachable endpoints do not guarantee a reachable shortest path: how prompts move matters, not only where they end. Project page: https://xixiaouab.github.io/Beyond-Endpoints/.

title: A source-of-truth schema for event dates, venues, and subsidy rules
description:
An event directory looks simple until a date changes, a venue is renamed, or a subsidy rule is replaced for the next policy year. If the database stores only the latest value, the team loses the ability to explain where that value came from and when it was checked.

A safer approach is to model the claim rather than only the event. The event can stay stable while each date, venue, organiser or subsidy condition becomes a time-stamped assertion backed by a source document.

Separate the entities

A useful minimum schema is:

  • event: the recurring series, such as a named trade fair.
  • edition: one dated occurrence, with its own venue, dates and organiser.
  • venue: a stable place record with city and country.
  • source_document: the official page, PDF notice or organiser announcement.
  • claim: one field-level statement linked to a source.
  • verification: who checked the claim, when, and what changed.

The key rule is that an edition never stores an unexplained date or venue. It points to one or more claims, and the currently published value is selected from those claims.

Add provenance to every field

A claim table can be small:

event_id
edition_id
field_name
value
source_url
source_type
observed_at
effective_from
effective_to
status

observed_at is not the same as effective_from. A subsidy page may be published in December for a policy that starts in January. A trade-fair website may announce dates two years ahead before the venue contract is final. Keeping both timestamps prevents a future-dated claim from silently overwriting today’s verified value.

Use status values such as proposed, verified, superseded and conflicted. Do not delete the losing record. A conflict is evidence that the source set needs review, not a database error to hide.

Make conflicts visible

When two official pages disagree, keep both claims and surface the conflict in the editorial queue. A simple rule set helps:

  1. Prefer the current organiser page over a third-party directory.
  2. Prefer a dated official notice over an undated marketing page.
  3. Prefer a specific exhibition edition over a generic industry page.
  4. Escalate when the sources are equally authoritative.

For a public exhibition database, the published page can show a compact evidence note: last checked date, source type and any unresolved conflict. This is more useful to readers than a confidence score with no explanation.

Treat subsidy rules as versioned records

Subsidy data needs its own structure because eligibility is not one number. At minimum, capture:

  • jurisdiction and responsible authority;
  • policy year and application window;
  • eligible exhibition catalogue or coverage rule;
  • eligible costs and caps;
  • required documents;
  • official notice URL and verification date.

A rule that was valid for one policy year must not be reused for the next without a new claim. Store the policy period explicitly and make the public page select the rule for the requested year. That prevents a stale amount from being presented as current guidance.

The overseas exhibition subsidy dataset is an example of publishing the source links and verification dates alongside the fields. The important design choice is not the file format; it is that every public value can be traced back to a dated official source.

Build a verification loop

A practical pipeline is:

  1. Ingest organiser pages, official notices and structured feeds.
  2. Normalise names, countries, dates and venue identifiers without discarding the raw text.
  3. Compare new claims with the current published values.
  4. Review only rows that changed, conflicted or expired.
  5. Publish the selected claim plus its evidence summary.
  6. Monitor source URLs for 404s, redirects and content changes.

The review queue should be the product of the comparison step, not a manual hunt through every record. This is where a source-linked trade fair directory becomes operationally useful: the team can see which editions need attention before a stale page reaches a visitor.

Keep the calendar disposable

A calendar view should be generated from the verified edition records, not edited by hand. The 2027 global exhibition calendar is a reader-facing projection; the underlying edition records remain the source of truth.

Generate the calendar with stable URLs, canonical dates and visible last-verified labels. When an edition changes, regenerate the view from the database instead of patching the page. That keeps every surface consistent and makes rollback simple.

The small discipline that matters

The hard part is not choosing a database. It is refusing to publish an unsourced field just because the layout expects a value. An empty state with a clear "not verified" label is better than a plausible-looking date that nobody can defend.

Model claims, keep provenance, expose conflicts and version the rules. Those four choices make an event directory easier to audit, cheaper to maintain and more trustworthy for the people using it.
