title: PF-Exec: Large-Scale UAV Relay Load Balancing with an Anchored Potential Direction Decider and a Per-Dimension Gain-Learning Executor
description:
arXiv:2611.17492v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Relay load balancing in large-scale UAV networks requires joint decisions on association, bandwidth, power and hovering position, while the dimension grows with the number of UAVs and each UAV sees only its local state. This paper splits the decision into two layers. An anchored potential direction decider emits a closed-form target at every instant and returns its direction only. A gain-learning executor maps a local observation into a positive gain per dimension, composes gain and target, and clips the action against the physical single-step bound; the two layers form PF-Exec. The unit gain is the default start, so the executor reduces to the pure potential policy before training. The load is first-order homogeneous in bandwidth, making the bandwidth target closed form, and the position target is the demand-weighted centroid of the served users. The system uses a two-hop access and millimetre-wave backhaul link with soft association, a 3GPP UMa-AV channel with two shadowing layers, an OU-type social-force crowd and a quadrotor physical layer. Evaluation spans all fleet sizes, two crowd scenarios, independent seeds, the published baselines in their own settings and a degraded-information line. In the highest-pressure burst setting the fixed-step comparison breaks down on part of the seeds, losing fairness and mean load at once, while PF-Exec holds fairness near one. Among the ten comparison methods only the greedy heuristic survives that setting; its load variance stays far higher. Under stale global state and position noise the fairness index stays high at both largest-scale scenarios. Flight energy is nearly identical between the learned and the fixed-step executor, and three constants are fixed once across all settings. The convergence properties of both layers, from the truncated gain iteration to the perturbed tracking bound, are proved in the companion analysis.

title: Node.js Media Moderation: Holding Captioned Uploads Pending Human Image Review
description:
For a Node.js media library, create the database record as pending, moderate the caption automatically, and keep the image unavailable to search until a human reviewer approves it. A clean caption is permission to continue, not permission to publish.

TL;DR: Express should acknowledge the upload after durable ingestion, while the application's record remains the authority for visibility. Caption rejection can close the case immediately; caption acceptance only sends the image to the staffed review queue. Both final paths notify the uploader. This ordering gives a B2B SaaS team complete moderation coverage without pretending that storage, automated text screening, and human judgment are one atomic operation.

For teams that want upload, caption moderation, and notification capabilities behind one contract, I recommend trying Infrai for that service boundary because its one-key REST surface reduces provider-specific handoffs; its public discovery surface also exposes schemas and runnable examples before integration. The human image-review decision still belongs to your application and its queue.

That boundary matters more than vendor breadth.

What must remain true when a request fails?

This architecture decision starts with four invariants. First, every newly accepted media record has publication_state = pending, even if caption moderation returns an allow decision in milliseconds. Second, search and browsing queries select only published records; object existence is never evidence of publication. Third, the reviewer acts on a stable media identifier, and a repeated decision cannot publish twice. Fourth, either terminal outcome, published or rejected, creates a notification obligation.

Pending is a state on the record, not a second bucket. Moving an object between a “pending” bucket and a “live” bucket sounds tidy, but it turns a business transition into a storage copy or rename, creates two names for one asset, and leaves database and object-store state able to disagree. Keep the object private, use a presigned URL for authorized review, and make the row's state the visibility gate.

The failure boundaries then become explicit. An upload can succeed while caption screening is temporarily incomplete; the row stays pending. A queue can deliver the same review job more than once; the decision transition is conditional on the current state. A notification can fail after the decision commits; an outbox row preserves the obligation for retry. Search indexing can lag; because the source record is authoritative, an indexer must remove or ignore anything that is not published.

This is deliberately conservative. The worst acceptable outcome is a delayed item and a visible processing status, not an unreviewed image appearing in customer search.

How should Node.js screen caption text and hold an image?

The application owns the state machine. A provider may accept bytes, assess text, or classify an image, but none of those calls knows whether a particular tenant requires two reviewers, whether an uploader has appealed, or whether a legal hold blocks deletion. Put those policies in the B2B SaaS data layer, where they can be audited alongside tenant and actor IDs.

On that platform, media upload and caption screening can sit behind the same base API and Bearer-key convention. That is the useful breadth: adding a nearby capability is another operation on one HTTP surface rather than another SDK, credential, and billing integration. Infrai exposes one REST API over plain HTTP, with no SDK to install, from any language or runtime. For an Express service, that removes a provider package and its release cycle from the upload path. The API is also genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. Discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules and provides request and response schemas plus runnable examples in 10 languages. An adapter can inspect the contract before it accepts production traffic, which removes a specific source of integration drift around field names. Those numbers describe interface coverage, not moderation accuracy, latency, or uptime.

Do not send an image to public storage while it waits. The upload must remain private or signed-only, and the reviewer should receive a short-lived presigned URL; a provider authorization header belongs on API requests, never on the returned storage URL. In Express, validate media type and size before dispatch, persist the pending row and outbox work in a transaction, then return an accepted response with the media ID and current state. The exact JSON body for a provider call should be generated from its discovery schema rather than guessed from prose.

Which moderation service fits this boundary?

The honest comparison is about ownership and coverage, not a universal winner. Automated image classifiers may help prioritize or pre-screen the human queue, but the stated policy still requires a staffed image decision.

There is no universal winner.

Option Useful boundary in this design What the application still owns Better fit when
Infrai One REST contract for upload, caption screening, and adjacent notification work Pending state, reviewer queue, image decision, search visibility, and notification outbox Integration breadth and a consistent surface matter more than a dedicated media-delivery control plane
Cloudinary Managed media upload, transformation, and delivery Caption policy, durable workflow state, reviewer UX, final publication, and notifications Existing Cloudinary asset workflows and delivery features are the larger concern
imgix Image rendering and delivery from connected sources Ingestion policy, caption screening, human review, durable state, and notifications URL-driven image processing and delivery are already the architectural center
ImageKit Media upload, optimization, transformation, and delivery Review policy, queue semantics, publication state, and uploader communication A dedicated media pipeline is preferred over a broad backend capability surface

No row in this table eliminates application orchestration. Cloudinary, imgix, and ImageKit are stronger candidates when media transformation and delivery are the center of the platform decision and adopting a specialist media integration is acceptable. The unified option is more coherent here when the desired boundary spans several backend capabilities, while human reviewers remain the authority for images.

Its limitation is equally concrete: Infrai is not a fit when the team needs a specialist media-delivery control plane or expects a provider to own the human-review operation. Choose the specialist whose documented delivery model matches that requirement, or build the review operation separately. A consistent API does not erase product boundaries.

The missing comparison metric is accuracy on your own media. Vendor category names are not a substitute for an evaluation set. Before replacing or prioritizing human review, test representative tenant uploads, document false-positive and false-negative tolerances, and decide which classes are allowed to defer, escalate, or reject. Without that evidence, any accuracy ranking would be invented.

The critical path is one conditional state transition

The following runnable Python example performs one narrow but important provider-integration step: it fetches the live schema for POST /v1/image/upload before an adapter is implemented, with an explicit method, environment-based Bearer authentication, status checks, and bounded 429 retry handling. It then models the state transition that must survive framework changes: mandatory pending status for an accepted caption, idempotent human decisions, and an outbox event for both outcomes. The same conditional update belongs inside the Node.js transaction used by an Express handler. Schema discovery is used here because the contract does not justify inventing an upload body.

import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum
from typing import Callable


class State(str, Enum):
    PENDING = "pending"
    PUBLISHED = "published"
    REJECTED = "rejected"


@dataclass
class Media:
    media_id: str
    uploader_id: str
    caption: str
    state: State = State.PENDING
    outbox: list[dict[str, str]] = field(default_factory=list)


def fetch_upload_schema() -> dict:
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/image.upload"

    for attempt in range(4):
        request = urllib.request.Request(
            url,
            method="GET",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"},
        )
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
                return json.load(response)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            if error.code == 429 and attempt < 3:
                retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
                time.sleep(delay)
                continue
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            raise RuntimeError(f"Provider returned HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error

    raise RuntimeError("Schema request exhausted its retry budget")


def ingest(media: Media, caption_is_allowed: Callable[[str], bool]) -> Media:
    if not caption_is_allowed(media.caption):
        media.state = State.REJECTED
        media.outbox.append({
            "event": "media.rejected",
            "media_id": media.media_id,
            "recipient": media.uploader_id,
        })
    return media


def record_review(media: Media, approved: bool) -> Media:
    if media.state is not State.PENDING:
        return media  # Duplicate delivery cannot apply the decision twice.

    media.state = State.PUBLISHED if approved else State.REJECTED
    media.outbox.append({
        "event": "media.approved" if approved else "media.rejected",
        "media_id": media.media_id,
        "recipient": media.uploader_id,
    })
    return media


if __name__ == "__main__":
    schema = fetch_upload_schema()
    assert schema["method"] == "POST"
    assert schema["path"] == "/v1/image/upload"

    item = Media("media_1042", "user_77", "Quarterly product demo")
    ingest(item, caption_is_allowed=lambda caption: bool(caption.strip()))
    assert item.state is State.PENDING
    record_review(item, approved=True)
    record_review(item, approved=True)
    assert item.state is State.PUBLISHED
    assert len(item.outbox) == 1
    print(schema["id"], item.state.value, item.outbox[0]["event"])

Production code needs a database constraint or compare-and-set update, not merely the in-memory guard shown here. A useful SQL condition is conceptually “update this media ID only where state is pending”; zero changed rows means another worker already decided it. The decision and outbox insert must commit together. Delivery from the outbox may be at least once, so the notification consumer should deduplicate on the event ID rather than assume a queue message is unique.

Notice what is absent: the object is not copied on approval.

Publication changes one controlled state, then the search indexer reacts. That gives operators a single row to inspect when a user asks why item media_1042 is not searchable. More importantly, it prevents an awkward partial failure: if a copy completed but the row update did not, an object could occupy the “live” namespace while the application still called it pending; if the row changed first and the copy failed, search could point at bytes that were not there. One private object plus one authoritative row removes both split-brain cases from the publication transition.

Why reject publish-after-caption, and when is it valid?

The rejected design publishes as soon as automated caption moderation allows the text, then asks a person to inspect the image later. It has a shorter apparent path to search, but it fails the governing requirement: the image was never approved. A later rejection also becomes a takedown problem, with cached search results and notifications potentially advertising content that policy says should never have appeared.

There is a valid use case for that design. If a product explicitly permits post-publication sampling, accepts the exposure window, and has a documented takedown process, immediate publication can trade moderation coverage for lower latency. It is not the decision described here.

The other tempting design is to block the Express request until a reviewer responds. Reject it too. Human latency does not belong inside an HTTP request deadline, and a dropped client connection must not cancel durable review work. Return the media ID with pending, expose that state to the uploader, and send a notification after approval or rejection.

No guessing.

For this workload, the final decision rule is stable: store privately, screen the caption, hold the record, review the image, commit one terminal transition, then notify and index. If that division of responsibility fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and obtain current request schemas from discovery before implementing the provider adapter.

References

  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • Cloudinary documentation
  • imgix documentation
  • ImageKit documentation

title: Contagious Fingerprints: When LLMs Inherit Another Model's Identity
description:
arXiv:2611.18104v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The fingerprint by which a classifier recognizes the LLM behind a text is usually treated as a fixed property of the model. We show that it is contagious: a model that continues a conversation begun by another model inherits that model's fingerprint. This undermines audits of API relays, which can serve the first turns of a conversation with the model a customer pays for and silently hand the rest to a cheaper one. After such a handoff, detection of the substitute by a text classifier drops from 0.97 to 0.72 (DeepSeek replacing Claude Sonnet) and from 0.87 to 0.54 for a same-vendor downgrade (Haiku), and retraining on handoff data repairs only substitutes seen in training. Preregistered experiments trace the contagion to imitation of the history's style. History also moves a model away from its own fingerprint: active probes are not camouflaged, but when calibrated on fresh conversations they flag \emph{honest} models on long contexts at rates up to 1.00, and a standard MMD equality test rejects all nine models we test. Both failures come from comparing a history-dependent reply with a history-free reference. We propose \textsc{Lineup}, which samples references from the claimed model \emph{on the same history} and tests the audited reply by its rank among them. \textsc{Lineup} controls false positives by exchangeability and needs no fitted threshold or log-probabilities. With contemporaneous references on two closed models, its false-positive rate is 0.056 (preregistered bound 0.10), and it detects 0.81 of substitute sessions across six pairs after four audited turns.

title: Availability-Aware Historical Feedback Learning for Electric Arc Furnace Temperature and Chemical Composition Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.17463v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking plays an increasingly important role in recycled and lower-carbon steel production. However, variability in charged materials, energy input, and operating conditions makes accurate prediction of molten steel temperature and final chemical composition challenging. Intermittent or delayed measurements limit the information available for timely prediction. This study develops an availability-aware historical-feedback learning framework for predicting EAF endpoint temperature and the final concentrations of twelve chemical elements. Eight industrial data sources are integrated into three progressively enriched predictor representations comprising 19 static, 39 temporal, and 47 history-informed features. Historical outcomes are incorporated only when eligible under an assumed 60-minute measurement-release delay. Using 19,738 temperature heats and 3,341 chemistry heats, twelve tuned regression algorithms are evaluated through chronological forward validation. The proposed historical-feedback representation reduces root mean squared error (RMSE) in 147 of 156 matched algorithm-target comparisons. For temperature prediction, ExtraTrees achieves an RMSE of 12.290 degrees C, representing a 5.54 percent reduction compared with its temporal-only counterpart. Historical-feature ablation and feedback-delay sensitivity analyses demonstrate the importance of recent outcome information and its availability. In a separate retrospective later-period evaluation, lightweight adaptive residual correction reduces temperature RMSE from 12.502 to 12.275 degrees C without retraining the underlying model. Exploratory deep learning comparisons and target-specific feature-attribution analyses provide additional insights into predictive behavior. The results establish historical outcome availability and sequential feedback as important considerations for EAF endpoint prediction.

title: PADSNet: Physics-Aware Dual-Stream Network with Biomechanical Priors for Laryngeal Lesion Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.17852v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Precise classification of laryngeal lesions is clinically crucial yet highly challenging, as inter-class visual differences are often subtle. While abnormalities in vocal fold vibratory dynamics provide complementary discriminative information, existing deep learning models predominantly rely on visual appearance and lack explicit mechanisms for modeling clinically meaningful vibratory dynamics. To address this, we propose PADSNet, a Physics-Aware Dual-Stream Network for laryngeal lesion classification that integrates visual representations with explicit biomechanical reasoning. Specifically, a Wavelet-Attention Enhancement Module (WAEM) is designed to bridge the spectral-semantic gap, enabling complementary learning of spatial texture and dynamic frequency representations. Meanwhile, a Knowledge Computing Module (KCM) extracts interpretable biomechanical indices from temporal glottal distance waveforms, including indicators of mobility, symmetry, glottal closure, and vibration stability. These descriptors are subsequently incorporated into a Physics-Aware Gating Module (PAGM) as biomechanical priors to adaptively recalibrate visual feature toward pathology-relevant vibratory patterns. Extensive experiments on a clinical dataset demonstrate that PADSNet achieves an accuracy of 0.8452, an F1-score of 0.8090, a sensitivity of 0.7953, and a specificity of 0.8866. These results indicate that explicitly integrating biomechanical priors with deep visual representations provides a more accurate, robust, and clinically interpretable framework for automated laryngeal lesion classification.

title: When Does Oversampling Help? A Decision Framework for Imbalanced Data Streams Under Label Delay and Concept Drift
description:
arXiv:2611.17981v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: For imbalanced data streams with delayed labels, is it worth adding a streaming oversampler, or does continuous re-evaluation of earlier predictions already recover the cost of the delay? We address this through an extensive experimental comparison of streaming oversampling and continuous re-evaluation under joint class imbalance, concept drift, and label delay. Streaming oversamplers are typically evaluated under the test-then-train assumption of immediate labels; their behaviour under these conditions, assessed through re-evaluation, has not been systematically studied. We close this gap with a decision framework that predicts when oversampling adds value over re-evaluation, organised around three axes: drift density, minority-class learnability, and delay relative to the refinement window, and operationalised as a competition between a recovery channel (re-evaluation) and a minority-coverage channel (oversampling). Evaluating $15$ classifiers on $6$ synthetic and $6$ real streams, we find: re-evaluation recovers delay-induced loss on drift-active streams but is silent on stationary ones; oversampling's marginal contribution over re-evaluation is statistically detectable in only one real-data configuration; and cost--performance Pareto recommendations from synthetic streams do not transfer to real data, where fronts partition by drift regime. Method selection should therefore be conditioned on the stream's profile and re-estimated as it evolves, not inherited from synthetic benchmarks.

title: When the customer changes, forget the contact - a stale id in a Uniface master-detail form
description:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 got a form for contact persons in stage 30. The upper part selects a customer, the lower part edits one contact person of that customer. The service behind it has simple operations: load the contacts of a customer, save one contact, delete one contact by id and version.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. The app uses SQLite through the SLE driver (SQLite 3.50.2).

The form state

The form keeps three component variables:

  • $cCust$: the customer that is shown,
  • $cContact$: the contact person that is loaded (0 = none, a new one is created on save),
  • $cVersion$: the version of that contact for the optimistic locking check.

The delete operation of the service only gets the contact id and the version:

public operation DELETE_CONTACT
params
    numeric pContactId : IN
    numeric pVersion : IN
    string pError : OUT
endparams
...

So the service cannot know which customer the form shows. Keeping the contact id in line with the customer is the job of the form.

The click test that found it

  1. Load customer 1, create the contact "Jordan Example", save. The form now has $cContact$ = 1.
  2. Load customer 2 in the same form. The list correctly says "No contact persons for this customer." The edit fields still showed Jordan's data.
  3. Type contact id 1 and press "Load contact": "Contact 1 does not belong to this customer." Correct - the load checks the list of the current customer.
  4. Press "Delete contact...". The question was: "Delete contact person 1 (Jordan Example)?" - for a contact of customer 1 while customer 2 was shown. The answer in the test was No.

The load check in step 3 was fine, but it did not touch the state. And the customer switch in step 2 did not reset it either.

Before

The tail of the entry that sets the customer:

    $cCust$ = pId
    C_ID.CT2_DMY = pId
    CUST_NAME.CT2_DMY = "%%(vLast), %%(vFirst) (#%%(pId))"
    activate "WORKSET_SVC".ADD_RECENT(pId, vError)
    if ($status < 0)
        rollback
    else
        commit
    endif
    call DO_LIST
    return 0
end

The not-found branch of the entry that loads a contact:

    if (vFound = 0)
        INFO.CT2_DMY = "Contact %%(K_ID.CT2_DMY) does not belong to this customer."
        return -1
    endif

After

The form already had an entry for the button "New contact" that resets the state and empties the fields:

entry DO_NEW
    $cContact$ = 0
    $cVersion$ = 0
    K_ID.CT2_DMY = ""
    K_NAME.CT2_DMY = ""
    K_TITLE.CT2_DMY = ""
    K_PHONE.CT2_DMY = ""
    K_EMAIL.CT2_DMY = ""
    K_MAIN.CT2_DMY = "0"
    INFO.CT2_DMY = "New contact person; Save contact creates it."
    return 0
end

It is now called when the customer changes:

    $cCust$ = pId
    C_ID.CT2_DMY = pId
    CUST_NAME.CT2_DMY = "%%(vLast), %%(vFirst) (#%%(pId))"
    activate "WORKSET_SVC".ADD_RECENT(pId, vError)
    if ($status < 0)
        rollback
    else
        commit
    endif
    call DO_NEW
    call DO_LIST
    return 0
end

DO_LIST runs afterwards and overwrites the info line, so the user sees the contact count of the new customer, not the text of DO_NEW.

A failed load resets as well and keeps only the typed id for the message:

    if (vFound = 0)
        vId = K_ID.CT2_DMY
        call DO_NEW
        K_ID.CT2_DMY = vId
        INFO.CT2_DMY = "Contact %%(vId) does not belong to this customer."
        return -1
    endif

With these two changes $cContact$ only gets a contact id in two places: after a successful load from the list of the current customer and after a save for the current customer. The delete entry itself did not need a change; it already refuses to work without a loaded contact:

entry DO_DELETE
variables
    string vError
endvariables
    if ($cContact$ <= 0)
        INFO.CT2_DMY = "Please load a contact person first."
        return -1
    endif

Retest

  • Customer 1, load contact 1, switch to customer 2: the fields are empty, "0 contact person(s)."
  • "Delete contact..." on customer 2: "Please load a contact person first." No question.
  • Contact id 1 on customer 2, "Load contact": "Contact 1 does not belong to this customer.", fields empty.
  • Back to customer 1, load contact 1, "Delete contact...", Yes: "Contact person deleted.", the list is empty.
  • The form compiled with 0 errors and the usual warning 1016 for the non-database entity.

Notes

  • A confirmation dialog that names the record helped here: the name in the question made the wrong state visible. It would not have helped a user who reads quickly.
  • The lesson for master-detail forms: every change of the master resets the detail state, and every failed detail load resets it as well.

title: Step-Up Authentication for Sensitive Actions
description:
A few years ago a client's support team got a call from a customer whose payout bank account had been changed overnight. The login itself looked normal: correct password, a known browser, a session that had been open for eleven days on a shared office machine. Someone had simply walked up to an unlocked laptop, opened the billing page and swapped the IBAN. Nothing in our stack asked "are you still you?" before a change that moved real money. The fix was not a stronger password policy. It was step-up authentication on the handful of actions that actually matter.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every snippet against current OWASP Authentication and Session Management cheat sheets, NIST SP 800-63B, the WebAuthn Level 3 spec, Laravel 11 and Node 22. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi with 9+ years across PHP/Laravel, Vue, Node and .NET microservices, and I build the free developer tools at PixelValut. This is the final part of the series, and everything here is about hardening an app you own.

📚 Series Navigation — Passkeys & Session Hardening for Web Apps

  • Part 1: Rolling Out Passkeys Without Locking Users Out
  • Part 2: Session Lifecycle Hardening: Rotation, Timeouts & Server-Side Revocation
  • Part 3: CSRF in 2026: SameSite, Fetch Metadata & Origin Checks
  • Part 4: Account Recovery Hardening: The Side Door Next to Your Passkey
  • Part 5: Protecting Login Endpoints: Credential-Stuffing Signals & Adaptive Rate Limits
  • Part 6 (This Post): Step-Up Authentication for Sensitive Actions

Related earlier posts: Browser Secrets That Leak: Token Storage, Quotas & Outbound Controls · OAuth 2.1, OIDC ID Tokens & PKCE Forensics

What is step-up authentication and when should you use it?

Direct answer: Step-up authentication asks an already signed-in user to prove their identity again, freshly and often more strongly, before a sensitive action. Use it for money movement, credential and MFA changes, data exports, role changes and destructive deletes. Record when and how the user re-authenticated, allow the action only within a short window, and log every elevated action.

Classify actions before writing code

The mistake I see most is protecting everything or nothing. If every settings page asks for a passkey, users learn to click through prompts and complain until you remove them. Start by putting actions into tiers:

Tier Example actions Required proof Freshness window Notify user?
0 – Normal Read dashboards, edit profile name Valid session Session lifetime No
1 – Sensitive View API keys, export personal data, invite users Re-auth with any enrolled factor 15 minutes Optional
2 – Critical Change email, password, MFA, payout account; create API keys Phishing-resistant factor (passkey) preferred, else TOTP 5 minutes Yes, to old and new contact
3 – Destructive Delete organisation, transfer ownership, disable audit log Passkey + typed confirmation; optional second approver Single use Yes, to all admins

Keep this table in your repository. When someone adds a new endpoint, the review question becomes "which tier is this?" instead of a debate.

Record how and when the user authenticated

Step-up only works if the server knows how fresh and how strong the current authentication is. OpenID Connect already has the vocabulary: auth_time for when the user last actively authenticated, amr for the methods used and acr for the assurance level. Even if you do not use OIDC, store the same facts in your session.

In Laravel, I set them on every successful login or re-auth:

// app/Support/AuthContext.php
final class AuthContext
{
    public static function record(Request $request, string $method, int $level): void
    {
        $request->session()->put('auth.time', now()->timestamp);
        $request->session()->put('auth.amr', $method);   // 'pwd', 'otp', 'hwk'
        $request->session()->put('auth.level', $level);  // 1 = password, 2 = passkey/otp
        $request->session()->regenerate();               // new ID on privilege change
    }

    public static function satisfies(Request $request, int $level, int $maxAgeSeconds): bool
    {
        $time = (int) $request->session()->get('auth.time', 0);
        $have = (int) $request->session()->get('auth.level', 0);

        return $have >= $level && (now()->timestamp - $time) <= $maxAgeSeconds;
    }
}

Regenerating the session ID on elevation matters for the same reason as on login: privilege changed, so the identifier should too (Part 2 covers rotation in detail).

Enforce it with middleware, not page logic

Put the check in one middleware so no controller forgets it. When the check fails, return a clear machine-readable error that tells the frontend what to ask for:

// app/Http/Middleware/RequireStepUp.php
public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next, int $level = 2, int $maxAge = 300)
{
    if (AuthContext::satisfies($request, $level, $maxAge)) {
        return $next($request);
    }

    $request->session()->put('stepup.intended', $request->fullUrl());

    return response()->json([
        'error'      => 'step_up_required',
        'acr_values' => $level >= 2 ? 'passkey otp' : 'any',
        'max_age'    => $maxAge,
    ], 401)->header('WWW-Authenticate', 'Bearer error="insufficient_user_authentication"');
}

// routes/web.php
Route::put('/billing/payout-account', UpdatePayoutAccount::class)
    ->middleware(['auth', 'stepup:2,300']);
Route::delete('/org', DeleteOrganisation::class)
    ->middleware(['auth', 'stepup:2,60', 'confirm.typed']);

The insufficient_user_authentication error code comes from RFC 9470 (OAuth 2.0 Step-Up Authentication Challenge). If you run an API with access tokens, follow that RFC and let the client request a new token with acr_values and max_age.

Node/Express version with short-lived elevated tokens

For APIs and SPAs, I avoid making the whole session elevated. Instead, the re-auth endpoint issues a separate, short-lived token scoped to the action:

// stepup.js
import { SignJWT, jwtVerify } from 'jose';
const key = new TextEncoder().encode(process.env.STEPUP_SECRET);

export async function issueElevation(userId, action, amr) {
  return new SignJWT({ act: action, amr: [amr] })
    .setProtectedHeader({ alg: 'HS256' })
    .setSubject(String(userId))
    .setIssuedAt()
    .setExpirationTime('5m')
    .setJti(crypto.randomUUID())
    .sign(key);
}

export function requireElevation(action) {
  return async (req, res, next) => {
    try {
      const token = req.get('X-Step-Up-Token');
      const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, key, { algorithms: ['HS256'] });
      if (payload.sub !== String(req.user.id) || payload.act !== action) throw new Error('scope');
      if (await usedJti(payload.jti)) throw new Error('replay');   // single use
      await markJtiUsed(payload.jti, payload.exp);
      return next();
    } catch {
      return res.status(401).json({ error: 'step_up_required', action });
    }
  };
}

app.put('/billing/payout-account', requireElevation('payout.update'), updatePayout);

Binding the token to one user, one action and one use stops an elevated token from being reused for something else. When I debug these, I paste the token into the JWT decoder to check sub, act and exp, and use the JWT signature verifier with a test key to confirm the signing setup. Never paste production secrets into any web tool.

Use passkeys for the re-auth itself

Passkeys from Part 1 make step-up fast: one fingerprint or face check. The important detail is to require user verification, not just presence, so the authenticator actually confirms the person:

// Browser: request a fresh assertion for step-up
const options = await fetch('/webauthn/stepup/options', { method: 'POST' }).then(r => r.json());
const assertion = await navigator.credentials.get({
  publicKey: {
    ...decodeOptions(options),
    userVerification: 'required',          // biometric or PIN, not just a tap
    allowCredentials: options.allowCredentials, // only this user's credentials
  },
});
await fetch('/webauthn/stepup/verify', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(encode(assertion)) });

On the server, verify that the UV flag is set, the challenge is fresh and single-use, and the credential belongs to the signed-in user. Only then record auth.level = 2 and the new auth.time. If the user has no passkey, fall back to TOTP; avoid SMS for critical tiers where you can.

UX rules that keep step-up from becoming nagware

  • Ask at the moment of action, not on page load. Show what is about to happen: "Confirm to change payout account ending 4421."
  • Reuse a fresh elevation within its window, so three related edits do not trigger three prompts.
  • Keep the user's input. After re-auth, replay the pending request instead of making them fill the form again.
  • Show a clear cancel path that leaves nothing half-changed.
  • For destructive actions, add a typed confirmation (the organisation name) on top of re-auth.

Log, notify and allow undo

Every tier 2+ action should produce an audit entry and a notification:

{
  "event": "payout_account.updated",
  "user_id": 4821,
  "auth_time": 1763271840,
  "amr": "hwk",
  "ip": "203.0.113.24",
  "user_agent_hash": "9f2c…",
  "old_value_suffix": "1180",
  "new_value_suffix": "4421",
  "request_id": "a1b2c3"
}

Send the notification to the old contact details as well as the new ones, include a "this wasn't me" link that freezes the change and revokes sessions, and for payout changes consider a short hold before the first transfer. This is the same side-door thinking from Part 4: assume one control will eventually fail and make the damage reversible.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] Every sensitive endpoint is assigned a tier in a version-controlled table
  • [ ] Sessions record auth_time, method (amr) and level after login and re-auth
  • [ ] Session ID rotates on every elevation
  • [ ] Step-up enforced in middleware, not in individual controllers or the UI
  • [ ] API responses use a clear step_up_required / insufficient_user_authentication error
  • [ ] Elevated tokens are bound to user, action and single use, with ≤5 minute expiry
  • [ ] Passkey step-up requires user verification and a fresh challenge
  • [ ] SMS not accepted for critical or destructive tiers where alternatives exist
  • [ ] Pending request is replayed after re-auth; elevation reused within its window
  • [ ] Tier 2+ actions audited and notified to old and new contacts with a freeze link
  • [ ] Payout and ownership changes have a short delay or second approver

FAQs

Isn't a short session timeout enough?

No. Short timeouts annoy everyone and still leave the riskiest minutes unprotected. Step-up lets normal sessions stay comfortable while the few critical actions get fresh proof.

What if the user has no second factor enrolled?

Ask for the password again at minimum, and use the moment to prompt passkey enrolment. For tier 3 actions, consider requiring enrolment before allowing the action at all.

How does this work with SSO users?

Send the user back to the identity provider with prompt=login or max_age=0 and the desired acr_values, then check auth_time and acr in the returned ID token before allowing the action.

Should admins be exempt?

The opposite. Admin and support accounts can do the most damage, so they should face step-up on impersonation, role changes and data exports, with every use logged.

Can I store the elevated state in localStorage?

Avoid it. Keep elevation server-side in the session, or in a short-lived token held in memory and sent per request. My earlier token-storage post explains why long-lived secrets in browser storage are risky.

How do I test step-up flows?

Write feature tests that call each protected endpoint with a stale auth_time, a low level and a replayed token, and assert a 401 step_up_required. Then test the happy path within the window.

That wraps up Passkeys & Session Hardening for Web Apps. The thread across all six parts: authentication is not a single gate at login. It is a lifecycle — enrolment, sessions, CSRF, recovery, login defences and step-up — and each stage needs its own control.

title: From Paas Comfort To IaaS Reality:Deploying a Go and React App on Oracle Cloud
description:
If most of your deployment experience comes from platforms like Render, Railway, or Vercel, your mental model of "deploying" probably looks like this:

  1. Push your code to GitHub.
  2. Paste some environment variables into a clean dashboard.
  3. Watch a build log scroll by for three minutes.
  4. Click a *.onrender.com URL that already has HTTPS. It's fast, predictable, and asks you to know almost nothing about what happens underneath your code. I loved it. Then I built something that PaaS couldn't host, and I got a crash course in everything it had been quietly doing for me.

The Project That Broke My Comfort Zone

I was deploying dns-blocker, a project with a Go backend (nullify) and a React dashboard, onto an Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Always Free VM.

The reason was simple: a DNS resolver needs port 53 and persistent control over the network. Web-focused PaaS platforms aren't built to give you that. So moving to Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) wasn't an experiment. It was the only option.

What follows is the honest version of that journey: the silent freezes, the debugging, the fixes, and what I'd tell anyone about to make the same jump.

The Mental Shift: Ordering Delivery vs. Renting a Kitchen

Before I touched a single config file, the biggest hurdle was conceptual.

On a PaaS, you're paying for an abstraction layer. Most PaaS companies don't own bare-metal data centers. They rent big pools of IaaS servers from AWS, GCP, or Oracle and build orchestration on top. When you click "Deploy," a pipeline provisions a container, injects your secrets, configures a reverse proxy, issues a TLS certificate, and wires up a GitHub webhook.

On IaaS, you get an empty Linux box and a public IP address. That's it. There's no git push trigger, no automatic domain, and no friendly UI for environment variables. My first thought, while SSHing in just to run docker compose up, was that this felt less like "real deployment" and more like running my app on a remote laptop.

Then it clicked: this is production. Everything PaaS gave me for free is still available. I just have to assemble it myself.

It's the difference between ordering delivery and renting a kitchen. The food can be just as good, but now you're the one who has to find the pans.

Challenge 1: The Silent SSH Freeze

The first wake-up call came the morning after my initial setup. I'd connected to my Ubuntu instance fine the day before, set up a few things, and logged off. The next morning I ran my SSH command and got... nothing. No "permission denied." No timeout. Just a blinking cursor.

If you're used to PaaS dashboards with clear status badges (Building, Live, Deploy Failed), a silent terminal is genuinely disorienting. I even wondered whether I needed the Oracle Cloud console open while connecting. (You don't. Once an instance is running, it lives on its own on the public internet.)

Instead of guessing, I reran SSH in verbose mode:

ssh -v -i ~/Downloads/ssh-key.key ubuntu@<PUBLIC_IP>

The output stopped after two crucial lines:

debug1: Connection established.
...
debug1: Local version string SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_10.2p1 Ubuntu-2ubuntu3.8

What that actually meant

Connection established ruled out half the usual suspects at once. Oracle's Security List wasn't blocking me, and port 22 was open. My laptop had completed the TCP handshake and sent its SSH greeting, and it was now waiting for the server to answer with its own banner.

When a Linux server accepts a TCP connection at the kernel level but never replies from userspace (sshd), it usually means one thing: the machine is so starved for RAM that the SSH daemon can't get any CPU time to respond.

Lesson one: ssh -v is your new status badge. Learn to read it.

Challenge 2: Out-of-Memory Thrashing During docker compose up

After force-rebooting from the Oracle console and getting back in, I wanted to see the freeze happen in real time. So I went to my dns-blocker directory and ran:

docker compose up -d

Docker pulled the base images (golang:1.26-alpine and alpine:3.20), downloaded the Go modules, copied the source, and reached the last step:

=> [builder 6/6] RUN go build -o nullify .

At 401.6s, the terminal froze. SSH went dead again. Mystery solved.

Why PaaS hides this problem

On a PaaS, builds often run on separate, beefier workers before your app ever lands on a small runtime container. On a 1 GB IaaS instance (VM.Standard.E2.1.Micro), your build environment and your production environment are the same constrained machine.

By default, go build spreads work across every available CPU core and holds a lot in memory at once. Add the linker at the end, and a build can spike past what a 1 GB box can handle. With no swap configured, Linux spends nearly all its CPU time trying to free memory pages, and the whole machine locks up before the OOM killer can even step in.

The two-part fix

First, I added a 2 GB swap file so memory spikes spill onto disk instead of freezing the kernel:

sudo fallocate -l 2G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

Pro tip: double-check your terminal prompt before running system-level commands like these. Running them in the wrong tab will happily allocate swap on your laptop instead of your server.

Second, I changed the Dockerfile to trade a few extra seconds of build time for much lower peak memory:

FROM golang:1.26-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app

COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download

COPY . .

# -p 1: compile one package at a time (prevents parallel RAM spikes)
# GOMEMLIMIT & GOGC=50: force aggressive garbage collection during compilation
# -ldflags="-s -w": strip debug symbols to reduce linker memory & binary size
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOMEMLIMIT=450MiB GOGC=50 go build -p 1 -ldflags="-s -w" -o nullify .

FROM alpine:3.20
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/nullify .
CMD ["./nullify"]

With swap enabled and -p 1 limiting compiler concurrency, the build finished cleanly. No freeze, no drama, and a very satisfying green checkmark.

Challenge 3: Rebuilding PaaS Conveniences by Hand

With the container running, the next question was: how do people actually use this?

For dns-blocker, I needed two things exposed to the world:

  1. Port 53 (TCP and UDP) so devices can send DNS queries to the server.
  2. Ports 80 and 443 so users can open the React dashboard in a browser without typing http://<IP>:3000. On IaaS, exposing an app means touching layers PaaS never shows you:
  • Two layers of firewall. In Oracle Cloud, opening a port in your VCN Security List is only half the job. Ubuntu images on OCI also ship with strict iptables rules by default. Traffic has to be allowed at both the cloud perimeter and the OS level. Forgetting the second one is a classic "I opened the port, why is it still closed?" moment.
  • A domain and a reverse proxy. Point a domain (or a free dynamic DNS subdomain like DuckDNS) at your public IP with an A record. Then put Caddy in front of your containers. It routes yourdomain.com to the React frontend and something like api.yourdomain.com to the Go backend, and it provisions Let's Encrypt certificates automatically. That's the same HTTPS experience PaaS gives you, in a few lines of config.
  • Secrets and CI/CD. Instead of a settings tab, secrets live in a git-ignored .env file on the server, referenced by docker-compose.yml. Instead of a built-in GitHub integration, a short GitHub Actions workflow can SSH in on every push to main, pull, and rebuild. Even better, build the React frontend and Go binary inside GitHub's CI runners and scp the compiled artifacts over, so the 1 GB server never has to compile anything again. None of this is hard, exactly. It's just a lot of small things that a PaaS bundles into one button.

Challenge 4: Never Compile on the Server Again

The swap file saved me, but it also felt like a bandage. A 1 GB machine shouldn't be doing the heaviest job in the whole pipeline. The better fix is to move the build somewhere with real resources and send the server only the finished product.

GitHub Actions is a good fit. Its runners have far more RAM than my VM, and they're free for public repos (with a generous allowance for private ones). The plan:

  1. On every push to main, build the Go binary and the React frontend on a GitHub runner.
  2. Copy the compiled artifacts to the server over SSH.
  3. Restart the containers, which now only run code and never build it. ### Step 1: Add secrets to your repo

Under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions, add three secrets:

  • SSH_HOST: your server's public IP or domain
  • SSH_USER: ubuntu on my instance
  • SSH_KEY: the full contents of your private key file I'd strongly recommend generating a dedicated deploy key for this instead of reusing your personal one. If it ever leaks, you revoke one key and nothing else.

Step 2: Write the workflow

Create .github/workflows/deploy.yml:

name: Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-go@v5
        with:
          go-version-file: go.mod

      # OCI's E2.1.Micro is x86_64, so target amd64
      - name: Build Go binary
        run: |
          CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 \
          go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o nullify .

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: frontend/package-lock.json

      - name: Build React frontend
        working-directory: frontend
        run: |
          npm ci
          npm run build

      - name: Copy artifacts to server
        uses: appleboy/scp-action@v0.1.7
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SSH_HOST }}
          username: ${{ secrets.SSH_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.SSH_KEY }}
          source: "nullify,frontend/dist/*"
          target: "~/dns-blocker/deploy"

      - name: Restart services
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1.0.3
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SSH_HOST }}
          username: ${{ secrets.SSH_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.SSH_KEY }}
          script: |
            cd ~/dns-blocker
            docker compose up -d --force-recreate

Adjust the frontend/ paths to match your repo layout. Mine keeps the React app in its own folder.

Step 3: Slim down the Dockerfile

Since the binary arrives pre-built, the runtime image no longer needs the Go toolchain at all. The Dockerfile I sweated over in Challenge 2 shrinks to this:

FROM alpine:3.20
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates
WORKDIR /app
COPY deploy/nullify .
CMD ["./nullify"]

No compiler, no memory spikes, and an image that builds in seconds.

What I like about this setup

A push to main now triggers a deploy with no SSH session from me, which is the closest thing to PaaS's "just push" feeling I could recreate. When something breaks, the Actions log tells me exactly which step failed, so I get my status badges back too (Building, Live, Deploy Failed, just with different names).

It does have rough edges. There's no automatic rollback, and --force-recreate means a few seconds of downtime. For a personal DNS blocker, I'll take that trade. If you can't, look at tagging images and keeping the previous version around so you can switch back.

The Trade-Offs: PaaS vs. IaaS

After going through this, the trade-offs felt a lot clearer:

Dimension PaaS (Render, Railway) IaaS (Oracle Cloud, AWS EC2)
Setup speed Minutes. Connect repo, add env vars, ship. Hours. Provision the VM, harden SSH, configure swap, firewalls, and a reverse proxy.
Network and protocol control Restricted, usually HTTP/HTTPS on standard ports. Total control: custom DNS servers (port 53), VPNs, raw TCP/UDP sockets, background daemons.
Resource limits and cost Predictable tiers, but free tiers often spin down when idle and costs climb quickly. Generous always-on compute (like OCI's Always Free tier), but you manage tight RAM and CPU budgets yourself.
Build pipeline Handled on separate build infrastructure. Runs on your server unless you offload to GitHub Actions or cross-compile locally.
Maintenance No OS patching, no SSL renewals. You own security updates, disk cleanup (docker builder prune), and crash recovery.

What I Took Away From It

Stepping down a layer in the cloud stack came with friction, but it gave me things I couldn't get on a standard PaaS:

  1. True protocol freedom. A custom Go DNS blocker and a React dashboard on one always-on IP, with no cold starts and no HTTP-only restrictions. That's exactly why IaaS exists.
  2. Sharper debugging instincts. Reading ssh -v output, recognizing OOM thrashing, adding swap, and tuning Go compiler flags (GOMEMLIMIT, -p 1) turned "the cloud" from a magic black box into ordinary Linux processes I can reason about.
  3. Don't build on tiny servers. Just because a small VM can compile Go or bundle React doesn't mean it should. Build locally or in GitHub Actions and ship lightweight binaries and static assets.
  4. PaaS makes more sense after IaaS. You don't fully appreciate what those platforms automate until you've set up firewalls, swap, a reverse proxy, and a deploy pipeline by hand. ## So, PaaS or IaaS?

If you're building a standard web app or REST API and want to focus on product features, stick with PaaS. Paying for abstraction is a smart engineering trade.

But if your app needs custom network ports, always-on background services, tight cost control, or you just want to understand how production infrastructure works under the hood, spin up a raw Linux VM. When it inevitably freezes on your first build, you'll learn more in two hours of debugging than in twenty one-click deploys.

Have you made the PaaS-to-IaaS jump? I'd love to hear what bit you first. Drop it in the comments.

title: Multi-level latent-diffusion adaptation for cross-region point cloud segmentation of ancient terraces
description:
arXiv:2611.18033v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated lidar feature detection from lidar point clouds can support archaeological surveys, but models trained in one landscape may transfer poorly to another because of differences in terrain, vegetation, acquisition characteristics, and feature morphology. We address this problem for cross-region detection of ancient terraces using transductive unsupervised domain adaptation that exploits an unlabelled target survey. We propose MELD (Multi-level Embedding-space Latent Diffusion), which trains separate diffusion denoisers on target-domain representations at four hierarchical PointNet++ feature levels. These target distribution priors are then used to refine source representations during supervised training and target representations during inference, allowing adaptation to act directly on the multi-scale features consumed by the segmentation decoder. We additionally investigate local geometric descriptors derived from K-nearest-neighbour neighbourhoods, including surface normals, slope, and aspect. MELD is evaluated bidirectionally between the Teyuna and Miraflores lidar surveys in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Colombia, against a source-only model and nine configurations of established domain adaptation approaches. MELD raises F1 over the source-only model from 0.397 to 0.459 for Teyuna-to-Miraflores transfer and from 0.557 to 0.594 in the reverse direction, achieving the highest F1 among the evaluated adaptation methods in both directions. Adding local geometry further raises F1 to 0.542 and 0.606, respectively. Multi-level ablation shows that refining all four PointNet++ levels provides the strongest performance in both directions. These results show that explicit modelling of target feature distributions in hierarchical point cloud feature space, complemented by local geometry, provides an effective route to cross-region archaeological mapping without target labels.

title: A Multi-Layered AI Pipeline for BPMN Generation from Natural Language
description:
arXiv:2611.18157v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The automated transformation of unstructured natural language process descriptions into Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams remains a challenging task, due to linguistic ambiguity and the difficulty to detect non-adjacent control-flow relationships. This paper proposes a solution for generating BPMN models from natural language descriptions through a multi-layered pipeline that integrates transformer-based architectures, Large Language Models and ontology population. The proposed method starts with natural language descriptions and separates textual processing, control-flow relation extraction, and structural validation into dedicated components. Entity extraction is performed using a fine-tuned RoBERTa-based transformer model while a control-flow engine captures non-adjacent relationships through LLM-based inference. To improve generalization under limited available data, the approach uses a dynamic few-shot strategy with con- trolled template input construction, enabling improved generalization under limited data availability. Additionally, an ontology population mechanism is introduced to represent the generated process models as semantic knowledge structures. For evaluation purposes we have used from the literature and industry reference processes. Additionally, we have validated the proposed method on a real-world heart disease patients transitional care process, capturing practical constraints and multi-actor collaboration, and serving as an expert-defined benchmark scenario. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance in the relation extraction task, achieving an accuracy of 90.7%, as well as maintaining structural alignment between the generated and reference BPMN models across multiple evaluation scenarios scenarios.

title: Photogrammetric 3D Model-Based Animal Behavior Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.17881v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video-based behavior estimation is often implemented end-to-end from image sequences. We advocate a two-stage alternative: reconstruct 3D body and object geometry before classifying behavior. This makes ambiguities of the ill-posed 2D-to-3D inverse problem explicit and potentially correctable. We demonstrate the strategy with simulated interacting mice and extend it to real video.

title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models
description:
arXiv:2611.17462v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.

title: React useState – Interview Questions & Answers
description:
Q1. What is useState in React?

  • useState is a React Hook that allows us to create and manage state (data) inside a functional component. 
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Here:
count – current state value.
setCount – function to update the state.
0 – initial value.

Q2. Why do we use useState?

  • We use useState to store and update data in a component. When the state changes, React automatically re-renders the component and updates the UI. 
import { useState } from "react";

function Counter() {

    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    return (
        <>
            <h2>{count}</h2>
            <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
                Increase
            </button>
        </>
    );
}

export default Counter;

When we click the button, the count increases and the UI updates.

Q3. What is the difference between normal variables and useState?

  • Normal variables do not trigger a re-render when their values change, but useState updates the component UI when its state changes. Normal variable: 
function App() {

    let count = 0;

    return (
        <>
            <h2>{count}</h2>
            <button onClick={() => count++}>
                Increase
            </button>
        </>
    );
}

The UI will not update when you click the button.
Using useState:

function App() {

    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    return (
        <>
            <h2>{count}</h2>
            <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
                Increase
            </button>
        </>
    );
}

Now the UI updates automatically.

title: EcoVGGT: Pinned-Key Inference for Efficient and Streamable Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Long Videos
description:
arXiv:2611.18099v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content, and our experiments on VGGT and $\pi^3$ support it: a few dozen evenly spread frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) matches the success rate of $\pi^3$ on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos at 13.8 times its speed. With refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate of VGGT from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times its speed on 500 frames. EcoVGGT reconstructs 4,000 frames on one GPU, and EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 frames per second with the lowest online absolute trajectory error.

title: How do I get ChatGPT responses programmatically without using the OpenAI API?
description:
Drive ChatGPT's web app with a browser automation library such as Playwright, or call a scraping API that runs that browser for you. Both give you what ChatGPT shows a visitor, and that is a different result from what the OpenAI API returns for the same prompt.

  • A short Playwright script works, with one condition. On 16 November 2026 a headed Chromium got ChatGPT's logged-out page and a full answer with its links. A headless Chromium got Cloudflare's "Just a moment..." page with HTTP 403.
  • The page has few stable hooks. The answer's elements carry generated class names such as x78zum5. The fixed hooks we found were a form field name and two aria-label values.
  • The API and the web app cite different pages. A 2026 preprint found that the Responses API and Google Search together recover only about a quarter of the URLs the web app cites.

The steps for the browser route:

  1. Install Playwright and its Chromium: pip install playwright, then playwright install chromium.
  2. Open https://chatgpt.com/ in a headed browser.
  3. Type the prompt into textarea[name="prompt"] and click the button labelled "Send message".
  4. Wait for section[aria-label="DIL content"], then wait until its text stops changing.
  5. Read the answer text and its links, and store them with the time and the country of your exit IP.

How do I get ChatGPT responses programmatically without using the OpenAI API?

There are two routes, and both read the same page, ChatGPT's web interface. With your own browser automation you run the browsers, proxies and parser. With a scraping API the vendor runs them and you send one HTTP request.

This is the browser route. We ran it on 16 November 2026 against the logged-out page:

import time

from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

PROMPT = "What are the best project management tools for remote teams?"

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=False)  # headless got a 403
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://chatgpt.com/")
    page.locator('textarea[name="prompt"]').fill(PROMPT)
    page.locator('button[aria-label="Send message"]').click()

    answer = page.locator('section[aria-label="DIL content"]').last
    answer.wait_for(timeout=120_000)

    # The answer streams in. Wait until the text stops changing.
    text, stable = "", 0
    while stable < 3:
        time.sleep(2)
        current = answer.inner_text()
        stable = stable + 1 if current == text else 0
        text = current

    links = answer.locator("a[href^='http']").evaluate_all(
        "els => els.map(e => e.href)"
    )
    print(text[:500])
    print(links)
    browser.close()

It printed the answer (Asana, ClickUp, monday.com, Notion, Jira and Trello) and six links, each tagged utm_source=chatgpt.com. Three things about this page matter for the code:

  • The logged-out page served a compact layout: a textarea named prompt and a form that posts to /unauth-mweb/conversation. A signed-in session gets a different layout with different selectors.
  • The answer has no data- attribute that names it. The aria-label "DIL content" was the only label on its section, and the elements inside it use generated class names.
  • The links are the inline links of the answer. The script does not read the sources panel or the model name, which need more parsing.

What does the browser route take at scale?

One answer on one laptop is the easy part. A schedule of prompts in several countries adds these parts, and you keep each one running:

Part What it takes
Browsers One Chromium per concurrent prompt. Headed mode needs a display, or a virtual one such as Xvfb on a server
Proxies An exit IP in each country you sample, because the answer and its links follow the location
The bot check Cloudflare sits in front of chatgpt.com. In our test it stopped headless Chromium with a 403 and let a headed one through. Cloudflare documents its bot detection engines, and the result can change with any update
Selectors The three hooks in the script are labels and a field name. A layout change removes them without an error, and the script then waits until it times out
Monitoring Alert on the share of empty or timed-out answers, not only on exceptions

The public record of the old wrappers shows where the work goes. pyChatGPT moved from plain HTTP to undetected_chromedriver to get past Cloudflare, and its repository is now archived.

If you need a few hundred answers a month from one country, the browser route can be the cheaper one. Count the hours you spend on fixes before you compare it with a per-answer price.

Which scraping APIs run the browser for you?

Several vendors sell ChatGPT's web answers as an API. Each request below is from the vendor's own page, read on 16 November 2026:

Vendor Request What comes back
Bright Data ChatGPT Scraper API A list of {"url": "https://chatgpt.com/", "prompt": ..., "country": ...} Answer text, answer HTML, citations, attached links, recommendations, country
Oxylabs ChatGPT scraper {"source": "chatgpt", "prompt": ..., "parse": true} markdown_text and citations
cloro POST /v1/monitor/chatgpt with prompt and country text, markdown, sources, citationPills and model

All three route each request through the country you set and hand back JSON. They differ in the fields, in whether they return the model ChatGPT chose, and in how they bill: per record, per result or per credit. Compare them on a sample of your own prompts.

Why not use the OpenAI API with web search?

The OpenAI API is the right tool when you want a model's output. It is a weak stand-in for what ChatGPT tells its users, and two independent studies measured the gap.

The preprint by Jiang and others (arXiv, 11 October 2026) recorded citations from signed-in ChatGPT web sessions across model versions 5.2 to 5.5, then ran the same questions through the Responses API with web search and through Google. Combined, the two recovered only about one quarter of the URLs the web app cited.

Researchers in Hamburg compared the web interface and the API on more than 24,000 German news answers over five weeks, as The Decoder reported. The API leaned on encyclopedias, with Wikipedia at almost 15% of its citations. welt.de and bild.de made up about 13% of web references and 2% of API citations.

Which route should you pick?

Your case Route
You want the model's answer in your own product The OpenAI API
A few hundred answers a month, one country, and you already run browsers Your own Playwright script
Several countries, a schedule, or the sources panel and model name parsed A scraping API

What are the limits?

Both routes see what a logged-out visitor sees. Anything that needs a signed-in session is out of reach. If ChatGPT asks for a login in one country, requests from that country fail until it stops. ChatGPT picks the model for each request, so the same prompt can get a different model on the next run.

The browser test ran once, from one machine in one country, on 16 November 2026. The study figures are from the linked pages; the preprint is not peer-reviewed, and it used signed-in sessions. This post is published by cloro, one of the three APIs in the table above.

title: Diagnose Vercel CLI setup problems with vercel doctor
description:
Vercel CLI now includes vercel doctor, which checks your setup and shows the command that fixes each problem it finds.

It checks the CLI version and install, your login and current team, the project link, and your project configuration in vercel.json. It also reports active incidents from the Vercel status page.

Each check reports OK, Warning, Failed, or Skipped. When vercel upgrade can't update the installed CLI, the install check shows where the CLI runs from and how to reinstall it.

Doctor runs without a login or a linked project, and it never prompts, logs in, or links a project, so coding agents can run it before guessing at a fix. Add --json to get each check's status and suggested commands as structured output.

Update to the latest CLI version and run vercel doctor to check your setup, or read the doctor command reference.

title: What Balanced Accuracy Cannot Identify in Neural-Signal Decoding under Test-Time Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2611.17925v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adaptation for neural-signal classification is usually transductive: each batch is scored after updating on it, and the gain depends on the adapted model [4]. This paper asks what an aggregate change fails to characterise inside the cohort. Full test-time adaptation (full_ttt) was evaluated in 11 dataset-encoder cells (four each on Siena/EEG and PTB-XL/ECG, three on Sleep-EDF/EEG), with splits and source-model evaluation fixed; the subject was the unit, exact sign tests were Holm-corrected and conditional on the shared stream, and bootstrap intervals accompanied a dependence audit. Two results of different kinds follow. In the binary case balanced accuracy gives a one-class decoder the same value as one reporting both classes at 50%, so the aggregate cannot identify a class that stopped being reported; a class covering a tenth of a subject's samples went unpredicted in 26-47 of 112 subject-cells, against 7-9 for the controls, which is a descriptive count. With cohort, split and update rule fixed, the within-subject class contrast follows the encoder, tested directly rather than inferred from tests against zero: two of six Siena encoder pairs survive the dependence readings at their nominal reference and one at a fold-level reference, while two of ten Sleep-EDF stage pairs pass the run-clustered gate at its nominal reference; aggregate and contrast named different encoders in 10 of 11. The protocol bounds both results, since a stream-interleaving effect reverses sign with state sharing (+3.5 to -2.4 pp). An aggregate score can hide individual harm, as [1] showed, but it cannot distinguish a uniform loss from a deleted class; class-level change should therefore be reported alongside the aggregate and subject-level change alongside it, with both results conditional on the cell, the rule and the stream construction.

title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
description:
arXiv:2611.18397v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

title: OCTAVE: A Capability-Resolved Benchmark for End-to-End HTML5 Game Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.17681v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Complete game generation requires agents to coordinate rules, interactions, states, and presentation over a long development process. A single aggregate score obscures which capabilities are implemented and which requirements remain unmet. We present OCTAVE, a benchmark for complete HTML5 game generation organized around eight Capability Dimensions, with 180 tasks and 1,800 Evaluation Requirements drawn from real player requests, commercial-mechanics reconstruction, and human expert design. It covers PC Web, Mobile Web, 2D, and 3D. Requirements distinguish Completeness, assessing publicly specified core implementation, from Richness, assessing hidden, deeper system relationships. Static source-code judgments provide requirement-level diagnosis across capabilities and task conditions. Evaluation of 11 model-harness combinations yields 33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness; 19.9% of generation records are static gate failures or missing artifacts. Excluding same-model self-evaluation, even the best combination remains below 50% on both public and hidden requirements. Richness is not harder than Completeness under every task condition. Systems perform relatively better on Core Rules and Numerical Design, while AI/NPC and Feedback and Game Feel show more prominent gaps. Requirement difficulty offers coarse stratification but is only weakly negatively correlated with pass rates. A limited human cross-check finds that requirements judged satisfied by humans but failed by the automated evaluator are the main direction of disagreement. OCTAVE extends evaluation beyond aggregate scores to diagnosis localized by requirement, capability, and task condition.

title: Figma Is a Canvas for Pictures. ExodeUI Is an Engine for Working Software.
description:
Figma Is a Canvas for Pictures. ExodeUI Is an Engine for Working Software.

Let's state an uncomfortable truth that every frontend developer knows in their heart:

Figma doesn't design software. Figma designs posters that look like software.

The Illusion of Prototyping

When you present a Figma prototype to stakeholders:

  • Clicking a button doesn't mutate actual application state.
  • Typing into an input doesn't validate regex or test sanitization.
  • Scrolling a list doesn't trigger virtualized windowing or lazy pagination.
  • It is a smoke-and-mirrors slideshow masquerading as an application.

What Working Software Actually Requires

Real software demands:

  1. Deterministic State Transitions: Handled via Finite State Machines (FSM).
  2. Fluid Physics: Damped harmonic motion that reacts to real touch inputs.
  3. Data Binding: Real API endpoints feeding live json structures into views.
  4. Accessible Semantics: Clean DOM trees with proper ARIA attributes.

Enter ExodeUI

Engineered by an ambitious team in India, ExodeUI bridges the chasm between visual expression and executable code:

// Exported from ExodeUI: Real functional UI with built-in state machine
export const AuthModal = ({ isOpen, onClose, onAuthSuccess }) => {
  return (
    <CanvasViewport responsive="domless" preset="liquid-glass">
      <LogicNode event="pointerdown" transition="spring-pop" />
      {/* Real interactive form inputs & validated state */}
    </CanvasViewport>
  );
};

Stop spending months translating dead mockups. Build with an engine designed for working software.

🚀 Experience the Post-Figma Era Built in India

If you are tired of drawing dead pictures in Figma and spending months translating mockups into code, try the next-generation interactive UI engine built right here in India:
