title: Node.js Browser Download Link 404s — Object Storage Export Job Race Conditions
description:
Short answer: treat a tenant export as unpublished until the worker has stored the exact completed-object identity in a durable record. A browser download link should be derived from that record, never from a filename guessed when the job was queued. This turns a confusing object-storage 404 into a small set of inspectable state transitions.

For a healthtech system that stores product images and builds a tenant-scoped ZIP, large-file throughput makes the distinction matter. The HTTP request that starts the work and the worker that completes the archive are separate owners. A fast queue can widen that gap; it cannot make an unfinished archive downloadable.

Why does a browser download link hit an object storage 404 after an export?

Start with the requested object key, copied byte for byte from the access log, and compare it with the key on the completed export record. Do not reconstruct it from a display filename, an object listing, or a route parameter. A missing tenant segment, a URL-encoding change, or a retry suffix is enough to make a plausible-looking link point nowhere.

The browser is just the witness.

For multipart uploads, completion is a real boundary: the upload is not an object available for download until the multipart completion operation succeeds. A worker that updates its database row before that operation has created an application-level race, even where the storage system offers strong read-after-write behavior. A HEAD-style metadata lookup after the final write provides evidence about the precise key the worker intends to publish; it does not prove that a CDN, retention worker, or a different retry will honor the same lifecycle.

The failure report I want has six fields: export ID, tenant ID, attempt ID, requested key, recorded key, and lifecycle state. Keep signed query strings out of it. For notification-heavy systems, that restraint matters: a copied URL in an email or SMS log is a credential, not useful diagnostic context.

Do not retry blind.

ADR: publish an immutable object identity, not a predicted path

Decision: the export worker alone moves an export from generating to ready, in the same durable update that records the final key and, where available, its version or generation. The link service reads a ready record scoped to the authenticated tenant. It does not accept an object key from the browser.

The invariants are deliberately boring. One completed attempt has one tenant ID and one object identity. ready means the storage write completed and the identity was persisted. Cleanup first changes ready to expired; only then may it delete the associated bytes. A request that loses that race gets an unavailable response rather than a freshly signed link to an object being removed.

Publication design What the 404 means Throughput effect Appropriate use
Sign a predicted key at job creation The queue, retry, or prefix construction disagreed with the link No finalization wait, but failures surface at click time A status page link, not a completed file
Record the completed identity, then sign it The record or retention state is stale, and has a narrow audit trail One metadata check per completed archive Tenant-scoped asynchronous exports
Stream the archive through the application The application policy or stream failed Adds application bandwidth and connection pressure Small artifacts requiring per-download inspection

The second row adds a pending state that some teams dislike. Keep it. Honest latency is easier to explain than a link that sometimes fails after a notification has already been delivered.

This decision has a cost beyond one database update. The job table becomes part of the download-serving path, so its retention, tenant index, and transition rules deserve the same review as the bucket policy. An export that reaches ready must retain the attempt identity long enough for a support trace to join the browser request to the worker write; deleting that row early recreates the mystery under a different name. The database also needs a unique rule that says which attempt is current for an export. Without it, two workers can both finish successfully, and a later transaction can silently replace the object identity that an earlier notification described. Use a conditional transition rather than an unconditional update, and alert when it affects zero rows. That outcome is useful evidence: either cleanup expired the export, a cancellation won, or another attempt already published. It should not become an automatic retry that writes another archive. For a service sending delivery messages, make the outbox entry reference the committed export ID. The message sender can retry its own delivery without reopening the storage lifecycle.

The critical path is a state transition, not a URL formatter

The adapter below is intentionally generic. It uses a unique attempt key, so a retry cannot overwrite bytes that a reader has already been authorized to fetch. The database predicate is what keeps two workers from publishing competing attempts.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta
from uuid import UUID


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CompletedObject:
    key: str
    size: int
    version: str | None


def archive_key(tenant_id: UUID, export_id: UUID, attempt_id: UUID) -> str:
    return f"tenants/{tenant_id}/image-exports/{export_id}/{attempt_id}.zip"


def finalize_export(db, storage, tenant_id: UUID, export_id: UUID,
                    attempt_id: UUID, archive: bytes) -> None:
    key = archive_key(tenant_id, export_id, attempt_id)
    storage.put(key=key, body=archive, content_type="application/zip")
    metadata = storage.head(key=key)
    if metadata.size != len(archive):
        raise RuntimeError("completed archive size differs from uploaded bytes")

    completed = CompletedObject(key=key, size=metadata.size,
                                version=getattr(metadata, "version", None))
    changed = db.publish_if_generating(
        export_id=export_id,
        tenant_id=tenant_id,
        attempt_id=attempt_id,
        object_key=completed.key,
        object_version=completed.version,
        expires_at=datetime.now(UTC) + timedelta(days=7),
    )
    if not changed:
        raise RuntimeError("another lifecycle transition won")


def issue_download(db, storage, tenant_id: UUID, export_id: UUID) -> str:
    export = db.get_ready_export(export_id=export_id, tenant_id=tenant_id)
    if export is None or export.expires_at <= datetime.now(UTC):
        raise PermissionError("export is unavailable")
    return storage.signed_download(key=export.object_key, expires_in=300)

For a large archive, avoid buffering all image bytes in the web process just to preserve this ordering. The worker can stream archive production into the storage writer, then execute its completion and metadata steps before publishing the record. The exact checksum, version, and replacement semantics differ by backend, so persist only identifiers whose documented meaning the adapter can verify. A size check catches truncation; it cannot establish content equivalence on its own.

What should the timeline show before blaming consistency?

Trace the job creation, upload start, upload completion, metadata result, database publication, link issuance, and cleanup transition with one correlation ID. The interesting cases usually become obvious when these events are ordered. A ready row before upload completion is a publisher bug. A requested key that differs from the recorded key is prefix drift. A recorded key that existed at publication but disappeared after expired is a retention question.

Test the awkward timings: cleanup one second before a click, two jobs with the same displayed ZIP name, a retry after a failed multipart completion, and a tenant A request carrying tenant B's export ID. Also test the notification boundary. Send the message after the ready transition commits, and make notification retries reuse that committed export rather than create a new archive.

Watch the count of exports stuck in generating, attempts to sign non-ready records, and storage-not-found results partitioned by lifecycle state. Those three signals identify whether throughput pressure is leaving work unfinished, authorization is bypassing publication, or retention is doing exactly what it was told to do.

The 300-second download lifetime is a policy input, not proof of availability.

Rejected option: deterministic overwrite keys

Using tenants/{tenant}/exports/{export}.zip for every attempt looks tidy and can reduce cleanup bookkeeping. It is a poor fit when a retry can overlap a download, because the system must then define what readers see during replacement and how the old version remains addressable. Choose it only when the storage adapter exposes documented conditional replacement and version semantics that the application actually enforces.

A real limitation of the publication-ledger pattern is its extra durable state and database dependency. The trade-off is not suitable for an export whose only consumer is an internal service and whose bytes are small; choose synchronous generation followed by direct application streaming there. It is not a throughput strategy for a ZIP assembled from many product images. The decision here is about an explicit handoff between asynchronous producers and browsers, not the name on a storage account.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: How We Built a Remote 10-Tool Streamable HTTP MCP Server and 13.3 KiB Link-in-Bio in Go
description:
Public link-in-bio pages are structurally simple documents: an avatar, a name, a contact bar, and 5 to 20 links. Yet most commercial bio-link platforms render them as client-heavy Single-Page Applications that download hundreds of kilobytes of framework JavaScript inside Instagram, TikTok, or WhatsApp in-app WebViews before painting a button.

When we built Linq.es and its Official Remote MCP Server (https://linq.es/mcp), we took the opposite path on both the public frontend and the AI agent layer:

  1. Public profiles render server-side in Go (html/template) with inline critical CSS, 5.1 KiB of gzipped async CSS, 8.2 KiB of gzipped defer vanilla JS, and zero React, Next.js, or Vue runtime (13.3 KiB total gzipped first-party CSS + JS).
  2. AI agents connect directly to https://linq.es/mcp over Streamable HTTP (JSON-RPC 2.0, MCP spec 2025-03-26) using a Personal API Key (lnq_live_...), without installing a local npx or Python stdio wrapper.

Below are the main architectural lessons we learned building both layers in Go.

1. Why Go HTML SSR beats heavy SPA bundles inside social WebViews

Most link-in-bio clicks happen inside constrained mobile WebViews (Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, X, and WhatsApp) over variable cellular connections. Every extra script tag, font round-trip, and client hydration pass delays First Contentful Paint and increases bounce rates before a visitor taps a wa.me button or downloads a .vcf contact card.

On Linq.es, public profiles render complete semantic HTML in the European Union behind a multi-tier cache (in-memory L1, persistent object storage L2, and Cloudflare Edge CDN):

Async stylesheet:     ~5.1 KiB gzipped (loaded non-blocking)
Deferred vanilla JS:  ~8.2 KiB gzipped (loaded with defer)
Total external CSS+JS: 13.3 KiB gzipped (zero client SPA framework)

No third-party ad pixels (Meta, TikTok, or GA4) are injected on public pages unless a Pro profile owner explicitly configures their own measurement IDs.

2. Streamable HTTP MCP (2025-03-26) vs local stdio wrappers

Many early MCP integrations wrap an existing REST API inside a local Node.js stdio package that users run via npx -y @vendor/mcp-server. That introduces three recurring friction points:

  • Node or Python version mismatches on developer machines
  • Stale local npm packages when tool schemas or annotations evolve
  • No support on cloud, browser, or mobile MCP hosts that cannot spawn local subprocesses

With the 2025-03-26 Streamable HTTP specification, an MCP server runs as a standard HTTPS JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint:

  • GET https://linq.es/mcp serves human-readable discovery metadata (name: "linqes-mcp", protocolVersion: "2025-03-26", transport: "streamable-http").
  • POST https://linq.es/mcp handles initialize, notifications/initialized, ping, tools/list, and authenticated tools/call executions.

Lesson #1: notifications/initialized must return 202 Accepted with an empty body

During the MCP handshake, right after initialize succeeds, strict clients send a JSON-RPC notification ({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"}) that omits the id field. If your HTTP router wraps every return path in a 200 OK JSON-RPC envelope with "id": null, strict clients treat the unexpected body as a protocol error.

In Go + Gin, handling JSON-RPC notifications before dispatching methods keeps the handshake clean:

// JSON-RPC notifications omit "id" and must not return a JSON-RPC response body.
if strings.HasPrefix(req.Method, "notifications/") || len(req.ID) == 0 {
    c.Status(http.StatusAccepted)
    return
}

Lesson #2: Evict edge caches synchronously on serverless runtimes

On serverless container platforms, CPU allocation drops as soon as the HTTP response finishes writing. If an AI agent calls add_profile_link or update_profile_link and you trigger CDN cache purges in detached background goroutines, the container can be throttled before the outbound purge completes, leaving visitors looking at stale HTML when the agent reports the link is live.

Running storage and CDN cache invalidations concurrently inside a sync.WaitGroup before returning the tools/call response guarantees that by the time Claude or Cursor replies "Done, live at https://linq.es/handle", public visitors already see the updated page:

var wg sync.WaitGroup
wg.Add(2)
go func() {
    defer wg.Done()
    purgeObjectCache(ctx, profileHandle)
}()
go func() {
    defer wg.Done()
    purgeEdgeCDN(ctx, profileHandle)
}()
wg.Wait()

Lesson #3: Explicit MCP Tool Annotations (2025-03-26) matter for agent safety

When exposing read, write, and delete operations side by side, tool descriptions alone should not force an LLM host to guess which calls are safe to auto-approve and which require human confirmation.

Adding standard MCP annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, and openWorldHint) using explicit boolean pointers in Go ensures false values serialize cleanly instead of being dropped by omitempty:

type MCPToolAnnotations struct {
    Title           string `json:"title,omitempty"`
    ReadOnlyHint    *bool  `json:"readOnlyHint,omitempty"`
    DestructiveHint *bool  `json:"destructiveHint,omitempty"`
    IdempotentHint  *bool  `json:"idempotentHint,omitempty"`
    OpenWorldHint   *bool  `json:"openWorldHint,omitempty"`
}

Combined with "additionalProperties": false on every tool's inputSchema and clear prerequisite notes (e.g., calling list_profiles to discover handles and list_profile_links before update_profile_link or delete_profile_link), agents avoid hallucinating parameters or accidentally deleting links when a user only asked to hide one (active: false).

Connecting to https://linq.es/mcp

Once you generate a Personal API Key in Account Settings, you can connect Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json), Claude Desktop, Windsurf, or Gemini CLI (~/.gemini/settings.json) directly over HTTPS:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "linqes": {
      "url": "https://linq.es/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer lnq_live_YOUR_PERSONAL_API_KEY"
      }
    }
  }
}

From there, your agent can use all 10 tools across up to 5 profiles and 500 /s/ shortlinks:

  • list_profiles: List owned profiles, themes, public URLs, and cumulative view counts.
  • get_profile_analytics: Pull 1-to-90-day views, clicks, CTR percentage, referrers, countries, devices, and daily time series.
  • list_profile_links: Inspect every link's key, url, active state, click count, and iOS/Android overrides.
  • add_profile_link: Publish a link or social icon with optional badgeText, iosUrl, androidUrl, scheduleStart/scheduleEnd (RFC3339), live countdown, or click badge.
  • update_profile_link & delete_profile_link: Edit, toggle (active: false), or permanently remove links with immediate cache invalidation.
  • import_bio_links: Migrate public links from an existing Linktree, Beacons, or Bio.link URL in one call.
  • list_shortlinks & create_shortlink: Create and audit https://linq.es/s/:code shortlinks with custom 3-50 character slugs, iOS/Android routing, and utm_source through utm_content tags.

title: When an empty field means "delete" - a silent removal in a Uniface service and how the form now guards it
description:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 has a supplier form. One of its features was still open: "remove a product from a supplier". The plan was to add a remove operation to the supplier service. While reading the service to plan it, it turned out that the removal already existed - hidden in an empty field.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. The app uses SQLite through the SLE driver (SQLite 3.50.2).

The operation

The service operation that links a product to a supplier has this signature:

public operation SET_SUPPLIER_PRODUCT
params
    numeric pSupplierId : IN
    numeric pProductId : IN
    string pSupplierSku : IN
    string pPrice : IN
    numeric pLeadDays : IN
    string pMinQty : IN
    string pError : OUT
endparams

After the checks for supplier and product, this branch follows:

    if (pPrice = "")
        call COUNT_SQL("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM SUPPLIER_PRODUCT WHERE SUPPLIER_ID = %%(pSupplierId) AND PRODUCT_ID = %%(pProductId) AND IS_MAIN = 1", vMain)
        sql "DELETE FROM SUPPLIER_PRODUCT WHERE SUPPLIER_ID = %%(pSupplierId) AND PRODUCT_ID = %%(pProductId)", "CUSTOMERS"
        if ($status < 0)
            pError = $concat("The supplier product could not be removed (error ", $procerror, ").")
            return -1
        endif
        if (vMain = 1)
            sql "UPDATE SUPPLIER_PRODUCT SET IS_MAIN = 1 WHERE PRODUCT_ID = %%(pProductId) AND SUPPLIER_ID = (SELECT SUPPLIER_ID FROM SUPPLIER_PRODUCT WHERE PRODUCT_ID = %%(pProductId) ORDER BY PURCHASE_CENTS, SUPPLIER_ID LIMIT 1)", "CUSTOMERS"
        endif
        return 0
    endif

An empty price means "remove the link". The branch even takes care of the details: if the removed supplier was the main supplier for the product, the cheapest remaining supplier becomes the new main supplier.

As a service function, that is a complete remove operation. As an interface, it is a trap.

Why it is a trap

The supplier form had one button for this operation, Set product, and passed the price field straight through. A user who forgot to enter a price and clicked Set product would not get "please enter a price". The link would be deleted, the form would commit, and the message line would say:

Supplier product saved.

Nothing in the form says that an empty price deletes anything. The code is not wrong; the meaning of the empty value was simply never visible where the value is entered. It was found by reading the service, not by an error report.

The fix: two buttons, two intentions

The service already did the right thing and is covered by the existing service tests, so it stayed unchanged. The form now separates the two intentions.

Set product refuses an empty price and points to the other button:

    if (P_PRICE.SUP_DMY = "")
        INFO.SUP_DMY = "Please enter a purchase price (use Remove product to remove it)."
        return -1
    endif
    vLead = P_LEAD.SUP_DMY
    activate "SUPPLIER_SVC".SET_SUPPLIER_PRODUCT($cId$, vProd, P_SSKU.SUP_DMY, P_PRICE.SUP_DMY, vLead, P_MIN.SUP_DMY, vError)

Remove product is a new button with its own entry. It passes the empty price on purpose, but only after two checks:

entry DO_REMOVE_PRODUCT
variables
    numeric vProd, vCount
    string vError, vData, vRow
endvariables
    call NEED_SUP
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    call PRODUCT_ID(vProd)
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    sql/data "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM SUPPLIER_PRODUCT WHERE SUPPLIER_ID = %%($cId$) AND PRODUCT_ID = %%(vProd)", "CUSTOMERS"
    vData = $result
    getitem vRow, vData, 1
    getitem vCount, vRow, 1
    if (vCount = 0)
        INFO.SUP_DMY = "This supplier does not deliver %%(P_SKU.SUP_DMY)."
        return -1
    endif
    askmess/question "Remove %%(P_SKU.SUP_DMY) from this supplier?~Remove product", "Yes,No"
    if ($status != 1)
        return 0
    endif
    activate "SUPPLIER_SVC".SET_SUPPLIER_PRODUCT($cId$, vProd, "", "", 0, "", vError)
    if ($status < 0)
        rollback
        INFO.SUP_DMY = vError
        return -1
    endif
    commit
    call SHOW_PRODUCTS
    INFO.SUP_DMY = "Supplier product removed."
    return 0
end
  • The read-only check is needed because the service reports success when the DELETE hits no row. Without it, removing a product the supplier never delivered would also say "removed". Both values in the SQL text are numeric variables, so no text from an input field ends up in the statement.
  • The confirmation uses askmess/question, where $status 1 means the first button, "Yes".

The click test

In the test, an empty price on Set product showed the new message and changed nothing. With a price, the link was saved. Remove product with "No" kept the link, with "Yes" removed it, and a second click reported "This supplier does not deliver TST-PO-1." The test database was backed up before and restored afterwards.

Takeaways

  • An empty value with a special meaning is invisible in the user interface. Give that meaning its own button.
  • "Saved" after a delete is worse than an error. Messages should name what actually happened.
  • If a delete is silent when nothing matches, check in the caller before you report success.
  • Read existing services before adding new operations. Sometimes the operation is already there, and only the interface around it is missing.

title: Creative Product Design under Brand Image Constraints
description:
arXiv:2611.17762v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Industrial design requires creative visual exploration while satisfying constraints that are often product-specific and implicit. Existing text-to-image (T2I) approaches can generate creative designs through concept blending or multi-agent self-enhancement, but they provide limited mechanisms for ensuring that generated designs remain consistent with such constraints. We focus on brand image as a representative design constraint and propose a framework for brand-aware redesign generation. Given a product name, the framework constructs a brand image survey report that summarizes product and market information, derives a creative direction from the report, and integrates this direction into a self-enhancement loop in which generated images are critiqued and prompts are revised. We evaluate the framework on 50 redesign tasks across five product categories, comparing it with Naive T2I, IP-Adapter/IT-Blender, and unconstrained self-enhancement under the same T2I backbone. By a VLM-as-Judge protocol to measure creativity and brand identifiability, the proposed framework achieves a more favorable trade-off between the two objectives, with particularly clear gains in highly constrained categories such as automotive and motorcycle, where the plausible design space is relatively limited compared with that of other product categories. These results suggest that dynamically eliciting and textualizing brand image can guide creative product design generation under brand image constraints.

title: In the Eye of the Beholder: Human Label Variation in Textual and Visual Entailment
description:
arXiv:2611.17954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human Label Variation (HLV) is increasingly recognised as an informative signal that reflects meaningful differences in how people interpret the same input. While HLV has been studied extensively in Natural Language Inference (NLI), much less is known about HLV in Visual Entailment (VE; Xie et al., 2019), where the textual premise is replaced by an image, keeping the hypothesis and label space fixed. We introduce VariNLI-VE, a dataset for studying how HLV changes between paired NLI and VE instances. We re-annotate a subset of originally neutral SNLI (Bowman et al., 2015) instances and their visual counterparts, with the same annotators evaluating both the textual and visual versions. Each annotation includes a label, confidence score, and explanation, yielding 2,250 annotations. Labels and explanations are collected jointly, providing ecologically valid explanations. Because the image may reveal information not stated in the text, one might expect disagreement to decrease in VE. Instead, we find no clear overall reduction: disagreement decreases for some instances while it increases for others. Explanations reveal further variation, as annotators can retain the same label while changing their rationale. When evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on the paired data, we find lower accuracy, weaker alignment with human label distributions, and generally higher uncertainty in VE than in NLI.

title: The Paradox of Silicon Valley’s Most Loved “Cheater” CEO — JENSEN HUANG
description:
On November 12, 2026, Jensen Huang resigned as the CEO of Nvidia, ending a 33-year run that built a $4 trillion artificial intelligence empire. His sudden departure erased nearly $600 billion in market value in a matter of days. The cause was a string of extramarital affairs that escalated into a national security crisis.

Yet, in a rare twist for a corporate scandal, the tech industry immediately rallied to defend him. Over 165,000 industry leaders, including Elon Musk, alongside 7,500 of Nvidia's own employees, signed a petition demanding his return.

Here is the wild, paradoxical truth about why the tech world is utterly terrified to lose him, and why the empire he left behind is a trap no competitor can escape.

  1. The Spy, The Smuggler, and the CEO

The crisis started as a standard corporate scandal. Huang confessed to an affair, and shortly after, a second relationship with a direct report was exposed.

Then came the kicker.

One of the women, Alice Huang, was allegedly acting as an intelligence asset for the Chinese government. She wasn't just a mistress; she was a geopolitical backdoor. Her former company, Megaspeed, was already under federal investigation for buying up $12 billion worth of restricted Nvidia chips and smuggling them into China. The board of directors panicked, Washington politicians demanded answers, and Huang was forced out.

A messy personal life is a PR crisis. A messy personal life that hands supercomputers to a geopolitical rival is an FBI raid waiting to happen.

  1. The Plot Twist: "We Want the Cheater Back"

Normally, a CEO is completely radioactive after a scandal of this magnitude.

Instead, over 165,000 tech leaders (including Elon Musk)and more than 7,500 of Nvidia's own employees signed a petition demanding his immediate return. Why on earth would they back him?

Because Jensen didn't just run a company. He bled for his team. Back in 2006, he burned billions of dollars to build CUDA, the software that makes modern AI possible. Wall Street hated it. They laughed at him and crashed Nvidia's stock. But Huang took the financial beating in total silence for ten years just to protect his engineers, allowing them to build the future without corporate interference.

He also ran a $4 trillion company with zero bureaucracy. He managed 60 people directly and read thousands of emails from junior coders every single day. He cut out the middle managers and built a culture of absolute, fierce loyalty.

Silicon Valley doesn't care about his morals. They care about his mind.

  1. The Irreplaceable Trap

Why can't anyone just replace him? Because Huang didn't just build fast chips. He built a prison for his competitors

CUDA: If a rival builds a faster chip tomorrow, developers still will not buy it. Why? Because they would have to completely rewrite 18 years of deeply ingrained code just to use it.

Blackwell: He stopped selling individual chips. Now, he sells entire liquid-cooled racks that act as one massive, perfectly synced super-brain, entirely eliminating data delays.

The Assembly Line: This is his craziest move. Huang used Nvidia's massive cash pile to buy up roughly 60% of the world's highly specialized chip-manufacturing space at TSMC. Even if competitors design a better chip, they literally have no factories left to build them.

Jensen didn't just beat the competition. He bought the battlefield.

  1. The Empire Without the Emperor

Now, he is gone. Interim CEO Colette Kress is a financial genius, but she is inheriting an empire under siege.

Competitors like AMD are finally catching up to Nvidia's speeds. Giants like Google, Microsoft, and Amazon are sick of paying Nvidia's insane markups and are aggressively building their own internal chips.

But the real threat? Chinese AI labs like DeepSeek, starved of Nvidia chips due to US bans, just figured out how to run AI using three times less hardware.

The world is finally figuring out how to do more with less just as Nvidia loses the one man who always knew how to do the most.

What do you think ,can NVIDIA actually survive losing its only one CEO?

title: Stage-wise Lineage-aware Dropout for Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting
description:
arXiv:2611.17752v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is prone to overfitting because only a limited number of images are available to constrain scene geometry. Dropout is one regularization strategy for alleviating this problem. We introduce the concept of a lineage family to describe a set of Gaussian primitives derived from the same founder through cloning or splitting operations. The founder Gaussians refer to all Gaussian primitives generated during initialization. Descendants within the same family often jointly contribute to the refinement of adjacent local regions. However, dropping individual Gaussians can be less effective due to the compensation effect from neighboring Gaussians for the dropped ones. To address this issue, we propose Stage-wise Lineage-aware Dropout(SLD), which applies lineage-family dropout during the structural regularization stage and switches to individual dropout during the later refinement stage. We further propose Lineage-Balanced Densification(LBD), which operates during densification by constructing an expanded candidate pool and reallocating the densification budget according to the mean gradient scores and existing descendant sizes of different families. Experiments on the LLFF, MipNeRF360, and Blender datasets show that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance in sparse-view reconstruction

title: 5 Uncopyable macOS Errors Developers Hit Weekly (Gatekeeper, Xcode codesign, Rust ld, Homebrew, Two-Column PDFs) — Real Screenshots & Quick Triage
description:
The common thread

Some macOS errors are not selectable text. They are drawn: dialogs, IDE overlays, console panes, the page image of a PDF. You cannot drag-select them, you cannot copy them, and Cmd+F finds nothing.

That changes the workflow. Normally you copy the message, paste it into a search engine, and read. Here you first have to get the text out. Below are five errors I hit repeatedly, each with the real triage commands first — and a note on the reading problem second.

Every screenshot is a real screen, reproduced as a before/after comparison.

1. Gatekeeper: "cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified" 


"AppName" cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified.

The variant that makes people panic:

"AppName" is damaged and can't be opened. You should move it to the Trash.

Neither means the binary is corrupt. Check, in order:

# 1. is the quarantine attribute attached?
xattr -l /Applications/AppName.app

# 2. what does Gatekeeper think?
spctl --assess --type execute -vv /Applications/AppName.app

# 3. is it signed at all?
codesign -dv --verbose=4 /Applications/AppName.app

If codesign reports code object is not signed at all, the build is unsigned — usually an ad-hoc distribution. If the distributor is trustworthy and only the quarantine flag blocks it:

xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/AppName.app

Or from the GUI: right-click → Open → Open once.

The expensive mistake is deleting the app because the dialog said "damaged".

→ Gatekeeper triage page

2. Xcode: codesign failed with exit code 1 


Command /usr/bin/codesign failed with exit code 1

Three things determine this, in this order: certificate → provisioning profile → Bundle ID.

# 1. do we have a usable signing identity?
security find-identity -v -p codesigning

# 2. what is the build actually going to use?
xcodebuild -showBuildSettings 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -iE "CODE_SIGN|provisioning|DEVELOPMENT_TEAM"

# 3. what happened, verbosely?
xcodebuild -scheme YourScheme -configuration Debug build 2>&1 \
  | grep -iE "codesign|signing|profile"

The three common causes:

  • security find-identity returns 0 valid identities → no certificate in the keychain
  • DEVELOPMENT_TEAM is empty → no team selected
  • profile Bundle ID ≠ target Bundle ID

Verify an already-built product:

codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=2 App.app

→ Xcode codesign triage page

3. Rust / Cargo: the linker error is a result, not a cause 


error: linking with `cc` failed: exit code: 1

The cause is a few lines above:

ld: symbol(s) not found for architecture arm64
clang: error: linker command failed with exit code 1

So read backwards:

# pull the linker lines, not only the last line
cargo build 2>&1 | grep -nE "ld:|undefined|note: reference|error:" | head -40

# what did the linker actually try?
cargo build -v 2>&1 | tail -60

# what does the binary ask for?
otool -L target/debug/your_bin | head
nm -u target/debug/your_bin | head

Typical causes: architecture mismatch (arm64 vs x86_64), an unresolved C/Objective-C symbol from build.rs, or a library path that needs RUSTFLAGS="-L /opt/homebrew/lib".

→ Rust linker triage page

4. Homebrew: undefined method / invalid option 


Error: undefined method `writable?' for nil:NilClass

Error: invalid option: --with-python3.8

Homebrew puts the conclusion on line 1. brew doctor comes second, not first.

# 1. sync the core first
brew update

# 2. then read errors only (warnings are normal and noisy)
brew doctor 2>&1 | grep -nE "^Error|Warning: " | head -20

# 3. which prefix are we even using?
brew --prefix
  • invalid option → the flag was removed (--with-* is largely gone)
  • undefined method → core/formula version mismatch, usually fixed by brew update
  • still broken → brew reinstall <name>

→ Homebrew triage page

5. Two-column PDFs: copy-paste scrambles the columns

Copy a paragraph from a two-column paper and the right column's opening gets glued to the left column's ending. Nothing is corrupted — the reading order is wrong, because extraction walks the row, not the column.

# does the PDF even have a text layer?
pdffonts paper.pdf

# extract preserving layout, then check the order
pdftotext -layout paper.pdf out.txt

Two fixes that work:

  1. Copy per column — select only the left column, then only the right one.
  2. Read a region instead of the stream — in Preview, hold ⌥ while dragging to force a rectangular selection, or capture the region and read it in place.

→ Two-column triage page

Reading the ones you cannot copy

The commands above all assume you can read the message. Half the time you cannot: the dialog has no text layer, the IDE overlay disappears when the pointer moves, the console pane refuses selection.

What I do instead of re-typing error messages by hand: press ⌃S, drag a box over the region, read the result in place. Escape closes it.

How it is wired, because the boundary matters for anyone under an NDA:

  • Recognition runs on-device via Apple Vision. The screen capture is not uploaded — the image stays local.
  • Translation is online. Only the recognized text is sent; the image never is.
  • Offline: recognition still works, translation does not.

Environment: macOS 13 or later, Apple silicon (arm64) only — it does not run on Intel Macs. The build is not notarized, so first launch is right-click → Open (see section 1 for why that warning is not corruption).

The full gallery — 18 real errors, same triage format for each entry:
Unity の Metal シェーダ警告の切り分け

The pattern worth keeping

  1. Dialogs are drawings. Check spctl / codesign / xattr before trusting the wording.
  2. Linker and build errors are bottom-up. The last line is the result; the cause is above it.
  3. Package managers put the conclusion first. Read line 1 before running the doctor.
  4. Column order is a layout problem, not an OCR accuracy problem. Changing the extraction route fixes the symptom.
  5. Get the text out without retyping it. Re-typing cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified from a screenshot is where the hour goes.

title: SQL Server to PostgreSQL: five details that break a data migration (and how to check them)
description:
Disclosure: I'm the author of dbSlice, a Windows tool, and I use it in the example. The five details below apply to any tool, and to a hand-written script too.

When an application moves from SQL Server to PostgreSQL, the schema usually gets the attention. The data is where the surprises are.

1. datetimeoffset loses its offset

A common mapping is TIMESTAMP, with values written in UTC. If the application needs the time zone, declare the column TIMESTAMPTZ in the CREATE TABLE before the load.

2. bit becomes BOOLEAN

1 and 0 arrive as true and false. Every query that compares with = 1 has to change.

3. nvarchar(max), ntext and xml

Use TEXT. PostgreSQL text is Unicode, so there is no N prefix. Declare XML yourself if you query it as XML.

4. rowversion / timestamp is not a date

It is binary in SQL Server (BYTEA in PostgreSQL). Leave it out of the copy unless the application reads it.

5. Case and collation

SQL Server usually compares text case-insensitively; PostgreSQL does not by default. Plan ILIKE, citext or a case-insensitive collation wherever the application relies on it.

How I check it

  1. Create the target tables from reviewed DDL. dbSlice does not create anything in your database by default: if the PostgreSQL table is missing it stops and shows a CREATE TABLE translated from SQL Server, for you or your DBA to review and run. That is where fixes 1 to 4 go.
  2. Initial load, then a nightly upsert by key (use a column that only grows, like updated_at or the IDENTITY id) so PostgreSQL stays in step until cutover.
  3. Fix the sequences. After rows are copied with their IDENTITY values, the PostgreSQL sequence can be behind the highest id. The tool can move it past the max id, or show the command.
  4. Compare key by key before the switch. The compare saves the list of divergent keys to a file.

What it does not do

It moves data, not T-SQL: stored procedures, triggers and views have to be rewritten for PostgreSQL. Incremental runs do not detect deletes at the source, so compare or reload before cutover. No CDC or SQL Server Agent is needed: it reads with ordinary queries.

Try it

There is a free version on the Microsoft Store (connects, browses, compares, exports CSV). Writing to the target needs a license.

  • Guide: https://dbslice.net/migrate/sql-server-to-postgresql
  • Nightly sync routine: https://dbslice.net/sync/sql-server-to-postgresql
  • Comparing tools (pgloader and others): https://dbslice.net/compare/sql-server-to-postgresql-migration-tools
  • Free version: https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9PMS69X1T53Z

Which of these has bitten you? I'm happy to answer questions about the type mapping.

title: How to Deploy a Web Application to AWS Amplify Without Git: A Step-by-Step Guide Using a ZIP Folder
description:
Introduction

When developers think about deploying a frontend application to AWS Amplify, one of the first things that comes to mind is connecting a Git repository.

The typical workflow involves pushing application code to GitHub, connecting the repository to AWS Amplify, configuring the build process, and allowing Amplify to automatically deploy the application whenever changes are pushed to the selected branch.

However, connecting a Git repository is not the only way to deploy an application with AWS Amplify.

AWS Amplify also supports manual deployments, which allow developers to deploy frontend applications by uploading a ZIP archive containing their application files.

This is particularly useful when:

  • You have a static website that does not require a build process.
  • You want to deploy a frontend application without creating a Git repository.
  • You are working with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files.
  • You want to host a frontend application independently of your backend infrastructure.
  • You need a straightforward way to publish a website directly from your local machine.

In this guide, we will walk through the process of deploying a frontend application to AWS Amplify without using Git.

We will use a simple static frontend application containing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files to demonstrate the process.

By the end of this tutorial, you should have a publicly accessible website hosted on AWS Amplify.

1. Understanding AWS Amplify Hosting

Before deploying anything, it is important to understand what AWS Amplify does.

AWS Amplify Hosting is a managed hosting service designed for modern web applications and static websites.

It provides infrastructure for hosting frontend applications without requiring developers to manually configure web servers, manage operating systems, or maintain hosting infrastructure.

When you deploy an application using Amplify, AWS handles several hosting responsibilities, including:

  • Hosting and serving your frontend files.
  • Providing a publicly accessible application URL.
  • Distributing application content through its hosting infrastructure.
  • Supporting HTTPS for deployed applications.
  • Managing deployment versions.

For this tutorial, we will use Amplify's manual deployment capability.

Unlike repository-based deployments, manual deployments do not require Amplify to connect to a source code repository.

Instead, we prepare our application files locally, compress them into a ZIP archive, and upload that archive through the Amplify Console.

The deployment process looks like this:

Local application files → ZIP archive → AWS Amplify Console → Manual upload → Deployment → Live application.

2. Prerequisites

Before proceeding, make sure you have the following:

  1. An active AWS account.
  2. Access to the AWS Management Console.
  3. A frontend application you want to deploy.
  4. A ZIP utility or the ability to create ZIP archives from your operating system.
  5. A modern web browser.

You do not need:

  • A GitHub account.
  • A GitLab account.
  • A Bitbucket account.
  • A connected Git repository.
  • A configured CI/CD pipeline.
  • An EC2 instance or web server.

For this demonstration, we will use a simple frontend project with the following structure:

my-frontend-app/
│
├── index.html
├── styles.css
└── main.js

These files represent a basic static frontend application.

If your application uses React, Vue, Angular, or another frontend framework, you can also deploy it this way, provided you first generate its production build output.

For example, a React application built with Vite typically produces a dist directory. The contents of that directory, rather than the entire development project, are what you would package for deployment.

3. Prepare Your Application Files

The first step is to prepare the files that Amplify will serve.

Navigate to your frontend project directory.

Before proceeding, make sure that:

  • Your HTML file exists.
  • Your CSS and JavaScript references point to the correct paths.
  • Your application works locally.
  • All assets required by the application are included.

For applications that communicate with backend services, check that API endpoints and other environment-specific configuration values are correct for the environment you are deploying.

4. Create a ZIP Archive of Your Application

This is one of the most important steps in the entire process.

AWS Amplify expects the ZIP archive to contain the files that should be deployed.

A common mistake is compressing the entire project folder instead of compressing the contents of the folder.

For example, consider this ZIP structure:

my-frontend-app.zip
│
└── my-frontend-app/
    ├── index.html
    ├── styles.css
    └── main.js

This structure introduces an unnecessary directory level.

For a simple static application, the preferred structure is:

my-frontend-app.zip
│
├── index.html
├── styles.css
└── main.js

The index.html file should be at the root of the archive so Amplify can serve it as the website's entry point.

Creating the ZIP file using Linux or WSL

If you are using Ubuntu, Linux, or Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), navigate into your frontend directory:

cd my-frontend-app

Run:

zip -r ../frontend-deploy.zip .

This creates a ZIP archive in the parent directory.

The important detail is the final dot (.).

It tells the zip command to archive the contents of the current directory rather than placing the entire directory inside the archive.

Creating the ZIP file using Windows

You can also create the archive using Windows File Explorer.

  1. Open your frontend project folder.
  2. Select the files you want to deploy.
  3. Right-click the selected files.
  4. Select Compress to ZIP file or Send to → Compressed (zipped) folder, depending on your Windows version.
  5. Give the archive a descriptive name, such as frontend-deploy.zip.

Make sure you select the application files inside the folder rather than compressing the parent folder itself.

Verify the ZIP archive

Before uploading, inspect the contents of your ZIP file.

On Linux or WSL, run:

unzip -l frontend-deploy.zip

The output should resemble:

index.html
styles.css
main.js

If you see an additional enclosing project directory, recreate the archive with the correct structure.

This small verification step can prevent unnecessary deployment problems.

5. Open the AWS Amplify Console

Now that your ZIP archive is ready, we can move to AWS.

  1. Sign in to the AWS Management Console.
  2. Search for AWS Amplify in the services search bar.
  3. Open the AWS Amplify service.
  4. Navigate to the Amplify applications dashboard.

You can also access the service directly:

https://console.aws.amazon.com/amplify/

Make sure you are working in the AWS Region where you intend to manage your application.

6. Create a New

Inside the Amplify Console:

  1. Select Create new app.

  1. Look for the option to deploy without connecting a Git provider.

  1. Select the manual deployment workflow.

Depending on the current Amplify Console interface, this option may appear as Deploy without Git provider or under a manual deployment section.

The important thing is to avoid selecting GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or another repository provider.

You are creating an application that will receive its deployment files through manual uploads.

7. Configure Your Application

The next step is to provide basic application details.

You may be asked to specify:

  • Application name.
  • Branch name.
  • Deployment method.

For example:

Setting Example value
Application name my-frontend-app
Branch name production
Deployment method Manual deployment

The application name helps identify your project in the Amplify Console.

The branch name is a deployment identifier. It does not mean you need to create or connect a Git branch.

You can use a name such as production to represent the deployment environment.

After entering the required information, proceed to the deployment configuration screen.

8. Upload Your ZIP Archive

This is where the actual deployment package is provided.

On the manual deployment screen:

  1. Locate the ZIP file upload section.
  2. Select your frontend-deploy.zip archive.
  3. If the console requests an application or branch selection, ensure you have selected the correct application and deployment branch.
  4. Review the deployment details.
  5. Start the deployment.

AWS Amplify will upload and process the archive.

Since we are deploying a static application without a build process, there is no need to configure a build specification such as amplify.yml.

Amplify can host the supplied static files directly.

Wait for the deployment to finish.

9. Verify the Deployment

Once Amplify successfully deploys your application, the deployment status should indicate that the application has been deployed.

The console will provide a default application URL.

It typically follows this format:

https://branch-name.application-id.amplifyapp.com

Open the URL in your browser.

You should see your deployed application.

If you deployed the example from this tutorial, you should see:

Welcome to My Website

This application is hosted on AWS Amplify.

Also open your browser's developer tools and inspect the Console and Network tabs.

Check for:

  • JavaScript errors.
  • Missing CSS files.
  • Missing JavaScript files.
  • Failed asset requests.
  • Incorrect API requests.

A successful deployment does not automatically mean every part of the application is functioning correctly. Always test the deployed application itself.

10. Updating Your Application Without Git

One advantage of manual deployment is that you can publish updates without pushing code to a repository.

Suppose you make changes to your frontend application.

For example, you update:

  • index.html
  • styles.css
  • main.js

The process is straightforward.

Step 1: Modify your local application files.

Step 2: Test the changes locally.

Step 3: Create a new ZIP archive containing the updated application files.

Step 4: Open the AWS Amplify Console.

Step 5: Select your existing Amplify application and deployment branch.

Step 6: Start another manual deployment using the updated ZIP archive.

Step 7: Wait for Amplify to finish deploying.

Step 8: Open your application URL and verify the changes.

You do not need to create another Amplify application every time you update your website.

You simply create a new deployment for the existing application.

11. Common Problems and How to Fix Them

Although manual deployment is relatively straightforward, a few issues can prevent an application from working correctly.

Problem 1: The deployed website displays a 404 error

One possible cause is an incorrect ZIP archive structure.

For example:

frontend-deploy.zip
└── frontend/
    └── index.html

For a simple static application, the entry point should be at the archive root:

frontend-deploy.zip
└── index.html

Solution: Recreate the ZIP archive using the contents of the frontend directory rather than the directory itself.

Problem 2: CSS files are not loading

This can happen when the paths specified in your HTML file do not match the deployed file structure.

For example:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="./styles.css">

This expects styles.css to be available relative to the HTML file.

Solution: Verify the paths and ensure all required files are included in the ZIP archive.

Problem 3: JavaScript files are not loading

Check that the JavaScript file exists and that its reference in your HTML file is correct.

For example:

<script src="./main.js"></script>

Also inspect the browser's developer console for JavaScript errors.

Problem 4: The application loads, but API requests fail

This is particularly important for applications that communicate with backend services.

Your frontend might load successfully while requests to API Gateway, Lambda-backed endpoints, or other backend services fail.

Possible causes include:

  • Incorrect API endpoint configuration.
  • CORS configuration problems.
  • Incorrect authentication tokens.
  • Invalid Cognito callback or logout URLs.
  • Backend authorization failures.

Solution: Verify the frontend configuration and inspect the browser's Network tab to identify the actual failing request.

If your application uses Amazon Cognito for authentication, make sure the deployed Amplify URL is registered as an authorized callback URL and logout URL in the Cognito app client.

Problem 5: Changes are not appearing after deployment

Sometimes your browser may continue displaying an older cached version of your application.

Solution:

  1. Confirm that the latest deployment completed successfully.
  2. Open the application in a private browsing window.
  3. Perform a hard refresh.
  4. Inspect the Network tab to verify which files are being loaded.

Also check whether your application uses a service worker or other caching mechanism.

12. Important Considerations When Using Manual Deployments

Manual ZIP deployments are convenient, but there are some limitations worth understanding.

No automatic deployment from Git

Because your application is not connected to a Git repository, Amplify will not automatically detect changes in your local project.

You must create and upload a new ZIP archive whenever you want to publish an update.

No automatic build process

A manual ZIP deployment is suitable for files that are already prepared for hosting.

For frameworks such as React, Vue, and Angular, generate the production build first and upload the resulting build output.

For example, with Vite:

npm run build

This normally generates a dist directory.

You should package the contents of that directory, ensuring that index.html is at the root of the archive.

Do not upload your entire development project with node_modules and source files when the production build output is all that is required.

Backend services are not automatically deployed

Uploading a frontend ZIP archive does not deploy your backend infrastructure.

If your application depends on services such as:

  • Amazon API Gateway
  • AWS Lambda
  • Amazon Cognito
  • Amazon DynamoDB
  • Amazon S3
  • Amazon Bedrock

Those services must already be provisioned and configured separately.

Amplify Hosting is responsible for hosting the frontend files in this deployment workflow.

Authentication and API configuration still matter

For applications that use authentication or communicate with backend services, make sure the production configuration is correct before uploading your archive.

A website can be successfully deployed while authentication or backend integration remains broken.

13. Conclusion

Deploying a frontend application to AWS Amplify does not always require a Git repository.

With manual deployments, developers can prepare their application files locally, package them into a ZIP archive, and upload the archive directly through the AWS Amplify Console.

The process is particularly useful for static websites, small frontend applications, prototypes, and projects where a repository-based deployment pipeline is unnecessary.

The overall workflow is simple:

  1. Prepare your frontend application.
  2. Ensure the required files are available.
  3. Create a ZIP archive with the correct directory structure.
  4. Open the AWS Amplify Console.
  5. Choose the manual deployment option.
  6. Upload the ZIP archive.
  7. Deploy the application.
  8. Verify the live website.
  9. Repeat the process whenever you need to publish an update.

The important lesson is that Git is not a mandatory requirement for hosting a frontend application on AWS Amplify.

If your application is already prepared for production, a ZIP archive is enough to get it deployed.

Additional Resources

  • AWS Amplify Documentation
  • AWS Amplify Hosting Documentation
  • AWS Amplify Console
  • AWS Amplify Pricing

Disclaimer: AWS Console labels and deployment screens may change over time. The exact wording of the manual deployment option may vary, but the ZIP-based deployment workflow remains the central approach described in this guide.

title: Towards Seconds-level Video Representation: Quadratically Gated Feature Grid with Adaptive, Prediction-free Sampling
description:
arXiv:2611.17786v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Implicit neural video representations are notoriously slow to build, which does not cross the basic practical threshold for most industrial applications. Here, we present Q-GAS, a coordinate-queryable video representation that couples multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids with a compact SwiGLU-style quadratic-gating (QG) decoder and an error-aware, prediction-free sampler. The explicit grids avoid hash-collision coefficient sharing at the cost of modestly higher storage yet greatly boost the expressive capacity; the QG decoder introduces low-rank local second-order interactions to improve the nonlinear feature response. During fitting, a global error map periodically refreshes a high-error pool, and each batch mixes pool samples with uniform samples, which is free from the auxiliary model to predict difficult samples, thereby further escalating the efficiency. On UVG Beauty/Bosphorus/Jockey, Q-GAS fits and quantizes under 50 s on one RTX PRO 6000, decodes at over 370 FPS with mixed precision and about 146 FPS in FP32. In our PyTorch implementation, Q-GAS trains and quantizes 5.5-7.2 times faster than the evaluated Instant-NGP baseline and 19-28 times faster than RNeRV. Under a 90 s budget, it improves PSNR/MS-SSIM/LPIPS over the evaluated NeRV-family pipelines at comparable BPP over the measured overlap. We have shared our code at https://github.com/MillenRosen/Q-GAS for readers' free use.

title: Go Token Expiry UX in Live Stock Watchlists: Deterministic Session Tests
description:
Short answer: keep the watchlist token short-lived, make expiry an explicit state transition, and test that transition with a fake clock and a replayable event log. The client should never infer authorization from whether a socket happens to be open.

In a stock trading watchlist, a live poll is a deceptively small feature. Prices arrive while a user edits symbols, the session token expires, and the UI must say what is still trustworthy. A stale quote is annoying; a stale permission boundary is a ledger problem waiting to happen.

Start with the bill, then decide what to retain

The largest recurring term is usually event delivery, not token issuance. A useful first estimate is subscribers × updates per second × encoded bytes per update; it gives the team a concrete number to measure before debating transports. Token minting and refresh calls are comparatively sparse, while retaining every transient quote event for replay can quietly turn a UX feature into a storage and compliance obligation.

For a watchlist, I retain an append-only audit record of authorization decisions, symbol changes, and the final session state. I do not retain every duplicate price tick by default. That choice reduces replay fidelity, so the recovery path uses a timestamped snapshot plus a sequence number; an operator can prove which quote version was displayed without preserving an unlimited stream of ephemeral values.

The catch is operational. If a regulator or incident responder needs tick-level reconstruction, dropping those events is not suitable. In that case, route the raw feed to a separately governed market-data archive and keep the product's audit log focused on user-visible decisions. Mixing the two retention policies makes deletion, access reviews, and cost attribution harder.

A simple budget worksheet should include fan-out bandwidth, connection counts, refresh traffic, and retained bytes. Cost is a constraint, not a selection criterion: a cheaper transport that makes expiry ambiguous creates more support work and a larger reconciliation surface.

Measure first.

How should token expiry shape a trusted watchlist session?

Treat authorization as a state machine shared by server and client: active, expiring, expired, and reconnecting. The server validates the token on connection and on privileged actions; the client displays quotes as provisional once the lease ends, stops submitting symbol mutations, and offers a deliberate re-authentication action. An open WebRTC data channel, WebSocket, or long poll is only a delivery mechanism. It is not proof that the lease remains valid.

Use an absolute expiry timestamp issued by the server, plus a small safety margin for clock skew. Do not schedule a single browser timer and call the job done. Background tabs throttle timers, laptops sleep, and a reconnect can race with a refresh response. On every message and before every mutation, compare the server-derived deadline with the current monotonic clock.

The UX should make the boundary legible: show “updates paused; sign in to continue,” preserve the last known quote with its age, and never silently re-submit a queued edit after a new token arrives. A fresh token starts a new authorization epoch. The epoch and the last accepted event sequence belong in the audit trail so duplicate callbacks remain harmless.

That is the trust boundary.

Here is the core of a deterministic test harness in Go. The production adapter can use a real clock; tests inject the fake one and advance it explicitly.

package session

import "time"

type Clock interface {
    Now() time.Time
}

type FakeClock struct{ current time.Time }

func (c *FakeClock) Now() time.Time { return c.current }
func (c *FakeClock) Advance(d time.Duration) { c.current = c.current.Add(d) }

type Lease struct {
    Epoch     uint64
    ExpiresAt time.Time
}

type State int

const (
    Active State = iota
    Expiring
    Expired
)

func SessionState(clock Clock, lease Lease, margin time.Duration) State {
    remaining := lease.ExpiresAt.Sub(clock.Now())
    if remaining <= 0 {
        return Expired
    }
    if remaining <= margin {
        return Expiring
    }
    return Active
}

The test should assert observable transitions, not sleep for five minutes. Advance to one second before expiry, verify that mutations are blocked in Expiring, then advance one second and verify that delivery is marked stale in Expired. Include a duplicate event with the same sequence number and assert that the audit writer records it once. This is an exactly-once mindset applied at the boundary where it matters; the network itself will not provide exactly-once delivery.

Testing reconnects without flaky timing

Build tests around a scripted event log. Each record contains epoch, sequence, received_at, and kind (quote, authorization, or mutation result). Feed the same log through a state reducer in unit tests, then run a smaller set of browser tests for rendering and focus behavior. The reducer gives you deterministic coverage for races such as “expiry arrives while a quote is buffered” and “refresh completes after reconnect.”

type Event struct {
    Epoch uint64
    Seq   uint64
    Kind  string
}

type Reducer struct {
    Epoch      uint64
    LastSeq    uint64
    Authorized bool
}

func (r *Reducer) Apply(e Event) bool {
    if e.Epoch != r.Epoch || e.Seq <= r.LastSeq {
        return false
    }
    r.LastSeq = e.Seq
    if e.Kind == "authorized" {
        r.Authorized = true
    }
    if e.Kind == "expired" {
        r.Authorized = false
    }
    return true
}

The important assertion is not “the reconnect finished within 200 ms.” It is “an event from epoch 4 cannot mutate state in epoch 5.” For example, imagine a trader's token expires just after sequence 881 carries a quote for NVDA, while the browser has already sent a symbol-removal request and the refresh endpoint is waiting behind a sleeping mobile radio. When the device wakes, the feed may deliver sequence 882, the refresh may complete, and the old mutation response may arrive in either order; the reducer must reject any record from the old epoch, retain the age of the last quote, and require the user to repeat the edit under the new lease. Add property tests that randomize event order, duplicate delivery, and reconnect count while keeping the clock fixed. Your mileage may vary with browser scheduling, but the authorization and ordering rules should remain invariant.

For integration tests, put the feed behind a controllable test server that can close the channel, delay a refresh response, and replay a sequence. Avoid monkey-patching wall-clock APIs in the browser; it often hides the exact race you are trying to expose. A short end-to-end suite can then verify accessible status text, disabled controls, and focus returning to the sign-in action.

Delivery choices and explicit limits

WebRTC data channels, WebSockets, and server-sent events each solve delivery, not authorization. WebRTC adds ICE and connection-state concerns; WebSockets offer a familiar bidirectional stream but still need application-level sequencing; server-sent events simplify one-way updates and browser reconnection while leaving mutations on ordinary HTTPS. The standards document for WebRTC describes its connection and data-channel states, which are useful signals for transport health, but none of them extend a token's lifetime.

Pick the least complex transport that matches the direction of traffic. For a read-heavy watchlist with separate HTTPS mutations, one-way events may be sufficient. Stay with a bidirectional channel when the session genuinely needs low-latency commands and you can operate its reconnect and backpressure behavior. Do not choose based on a benchmark that omits token refresh, audit writes, and mobile sleep.

I initially treated expiry as a timer concern. That was the wrong boundary. The durable boundary is an authorization epoch recorded beside the user's intent, because that is what reconciliation can explain after a reconnect or a disputed order. Keep transport telemetry (connect, close, retry, buffered bytes) separate from financial audit events, and sample high-volume quote metrics without sampling security decisions.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449

title: Object Storage App Data Backups Explained — Large-File Uploads and Presigned Recovery
description:
Short answer: for a marketplace that accepts private uploads, treat a backup as a verifiable object plus a restore contract. Stream the database dump and archive to private object storage, record an immutable manifest, and issue short-lived presigned downloads only after authorization. The throughput decision is about multipart transfer and retry behavior, not about which dashboard has the nicest button.

Start with the restore contract

A cron job that creates a ZIP and gets a 200 response has not proved that the backup is usable. A restore needs an object key, byte length, checksum, creation time, schema version, and the list of included tenant or marketplace partitions. Keep that manifest beside the archive, and write a separate record in the application database so an operator can find the latest complete set without listing a bucket.

The private-upload path should have a different namespace from backups. For example, uploads/{tenant_id}/{asset_id} and backups/{date}/{run_id}/data.zip make accidental cross-use harder to miss in logs. Encryption at rest is a baseline; authorization still belongs in your service because a presigned URL is a bearer capability.

One rule saves painful nights: a backup is complete only after a read-after-write verification. Check the returned length and checksum, then read a bounded range or the full object from a worker account. A successful upload request alone can hide a truncated stream, a wrong content type, or a manifest that was written before the archive finished.

Verify twice.

How should a Node.js cron upload a database dump zip to object storage?

The implementation can stay boring. Run the database-native dump, pipe it into a compressor, and send the resulting stream with a multipart-capable client. Node.js cron should limit concurrency so four large jobs do not consume the same disk and network budget as customer traffic. If your dump is 18 GB, a 64 MB part size means about 288 parts; that is a planning input for memory, retry windows, and provider limits.

Here is a deliberately generic Python sketch of the worker contract. The storage SDK is an interchangeable adapter; the important pieces are the manifest and the verify step.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from hashlib import sha256
from datetime import datetime, timezone


@dataclass
class BackupManifest:
    run_id: str
    object_key: str
    bytes: int
    sha256: str
    schema_version: str
    created_at: str


def stream_backup(source, bucket, key, put_object, head_object):
    digest = sha256()
    size = 0
    with source as chunks:
        for chunk in chunks:
            digest.update(chunk)
            size += len(chunk)
            put_object.write_part(bucket=bucket, key=key, data=chunk)
    remote = head_object(bucket=bucket, key=key)
    if remote["content_length"] != size:
        raise ValueError("backup length mismatch")
    return BackupManifest(
        run_id="run-2026-09-09T010000Z",
        object_key=key,
        bytes=size,
        sha256=digest.hexdigest(),
        schema_version="orders-v7",
        created_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    )

The production adapter should use bounded retries with jitter, abort incomplete multipart uploads, and emit one metric for each part retry. Do not retry a complete-part commit blindly: make the operation idempotent with a run ID, or you can create two manifests for one schedule. I once traced a restore delay to a cron process that kept the ZIP on an almost-full ephemeral volume; streaming removed that disk-pressure edge case.

That failure was quiet. The scheduler reported success, the database row existed, and the object listing looked normal until a restore worker compared the manifest's byte count. The fix was procedural as much as technical: the worker now closes the dump stream, finalizes the multipart upload, verifies metadata from a separate credential, and writes the “complete” state last. If any stage is interrupted, the run remains explicitly incomplete and the next cron cycle gets a fresh run ID. This ordering also gives on-call staff a useful answer at 02:00: there is either a complete object with a checksum, or there is no backup to restore.

No guesswork.

What fails first at marketplace scale?

Large-file throughput is usually constrained by the slowest shared resource. Database dump CPU, compressor CPU, egress bandwidth, object-store part limits, and the worker's file descriptors all compete. Measure them separately. A single end-to-end timer tells you only that the job was slow.

The failure modes are predictable:

Failure Detection Design response
Dump succeeds, upload is partial byte/checksum mismatch abort the multipart upload and mark the run incomplete
Presigned link leaks unexpected download principal or volume short expiry, authorization check, audit event
Retention deletes the only good copy restore drill finds a missing generation keep overlapping generations and test lifecycle rules
Tenant data crosses a boundary manifest has an unexpected tenant ID partition keys, policy tests, and a deny-by-default reader

Lifecycle rules are useful for stale temporary parts and old generations, but deletion is a data-governance action. AWS documents lifecycle transitions and expiration as rules evaluated by the service, so your runbook should allow for timing rather than assuming a deletion happens at an exact minute. Firebase Cloud Storage documentation makes a similar security point in a different product context: access control is separate from object retention.

Keep an offline restore fixture under version control: a tiny database dump, one representative upload, and its manifest. It catches schema drift and ZIP layout changes before a six-hour restore drill does. Your mileage may vary on compression ratio; it depends heavily on whether uploads are already compressed media.

Comparing compatible backends without choosing a winner

S3-compatible services, self-hosted object stores, and hyperscale buckets can all implement private objects and presigned requests, but their operational edges differ. AWS S3 has mature lifecycle and multipart controls; Cloudflare R2 removes some egress charges but changes the cost profile of reads; MinIO gives teams direct control of hardware and upgrades. Those are constraints, not a ranking.

Ask each candidate for documented limits on part count, minimum part size, checksum algorithms, lifecycle timing, replication, and audit-log retention. Then run the same restore fixture through each endpoint. A backend that wins a synthetic upload benchmark can still lose when a presigned URL must be denied after a user is suspended, or when a region cannot meet your recovery point objective.

Benchmarks are clues, not contracts.

The catch is that a self-hosted option is not suitable when your team cannot operate disks, replication, and key rotation. Stick with a managed bucket when the operational burden matters more than placement control; choose self-hosting when data residency or predictable hardware access is the hard requirement. Either way, keep the adapter narrow so changing the backend does not rewrite backup semantics.

Roll out with a reversible restore drill

Ship the manifest schema first, then dual-write one scheduled run while the existing backup remains authoritative. Compare checksums and restore duration for at least seven runs, including a deliberately interrupted upload. Only after the new path passes a full restore should the retention policy remove older copies.

During the drill, revoke the operator's session, expire a presigned URL, and attempt a cross-tenant key. These are cheap tests with expensive production consequences. Record recovery point and recovery time objectives next to the run, not in a separate wiki page that will drift.

The final decision is small: select the backend that meets throughput, isolation, retention, and restore-time targets with an operating model your team can sustain. The archive format is an implementation detail; the contract is what keeps app data recoverable.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://firebase.google.com/docs/storage
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html

title: The Death of Dead Mockups: Why India’s ExodeUI Is the Real Figma Competitor We Needed
description:
The Death of Dead Mockups: Why India’s ExodeUI Is the Real Figma Competitor We Needed

We need to talk about the great lie of modern UI/UX design: The Prototype Slideshow.

You spend weeks creating high-fidelity artboards in Figma. You wire up 80 connection noodles in Smart Animate. You demo the prototype to the executive team, everyone nods enthusiastically, and then...

The engineering sprint begins.

Proudly Made in India

Seeing this level of graphics engineering emerge from India’s tech capital is exhilarating. The post-Figma era is no longer a theoretical debate—it is live in the browser.

title: unumsearch: a trigram index so coding agents stop re-reading 258,000 files
description:
An AI coding agent asks the same sort of question hundreds of times a day: where is this function called, which files mention that setting. A plain rg answers each one by reading every file again. That is fine on one repository. It gets slow when you run many checkouts on one machine, which is our situation.

So we built unumsearch, a search CLI for code and files that keeps an index and answers like ripgrep, usually in milliseconds. It is open source (Apache-2.0), written in Rust, and has no GPU, model or network dependency. This post is what it does, what we measured, and where it loses.

How it works

The index is a list of every three-letter piece of text and the files it appears in. A query is cut into those pieces, the index names the few files that contain all of them, and only those files are opened and checked line by line against their real contents. The index only narrows what to read; the answer always comes from the file.

Two properties matter for agents:

  • It says when it might be stale. A file watcher marks edits, changed files are searched directly until the index catches up, and every JSON answer carries fresh, backend, covered, truncated and complete fields so a client knows when to scan for itself.
  • It does not index secrets. .ssh/, .aws/, .env*, *.key, *.pem and similar are never indexed, whatever the configuration says.

What we measured

The test set is 20 regexes mined from a week of real coding-agent tool calls, on the author's machine, dated 2026-10-09.

Over the whole tree (247,535 files, warm page cache, median of three passes), ripgrep 15.1 took 347 ms per query. The unumsearch daemon took 64 ms and the one-shot CLI took 91 ms.

In a separate race of 12 patterns our agents actually issued, over about 180 worktrees (258k files), ripgrep needed 4.03 s in total and the daemon needed 217 ms, 18.6x faster, with the same files as rg on 12 of 12.

On answers: 19 of 20 queries returned exactly rg's files; the 20th differs only by .env.example files, which unumsearch never indexes on purpose. During git checkout of a branch that rewrites 44,686 Linux kernel files, the index caught up 6.4 to 7.5 s after the checkout began. Until then answers said fresh: false, and 0 of 64,454 fresh answers differed from ripgrep.

Where it loses

On a single repository of 3.7k files, ripgrep takes a median 9.8 ms. The daemon takes 2.3 ms, but the one-shot CLI, which starts a new process per query, takes 12 ms. That is slower than rg. The speed comes from a process that keeps the index open, so if you run it as a daemon, MCP server or rpc, you get the gain; if you shell out once per query on a small repo, you do not.

The benchmark file lists further weak spots, including that a busier machine made every engine about 1.7x slower in one run, so read the absolute times with that in mind.

Try it 

curl -fsSL https://github.com/corpunum/unumsearch/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
unumsearch --root ~/src/myrepo index
unumsearch search 'fn\s+main' ~/src/myrepo --text

For agents, unumsearch mcp runs it as a stdio MCP server, and the README lists setup for Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and others. The latest release at the time of writing is v0.1.12, which fixed a case where a daemon reported fresh before it had looked at its roots.

You can reproduce the race on your own code with python3 bench/race.py --root .; your numbers will differ.

Source and benchmark method: github.com/corpunum/unumsearch.

How this was written

This article was drafted by an AI model (Claude, from Anthropic) working for CorpUnum Labs, from the project's README, benchmark notes and published project facts. Its figures were checked against those files before posting. The numbers come from those files; none were measured by the model.

We are CorpUnum Labs, in Athens, building OpenUnum, a local-first runtime for user-owned agents. If you want to see what our agents do on that one mini PC, there is a playable lab here: corpunum.com/play.
