title: Disentangling Forgetting from Utility: Lightweight LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Null-Space Projection
description:
arXiv:2611.17864v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) pose significant security risks by retaining private or hazardous information, creating an urgent need for unlearning techniques that excise specific knowledge without compromising general utility. However, prevailing fine-tuning-based unlearning methods struggle to achieve this balance, often suffering from computational inefficiency and unintended utility degradation due to the entangled nature of knowledge within model parameters. To disentangle forgetting from utility, we propose UUE, a theoretically grounded framework that reformulates unlearning as controllable model editing. First, UUE projects parameter updates into the orthogonal left null space of retained knowledge representations, strictly ensuring that the editing process causes minimal interference to the model's general capabilities. Second, distinct from targeted mapping, we introduce a convex untargeted objective that derives a closed-form analytical solution to effectively disrupt undesired knowledge by pushing forget-set embeddings toward their antipodal points. We implement UUE via lightweight, pluggable adapters (including a low-rank variant, UUE-L), enabling efficient deployment without modifying the frozen backbone. Extensive experiments on TOFU and WMDP benchmarks demonstrate that UUE and UUE-L achieve superior unlearning efficacy, significantly outperforming existing methods.

title: Cross-Linguistic Acoustic Biomarkers of Cognitive Impairment Across Interactive and Single-Speaker Speech Tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.17710v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multilingual dementia detection is essential for scalable and equitable screening. In recent years, automated speech analysis has emerged as a promising approach for supporting dementia detection by enabling non-invasive and scalable assessment of cognitive function. However, existing studies that use automated speech analysis often rely on one type of task, such as picture description, and use black-box models. These studies often neglect the role of task and language. To address these gaps, we performed a cross-linguistic and cross-task acoustic analysis that integrates a conversational dataset with structured speech tasks across four languages (Spanish, Mandarin, English, Japanese). We applied statistical, linguist-/clinician-guided, and machine learning model-based feature selection to derive compact acoustic feature sets while maintaining classification performance. This enabled systematic comparison of cognitive impairment-relevant features across datasets and tasks. Our results revealed that acoustic features did not generalize uniformly across tasks and languages. Temporal features remained robust across all datasets, consistently capturing timing disruption regardless of language or task. In contrast, speech rate showed strong task dependence -- emerging as informative mainly in single-speaker tasks with externally anchored content and pacing, but becoming less reliable when speech content was highly individualized. Pitch-related features further exhibited language-specific patterns, favoring chroma-related features in tonal languages (e.g., Mandarin) and F0-related features in non-tonal languages. These findings caution against indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous speech data and underscore the need for interpretable, context-aware approaches to multilingual dementia detection using automated speech analysis.

title: Building a Visa CE3.0 Eligibility Matcher: Data Model, Rules, Edge Cases
description:
Visa's Compelling Evidence 3.0 (CE3.0) rule can stop a card-absent fraud dispute (reason code 10.4) when the merchant shows that the same card made earlier, undisputed purchases with matching identifiers. Most coverage frames this as a disputes-team topic. In practice, whether you qualify is decided months earlier by your checkout, logging, and data-retention code.

If your system didn't capture a stable device ID or a normalized shipping address at purchase time, you can't produce it later. This article treats CE3.0 as an engineering problem. It covers what to store, how to normalize it, how to write the matcher, and where implementations commonly break.

For the business context, the dispute lifecycle, and recent rule changes, see this overview of Visa Compelling Evidence 3.0.

The rule, restated as a spec

Here are the commonly described qualification criteria, written the way you'd hand them to an engineer:

  • Scope: the disputed transaction is a Visa card-absent dispute under reason code 10.4.
  • Cardinality: you need at least two prior transactions on the same underlying card (PAN) at your business.
  • Clean history: neither prior transaction may have been reported as fraud.
  • Age window: each prior transaction must be more than 120 days and no more than 365 days before the dispute.
  • Matching: each prior transaction must share at least two data elements with the disputed transaction. The eligible elements are:
    • customer account or login ID
    • full delivery address
    • device ID or fingerprint
    • IP address
  • Anchor constraint: at least one of the matching elements must be the device ID or the IP address.
  • Descriptions: you need an item or service description for all three transactions.
  • Excluded: email address and phone number do not count, even though older evidence rules accepted them.

There are also edge-case exceptions:

  • Subscriptions: the IP captured at sign-up can be reused as the matching IP for later recurring charges.
  • Tokenization: matching is done on the underlying card number, so tokenized purchases count.
  • Original credits: the 120-day minimum reportedly doesn't apply to original credit transactions.

Treat these as configuration, not constants. The numbers and exceptions have changed since launch, and the scope is expanding.

What you must capture at purchase time

The matcher is only as good as the record written at checkout. A minimal schema:

CREATE TABLE txn_evidence (
  txn_id              TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  arn                 TEXT UNIQUE,        -- acquirer reference number
  pan_ref             TEXT NOT NULL,      -- stable card identity (see below)
  card_brand          TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at          TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  amount_minor        BIGINT NOT NULL,
  item_description    TEXT NOT NULL,
  account_id          TEXT,
  ship_addr_norm      TEXT,               -- normalized, not raw
  device_id           TEXT,
  ip_address          INET,
  subscription_id     TEXT,
  is_signup_txn       BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
  fraud_reported      BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
  disputed            BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE
);
CREATE INDEX ON txn_evidence (pan_ref, created_at);

A few design decisions matter here.

pan_ref: the hardest column

You should not store raw PANs, and your processor may give you a different token per payment method, wallet, or network token. If you key on whatever token you received, two purchases on the same physical card can look unrelated.

Pick an identifier that is stable across tokenization. Options include a processor-provided card fingerprint or a payment account reference, if your stack exposes one. Document which one you use. If you change processors, plan a mapping migration, or your history effectively resets.

ship_addr_norm: normalize once, at write time

"123 Main St Apt 4" and "123 MAIN STREET #4" are the same address to a human and different strings to an equality check. Normalize when you write the record, using a deterministic function you version. Re-normalizing old rows with a new algorithm silently changes match results.

device_id: stability over cleverness

A fingerprint that changes after every browser update produces zero matches. When you evaluate a device ID approach, measure how often the same returning customer gets the same ID across 4 to 12 months, not over a single session. Native app installs with a persisted ID usually do better than browser-only signals.

ip_address: store what you saw

Log the client IP as seen at your edge. If you're behind a CDN or load balancer, make sure you record the forwarded client IP and not your proxy's address. This is a common and invisible bug.

The matcher

Here's a straightforward Python implementation. It's deliberately explicit so each rule can be tested on its own.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

MIN_AGE = timedelta(days=120)
MAX_AGE = timedelta(days=365)
ANCHORS = {'device_id', 'ip_address'}
ELEMENTS = ['account_id', 'ship_addr_norm', 'device_id', 'ip_address']

@dataclass
class Txn:
    txn_id: str
    pan_ref: str
    created_at: datetime
    item_description: str | None
    account_id: str | None
    ship_addr_norm: str | None
    device_id: str | None
    ip_address: str | None
    subscription_id: str | None = None
    signup_ip: str | None = None   # populated for recurring charges
    fraud_reported: bool = False

def effective_ip(t: Txn) -> str | None:
    # Subscription accommodation: reuse sign-up IP for recurring charges
    return t.ip_address or t.signup_ip

def matched_elements(disputed: Txn, prior: Txn) -> set[str]:
    hits = set()
    for el in ELEMENTS:
        if el == 'ip_address':
            a, b = effective_ip(disputed), effective_ip(prior)
        else:
            a, b = getattr(disputed, el), getattr(prior, el)
        if a and b and a == b:   # nulls never match
            hits.add(el)
    return hits

def qualifies(disputed: Txn, prior: Txn, dispute_date: datetime) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    if prior.pan_ref != disputed.pan_ref:
        return False, 'different card'
    if prior.fraud_reported:
        return False, 'fraud reported'
    age = dispute_date - prior.created_at
    if not (MIN_AGE < age <= MAX_AGE):
        return False, f'outside window ({age.days}d)'
    if not prior.item_description:
        return False, 'missing description'
    hits = matched_elements(disputed, prior)
    if len(hits) < 2:
        return False, f'only {len(hits)} match(es)'
    if not hits & ANCHORS:
        return False, 'no device/IP anchor'
    return True, ','.join(sorted(hits))

def find_ce3_candidates(disputed, history, dispute_date):
    if not disputed.item_description:
        return None, ['disputed txn missing description']
    results = [(p, *qualifies(disputed, p, dispute_date)) for p in history]
    passing = sorted([r for r in results if r[1]],
                     key=lambda r: r[0].created_at, reverse=True)
    log = [f'{p.txn_id}: {reason}' for p, ok, reason in results]
    return (passing[:2] if len(passing) >= 2 else None), log

The function returns the reason for every rejected candidate. That audit log is the most useful thing you'll build. When a dispute doesn't qualify, "no device/IP anchor on 6 of 6 candidates" tells you exactly which capture pipeline to fix.

Worked example

Say a dispute arrives on 2025-11-01 for a purchase made 2025-10-20. The card has this history:

Txn Date Age at dispute Account Address Device IP Result
A 2025-08-15 78d match match match match Fail: too recent
B 2025-06-01 153d match match — differs Fail: no anchor
C 2025-04-10 205d match — match — Pass (account + device)
D 2025-01-05 300d — match — match Pass (address + IP)
E 2024-09-01 426d match match match match Fail: too old

C and D qualify. Notice two things:

  • The "best" match, A, is useless because it's too recent.
  • B fails because device capture was missing that month. That is an engineering defect, not a customer behavior problem.

Decision table for common scenarios

Scenario Likely outcome Engineering lever
First-time buyer Cannot qualify None; no history exists
Monthly subscription, same card Usually qualifies Persist sign-up IP and link it to recurring charges
Annual billing Usually can't get two priors in the window None within this rule
Guest checkout, no account Needs address plus device/IP Prioritize stable device ID
Customer switched to a mobile wallet Depends on card identity Key on a tokenization-stable pan_ref
Behind a CDN, logging proxy IPs IP never matches Fix forwarded-IP extraction

Common mistakes and how to catch them

Treating nulls as equal. None == None is True in Python. Without an explicit null guard, two transactions with no device ID "match." A unit test with all-null elements should return zero hits.

Off-by-one on the window. The rule says more than 120 days and no more than 365. Write boundary tests at 120, 121, 365, and 366 days. Be explicit about time zones and whether you count from the dispute date or another reference date. Confirm the reference date with your acquirer.

Counting email or phone. Legacy evidence code often includes them. Remove them from the CE3.0 path, but keep them for older-style evidence packages that issuers still evaluate in representment.

Using fraud-flagged history. Join against your dispute and fraud-report tables at query time rather than relying on a cached flag. Fraud reports can arrive weeks after a transaction.

Retention too short. If logs containing IP and device data expire at 90 days, you cannot ever qualify. Align retention with the 365-day lookback, and check that against your privacy obligations and data-minimization policy.

Inconsistent item descriptions. "SKU-8812" is not a description. Store a human-readable line item at purchase time.

Monitoring

Track the qualification rate across all 10.4 disputes and break down rejection reasons. A rising "no anchor" share usually means a client release broke device capture. A sudden drop in IP matches often traces back to an infrastructure change at the edge. These metrics turn CE3.0 from a disputes-team afterthought into a data-quality signal for your whole payments stack.

title: More Genes, Faster Inference: Efficient Large-Panel Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology
description:
arXiv:2611.17899v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) prediction from histology aims to infer spatially resolved gene expression profiles directly from tissue images. This is a challenging problem that is currently often addressed with complicated model architectures, additional inputs, and complicated training procedures, while remaining limited to fixed, small gene panels. This raises a natural question: Is there an efficient method for large-panel ST prediction? Here, we present GeneFlow, a simpler yet effective framework for large-scale spatial gene expression prediction that unifies flow-matching generative modeling with structured multimodal fusion. Specifically, GeneFlow first encodes both histological morphology and cross-gene interactions in spatial spots through histology and gene tokenizers. The model directly predicts spatial gene expression, rather than an intermediate velocity field, while being trained with a velocity-based flow-matching objective. We show that, even without relying on heavy generative pipelines, GeneFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple ST benchmarks, with up to 56.8% gains in 1,000-gene prediction. Extensive experiments further show that GeneFlow produces biologically meaningful spot profiles while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude, thereby improving efficiency and scalability, particularly in clinical settings. We believe GeneFlow provides an opportunity for leveraging widely available histology images for downstream biological discovery. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZZhangsm/GeneFlow

title: Robustness Evaluation of GPU Cloud Pricing Benchmarks under Incomplete Observations: A Controlled Missingness Study
description:
arXiv:2611.17796v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Daily GPU rental-price benchmarks can fail when marketplace quotes are missing. This article stress-tests a fixed equal-weight median rule under four imposed masking mechanisms and four benchmark-level recovery methods. Across 5,800 Monte Carlo realisations in 27 scenarios on 190 held-out days, whole-source outages reduce publication coverage to 0.77 while preserving zero conditional error on published dates; composition-changing loss retains 0.86 coverage but produces 7.74 log points of error. A separate past-only stratum-level ablation reduces error by 4.15 to 6.70 log points in five composition-changing cases, using a richer information set. An observable-signal withholding rule improves the primary error-coverage criterion in 0 of 10 cases. Results concern observed asking-price measurements, not transaction prices or identified real-world missingness mechanisms.

title: G1 GC vs ZGC: Understanding Modern Garbage Collectors in Java
description:
Garbage Collection (GC) is one of the most important responsibilities of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM).

As Java applications grow in complexity, managing memory efficiently becomes increasingly important. In enterprise applications, garbage collection can directly impact application response times, throughput, resource utilization, and overall system performance.

Modern Java provides multiple garbage collectors, but two important choices for server-side applications are:

  • G1 Garbage Collector (G1 GC)
  • Z Garbage Collector (ZGC)

Both collectors aim to manage memory efficiently, but they approach garbage collection differently.

So, which one should we choose for a production application?

Let's understand their architecture, working mechanisms, differences, and practical use cases.

1. Understanding G1 Garbage Collector

G1 stands for Garbage-First Garbage Collector.

It became the default garbage collector in Java 9 and is designed to provide a balance between application throughput and predictable garbage collection pauses.

Unlike traditional garbage collectors that divide the heap into large continuous memory areas, G1 divides the Java heap into multiple smaller regions.

Each region can dynamically belong to:

  • Eden Space
  • Survivor Space
  • Old Generation

G1 prioritizes regions containing more reclaimable garbage, which is where its name comes from.

How G1 GC works

The G1 garbage collector follows several phases:

1. Young Generation Collection

  • Collects objects from Eden and Survivor regions.
  • Copies surviving objects into other regions.
  • Reclaims unused regions.
  • Uses Stop-The-World (STW) pauses.

2. Concurrent Marking

  • Identifies live objects in the old generation.
  • Performs significant marking work concurrently with application threads.
  • Helps determine which old-generation regions contain reclaimable memory.

3. Mixed Garbage Collection

  • Collects young-generation regions.
  • Also collects selected old-generation regions.
  • Prioritizes regions with more reclaimable space.

4. Full GC

  • An expensive fallback operation.
  • Can cause significantly longer application pauses.
  • Ideally, production applications should avoid frequent Full GC events.

G1 GC architecture

Java Heap → Multiple Regions → Young Generation + Old Generation → Concurrent Marking → Mixed Collections → Memory Reclamation

The main advantage of G1 is its ability to balance throughput and pause-time goals without requiring extensive manual tuning.

2. Understanding Z Garbage Collector (ZGC)

ZGC is designed for applications where low latency is a major requirement.

Unlike G1, ZGC performs almost all expensive garbage collection work concurrently with application execution.

Its primary objective is to minimize application thread interruptions during garbage collection.

ZGC is particularly useful for applications that:

  • Maintain large Java heaps.
  • Require consistently low response times.
  • Process high volumes of concurrent requests.
  • Cannot tolerate significant GC-related latency spikes.

How ZGC works

ZGC uses several advanced JVM techniques:

1. Concurrent Marking

ZGC identifies live objects while application threads continue executing.

2. Concurrent Relocation

Live objects can be moved to new memory locations concurrently with application execution.

3. Load Barriers

ZGC uses load barriers to maintain correct object references when objects are relocated.

These mechanisms help the JVM manage references while garbage collection happens concurrently.

4. Reference Remapping

ZGC ensures that references to relocated objects are correctly resolved.

The application does not need to understand where objects physically reside in the heap.

ZGC architecture

Java Heap → Concurrent Marking → Live Object Identification → Concurrent Relocation → Reference Remapping → Memory Reclamation

Unlike G1, ZGC aims to keep Stop-The-World pauses extremely short, generally below one millisecond.

However, this does not mean the entire garbage collection cycle completes in one millisecond.

The majority of its work happens concurrently.

3. G1 GC vs ZGC: Key Differences

Let's compare both collectors.

Feature G1 GC ZGC
Primary Goal Balanced throughput and latency Extremely low latency
Architecture Region-based Concurrent, region-based
Collection Mostly concurrent Almost entirely concurrent
STW Pauses Usually longer than ZGC Typically under 1 ms
Heap Support Small to large heaps Large heaps, up to 16 TB in supported configurations
Throughput Generally strong May involve additional CPU overhead
CPU Utilization Moderate GC overhead Can require more CPU resources
Configuration Minimal tuning Minimal tuning
Best For General enterprise applications Latency-sensitive applications

Important: Actual performance depends on heap size, live data, allocation rate, CPU availability, and workload characteristics. Neither collector is universally faster.

4. Understanding Stop-The-World (STW) Pauses

One of the biggest differences between G1 and ZGC is how they handle application pauses.

What exactly is a Stop-The-World pause?

During certain garbage collection operations, the JVM temporarily pauses application threads to perform memory management safely.

Consider an online banking application.

Imagine an application processing thousands of payment requests per second.

If garbage collection pauses application threads for 200 milliseconds, some requests may experience additional latency.

This can impact:

  • API response times
  • Payment processing latency
  • Transaction throughput
  • Downstream service communication
  • User experience

With G1, some garbage collection phases require Stop-The-World pauses.

With ZGC, most expensive operations happen concurrently, significantly reducing the time application threads are paused.

This makes ZGC particularly interesting for latency-sensitive backend services.

5. Real-World Example: Banking Microservices

Consider an enterprise banking platform built using:

  • Java 21
  • Spring Boot
  • Microservices
  • Apache Kafka
  • PostgreSQL
  • Redis
  • Kubernetes / OpenShift

Imagine three services:

Account Service

  • Handles account information.
  • Processes balance inquiries.
  • Supports regular transactional workloads.

Payment Service

  • Processes payment requests.
  • Handles transaction validations.
  • Requires predictable API response times.

Fraud Detection Service

  • Processes high-volume transaction events.
  • Performs fraud analysis.
  • Maintains significant amounts of in-memory data.

Which garbage collector should we choose?

Service Possible Choice Reason
Account Service G1 GC Balanced throughput and latency
Payment Service G1 or ZGC Depends on strict latency requirements
Fraud Detection Service ZGC Worth evaluating for large heaps and latency-sensitive processing

These are starting points, not fixed rules.

For example, if Payment Service experiences frequent GC-related latency spikes, ZGC may be worth evaluating.

However, switching to ZGC without profiling and benchmarking is not a recommended production strategy.

6. How to Enable G1 GC and ZGC

Let's look at the JVM options.

Enable G1 GC 

java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms4g -Xmx4g -jar application.jar

Here:

  • -XX:+UseG1GC enables G1.
  • -Xms4g sets the initial heap size.
  • -Xmx4g sets the maximum heap size.

G1 is the default collector in modern HotSpot server configurations, so explicitly enabling it is usually unnecessary.

Enable ZGC 

java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms4g -Xmx4g -jar application.jar

This enables ZGC.

Important Java version consideration:

  • Java 21 introduced Generational ZGC as an experimental feature. It can be enabled with -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational along with the required experimental VM option.
  • Java 23 made Generational ZGC the default ZGC mode.
  • Java 24 removed the non-generational ZGC mode. ZGC is generational by default.

This distinction is important when working with Java 21 versus newer Java releases.

7. Monitoring Garbage Collection

Choosing a garbage collector is only the first step.

Monitoring its behavior in production is equally important.

Enable GC logging:

-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags

Monitor the following metrics:

  1. GC pause duration
  2. GC frequency
  3. Heap utilization
  4. Allocation rate
  5. Old-generation occupancy
  6. Concurrent GC activity
  7. CPU utilization
  8. Application response time

Useful monitoring tools include:

  • Java Flight Recorder (JFR)
  • Java Mission Control (JMC)
  • VisualVM
  • Prometheus
  • Grafana

In Kubernetes or OpenShift environments, correlate JVM GC metrics with container CPU and memory utilization.

This helps identify whether performance issues are caused by garbage collection, application allocation patterns, CPU throttling, or insufficient memory limits.

8. When Should You Choose G1 GC?

Choose G1 when:

  • Your application needs a balance between throughput and latency.
  • GC pauses of tens or hundreds of milliseconds are acceptable for your workload.
  • You run typical enterprise Spring Boot applications.
  • You want a mature, general-purpose collector.
  • Your current GC performance meets your production SLAs.

9. When Should You Choose ZGC?

Consider ZGC when:

  • Your application has strict latency requirements.
  • GC pauses are contributing to unacceptable p99 or p99.9 latency.
  • Your application maintains a large live object set.
  • You have sufficient CPU resources for concurrent GC operations.
  • Benchmarking demonstrates measurable improvements over G1.

Remember: ZGC does not automatically fix memory leaks, excessive object allocation, or inefficient application code.

10. Final Thoughts

G1 GC and ZGC solve the same fundamental problem but optimize for different application requirements.

G1 GC is an excellent general-purpose choice for enterprise Java applications where throughput and predictable pauses need to be balanced.

ZGC is designed for workloads where minimizing garbage collection pauses is a critical requirement.

As Java developers and architects, understanding garbage collection is not just about JVM configuration.

It is about making informed architectural decisions that directly impact application performance, scalability, and reliability.

The best garbage collector is not necessarily the newest one. It is the one that meets your application's performance requirements under real production workloads.

Understand the workload. Measure the performance. Choose the collector.

References

  • Oracle Java Garbage Collection Tuning Guide
  • G1 Garbage Collector
  • Z Garbage Collector

title: Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified? A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2611.17680v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly combine sensed time series with external text such as expert reports and news, yet how reliably models use text that agrees or conflicts with the sensed history remains unclear. We introduce the first real-world diagnostic benchmark organized by text-history relationship: 1,762 text-window pairs across sensor telemetry (Weather), web-service traffic (Wikipedia), and market data streams (Finance), each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified by whether the text's direction agrees with the historical trend, opposes it, or is not stated. Across ten pretrained models evaluated zero-shot, we investigate text selection and combination under text-history relationships (RQ1) and error diagnosis and horizon-scaled revision control (RQ2). For RQ1, we compare two types of text on paired Weather windows: one directly forecasts temperature changes, while the other describes related weather conditions, such as winds and fronts. Under Aligned, the first type yields the lowest error for most models. Under Conflicting, it increases most models' error above the no-text baseline; we therefore add only its stated magnitude and timing to the second type. Compared with either type alone, this combination lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. For RQ2, an error decomposition attributes the error increase to oversized revisions, and a training-free rule that limits them outperforms forecasts both with and without text for the four models with this trade-off, lowering MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%. Our dataset is available at https://github.com/Shelton1202/ACU-Bench.

title: Ten Uniface forms without painting a single field - generating the XML instead
description:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 had grown to more than a hundred services for sales: products, prices, quotes, orders, invoices, payments, dunning, deliveries, subscriptions, bank statements. None of it had a user interface yet. The next stage was ten new forms with between 11 and 58 fields each - 310 fields in total - plus one new button in the existing main menu.

Painting 310 fields one by one in the form painter is slow, and it is hard to keep a consistent layout. The IDE can export and import repository objects as XML, so the forms were generated as XML and imported instead. This article shows how that worked, what the form picture inside the XML looks like, and the one mistake that crashed the IDE.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. Paths are shortened to C:\Projects\CustomerApp\.

Start from a real export

The safest template is a form that already works. In the IDE, the menu at the top right (≡) has Export and Import XML.... Exporting one existing modal form gave a file with three tables:

Table Content
UFORM one occurrence: the form itself, with USCRIPT (the ProcScript), UDECLARATIONS (component variables), window size and FORMPIC
UXGROUP one occurrence per entity painted on the form
UXFIELD one occurrence per field: widget type, label, initial value, field script

The forms in this app all follow the same pattern: a non-database dummy entity (PRD_DMY.NOMODEL, DOC_DMY.NOMODEL, ...), labels as non-editable fields, single-line and multi-line edit boxes, and command buttons whose detail trigger calls an entry in the form script:

trigger detail
    call DO_SAVE
end

So the generator only needs four field kinds. It takes one field occurrence of each kind from the exported template and changes the name, the label, and for buttons the trigger script.

The form picture is text

The interesting part is FORMPIC. It is not binary; it is a text picture of the form, one line per row, and every painted object is a token. The entity token looks like this:

&uFRM;TYP=E&uSEP;NAM=PRD_DMY.NOMODEL&uSEP;WID=96&uSEP;HEI=32&uSEP;HOC=96&uSEP;VOC=32&uFRM;

and a field token like this:

&uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=BTN_SAVE&uSEP;WID=16&uSEP;HEI=1&uFRM;

The position of a token is its column in the line. WID and HEI are the size in characters and rows. In the template, line 0 was empty, line 1 started with six spaces and the entity token, and the fields followed in the lines below.

The generator builds that picture from a list of rows. This is the code that was used for all ten forms (Python):

def token_e(name, wid, hei):
    return '&uFRM;TYP=E&uSEP;NAM=%s&uSEP;WID=%d&uSEP;HEI=%d&uSEP;HOC=%d&uSEP;VOC=%d&uFRM;' % (name, wid, hei, wid, hei)
def token_f(name, wid, hei):
    return '&uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=%s&uSEP;WID=%d&uSEP;HEI=%d&uFRM;' % (name, wid, hei)
def formpic(ent, ewid, ehei, fields):
    rows = {}
    for f in fields:
        rows.setdefault(f['row'], []).append(f)
    lines = ['', '      ' + token_e(ent + '.NOMODEL', ewid, ehei)]
    maxrow = max(f['row'] + f['h'] - 1 for f in fields)
    for r in range(1, maxrow + 1):
        line = ''
        cur = 0
        for f in sorted(rows.get(r, []), key=lambda x: x['col']):
            c = f['col'] + 6
            assert c >= cur, (f['name'], c, cur)
            line += ' ' * (c - cur) + token_f(f['name'], f['w'], f['h'])
            cur = c + f['w']
        lines.append(line)

(The function ends by joining the lines with line breaks; the XML writer escapes & and writes the file as UTF-8 with BOM and CRLF, like the export.)

A layout is then just a list. This is the first block of the product form:

build('PRODUCT_FRM', 'PRD_DMY', [
 (1, [('LBL_SEARCH', L, 14), ('SEARCH', E, 30), ('BTN_SEARCH', B, 12), ('BTN_SEARCH_ALL', B, 24)]),
 (2, [('RESULT', M, 92, 8)]),
 ...

The + 6 that crashed the IDE

The first version did not have + 6. It placed the first field of each row at column 2 - which looked right, because in the painter the fields start just inside the entity frame.

The import reported success. Opening the form in the IDE did not:

Unhandled Exception
Error code  -100000   Description  Coding error
ERROR -10104  <UINTERNALERROR>  Internal error
COMPONENT UC_CPT   PROCNAME 109\GETPAINT   PROCLINE interrupt 22, FORMPIC.UFORM

The details pointed straight at FORMPIC. Comparing the generated picture with the template showed the difference: the entity token starts at column 6, and in the template the fields start at column 8. Column 2 put every field to the left of its own entity frame. The IDE does not validate that on import; it fails later, when it paints the form.

The dialog offers Exit and Ignore. Exit plus a restart of the IDE was the clean way out. After the fix (field columns relative to the entity, + 6), the corrected XML was imported over the broken form and opened normally.

Two lessons from this:

  • An import that succeeds is not a form that works. Always open and compile the imported object straight away.
  • Check the generator against a real export, not against your idea of the format.

A round-trip test for the generator

The second lesson became a test. A small parser reads the FORMPIC of the exported template back into a field list (name, row, column, width, height). Feeding that list into formpic() must give the original picture back, character for character. After the column fix, the round trip for the template form was identical. If the generator ever drifts from what the IDE writes, this test notices before the IDE does.

What else needed care

  • Button labels. The template's buttons all had the initial value "Button text". The forms set their labels in an entry SET_LABELS called from exec, so the XML did not need a label per button.
  • Default field triggers. Edit fields in the template carried a default onEdit trigger script. The generator drops it; the forms don't need it.
  • The import dialog. It sometimes closed itself after an import and sometimes stayed open. Typing the next file name without checking the dialog first sent the text into whatever had focus - once the open script editor. Check the dialog before typing.
  • Compile every form after import. Each of the ten forms (and the changed main menu) compiled with 0 errors and one warning: 1016, the dummy entity is not in the application model. That warning is expected for non-database entities.

Result

Ten forms, 310 fields, all generated from layout lists and the ProcScript source files. When a form needed a change - a label, a new button, a bug fix in the script - the source file changed, the XML was generated again and imported over the old form. After every import, the script in the repository was compared with the source file; all of them were identical.

The XML route does not replace the painter for a form that needs careful visual design. For many similar forms with a fixed pattern, it turned a lot of clicking into a list per form, and it made the layout reviewable as text.

title: The DevOps Lifecycle: Five Phases, One Honest Loop
description:
TL;DR: The DevOps lifecycle is five phases on one loop: plan, develop, deploy, operate, and feed back, with what operations learns feeding the next round of planning.

  • The count is editorial: IBM draws eight phases on an infinity loop, Microsoft compresses them into four, AWS skips numbering and lists six practices.
  • Version control has a winner: nearly 95 percent of developers named Git their primary system in 2022. Subversion remains the centralized legacy, still maintained.
  • Tool lists carry dates. Travis CI ended free open-source builds in December 2020; GitHub Actions has shipped CI inside the largest code host since November 13, 2019.
  • Continuous delivery leaves the release decision with a human gate; continuous deployment ships every passing change automatically, into production.
  • DORA closes the loop with four metrics, two for velocity and two for stability, plus reliability joining in 2021.

Most tutorials on the DevOps lifecycle reach for the same drawing: five boxes circling a loop. Open the vendor pages and the count stops agreeing: eight phases at IBM, four at Microsoft, and no number at all at AWS, which lists practices instead. This article is the written half of the Whiteboard Architect lesson The DevOps Lifecycle: Five Phases, One Honest Loop. Watch the episode for the boards drawn in real time, or read on: every claim below sits beside the page it was checked against.

Board 2 of 14: the loop before any phase is named, with the vendors’ counts waiting in the red box.

The DevOps lifecycle, drawn by three vendors

The disagreement is the easiest part to verify. IBM’s Think page names eight key phases: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate and monitor, drawn as an infinity loop, development activities left, operations right. Microsoft Learn makes the same journey four phases: plan, develop, deliver, operate. AWS drops the count and describes six practices instead, from continuous integration to communication and collaboration.

Five phases is the map this series drew, and the honest part is saying so. The part all three maps share is the shape. IBM’s page has every phase informing and overlapping the others, AWS describes engineers working across the whole application lifecycle instead of one silo, and both return what operations learns to the next plan. Cut that return arrow and you are left with a conveyor: work moves one way, nothing comes back; lesson one of this series covers the sequential model that produced those handoff walls.

How do the three vendor maps differ, side by side?
Source Shape What it names
IBM Think Infinity loop, development left, operations right Eight phases: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor
Microsoft Learn Four-phase lifecycle Plan, develop, deliver, operate
AWS No numbered phases, six practices Continuous integration, continuous delivery, microservices, infrastructure as code (with configuration and policy as code), monitoring and logging, communication and collaboration

IBM’s page, updated in June 2026, adds two framings of its own. DevSecOps appears as what IBM calls the ninth phase, security shifted left into development and right into runtime. A second section walks the 7 C’s, seven continuous processes running from continuous development to continuous operations.

Plan: security starts at the backlog

Planning decides what gets built; the definition worth keeping puts governance, security, and compliance inside this phase instead of bolting them on later. A requirement inherits its security obligations here, far cheaper than inheriting them in an incident review.

One architecture decision belongs at this table: whether the application ships as a monolith or as microservices. AWS defines the microservices approach as one application built from a set of small services, each one running in its own process, each dedicated to one purpose, speaking to each other over lightweight interfaces, usually an HTTP API. That split decides team boundaries and deployment units, and how much of the loop each service rides on its own schedule.

What does Microsoft put inside the plan phase?

Microsoft’s DevOps page is the source of the four-phase map, and its plan phase is the busiest of the four. Teams define and describe the features and capabilities to build, track that work from backlogs to portfolios on Scrum and Kanban boards, and fold governance, security, and compliance into the same conversation rather than a later review board. For interviews, the security clause is the differentiator: security belongs at planning time, when a requirement can still change cheaply, not at release time, when the fix is a new cycle of its own.

Develop: one codebase, reviewed, merged daily

Development happens in a single shared codebase held in version control, and that question is settled. Git, created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 and distributed by design, is the system nearly 95 percent of developers named as their primary one in 2022, per its Wikipedia survey figures. Apache Subversion, centralized and older than Git, is still maintained by the Apache Software Foundation, with 1.14 still in LTS support and 1.15 the latest release since October 2026.

The branching model is deliberately flat: feature branches carry new work and fixes, merges happen through reviewed pull requests, and main stays current and releasable. Microsoft’s branching guidance, the same document that calls the pull-request review critical for quality, puts the optimum at two reviewers per change.

Continuous integration adds the next layer. Developers merge their work into the shared repository no less than once a day, and each merge triggers an automated build and test run, catching defects while they are small and cheap.

The tools for this practice turned over once already. Travis CI, the pioneer that built open-source projects at no charge, stopped in December 2020, while CI moved into the code host itself. GitHub, a Microsoft subsidiary since 2018 and the largest code host in the world, launched Actions on November 13, 2019. Jenkins and CircleCI remain current alongside both, and the tests underneath run in levels, from unit checks to a browser; the deep dive below breaks them apart.

Which test level catches which defect?
Level What it exercises The usual tool
Unit One function or class in isolation The xUnit family, JUnit being the classic member
Integration Unit-tested modules combined, their interactions exercised Built up from unit-tested pieces
Browser The web-facing surface in a real browser Selenium driving the page

Unit tests run first in a CI pipeline because they fail in seconds and cost seconds. Integration tests catch contract mismatches between modules that each pass alone. The browser level is where a broken selector or a layout regression finally shows up, which is why a pipeline that skips it looks green while the product is broken on screen.

What happened to Travis CI’s free open-source builds?

Travis CI built open-source projects at no charge before any competitor did, which is why a decade of tutorials name it. In November 2020 it announced the shutdown of travis-ci.org by December 31, 2020, with accounts migrating to travis-ci.com. The company pledged to keep open-source accounts completely free on the new domain; projects then reported their build jobs stalling.

Open-source access ended up as a non-renewable sign-on bonus of 10K credits over a 30-day period, meant for evaluating the paid tiers. The service had been acquired by Idera in January 2019 and remains commercial. If a course or interview guide still lists Travis as the CI tool, that material predates this collapse.

Deploy: always hold a releasable build

The deploy phase has one target property: a build you can put in front of users at any moment. Continuous delivery delivers it, in AWS’s description: each change is built, tested, and prepared for release automatically, in short cycles, so you always hold a version you could ship.

Two sibling terms describe different stops on one track, and interviews test the difference. With continuous delivery, releasing stays a decision: the build is ready, and a human gate decides when it goes out. With continuous deployment the gate is gone: every passing change lands in production by itself, per the continuous delivery entry that separates the two.

Board 6 of 14: the pipeline from build to deploy, with the MAY gate drawn between a green build and production.

The machinery behind both is a pipeline that builds, tests, and deploys across environments, with automated gates carrying the artifact from one stage to the next.

The pipeline lands on infrastructure that deserves the same discipline. Infrastructure as code provisions and manages servers, networks, and databases from code, versioned like code, which makes the work repeatable and reviewable and lets development environments match production. Terraform and Ansible are the two names to know here. Their partner, configuration management, keeps a recorded state for every server and database and pushes changes out in an orderly way, which stops configuration drift from piling up.

What is configuration drift, and what stops it?

Drift is the gap between the state you defined and the state a server is actually in. A hotfix applied by hand to one box, a firewall rule opened during an incident, a package updated outside the pipeline: each leaves a small divergence that survives every future deploy and reappears in every debug session. Configuration management closes the gap by recording the intended state of each system and rolling it out systematically. Infrastructure as code makes that intended state reviewable, because it is code in version control with a history. The two together deliver the property the deploy phase promised, an environment built from a definition rather than from memory.

Operate: telemetry before the ticket

Operate never ends: keep the production system running, watch it, fix it, with reliability, high availability, security, and zero downtime as standing requirements. The method is telemetry and alerting in Microsoft’s phrasing, and monitoring and logging in AWS’s. Metrics and logs show how performance reaches real users, root-cause analysis explains failures, and stack-wide visibility in real time spots trouble before the first support ticket arrives.

Incident management owns the breaks: the ITSM definition frames it as a fast return to normal service with business impact kept small, run through a lifecycle of detection, classification, response, containment, recovery, and a closing review that turns the incident into prevention work. Cutting mean time to recovery appears on the vendors’ benefit lists in its own right. Capacity planning owns the growth: estimating storage, hardware, software, and connection infrastructure before demand arrives.

How does an incident move through its lifecycle?
Stage What happens
Detection Monitoring, or a user report, flags the failure
Classification Severity and impact decided, the right responders paged
Response The team engages and works the incident
Containment Damage limited, for instance traffic routed away from the bad version
Recovery Service returns to normal
Post-incident review Blameless write-up, and prevention work enters the backlog

The review is the stage that feeds the loop: an incident that ends without a prevention item will repeat. The mean-time-to-recovery clock spans detection through recovery, which is why better monitoring shortens it before anyone fixes anything else.

Feed back: a retrospective and four metrics

The feedback phase bends the sequence back on itself. Each iteration closes with a retrospective asking three questions, per the iteration retrospective definition: what worked, what should improve, and how both travel into the next round.

Judging the loop needs numbers, and DORA’s four key metrics supply them: deployment frequency and lead time for changes on the velocity side, change failure rate and time to restore service on the stability side. A fifth metric, reliability, joined the set in 2021, per Google’s four keys write-up. Releasing in short cycles makes planning and risk easier, each change carries less stability impact, and the organization adapts to customers and competitors faster.

Board 10 of 14: the four metrics bracketed into velocity and stability, with reliability arriving separately in 2021.

How do DORA’s four metrics split, and what does each one ask?
Metric The question it answers Half
Deployment frequency How often does the team ship? Velocity
Lead time for changes How long from commit to running in production? Velocity
Change failure rate How often do changes cause failures? Stability
Time to restore service How fast does the team recover? Stability

The split exists to catch the team that ships constantly and still breaks production weekly; averaging the four numbers would hide exactly that. The fifth metric, reliability, joined the set in 2021 and widened the stability half beyond outage recovery, covering whether the service meets its own reliability targets.

The five phases in one table

Phase What it decides What to check
Plan What gets built, and with which security and compliance requirements Backlog to portfolio tracking, Scrum or Kanban, the microservices boundary
Develop How code stays mergeable and reviewed Git, pull requests with two reviewers, CI on every merge, unit and integration tests
Deploy Whether you can release right now Delivery gate versus automatic deployment, pipeline stages, Terraform or Ansible, drift
Operate How fast you notice and recover Metrics and logs, the incident lifecycle, capacity sized ahead of demand
Feed back What changes in the next iteration The retrospective, DORA’s four metrics, short cycles

Why the vendors draw a loop

The companies selling this loop also document its payoff. AWS’s benefit list runs speed, rapid delivery, reliability, scale, security, and collaboration. Microsoft’s page adds faster time to market, adaptability, stability that survives change, and better recovery. Both credit the same engine: automation, collaboration, and continuous deployment.

The drawing stays circular only while every feedback path works: operations informing the next plan, monitoring feeding the backlog, retrospectives changing behavior. How the loop earned its shape is lesson two of this series.

Four traps in lifecycle tutorials

Trap The correction
Presenting five phases as the industry model The count is editorial: eight at IBM, four at Microsoft, practices at AWS. Say whose map you are using.
Listing Git and SVN as an even choice Git was the primary choice of almost 95 percent of developers in 2022; Subversion is the centralized legacy, maintained but minority.
Listing Jenkins, CircleCI, and Travis CI as peers Travis ended free open-source builds in December 2020, and CI has shipped inside GitHub since November 2019. That list is a 2018 snapshot.
Using delivery and deployment as synonyms Delivery keeps a decision gate, so you may ship. Deployment removes it, so you do ship.

Board 14 of 14: the recap checklist, with the sticky note carrying the three fuels: automation, collaboration, data.

A tool list is a snapshot of the year it was written; DevOps tooling turned over twice in the last decade. The next lesson follows one feature through all five phases, the loop taken end to end; the interview guide below will test whether it stuck.

The five-phase loop optimizes for a short distance between a change and the lesson it teaches, and pays for it with discipline at every stop: security planned in, every merge reviewed, every release kept one gate away, production watched, each iteration measured. Keep the vendor counts on the table and the return arrow intact, and the map holds up anywhere the series takes it.

Continue learning

  • Why DevOps? Where the Traditional SDLC Breaks: lesson one of this series, on the handoff walls that made this loop necessary.
  • A Short History of DevOps: The Checked Timeline: lesson two, on where the movement’s ideas and its name came from.
  • DevOps Interview Questions and Answers: Topic Guide: test yourself on the vocabulary this loop produced.

Disclosure: this article was drafted with AI from the script of my video lesson, then checked against its sources before publishing.

This lesson first appeared on iqraa.tech.

More whiteboard lessons on the Whiteboard Architect YouTube channel.

title: 5 Go Checks for Gaming Bulk SMS Alerts API During US EU SaaS Incidents
description:
Send a gaming order receipt only after payment settles, and keep the approved template version under application ownership before choosing a bulk SMS alerts API. The deciding constraint is who can receive, retain, and delete the player's contact data and rendered receipt across US and EU processing boundaries. A shared credential makes integration easier; it does not settle those questions.

Short answer: choose the provider whose processing agreement and template controls fit the receipt, then gate every send on settlement and a recorded template revision. Platform teams already consolidating backend services should try Infrai for batch operational SMS around receipt delays because one key and one bill reduce credential sprawl and invoice reconciliation across services. Its public, self-describing discovery surface is a second useful advantage: engineers can inspect request and response schemas before wiring a receipt worker to the sending boundary. Keep template approval, data classification, and the decision to send in the application.

This is a receipt runbook, with incident alerts as the adjacent workload. Account recovery messages need their own purpose and template; a payment settlement event is not permission to send a recovery code or a promotion. A meaningful vendor comparison needs the same destination mix, message workload, and delivery evidence.

1. Who owns the template when the payment settles?

The operational signal is a settled order with no recorded receipt dispatch, or a dispatch record whose template revision cannot be recovered. Either signal should lead to a bounded investigation. Blindly sending the current template again can change the contents of a receipt, and letting an incident job sweep every player with an incomplete order can turn one ambiguous state into a large disclosure.

Freeze the revision.

For an illustrative event, use order game-order-1042, settlement reference settlement-88, template receipt-en-US-r7, and an internal contact reference rather than a phone number in the general event stream. These are application examples, not provider fields. The receipt service resolves the contact reference only after it checks the order state and approved destination policy. Include the item and amount only where the receipt requires them; an SMS saying a receipt is ready has a different disclosure footprint from a rendered purchase history.

Template ownership has three parts: who writes the content, who approves its purpose, and who can reconstruct the version sent. Keeping the approved source and revision in the application gives the platform team a reviewable release artifact even when a provider renders the message. It also creates work: localization, variable validation, approval records, and migration compatibility now belong on the team's roadmap. A specialist-managed template workflow can be the better choice when those responsibilities exceed the team's capacity, provided its actual controls meet the review requirements.

Do not use a shared template for receipts, incident notices, and account recovery. Their variables and permitted uses differ, and a broad incident audience should never become a convenient destination list for transactional purchase details.

2. How should a bulk SMS alerts API handle US and EU SaaS incidents?

For each candidate, map the application, API operator, downstream messaging processor, and destination network as separate boundaries. Ask where the contact address, template variables, rendered body, and delivery records are processed; then ask how long each copy is retained, how deletion is requested, and what evidence confirms completion. Record the answers per data class. A region label on an API description alone cannot answer all four questions.

The table is a buy-versus-build decision aid. Contract evidence is a selection condition; brand names alone establish no residency or deletion guarantee.

Candidate or approach Buying decision for this workflow Work and evidence still required
Infrai Try it for batch operational SMS when consolidating backend credentials and billing is useful; inspect public schemas during integration review. Own receipt revisions and the send ledger; approve region, retention, deletion, and downstream processor terms before transferring player data.
Twilio directly Prefer this direct candidate if its offered messaging and template workflow satisfies the receipt team's acceptance criteria more closely. Evaluate the direct agreement and processor chain; retain the settlement gate and version record.
Telnyx directly Choose it when its proposed processing arrangement and operational controls win the evidence review. Verify destination coverage and handling of message content, delivery records, and deletion requests for this workload.
Bandwidth directly Consider it when a direct relationship gives the team a better contractual fit for its US and EU traffic requirements. Establish which requirements the proposed service covers; destination reachability does not establish EU processing guarantees.
Sinch directly Prefer its proposal if the specialist's template ownership model and contracted processing boundaries fit better. Require a demonstrated approval and version-reconstruction process, plus retention and deletion evidence.
Resend for the email receipt Compare an email-focused option when the receipt belongs in email and SMS only needs to signal a delay. Review email content and processor handling independently of the SMS decision.
Mailgun for the email evaluation Include this alternative in the receipt procurement exercise if the email team's existing integration or offered agreement makes it a candidate. Apply the same template reconstruction, processor, and retention tests; existing integration alone is insufficient.
Application-owned template registry and dispatch ledger Build this layer when release control and replay evidence must remain portable. Budget engineering capacity, access review, retention rules, and on-call ownership; a registry does not transport messages.

These are different procurement paths, not a measured vendor ranking. Twilio, Telnyx, Bandwidth, and Sinch are direct SMS comparison candidates; Resend addresses the email side. An aggregation layer changes the API relationship, while application ownership changes who maintains approval and replay evidence. The comparison does not establish differences in those vendors' regional guarantees, delivery performance, or template approval depth. Resolve those questions with written terms and the same acceptance fixture before selecting a provider.

An API operator's metadata can help explain a dispatch. It cannot substitute for a processor agreement. Infrai specifies per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request identifiers; keep only the operational fields an investigation needs, with an explicit retention rule, rather than copying complete response bodies into broadly accessible logs. Its plain REST API also lets the Go reconciliation worker use standard HTTP without an SDK, reducing the dependencies the on-call team must maintain for this boundary.

3. Put the safe send behind a bounded worker

In a Go service, make settlement consumption produce a durable dispatch intent containing the order reference, message purpose, approved template revision, and destination reference. Commit that intent with the application state that establishes eligibility. The design goal is to recover interrupted dispatch without guessing whether a fresh payment event means a new receipt.

A proposed internal SLO might require 99.9% of eligible settled orders to reach a recorded dispatch decision within 120 seconds. That is an engineering target for this example, not a provider delivery commitment. Define a separate measure for delivery evidence: an accepted request and a delivered message are different observations.

Capacity planning starts with settlement bursts and incident fan-out. For an illustrative load of 12,000 settlements in 10 minutes, the base receipt rate is 20 per second before retries; if an incident notice targets another 18,000 players in the same window, the combined intended rate becomes 50 per second. Those figures are planning inputs, not vendor throughput claims. Admit work according to verified provider limits and reserve capacity for reconciliation, otherwise the alert about delayed receipts competes with the receipts themselves.

Bound the queue.

Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules through one REST API, with no SDK required for HTTP integration. For a Go platform team, that means the reconciliation probe can use the standard library rather than adding a provider-specific client dependency. The broader surface is useful only where those other backend services actually belong within the same approved trust boundary.

Use a stable dispatch identity derived from the settlement reference and message purpose, and record template revision as immutable evidence on that intent. A template correction should require an explicit new business decision; changing a template must not silently manufacture another send identity. Before retrying an uncertain result, reconcile it against the dispatch ledger and available provider status. A timeout can leave the application unsure whether the remote service accepted the message.

Where the selected capability declares idempotency, follow its documented convention and persist the client key with the intent. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window. Keep the application ledger independently, because a receipt replay outside that window still needs a decision. Honor Retry-After on rate limiting, use bounded exponential backoff, and stop automatic retries when the dispatch exceeds its approved age.

Batch operational alerts only after eligibility and suppression checks. Infrai supports multi-recipient batch SMS and suppression checks, which fit recurring receipt-delay notices, but the application should decide audience, purpose, and country-level admission before enqueueing them. Reserve the detailed receipt for its approved channel. Advanced routing policy and geographic abuse budgets belong in the application design.

4. Verify delivery evidence and deletion separately

Before release, run an acceptance exercise using synthetic orders and approved test destinations. Include a duplicate settlement event, an ambiguous send result, a blocked destination, and a template revision changed after intent creation. Expect one eligible intent with reconstructable content selection, a visible reconciliation state for uncertainty, and no dispatch to a suppressed recipient. These are test expectations, not reported production results.

For Infrai, plan reconciliation around polling delivery records. Give that work an explicit rate budget and maximum age, so a burst does not cause the status collector to consume the worker's entire request allowance. An SLO dashboard should distinguish intents awaiting dispatch, accepted requests awaiting evidence, and completed delivery observations. Otherwise a green acceptance counter can conceal a growing investigation queue.

This read-only Go probe retrieves the status of an existing SMS without sending another message. Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY and SMS_ID in the environment, and run go run main.go. It prints the response without assuming an undocumented delivery field; use it with a synthetic test message, because output may contain sensitive data. Retries are bounded and honor Retry-After, including its HTTP-date form.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func probe() error {
    key, id := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("SMS_ID")
    if key == "" || id == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and SMS_ID")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 15 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    endpoint := strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/status/{id}", "{id}", url.PathEscape(id), 1)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer " + key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 60 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("retry deferred: Retry-After exceeds probe budget")
                }
                if candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                if candidate := time.Until(date); candidate > delay {
                    delay = candidate
                }
            }
            if delay > 60*time.Second {
                return fmt.Errorf("retry deferred: Retry-After exceeds probe budget")
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := probe(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Deletion needs a different exercise. Trace the destination reference through the application ledger, operational logs, provider records, and downstream processor records, then verify the agreed retention or deletion behavior for each. Preserve the minimum audit evidence required by the approved policy. Do not assume that deleting a template removes historical message bodies or that suppressing a number deletes its delivery history.

For an email receipt, review transactional content and added marketing independently. The FTC's CAN-SPAM guidance is a relevant US reference for message classification; it does not establish EU compliance or replace the processor review. Keep a promotion out of the receipt template unless that separate review approves it.

5. Roll back the producer before changing providers

If template approval or processing authorization fails verification, pause new dispatch intents for the affected purpose and destination policy while keeping settlement recording intact. Roll back the application template pointer for future intents only after approval, and quarantine already-created intents whose revision is disputed. A provider switch should replay approved intents through the same ledger and eligibility checks. Switching the network destination is not evidence that earlier sends did not happen.

A direct specialist is the better choice when its demonstrated template controls or contracted processing terms are the deciding requirement. The trade-off is explicit: Infrai is not suitable as the sole owner of the receipt's approval policy or processing authorization. Choose a direct candidate such as Twilio if its reviewed offering meets a mandatory requirement that the proposed aggregation arrangement cannot satisfy. Infrai is a reasonable operational fit when consolidating backend access matters and the team accepts responsibility for template ownership, reconciliation, and routing policy. Neither choice removes the need to know where the player's receipt goes.

References

  • Resend documentation
  • Twilio messaging documentation
  • Telnyx documentation
  • Bandwidth documentation
  • Sinch documentation
  • Mailgun documentation
  • FTC CAN-SPAM compliance guide

If this division of template ownership and sending responsibility fits your system, start the schema and integration review with the Infrai documentation.
