title: Pattern-Based Matrix Analysis Under Permutations
description:
arXiv:2611.17674v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-rank approximation captures one important notion of matrix simplicity: a matrix is simple if it is well described by a low-dimensional linear model. This paper studies a complementary notion. We consider matrices that become structurally simple only after permuting rows and columns, so that their mass concentrates in a prescribed geometric pattern such as a band, block-diagonal, arrowhead, or related form. We introduce a pattern distance that measures how close a matrix is to a given pattern after optimal reordering, giving a common framework for structural problems such as latent ordering, community detection, and bandwidth minimization. The problem is NP-hard in general; we derive an alternating algorithm based on Linear Assignment subproblems. We further introduce a pattern-plus-low-rank decomposition that combines permutation-structured fitting with a low-rank residual, whose permutation step is pattern fitting on the residual; its gains across pattern families persist at a matched parameter budget and are substantially reduced under a density-matched random-mask control. We evaluate the framework on synthetic recovery tasks, real correlation and graph adjacency matrices, and transformer attention heads, showing that a single universal algorithm recovers qualitatively different forms of matrix structure.

title: Folding Language Models into Themselves
description:
arXiv:2611.18113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge distillation usually trains a compact student from scratch, which needs a large amount of data even though the teacher's weights already encode most of what the student has to learn. In this work, we explore building the student directly from the teacher's weights. We propose Concertina, which folds every group of N adjacent teacher layers into one shared block that is executed N times. Each loop step carries a low-rank correction initialized from the layer it replaces, and a per-token gate mixes these corrections, to let every token recover the behavior of the original layers from a single shared block. We further design a distillation data recipe that balances general, mathematical, academic and targeted multiple-choice data, to recover all capabilities of the teacher together rather than one at the expense of another. On Qwen3-4B, a 2.27B Concertina model distilled on 22B tokens retains about 90% of the teacher on commonsense and mathematical reasoning and 84% on average across eight benchmarks. It outperforms same-size dense and layer-sharing baselines, as well as Qwen3-1.7B, which is trained on over a thousand times more data. These results suggest that a compact model need not be retrained at scale, since folding the teacher into itself and distilling it on the right data recovers most of its capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/myboker/concertina.

title: Your 100% Lighthouse A11y Score Is a Lie: The Visual Architecture Guide to the Browser Accessibility Tree
description:
You open Chrome DevTools. You navigate to the Lighthouse tab, click "Analyze page load," and wait thirty seconds while the audit completes.

The circular gauge spins, stops, and turns bright emerald green:

Accessibility: 100 / 100

You smile, push your code to production, and congratulate yourself on shipping an inclusive, accessible web application.

Then an actual screen reader user visits your website.

They press the Tab key to navigate your navigation menu, and the focus ring vanishes into thin air. They trigger a modal window to update their billing address, but the screen reader continues reading paragraphs hidden underneath the backdrop. They fill out a form, click your custom button, and hear nothing:

"Button. Unlabelled. Clickable."

When an error banner appears, the screen reader remains completely silent. The user has no idea whether their payment succeeded, failed, or timed out. Frustrated and disoriented, they abandon your application.

How could a website with a perfect 100% Lighthouse accessibility score be virtually unusable for someone relying on assistive technology?

Because automated accessibility audits only check static, programmatic rules: whether images have alt tags, whether color contrast meets basic thresholds, and whether input fields have matching labels.

Automated scanners catch roughly 30% to 40% of web accessibility barriers. They cannot test whether your keyboard tab order makes logical sense. They cannot verify whether your custom modal traps focus. And they cannot tell you if your ARIA attributes are actively breaking the browser's internal accessibility tree.

In fact, the annual WebAIM Million audit of the top one million websites repeatedly uncovers a staggering paradox: pages with ARIA attributes present an average of 41% more accessibility errors than pages without ARIA.

To build digital products that work for everyone, you must understand how assistive technology actually experiences your code: the Accessibility Tree, the First Rule of ARIA, CSS visibility traps, and focus management.

Here is the architectural reality of web accessibility.

1. The Dual-Tree Architecture: How Browsers Construct the Accessibility Tree

When a web developer thinks about a web page, they visualize the DOM (Document Object Model): a tree of HTML nodes that JavaScript inspects and modifies.

When the browser renders that page, it constructs a CSSOM (CSS Object Model), merges it with the DOM, and produces the Render Tree to paint pixels on your display.

However, screen readers (like VoiceOver on macOS/iOS, NVDA and JAWS on Windows, and TalkBack on Android) do not read your DOM, and they do not inspect your Render Tree.

Instead, the browser constructs a parallel, internal data structure: the Accessibility Tree (Accessibility Object Model / AOM).

The Anatomy of an Accessibility Node

Every node in the Accessibility Tree contains four fundamental attributes computed by the browser:

  1. Role: What the element is (e.g., button, heading, checkbox, dialog, link).
  2. Name: The human-readable label of the element (e.g., "Submit payment", "Close window").
  3. State: The current condition of the widget (e.g., focused, expanded: true, checked: false, disabled).
  4. Value: The current numerical or textual value (e.g., "50%", "John Doe").

How the Browser Communicates with the Operating System

The browser does not talk directly to screen reader software.

Instead, the browser translates the Accessibility Tree into platform-specific native operating system accessibility APIs:

  • Windows: UIAutomation, IAccessible2, MSAA
  • macOS / iOS: NSAccessibility, UIAccessibility
  • Linux: AT-SPI (Assistive Technology Service Provider Interface)

When a blind user presses the Tab key, their screen reader queries the operating system's accessibility API. The OS queries the browser's Accessibility Tree. The browser reports:
"Focused element is a Button, Name is 'Download Invoice', State is Enabled."

The screen reader synthesizes speech from that exact data. If an element does not exist in the Accessibility Tree, or if its role and name are garbled, it does not exist for the user.

2. The First Rule of ARIA: Why Your Custom Div Buttons Are Broken

ARIA stands for Accessible Rich Internet Applications. It is a W3C specification designed to supplement HTML when native elements cannot express complex dynamic behavior.

However, the official W3C specification opens with a principle so critical that the authors codified it as The First Rule of ARIA:

"If you can use a native HTML element or attribute with the semantics and behavior you require already built in, then do so instead of re-purposing an element and adding an ARIA role, state or property to make it accessible."

Why did the specification authors write this?

Because developers routinely write code like this:

<!-- DANGEROUS: The fake button anti-pattern -->
<div class="btn" role="button" onclick="handleSubmit()">
  Submit Order
</div>

A developer looks at this div, applies CSS to make it look like a button, adds role="button", and assumes they are done.

Lighthouse inspects the code, sees role="button" and readable text, and awards a green checkmark.

In reality, this fake button is completely broken.

The 6 Hidden Superpowers of a Native <button>

When you use a real HTML <button>, the browser provides six complex behaviors for free:

  1. Keyboard Focus: It is automatically included in the keyboard tab order without needing tabindex="0".
  2. Dual Key Activation: It fires click events on both the Enter key and the Space key.
  3. Space Key Scrolling Suppression: Pressing Space on a native button triggers the action without scrolling the entire web page down.
  4. Native Disabled State: Setting disabled automatically removes the button from the tab order and prevents click handlers from firing.
  5. Form Integration: Pressing Enter inside an input automatically submits the associated form through the button.
  6. OS High Contrast Support: The browser automatically renders high-contrast borders in Windows High Contrast Mode.

Rebuilding a Button from Scratch

If you insist on using <div role="button">, you must manually implement all six behaviors in JavaScript:

// Rebuilding what the browser gives you for free
const fakeButton = document.querySelector('.btn');

// 1. Make it focusable
fakeButton.setAttribute('tabindex', '0');

// 2. Listen for keyboard triggers
fakeButton.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  if (event.key === 'Enter' || event.key === ' ') {
    event.preventDefault(); // Stop spacebar scrolling
    handleSubmit();
  }
});

// 3. Handle disabled state manually
if (isDisabled) {
  fakeButton.setAttribute('aria-disabled', 'true');
  fakeButton.removeAttribute('tabindex');
}

You just wrote twenty lines of fragile, bug-prone JavaScript to recreate what <button>Submit Order</button> does in zero lines of code.

No ARIA is better than bad ARIA. Always prefer semantic HTML.

3. The CSS Visibility Trap: How Styles Alter the Accessibility Tree

Most frontend developers believe CSS only controls visual layout on screen.

In modern browsers, CSS properties directly alter the Accessibility Tree.

Choosing the wrong hiding technique creates invisible ghost elements that trap keyboard users, or accidentally silences screen readers when elements are supposed to be heard.

Case 1: display: none and visibility: hidden

When you apply display: none or visibility: hidden:

  • The element is completely removed from the visual Render Tree.
  • The element is completely removed from the Accessibility Tree.
  • Screen readers will never announce it, and keyboard users cannot tab to it.

This is the correct choice when content should be completely hidden from all users (such as an unexpanded accordion panel or a closed dropdown menu).

Case 2: opacity: 0 (The Ghost Tab Trap)

When an element has opacity: 0:

  • It is completely invisible on the visual screen.
  • It remains 100% active in the Accessibility Tree.
  • It remains fully focusable by the Tab key!

If you animate a mobile navigation drawer off-screen using opacity: 0 without setting visibility: hidden or display: none, keyboard users will tab through ten invisible menu links floating in empty space.

Case 3: The Visually Hidden Pattern (.sr-only)

What if you have an icon button (like a shopping cart or search magnifying glass) that visual users understand through iconography, but screen reader users need descriptive text for?

Do not use opacity: 0. Use the standardized .sr-only (screen-reader only) CSS utility:

.sr-only {
  position: absolute;
  width: 1px;
  height: 1px;
  padding: 0;
  margin: -1px;
  overflow: hidden;
  clip-path: inset(50%);
  white-space: nowrap;
  border: 0;
}

<button class="cart-btn">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" class="icon-cart"></svg>
  <span class="sr-only">View shopping cart (3 items)</span>
</button>

How this works:

  1. aria-hidden="true" removes the purely decorative SVG from the Accessibility Tree, preventing screen readers from announcing "graphic, path, vector".
  2. The .sr-only span shrinks to a 1-pixel clipped box that is invisible to the eye.
  3. The browser keeps the text inside the Accessibility Tree, so VoiceOver reads: "View shopping cart (3 items), button".

Case 4: The :focus-visible Revolution

For over a decade, frontend developers committed the ultimate accessibility crime:

/* NEVER DO THIS */
*:focus {
  outline: none;
}

Designers complained that clicking a button with a mouse created an ugly blue outline, so developers erased the focus ring entirely.

In doing so, they blinded millions of keyboard users who navigate using Tab and depend on that focus ring to know where they are on the page.

Modern CSS solved this conflict with the :focus-visible pseudo-class:

/* Remove outline ONLY for mouse clicks, preserve it for keyboard navigation */
button:focus {
  outline: none;
}

button:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #38BDF8;
  outline-offset: 4px;
}

:focus-visible only renders when the browser detects keyboard navigation or assistive device input. Mouse clicks stay clean, while keyboard users receive a crisp, high-contrast navigation ring.

4. Focus Architecture: Building Accessible Modals and Dialogs

Modals and dialogs are the single most common source of critical accessibility failures in modern web applications.

When an inaccessible modal opens:

  1. The user clicks "Edit Profile".
  2. The modal appears visually on screen.
  3. Keyboard focus remains stuck on the background page.
  4. Pressing Tab moves focus behind the dark modal backdrop, clicking unseen links and triggering unintended actions.
  5. Pressing Escape does nothing.
  6. Closing the modal causes focus to reset to the top of the <body>, forcing the user to tab through the entire navigation bar again.

An accessible modal requires a strict four-step lifecycle:

Step 1: Semantic Markup and ARIA Attributes

Your modal container must inform assistive technology that it is an isolated dialog:

<div 
  id="edit-modal" 
  role="dialog" 
  aria-modal="true" 
  aria-labelledby="modal-title"
  class="modal"
>
  <h2 id="modal-title">Edit Your Profile</h2>
  <!-- Form fields -->
  <button id="close-btn">Close</button>
</div>
  • role="dialog" announces to screen readers that an interactive dialog has opened.
  • aria-modal="true" instructs assistive technologies to treat the dialog as modal, ignoring elements outside it.
  • aria-labelledby="modal-title" automatically reads the heading when the modal opens.

Step 2: Focus Trapping

Focus must never escape the bounds of the active dialog:

  • When focus is on the last interactive element (e.g., the "Save" button) and the user presses Tab, focus must wrap back to the first interactive element (e.g., the "Close" button).
  • When focus is on the first element and the user presses Shift + Tab, focus must wrap to the last element.

Step 3: The Native inert Breakthrough

Historically, trapping focus required complex JavaScript listeners counting DOM elements.

Today, modern browsers support the native HTML inert attribute:

// Opening the modal
const mainContent = document.querySelector('#app-content');
const modal = document.querySelector('#edit-modal');

// Make the entire background page inert in one line!
mainContent.setAttribute('inert', '');
modal.classList.add('is-open');

When an element is marked inert, the browser automatically:

  1. Prevents all pointer and click events on background nodes.
  2. Removes all background elements from the keyboard tab order.
  3. Removes all background elements from the Accessibility Tree.

Step 4: Deterministic Focus Restoration

When the user closes the modal (either by clicking Close or pressing the Escape key):

// Remember the button that triggered the modal
let previousActiveElement = null;

function openModal(triggerElement) {
  previousActiveElement = triggerElement;
  modal.show();
  modal.querySelector('input').focus();
}

function closeModal() {
  modal.hide();
  mainContent.removeAttribute('inert');

  // Return focus back to where the user started!
  if (previousActiveElement) {
    previousActiveElement.focus();
  }
}

Restoring focus guarantees that keyboard users can resume navigating immediately without losing their place on the page.

5. Dynamic Real-Time Announcements: Mastering Live Regions (aria-live)

In traditional multi-page websites, submitting a form refreshed the entire browser tab. The screen reader detected a page load, moved to the top of the new document, and announced the heading.

In modern Single Page Applications (React, Vue, Svelte, Next.js), state updates occur asynchronously without page refreshes.

When a user clicks "Add to Cart":

  • A microtask runs.
  • A green toast notification appears in the bottom right corner: "Item added to cart."
  • A visual user sees the toast instantly.

To a screen reader user, absolutely nothing happened.

Unless you explicitly inform the browser, the Accessibility Tree does not announce dynamic visual changes.

The Solution: Live Regions

An ARIA Live Region is a DOM node designated to monitor content changes and announce them via assistive technology:

<!-- A polite notification container -->
<div aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true" class="sr-only toast-announcer" id="live-region">
  <!-- Dynamic messages injected here -->
</div>

The Difference Between polite and assertive

  • aria-live="polite": The screen reader waits until the user finishes their current sentence or action before reading the update. Use this for 95% of notifications (e.g., cart updates, form saved confirmations, search result counts).
  • aria-live="assertive": The screen reader immediately interrupts whatever it is currently saying to announce the message. Reserve this strictly for critical, time-sensitive emergencies (e.g., session timeout warnings, server connection lost, validation errors blocking submission).

The Golden Rule of Live Regions

The live region container must already exist in the DOM when the page loads.

If you dynamically create a <div aria-live="polite"> in JavaScript and immediately populate it with text, the browser will not register the live region in time to announce it.

Always render an empty live container in your root layout and update its textContent when events fire:

function announceToScreenReader(message) {
  const liveRegion = document.getElementById('live-region');
  liveRegion.textContent = ''; // Clear previous message
  setTimeout(() => {
    liveRegion.textContent = message; // Triggers fresh OS announcement
  }, 50);
}

6. The 5-Step Developer Accessibility Audit

You do not need an expensive third-party consultancy to ensure your web application is accessible.

Before opening a pull request, run this 5-minute manual engineering checklist:

Step 1: The No-Mouse Challenge (Keyboard Navigation)

Unplug your mouse or turn off your trackpad. Navigate your entire user flow using only Tab, Shift + Tab, Enter, Space, and Escape:

  • Can you see where the focus ring is at all times?
  • Can you reach every button, link, and input?
  • Do custom dropdowns open and close with the keyboard?
  • Does pressing Escape close modals and menus?

Step 2: The Screen Reader Dry Run

Turn on your operating system's built-in screen reader (press Cmd + F5 for VoiceOver on macOS, or Win + Ctrl + Enter for Narrator on Windows).
Close your eyes and try to complete the core user task (e.g., sign up, search, add an item to cart). Listen to the announcements. Are buttons labelled properly, or do you hear "clickable, unlabelled"?

Step 3: Zoom and Reflow Testing

Press Cmd + Plus (or Ctrl + Plus) until your browser zoom reaches 200%:

  • Does your layout break into overlapping text?
  • Does content get cut off inside fixed-height containers?
  • Does horizontal scrolling appear unnecessarily?

Step 4: Color and Contrast Verification

Use Chrome DevTools to inspect your text elements. Ensure standard text achieves at least a 4.5:1 contrast ratio against its background (3:1 for large 18pt+ headings). Never convey information through color alone (e.g., don't just turn an input border red on error; include an error text message and an icon).

Step 5: Inspect the Accessibility Tree

Open Chrome DevTools, click the Elements tab, and switch to the Accessibility sub-tab. Click any interactive widget on your page. Look at the computed Name and Role. If the computed name is empty or incorrect, fix your HTML semantics immediately.

The Mental Shift

Web accessibility is not an extra feature you bolt onto a web application during the final sprint before release.

Accessibility is fundamental web engineering quality.

  • Semantic HTML gives you keyboard support, focusability, and OS integrations for free.
  • ARIA is not a styling tool; it is a communication protocol with assistive technology.
  • The browser constructs an Accessibility Tree alongside your visual layout, and both trees must be maintained with equal engineering rigor.

When you stop treating accessibility as an afterthought and start respecting the browser's dual-tree architecture, your Lighthouse scores stay high, your code stays lean, and your digital products become usable for every human being on the internet.

How does your team handle accessibility audits and testing in your CI/CD pipelines? Have you encountered surprising bugs when inspecting the browser Accessibility Tree, or experienced the ARIA paradox in production? Share your thoughts and testing strategies in the comments below.

title: Fundamentos de Banco de Dados
description:
Os bancos de dados se configuram como uma tecnologia essencial na vida moderna. A utilização de aparelhos tecnológicos computacionais estruturou a sociedade em uma interação constante com dados armazenados para realização de tarefas cotidianas. Ao acessar uma ferramenta no celular, no computador ou pela internet, o usuário interage diretamente com algum banco de dados. Portanto, esses sistemas desempenham um papel crítico em quase todas as áreas nas quais os computadores são utilizados.

Dados podem ser definidos como observações ou medições sobre o mundo armazenadas em algum formato para consulta posterior. Elmasri e Navathe afirmam que dados são fatos conhecidos que podem ser registrados e que possuem significado implícito. Date, por sua vez, afirma que, em contextos práticos e computacionais, dado é aquilo que está armazenado no banco de dados.

Em contrapartida, Date apresenta o conceito de informação diferenciando-o de dados por conter significado contextualizado para determinado usuário. Nesse sentido, a informação resulta do processamento, da manipulação e da organização do dados, de modo a representar um acréscimo ao conhecimento. Contudo, na prática do desenvolvimento de sistemas, os termos “dados” e “informação” são frequentemente utilizados de forma intercambiável, embora mantenha suas distinções teóricas.

Dados estruturado são aqueles cuja arquitetura segue um modelo predefinido e rígido. Dessa forma, eles obedecem a um esquema de formatação fixa que especifica rigidamente suas características. Os dados não estruturados, como afirma Coronel, apresentam-se em seu estado bruto ou nativo, sendo armazenados da mesma forma que foram coletados. Segundo o autor, a utilização desse formato dificulta a extração de informações, exigindo um pré-processamento para a organização ou imposição de alguma estrutura.

De forma intermediária, os dados semiestruturados se apresentam como uma estrutura que contém uma formatação, mas não se mantém fixa e precisa. Embora apresentem regras em padrão próprio, não precisam conter de forma exata e precisa. Embora apresentem regras em padrão próprio, não precisam conter de forma exata as mesmas características entre si, podendo um tipo de dado ser armazenado de formas diferentes. Para organizar esse tipo de dado, costuma-se utilizar notações e linguagens flexíveis baseadas em tags e marcadores, como o XML (Extensible Markup Language) e JSON (JavaScript Object Notation).

Banco de Dados e SGBDs

A definição de um banco de dados pode ser apresentada como uma coleção organizada de dados inter-relacionados, que contêm significado e informações implícitas sobre um domínio específico. Dessa forma, para que os dados se configurem como um banco de dados, é necessário que estejam inseridos em um contexto e o representem. De acordo com Elmasri e Navathe, as propriedades necessárias para definir corretamente um banco de dados consistem em: representar algum aspecto do mundo real (domínio), denominado minimundo ou universo de discurso; construir uma coleção logicamente coerente de dados com significado inerente; e ser projetado, construído e populado com dados para uma finalidade específica.

Assim, o banco de dados descreve um recorte da realidade. Ao sofrer modificações, esse recorte deve se refletir nos dados armazenados, mantendo o paralelo com as ações do mundo real de forma precisa e confiável. Esses dados não devem ser apresentados de forma aleatória, mas sim em uma estrutura de relações e regras que lhes conferem sentido, perante a realidade, atendendo a um grupo definido de usuários e a aplicações que permitem, principalmente, a recuperação de informações.

A necessidade de operacionalizar e gerenciar um grande acervo de dados sujeitava os usuários a problemas como desorganização, perda e redundância de informações. Isso acarretava um ambiente inconsistente, no qual as regras e a coerência lógica eram constantemente violadas. A partir dessas problemáticas surgiram os Sistemas de Gerenciamento de banco de dados (SGBDs), os quais Elmasri e Navathe definem como uma coleção de programas de uso geral que possibilita a criação, manutenção e compartilhamento dos dados.

Os SGBDs permitem a definição e a construção de um banco de dados, com a especificação e as restrições de toda sua estrutura, bem como dos dados que estão ou serão armazenados. Além disso, permitem a manipulação e o compartilhamento das informações, possibilitando que diversos usuários e programas acessem de forma simultânea. Complementarmente, os SGBDs devem garantir a proteção e a segurança contra falhas de hardware e software, assim como a atuação contra o acesso não autorizado ou malicioso, garantindo sua manutenção e evolução ( adição de novos campos e atualizações das regras ) de forma segura.

O tamanho e a complexidade dos bancos de dados podem variar de forma considerável. Eles podem ser pequenos e simples, como uma lista de nomes e endereços com centenas de registros, ou grandes e complexos, como o sistema de um banco comercial com milhares de usuários e transações diárias.

Vale ressaltar que o SGBD não é absolutamente necessário para implementação de um banco de dados computadorizado. Assim, um software alternativo próprio pode ser desenvolvido para realizar as mesmas funcionalidades, mas a complexidade no desenvolvimento torna necessária a utilização de um SGBD já disponível, seja de código aberto ou privado. Assim, a união do banco de dados com um SGBD é denominada Sistema de Banco de Dados, o qual compreende, segundo Date, quatro componentes principais: dados, hardware, software e usuários.

A demanda pelo processamento cada vez mais complexo e de baixa latência tornou ineficiente o armazenamento estruturado diretamente pelos programas em arquivos isolados. Além disso, o compartilhamento de dados em locais diferentes gerava um problema crítico de inconsistência para as aplicações. Assim, a adoção de um banco de dados centralizado tornou-se a abordagem mais eficaz. A centralização por meio de um SGBD combate falhas graves, como a redundância de dados e a ineficiência operacional. Isso evita que as informações sejam duplicadas em vários locais, reduzindo o desperdício de espaço e o esforço necessário para realizar as atualizações.

Os SGBDs manipulam seus dados armazenados de forma correta a partir de uma autodescrição dos próprios dados. Essa estratégia é denominada natureza autodescritiva do sistema de banco de dados. Por meio do objeto chamado catálogo de dados, dicionário de dados ou metadados, os SGBDs guardam a descrição dos dados, assim como a definição completa e integrada de sua estrutura e suas restrições.

Sendo assim, os metadados são informações estruturadas adicionais, relativas a certo conjunto de dados, que podem ser utilizadas para descrevê-los, explicá-los, localizá-los e manipulá-los de forma eficiente, tornando-os mais fáceis de recuperar, usar ou gerenciar. Na prática, eles definem a estrutura do banco de dados, os tipos de dados ( inteiro, caractere, texto ), além de diversas restrições sobre esses dados — como permitir apenas números positivos.

Quanto à abstração e à independência proporcionadas pelos SGBDs, as aplicações interagem com os dados sem precisar conhecer sua estrutura física de armazenamento. Os programas apenas solicitam a informação, enquanto o sistema gerenciador se encarrega de buscá-la e entregá-la com precisão. Essa separação garante que mudanças na estrutura interna do banco não impactam o funcionamento das aplicações.

Como operam de forma centralizada, os SGBDs devem garantir que os usuários tenham acesso restrito às informações de acordo com suas categorias e permissões específicas. Para isso, a segurança é assegurada por meio do conceito de Visões de Dados (Views), que criam recortes personalizados das informações, limitando o que pode ser visualizado ou manipulado.

Por ser uma das características que distinguem os SGBDs das abordagens tradicionais, a operação multiusuário permite que diversas pessoas e aplicações acessem o banco simultaneamente. Entretanto, sem o devido gerenciamento, esse acesso concorrente pode causar a sobrescrita de dados e gerar inconsistências. Para evitar esse problema, os sistemas implementam mecanismos de controle de concorrência.

Transações e ACID

Segundo Date, as transações em um banco de dados mediado pelo SGBD representam uma unidade lógica de trabalho com começo e fim, envolvendo diversas operações. Elmasri e Navathe complementam essa ideia definindo transação como uma execução ou processo realizado por um programa que inclui um ou mais acessos ao banco de dados, como a leitura, atualização, apagamento ou inserção de novas informações nos registros.

A atomicidade, por sua vez, é a garantia de que a transação será concluída com sucesso ou totalmente cancelada, sendo tratada como uma operação lógica única, mesmo que diversas ações sejam realizadas. Isso estabelece a regra de que, caso qualquer instrução falhe, todo o processo será desfeito e o banco de dados permanecerá inalterado. Ou seja, ou a transação ocorre de forma completa (operação denominada commit) ou não ocorre de forma alguma (ação denominada rollback). A responsabilidade de garantir a atomicidade é destinada ao Subsistema de Recuperação do SGBD.

A consistência garante que a transação só levará o banco de dados de um estado consistente para outro igualmente consistente. Assim, uma transação só pode ser finalizada se todos os dados e regras forem preservados. Essa garantia é assegurada pelos próprios programadores, com auxílio do Módulo de Restrição de Integridade do SGBD.

O isolamento garante que as transações, mesmo sob execução concorrente, ocorram de forma independente umas das outras. Desse modo, vários usuários e programas realizam operações simultâneas no banco de dados sem interferir uns aos outros, assemelhando-se a uma execução sequencial (uma após a outra). A responsabilidade por garantir o isolamento cabe ao Subsistema de Controle de Concorrência do SGBD.

Já a durabilidade é a garantia de que uma transação confirmada (commit) seja persistida mesmo em caso de falha do sistema. Assim, os dados permanecem gravados em armazenamento permanente (não volátil), sem a ocorrência de eventos que modifiquem ou desfaçam a ação ao longo do tempo, cabendo também ao Subsistema de Recuperação do SGBD assegurar essa propriedade.

Arquitetura do Sistema de Banco de Dados

A arquitetura de banco de dados é o projeto estrutural que define como os dados são organizados, armazenados, acessados e gerenciados em um sistema. Como já informado anteriormente, esse sistema é composto por quatro elementos básicos: os dados, que contêm as informações reais salvas; o hardware, que consiste no computador ou servidor físico onde tudo está gravado; o software (SGBD), responsável por gerenciar o acesso, a segurança e a leitura/gravação; e os usuários, isto é, as pessoas ou sistemas que realizam as transações nos dados, alterando-os ou consultando-os.

Em 1975, o Comitê de Planejamento e Requisitos de Padrões ANSI/X3/SPARC propôs uma arquitetura em 3 esquemas, denominada arquitetura ANSI/SPARC, para os SGBDs. Essa arquitetura auxiliou no alcance das características de autodescrição, isolamento e suporte a múltiplos usuários. A primeira camada é denominada nível interno, também conhecido como nível de armazenamento. Ela descreve a estrutura do armazenamento físico do banco nos discos, detalhando a gravação e os caminhos de acesso aos dados, definidos por meio de um modelo interno (ou modelo físico). Cabe ressaltar que os dados reais encontram-se apenas nessa camada, gravados em disco.

Em sequência, tem-se o nível conceitual, ou nível lógico. Ele descreve a estrutura do banco de dados inteiro para uma comunidade de usuários, ocultando os detalhes das estruturas de armazenamento físico e concentrando-se na descrição de entidades, tipo de dados, relacionamentos, operações do usuário e restrições, descritos a partir de um modelo conceitual. Por fim, o nível externo, ou nível de visão, inclui uma série de esquemas ou visões de usuários. Essa camada apresenta estruturas que descrevem apenas uma parte do banco de dados de interesse de um grupo específico, ocultando o restante e diferenciando os dados a que cada perfil pode ter acesso.

A arquitetura em três camadas, ou esquemas, se configura como um modelo de SGBD que visa garantir a independência de dados. Esse conceito define-se como a capacidade de alteração do esquema de um nível sem afetar o nível imediatamente superior. Isso é possível porque o SGBD mantém mapeamentos ( links ) entre as camadas e os ajusta quando um objeto muda, permitindo que o nível superior continue a encontrá-lo.

Para isso, o esquema em três camadas necessita de dois tipos de mapeamento: o conceitual/interno e o externo/conceitual, que possibilita a independência física e lógica dos dados, respectivamente. O mapeamento conceitual/interno especifica como os campos do nível conceitual são representados no nível interno. Isso garante a independência física, permitindo alterar o esquema interno (estrutura de armazenamento físico do banco de dados) sem modificar o esquema conceitual. Contudo, pode ser necessária a alteração do mapeamento para que o nível conceitual permaneça invariável.

Já o mapeamento externo/conceitual define a correspondência entre uma visão externa — usada pelos programas de aplicação — e a visão conceitual. Isso garante a independência lógica, permitindo manipular o esquema conceitual (estrutura lógica) sem afetar o funcionamento dos esquemas externos ou dos programas que os utilizam. Assim como no caso anterior, pode ser necessária a alteração do mapeamento para que o esquema externo permaneça invariável.

Atores

Devido à complexidade de manter um banco de dados em grandes organizações, com variados tipos de usuários participando do projeto, do uso e da manutenção, é necessário um responsável por definir as regras da empresa. Em vez de cada área de negócio decidir o que guardar, como guardar e quem pode acessar, essas decisões ficam centralizadas em uma pessoa ou papel.

O Administrador de Dados (DA, Data Administrator) atua com foco estratégico e de gestão, sendo o principal responsável pela governança e pelas políticas de tratamento das informações dentro de uma organização. Em vez de lidar com as tarefas técnicas e cotidianas, esse profissional analisa o negócio como um todo para definir quais dados são relevantes, como devem ser geridos e quais regras precisam seguir. Dessa forma, o DA atua como um gestor de negócios que mantém a visão abstrata das informações, liderando a criação dos modelos lógico e conceitual do banco de dados para alinhá-los aos objetivos da empresa.

O Administrador de Banco de Dados (DBA, Database Administrator) é o profissional técnico responsável pela supervisão e gestão diária tanto do banco de dados quanto do SGBD. De acordo com o autor C. J. Date, suas funções principais incluem a criação da estrutura interna do banco, a definição de regras de segurança e integridade, bem como rotinas de cópia e migração de dados (como backup e restore). Além disso, o DBA atua diretamente no monitoramento de desempenho, na adaptação do sistema a novas demandas e na comunicação com os usuários para assegurar que as informações necessárias estejam sempre disponíveis.

De forma complementar, segundo Elmasri e Navathe, o DBA desempenha um papel essencial na manutenção operacional, segurança e eficiência do ambiente de dados. Na área de segurança, esse profissional gerencia usuários, perfis e permissões, além de auditar acessos e responder a incidentes para assegurar a integridade e a confidencialidade das informações. Para garantir a continuidade do negócio, o DBA realiza e testa backups, configura sistemas de replicação e alta disponibilidade e planeja atualizações. No âmbito da performance (tuning), ele otimiza consultas, particiona dados e monitora estatísticas e recursos de hardware, como CPU, memória e armazenamento. Além disso, completa suas funções aplicando correções (patches), automatizando rotinas, acompanhando alertas e dimensionando a infraestrutura conforme o crescimento da demanda.

Segundo Elmasri e Navathe, os Projetistas de Banco de Dados (ou Designers) atuam antes da implementação e inserção dos dados para identificar o que precisa ser armazenado e estruturar o sistema. Embora tenham um perfil mais voltado ao negócio do que os DBAs, eles desempenham um papel híbrido e essencial na equipe. Na prática, eles conversam com os usuários para levantar requisitos e entender quais informações e respostas o sistema precisa fornecer. Além de criar modelos conceituais de alto nível, esses profissionais também se aprofundam em detalhes técnicos para projetar a estrutura física do banco de dados em conjunto com os administradores.

Os usuários finais são profissionais que manipulam dados no dia a dia de trabalho e se dividem em quatro categorias principais, segundo os autores Elmasri e Navathe. Os usuários casuais, geralmente gerentes, acessam o banco de dados apenas ocasionalmente por meio de linguagens de consulta avançadas. Já os usuários iniciantes (ou paramétricos) realizam tarefas repetitivas e constantes usando telas e transações já padronizadas nos sistemas. Os usuários sofisticados, como engenheiros, cientistas e analistas, dominam as ferramentas do SGBD para criar suas próprias aplicações e resolver demandas complexas. Por fim, os usuários isolados gerenciam bancos de dados pessoais utilizando softwares prontos com interfaces gráficas simples e intuitivas.

Vantagens dos Bancos de Dados e SGBDs

Os Bancos de Dados e SGBDs oferecem vantagens técnicas essenciais para gerenciar informações com eficiência, segurança e confiabilidade. Em primeiro lugar, eles garantem o controle da redundância ao armazenar cada dado em um único local, evitando duplicações e incoerências (ou mantendo cópias sincronizadas sob regras rígidas quando o foco é desempenho). Além disso, o SGBD assegura a integridade e a persistência das informações, aplicando regras de validação para impedir valores inválidos e salvando objetos de programas de forma permanente, mesmo após o encerramento da execução.

No âmbito da estrutura e do uso, o sistema permite representar e atualizar relacionamentos complexos entre diferentes conjuntos de dados, contando com técnicas avançadas de armazenamento e busca que tornam as consultas muito mais rápidas. Somado a isso, a tecnologia protege os registros contra acessos não autorizados por meio de permissões e senhas, ao mesmo tempo em que oferece múltiplas interfaces, adaptando-se tanto a usuários casuais (via linguagens de consulta) quanto a desenvolvedores (via APIs).

Há também garantia na padronização dos dados, como a definição de formatos específicos para datas, além de assegurar a disponibilidade imediata de informações atualizadas para todos os usuários simultaneamente. Por fim, o uso de um SGBD oferece grande flexibilidade, permitindo alterar a estrutura do banco sem prejudicar os dados existentes ou as aplicações já criadas. Como resultado, o tempo de desenvolvimento de novos sistemas é reduzido e obtém-se economia de escala, já que a centralização das informações elimina custos gerados por redundâncias e sobreposições.

title: Judge Me by My Size, Do You? What Your Viewport Really Costs an AI Tester
description:
Yoda told Luke that size matters not. With all due respect to the little green guy, he never had to pay for a computer-use agent's screenshots.

Here's how I ended up down this rabbit hole. I recently pointed Claude at a web app to do some functional testing, and my usage went way up. My gut said screenshots were the culprit: the agent has to look at the screen before nearly every move, and every look costs tokens. So my tongue-in-cheek pitch for a blog post became "monitor size actually matters for AI-driven testing." But talk is cheap, so I had a small team of AI agents build and run an experiment to prove or disprove it. Let's see what happened.

Spoiler: size matters, just not in the direction you'd guess every time.

The Math You Can Do on a Napkin

Claude doesn't see pixels. It sees patches. Per Anthropic's vision docs, each image is chopped into 28×28-pixel blocks ("visual tokens"), and the cost is:

import math

def visual_tokens(width: int, height: int) -> int:
    # Anthropic vision docs: ceil(w / 28) * ceil(h / 28)
    return math.ceil(width / 28) * math.ceil(height / 28)

for w, h in [(1024, 768), (1280, 800), (1920, 1080), (2560, 1440)]:
    print(f"{w}x{h}: {visual_tokens(w, h):,} tokens")

# 1024x768: 1,036 tokens
# 1280x800: 1,334 tokens
# 1920x1080: 2,691 tokens
# 2560x1440: 4,784 tokens

(In my runs, each screenshot actually came in 21 tokens over the formula, so 1,057 at 1024x768 and 4,805 at 2560x1440. Close enough for napkin work.)

Two more things from the docs matter here. First, Claude 4.7 and later models sit on a high-resolution tier that tops out at 2,576 px on the long edge and 4,784 visual tokens per image. That means a 2560x1440 screen lands right at the ceiling. Second, the docs say screenshots you return to the computer-use and browser-use tools that exceed those limits are rejected with a validation error rather than quietly downscaled. If your screen is bigger, resizing (and scaling the click coordinates back) is your job.

So a 2560x1440 screenshot costs roughly four and a half times what a 1024x768 one does. Case closed? Not quite. The bill isn't per screenshot. It's per task.

The Experiment

The setup, in brief:

  • Model: claude-opus-5-5 with Anthropic's computer-use toolset, run on Nov 16, 2026.
  • Browser: Chrome in kiosk mode at exactly 1024x768, 1280x800, 1920x1080, and 2560x1440, at a device pixel ratio of 1, with a fresh profile every run.
  • Context policy: only the last 3 screenshots stay in history (older ones become a text placeholder), with prompt caching off.
  • Thinking: "adaptive, low." It can't be turned off on this model, and the API rejects sampling settings like temperature, so I couldn't pin those either.
  • Volume: 10 runs per viewport per flow, with the hypotheses written down before the full runs.

And two deliberately boring test flows:

  1. TodoMVC behind a demo login. Everything fits on screen at every size, so no scrolling.
  2. Bootstrap 5.3.9's checkout example. The form runs below the fold on smaller screens, so the agent has to scroll to finish it.

Every one of the 80 main runs succeeded, with zero retries or misclicks.

Flow 1: No Scrolling, No Mercy

When the page fits on every screen, the agent does about the same work at every size, and you just pay for bigger pictures.

Viewport Tokens/screenshot Median input tokens Mean API calls Median cost/run
1024x768 1,057 37,701 5.0 $0.184
1280x800 1,355 41,127 4.8 $0.199
1920x1080 2,712 57,425 5.0 $0.271
2560x1440 4,805 82,477 5.0 $0.382

2560x1440 used 2.19x the input tokens of 1024x768, or about 2.1x the cost per run. That's a 119% token premium for the privilege of a big monitor. Hot dang.

One honest wrinkle: 1280x800 doesn't clearly cost more than 1024x768. Two of its ten runs batched the last steps into 4 calls instead of 5, and that saved more tokens than the bigger screenshots added. On a page like this, a little run-to-run behavior can outweigh one step up in screen size.

Flow 2: Where the Big Screen Earns Its Keep

On the checkout form, the smaller screens scrolled in every run. At 2560x1440, the whole form fit, and the agent never scrolled once.

Viewport Tokens/screenshot Median input tokens Mean API calls Median cost/run
1024x768* 1,057 20,395 3.0 $0.103
1280x800* 1,355 22,183 3.1 $0.111
1920x1080 2,712 30,361 3.1 $0.149
2560x1440 4,805 23,693 2.0 $0.115

* Rerun with Chrome's payment-autofill popup turned off. More on that in a second.

Here 2560x1440 used only about 1.16x the input tokens of 1024x768 (about 1.12x the cost), and about 1.07x the tokens of 1280x800. Fewer steps shrank the big-screen token premium from roughly +119% to roughly +16%.

Why? Every API call resends the conversation, which on this flow meant roughly 5,000 tokens of non-image context per call, plus the screenshots it's carrying. Skip a scroll, skip a screenshot, skip a call, and the savings add up fast. Meanwhile, 1920x1080 is the cautionary middle child: it needed about as many calls as 1280x800 and paid for bigger screenshots, so it came out the most expensive of the bunch.

The Popup That Ate My Ratio

I would be remiss if I didn't mention how this almost went sideways. In the first pass, the big screen came out cheaper than 1024x768. Great headline. Also wrong.

When a card field got focus, Chrome showed a payment-autofill popup. At 1024x768, the agent dismissed it with Escape 9 times across 10 runs, re-scrolled, and took another screenshot, which cost it an extra call almost every time (3.9 calls on average and a median of 28,850 tokens, versus 3.0 and 20,395 with the popup off). So I had the agents run a follow-up at 1024x768 and 1280x800 with the popup disabled, as a separate comparison after the main results. The extra call at 1024x768 vanished entirely.

The lesson: one incidental browser popup moved the cost of a task by roughly 40%. Your test environment is part of your token bill.

Fine Print (Trust, but Verify)

This passes the smell test, but know the limits:

  • It's small. Two simple pages, one model, one browser at DPR 1.
  • The context policy matters. I kept only the last 3 screenshots. Keep the full history and the big-screen penalty grows, because every old screenshot rides along on every call.
  • The confidence intervals are tight because the runs were nearly deterministic (all ten 2560 runs on the checkout form cost exactly 23,693 tokens). They measure run-to-run noise, not how well this generalizes.
  • Not everything was rerun. 2560x1440 and 1920x1080 weren't rerun with the popup off. 2560 never pressed Escape, so I'm comfortable comparing it. But 1920 averaged about one Escape press per run, so its number may be slightly inflated.
  • One scoring rule changed after the pilot, before the full runs, and it's documented. The original rule would have flagged 4 successful runs as refusals just because of how the agent formatted its final message.
  • Thinking was "adaptive, low," not off. It showed up in 3 runs at 1920x1080, at 43 to 51 tokens each.
  • The absolute dollars are small: about $0.10 to $0.38 per run, at list price ($4/$20 per million input/output tokens) including a 1.1x US-inference multiplier. The ratios are the story, and they compound at scale.

So What Should You Do?

  1. Start at a modest viewport. 1024x768 and 1280x800 were the two cheapest sizes in both flows here. Don't hand your agent a 4K canvas just because your own monitor is one.
  2. Size the viewport to the task. If a bigger screen removes scrolling on your key pages, it can nearly pay for itself. If it doesn't, you're just buying bigger pictures.
  3. Count calls, not pixels. Cost tracked the number of steps more than resolution. Watch your loop's call count first.
  4. Clean up your test environment. Kill autofill popups, cookie banners, and anything else that makes the agent stop and swat at the screen.
  5. Mind the ceiling. At 2560 px wide you're at the high-resolution tier's limit. Anything bigger has to be resized in your code, or the API will reject it.
  6. Trim screenshot history. Every old screenshot you keep gets paid for again on every call.

Is monitor size a cost lever? Yes, just not a one-way one. Houston, we have a tradeoff.

I'm curious what you've seen. If you're running computer-use agents for testing, what viewport did you land on, and did anything (popups, banners, infinite scroll) quietly blow up your token bill?

title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
description:
arXiv:2611.17495v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not been modified to interpret as a different type of data. By construction, the resulting measure, NLS depth, can be adjudicated before training from an architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone, and is insensitive to ordinary post-training such as prompting, distillation, and RL. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. It would likely grow slowly under continued scaling of standard transformers, while latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could increase it by a large amount. We work through how NLS depth applies to a range of existing and proposed architectures, discuss alternative operationalizations, and give a worked example bounding the depth of Gemma3-1B. We argue that AI developers should track and report the NLS depth of their models as a complement to direct measurements of CoT monitorability.

title: I selected all the text on 76 pages and copied it: 653,476 characters, and not one button label came along
description:
Readers copy pages. They paste a pricing table into a spreadsheet, an email template into their drafts, a definition into a note. What arrives in the clipboard is not the HTML, not textContent, and not quite innerText: it is the rendered text of the selection, filtered by a CSS property most of us set without thinking.

I measured it across all 76 public pages of Nakodo with the browser's own selection:

const sel = getSelection();
sel.removeAllRanges();
const range = document.createRange();
range.selectNodeContents(document.body);
sel.addRange(range);
const copied = sel.toString();      // what Ctrl+C would put on the clipboard

653,476 characters

Characters copied across 76 pages 653,476
Lines 13,428
Largest page, /how-it-works 16,780
Smallest page, /alternatives 2,523
Footer, identical on every page 878
Header, identical on every page 45

The two constants are my favourite detail in this measurement. Every page on the site starts with the same 45 characters and ends with the same 878, so a reader who selects a whole page and pastes it gets a navigation menu, then the content, then 878 characters of site furniture. That is the shape of a copied web page and nothing in our markup makes it otherwise.

The header being exactly 45 characters is the first hint of what this post is about. The header holds a brand name, five links and a button, and the selectable part is:

nakodo
How it works
Guides
Blog
Pricing
About

Six lines, 45 characters, and no sign of the button that says "Open the app".

The clipboard gets less than innerText, and the gap is your buttons

On every one of the 76 pages, document.body.innerText was longer than what the selection produced. The gap ran from 52 to 178 characters, median 69.

On the home page the eight strings in innerText that never reach the clipboard are:

Open the app
Start free
https://
Compare every limit
Start free
Try Pro free for 7 days
Choose Business
Open the app

Those are every call to action on the page, plus the https:// prefix glued to the front of the website field. They are missing for one reason:

$ grep -n "select-none" src/components/ui/button.tsx
inline-flex shrink-0 items-center justify-center gap-2 select-none ...

user-select: none is in the base class of our button component, which is where the shadcn generator put it, and it is a perfectly sensible default: dragging across a button should not leave it highlighted. The side effect is that a reader who copies the page loses the words that tell them what to do next.

Unselectable elements per page, counted by computed style:

Page Elements with user-select: none
/tools/engagement-rate-calculator 35
/guides/youtube-outreach-email-templates 33
/how-it-works 9
/privacy 7

The outreach-templates guide earns its 33 honestly: it holds six example messages, each with its own Copy button, and each of those buttons is three unselectable elements (the button, its icon, the icon's path). Copy the whole guide and you get all six messages and not one of the six words "Copy", which is the right outcome by accident rather than by design.

The text written for screen readers does come along

Only two of the 76 pages have any sr-only text in them at all, and on both of them, all of it lands in the clipboard.

The pricing page has four, and they are the word "Yes" sitting behind the four ticks in the comparison table. Copy that table into a spreadsheet and you get "Yes" in the cells where a tick is, which is exactly what you wanted and would not have got from an icon alone. Visually hidden text is what makes a pasted table readable.

The home page has eight, and they are a different kind of thing: status words for the icons in a small example table, including "published", "not published", and a sentence explaining why one row has no email address. Pasting that sample gets you the labels interleaved with the rows. It is not wrong, and it is not what somebody copying an example table is after.

So sr-only has a second audience nobody designs for. The rule I would draw from the two pages is that hidden text standing in for a symbol (a tick, a status dot) is a gift to the clipboard, and hidden text explaining an interface is clutter in it.

Range, Selection and innerText are three different answers

This is the part that cost me a measurement. My first pass compared regions using Range.toString() and got a number larger than the whole page:

new Range().selectNodeContents(document.querySelector("main")).toString().length;  // 14,852
getSelection().toString().length;                                                 // 6,943 for the entire page

A Range concatenates text nodes. It does not care about CSS, and it does not care whether an element is rendered, so it happily includes the contents of <script> tags. On the home page that is 362,221 characters of framework payload, and on /how-it-works it is 334,451. Measure "how much text is on this page" with a Range and you are mostly measuring your own serialised component tree.

The three APIs, ranked by how close they are to the clipboard:

API Includes hidden elements Includes <script> Honours user-select
textContent yes yes no
Range.toString() yes yes no
innerText no no no
Selection.toString() no no yes

Only the last one answers the question a reader asks.

One selection rule, and one copy helper

Two small things found in passing.

There is exactly one ::selection rule in 154 KB of stylesheet:

::selection {
  background: var(--color-cyano-100);
  color: var(--color-cyano-950);
}
:root {
  caret-color: var(--color-cyano-700);
}

A pale brand blue behind the selected text and a brand-coloured caret. Two declarations, applied every time anybody drags across anything on the site, and the cheapest branding on the whole page.

And the only programmatic copying anywhere on the public site is 20 buttons across 8 guides, all of them driven by one 16-line helper:

export async function copyText(text: string, done?: string): Promise<boolean> {
  try {
    await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text);
    if (done) notify({ message: done });
    return true;
  } catch {
    notify({ error: "Couldn't copy. Select the text and copy it yourself." });
    return false;
  }
}

The clipboard API can refuse: no permission, an insecure origin, an older browser. The fallback is not a hidden textarea and an execCommand that has been deprecated for years. It is a sentence telling the reader to do the thing they already know how to do, which works because the text that button copies is in a paragraph, selectable, right next to it.

What came out of it

  1. Decide about select-none on link-shaped buttons. Our primary calls to action are links wearing a button class, and copying a page silently drops their wording. Dragging over a text link should select it. The property belongs on controls that behave like controls, not on everything that looks like one.
  2. Review the eight hidden strings on the home page. The four on the pricing table should stay: they are what makes a paste make sense. The ones narrating an example table probably should not be in a copy of it.
  3. Use Selection.toString() when you audit your own text. innerText is close but blind to user-select, and a Range will quietly hand you a quarter of a megabyte of your framework's payload.

Everything here is reproducible on the live site. Open the home page, press Ctrl+A and Ctrl+C, paste it into a text editor, and look for the words "Start free". Then do the same on the pricing page and look for the word "Yes".

title: InfiHall-Bench: A Benchmark for Hallucination Evaluation in Autoregressive Text-to-Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.18053v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hallucination benchmarks for text-to-image generation are predominantly designed around diffusion models, limiting their diagnostic value for visual autoregressive (VAR) models and the development of mitigation methods. We identify two limitations in existing prompt construction paradigms: many prompts are no longer challenging for modern generators, while category-based construction relies on recurring object-attribute-relation templates and rarely tests interactions among multiple visual requirements within a single image.
  We introduce InfiHall-Bench, a controlled benchmark of 411 prompts constructed by systematically composing five foundational and visually verifiable skills: attribute binding, spatial relation, action relation, part consistency, and scene consistency. Each prompt covers 4.05 annotated skills on average, enabling the evaluation of hallucinations under diverse combinations of visual requirements. Using this benchmark, we find that hallucinations in VAR models exhibit a scale-wise persistence pattern: semantic errors can emerge at different autoregressive scales and are rarely corrected by subsequent fine-scale steps.
  Motivated by this observation, we propose Confidence-Masked Hallucination Mitigation (CMHM), which estimates the prediction confidence of target visual tokens at each autoregressive scale during teacher-forced fine-tuning. CMHM downweights reliably predicted tokens, allowing optimization to focus on uncertain predictions across scales. Experiments show that InfiHall-Bench distinguishes models that existing compositional benchmarks rate as comparable, while CMHM consistently outperforms uniform LoRA fine-tuning for VAR-based text-to-image generation.

title: How to harness skills that AI can’t automate
description: With more teams moving faster than ever, the real differentiator is craft—the curiosity, intuition, taste, and intention behind every detail.

title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
description:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.
