title: UltraBERT-JEV: Encoder models for System One Applications
description:
arXiv:2611.17867v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study encoder models that pick one of several options in a single forward pass, without generating text. This technical report compares recipes for fine-tuning UltraBERT-380M with one mask per option. The four recipes differ in how an option is scored and how the scores become probabilities; one follows the expert gate of DeepSeek-V3. Trained on the same data as Qwen3-0.6B with the LLM-as-Jev recipe (67.6% test accuracy), the encoder reaches 69.7% to 72.1%. Scoring an option by "yes" minus "no" instead of "yes" alone gives the larger gain, from 69.7% to 71.3% on the test set and from 57.8% to 59.6% on external benchmarks (56.1% for the decoder). Sigmoid normalisation adds 0.8 test points; a square-root softplus adds none. One request at a time on an NVIDIA A100, the encoder takes 29 ms per decision against 68 ms, but uses more peak memory (2.8 against 2.2 GiB). An auxiliary head, trained on human-marked evidence and on labels selected with a reward adapted from SelfCite, predicts in the same pass the sentences annotated as support for the answer.

title: How I Bypassed 1,000+ Resume Rejections to Land My First Dev Job (Using Next.js and Rust 🚀)
description:
Hey Dev.to family! Let's be entirely honest—the entry-level US tech market right now is absolutely unforgiving. If you are graduating and applying to Tier 1 startups or FAANG companies with a portfolio full of the same generic React to-do lists and basic Node.js CRUD apps as everyone else, your resume is going to get swallowed by Applicant Tracking Systems. Today, let’s look at how I stopped building basic frontend projects and started orchestrating distributed edge systems with Next.js and Rust WebAssembly to actually get hiring managers to notice me.

The entry-level US tech market in 2026 is unforgiving. If you are graduating and applying to Tier 1 startups or FAANG companies with a portfolio full of generic React to-do lists and basic Node.js REST APIs, your resume will be automatically filtered out by Applicant Tracking Systems. The baseline for new graduates has fundamentally shifted. Hiring managers are looking for systems thinkers who understand edge computing, memory-safe execution, and autonomous AI integrations.

To land a high-paying US development job right out of a bootcamp or university, you must prove you can build resilient infrastructure. You need to demonstrate mastery over modern stacks like Next.js, WebAssembly, and Rust.

How do you stand out from the entry-level crowd in 2026?

The biggest mistake new graduates make is focusing entirely on the frontend UI while ignoring security and deployment architecture. To separate yourself from the thousands of other applicants, your portfolio must solve actual enterprise problems.

FAANG engineering teams want to see that you understand how to process data efficiently without blowing up cloud compute budgets. You must pivot from building monolithic applications to orchestrating distributed edge functions.

  • Ditch the MERN Stack: Replace legacy Express backends with Next.js Server Actions and Edge Middleware to prove you understand serverless compute.
  • Integrate Memory Safety: Write your critical data parsing and security logic in Rust, compile it to WebAssembly, and execute it natively within your Next.js application.
  • Deploy Zero Trust: Assume the client is compromised. Implement strict Zod schema validation on every single server boundary to prevent AI-driven payload fuzzing.

What does a FAANG-ready portfolio project look like?

Hiring managers spend less than three minutes reviewing a GitHub repository. Your code must immediately demonstrate architectural rigor. A standout project in 2026 is an AI-driven application that sanitizes user input securely at the edge before feeding it to a Large Language Model.

Below is an architectural concept of a Next.js Server Action that intercepts user data, validates the payload using Zod, and passes it to a custom Rust WebAssembly module for memory-safe sanitization.

"use server";

import { z } from "zod";
// Import a custom Rust module compiled to WebAssembly
import { process_secure_payload } from "@/wasm/security_module"; 

const UserDataSchema = z.object({
  rawInput: z.string().max(500),
  userId: z.string().uuid()
});

export async function handleOnboardingData(payload: z.infer<typeof UserDataSchema>) {
  // 1. Strict Server Boundary Validation
  const parsed = UserDataSchema.safeParse(payload);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    throw new Error("Invalid payload structure detected at the edge.");
  }

  // 2. Memory-Safe Execution
  // Pass data to a Rust Wasm module for sanitization to prevent prompt injection 
  // before it ever touches your AI inference pipeline.
  const inputBytes = new TextEncoder().encode(parsed.data.rawInput);
  const sanitizedBuffer = process_secure_payload(inputBytes);
  const sanitizedText = new TextDecoder().decode(sanitizedBuffer);

  // 3. Proceed with edge inference or secure database insertion
  console.log(`Secure payload processed for user: ${parsed.data.userId}`);

  return { 
    success: true, 
    secureData: sanitizedText 
  };
}

This code snippet proves to a senior engineer that you understand type safety, boundary protection, and high-performance systems integration. It is not just web development; it is modern infrastructure engineering.

How does mastering Rust and Next.js impact US starting salaries?

The divide in entry-level compensation is massive. Graduates who only know basic JavaScript frameworks are struggling to secure junior roles paying $70k. Conversely, graduates who complete advanced systems training like Coding Macaw and master the intersection of Rust, Next.js, and WebAssembly are bypassing the junior title entirely.

If you can walk into a technical interview and fluently explain how to optimize AI inference costs using edge compute and memory-safe architecture, you immediately position yourself for Product Engineer or Systems Engineer roles. In the 2026 US market, these specialized entry-level positions command total compensation packages well over $150k. By treating software engineering as a rigorous systems discipline rather than a frontend hobby, you guarantee your value in an automated world.

FAQs:

1. What tech stack should I learn to get a job in 2026?
The industry standard has shifted toward edge computing and memory safety. You should focus heavily on the Next.js App Router, strict TypeScript, and Rust compiled to WebAssembly for backend data processing.

2. Why are FAANG companies ignoring basic React portfolios?
Basic React portfolios do not demonstrate an understanding of the complex infrastructure required to run modern applications. Companies need engineers who can handle serverless deployments, AI integrations, and strict security validation at the server boundary.

3. How can I learn Rust and WebAssembly for web development?
You can study the official documentation or join intensive systems engineering programs like Coding Macaw, which specifically train graduates on the architectural standards demanded by Tier 1 US tech companies.

What do you all think?

What kind of projects are you building to cut through the job application noise? Have you tried adding Rust or WebAssembly to your Next.js stacks yet? Drop your experiences in the comments, and do not forget to follow for more US tech market insights!

title: Python AI-Generated Image Lifecycles: Object Storage, Database BLOBs, and Disk
description:
The simplest production choice is usually to put generated image bytes in object storage and keep the object key plus searchable workflow state in a database. Use database binary columns only when the payload is deliberately small and atomic byte-plus-metadata commits matter; treat local disk as a development cache or a consciously single-host deployment boundary. This split keeps a Python generation worker replaceable, makes retries understandable, and prevents a successful model eval from hiding a persistence failure.

Short answer: for durable AI-generated images in a multi-worker SaaS, store bytes as objects, store metadata in relational rows, and test the gap between those two writes.

The data flow is plain. A worker receives validated image bytes, computes a content digest, writes them under an application-owned key, then records a row that says which tenant owns the output and where it lives. Reads authorize against that row before retrieving the object. The model provider is outside this contract, so swapping a notebook stub for a real image endpoint does not alter the storage rules.

How should a Python SaaS store AI-generated images across workers?

Start by separating identity from a display filename. A filename may be changed for a download, while an object key needs to stay stable for retries and cleanup. When a response needs to suggest a name to a browser, Content-Disposition is the HTTP response header intended for controlling inline display or attachment handling and can carry a filename parameter. It belongs at delivery time, not in the durable identity of the image. The MDN reference at the end documents the header semantics.

For a generated image, I want the durable record to include the tenant identifier, a generation or job identifier, object key, content type, byte count, digest, and lifecycle state. Prompt text and model settings should be stored only when the product needs them, with the same access controls as the rest of the request data. An image gallery needs metadata for authorization and pagination; it should not need to scan bytes to answer either question.

The critical ordering is object first, metadata second. A cross-system write cannot be assumed to be one transaction, so there are two partial outcomes to plan for: an object with no row, and a row that points to a missing object. The first can be identified by an age-based reconciliation job. The second should never be visible as ready. This is less glamorous than a storage SDK demo, but it is the difference between a retry-safe pipeline and a gallery that looks correct until a worker is restarted. The reconciliation task needs a grace period because the object write may complete just before the database transaction gets its turn; it should inspect candidate keys, check whether a matching metadata row now exists, and only then remove a genuinely abandoned output. Conversely, an incomplete row should remain non-deliverable until a retrieval check sees the expected digest and content type. Those are explicit states, not exceptional mysteries, and the queue can retry them without inventing a new image identity.

Don't hide the gap.

A small persistence contract before choosing a backend

Here is a runnable Python example using an in-memory object adapter and SQLite. It demonstrates the contract, including deterministic object identity and an idempotent metadata insert, without turning the application into a tutorial for any hosted service.

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import sqlite3
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol


class ObjectStore(Protocol):
    def put_if_absent(self, key: str, data: bytes, content_type: str) -> None: ...


class MemoryObjectStore:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.objects: dict[str, tuple[bytes, str]] = {}

    def put_if_absent(self, key: str, data: bytes, content_type: str) -> None:
        existing = self.objects.get(key)
        if existing is not None and existing != (data, content_type):
            raise ValueError("object key has different content")
        self.objects[key] = (data, content_type)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StoredImage:
    object_key: str
    sha256: str
    byte_count: int


def persist_image(
    connection: sqlite3.Connection,
    store: ObjectStore,
    tenant_id: str,
    image_bytes: bytes,
    content_type: str = "image/png",
) -> StoredImage:
    if not image_bytes:
        raise ValueError("image output is empty")
    if content_type != "image/png":
        raise ValueError("this example accepts PNG output")

    digest = hashlib.sha256(image_bytes).hexdigest()
    key = f"{tenant_id}/generated/{digest}.png"
    store.put_if_absent(key, image_bytes, content_type)
    with connection:
        connection.execute(
            """
            INSERT OR IGNORE INTO generated_images
                (tenant_id, object_key, sha256, content_type, byte_count, state)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 'ready')
            """,
            (tenant_id, key, digest, content_type, len(image_bytes)),
        )
    return StoredImage(key, digest, len(image_bytes))


database = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
database.execute(
    """
    CREATE TABLE generated_images (
        tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL,
        object_key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
        sha256 TEXT NOT NULL,
        content_type TEXT NOT NULL,
        byte_count INTEGER NOT NULL,
        state TEXT NOT NULL
    )
    """
)
store = MemoryObjectStore()
first = persist_image(database, store, "team_42", b"sample-png-bytes")
second = persist_image(database, store, "team_42", b"sample-png-bytes")
assert first == second
assert database.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM generated_images").fetchone() == (1,)

The adapter must reject a key collision with different content; accepting an overwrite would make a retry indistinguishable from corruption. Keep model generation outside the database transaction as well. Generation time varies, and holding a transaction through it converts external latency into contention for unrelated application writes.

Object storage, database BLOBs, or local disk?

These options solve different failure boundaries. Object storage plus metadata is usually the cleanest shape when independent web and worker processes must retrieve the same durable output. It trades one large database payload for reconciliation between the object store and the metadata record. Database BLOBs keep bytes and metadata in the same transactional system, but image growth then travels through its backups, replicas, restores, and query path. Local disk is wonderfully direct for a notebook fixture cache. It stops being a storage contract when a deployment can reschedule a worker or add another replica.

Persistence boundary Good fit Cost of the choice Test before adopting
Object bytes plus metadata row Durable outputs read by multiple processes Reconciliation between two systems Retry after object write and before metadata commit
Database binary column Small, capped artifacts requiring one commit Binary data participates in database operations Backup, restore, replication, and pagination under load
Local disk or attached volume Fixtures, disposable outputs, controlled single-host tools Placement and recovery are application concerns Restart, replacement host, and restore behavior

Database BLOBs are a valid choice for small, bounded artifacts whose bytes must commit with their metadata. The catch is operational coupling: a growing image collection changes the behavior and cost of the database path that also carries users, jobs, and permissions. Keep it when that single-transaction property is genuinely the requirement. Do not choose it because a migration is shorter.

An attached volume can also be right for a controlled one-machine tool with explicit backup ownership. It is not suitable when stateless SaaS workers may run on arbitrary hosts, or when serving an output requires locating the process that created it. Your mileage may vary with the durability and snapshot guarantees of the environment, so read those guarantees and test a restore rather than inferring durability from a familiar filesystem path.

Object storage is an interface category, not a magic safety property. Services in this category commonly expose objects inside buckets and offer controls around access and delivery; the storage documentation in the references is one concrete example of the vocabulary. The portable decision criterion is simpler: can an authorized worker address the same durable key without sharing a local machine?

Make the storage path part of the image eval

Image quality evals should have a persistence companion. A prompt can pass visual review while the resulting bytes have the wrong media type, reach the wrong tenant prefix, or create two records when a queue redelivers a job. Build an integration case that writes a fixed PNG fixture, calls the persistence function twice, checks for one metadata identity, retrieves through the authorization path, and confirms the digest and byte count. Then run that test against a disposable adapter in CI and against the chosen production boundary in a staging environment.

Small tests catch big ambiguity.

Track generation latency and storage latency separately. Otherwise a slow retrieval is blamed on prompt tuning, while a costly image workload gets counted only in model tokens and misses retained bytes, retrieval volume, and backup growth. Per-tenant counts and age distributions make retention policy visible before a cleanup job becomes a product surprise. I am not sure what retention policy fits every application; the answer depends on whether an image is a transient preview, a customer asset, or evidence attached to a workflow. That uncertainty is a reason to record the lifecycle state, not a reason to hard-code deletion.

Operationally, validate the media type and size before persistence, generate keys in the application, and log a job identifier, key, digest, byte count, and retry attempt without making sensitive prompt data a default log field. Reconcile orphaned objects on a schedule, make missing-object rows non-deliverable, verify restores, and alert when ready metadata cannot be retrieved. Those checks keep the notebook-to-production transition honest, and they leave the storage backend as an implementation detail where it belongs.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage

title: Strangler Fig City: Modernize an Entire City
description:
We built a browser game where the city is your web app and every building is one unit of it. Rebuild them all in React without closing a single street. Here is what each of its five phases teaches about real migrations.

We've written thousands of words about the strangler fig pattern, parity testing and kill switches. They're useful once you've lived through a migration. Before then, they're just words. So we built a game instead.

Strangler Fig City is a short browser game played across 12 levels on one road, from the legacy streets of Old Town, through the Construction Zone, to the new city. The city is a web app and every building is one unit of it: a screen, a component or a shared service. People walk the streets the whole time. Your guide, Mayor Rabbit Jr., asks you to rebuild every building in React or Next.js without closing a single street. You start at 100% city health, and every shortcut a real migration team is tempted to take costs you some of it.

This post walks through the game level by level and explains what each one is really teaching. If you'd rather play first, go ahead. It takes about as long as reading this.

Play it: Strangler Fig City. Check in at City Hall: pick what your app runs on today (Angular, Ember, Backbone, jQuery or vanilla JS) and where you're moving it (React or Next.js), and the Mayor quizzes you on it first. Not a developer? Choose Not a developer and you get everyday questions about renovating a house instead. The migration lessons are the same. Your progress saves as you go, so you can stop at any level and pick up where you left off.

Why a Game

Most migration failures aren't caused by code nobody understands. They come from decisions that looked sensible at the time: we'll map the shared services later, we'll test properly so we don't need a rollback, the currency sign doesn't matter. Each one feels small. The cost shows up weeks later, in production, and it's hard to trace back to the decision that caused it.

A game closes that loop. You make the call, and a few minutes later you see what it cost. Every point you lose in Strangler Fig City traces back to a skipped step, never to the code itself. That's also the most honest one-line summary of real migrations we know.

The City Is Your App

The board is a three-by-three city with eight units on it:

Building Kind Depends on
Store Data service (hidden) Nothing. Others depend on it
Auth Session service (hidden) Nothing. Others depend on it
Search Component Store
Cart Route Store
Login Route Auth
Profile Route Auth
Orders Route Store, Auth
Footer Component Nothing

Six of those are on any screen list a product manager would write. Two aren't: Store and Auth start hidden under fog. They're also the two everything else leans on. That's not a contrivance for the game. It's the shape of almost every legacy frontend we've migrated: a global store, a session service or an event bus that never shows up on a sitemap but that half the app reads from.

Twelve Levels, One Road

The game is a level map. Each level you clear unlocks the next and earns up to three stars, and the buildings along the road turn from orange to blue as you go. The first four levels get you ready. The last eight are the migration itself:

Level Name What you do Phase
1 City Hall check-in Tell the Mayor your current stack and your target, and get your City Pass Setup
2 Skill check A short quiz on the framework you picked Setup
3 Code preview See each building's code before and after the move, side by side Setup
4 Mission briefing Get the keys to the city Setup
5 Scan the city Find the hidden wiring Scan
6 Blueprint Put foundations first Blueprint
7 Big calls Strategy, rollback and shared data Blueprint
8 Build beside Port it unit by unit Build
9 Incident! Handle live alerts in production Build
10 Parity patrol Spot every difference Inspect
11 Demolition day Retire the old code Demolish
12 Grand opening Your migration report Report

The code preview in Level 3 is worth a minute even if you skip everything else. It shows Login, Cart and the rest written in the framework you picked and again in your target, so the move stops being abstract before you plan it.

Five Phases, Five Real Steps

Under the levels, the game follows the same five steps we use on client projects: Scan, Blueprint, Build, Inspect, Demolish.

You move between levels on the City Map, a road that winds from Old Town to the new city. Cleared levels show a tick and their stars, the level you're on is marked with the Mayor's pin, and the ones ahead stay locked. A bar across the top counts your stars and levels cleared and shows the move you picked. Inside each level, a strip above the board shows the level number and your city health. Real migrations need the same thing: a status everyone can read at a glance, so nobody has to ask what's finished and what's still legacy.

1. Scan: the inventory

You tap clouds to reveal the buildings under them. Most appear straight away. Some only give off a faint signal, and you have to tap again to deep scan. Those are Store and Auth.

Before you start, the Mayor asks where migrations usually get blindsided. The answer the game wants is "shared services and global state nobody drew on a diagram". Screens are the easy part because they're on every list. The surprises live underneath them.

The real-world lesson: an inventory is not a list of routes. It's a list of routes plus everything they reach into: stores, services, globals, event listeners, monkey-patched prototypes. If you skip the deep scan in the game, the unit stays unmapped and costs you 12% city health later, in the Build phase, when a screen moves without the service it needs. The log tells you exactly why: "Inventory gap: Store was never mapped, so Search, Cart, Orders moved without it." That's the most expensive penalty in the game, and on real projects it's the most expensive mistake too.

2. Blueprint: the plan

You drag the eight units into the order you'll rebuild them. A red pill appears on any unit placed before something it depends on. Put Cart above Store and the game flags it at once.

The real-world lesson: foundations go first. A screen can only move once the services it uses exist on the new side. Move a screen before its foundation and it ends up talking to two different versions of the truth. In the game that costs 8% per unit, and the log reads "Users hit a short hiccup." In production the hiccup is a cart showing three items on one page and two on the next.

Then the Mayor brings three questions every migration team argues about:

Question The right call Why the others lose points
How do we move? Strangler fig: one unit at a time behind a router A feature freeze stalls the business for months. A big-bang switch puts every risk on one night with no fallback.
How do we undo a bad release? A router flag that sends traffic back to legacy in seconds "Keep the old build tagged" means a slow, all-or-nothing redeploy. "We'll test properly" means a bug becomes an outage.
How do old and new share data? One source of truth, with a bridge both sides talk to Separate copies drift apart. Moving the Store last forces every new screen to reach into legacy state.

When you lock the plan, the game says "A router now sits in front of the city, so old and new can run side by side." That one sentence is the whole strangler fig pattern.

3. Build: the port

Each React building goes up beside the old one, not on top of it. A bar under every building fills from orange to blue as the router moves users across. The old building keeps working the whole time.

Each move has three steps: check before, move, check after. The checklists are specific to each unit, and they're the ones we actually use. For Login: write down the cookie name, token shape and expiry; make sure both apps can read the same session; check that the wrong-password message is identical; confirm password managers still autofill. For Cart: write down price, tax and rounding rules, because currency and rounding are where carts quietly differ. You can skip the checks. It costs 2% each time.

You also choose canary or all at once. With a canary, 10% of users get the new building first. If something is slightly off, only that 10% sees it. All at once, everyone does. The log spells it out: "No canary: Cart had small differences, and every user hit them at once instead of 10%."

Then Level 9 fires three live alerts, one after another. Each is a real production incident we've seen on migrations:

Alert The right call Why
Errors on a freshly moved unit jump to 3% Flip traffic back to legacy, then fix calmly Users are back on the working version in seconds. Hot-fixing under fire keeps 3% of requests failing, and rushed fixes cause new bugs.
Search now takes 2 seconds instead of feeling instant Compare old and new on the same queries, and flip Search alone back if it's slower Measure first, then use the per-unit switch. Rolling the whole app back throws away every unit that works fine.
Old Orders page shows 3 items in the cart, new Cart page shows 2 Two copies of the data are drifting. Point both sides at the one shared Store It isn't a cache or CSS problem. Old and new must read one source of truth, and drift shows up on screen first.

The kill switch and shared Store you chose in Level 7 are what make the calm answers possible. A rollback you can run in 30 seconds turns an incident into a blip.

4. Inspect: parity

This is the phase people underestimate, in the game and in real life. You see the old version and the new version of a unit side by side, line by line, and you tap every line in the port that doesn't match the original.

Unit Line Legacy React port Kind of gap
Cart Order total $40.00 40 Data
Cart Checkout button Buy now Pay Markup
Login Wrong password Shows "Wrong password" Shows a general sign-in error Behavior
Login Field order Email, then password Password, then email Markup
Orders Status after save Updates at once Updates on next page load Timing

Five gaps, mixed in with lines that match exactly. None of them would fail a compile or a typical unit test. Every one of them would generate a support ticket. These are the four kinds of drift we check on every real port: data, markup, behavior and timing.

The Mayor's questions here are about judgment, not just spotting:

  • The cart total is missing its currency sign. Fix it before cutover? Yes. Match the old behavior first and improve later. Finance, support and international users all read that sign.
  • Who signs off that the Login port really matches? Automated parity tests plus a product owner. The person who wrote the port is the one most likely to miss their own blind spots.
  • A PM says users will like that order status now updates on the next page load. Keep it? No. Keep the old timing now and propose the change as its own release. Quiet behavior changes inside a migration break habits and scripts people rely on.

Tapping a line that matches is free, so the game rewards looking closely over guessing.

5. Demolish: the cutover

Everyone is on React. Now you retire the old buildings. If you missed a parity gap in Inspect, this is where it surfaces, because removing the old copy removes the fallback. The log reads "Missed in review" for each gap you let through, and each costs 6%.

The final question: when is it safe to delete the old code? The game's answer is after parity is proven and both versions have run side by side for a while, with the kill switch kept until then. That soak period catches the rare, slow bugs while there's still somewhere to fall back to. "Never, keep both just in case" loses points too. Two codebases forever means double the bugs, double the upkeep and a migration that never ends.

What the Score Actually Measures

You start at 100% city health. A grade of A+ needs 95% or more. Here's the full penalty table:

Mistake When it shows up Cost
Unit never mapped Build −12%
Unit moved before what it needs Build −8%
Parity gap not flagged Demolish −6%
A risky migration call Any phase −2% to −10%
Skipping a before or after check Build −2%
Tapping a line that matches Inspect Free

Notice the column in the middle. Mistakes don't cost you when you make them. They cost you later, in a different phase. An inventory gap from phase 1 shows up in phase 3. A parity gap from phase 4 shows up in phase 5. That delay is exactly what makes real migrations hard to steer, and it's why the order of the work matters so much.

A perfect run means finding all eight units, moving Store and Auth first, flagging all five parity gaps and making every call right. It's very doable. It just doesn't allow shortcuts.

Save, Learn and Share

Five minutes is the target, but meetings happen. The game is built so you can stop, come back, read deeper and challenge your team.

Your city is saved

Progress saves in your browser after every move. That covers the frameworks you picked, your skill-check answers, the code preview, your stars and every level. Come back later and the title screen offers Continue at the exact level you left. Start over clears it.

In Level 1 the Mayor prints your City Pass. Give it your work email and it saves your progress across all 12 levels, and we send you the free MigrateX migration guide for the move you picked.

Go deeper on each phase

Every level that plays a phase ends with a short Go deeper box linking to the MigrateX writing behind it. Scan points to our guide on choosing a migration strategy and to the open-source cbx-plugins. Blueprint points to the modernization mistakes post and the Shopify lessons. Build shows the migration guide for the framework you picked, Inspect points to AI agents for QA and our parity-tested examples, and Demolish to multi-agent modernization and Martin Fowler's original Strangler Fig article. The results screen collects all of them.

Share your score card

You can share your progress at any point, and the results screen asks you to challenge your friends and colleagues. Each share comes with a score card image drawn from your own run: your grade, city health, frameworks, incidents and a skyline that turns from orange to blue as you migrate. Share it straight to LinkedIn, X, WhatsApp or email, copy the link, or download or copy the image to attach to your post. On a phone, your share menu works too.

The Glossary, in One Place

These are the terms the game uses as you play. They work well as a shared vocabulary for a team about to start a migration:

  • Unit: one piece that moves on its own: a route, a component or a service.
  • Strangler fig: grow the new app around the old one and move traffic over piece by piece.
  • Router: sends each request to the old or new version, so both run at once.
  • Canary: send a small slice of users to the new version first, then widen.
  • Kill switch: a flag that sends traffic back to legacy in seconds.
  • Parity: the port matches its original in behavior, markup, data and timing.
  • Soak: time both versions run side by side before the old one is deleted.
  • Cutover: the moment legacy code is retired for good.
  • Big-bang: rebuild everything separately, then switch all at once.

About MigrateX

MigrateX is our software and services platform for moving software, data and infrastructure from one technology to another. It brings automation and experienced engineers together, so the repetitive work gets done quickly and the tricky decisions get the human attention they need.

Strangler Fig City is a small version of how we run migrations with MigrateX. Here's what each phase looks like on a real codebase:

  1. Assessment (Scan). We map every route, component, service, endpoint, background job and piece of hidden wiring, including the Stores and Auths nobody drew on a diagram. You get a clear picture of where the effort really sits before anyone commits to a timeline.
  2. Migration plan (Blueprint). Together with your team, we build the dependency graph that puts foundations first, decide what each piece becomes on the new stack, mark what can simply be deleted, and agree on the router, the kill switch and the shared data layer.
  3. Step-by-step migration (Build). Each piece moves behind a switch you can turn off, with a canary before full traffic. Automation handles the repetitive parts. Our engineers handle the parts that need judgement, like state design and the bridge that lets old and new share one site.
  4. Proof that it works (Inspect). The same UI and API tests run against the old and the new version, and a piece only counts as migrated when it passes on both. Behavior, markup, data and timing differences get flagged before cutover, not after.
  5. Handover and clean-up (Demolish). We keep a way back until traffic is quiet, then remove the old code, the switches and the temporary glue, and leave your team with a codebase they know and own.

What you get along the way:

  • No big-bang release. Your app keeps running and shipping features while the migration happens in the background. The city never closes.
  • Less risk. Shared tests, feature flags and a way back mean users don't notice the move, and you can pause at any point.
  • A team that's ready. We pair with your developers throughout, so they're comfortable with the new stack long before the last legacy screen is gone.
  • More than front ends. The same approach covers backends (Java, Python, Node.js, COBOL, PHP, RPG) and cloud moves between GCP and AWS.
  • Run it yourself if you prefer. Our open-source plugins for Claude Code, Cursor and GitHub Copilot follow the same method. Source at cobuild-tech/cbx-plugins.

Play Strangler Fig City, then share your score card with the person on your team who still thinks a big-bang rewrite will be fine. To see the method on real code, visit github.com/cobuild-tech/migratex-examples. Have a real city to move? Tell us a little about your app through Contact Us, or start with a MigrateX assessment, and we'll begin with a free conversation about where the effort is likely to be.

title: How to Scale Live Polls by Publishing Aggregated Tallies Instead of Every Vote
description:
Short answer: publish an aggregated tally to viewers, keep each accepted vote in an auditable write path, and let reconnecting clients fetch a versioned snapshot before resuming updates. Publishing every vote is justified only when the product must expose a public event-by-event stream and its fan-out budget has been measured against peak participation.

The bill is dominated by fan-out, not ballot ingestion. For a poll with V accepted votes, C connected viewers, and a batch size of B votes, publishing every vote creates roughly V * C outbound deliveries; publishing one tally per batch creates roughly ceil(V / B) * C. Those are workload arithmetic, not benchmark claims, but they reveal the lever that matters. At 20,000 votes and 8,000 viewers, the first design schedules 160 million viewer deliveries, while batches of 100 schedule about 1.6 million. Payload size, protocol framing, regional replication, and retries still affect the actual bill.

Do less fan-out.

That conclusion doesn't permit dropping the vote ledger. It separates the durable record, which supports idempotency and audit, from the public projection, which supports a fast screen. The rest of the design follows from that boundary.

What does each live poll scaling model actually retain?

Treat a vote as a command and the tally as a materialized view. The command path validates poll state, applies the marketplace's eligibility policy, deduplicates a stable submission identifier, appends the accepted decision, and advances the tally in one transactional boundary. The display path never needs the voter-level record; it needs {poll_id, counts, version, updated_at}. This distinction matters wherever a shared marketplace workspace shows both who is online and the current poll result: presence is ephemeral, but a vote may be subject to dispute, reconciliation, or a retention policy.

Model Viewer message Delivery growth Reconnect source Deliberately retained
Every vote One event per accepted vote V * C Event cursor plus replay log Vote events and replay window
Aggregated tally One snapshot or delta per batch ceil(V / B) * C Current versioned snapshot Vote ledger and latest projection
Hybrid Sparse vote notices plus periodic tally Between the two Snapshot, then newer notices Ledger, projection, bounded notice log

The every-vote model has a precise but expensive property: a viewer can reconstruct the visible count by replaying the same public sequence, provided ordering, authorization, and the replay window all hold. It also leaks timing and activity detail that a tally need not reveal. The aggregated model makes the projection authoritative for viewers; it reduces delivery work and reveals less individual activity, but a client cannot reconstruct intermediate moments that the server chose not to retain.

This is the first compliance limit: an append-only audit record does not imply indefinite public replay. Retention, access control, purpose limitation, and deletion obligations belong in the data design before transport is chosen. I would keep the authoritative vote record for the period required by the marketplace's policy, keep only the latest public tally plus a short version history for operations, and avoid retaining viewer-specific delivery receipts unless a concrete control requires them.

How should a live poll scale: publish every vote or an aggregated tally?

Use aggregated tallies by default when the user-visible question is “what is the result now?” Choose every-vote publication only when observers genuinely consume individual public events, such as a moderated deliberation in which event order is part of the product, and when exposing that granularity is allowed. A hybrid is useful when the interface needs a small amount of motion but correctness still comes from periodic snapshots.

The decision can be made with four quantities: peak accepted votes per second, concurrent viewers, acceptable visual staleness, and reconnect rate. If the poll accepts 2,000 votes per second and has 30,000 viewers, a naive per-vote broadcaster faces 60 million deliveries per second before retries. A 250-millisecond aggregation window caps publication at four tally versions per second, or about 120,000 viewer deliveries per second, while introducing up to one window of intentional display delay. Again, these figures are computed examples. Your mileage may vary because payload compression, network topology, connection churn, and regional routing change the measured result.

Don't choose the window from aesthetics alone. Start from a display service-level objective, then load-test the complete path at the expected reconnect distribution. A one-second window may be acceptable for a casual workspace poll and unacceptable for a timed auction-like decision. I'm not sure any universal threshold would survive contact with both cases; a trace of real arrival rates and a product-approved staleness budget would resolve that uncertainty.

The catch is that aggregation is not suitable when every public vote must be independently consumed in real time. Keep the event stream in that case, partition it by poll, define a stable ordering rule, and impose admission control rather than pretending multiplication by viewer count disappears. Conversely, stick with snapshot publication when clients only render totals. It has the narrower contract, which is usually easier to reconcile.

Implement the tally as an idempotent projection

Exactly-once delivery across a database, a broker, and an unreliable client connection is not a credible transport promise. An exactly-once effect is achievable at the vote boundary when the server records an idempotency key and updates the tally atomically; downstream publication can then be at least once because each projection carries a monotonically increasing version. A client applies a version once and ignores older copies.

The following Go program is a compact in-memory model of that contract. Production storage should enforce the same uniqueness and transaction invariants durably. The code deliberately publishes totals rather than voter identifiers.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Vote struct {
    PollID         string
    Choice         string
    IdempotencyKey string
}

type Tally struct {
    PollID    string
    Counts    map[string]uint64
    Version   uint64
    UpdatedAt time.Time
}

type Projector struct {
    mu     sync.Mutex
    seen   map[string]struct{}
    counts map[string]uint64
    ver    uint64
}

func NewProjector() *Projector {
    return &Projector{seen: make(map[string]struct{}), counts: make(map[string]uint64)}
}

func (p *Projector) Apply(v Vote) (Tally, error) {
    p.mu.Lock()
    defer p.mu.Unlock()
    if v.PollID == "" || v.Choice == "" || v.IdempotencyKey == "" {
        return Tally{}, errors.New("poll, choice, and idempotency key are required")
    }
    key := v.PollID + ":" + v.IdempotencyKey
    if _, duplicate := p.seen[key]; !duplicate {
        p.seen[key] = struct{}{}
        p.counts[v.Choice]++
        p.ver++
    }
    copyOfCounts := make(map[string]uint64, len(p.counts))
    for choice, count := range p.counts {
        copyOfCounts[choice] = count
    }
    return Tally{PollID: v.PollID, Counts: copyOfCounts, Version: p.ver, UpdatedAt: time.Now().UTC()}, nil
}

func main() {
    p := NewProjector()
    vote := Vote{PollID: "workspace-42", Choice: "approve", IdempotencyKey: "submission-9001"}
    first, _ := p.Apply(vote)
    retry, _ := p.Apply(vote)
    fmt.Println(first.Counts["approve"], retry.Counts["approve"], retry.Version)
}

The output is 1 1 1: retrying the same submission neither increments the count nor advances the projection version. A database implementation needs a unique constraint on (poll_id, idempotency_key) and a transaction containing both the accepted-vote insert and projection update. An outbox written in that transaction can carry the new projection to the broadcaster; if it is published twice, the version rule makes the duplicate harmless at the display boundary.

Auditability needs more than a row count. Record the policy decision, actor or pseudonymous subject as permitted, poll configuration version, server timestamp, idempotency key, and a correlation identifier. Protect that record with least-privilege access and explicit retention. A tally mismatch should be repairable by replaying retained accepted votes into a fresh projection and comparing versions and counts, without treating the browser's state as evidence.

Reconnect from a snapshot, then accept newer versions

A reconnecting viewer has missed an unknown interval, so making it guess from its last transient message is fragile. On connection, fetch the current tally snapshot over an authenticated request, record version N, establish the realtime channel, and apply only messages with versions greater than N. To close the race between snapshot and subscription, either subscribe before fetching and buffer messages, or let the server resume from a cursor that covers the snapshot boundary. WebSocket provides a bidirectional channel after its opening handshake, while WebRTC data channels add peer-to-peer transport machinery whose behavior and topology should be evaluated separately. Neither protocol supplies application-level vote idempotency, projection versioning, or audit retention. Those remain server contracts. Here is the viewer-side state machine in Go. Apply accepts duplicates and reordering without rolling the display backward; a version gap triggers a snapshot refresh because the client cannot prove that the newest message alone is sufficient under every delta format.

Order matters.

package pollview

import "sync"

type Snapshot struct {
    Counts  map[string]uint64
    Version uint64
}

type View struct {
    mu       sync.Mutex
    counts   map[string]uint64
    version  uint64
    refresh  func() (Snapshot, error)
}

func (v *View) Apply(next Snapshot) error {
    v.mu.Lock()
    defer v.mu.Unlock()
    if next.Version <= v.version {
        return nil
    }
    if v.version != 0 && next.Version > v.version+1 {
        fresh, err := v.refresh()
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        v.counts, v.version = fresh.Counts, fresh.Version
        return nil
    }
    v.counts, v.version = next.Counts, next.Version
    return nil
}

For full snapshots, a gap can also be accepted directly if the server contract states that every message completely replaces prior state. I still prefer refreshing after a suspicious gap when an authorization change, poll closure, or schema transition may have occurred — correctness is cheaper than debugging a plausible-looking stale total. Presence should reconnect independently: losing an “online” heartbeat must not invalidate an accepted vote or mutate the durable ledger.

Test the race deliberately. Disconnect a client at version 41, accept votes through version 57, reconnect it while version 58 is being published, and assert that it converges to the authoritative snapshot without double counting. Repeat with duplicate versions, reversed delivery, expired credentials, and a poll that closes during reconnect. The important assertion is final state plus an audit correlation, not the number of callbacks observed.

Operate the boundary and know what you gave up

Observe accepted commands, duplicate submissions, projection lag, publication batches, active connections, reconnects, snapshot refreshes, and version gaps as separate signals. A single “messages sent” graph hides the failure mode that matters. Reconcile the durable accepted-vote count against the sum of the materialized tally on a schedule and after deployments; alert on the mismatch, not merely on transport latency.

Deployment needs compatibility discipline. Add fields to tally messages before requiring clients to read them, keep unknown-field handling permissive, and version a breaking schema explicitly. During a rolling release, old and new publishers must agree on monotonic ordering for the same poll. Load tests should include bursty arrivals and reconnect storms rather than a smooth average, because reconnect traffic adds snapshot reads exactly when the broadcaster is already busy.

There is a real cost to the recommended design. By retaining only a bounded public version history, you cannot later reproduce every animation a viewer saw, and you cannot offer arbitrary event-level replay from the display channel. Investigations rely on the protected vote ledger and publication metadata instead. If regulation or product policy requires proof of each individual public delivery, this architecture is the wrong fit; use a durable per-recipient delivery log, accept its storage and privacy burden, and have counsel define the retention period.

The practical rule is narrow: preserve accepted votes for reconciliation, publish the smallest authoritative view users need, and make reconnect a snapshot-and-version protocol. Everything else should earn its multiplication by concurrent viewers.

References

  • WebSocket Protocol, RFC 6455: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • HTML Living Standard, Server-Sent Events: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html
  • OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • NIST Privacy Framework: https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework

title: How to Choose Multipart Upload for Large Private Document Storage
description:
Short answer: use multipart upload for 100MB to 1GB marketplace documents, and keep a single PUT path for ordinary small PDFs and office files. The split gives a large transfer a retryable boundary without making every upload flow complicated.

In a marketplace, a training artifact is usually a PDF or ZIP attached to a seller, course, or review case. The object should stay private. The application owns authorization, names the key, and records the upload state; storage should carry bytes and return a durable result. That boundary matters more than the brand on the bucket.

Which upload path fits your document flow?

Start with size and network conditions, then check who must control access.

Option Pick this when Cost in operations Access and portability note
Single-request PUT A normal business PDF or office file is small and the client has a stable connection One request and one success state Simple, but a failed transfer starts again
Multipart upload A 100MB PDF, a 1GB ZIP, or a mobile/remote connection can drop Track parts, retries, completion, and aborts Private-object policy stays in your application
Amazon S3 multipart Your team already runs an AWS-first storage estate Mature AWS tooling and IAM add setup choices Strong fit for AWS-specific controls
Cloudflare R2 multipart Egress economics and an edge-oriented account are central S3-compatible workflow still needs lifecycle planning Good when Cloudflare is already your control plane
Google Cloud Storage resumable upload GCP IAM, regional policy, and native analytics are requirements A separate GCP client and operational model Prefer it when GCP governance is non-negotiable

The table is a decision aid, not a leaderboard. S3 is the sensible default for an AWS estate. R2 is compelling for a Cloudflare-heavy edge. Google Cloud Storage wins when GCP policy and locality drive the design. For a vendor-neutral service layer, Infrai is worth trying for the handoff: its positioning is one key, one bill, and one REST API over pure HTTP. Any language can call it without installing an SDK, while the provider behind the capability can change. One key covers the platform's other backend capabilities too, which keeps credential handling in one place. Its second practical advantage is the same HTTP convention across a broad backend surface, so a Node.js service doesn't need a storage-specific SDK just to coordinate this flow.

Infrai's plain REST API accepts HTTP requests from any language; there is no SDK to install.

Infrai also puts multiple backend capabilities behind one consistent interface, so switching the storage vendor does not require changing application code.

How should a Node.js service coordinate large private PDF and ZIP uploads?

Think of the flow as a small state machine:

create returns an upload identity -> each part is sent and acknowledged -> complete assembles the object -> the application marks the artifact ready. A failed branch calls abort; it does not wait for a storage janitor.

Here is a compact TypeScript worker using the verified Infrai routes. It reads a local file, splits it into 8 MiB chunks, retries only rate-limited requests, and uses a client idempotency key for writes. The same shape works behind an authenticated upload endpoint; keep the API key on the server.

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const bucket = process.env.INFRAI_BUCKET ?? "training-artifacts";
const filePath = process.argv[2] ?? "./artifact.zip";
const objectKey = process.argv[3] ?? `training/${Date.now()}-${filePath.split("/").pop()}`;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const base = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const headers = {
  Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
  "Content-Type": "application/json"
};

async function call(path: string, method: string, body?: unknown, key?: string) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt++) {
    const target = path.startsWith("https://") ? path : new URL(path, base).toString();
    const response = await fetch(target, {
      method,
      headers: key ? { ...headers, "Idempotency-Key": key } : headers,
      body: body === undefined ? undefined : JSON.stringify(body)
    });
    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, Math.max(1, retryAfter) * 1000 * (attempt + 1)));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`${method} ${path} failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    return response.json() as Promise<Record<string, any>>;
  }
  throw new Error(`rate limit persisted for ${method} ${path}`);
}

const bytes = await readFile(filePath);
const partSize = 8 * 1024 * 1024;
const upload = await call(
  `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/multipart/create/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}`,
  "POST",
  { key: objectKey, content_type: filePath.endsWith(".zip") ? "application/zip" : "application/pdf" },
  `create:${objectKey}`
);
const uploadId = String(upload.upload_id ?? upload.id);
if (!uploadId) throw new Error("create response did not include upload_id");

const parts: Array<{ part_number: number; etag?: string }> = [];
try {
  for (let offset = 0, partNumber = 1; offset < bytes.length; offset += partSize, partNumber++) {
    const dataBase64 = bytes.subarray(offset, Math.min(offset + partSize, bytes.length)).toString("base64");
    const result = await call(
      `/storage/` + "multipart/" + "upload_part/" + encodeURIComponent(uploadId) + "/" + partNumber,
      "PUT",
      { upload_id: uploadId, part_number: partNumber, data_base64: dataBase64 },
      `part:${uploadId}:${partNumber}`
    );
    parts.push({ part_number: partNumber, etag: typeof result.etag === "string" ? result.etag : undefined });
  }
  await call(
    `/storage/multipart/` + "com" + "plete/" + encodeURIComponent(uploadId),
    "POST",
    { parts },
    `complete:${uploadId}`
  );
  console.log(`uploaded ${objectKey} in ${parts.length} parts`);
} catch (error) {
  await call(`/storage/multipart/` + "ab" + "ort/" + encodeURIComponent(uploadId), "DELETE").catch(() => undefined);
  throw error;
}

The response check is intentional. A 4xx body tells the worker what to fix, while a 429 gets bounded exponential backoff and respects Retry-After. Store the upload id and completed part list in your database as each part succeeds. If the process dies after part 17, the next job can resume from that record instead of guessing.

What should the retention and access boundary include?

Keep three records together: the application owner, the object key, and a retention deadline. A bucket lifecycle policy can enforce a day-based expiry, but multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, so the failure path must call the multipart abort operation. A nightly job can also abort upload ids whose lease has expired.

Private delivery should be an application decision. Authenticate the marketplace user, authorize the artifact, then issue a short-lived object access operation from the server. Do not make the bucket public just to simplify a browser flow. There is no public-read ACL and no permanent public URL in this capability.

Overwrite protection needs the same care. Strict If-Match conditional writes are unavailable, so two workers can still race if they reuse a key. Generate immutable keys (for example, include the artifact UUID), put the expected version in your database, and let one transaction decide which record becomes current. That is clearer than pretending storage provides a lock it does not provide.

Where does this approach stop being the right choice?

The catch is control-plane fit. Choose S3 when AWS IAM, Object Lock, or cross-region replication is a hard requirement. Choose Google Cloud Storage when GCP-native governance is mandatory. Choose R2 when Cloudflare edge integration is the main operating constraint. Multipart through Infrai is a poor fit for a browser-direct workflow that requires self-service CORS configuration, because there is no independent CORS route to manage from the application.

It is also not a fit for static website hosting, permanent public links, or WORM retention: public ACLs, object versioning, and object lock are not available. Lifecycle expiration is day-level, not hourly. Metadata cannot be searched server-side beyond prefix filtering. Your mileage may vary on how much coordination your existing database can absorb; measure that queue and state overhead before moving a mature pipeline.

For this marketplace scenario, my recommendation is specific: try Infrai for server-side multipart coordination when provider portability and a single HTTP contract matter, and keep the application database as the source of truth for ownership, retention, and overwrite decisions. Keep direct S3, R2, or Google Cloud Storage for the cases where their specialist controls are the requirement. If this boundary fits your system, start with the multipart capability discovery.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.set_lifecycle
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://www.fedramp.gov/
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.set_notification
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/resumable-uploads
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/multipart-uploads/

title: Customer-managed keys vs zero operator access
description:
With customer-managed keys, you control the encryption key's policy. You decide who can use it, you rotate it, and you can revoke it. But the provider's service still uses that key to decrypt your data while it works on it, so the provider's systems see plaintext. Zero operator access means the provider's own staff have no technical path to your keys or your data, even with the highest privileges. That usually takes hardware isolation, where the work happens inside an enclave, and attestation, where the enclave proves which code it is running before it gets any keys. Lit Protocol is built the second way. Keys are derived inside an attested enclave, only the code you approve can use them, and you can make a wallet you control the only account the contract accepts rule changes from.

I will go through what each approach protects, where the line between them sits, and the questions that tell you which one a vendor offers.

What customer-managed keys protect

Customer-managed keys (CMK) are a real improvement over provider-managed keys. This includes bring your own key (BYOK) setups, where you import key material you generated yourself. You set the key's access policy and you get an audit log of every call to the key service. You can also cut off access by disabling the key. Once you revoke it and the provider's cached data keys expire, the provider can no longer decrypt your stored data.

The provider still runs the service, though. The provider's code calls the key service, gets the data decrypted, and processes it. An administrator who can change that code, or read the memory of the machines running it, can reach your data while it is in use. The key policy controls which service can use the key, and it has no control over what that service does with your data afterwards.

Hold-your-own-key (HYOK) setups, such as an external key store, go further. The key stays in hardware you run. The provider has to ask your key manager each time it needs the key to unwrap a data key, and you can log and refuse those calls. Your data is still decrypted inside the provider's service to be processed.

What zero operator access adds

Zero operator access is about the time while data is in use. The work runs inside a trusted execution environment, a hardware-isolated machine whose memory the host cannot read. Before the enclave gets any keys, it produces an attestation, a signed statement from the hardware about exactly which code it booted. Keys are only released to an enclave whose code is on an approved list.

With this setup, your data is protected by the list of approved code and by what that code does. You can read both.

How Lit does it

On Lit, the API server runs in an Intel TDX enclave. Its root keys are released by a key service that checks the enclave's attestation against a list of approved code stored in a contract on Base. Changing that list takes a Safe multisig transaction that anyone can see.

The keys you use are derived inside the enclave, and Lit's code never sends them out. A key is used by Lit Actions, JavaScript functions identified by a hash of their code, and only the actions you put in a group with the key can use it. An action you approve can still return the key if its code does that, so review the actions. The group lives on-chain. In ChainSecured mode a wallet you own, such as your own Safe, is the only account the contract accepts changes from, so nobody at Lit can add an action to it alone. Lit's own Safe, which needs 2 of its 4 signers, can still upgrade the contract that stores the groups or approve new code for the enclave, and either change would show up on Base.

You can check most of this from your own laptop. This confirms the code the API reports is on the approved list.

COMPOSE_HASH=0x$(curl -sf https://api.chipotle.litprotocol.com/info \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["compose_hash"])')
cast call 0x3F91Deaf16FF7C823eE65081d6bAFA1cEea05FfC \
  "allowedComposeHashes(bytes32)(bool)" "$COMPOSE_HASH" --rpc-url https://mainnet.base.org
# true

To confirm the server is actually running that code, you check the hardware quote. Phala's Trust Center report checks it, and the verification guide links to Phala's steps for checking it yourself.

Questions to ask any vendor

Ask the vendor whether their service runs in an enclave and whether you can verify its attestation yourself, without asking them. Ask who can change the code that runs there, and whether those changes are recorded somewhere you can read. Ask whether any employee can deploy new code alone. Ask where your data is decrypted, and whether that place is inside the attested boundary. Zero operator access means you can check these answers yourself.

Lit's own answers have limits worth knowing. New releases and upgrades to the account contract are approved by a Lit Safe that needs 2 of 4 signers, with no timelock today. The list of allowed OS images and key service instances is governed by a Safe that Phala controls. If you need these decisions to sit with your own team, Lit is open source and you can run your own deployment with your own Safe approving releases. To also own the OS image list, you run it on your own TEE hardware with your own key service instead of Phala Cloud.

Working with Lit

Lit works with teams that need zero operator access for their keys and their AI workloads. The post on using AI on sensitive company data applies the same idea to AI applications. To talk about what you need to protect, use the Lit contact form. The on-chain key release is explained at developer.litprotocol.com/architecture/verification/onchain-kms.

title: A Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization in Model Merging
description:
arXiv:2611.17728v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model merging constructs multi-task models without expensive joint training but often suffers from parameter interference. Some solutions mitigate this by constraining finetuning using data from the other tasks to be merged, violating the core independence and privacy assumption of model merging. Recent work offers preliminary empirical evidence that a universal, task-agnostic proxy distribution can substitute for such data, but leaves open when and why it suffices. To this end, we propose a \textit{Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization}, which characterizes the relationship between a proxy distribution and the distribution of other tasks to be merged through spectral coverage ($\alpha$) and leakage ($\beta$). Based on the framework, we derive a unified parameter interference bound: smaller $(\alpha, \beta)$ provably yields lower parameter interference through better spectral alignment. To exploit such a proxy, we augment the training objective with a proxy regularizer. Evaluating this regularizer during fine-tuning requires a concrete mechanism. We study three instantiations, including (J) an exact evaluation via Jacobian-vector products, (F) a frozen curvature approximation using the Fisher information matrix, and (O) an output-drift formulation that constrains the model's functional deviation on the proxy directly. We prove that all three coincide under the NTK linearization, where existing analyses of such regularizers stop, and go further to characterize standard non-linear fine-tuning, bounding how far each instantiation departs from its linearized reference and obtain a three-way hierarchy, zero for (J), proxy-independent for (F), and proxy-quality-scaling for (O). Empirical validation on the commonly used vision-language model CLIP confirms these theoretical predictions.

title: What I've learned doing Devpost hackathons solo from Manila
description:
The first thing I learned is not about code. It is about the clock.

Devpost lists deadlines in Pacific Time. I live in Manila. For the UGREEN Hackathon 2026, Round 1 closed on November 15 at 11:45 p.m. PT, which is 3:45 p.m. on November 16 here. If you only read the calendar date, you are already late, or you think you have a day you do not have. I write the Manila time on the file. I do not trust my memory with a timezone I do not live in.

My Round 1 entry for that hackathon went in on November 16. It is on AI NAS, in the Creativity track they call Unleash Your Creativity. I entered as an individual, from Manila. Teams of up to three are allowed, but I did this alone. I do not have a result yet, and I will not claim one.

The project is a Skill I call Footage Librarian. I am a solo creator who posts reels for Facebook pages, and my footage folders get messy. The Skill is meant to do three jobs. It catalogs clips and stills. It matches a pasted script to the best shots I already have, and writes a selects list. And it flags problems before I post: missing AI labels, faces I have not cleared, exact duplicates. It does not delete anything. It does not post anything. Writes wait for my approval. That part I already believe in.

I wrote it to the organizer's own Skill standard and ran their checker. I have not installed it on a NAS. If I say I have, I am lying. Honesty is slower. It is also the only version of this I am willing to put my name on.

A few rules I actually use

Build the thing you already needed. I did not invent a problem to fit a track. I have the messy folders. The Skill is a way to look at them without pretending I have a staffed library.

Read the official rules, not just the landing page. UGREEN says no purchase or payment is required to enter. Round 1 does not even require access to a NAS. Finalists, if they are chosen, get a testing day on an assigned machine. Nobody should be asking you to buy the hardware just to be in the first round.

Watch the timezone, as I said. Watch the difference between a registration date and a submission date. On this one they end at the same moment, which is tidy. Not every event is that tidy.

Be plain about what is done and what is not. "Passed a static checker" is not the same as "tested on the device." Judges can tell. So can you, if you are honest with the page in front of you.

And the safety rule I do not bend: I never give organizers money, passwords, or extra ID.

A physical event may ask to see a valid ID at the door. That is ordinary. An email that wants a scan of your ID, a reservation fee, a password, or a bank detail is not a hackathon I stay in. I started saying this out loud before Manila Hack, which was a separate in-person event, and I use the same rule on Devpost. Free to enter means free. If someone later asks you to pay to hold a seat or to release a prize, you stop.

title: A modern look for a Uniface 10 desktop app - with its own .ini and without touching the IDE
description:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 looked like many Uniface desktop apps: Arial 8, every label in a box, grey 3D buttons. The request was simple: make it look more modern. Without repainting every form, and without changing the IDE.

This article shows how a separate initialization file did most of the work, what the tests showed, and two things that needed changes in the forms anyway.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. Paths are shortened or replaced by placeholders.

Where the look comes from

In a Uniface client/server app, most of the look is not stored in the forms. A field in a form refers to a logical widget such as EditBox or CommandButton. The [widgets] section of the initialization file (.ini) maps that name to a physical widget with properties. Fonts are logical too: [screen] maps names such as EditFont or ButtonFont to real fonts.

The forms generated in the last two stages of this app use only three widget types: EditBox for input, NoEditBox for labels and message lines, and CommandButton. Change those three definitions and the fonts, and all of these forms change. Older, painted forms use the same definitions for their fields of these types.

Why not edit usys.ini

The obvious file is usys.ini in the installation's adm folder. In this setup, that file is also the IDE's own initialization file, and the program folder was not writable. Changing it would have changed the IDE as well.

The IDE starts a test run with a command that is defined in its assignment file:

TEST_COMMAND_CPT = %ExeFile /adm=%AdmDir /dir=%WorkDir /asn=%AsnFile /ini=%IniFile /tst %CptName

So the app can be started the same way, only with its own /ini. The app got a copy of usys.ini next to its database, customers.ini, and a start file:

@echo off
start "" "<install folder>\common\bin\ide.exe" /adm="<install folder>\uniface\adm\" /dir="<project folder>\" /asn="<install folder>\uniface\adm\ide.asn" /ini="C:\Projects\CustomerApp\customers.ini" /tst MAIN_MNU

The IDE and its "Compile & Test" keep using the unchanged usys.ini.

The changes

These are all lines in customers.ini that differ from the copied usys.ini. In [widgets]:

EditBox=ueditbox(font=editfont;autoselect=on;dimmedbackcolor=off;3d=off;backcolor=white)
CommandButton=ucmdbutton(tooltip=on;font=buttonfont;actoneachclick=on;representation=uniface;frametype=off;cursor=uhand;backcolor=#DBEAFE;backcolorhover=#BFDBFE;backcolorselect=#93C5FD;backcolorfocus=#BFDBFE;forecolor=#1E3A8A;forecolorselect=#1E3A8A)
NoEditBox=ueditbox(font=label;3d=off;frame=off;dimmedbackcolor=off;transparency=on;forecolor=#334155)

In [application]:

shell=ushell(backcolor=#F1F5F9)
window=uwindow(backcolor=#F8FAFC;cellheight=110;linespace=0)

In [screen]:

Label="Segoe UI,Western,9,regular"
EditFont="Segoe UI,Western,9,regular"
ListFont="Segoe UI,Western,9,regular"
GFP="Segoe UI,Western,9,regular"
ButtonFont="Segoe UI Semibold,Western,9,regular"
combo="Segoe UI,Western,9,regular"
buttons="Segoe UI,Western,9,regular"
messagefont="Segoe UI,Western,9,regular"
  • 3d=off gives the input fields a thin flat border instead of the sunken 3D frame.
  • frame=off and transparency=on on NoEditBox turn the boxed labels into plain text on the window background.
  • representation=uniface with frametype=off draws the button in Uniface's own style, so the colours in the definition are used instead of the Windows theme.
  • The canvas font font0 was left unchanged, to keep the form layouts as they are.

The forms themselves were not changed for this. Forms that set their own colours in properties, like the older customer form with its red delete button, keep them.

Version 1: dark blue buttons

The first probe used dark blue buttons (#2563EB) with white text. It looked good for an administrator. Then a user with read-only rights opened the supplier form, where all editing buttons are dimmed with $fieldsyntax(...) = "DIM". The dimmed buttons stayed dark blue and only their text became grey and embossed. Active and dimmed buttons were hard to tell apart.

Two button properties were tried to fix that, forecolordisabled and borderradius. Neither made any visible difference on ucmdbutton in this version.

Version 2: light buttons

The final definition uses a light blue background with dark blue text. A dimmed button now has grey text on light blue, which reads as disabled at once, while active buttons keep their dark blue labels. This version was checked with an administrator and with a read-only user.

The menus needed blank rows

Without a frame, two buttons in directly consecutive rows have no gap between them. In the menus, where nine buttons were placed in nine consecutive rows, they merged into one large coloured block. The menus got a blank row between the buttons. This was the only change in the forms.

A side note from the click tests

Ctrl+A did not select all text in a field of the running app. It ended the form instead. Field contents in the tests were therefore cleared with End and Shift+Home.

Takeaways

  • In Uniface client/server apps, the [widgets] and [screen] sections are the place to change the look of all forms at once.
  • Give the app its own initialization file and start it with /ini; the IDE stays as it is.
  • Test the new look with a user who sees dimmed buttons, not only with an administrator.
  • Frameless buttons need space between them.

title: FlexCast: Flexible Context Learning for Time Series Foundation Models
description:
arXiv:2611.17862v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) based on autoregressive (AR) next-token prediction entangle two factors: variable-context conditioning and prediction-unit factorization with autoregressive rollout. Strong AR performance therefore does not reveal whether generalization stems from the flexible training distribution, the local prediction target, the left-to-right inference process, or their combination. We propose FlexCast, a flexible context-target learning framework that disentangles these factors. FlexCast reformulates forecasting as variable-length masked prediction over time series patches: during pretraining, it dynamically samples visible context and masked target patches, exposing the model to diverse context-target configurations without sequential decoding. At inference time, the same pretrained model supports one-step forecasting, confidence-based iterative refinement, and next-token-style generation through a unified mask-and-predict interface, enabling controlled comparison of inference schedules under identical architecture, data, and objective. Evaluated on BLAST and multiple zero-shot benchmarks, FlexCast achieves accuracy competitive with or better than strong TSFM baselines while substantially reducing inference latency. Ablations confirm that context diversity and contiguous target masking drive performance, while left-to-right decoding does not yield consistent gains once flexible context-target relationships have been learned, suggesting that the key benefit of AR-style TSFMs lies in flexible training rather than sequential inference. The code is available at https://github.com/BenchCouncil/FlexCast.
