title: See what your agent sees, and keep your Terminals in tabs
description:
When an agent takes a screenshot through the browser or computer tools, this is what comes back to your terminal: a line of text. "Successfully captured screenshot," a size, an ID. The picture itself went to the agent. You never see it.

I ran into why that matters while an agent was debugging a desktop app. The app's window was on my other monitor, so every screenshot showed something else, and the agent kept describing a window it had never seen. From the terminal there was nothing to notice. I could only guess.

PonyMux 0.18 adds Agent View. When an agent takes a screenshot of a browser or your screen, or reads an image, the picture now shows up in a small window over its Terminal, and in the Inspector, where you can flip back through the last 20. It also lets you show your Terminals as tabs above the terminal instead of a column, and it adds a pace mark to the usage card so you can tell when you are burning through a plan too fast. macOS and Windows each have their own 0.18.0.

What does Agent View show?

The screenshots and images your agent receives from its tools: a browser it is driving, your screen when it uses computer use, or an image file it reads. Not the files it hands you at the end. For those there are outputs and links.

A small window opens in the corner of the Terminal while the agent works. Rest the pointer on it for the counter and the previous and next buttons. Select the picture and it opens larger, and the arrow keys step through the last 20. A tall screenshot shows its top and fades out at the bottom instead of making the window as tall as the page.

With the picture in view, the wrong-monitor case is obvious at a glance, and so is the fix: tell the agent to capture the other display.

Nothing is saved to disk. PonyMux keeps the pictures in memory, and when you open a conversation it reads its recent ones back from the transcript. Turn the floating window off with Show Agent View automatically in Settings → General and the pictures wait in the Inspector instead.

The agent already had eyes. I wanted a seat next to it.

Why tabs?

Because a column is a list, and a tab bar is a row of names you can read at a glance.

I wrote the column first and I still like it for a pile of agents. But a lot of people run a handful of sessions and want the whole width for the terminal. The complaint is old and it keeps coming back: tabs that all read "claude," and no way to tell which session is which. A tab here carries the Terminal's name, a status icon, and a hover card with the process, the Folder and List it lives in, and what it is waiting for.

Turn it on with ⌥⌘T on macOS or Ctrl+Shift+T on Windows, or with the layout switch. Drag tabs to reorder them. When they run out of room, the ⌄ at the end lists every Terminal in the collection, with a search box once there are more than 12.

Tabs are for All Terminals, Agents, and your Lists. Archive, Trash, and Search stay a column. Every collection also gets a header now, with its name, Select All, the layout switch, and a New Terminal button.

How do I know I am ahead of my usage?

Open a usage card and each window is a row of equal segments with a thin mark. The mark is where an even pace would have you by now. It follows the clock, and it turns to a warning colour when your usage is more than one percentage point past it.

People ask for this in other places too. There are requests to show the live weekly percentage and the reset time in the CLI and to put them in the status line, and a small crowd of status line scripts that draw a bar. A percentage on its own tells you how much is gone. It doesn't tell you whether that is too much for a Tuesday.

A 5-hour window gets one segment per hour, a 7-day window one per day. For Grok, a period that has ended now shows an unknown percent instead of a misleading 0%.

Can I check this from my phone?

Yes. Remote Control shows the same pictures, with a swipe between them, and has a usage panel that answers with that computer's own numbers for Claude Code, Codex, and Grok. The pictures are fetched from your computer when you look at them, and the service doesn't keep them.

What else is in 0.18?

Archive and Trash get date headings once they hold more than 10 Terminals: Today, Yesterday, Previous 7 days, and so on. Hover a Terminal there to see exactly when it went in. If you drag Terminals onto Archive or Trash, PonyMux now lists the ones that will change first, and marks the ones that are still running.

If you don't like the card that opens when you rest the pointer on a Terminal, turn it off in Settings → General.

On Windows, the update button opens a dialog with what changed in the new version and how many running agents the restart will end, and the ≡ menu is now in three groups with a Window menu for Debug Log.

Start with Agent View and Show Terminals as tabs. The usage pace is explained in Usage limits.

PonyMux is free for macOS and Windows: download it.

title: Your API URL lives in 3 dashboards. Which copy is right?
description:
Most teams do not plan to spread one app across three services. It happens a service at a time, and then the same environment variable has to be set in every place the app runs.

The Twelve-Factor App method puts config in the environment, apart from code, and asks you to keep development, staging and production as similar as possible. A database address is config too. The test it suggests is simple: your codebase should be openable to anyone without exposing a credential.
Sooner or later one copy drifts. An API URL that was updated in two dashboards but not the third. A key that was rotated in one place and left alone in two others. Nobody broke anything on purpose. The change was just made three times.

How to check it in 5 minutes:

  1. List the variables of each service in each environment.
  2. Compare them line by line.
  3. Any difference you cannot explain is drift.

How to reduce it: one source of truth for config, and rotate secrets from one place.
Source: The Twelve-Factor App, sections "Config" and "Dev/prod parity" (12factor.net).
Save this for your next deploy, and send it to the teammate who owns your environment variables.

title: Projeto de Banco de Dados - Modelo Conceitual
description:
Como um processo padrão na engenharia, a modelagem de um banco de dados torna-se indispensável para mitigar problemas em sua construção. Antes de desenvolvê-lo e alimentá-lo com informações, é fundamental planejar sua estrutura e como o mundo real será representado por meio dos dados. A etapa de modelagem de dados consiste no planejamento estrutural do sistema, a fim de garantir que a representação seja precisa e eficiente, padronizando a forma como os dados são descritos.

De forma complementar, os modelos de dados atuam como ferramentas que ilustram como as estruturas de suporte aos processos de negócio serão construídas, além de detalharem a organização dessas informações e os relacionamentos estabelecidos entre elas. Dessa maneira, a modelagem de dados distingue-se do modelo de dados porque a primeira refere-se ao processo de criação, enquanto o segundo constitui o produto final.
A construção efetiva de um banco de dados passa por processos de especificação que vão de modelos mais abstratos a mais detalhados. Os conceitos e as necessidades do sistema são estruturados para que possam ser validados com os usuários em um nível compreensível, mas também apresentam regras definidas e maior complexidade para que os analistas possam consolidá-los.

O projeto deve iniciar com a análise de requisitos, levantados por meio de reuniões com diversos grupos de interesse. Esses encontros têm como objetivo extrair informações sobre o armazenamento exigido pelas aplicações, bem como identificar as operações mais frequentes que demandam otimização. Posteriormente, utilizam-se essas informações para construir o projeto conceitual, contemplando os requisitos validados pelos usuários. Esses modelos — denominados modelos de dados de alto nível, conceituais ou semânticos — são elaborados de forma abstrata e independente de tecnologias específicas, pois têm maior proximidade com os usuários de negócio e facilitam o entendimento.

Subsequentemente, ocorre a fase de construção do projeto lógico do banco de dados. Essa etapa consiste no refinamento do modelo conceitual anterior para abranger maiores detalhes, originando o modelo de dados lógico, também denominado representativo ou representacional. Nesse nível, os conceitos ainda podem ser compreendidos pelos usuários de negócio, mas já refletem a estrutura de organização dos dados. Assim, a documentação é preparada para ser mapeada no SGBD escolhido, embora ainda oculte os detalhes físicos de armazenamento em disco. Ramakrishnan e Gehrke afirmam que essa é uma etapa apropriada para adoção de refinamento dos modelos, revisando a qualidade do que já foi produzido.

Na etapa seguinte, a etapa de projeto físico de banco de dados, o modelo produzido anteriormente é traduzido em um modelo de baixo nível, também denominado modelo físico. Esse modelo deve descrever a estrutura do banco de dados de modo próximo a como os dados serão armazenados, de forma mais técnica, incluindo detalhes de acesso físico, desempenho, armazenamento, partições. Para a construção desse modelo, já se deve ter como base o SGBD específico e as estruturas técnicas para implementação. Por fim, o fluxo conclui-se com o desenvolvimento do aplicativo que consumirá os dados armazenados, considerando aspectos como segurança e permissões de visualização por perfil de usuário.

Modelo Entidade Relacionamento

O modelo entidade-relacionamento, ou modelo ER, tem como base a estruturação de um conjunto de entidades e seus relacionamentos a fim de descrever o contexto, ou minimundo. As notações mais comuns para representar graficamente o modelo ER se dão a partir dos diagramas ER, nos quais os mais frequentemente utilizados são denominados Pé de Galinha (Crow's Foot), Peter Chen, IDEF1X, Barker e UML. Cada estilo varia na forma como representa as entidades, os atributos e as cardinalidades dos relacionamentos.

Nesse contexto, as entidades são os elementos fundamentais do diagrama, representando os objetos, sejam eles concretos ou conceitos abstratos do mundo real. A notação de Peter Chen é a representação clássica e original do modelo entidade-relacionamento, muito utilizada no meio acadêmico e na fase conceitual. Ela ilustra entidades como retângulos, atributos como elipses e relacionamentos como losangos conectados por linhas com números ou letras (1, N, M) para indicação das cardinalidades. Complementarmente, cada entidade possui atributos, ou propriedades que descrevem suas características específicas.

Os relacionamentos entre duas entidades é estruturada a partir de representações na forma de losangos ligando os retângulos e seus atributos que representam as entidades e suas características. Outra representação comumente utilizada é sem a indicação dos atributos, omitindo-os para que não haja sobrecarga visual. Os relacionamentos também podem ser apresentados de forma auto-relacionada ou relacionamento recursivo, ocorrendo quando as ocorrências de uma entidade se relacionam com outras ocorrências dessa mesma entidade.

Classificação dos Atributos

No contexto de Modelagem de Dados, ou Modelo Entidade-Relacionamento, os atributos (características que descrevem a entidade) são classicamente divididos em quatro categorias principais e outras variações importantes. Os simples, ou atômicos, não podem ser divididos em partes menores e representam um único valor elementar (ex: CPF ou Idade). Os compostos podem ser divididos em subatributos com significados próprios (ex: Endereço, dividido em Rua, Número e CEP). Os multivalorados podem ter um conjunto de múltiplos valores para uma mesma instância de entidade (ex: Telefones de um mesmo cliente), diferente dos monovalorados, que possuem apenas um único valor para cada instância.

Outras variações importantes são os atributos-chave (ou identificadores), os derivados e os armazenados. Os atributos-chave identificam de forma única cada instância de uma entidade, impedindo valores repetidos (ex.: Matrícula ou ID). Embora atuem como chaves primárias, no modelo ER eles são chamados apenas de chaves ou identificadores, comportando-se como chaves candidatas — diferentemente do modelo relacional, que formaliza o conceito de 'chave primária'.

Já o atributo derivado consolida um valor não armazenado fisicamente, mas calculado a partir de outros dados (ex.: Idade, obtida pela data de nascimento e pela data atual). O atributo armazenado tem seu valor efetivamente gravado no banco de dados (ex.: Data de Nascimento). Os atributos descritivos têm a intenção de descrever as características de determinada entidade e o atributo nominativo é usado para identificar a entidade. Por fim, o atributo referencial não se comporta como atributo da entidade, mas sim do relacionamento entre as entidades, fornecendo informações sobre as ligações entre elas.

Cardinalidade dos relacionamentos

A cardinalidade em banco de dados define a quantidade mínima e máxima de ocorrências de uma entidade que podem se associar a outra dentro de um relacionamento. Ela funciona como uma tradução direta das regras de negócio para o Diagrama Entidade-Relacionamento (DER) e garante que o mundo real seja representado corretamente nas tabelas do sistema.

Na prática, a cardinalidade é dividida em dois aspectos fundamentais: a cardinalidade máxima e a cardinalidade mínima. A cardinalidade máxima indica o limite superior de registros que podem se relacionar, respondendo à pergunta de quantos elementos no máximo participam daquela ligação. Já a cardinalidade mínima aponta a obrigatoriedade do relacionamento, definindo se a associação é opcional, representada pelo número zero, ou obrigatória, representada pelo número um.

O relacionamento um para um (1:1) ocorre quando um registro de uma tabela A pode estar ligado a no máximo um registro de uma tabela B, e vice-versa. Um exemplo clássico é a relação entre um funcionário e seu crachá de identificação exclusivo, onde cada pessoa possui apenas um crachá ativo e cada crachá pertence a somente um trabalhador. Na implementação no banco de dados, a chave primária de uma das tabelas costuma ser usada como chave estrangeira para a outra, geralmente aplicando uma restrição de unicidade para impedir duplicidade.

O relacionamento um para muitos (1:N) é o mais comum nos sistemas e acontece quando um registro da tabela A pode se associar a vários registros da tabela B, mas cada registro da tabela B está ligado a apenas um registro da tabela A. A representação pode ser contextualizada na relação entre um cliente e seus pedidos em uma loja virtual, pois um único cliente pode fazer dezenas de compras ao longo do tempo, mas cada pedido específico pertence a um único comprador. No modelo relacional, esse cenário é resolvido colocando a chave primária do lado “um” como chave estrangeira na tabela do lado “muitos”.

O relacionamento muitos para muitos (N:N) acontece quando vários registros da tabela A podem se conectar a vários registros da tabela B simultaneamente. Um bom exemplo é a ligação entre alunos e disciplinas em uma faculdade, já que um estudante se matricula em várias matérias e cada matéria possui diversos estudantes inscritos. Como os bancos de dados relacionais não suportam essa ligação diretamente entre as duas tabelas, cria-se uma terceira tabela intermediária, conhecida como tabela associativa, que recebe as chaves primárias das duas tabelas originais para organizar as combinações.

A leitura de um Diagrama Entidade-Relacionamento exige atenção ao posicionamento dos símbolos, pois existem duas convenções visuais muito comuns no mercado: a notação de Peter Chen (com parênteses) e a notação Pé de Galinha (Crow's Foot). Na notação de Peter Chen, a leitura é feita cruzando as entidades e olhando para a extremidade oposta da linha. Para ler a relação da entidade A para a entidade B, você parte do nome da entidade A, passa pelo verbo do losango de relacionamento e lê o par de números que está encostado na entidade B. Por exemplo, se entre Cliente e Pedido houver o par (0,N) encostado em Pedido, lê-se: "Um Cliente pode realizar no mínimo zero e no máximo vários Pedidos". Fazendo o caminho inverso, se houver (1,1) encostado em Cliente, lê-se: "Um Pedido pertence a, no mínimo, um e, no máximo, um Cliente".

Na notação Pé de Galinha (Crow's Foot), muito utilizada em ferramentas modernas como MySQL Workbench e brModelo (em modo lógico), os números são substituídos por símbolos gráficos na ponta das linhas. Um traço vertical (|) significa "um", um círculo (O) significa "zero" e três linhas abertas formando um pé de galinha (<) significam "muitos". A leitura segue a mesma direção cruzada: olha-se para os dois símbolos mais próximos da entidade de destino, sendo que o símbolo mais interno (longe da caixa) representa a cardinalidade mínima e o símbolo mais externo (encostado na caixa) representa a cardinalidade máxima.

Grau dos relacionamentos

O grau de um relacionamento em banco de dados indica quantas entidades diferentes participam simultaneamente de uma mesma associação na modelagem conceitual. Enquanto a cardinalidade define a quantidade de registros que se conectam, o grau foca na quantidade de conjuntos de entidades envolvidos no vínculo, sendo dividido principalmente em unitário, binário, ternário e n-ário.

O relacionamento unitário, também chamado de autorelacionamento, ocorre quando uma entidade se relaciona com ela mesma. Isso significa que registros dentro de uma mesma tabela possuem algum tipo de vínculo hierárquico ou de associação direta entre si. Um exemplo clássico é a entidade Funcionário em uma empresa, na qual um funcionário pode gerenciar outros funcionários. Na prática, esse modelo exige que a tabela possua uma chave estrangeira que aponta para a própria chave primária, permitindo identificar quem é o superior imediato de cada colaborador sem a necessidade de criar uma tabela separada para gerentes.

O relacionamento binário é o mais comum na modelagem de banco de dados e acontece quando duas entidades distintas são conectadas por um relacionamento. A grande maioria das regras de negócio no mundo real pode ser representada dessa forma, ligando dois conceitos diferentes do sistema. Por exemplo, considerando as entidades Cliente e Pedido em uma loja virtual, o relacionamento entre elas envolve exatamente essas duas partes, em que um cliente realiza vários pedidos e cada pedido pertence a um único cliente, estabelecendo uma ponte direta entre os dados cadastrais e as compras efetuadas.

O relacionamento ternário surge quando três entidades distintas precisam estar associadas ao mesmo tempo para que o fato faça sentido no negócio. Ele é utilizado quando a conexão entre apenas duas entidades não é suficiente para representar a informação completa, exigindo uma terceira parte para dar contexto. O exemplo representativo pode se dar em um sistema hospitalar com as entidades Médico, Paciente e Medicamento, ligadas pelo relacionamento Prescreve. Não basta apenas saber qual médico atendeu qual paciente, nem apenas qual remédio o paciente tomou, pois é necessário registrar simultaneamente qual médico receitou qual medicamento específico para determinado paciente em uma consulta.

Por fim, o relacionamento n-ário é a generalização para casos mais complexos em que quatro ou mais entidades participam juntas de uma mesma associação. Embora sejam menos frequentes, eles aparecem em cenários altamente específicos que demandam o cruzamento simultâneo de múltiplos fatores. Um exemplo seria um sistema de alocação universitária que conecta Professor, Disciplina, Sala e Horário ao mesmo tempo para definir uma aula. Na hora de transformar esse modelo conceitual para o banco de dados físico, tanto os relacionamentos ternários quanto os n-ários costumam virar uma tabela associativa própria, que guarda as chaves primárias de todas as entidades envolvidas.

Classificação das entidades

Na modelagem de dados, as entidades representam objetos, pessoas, locais, ou conceitos do mundo real sobre os quais desejamos armazenar informações. Para organizar e estruturar corretamente um banco de dados, essas entidades são classificadas de acordo com sua dependência, existência e função dentro do sistema.

A classificação fundamental divide as entidades em dois grandes grupos: Entidades Fortes e Entidades Fracas. Uma Entidade Forte é aquela que possui existência própria independente do banco de dados. Ela tem uma chave exclusiva capaz de identificar cada um de seus registros de forma única, sem precisar de ajuda de nenhuma outra tabela. Um exemplo clássico é a entidade “Cliente”, pois um cliente existe no sistema por si só, identificado pelo seu CPF ou código interno.

Por outro lado, a Entidade Fraca (também chamada de subordinada ou filha) é aquela que não possui existência própria e depende totalmente de uma Entidade Forte (chamada de entidade proprietária ou identificadora) para existir e ser identificada. Ela não possui uma chave completa por si só, utilizando uma chave parcial, podendo ser atributos da própria entidade fraca, combinada com a chave da entidade forte à qual está ligada. Um exemplo é a entidade “Dependente” em um sistema de recursos humanos: o registro de um dependente só faz sentido se estiver vinculado a um “Funcionário” ativo, e se o funcionário for excluído, os dados de seus dependentes também perdem o sentido de existir.

Além da dependência de existência, existe a Entidade Associativa, que surge para resolver um problema estrutural específico. Quando existe um relacionamento do tipo muito-para-muitos (N:N) entre duas entidades e há necessidade de armazenar informações próprias dessa conexão, o relacionamento ganha status de entidade. Por exemplo, entre as entidades “Aluno” e “Disciplina”, surge a entidade associativa “Matrícula”, que guarda atributos como a data de inscrição e a nota final, permitindo que o banco de dados relacional represente essa ligação de maneira eficiente.

Por fim, na modelagem avançada (MER Estendido), encontra-se a classificação hierárquica entre Superentidades (ou entidades genéricas) e Subentidades (ou entidades especializadas). A superentidade agrupa atributos comuns a vários elementos, enquanto as subentidades herdam essas características e adicionam atributos específicos. Por exemplo, pode-se contemplar a superentidade “Pessoa” (com nome e endereço) e as subentidades “Pessoa Física” (com CPF) e “Pessoa Jurídica” (com CNPJ), evitando a repetição desnecessária de dados e tornando o projeto mais limpo e organizado.

Agregação

A agregação em banco de dados é uma técnica de modelagem que trata um relacionamento e suas entidades participantes como uma única entidade de nível superior. Esse recurso resolve uma limitação clássica do Modelo Entidades-Relacionamento, que não permite conectar um relacionamento diretamente a outro.

Na modelagem tradicional de dados, os relacionamentos servem apenas para conectar entidades entre si. Quando uma regra de negócio exige registrar informações sobre um vínculo que já existe entre duas ou mais entidades, o modelo padrão trava. Em um cenário em que um Médico realiza uma Consulta com um Paciente, essa consulta gera uma prescrição de medicamentos. A prescrição não pertence apenas ao médico ou apenas ao paciente de forma isolada. Ela depende diretamente do ato da consulta já ocorrido entre os dois, exigindo que o relacionamento “Consulta” seja tratado como um objeto próprio para se ligar à entidade “Medicamento”.

Para aplicar a agregação, desenha-se um retângulo ao redor do relacionamento e das entidades que o compõem. Esse bloco inteiro passa a funcionar visualmente e logicamente como uma nova entidade abstrata, capaz de participar de outros relacionamentos no diagrama. Quando o diagrama com agregação é levado para o projeto lógico (tabelas), não se cria uma tabela extra apenas para a caixa de agregação em si. Na prática, a estrutura é convertida usando as chaves primárias das entidades envolvidas para formar uma tabela associativa. A tabela resultante do relacionamento principal recebe as chaves das entidades originais, formando uma chave composta. Em seguida, a nova entidade ou relacionamento ligado à agregação referencia essa chave composta para manter a integridade dos dados.

Embora os termos Agregação e Composição apareçam juntos na engenharia de software, eles possuem focos distintos no contexto de dados. A agregação no MER foca em abstrair um relacionamento inteiro para conectá-lo a outras partes do sistema. Já na programação orientada a objetos e na UML, a agregação indica uma relação de "todo e parte" onde as partes podem existir de forma independente do todo. No banco de dados conceitual, o objetivo principal é evitar redundâncias e representar dependências complexas de negócio sem quebrar as regras do diagrama.

IDEF1X

O IDEF1X é uma linguagem visual padronizada utilizada para representar modelos lógicos de dados relacionais. Graficamente, as entidades são representadas por retângulos com pontas retas para entidades independentes e pontas arredondadas para entidades dependentes ou fracas, contendo seus nomes no topo. Os atributos, que definem as características dessas entidades, incluem as chaves primárias (PK) separadas por uma linha horizontal, chaves alternativas (AK) e chaves estrangeiras (FK) que resultam da migração de identificadores para conectar diferentes tabelas.

Os relacionamentos exibem as associações entre instâncias das entidades e classificam-se em não-específicos e específicos. O relacionamento não-específico ocorre na proporção de muitos para muitos (N:M), representado graficamente por uma linha com dois círculos nas pontas. Já os relacionamentos específicos abrangem as cardinalidades 1:1 e 1:N, subdividindo-se em categorização e conexão. A categorização modela a herança ou generalização entre uma entidade genérica e categorias que podem formar um grupo completo (representado por linha dupla sob uma circunferência) ou incompleto (linha simples). Os relacionamentos de conexão, por sua vez, ligam uma entidade genitora a uma filha e podem ser identificadores — quando a chave da genitora compõe a chave primária da filha fraca — ou não-identificadores, representados por linhas pontilhadas que podem ser mandatórias ou opcionais conforme a cardinalidade mínima.

title: RecMem: Recurrent Memory Compression for Long-Sequence Generative Recommendation
description:
arXiv:2611.17921v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but the cost of processing them directly grows with history length. We propose RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework guided by three desiderata: space invariance, semantic fidelity, and lifelong evolvability. RecMem compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and slot-wise forget-gated updates. Recommendation supervision trains the memory to preserve predictive information, while stream-consistency training aligns predictions from sequential and packed processing. By construction, the memory state and decoder context are independent of history length; under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency, we further derive a horizon-independent bound on the state discrepancy between these two processing orders. On MerRec, RecMem uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context, compared with 1,200 tokens for HSTU-1200, while retaining 87.9% of HSTU-1200's Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200. It outperforms PHSTU and the evaluated recent-only and retrieval baselines, and analyses of distant history show that archived interactions contribute predictive signal.

title: How Peer-to-Peer GPU Marketplaces Work
description:
If you size GPU jobs, our open-source GPU VRAM calculator estimates the GPU memory an LLM needs and which GPUs fit it.

GPU capacity is unevenly distributed, and peer-to-peer marketplaces are one way to match spare GPUs with short-term demand. This is a plain explanation of how they work, using EverXCloud as the example.

The Short Answer

A peer-to-peer GPU marketplace lets suppliers list GPU machines they own and lets customers rent them by the hour. The marketplace sits between them: it lists the offers, takes the order, collects the payment and connects the customer to the machine.

This guide explains each step, using EverXCloud as the example. Other marketplaces make different choices.

Why These Marketplaces Exist

GPU capacity is unevenly distributed. Some data centers have servers that are not fully booked, and some individuals own GPUs that sit idle for much of the day. Meanwhile, AI teams, researchers and 3D studios often need GPUs for a few hours or a few weeks, not for years.

Peer-to-peer does not always mean that two individuals deal directly. The key difference from a conventional cloud is where the hardware comes from: a conventional provider operates its own fleet, while a marketplace aggregates capacity owned by many suppliers.

The Three Roles

Customers are developers, researchers, studios and companies that need GPU hours. They choose a GPU, a rental model and a region.

Suppliers own the hardware: verified individuals, companies and data centers. They decide what to list and under which rental models.

The marketplace operator matches orders to machines, handles payment and issues invoices. On EverXCloud, EverXCloud Inc., a Delaware corporation, is the merchant of record for every rental, so the customer buys from one company whichever supplier's machine runs the workload.

Step 1: Listing and Verification

The hardest problem in a marketplace is trust: is this machine what it claims to be? A common approach is an agent installed on the supplier's machine that reports the GPUs, memory and network it actually has, instead of what the supplier typed into a form.

The operator then reviews the machine before it is shown to customers. On EverXCloud, that review covers the hardware, the connection and the isolation between customers. Individual suppliers provide their contact details and confirm they are at least 18. Identity is verified before the first payout. Selling is not open in every country.

Step 2: Choosing How to Rent

Marketplaces usually offer several rental models. EverXCloud has four: On-Demand, a whole GPU billed for the time it runs; Time-Sliced, a guaranteed share of a GPU's time alongside other customers; Pay per task, a container that runs, stops on its own and is billed for its real runtime; and Reserved, future hours booked in a calendar, available only in EverXCloud Premium.

Each model can be Dedicated, where the machine stays yours for the whole rental, or Interruptible, where capacity may be stopped when the machine is needed. Operators can also divide a large server with NVIDIA MIG or time slicing, so one machine serves several customers.

Step 3: Payment and Responsibility

In many marketplaces the customer pays the operator, not the supplier. On EverXCloud, customers add funds to a prepaid balance in US dollars and rentals draw on it; the balance never goes negative.

The operator collects the payment, issues the invoice and credits the supplier's earnings after deducting a commission. The customer has one counterparty when something goes wrong, and the supplier is paid by the operator rather than chasing each customer. On EverXCloud, a supplier sees the commission in their account after the machine review, before the listing is published.

Step 4: Connecting and Running the Workload

Customers usually connect over SSH or manage rentals through an API, run their code in a container or a machine image, and release the machine when done. On EverXCloud, rentals are managed from the web portal or the REST API, with scoped API keys and signed webhooks.

Save outputs and checkpoints before releasing a machine. What remains on a third-party machine after a rental depends on the operator's terms, so check them before you start.

Strengths and Trade-Offs

Marketplaces give access to a wider range of GPU models than one provider stocks, including consumer cards that data centers do not usually offer. They allow flexible rental lengths, from short experiments to batch jobs, and give owners a way to earn from idle hardware.

They also have weaknesses. Two machines with the same GPU can differ in network, CPU and storage, so reproducible measurements need a recorded environment. You run on hardware someone else controls: do not place secrets you cannot afford to expose on any third-party machine. And supply depends on suppliers, so a specific model in a specific region may not always be available.

For stricter needs, some operators offer a tier of machines they run themselves or place in verified data centers. On EverXCloud, that tier is EverXCloud Premium.

How to Evaluate a Marketplace

Before committing a workload, ask who the merchant of record is and who you contact when something fails, how machines are verified and customers isolated, which rental models are interruptible, what the invoice shows, and what happens to your data when a rental ends.

Then run your own workload on the candidate configuration and record runtime, total cost and failed requests. A test of your workload is more reliable than any specification table.

Five questions to ask any GPU marketplace

  1. Who is the merchant of record? It is your counterparty for payment, invoices and failures.

  2. How are machines verified? A reported configuration is more reliable than a declared one.

  3. How is isolation between customers handled? Your workload runs on hardware someone else controls.

  4. Which rental models are interruptible? Interruptible capacity can be reclaimed during a job.

  5. What happens to your data when a rental ends? Outputs must be saved before the machine is released.

Originally published at everxcloud.ai. EverXCloud is a GPU cloud marketplace: see how it works or sell your GPU time.

title: Fractional Product Designer or Full-Time Hire? How to Decide
description:
Originally published on ayurchenko.xyz.

Hire a full-time product designer when there is design work every day and someone to lead it. Bring in a fractional one when the work is real but not daily, when you need senior judgment before you can justify a senior salary, or when a first version or a relaunch needs an owner for a few months. On independent designers’ published prices, part-time senior work costs $4,000 to $8,000 a month; one designer’s comparison estimates a full-time senior product designer in the US at $14,000 to $19,000 a month, and about three months to hire. The two buy different things, so the sums alone do not decide it.

Signs you need a fractional designer

  • A first version has to be defined, and nobody on the team has done it before.
  • The product works but has become hard to use and hard to change.
  • You are about to raise or launch, and the product has to look like the company it says it is.
  • Engineers ship every week, partly with coding agents, and nobody owns how the product behaves.
  • You need a senior person now, and a senior hire would take months to find.

Signs you need a full-time designer

  • There is design work every day, across several teams or products.
  • Research, design and the design system all need an owner at once.
  • Someone on the team can lead a designer, or the hire will lead others.
  • The product will be the company’s core for years, and the knowledge has to stay inside.

What each costs, and how fast it starts

Option Cost a month Before work starts
Fractional, part-time senior $4,000 to $8,000 on published prices Days, once the scope is agreed
Full-time senior product designer, US $14,000 to $19,000, by one designer’s estimate About three months to hire, by the same estimate
Design agency $15,000 to $40,000, by the same comparison Three to six weeks

The sources and the full price table: What a freelance product designer costs.

What you give up with each

  • Fractional: fewer hours, so usually one stream of work at a time; less time in the team’s daily conversations; and what the designer learns leaves with them unless it is written down.
  • Full-time: months to hire, a salary whether or not the work fills the week, and someone to manage. In return, every day of attention, several streams at once, and knowledge that stays in the company.

What a fractional designer should own

Not tickets. The product side: what goes into the next release and what waits, how the system behaves behind the screens, and what it looks like. If the person only takes requests, you are paying senior rates for production work.

  • A seat in planning, and a say in scope.
  • Access to the repository, so they can read what ships and, if they write code, fix it.
  • One design system, kept in code, that engineers and their coding agents build from.
  • A fixed number of days a week, agreed at the start and adjusted month to month.

How to make it work

  • Start with a small, fixed piece of work, like a one-week Product Diagnosis, so both sides know what the work is before committing to months.
  • Give one founder the job of deciding with the designer, so decisions do not wait for a meeting.
  • Review what shipped every week, not what was designed.
  • Write down what the designer owns and what they do not, so nothing falls between them and the engineers.

When to switch to full-time

When the fractional days are always full and the backlog keeps growing, or when the design work splits into several streams. A good fractional designer helps you write the job description and hire for it.

Questions founders ask

Is a fractional product designer cheaper than a full-time hire?

Per month, often: $4,000 to $8,000 for part-time senior work against $14,000 to $19,000 for a full-time senior designer in the US, by one designer’s estimate. But a full-time designer is there every day and what they learn stays with you, so compare what each would own.

How many days a week does a fractional designer work?

Whatever the stage needs: agreed at the start, adjusted month to month.

Can a fractional designer lead design for the company?

Yes, for a small team: decide, design and set the system. Once there are several designers to lead, hire a full-time lead.

What does fractional product design cost with you?

From $8,000 a month. See fractional product design.

Deciding on your first designer? Send a few lines about the product and the team. I’ll tell you which one I would pick in your place. Write to me through ayurchenko.xyz.

title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.17790v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.

title: ParseBench-2: Severity-Aware Evaluation of Document Parsing
description:
arXiv:2611.17400v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Document-parsing metrics can give high scores to outputs that change important facts and penalize changes that preserve meaning. People can often judge these consequences more easily than they can design a metric to measure them. We introduce a method for developing parsing metrics from severity policies that specify how each error type should affect the score. We express these policies through test scenarios that specify how a metric should behave. We then optimize the metric implementations against these fixed expectations, using coding agents to refine comparison rules, error detectors and weights under human review. This makes stated human priorities an explicit objective of metric design. We apply this method in ParseBench-2, a comprehensive document-parsing benchmark that combines broad capability coverage with metrics calibrated to error severity. It covers 4,317 pages across six dimensions of parsing quality: text, formatting, tables, charts, visual grounding, and forms. We use detailed annotations and targeted difficult cases to check for changed facts, broken structural relationships, and missing content. We take the lower of a parsing score that measures content recovery and a severity cap that penalizes detected errors, so recovering most of a page cannot hide a serious error. Across six severity test suites, our metrics more closely match the expert judgments expressed by the scenario targets than existing metrics and penalize at most 3.4% of the tested benign variations. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation spanning frontier vision-language models, specialized document parsers and open-weight systems, comparing their overall rankings, performance across parsing capabilities and tradeoffs between accuracy and cost.

title: Agentless CSPM Explained: How It Works, What It Sees, and Where It Falls Short
description:
Few topics in cloud security generate as much debate as the question of agents. Should you install software on every workload, or collect information without touching the workload at all? Vendors have strong opinions, usually aligned with what they sell. This article offers a more neutral look at agentless CSPM: how the approach works technically, what it does well, where it has limits, and how to decide whether it fits your environment.

What "agentless" actually means

In this context, agentless means the security platform gathers data without installing its own software on your servers, containers, or virtual machines. Instead, it relies on access that the cloud provider already offers.

There are generally three data sources.

Control plane APIs. Every major cloud exposes APIs describing how resources are configured: networks, identity policies, storage settings, database options, and so on. A posture platform given read-only credentials can query these continuously and build a detailed picture of the environment.

Snapshot analysis. Some platforms go further by reading copies of disk volumes. The platform creates or accesses a snapshot of a virtual machine's storage and analyzes it outside the running system. This can reveal installed software, operating system versions, vulnerabilities, and sometimes secrets or sensitive data, without running anything on the workload.

Cloud logs and events. Audit logs, flow logs, and event streams provide information about changes and activity, which helps detect drift and unusual behavior.

Together, these sources allow broad visibility with relatively little deployment work.

Why teams like the approach

Fast time to value

Because there is nothing to install on workloads, onboarding can be quick. Connecting an account through a read-only role may take minutes, and an initial picture of risk can appear within hours. For organizations with hundreds of accounts, that speed is a major advantage.

Broad coverage by default

Agent deployments depend on every workload being enrolled. Workloads that are missed, short-lived, or managed by someone else go uncovered. API-based collection sees everything in the account automatically, including new resources as they appear.

Low operational burden

No agent means no agent updates, compatibility testing, performance tuning, or conflicts with other software. For teams that already struggle to maintain endpoint tooling, this matters.

Lower friction with engineering

Developers are often wary of additional software on production systems. Avoiding it removes a common source of resistance and reduces the risk of performance impact.

Works with services that cannot host agents

Many modern services, such as managed databases, serverless functions, and storage services, cannot run third-party agents at all. API-based assessment is the only practical way to evaluate their configuration.

What it does particularly well

  • Identifying misconfigurations across identity, networking, storage, and data services.
  • Building an accurate, near-real-time inventory.
  • Mapping relationships between resources, such as which instance can reach which database.
  • Flagging exposure, such as public endpoints and overly permissive roles.
  • Finding known vulnerabilities and installed packages through snapshot analysis.
  • Supporting compliance reporting against recognized benchmarks.
  • Highlighting attack paths, where several moderate weaknesses combine into a serious route to valuable assets. Understanding attack path analysis is increasingly central to how teams prioritize limited remediation capacity.

Where it has limits

An honest assessment should include the trade-offs.

Limited runtime visibility. Without something running on the workload, it is hard to see live behavior: which processes are executing, which network connections are active at this moment, or whether a file is being modified. Snapshots capture a point in time, not continuous activity.

Delay. Snapshot scans often run on a schedule, such as every day. A vulnerability introduced this morning may not appear until the next cycle.

Reduced ability to respond. Agents can block or kill a malicious process. A system that only observes through APIs cannot easily do that inside a workload, although it may be able to change cloud-level settings, such as isolating an instance through network controls.

Dependence on permissions. The platform can only see what its credentials allow. Overly restrictive roles produce blind spots, while overly generous ones create risk of their own.

Provider constraints. API rate limits, snapshot costs, and regional behavior can affect performance and expense, especially at large scale.

Encrypted data. Disks encrypted with customer-managed keys require additional permissions for snapshot analysis, and some organizations are uncomfortable granting them.

Agent-based approaches: when they add value

Agents are not obsolete. They shine where continuous, in-workload insight is needed.

  • Detecting active threats such as malware execution or suspicious process behavior.
  • Monitoring file integrity and runtime drift in sensitive systems.
  • Providing real-time protection for containers and hosts.
  • Supporting environments with limited cloud API visibility, such as some hybrid or on-premises estates.

Many organizations use agentless methods for broad posture coverage and add agents only to the workloads where runtime protection justifies the effort, such as internet-facing servers or systems holding regulated data.

Questions to ask when evaluating agentless platforms

  1. What permissions do you require, and can they be limited further?
  2. How often are snapshots taken, and can the frequency be adjusted?
  3. Where is snapshot analysis performed: in my account or in yours?
  4. What is stored after analysis, and for how long?
  5. How are encrypted volumes handled?
  6. What is the impact on cloud costs, such as snapshot storage and API calls?
  7. How do you handle very large environments and rate limits?
  8. Can the platform integrate with runtime tools if I need both?

Security and privacy considerations

Because agentless platforms hold powerful read access and sometimes copies of disk data, their own security matters. Check how credentials are protected, whether access is scoped to least privilege, how data is isolated between customers, and what certifications the vendor holds. Where snapshot analysis runs inside your own account rather than the vendor's, sensitive data may never leave your control, which can simplify compliance for regulated industries.

A pragmatic way to decide

Consider three questions.

Is speed of coverage your priority? If you need broad visibility quickly across many accounts, agentless is hard to beat.

Do you need runtime protection? If you are defending against active threats on workloads, plan for agents on the systems that warrant them.

What does your workload mix look like? Environments heavy on managed and serverless services lean toward agentless by necessity, while those dominated by long-lived virtual machines may benefit from a hybrid.

Closing thoughts

The agent versus agentless debate is often framed as a contest, but it is better understood as a question of fit. API and snapshot-based collection offers speed, breadth, and low overhead, making it an excellent foundation for posture work. Runtime agents add depth where active defense is required. Understanding what each can and cannot see allows you to combine them sensibly rather than overpaying for overlap or leaving blind spots you did not realize existed.

title: Representational Geometry as a Diagnostic for Adversarial Robustness
description:
arXiv:2611.17684v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adversarial training is a common technique for making neural networks more robust to small, intentionally crafted input perturbations, and robustness is commonly measured through accuracy under attack. By exploring inter-network representations across different adversarial training objectives, we can analyze whether multiple networks organize their latent representations similarly. We study Multilayer Perceptrons trained on MNIST under three adversarial training regimes and compare the resulting population training dynamics and geometry to those of a vanilla network. We use M-PHATE to embed data samples across training epochs and examine how the geometry of the data changes during training under adversarial objectives. On penultimate-layer representations we measure displacement between clean and perturbed points, distributional distance through maximum mean discrepancy, and nearest-neighbor recovery. Our visualizations and quantitative analyses show that adversarial training leads to structural changes in how networks organize internal data representations, and robust accuracy and representational stability can rank the same defenses in opposite ways. These findings support a discussion of re-evaluating how practitioners approach the auditing of model robustness by treating latent representations and their training trajectories as diagnostic artifacts across sets of networks.

title: "Why we built Apium Cloud OS: running a multi-protocol gateway without gluing together four different VPN stacks"
description:
If you have ever set up a private network gateway for a company, a distributed dev team, or your own commercial service, you know how quickly a simple setup turns into a mess of incompatible tools.

Developers want VLESS Reality or Hysteria 2 because their ISP throttles standard VPN protocols or drops packets on unstable Wi-Fi. Non-technical colleagues on Windows refuse to install third-party proxy clients and configure JSON files. The office administrator needs a site-to-site tunnel with a static IP for a MikroTik, Keenetic, or OpenWrt router. Meanwhile, you have to track bandwidth quotas, block BitTorrent traffic so your hosting provider doesn't suspend your VPS, and cut off expired accounts immediately.

Usually, solving this means running three different panels and a pile of custom bash scripts on separate servers. We built Apium Cloud OS (https://apium.cloud/) to put all of this into a single self-hosted system that installs on a clean Linux VPS in under five minutes.

Here is how it works in real-world scenarios.

Scenario 1: One gateway for developers, non-tech staff, and office routers

When onboarding a team of 50 people, client software is always the biggest headache. In Apium Cloud OS, all four core protocols run concurrently and share a single user database, quota counter, and bandwidth shaper:

  • For Windows laptops without extra software: You create an SSTP or L2TP user, copy a one-line PowerShell command from the dashboard, and send it to the employee. They paste it into PowerShell, and a native Windows VPN profile is registered automatically. Because SSTP runs over standard TCP port 443 (HTTPS), it passes cleanly through strict corporate and hotel firewalls.
  • For hardware routers: You create a router account with a dedicated static IP inside the subnet and connect your Keenetic, OpenWrt, or MikroTik router via standard L2TP/IPsec. The whole office or home network is now routed without configuring individual devices.
  • For mobile devices and strict ISP filtering: Users connect via VLESS Reality (which looks identical to standard TLS 1.3 web traffic and doesn't even require you to buy a domain) or Hysteria 2 over QUIC, which keeps connections fast even when a mobile or hotel network has 30 to 40 percent packet loss.

Scenario 2: Uninterrupted access to overseas APIs and AI tools via Cascade Routing

Many engineering teams today need stable access to international cloud consoles and AI platforms like Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini from regions where direct routes are degraded or restricted. Connecting directly to a distant overseas server often results in high latency or blocked handshakes.

To solve this, we built Cascade VPN directly into the routing engine. You deploy an Apium ingress node on a nearby VPS with low ping to your users, and chain it to several remote exit nodes in Europe, the US, or Asia.

Apium probes every upstream exit node every 15 seconds. You can route traffic in four modes: direct, pinned to a specific node, load-balanced (evenly or by priority), or automatic failover. If an overseas provider has an outage or a route drops, traffic switches to a healthy exit node in the background without dropping active user sessions.

Scenario 3: Protecting your VPS from abuse notices and enforcing hard limits

Anyone who runs a gateway for multiple users eventually runs into two classic Linux networking problems: hosting abuse tickets and zombie sessions.

First, if a single user forgets to turn off a torrent client, your hosting provider will flag the server IP for DMCA or abuse violations. Apium Cloud OS includes a built-in packet filter that drops BitTorrent and DHT traffic automatically, alongside client-to-client isolation and flood protection. You can also switch the global firewall between three modes depending on your paranoia level: Basic (all ports open), Restricted (only Web, Mail, SSH/Git, DNS, and NTP), or Paranoid (strictly HTTP/HTTPS and local DNS). On top of that, a local dnsmasq resolver blocks over 78,000 ad and tracker domains right in RAM without sending telemetry outside your server.

Second, on many panels, when you disable a user or their traffic runs out, their existing TCP/UDP connections stay alive in the Linux kernel state table. In Apium, revoking an account terminates the session daemon, flushes the user's Linux kernel conntrack entries, and updates firewall DROP rules at the exact same moment. Speed limits per user or group are enforced at the kernel level via Linux tc (HTB/TBF), so one heavy downloader cannot choke the channel for everyone else.

Scenario 4: Hooking up your own billing or Telegram bot via REST API

If you are a service provider, reseller, or automating internal IT onboarding, clicking through a web UI doesn't scale. Everything in Apium Cloud OS can be automated over an OpenAPI 3.0 REST interface using scoped, IP-whitelisted API keys.

You can set up tariff plans once, create up to 500 users in a single bulk request, generate public Base64 subscription links (with standard Subscription-Userinfo headers for client apps), and receive HMAC-SHA256 signed webhooks when a user's quota runs out.

We separated the billing portal on apium.cloud from the actual software running on your VPS. When you enter your server's SSH credentials in the 5-minute installation wizard, they exist only in volatile RAM for the duration of the setup and are wiped immediately once provisioning finishes. After that, the node runs completely autonomously—we have no SSH keys, no backdoor agents, and no access to your user database.

Even the built-in DPI traffic inspector (useful when an admin needs to debug which domains are eating up bandwidth) only reads connection metadata like TLS SNI and HTTP Host headers without decrypting payloads, and stores those logs strictly on your own disk.

If you want to test it on your own VPS or read more about the protocol setup, check out

https://apium.cloud/
https://apium.cloud/en/faq and the technical FAQ

I would be glad to answer any questions about the Linux networking stack or hear how you currently handle multi-protocol routing in your infrastructure.

title: Why Netrix uses separate SSH connections for SFTP
description:
A desktop SSH client can show an interactive shell and a remote file browser for the same host. Their lifetimes are different: a user may close Files, cancel an upload, or switch hosts while keeping a shell open.

That creates a useful design question: which component owns the connection that a cancellation is allowed to close?

I'm the maintainer of Netrix, a desktop terminal client. This article examines the SFTP connection lifecycle in its public 0.3.0-beta.8 source snapshot. The implementation is in Rust, using Tokio and russh.

SSH channels and connection ownership

SSH supports multiple channels within one encrypted connection. A shell and an SFTP subsystem can use different channels on a shared connection; the protocol does not require a separate connection for every feature. RFC 4254 describes the channel mechanism.

Sharing can avoid additional connection setup and authentication. It also means the application needs a clear owner for the shared transport. Closing one channel and disconnecting the entire SSH connection have different consequences.

Netrix gives SFTP its own SSH transports. The terminal manager retains ownership of interactive terminal connections, while the SFTP manager owns file-operation connections:

Saved host profile and credential loading
                  |
          Shared host-key trust
                  |
          +-------+-------+
          |               |
   Terminal manager   SFTP manager
          |               |
   SSH connection A   SSH connection B
          |               |
     Shell channel    SFTP subsystem

An SFTP failure can therefore discard its own transport without asking the terminal manager to reset a shell. This is a lifecycle boundary: both features still depend on the same backend process, network and remote server.

The Files view has a connection lifecycle separate from terminal tabs. Identifying details in this screenshot are masked.

Bound the cost of isolation

Separate transports have a cost: more sockets, authentication work and server-side connections. Opening a new SSH connection for every directory click would make that cost visible quickly.

The SFTP connection manager uses leases and bounded reuse. A lease gives one operation exclusive access to an SFTP connection. A healthy connection can return to the idle pool when the operation finishes.

The current implementation has these bounds:

Resource Limit
Concurrent SFTP leases 4
Retained idle connections 8
Idle connection lifetime 60 seconds
Idle cleanup interval 15 seconds

The four-lease limit is a concurrency limit, not a claim that the application can only hold four SSH sockets in total. Idle SFTP transports and interactive terminals have separate lifetimes.

Setup also has a deadline covering the wait for a pool slot, connection establishment, authentication and subsystem initialization. A stalled authentication attempt should not reserve work indefinitely. Failed or timed-out operations do not return their connection as healthy.

The disconnect race is more interesting than the happy path

Consider this sequence:

  1. A directory listing borrows a connection.
  2. The user disconnects that saved host's Files session.
  3. The disconnect handler removes its idle connections.
  4. The listing finishes and tries to return its borrowed connection.

If disconnect only clears the idle map, step four can repopulate it. The UI says disconnected, but the old connection has quietly become reusable again.

Netrix associates leases with a per-profile cancellation scope. Disconnect cancels that scope and removes the profile's idle entries. The lease-return path checks the scope while holding the pool-state lock; a lease from a cancelled lifetime cannot re-enter the pool.

The saved profile ID matters too. Two profiles can point at the same address and port while representing different connection choices. Disconnecting one profile should not invalidate the other's pool lifetime. A later connection for the disconnected profile gets a new scope.

This pattern applies beyond SSH: when async work can outlive a view or session, cache eviction alone may not invalidate work already in flight.

Keep trust shared across the boundary

Transport isolation should not create competing answers to “is this the same server?” Terminal and SFTP connections share the application's host-key trust model.

Pool reuse also depends on more than the endpoint. Its key includes the saved profile, authentication inputs, host-key policy and current known-host entry, represented by a process-salted SHA-256 digest. A changed credential or trust entry produces a different reuse key. This digest is a cache identity mechanism; it does not replace credential-vault encryption or SSH host-key verification.

Cancellation does not undo a remote write

Independent transports make it clearer which connection can be closed. They do not make a mutation transactional across the network.

For uploads, the implementation writes a temporary sibling file, checks completion, then commits through a rename. The transfer registry serializes cancellation with entry into the commit phase. Once the rename is starting, cancellation returns a conflict instead of promising rollback.

A lost rename reply is another important case: the server may have committed even though the client cannot confirm success. The operation reports failure with instructions to inspect the destination before retrying. It does not automatically replay the write.

The SFTP implementation notes describe the cleanup rules and limits. Cleanup can leave a temporary file when the server is unreachable. Recursive directory transfer, synchronization and resume after application restart are not implemented.

Test the lifetime boundaries

A useful verification plan should include more than a successful upload:

  • Disconnect while a directory response is deliberately delayed, then confirm the late lease cannot revive the pool.
  • Use two profiles for the same endpoint and disconnect only one.
  • Stall SSH authentication and disconnect during setup.
  • Cancel an upload before commit, and separately exercise cancellation at the commit boundary.
  • Inject an SFTP failure while a terminal remains connected and check both lifecycles independently.

The repository documents an opt-in local SSH/SFTP smoke fixture for several of these cases, alongside packet, API and cancellation tests. Those checks still need complementary testing against real server implementations and the native file-saving UI.

The design choice is about ownership: give each workflow a clear connection lifetime, preserve shared trust checks, and make cancellation semantics explicit all the way through to the remote commit.

AI disclosure: This article was drafted by an AI assistant from Netrix's public source code and documentation. The screenshots show the application with identifying details masked.

title: From Local Prediction Error to Final Outputs: A Theory of Expert Sharing in Multi-Step Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.17879v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can share experts across layers or computational steps, pooling training information from different contexts. This can reduce local prediction error, but multi-step systems are ultimately evaluated by their final outputs. We study when these local gains survive composition. In specified linear regression models, we derive exact sharing and merging criteria by balancing variance savings against bias from sharing across roles with different target behavior. Under a common fixed linear propagation map, we characterize expected squared final-output risk, retaining error directions and correlations. We construct cases where sharing lowers average local error yet increases final-output error. Within this setting, we also identify when orthogonal full pooling with isotropic noise preserves every local improvement at the final output. For general routed computations, we derive conditional end-to-end error bounds that account for distribution shifts, errors in surrounding components, and changes in expert selection. Separately, we show that correct predictions and route labels alone do not establish that individual experts implement the attributed operations. Controlled experiments realize a strict local-to-final risk reversal. In low-data symbolic settings, trained Transformers exhibit statistically supported teacher-forced one-step gains without statistically resolved free-running final-output gains. Separate intervention tests distinguish successful multi-layer actions from single-expert attribution and generalization to unseen transitions. Together, these results distinguish when sharing improves local estimation, when those gains survive to the final output, and what evidence is needed to attribute reusable operations to individual experts.

title: Zoom In, Scale Out: Metric Depth Models Mistake Digital Zoom for Moving Closer
description:
arXiv:2611.17903v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many new AI models estimate how far away things are, in metres, from a single photo. To do this they must also work out what camera took the photo. We check whether they really do with a simple test: digital zoom, that is, cropping a photo and enlarging the crop back to full size. Zooming moves nothing in the scene, so a correct model should give the same distance for every point still in the picture. The test is free, exact and needs no labels. Two numbers describe a model's reaction: its depth changes like $s^{-\alpha}$ (ideal $\alpha=0$) and its focal-length estimate like $s^{\beta}$ (ideal $\beta=1$), for zoom factor $s$. On 800 images from KITTI, NYUv2 and DIODE, the widely used Depth Anything V2 has $\alpha=0.95$: it treats a zoomed photo almost as if the camera had moved closer, because it judges distance mainly from how large things look. Models that also predict the camera remove only part of this error ($\alpha\approx0.31$-$0.36$), because their focal estimate grows too little. Given the true camera, Depth Pro and DA3-Nested keep their depth ($\alpha\approx0$), so the error lies in their camera estimate. The reason: a zoomed photo is, pixel for pixel, a normal photo of a scene squashed in depth, so size alone cannot tell the two apart, and a focal estimator trained by regression stays close to the cameras it saw in training. Undoing this needs no labels or training and makes Depth Pro pass the test ($\alpha=0.04$) at almost no cost on normal photos. Controls, including a real optical zoom lens, rule out blur and resizing artefacts. Finally, label-free fine-tuning for self-consistency lowers $\alpha$ to 0.05 on KITTI and 0.07 on NYUv2 once a "blurry means zoomed" shortcut is removed; we report what this costs on normal and unseen photos.

title: Finding two ClickHouse time zone bugs with a differential test
description:
I wanted a cheap way to find real bugs in a large database, so I stopped reading code and compared answers instead. Two of the comparisons found genuine bugs in ClickHouse's date functions, both in time zones with a UTC offset that is not a whole number of hours. The other three comparisons found nothing, which is also worth knowing.

Both fixes are open pull requests, not merged. I say so up front because the title of a post like this tends to promise more than the state of the work.

The method: ask the same question two ways

A differential test needs no expected values. You run the same logical query through two routes that must agree, and print any disagreement:

  • Against a reference. ClickHouse's date functions against Python's zoneinfo.
  • Against itself. The same JOIN with every join algorithm. The same filter with the primary key, skip indexes and PREWHERE on and off. The same GROUP BY with two-level, external and in-order aggregation.

Each probe is about 40-70 lines of Python that shells out to clickhouse local. They are public gists, with the setup in the header: date functions, JOIN algorithms, index analysis, aggregation settings.

Bug 1: toStartOfHour returns :30 on a day when the clocks move by 30 minutes

Australia/Lord_Howe shifts by 30 minutes twice a year. The probe compares toStartOfHour over thousands of timestamps with what Python says the wall clock hour is. Only two samples out of 4,000 disagreed, both on a transition day:

SELECT toStartOfHour(toDateTime('2024-04-07 03:10:00', 'Australia/Lord_Howe'));
-- 2024-04-07 02:30:00   (expected 03:00:00)

Every other sample, including all the other days of the year in that zone, was right. The test only found this because it sampled around transitions on purpose. The cause is that toStartOfHour ends in a function that rounds on a grid anchored at the local midnight. After a 30 minute shift, that grid no longer lines up with the clock. toStartOfInterval(..., INTERVAL 2 HOUR) already compensated for the shift, so the 2-hour answer was right and the 1-hour answer wrong for the same input.

The fix applies the same compensation to the 1-hour case, only when the day's shift is not a whole number of hours.

Two things I learned from the CI run:

  1. I could not build ClickHouse here, so CI was the first time the test ran. It passed.
  2. The performance comparison, which is part of the CI, flagged date_time_long at +51.7% on my first push. I had added a second lookup of the day to the hot path. Looking the day up once removed it. A correct fix can still be a regression, and the benchmark caught it before a reviewer had to.

Pull request: ClickHouse #131620.

Bug 2: minute intervals before 1970 round to the wrong boundary 

SET enable_extended_results_for_datetime_functions = 1;
SELECT toStartOfFifteenMinutes(toDateTime64('1910-06-15 12:07:00', 0, 'Europe/Warsaw'));          -- 12:00:00
SELECT toStartOfInterval(toDateTime64('1910-06-15 12:07:00', 0, 'Europe/Warsaw'), INTERVAL 15 MINUTE);  -- 11:54:00

toStartOfInterval has an arithmetic shortcut that rounds the Unix timestamp. Before 1970 it was allowed whenever the offsets were whole minutes. The dedicated functions round from the local midnight there. The two agree only if the offset is a multiple of the interval, and Warsaw was at +01:24 until 1915. Checking the neighbours turned up Pacific/Chatham (+12:45), where even INTERVAL 10 MINUTE was wrong in 1960.

The fix narrows the condition: whole hours that divide into the interval. Other zones take the slower generic path before the epoch, which is what the dedicated functions use.

Pull request: ClickHouse #131915.

What found nothing

  • JOIN algorithms (hash, parallel_hash, grace_hash, full_sorting_merge, partial_merge, direct, auto) over NULL, NaN, tuple, array, map, LowCardinality and decimal keys: no disagreement over 7 random seeds.
  • Index analysis (primary key, three skip index types, PREWHERE, the old analyzer, the query condition cache) against a full scan over 14 key types: about 6,000 comparisons, no disagreement.
  • Aggregation settings against GROUP BY, DISTINCT, ROLLUP, window functions on composite keys: about 3,200 comparisons, no disagreement.

That is a useful result about the database. It is also a reminder that most of a mature system is correct, and the bugs live in the corners where two correct-looking pieces of logic meet, here "round to the hour" and "the offset changed by 30 minutes today".

The probes lied to me first

Most of my debugging time went on the harness, not on ClickHouse:

  • A first run reported thousands of mismatches. DateTime is unsigned, so negative timestamps clamp to 1970, and my Python side disagreed with that. I limited the range.
  • toStartOfMonth returns a Date, which has no time zone, so comparing its Unix timestamp with Python's local midnight is meaningless. I compared dates instead.
  • -0.0 and 0.0 group together but print differently, so the probe flagged a representative choice as a bug. I removed -0.0 from the value pool.
  • clickhouse local keeps tables between runs, and running several seeds in parallel locked its directory. I gave each run its own path and a DROP TABLE IF EXISTS.

If your first differential test reports a flood of bugs, it is almost always the test.

Takeaways

  • A reference implementation in another language is a good oracle for date and time code, because the two have different bugs.
  • Sample around the edges on purpose. The Lord Howe bug showed up in 2 of 4,000 timestamps.
  • When a fix touches a hot path, read the performance results, not only the tests.
  • Say whether your fix is merged. Mine are not, yet.

title: SURFACE: Preference Distribution Matching on Pareto Fronts via Scalarization Steering
description:
arXiv:2611.17484v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Constructing a finite Pareto representation requires allocating a limited number of solutions across the Pareto front (PF). A desired preference distribution specifies this allocation by assigning more solutions to some PF regions and fewer to others. Scalarization generates Pareto solutions by varying objective weights and solving single-objective problems. However, a distribution of scalarization weights generally does not translate into the same distribution of Pareto solutions along the PF, because the weight-to-solution map is nonlinear and unknown in advance.To account for this distortion, we introduce SURFACE (Scalarization Updates for Redistributing Finite Approximations with Chart Estimation}), which adaptively updates scalarization weights to match a desired PF distribution. SURFACE estimates how each region of the weight grid corresponds to an area of the PF from the current scalarized solutions, then redistributes the weights accordingly. The method supports parallel, warm-started, inexact optimization with standard single-objective solvers. Theoretically, we establish that, under the stated regularity conditions, SURFACE achieves linear convergence of the preference distribution mismatch to a finite-resolution error floor of $\mathcal{O}(N^{-2/(M-1)})$, where $N$ is the number of adaptive weights and $M$ is the number of objectives. Empirically, experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate improved target-mass balance and PF coverage compared with established baselines.

title: My Edge Add-ons submission failed validation: the store package contained two manifest.json files
description:
I submitted my extension ConvoExport to the Microsoft Edge Add-ons store, and the first package failed validation. The reason was not in the code at all. The zip contained two manifest.json files: one at the root, and one inside src/.

How it happened

My packaging script builds a staging directory, copies the src/ tree into it, and writes a derived manifest.json at the staging root. The src/ tree already contained a manifest.json (the source manifest the extension loads during development). The packager copied it along with everything else, then wrote a second manifest at the root. The resulting zip had 30 entries, two of them manifests.

Why my own checks missed it

The packaging self-check verified that a manifest.json existed at the package root, and that its fields were correct. It never checked that it was the only one. A check that asserts presence cannot catch a duplicate.

The fix

Two changes, both in the packager:

  1. Strip manifest.json out of the src/ tree when staging, so only the derived root manifest is packaged.
  2. Add a self-check that fails the build if more than one manifest.json exists anywhere in the package.

After the fix I re-packed both targets: Chrome 38,223 bytes and Firefox 38,303 bytes, 29 entries each, exactly one manifest.json at the root. The corrected package passed Edge validation and the submission went to In review.

The general lesson is boring and worth writing down: validate the package the way the store does, not the way your build does. My checks verified the source tree; the store verifies the zip. Anything the packager adds, moves, or duplicates between those two steps is invisible to source-level checks. A one-line assertion — "exactly one manifest.json in the archive" — would have caught this before the first submission.
