title: Classification with Large-Step Gradient Descent: Unifying Self-Stabilization and Convergence Rates
description:
arXiv:2611.17459v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural networks are often trained with gradient descent (GD) using step sizes that exceed classical stability thresholds, a regime where standard convergence theory no longer applies. Despite exhibiting non-monotonic loss and oscillatory dynamics, this regime frequently leads to faster convergence and better generalization. Existing theoretical perspectives offer complementary but incomplete insights: one identifies a self-stabilization mechanism that drives GD toward flat regions but does not yield convergence rates; another derives rigorous rates for specific losses but does not explain the underlying stabilization mechanism; and a third unifies these views for overparameterized least squares, but relies on the existence of a minimizer manifold, which is absent in classification settings. In this work, we extend this unified geometric perspective to exponential-tail losses, including logistic and cross-entropy losses in separable linear classification, where the loss infimum is not attained at any finite parameter. We identify a curvature-defined reference subspace that replaces the role of the minimizer manifold, yielding a coupled dynamical system in which orthogonal oscillations are damped by parallel progress along directions of decreasing sharpness. Under regularity conditions, which we verify for logistic and multiclass cross-entropy losses on symmetric data models, we derive explicit bounds for the iterates, not just the loss, covering both the unstable and stable regimes, and revealing a three-phase damping structure in the latter. Our analysis further uncovers a transient implicit bias induced by large step sizes: although GD converges asymptotically to the max-margin direction, large steps can leave persistent orthogonal residuals and, in certain geometries, amplify them, affecting finite-time alignment with the max-margin direction.

title: DECODE: Diagnosing Interpretability Failures in Automated Interpretation Process
description:
arXiv:2611.17856v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on LLMs themselves to both generate and evaluate explanations, creating a self-referential automated interpretation process with minimal human oversight. This automation raises significant reliability concerns, which are exacerbated by the absence of ground truth. In practice, it is difficult to validate explanations or to attribute interpretability failures to their source -- whether they originate from the tool's extracted representations or from the LLM used in the process. To address these challenges, we present DECODE, a visual analytics system that reintroduces human oversight into the automated interpretation process. Our approach decomposes the diagnostic workflow into three progressive stages, isolating failure sources ranging from structural defects to explanation-level misalignments. Drawing inspiration from inter-coder consensus in qualitative analysis, we utilize consensus among independently generated explanations and their evaluation metrics as a proxy for reliability. To further scale human inspection, we employ a three-phase active seeding protocol that strategically recommends high-priority instances for manual review. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features, showing that it can efficiently identify and attribute interpretability failures at scale.

title: Federated Physics-Informed Thermal Field Prediction Across Unseen Geometries in Distributed Additive Manufacturing
description:
arXiv:2611.17794v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In additive manufacturing (AM), each change in part geometry requires a new thermal simulation, which makes design evaluation over many candidates costly. Geometry-aware models reduce this cost by predicting thermal fields on unseen parts with a single learned model, but they assume that diverse geometries are available centrally. This assumption is restrictive when each manufacturing site holds only a limited set of proprietary part designs that it cannot share. We propose Fed-PIGANO, a federated framework that trains physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator (PI-GANO) models at individual sites and aggregates their geometry encoders and prediction networks without sharing part geometries. We evaluate the framework on a 2D steady-state thermal benchmark for metal AM, with geometries from five polygonal families distributed across three sites under four scenarios that range from identical to strongly different family compositions. Over seven replications, Fed-PIGANO achieves mean relative L2 errors of 1.83% to 2.04% across all 12 scenario-site cases, compared with up to 20.46% for local-only training, and consistently yields lower PDE residuals. Its prediction accuracy is comparable to that of a centralized model trained on the pooled geometries of all sites. These results demonstrate that federated learning lets manufacturing sites benefit from each other's geometries without sharing them, enabling rapid thermal prediction on new part designs for tasks such as shape optimization, inverse design, and uncertainty quantification.

title: Beyond a Single Sign: BiTE for Branch-Preserving Binary Threshold Expansion
description:
arXiv:2611.17576v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Binary neural networks (BNNs) reduce model storage and replace many arithmetic operations with efficient bitwise computations, but the single-sign activation limits their representational capacity. Each preactivation direction is compared with one threshold and reduced to one of two values, discarding variation within each sign region. We propose \textbf{BiTE} (Branch-Preserving Binary Threshold Expansion), which evaluates each feature direction against $K$ ordered thresholds and retains the resulting binary responses as separate inputs to the following learned operator. BiTE can distinguish up to $K+1$ ordered activation states while allowing the following operator to learn a separate transformation for each threshold response. It also enables a controllable trade-off between the number of independently constructed feature directions and the number of ordered responses extracted from each direction. On BinaryViT, BiTE improves mean final-epoch Top-1 accuracy from $74.60\pm0.30\%$ to $75.83\pm0.15\%$ on CIFAR-10 and from $42.80\pm0.46\%$ to $44.07\pm0.32\%$ on CIFAR-100, with nearly unchanged trainable parameter counts. A matched uniform-collapse control reaches $75.33\pm0.15\%$ on CIFAR-10, supporting the value of retaining the threshold responses separately relative to the evaluated scalar collapse. Binary VGG-16 experiments further show a favorable observed parameter--accuracy trade-off, including a configuration that achieves $0.64$ percentage points higher mean accuracy with $21.8\%$ fewer parameters than conventional width scaling. Overall, these results support branch-preserving threshold expansion as an effective way to improve binary representations and the observed parameter--accuracy trade-off.

title: Datasette 1.0a43：流式导出、安全修复与跨页过渡
description:
Datasette 1.0a43 的重点是输出渲染器的流式支持、安全修复，以及基于 CSS 的跨文档视图过渡。此次更新后，1.0 里程碑的完成进度达到 53%。

面向关注数据工具与 Web 开发的写好标智库读者，本文按导出接口、安全边界和页面交互三个方向梳理这次更新。

输出渲染器支持流式响应

本次面向 1.0 的主要改动，是为输出渲染器加入流式支持：

  • 内置 TSV、CSV 导出已采用这一机制。
  • 插件可以声明自身支持流式输出。
  • 新增 Response.stream() 方法，支持在一次响应中流式输出表内全部行。

对于输出渲染器插件的开发者来说，流式输出是此次值得关注的接口变化。

安全修复：私有查询信息可能泄露

本次包含多项安全修复，其中一项涉及私有存储查询的信息暴露，并已发布安全公告。

该问题可能导致查询标题与 SQL 内容被读取，但不会允许访问者执行该查询。

这里需要区分两个权限边界：

  • 信息可见性：访问者能否读取查询标题和 SQL。
  • 查询执行权限：访问者能否运行该查询。

此次问题涉及前者，不能将其理解为访问者可以直接执行私有查询。

行页面与插件接口改进

围绕行页面、复制操作和插件开发，本次还包括以下更新：

  • 调整行页面的 JSON 表示，为 1.0 做准备。
  • 新增 <datasette-copy-button> Web Component，在多处提供数据库结构复制功能。
  • 行页面中的 JSON 列内容支持格式化显示。
  • 新增 JavaScript 工具方法 DatasetteModal.confirm()。
  • 修复数十项问题。

用 CSS 改善多页导航体验

Datasette 仍然是多页应用。新增的跨文档视图过渡并未改变这一架构，而是让页面间导航在视觉上更接近单页应用。

关键 CSS 如下：

/* 仅在用户未要求减少动态效果时启用跨文档视图过渡 */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  @view-transition {
    navigation: auto;
  }
}

/* 让分面结果区域在新旧位置之间过渡 */
html:active-view-transition .content > .facet-results {
  view-transition-name: facet-results;
}

/* 为包含数据表格的容器设置过渡名称 */
html:active-view-transition .table-wrapper:has(> table.rows-and-columns) {
  view-transition-name: rows-table;
}

这段实现可以分为两部分：

  1. 启用跨文档过渡：通过 @view-transition 中的 navigation: auto 开启导航过渡，并用 prefers-reduced-motion 尊重用户的减少动态效果偏好。
  2. 指定参与过渡的区域：为分面结果和表格容器设置 view-transition-name，让对应区域参与页面切换动画。

需要注意，这属于导航体验的增强，不代表 Datasette 已改为单页应用。

浏览器兼容性需区分现状与预期

该版本说明称，Safari 和 Chrome 已可使用这一效果；Firefox 162 则被预计将于 2026 年 12 月 8 日加入支持。

后者是预期时间，并非已经完成的兼容性确认。实际采用时，应以目标浏览器版本的支持情况为准。

title: LitArc-Bench: Disentangling Text-Specific Reader-Response Dynamics from Position and Lexical Affect
description:
arXiv:2611.18412v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When model predictions track an unfolding human affect trajectory, alignment may reflect narrative position, affective words, or text-specific reader-response dynamics. We introduce LitArc-Bench to separate these explanations: 39 Chinese-language literary excerpts segmented into seven checkpoints, with 430 questionnaires from 81 adults in two classroom groups (9,020 VAD ratings). We compare three future-blind model runs with leave-one-text-out position priors, lexical affect, and human-human references. Position alone reaches r = .470 for arousal, making raw alignment insufficient. Yet all six V/A transition advantages over a joint position-lexicon control have text-bootstrap intervals above zero. Cross-fitted models match the correct human text better than 38 mismatched texts in all nine model-dimension cells (p < .0001); a text-invariant negative control returns chance (p = 1). On human transitions at least 0.5 points against the position trend, models recover 69-76% of valence directions and 53-68% for arousal and dominance. Under crossed participant-text resampling, all nine identity intervals remain above zero; joint-control advantages are robust for valence and directional but less certain for arousal. High shape agreement still coexists with scale bias. LitArc-Bench identifies which components of literary reader response are recoverable beyond shallow explanations and why shape, calibration, and human variability require separate evaluation.

title: Node.js Setup for Creating a Message Queue and Publishing Game Cleanup Tasks
description:
A game session cleanup job should leave the web request quickly, then make its delivery contract explicit. For expired sessions, I would publish one idempotent message per cleanup unit, let a worker claim it, and delete the message only after the write succeeds. The important choice is not the queue brand. It is what happens when a worker dies after claiming work.

The practical rule is this: use at-least-once delivery, make the handler safe to repeat, and set the visibility window longer than the normal cleanup attempt. A queue is a delivery mechanism, not a transaction around every database and game-service write.

That boundary matters.

Suppose the API receives a request to end a match. It records the match as finished and enqueues cleanup for abandoned room membership, temporary inventory reservations, and the session presence record. The request returns after the durable handoff, not after every cleanup operation. That keeps the request path bounded.

The worker receives a payload like this:

type CleanupMessage = {
  jobId: string;
  sessionId: string;
  reason: "expired" | "match-ended";
  createdAt: string;
};

jobId is the useful field. The worker stores it, or uses a database constraint around it, so a retry cannot remove a newly created session that happens to reuse an identifier. The cleanup operation itself should also be idempotent: deleting an already absent presence row is success, and releasing an already released reservation is success.

That is the difference between “the message was delivered” and “the game reached the desired state.” The queue can provide the first property. The application has to design the second.

How should a Node.js setup create and publish a message queue?

Keep the queue behind a narrow interface. This makes the publisher and worker testable without tying the article to a commercial service or a particular broker protocol.

type QueueMessage<T> = {
  receipt: string;
  body: T;
};

interface TaskQueue<T> {
  publish(message: T): Promise<void>;
  receive(): Promise<QueueMessage<T> | undefined>;
  acknowledge(receipt: string): Promise<void>;
  extendVisibility(receipt: string, seconds: number): Promise<void>;
}

async function enqueueSessionCleanup(
  queue: TaskQueue<CleanupMessage>,
  sessionId: string,
  reason: CleanupMessage["reason"],
): Promise<void> {
  const message: CleanupMessage = {
    jobId: crypto.randomUUID(),
    sessionId,
    reason,
    createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  };

  await queue.publish(message);
}

async function runCleanupWorker(
  queue: TaskQueue<CleanupMessage>,
  cleanup: (message: CleanupMessage) => Promise<void>,
): Promise<void> {
  for (;;) {
    const item = await queue.receive();
    if (!item) {
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 250));
      continue;
    }

    try {
      await cleanup(item.body);
      await queue.acknowledge(item.receipt);
    } catch (error) {
      console.error("cleanup failed; leaving message for retry", {
        receipt: item.receipt,
        error,
      });
    }
  }
}

The adapter owns persistence, claiming, visibility timeout, and retry policy. The worker owns business correctness. A failed handler deliberately does not acknowledge the message. A broker can then make it visible again after its visibility timeout. A worker crash follows the same path because the acknowledgement never happens. This split trades a little adapter code for a testable worker and a recovery path that does not depend on a request staying open.

The example uses crypto.randomUUID(), so the module also needs the Node.js import below when the file is compiled as a module:

import crypto from "node:crypto";

In a real process, add a shutdown handler that stops taking new messages and waits for the current cleanup to finish. Do not treat process termination as an acknowledgement.

How long should a message stay invisible?

This is where the delivery guarantee turns into an operational number. If a cleanup normally takes 8 seconds but occasionally waits on a database lock for 20, a 10-second visibility window is too short. Another worker can receive the same message while the first one is still changing state. That is a duplicate execution, not necessarily data loss, but it exposes every non-idempotent side effect.

Start with a measured upper bound, add room for the downstream timeout, and extend visibility during unusually long work. The queue documentation for this pattern describes visibility timeout as the period in which a received message is hidden from other consumers; it does not remove the message. An acknowledgement or delete is still required after successful processing.

There is a second limit: a poisoned message should not retry forever. Track receive attempts in the adapter, move messages beyond the retry budget to a dead-letter destination, and alert on that destination. The alert should include jobId, sessionId, and the last error. A dashboard showing only queue depth will miss a queue that is empty because all the bad work has been quarantined.

What breaks first in production?

The first trap is publishing before the match completion is committed. The queue can contain cleanup for a match state that later rolls back. The opposite trap is committing first and crashing before publish. That leaves a finished match with no cleanup message.

For a solo SaaS, I would use an outbox table when the database transaction and the background task must agree. Write the business change and an outbox row in one transaction. A small publisher reads unsent rows, publishes them, and marks them sent. The publisher can repeat its own work, so the outbox message also needs a stable jobId and a consumer that tolerates duplicates. This costs a table and a polling loop. It buys a clear recovery path.

The other failure is a worker that performs three side effects and fails between the second and third. There is no universal rollback for external systems. Break cleanup into independently retryable operations, record progress where useful, and make each operation converge toward the same final state. “Run once” sounds attractive, but “safe to run again” is the property that survives a crash.

Make retries boring.

What I would change at scale

With a few hundred cleanup messages per hour, one worker process and a durable queue are enough. I would spend the next hour on tests: publish failure, crash after receive, timeout during cleanup, duplicate delivery, and dead-letter recovery. Those tests protect more revenue per hour than a custom scheduler.

At higher volume, separate queues by work profile. Presence cleanup and inventory release have different downstream limits, so one busy category should not consume all worker capacity. Add a concurrency cap per dependency, structured logs keyed by jobId, queue age metrics, retry counts, and an alert on oldest-message age. Autoscaling on depth alone is too blunt when each task has a different runtime.

I would also keep the message small. Put identifiers and the reason in the queue; fetch current state in the worker. Large snapshots become stale while waiting and make retries harder to reason about. The trade-off is an extra read. For cleanup, current state is usually the safer input.

The decision rule is straightforward: if losing a cleanup task is acceptable, an in-process timer may be enough. If the task must survive a web process restart, use durable queue storage. If duplicate cleanup would be dangerous, fix idempotency before increasing worker count. Delivery guarantees are selected in the application boundary, then enforced by the queue adapter and the data model.

Sources

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://nodejs.org/api/crypto.html#cryptorandomuuidoptions

title: Differentially Private Federated Class-Incremental Learning for EEG Mental State Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.17944v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated learning (FL) under differential privacy (DP) is typically evaluated on large client cohorts, where subsampling and cross-client averaging amplify privacy and smooth injected noise. Personal biosignal applications such as wearable EEG instead involve small federations of a handful of subjects, a regime whose interaction with formal client-level DP is largely uncharacterized. We study differentially private federated class-incremental learning in this small-cohort regime, combining a public EEG dataset with a custom four-channel MUSE 2 recording set into a K=5-client federation, and give a masked per-class training protocol that avoids degenerate gradients and missing negative supervision under class-incremental streaming. We propose FedEEG, combining Synaptic-Intelligence consolidation with a lagged adaptive FedProx term, and show it reduces catastrophic forgetting relative to FedAvg, FedProx, and a federated Learning-without-Forgetting baseline; on-device balanced-batch replay reduces mean forgetting by a further 56.7%. A class-scoping diagnosis yields $50.5\%\pm3.6\%$ accuracy with 6 seeds and 2.02 times chance. We also introduce head-scoped client-level DP, which protects the classification head and alone reduces the achievable $\varepsilon$ by 200 times at a matched round budget; combined with fewer communication rounds it reaches $\varepsilon\!\approx\!10.4$ with utility not statistically distinguishable from non-private training.

title: We counted which apps send OTP codes to shared virtual numbers (900 tries, Nov 2026)
description:
If you test sign-up flows, run QA across countries, or just wonder why a free online number never got your code, here is some real data. We run a receive-SMS service, and between 27 October and 16 November 2026 about 900 free shared numbers on one pool either received an OTP or timed out. We counted the results per app and country.

How we counted

A try is a free number that either received the code or waited the full time without it. Numbers the visitor gave back early are left out, because that says more about patience than about the app. Only app and country pairs with at least 8 tries are shown below.

Apps that usually deliver

App (country) Codes / tries Success
Marktplaats (FR) 45 / 46 98%
YouTube (PK) 13 / 16 81%
OpenAI (IN) 19 / 27 70%
Airtel (IN) 14 / 21 67%
Opay (NG) 14 / 21 67%
Fiverr (DE) 16 / 26 62%
Discord (DE) 8 / 13 62%

Apps that rarely deliver

App (country) Codes / tries Success
Telegram (IN) 2 / 39 5%
Telegram (NG) 1 / 13 8%
Telegram (PK) 0 / 11 0%
YouTube (PH) 4 / 31 13%
Foodpanda (PK) 0 / 8 0%

Three things that surprised us

1. Country matters as much as the app. YouTube delivered 81% of codes in Pakistan and 13% in the Philippines. By country overall, France delivered on almost 9 of 10 tries, Germany and Nigeria on more than 4 in 10, India on about a third, and Mexico and the Philippines rarely worked.

2. Some big apps simply refuse shared numbers. Telegram delivered 8 codes out of 127 tries across all countries. Amazon delivered 2 out of 50 in our wider logs. Waiting longer does not help; the SMS is never sent. We have since removed apps like these from our free list so people stop wasting time.

3. People give up too early. A large share of numbers were cancelled about a minute and a half after they were issued. International SMS can take several minutes. Give it the full 10 to 15 minutes before you conclude it failed.

What this means for your tests

  • For automated end-to-end tests, a free shared number is only reliable for apps and countries in the first table. Do not build CI on it.
  • For anything that must work every time, or for apps like Telegram, use a private number (one-time or rented) that only your test account receives SMS on.
  • If you send OTPs yourself and see users from shared-number ranges, expect them. Blocking them is a product choice, but it explains some of your "never received" tickets.

The data

The full table (132 app and country pairs, counts only, no phone numbers or user data) is on Kaggle under CC BY 4.0: SMS code delivery to free virtual numbers by app. There is also an interactive chart on Observable.

Disclosure: I'm part of the team behind receive-smss.net, which offers free numbers, private one-time numbers and rentals. The figures come from our own logs and change over time.

title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2611.18471v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.

title: Projeto de Banco de Dados - Normalização
description:
O processo de normalização de banco de dados relacionais, proposto por Edgar F. Codd na IBM, visa organizar o armazenamento das informações para garantir a eficácia das restrições de integridade e eliminar dependências indesejadas estruturadas incorretamente, conhecidas como anomalias. Essas falhas manifestam-se na inserção, quando a rigidez de tabelas mistas impede o registro de novos dados por falta de informações complementares ainda inexistentes; na exclusão, quando a remoção de um registro apaga acidentalmente dados de outra entidade associada; e na atualização, provocada pela duplicação de dados em várias linhas, o que gera inconsistências e dados contraditórios caso a alteração seja feita de forma incompleta.

Para solucionar essas falhas, a normalização utiliza um conjunto progressivo de regras chamadas Formas Normais. Esse processo opera de maneira cumulativa, de modo que cada nova etapa impõe critérios mais rigorosos e herda integralmente as exigências das formas anteriores, garantindo uma evolução consistente na estruturação e no refinamento lógico do banco de dados.

Como resultado desse rigor metodológico, o projeto obtém vantagens, como a prevenção de anomalias, a mitigação da redundância não intencional, a economia direta de custos de armazenamento — especialmente relevante em servidores locais e em ambientes de computação em nuvem —, e a recuperação mais ágil de dados por meio de consultas otimizadas que exigem menor esforço de processamento.

Dependências Funcionais

As dependências funcionais (DFs) refletem as regras de negócio e as verdades do mundo real que o banco de dados deve respeitar rigidamente. Elas ocorrem quando os valores de um conjunto de atributos (o conjunto determinante, localizado à esquerda) determinam obrigatoriamente os valores de outros (o conjunto dependente, à direita), representadas pela notação A → B. Esse conceito é fundamental para a aplicação das Formas Normais (2ª, 3ª e Boyce-Codd) e para a identificação de chaves, uma vez que um conjunto de atributos capaz de determinar todos os demais da tabela constitui, por definição, uma chave.

Para descobrir novas dependências a partir das regras iniciais fornecidas pelos projetistas, utilizam-se os Axiomas de Armstrong. A reflexividade dita que um conjunto de atributos sempre determina suas partes ou a si mesmo (gerando DFs triviais úteis para provar superchaves); a augmentação permite adicionar atributos extras a ambos os lados de uma dependência sem invalidá-la, auxiliando na composição de chaves; e a transitividade possibilita encadear dependências quando o determinante de uma é determinado por outra (X → Y e Y → Z ⇒ X → Z ), revelando chaves ocultas no modelo.

  1. Reflexividade: Se Y é um subconjunto de X, então X determina Y.
    • Conceito: Um conjunto de atributos sempre determina a si mesmo ou a qualquer parte de si.
    • Exemplo: {CPF_Cliente,Cod_Produto}→CPF_Cliente (É uma DF trivial, mas válida).
  2. Augmentação: Se XY, então XZYZ.
    • Conceito: Adicionar o mesmo atributo (Z) a ambos os lados de uma dependência não a invalida. Isso é crucial para a formação de chaves compostas.
    • Exemplo: Se Cod_Produto→Preço_Unitário, então {Cod_Produto,CPF_Cliente}→{Preço_Unitário,CPF_Cliente}.
  3. Transitividade: Se XY e YZ, então XZ.
    • Conceito: Permite encadear dependências. Se X define Y, e Y define Z, então X define Z indiretamente.
    • Exemplo: Se tivermos as DFs: CPF_Cliente→ID_Endereco e ID_Endereco→Cidade, podemos inferir que CPF_Cliente→Cidade.

Complementando os axiomas, regras derivadas otimizam a manipulação lógica dessas dependências. A união estabelece que, se um mesmo determinante gera dependências separadas, ele também pode determiná-las conjuntamente (X→Y e X→Z ⇒ X →YZ ). Inversamente, a regra da decomposição permite separar um conjunto de dependentes no lado direito quando determinados em bloco por um único determinante (X→YZ ⇒ X →Y e X→Z).

  1. União: Se X→Y e X→Z, então X→YZ.
    • Conceito: Se um determinante define dois atributos separadamente, ele também pode defini-los como um conjunto.
    • Exemplo: Se Cod_Produto→Nome_Produto e Cod_Produto→Preço_Unitário, então Cod_Produto→{Nome_Produto,Preço_Unitário}.
  2. Decomposição: Se X→YZ, então X→Y e X→Z.
    • Conceito: O inverso da união. Se um determinante define um conjunto de atributos, ele também define cada um individualmente.
    • Exemplo: Se Cod_Produto→{Nome_Produto,Preço_Unitário}, podemos decompor em Cod_Produto→Nome_Produto e Cod_Produto→Preço_Unitário.

Formas Normais

O processo de normalização inicia-se com a 1ª Forma Normal (1FN), considerada obrigatória para a existência conceitual e matemática de um banco relacional. Ela exige que cada tabela possua obrigatoriamente uma chave primária para a identificação unívoca de seus registros e impõe a atomicidade dos atributos, proibindo estritamente a presença de grupos repetitivos, tais como atributos multivalorados, compostos, repetitivos em série ou estruturas aninhadas do tipo tabela dentro de tabela.

Evoluindo para a 2ª Forma Normal (2FN), a tabela precisa primeiro estar na 1FN e eliminar totalmente as dependências parciais, o que significa que todos os atributos não-chave devem depender de forma integral e total de toda a chave primária composta. Caso exista dependência de apenas uma parte da chave, a tabela deve ser decomposta em estruturas menores e independentes focadas em suas respectivas dependências funcionais.

A 3ª Forma Normal (3FN) introduz o conceito de combate às dependências transitivas, estabelecendo que atributos comuns (não-chave) não podem determinar outros atributos comuns. Desse modo, o modelo não tolera correntes indiretas do tipo em que a chave determina um atributo comum, e este por sua vez determina outro, exigindo que a cadeia seja quebrada e isolada em tabelas específicas.

A Forma Normal de Boyce-Codd (FNBC) é uma versão mais rigorosa da Terceira Forma Normal (3FN). Uma tabela está na FNBC quando já se encontra na 3FN e, para cada dependência funcional não trivial, o determinante é obrigatoriamente uma superchave da tabela. Isso significa que nenhum atributo não chave ou parte de uma chave candidata pode determinar outro atributo que faça parte de uma chave candidata.

Para entender na prática, imagine uma tabela de monitoria universitária com as colunas Aluno, Disciplina e Monitor. Considere que um aluno pode ter vários monitores em disciplinas diferentes, mas cada monitor auxilia em apenas uma disciplina, e cada aluno tem apenas um monitor por disciplina. A chave primária composta pode ser (Aluno, Disciplina), porém o atributo Monitor determina sozinho a Disciplina. Como o Monitor não é uma superchave da tabela, ocorre redundância ao repetir o nome da disciplina toda vez que o monitor aparece. A solução é dividir a tabela original em duas: uma tabela relacionando Aluno e Monitor e outra relacionando Monitor e Disciplina.

A Quarta Forma Normal (4FN) trata da eliminação das chamadas dependências multivaloradas. Uma tabela está na 4FN se já estiver na FNBC e não contiver duas ou mais características independentes entre si e multivaloradas sobre a mesma entidade. Em outras palavras, não devemos misturar na mesma tabela diferentes listas de atributos que não possuem relação direta um com o outro.

Como exemplo didático, pense em uma tabela chamada Funcionario_Info com as colunas Funcionario, Idioma e Ferramenta. Suponha que o funcionário Carlos fale Inglês e Espanhol, e também saiba usar Excel e Python. Como os idiomas que ele fala não têm relação com as ferramentas que ele domina, somos obrigados a criar todas as combinações possíveis na mesma tabela para não perder dados (Carlos com Inglês e Excel, Carlos com Inglês e Python, Carlos com Espanhol e Excel, etc.). Para atingir a 4FN, dividimos essa estrutura em duas tabelas independentes: Funcionario_Idioma e Funcionario_Ferramenta.

A Quinta Forma Normal (5FN), também conhecida como Forma Normal de Projeção-Junção (PJ/NF), tem como objetivo eliminar redundâncias causadas por dependências de junção. Uma tabela está na 5FN quando já está na 4FN e não pode ser decomposta em tabelas menores sem que haja perda de informação ou criação de registros falsos (tuplas espúrias) ao juntá-las novamente. Ela lida com relacionamentos ternários onde três entidades precisam estar associadas simultaneamente sob regras de negócio específicas.

Considere um cenário de logística com uma tabela contendo Fornecedor, Peca e Projeto. Suponha que exista uma regra de negócio indicando que, se um fornecedor fornece uma determinada peça, e essa peça é usada em um projeto, e esse fornecedor também atende a esse projeto, então o fornecedor obrigatoriamente fornece aquela peça para aquele projeto. Quando essa regra cíclica existe, manter os três dados juntos gera repetições desnecessárias sempre que um novo vínculo é criado. A solução na 5FN é quebrar a tabela original em três tabelas binárias: Fornecedor_Peca, Peca_Projeto e Fornecedor_Projeto, pois a junção natural dessas três reconstruirá exatamente os dados originais sem redundância.

Dependências funcionais na prática

A materialização prática das dependências funcionais, chaves e formas normais em bancos de dados relacionais ocorre por meio de comandos da linguagem SQL, destacando-se o PRIMARY KEY para definir a chave primária e o UNIQUE para as chaves alternativas. Essa estruturação permite certificar se as regras de negócio foram implementadas corretamente na modelagem física, pois a definição de um atributo como chave assegura diretamente a validade de dependências funcionais em que esse identificador determina todos os demais elementos do registro.

Além do código de criação, a validade de uma dependência funcional (XY) pode ser testada empiricamente sobre os dados armazenados em uma instância de tabela. A regra prática consiste em verificar se existe qualquer par de linhas que compartilhe o mesmo valor em X mas apresente valores distintos em Y. Caso um mesmo determinante aponte para dados diferentes no lado dependente, encontra-se uma contradição e a dependência funcional torna-se inválida; se nunca houver divergência, a dependência se sustenta para aquela instância analisada.

Desnormalização

Embora a normalização até a 3ª Forma Normal (3FN) seja o padrão ideal para eliminar anomalias e garantir a integridade dos dados, ela gera o efeito colateral de fragmentar a informação em numerosas tabelas. Essa segmentação excessiva exige operações complexas de junção (JOINs) que consomem tempo e recursos computacionais elevados, abrindo espaço para a desnormalização intencional em cenários de grande volume de dados ou exigências estritas de velocidade, onde se aceita deliberadamente certa redundância em prol do desempenho e da otimização de consultas.

Para concretizar esse equilíbrio entre agilidade e integridade, aplicam-se estratégias práticas específicas de desnormalização, começando pelo uso de dados redundantes, em que a mesma informação é armazenada em tabelas diferentes para evitar junções custosas, transferindo ao sistema a responsabilidade de manter os registros sincronizados. Outra abordagem é o dado derivado, que armazena um atributo calculado de antemão para reduzir o custo de processamento em tempo real em troca de um maior custo de armazenamento, sendo um desdobramento direto do dado pré-agregado, que salva resultados de operações como somas, médias ou contagens calculadas previamente e atualizadas sempre que a origem sofre modificações.

Por fim, a técnica de tabela temporária para relatório resolve situações em que a rigidez da estrutura normalizada torna inviável a extração de informações complexas diretamente pelo modelo padrão. Nesses casos, constrói-se uma estrutura desnormalizada exclusiva para a montagem do relatório, sendo descartada logo após o uso e isenta de qualquer preocupação com a consistência ou sincronização contínua dos dados, funcionando como uma ferramenta de suporte pontual à tomada de decisão.

title: eBPF Ring Buffer Backpressure in Go Services: Kernel-to-User Data Loss, Perf Event Semantics, and the Sampling Tradeoff
description:
eBPF Ring Buffer Backpressure in Go Services: Kernel-to-User Data Loss, Perf Event Semantics, and the Sampling Tradeoff

eBPF-based observability tooling—network tracing, syscall auditing, latency histograms—sits inside production Go services today not as a curiosity but as a load-bearing instrumentation layer. The appeal is real: zero application recompilation, nanosecond-accurate timestamps, kernel-side aggregation. The failure mode is subtle and almost never surfaced in vendor documentation: the ring buffer fills, the kernel drops events silently, and your dashboards look completely healthy while you are blind to entire request classes.

This article walks through the mechanics of that failure, compares the two primary kernel-to-user transport mechanisms, and proposes a concrete adaptive sampling strategy implementable in a Go consumer.

Two Transports, Two Failure Modes

Perf Event Array (BPF_MAP_TYPE_PERF_EVENT_ARRAY)

The older mechanism. Each CPU core writes to its own per-CPU ring buffer via bpf_perf_event_output. The Go side—typically cilium/ebpf or libbpf-go—opens an epoll file descriptor per CPU and drains records in a polling loop.

The critical property: when the per-CPU buffer is full, the kernel drops the event and increments a lost-samples counter accessible only by reading the perf event header's PERF_RECORD_LOST records inline with data records. If your consumer loop is not reading that header type explicitly, you never see the loss count. The buffer is sized at map creation time in pages (must be a power of two). Default tooling often uses 8–64 pages (32–256 KB per CPU). On a 32-core host tracing every syscall, that fills in under a millisecond under load.

Ring Buffer (BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF)

Introduced in kernel 5.8. A single shared ring buffer across all CPUs, avoiding the per-CPU fragmentation problem. The eBPF program reserves space atomically with bpf_ringbuf_reserve, writes, then commits. If reservation fails (buffer full), your eBPF program receives a NULL pointer—and must explicitly handle that path or silently skip the event.

The Go consumer uses a single file descriptor with epoll. Reads are lock-free via a pair of producer/consumer position counters in a shared memory region. Throughput is higher and memory utilization is better, but the single buffer means a slow Go consumer blocks all CPU cores from committing new records, not just one.

The failure modes differ:

  • Perf array: per-CPU isolation means one hot core hurts only its own queue, but loss counters are buried in stream.
  • Ring buffer: global contention, but the fd-based notification model makes watermark-driven wakeup straightforward.

Where Go Consumer Latency Causes Drops

A Go eBPF consumer is structurally a tight loop:

rd, err := ringbuf.NewReader(objs.Events)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
defer rd.Close()

for {
    record, err := rd.Read()
    if errors.Is(err, ringbuf.ErrClosed) {
        return
    }
    if err != nil {
        continue
    }
    processEvent(record.RawSample)
}

processEvent is where latency accumulates. If it does anything synchronous—a MongoDB write, a JSON marshal with allocation, a channel send to a blocked goroutine—the Read call is delayed. During that delay, the kernel continues writing. When the buffer reaches capacity, bpf_ringbuf_reserve returns NULL in your eBPF C program and the event is dropped. The kernel does expose a lost counter in the ring buffer's metadata page, but cilium/ebpf's Reader does not surface it directly; you must memory-map the consumer page yourself and read offset 24 bytes in (the lost u64 field).

The runtime scheduler compounds this. A goroutine blocked on a channel send while another goroutine holds the P can delay the consumer loop by an entire scheduler quantum (~10ms in the worst case with a saturated GOMAXPROCS). Unlike a C consumer that owns its thread, a Go consumer is subject to preemption. Pinning the consumer goroutine to an OS thread with runtime.LockOSThread() reduces jitter but does not eliminate GC stop-the-world pauses.

Adaptive Sampling: The Correct Mitigation

Buffer resizing is the blunt instrument. Doubling the ring buffer from 64 pages to 512 pages absorbs spikes but adds 1.75 MB of locked kernel memory per buffer instance and does not help if the consumer is structurally slow. The better approach is kernel-side adaptive sampling driven by a feedback signal from the user-space consumer.

The architecture:

  1. A BPF map of type BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY holds a single u32 sample_rate. The eBPF program reads it on each event and emits only when bpf_get_prandom_u32() % sample_rate == 0.
  2. The Go consumer tracks the fill ratio of the ring buffer by reading the producer and consumer position counters from the mmap'd metadata page.
  3. A control goroutine adjusts sample_rate up (more dropping) when fill ratio crosses a high-water mark, and down (more recording) when it drops below a low-water mark. 
type SamplingController struct {
    sampleRateMap *ebpf.Map
    metaPage      []byte // mmap of ring buffer consumer page
    mu            sync.Mutex
    current       uint32
}

func (sc *SamplingController) Adjust() {
    prod := atomic.LoadUint64((*uint64)(unsafe.Pointer(&sc.metaPage[0])))
    cons := atomic.LoadUint64((*uint64)(unsafe.Pointer(&sc.metaPage[8])))
    // ring size is known at construction; derive fill ratio
    inflight := prod - cons
    ratio := float64(inflight) / float64(sc.ringSize)

    sc.mu.Lock()
    defer sc.mu.Unlock()
    switch {
    case ratio > 0.75 && sc.current < 64:
        sc.current = min(sc.current*2, 64)
    case ratio < 0.25 && sc.current > 1:
        sc.current = max(sc.current/2, 1)
    }
    val := sc.current
    _ = sc.sampleRateMap.Put(uint32(0), val)
}

Run Adjust on a 500ms ticker. The convergence is coarse but sufficient: a sudden 10× traffic spike raises sample_rate to 8 within 1.5 seconds (three ticks), dropping 87.5% of events, which is far preferable to dropping 100% while the buffer saturates and losing the lost-count signal itself.

Operational Consequences

Sampling breaks rate-based alerting. If you emit events for every inbound request and drive a Prometheus counter from the Go consumer, sampling invalidates the counter without correction. The fix: maintain a total_events_seen counter in the eBPF program (a per-CPU array, summed in user space) and expose it alongside total_events_emitted. Compute effective sample rate as their ratio and apply it as a multiplier in your recording rules.

The lost counter is not a replacement for structured drop attribution. The ring buffer's metadata-page lost count tells you how many reservations failed but not which event types were dropped. Under mixed workload tracing—syscalls, network events, uprobe hits—you cannot diagnose which probe is the hot path from the aggregate. Instrument per-probe drop counters in a second BPF map keyed by probe ID.

Memory-mapping the metadata page is not documented in cilium/ebpf as a stable API. The page layout matches kernel bpf_ringbuf internals. Pin a kernel version test in CI that validates the offsets have not shifted. Alternatively, use BPF_OBJ_GET_INFO_BY_FD to retrieve ring_buffer_max_entries and correlate with the fd's seek position—noisier but kernel-API-stable.

Decision Framework

Choose your transport and mitigation path based on these axes:

Condition Recommendation
Kernel < 5.8 Perf event array; read LOST records explicitly
Single hot CPU core (e.g., network RX softirq affinity) Perf array preferred; ring buffer will serialize all cores
Mixed multi-probe workload, kernel ≥ 5.8 Ring buffer; lower total memory, single wakeup fd
Go consumer does synchronous I/O in hot path Decouple: channel → worker pool; never block Read loop
Consumer latency p99 > 5ms Add adaptive sampling controller; do not just enlarge buffer
Need event-type-level drop attribution Per-probe drop counter map; aggregate in user space
Rate-based alerting downstream Emit total-seen counter from eBPF; apply ratio correction in Prometheus rules

The ring buffer is the right default for Go services on modern kernels—its throughput and memory profile are better, and the notification model suits Go's epoll integration. But treating it as a lossless channel is the architectural mistake. Build the sampling controller, expose the drop signal, and correct derived metrics at the recording layer. Observability infrastructure that can silently lose data under its own load is not infrastructure—it is a liability dressed as insight.

title: Background Jobs in Python: Celery vs Simpler Queues
description:
Long-running work should not sit inside an HTTP request. Sending a transactional email, generating a PDF, processing an upload, or embedding a batch of documents for a search or RAG pipeline can take seconds or minutes. If that work runs in the request-response cycle, users wait, workers time out, and a retry from the client can start the same job twice.

Python gives you several ways to move that work into a background job. The useful question is not “which tool is best,” but which one matches the shape of your app: a small FastAPI service, a growing backend with Redis, or a distributed system that needs retries, schedules, and multiple queues.

This guide compares four options you will actually see in Python backends: FastAPI BackgroundTasks, RQ, ARQ, and Celery. It stays on the job-queue choice itself, not general async syntax or concurrency models.

What a background job needs to get right

A queue is more than “run this later.” For anything you care about, the setup should give you:

  • Durability. If the API process restarts, the job is still waiting in a broker such as Redis or RabbitMQ.
  • A separate worker. Heavy work runs in another process, so the web process stays free for requests.
  • Retries with limits. Transient failures (a mail provider timeout, a locked row, a brief Redis blip) can be retried without blocking the user.
  • Idempotency. The same job can safely run twice. That matters because retries and at-least-once delivery are normal.
  • Visibility. You can see queued, running, failed, and completed jobs, and inspect why a job failed.

FastAPI BackgroundTasks only covers the “run this after the response” part. RQ, ARQ, and Celery add a broker and a worker. That is the line between a convenience helper and a real job queue.

Option comparison 

Queue Broker Worker model Best fit Complexity     FastAPI `BackgroundTasks` None (in-process) Same API process Non-critical, short, fire-and-forget work Very low   RQ (Redis Queue) Redis Synchronous Python workers Straightforward jobs in a sync or mixed codebase Low   ARQ (Async Redis Queue) Redis Asyncio workers Native async jobs in FastAPI or other asyncio apps Medium   Celery Redis or RabbitMQ Distributed workers, optional scheduling Multiple queues, workflows, scheduled tasks, and larger systems High   If you only need to send a welcome email and can accept lost work on a process restart, start with `BackgroundTasks`. If the job must survive a deploy, move to RQ or ARQ. Reach for Celery when you need more than a simple Redis-backed queue: several worker pools, a scheduler, or chained workflows.

FastAPI BackgroundTasks: useful, but not a queue

FastAPI can run a function after it sends the response. You do not need Redis, a worker service, or a new deployment unit. That is perfect for short, non-critical work such as writing an audit log or sending a welcome email.

from fastapi import BackgroundTasks, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

def send_welcome_email(email: str) -> None:
    # Keep this short. It still runs inside the API process.
    print(f"Sent welcome email to {email}")

@app.post("/register")
async def register(email: str, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    background_tasks.add_task(send_welcome_email, email)
    return {"message": "Registration successful. Email will be sent shortly."}

The limitation is the same as the convenience: the job lives in memory in the API process. If the process is killed, restarted, or replaced during a deploy before the function finishes, the job is gone. There is no built-in retry dashboard, no dead-letter queue, and no way to scale that work independently of your web workers.

Do not use BackgroundTasks for payments, invoice generation, video processing, document embedding, or anything you cannot afford to lose. Also avoid long or blocking work here. It still shares the process with your API, so a slow job can hurt request latency.

RQ: the simple Redis-backed queue

RQ (Redis Queue) is a small, readable library for enqueueing Python callables and running them in a separate worker process. Jobs are stored in Redis, so they survive an API restart. The mental model is easy to teach and easy to operate: enqueue a function, run rq worker, and inspect failures with RQ’s tools.

from redis import Redis
from rq import Queue

queue = Queue("reports", connection=Redis())

def generate_report(user_id: int) -> str:
    # Long-running CPU or I/O work belongs here, not in the request handler.
    return f"report-{user_id}.pdf"

# In your API process, after the request is validated:
job = queue.enqueue(generate_report, 42)


python

Start a worker in another process with rq worker reports. That separation is the main upgrade over BackgroundTasks: you can restart the API without dropping queued jobs, and you can run more workers when the report backlog grows.

RQ is a strong default when your tasks are ordinary synchronous Python. That is common in backends that already use a sync database driver, SDK, or report library. The trade-off is that the worker itself is sync. If your FastAPI app is fully async and the jobs are mostly async I/O (HTTP calls, async database drivers, embedding APIs), ARQ is usually a better fit than forcing that work into RQ.

ARQ: a Redis queue that fits asyncio and FastAPI

ARQ is a lightweight job queue built on Redis and asyncio. Jobs and workers are async functions, which matches a modern FastAPI service. You still get durability and a dedicated worker, without bringing in Celery’s broader feature set.

# worker.py
from arq.connections import RedisSettings

async def download_and_embed_pdf(ctx, url: str) -> str:
    # Long-running RAG or document work in a worker, not in the API request.
    return f"Processed {url}"

class WorkerSettings:
    functions = [download_and_embed_pdf]
    redis_settings = RedisSettings(host="localhost", port=6379)


# Inside an async FastAPI route, after you accept the request:
from arq import create_pool
from arq.connections import RedisSettings

redis = await create_pool(RedisSettings(host="localhost", port=6379))
await redis.enqueue_job(
    "download_and_embed_pdf",
    "https://example.com/doc.pdf",
)

Run the worker with arq worker.WorkerSettings. Keep the API process responsible for validation, auth, and enqueueing. Keep the worker responsible for the slow work. That split stays clean as the service grows.

ARQ also supports deferred and scheduled jobs, which is enough for many product features: “send this reminder in an hour,” “retry this embedding later,” or “run this cleanup on a timetable.” If you later need multi-step workflows, routing across many queues, or a broker other than Redis, that is usually the point where Celery starts to earn its complexity.

Celery: when the simpler queues are not enough

Celery is the option people jump to first, and often earlier than they need to. It is a full distributed task queue, not just a Redis worker. That power is useful, but it also means more moving parts: a broker, a result backend, worker processes, and, in many production setups, a scheduler.

Use Celery when at least one of these is true:

  • You need several queues and worker pools, for example a fast “email” queue that must not wait behind a slow “video” or “embedding” queue.
  • You need workflow primitives: chaining steps, grouping tasks, or coordinating a set of jobs before the next step runs.
  • You need a first-class scheduler (Celery Beat) for recurring work.
  • You want a battle-tested retry, routing, and monitoring ecosystem, or you may later use RabbitMQ instead of Redis. 
# tasks.py
from celery import Celery

app = Celery(
    "jobs",
    broker="redis://localhost:6379/0",
    backend="redis://localhost:6379/1",
)

@app.task(
    bind=True,
    autoretry_for=(Exception,),
    retry_backoff=True,
    retry_kwargs={"max_retries": 5},
)
def generate_report(self, user_id: int) -> str:
    return f"report-{user_id}.pdf"


python

# From the API process, after validation:
from tasks import generate_report

generate_report.delay(42)

The FastAPI (or other web) process should only enqueue the job. The Celery worker runs in its own process or container. That is the same shape as RQ and ARQ; Celery just gives you more control over routing, retries, and orchestration once the backlog is no longer a single queue of similar tasks.

The cost is operational. You will need to define queues, supervise workers, think about task serialization, and decide what belongs in the result backend. For a small FastAPI service with a handful of Redis-backed jobs, that overhead is usually not worth it. For a backend that already has mixed workloads and a need to isolate them, Celery is still the most complete Python option.

How to choose

  • Choose FastAPI BackgroundTasks when the work is short, non-critical, and acceptable to lose on a restart. Think log writes or a best-effort notification.
  • Choose RQ when you want a durable Redis queue, your jobs are mostly synchronous, and you want the smallest production setup.
  • Choose ARQ when the API and the jobs are already async, especially in FastAPI services that call other APIs, async database drivers, or embedding endpoints.
  • Choose Celery when you need multiple queues, workflows, scheduled tasks, or a broker choice beyond a simple Redis worker.

A practical path for many FastAPI products is to start with BackgroundTasks for the truly disposable work, add ARQ (or RQ) as soon as a job must be durable, and only introduce Celery when the queue itself becomes a system: mixed priorities, several worker types, or scheduled pipelines.

Do not pick Celery only because it is the most famous name. And do not stay on BackgroundTasks because it is already in the framework. The wrong choice usually shows up as lost jobs after a deploy, or as a week spent operating a platform you did not need yet.

Production habits that matter more than the library

Once you have a real broker and worker, the same habits apply to RQ, ARQ, and Celery:

  • Keep handlers thin. Validate and persist the request in the API, then enqueue an ID, not a huge payload.
  • Make jobs idempotent. Use a unique job key, a processed-flag in the database, or an upsert so a retry cannot bill twice or embed the same document twice.
  • Retry only transient errors. A typo in an email address or a missing file should fail clearly. A timeout can retry with backoff and a max attempt count.
  • Separate slow and fast queues. A 20-minute export should not sit in front of password-reset emails.
  • Watch the backlog. Queue depth, failed jobs, and worker heartbeats tell you about production health earlier than user complaints.
  • Run workers as supervised processes. Treat them like the API: deploy them, restart them cleanly, and give them their own resource limits.

Those practices matter more than micro-differences between libraries. A small RQ or ARQ setup with idempotent jobs and a failed-job view will beat a large Celery install that retries unsafe work and shares one queue for every task type.

Summary

Use FastAPI BackgroundTasks for short, non-critical work that can disappear when the process restarts. Step up to RQ or ARQ when the job must live in Redis and run in a worker. Reserve Celery for the cases that actually need a distributed task platform: multiple queues, workflows, scheduling, or a more demanding backend.

If you are choosing a queue for a FastAPI or Python backend, or you already have jobs that disappear during deploys, get in touch. I can help you pick a setup that fits the app you have now, and keep a path open for the one you will need next.

Originally published at https://prakashtank.com/blog/background-jobs-in-python-celery-vs-simpler-queues.

title: Upgrading AG Grid from v21 to v36: Skipping 15 Major Versions, One Screen at a Time
description:
TL;DR

  • Our frontend grids (AG Grid) were a mix of v21 and v33, so we are migrating everything to v36
  • Instead of upgrading all at once, we run v21 and v36 side by side in the same app and migrate and release screen by screen
  • We turned the per-screen workflow into a fixed template (a "harness"), so an AI agent (Claude Code) or a human gets the same quality every time

Background

Where we started

Item Details
Target Web frontend of a sales-support SaaS (React 17 + TypeScript)
AG Grid usage About 40 grids across lists, detail pages, settings, and reports; about 220 files to migrate
Versions Mostly v21 (released 2019), with v33 on a few screens
License AG Grid Enterprise. Our current license covers the latest release, 36.2.0 (released September 2026)

Problems

  • Not using newer features: Although we use the Enterprise edition, we were on a version more than six years old and missed most of the features and improvements added since then
  • Two versions living together: The v21 and v33 stylesheets conflict, so the v33 screens relied on a workaround that loads their CSS only while they are displayed. Maintaining that workaround was a burden
  • Blocked on a feature we wanted: We want to expand a row in a parent list to show its related child list directly beneath it (Master/Detail). But the parent list was built on v21 and the child list on v33, and different versions can't be combined
    • Reference: AG Grid - Master / Detail

Goals

  • Standardize on AG Grid 36.2.0 and remove both the v21/v33 coexistence and the CSS workaround
  • ag-grid-react@36.2.0 supports React 16.8–19, so no React upgrade is needed

What makes it hard

  • About 220 files are affected, and the largest list is about 1,700 lines on its own
  • v21 and v36 coexist during the migration, so their CSS must not conflict
  • After migrating, infinite scrolling, sorting, row selection, range selection and copy, saving and restoring column settings, CSV export, grouping, and so on must all keep working as before

Main differences between v21 and v36

Simple renames (excerpt)

v21 v36
columnApi.xxx() api.xxx() (columnApi was removed)
cellRendererFramework cellRenderer (pass the component directly)
getRowNodeId: (data) => id getRowId: (params) => id
api.setRowData(rows) api.setGridOption('rowData', rows)
api.updateRowData(...) api.applyTransaction(...)
purgeServerSideCache() refreshServerSide({ purge: true })
stopEditingWhenGridLosesFocus stopEditingWhenCellsLoseFocus
suppressMenu suppressHeaderMenuButton
Cell editors as classes (getGui / getValue) React components (onValueChange / useGridCellEditor)

Renames that change behavior (handled with helpers)

Target If you just rename it What our helper does
Applying column state (applyColumnState) Saved column order is not restored Applies the column order as well
Getting column state (getColumnState) sort and other fields get saved, so sorting is applied twice Keeps only the fields v21 had
Resetting column state (resetColumnState) Sorting is cleared too, and the list goes empty Resets only column order, width, visibility, and pinning
getSortModel / setSortModel Removed Builds the sort model from the column state

Event and option differences

Target v21 v36 What happened
Event source for column move / resize Both uiColumnDragged Split into uiColumnMoved / uiColumnResized Column state stopped being saved
suppressSetColumnStateEvents Available Removed Applying column state through the API triggers our save logic
infiniteInitialRowCount: 0 Rows load Rows never load The list stays empty
context Later changes are reflected Only the initial value is used Updated values such as names don't reach the cells
Cell renderers returning HTML strings Rendered as HTML Shown as plain text Raw tags appear on screen
Server-side row model getRowId optional Effectively required Row selection is not kept
Line breaks in range copy \n \r\n Accepted, since pasting into Excel and similar tools works the same
Zero results Nothing shown "No Rows To Show" overlay Kept the v36 behavior

Visuals (restored to v21 in our shared wrapper)

Target v21 v36 default
Minimum column width 10px 28px
Header text 12px, system font 14px, page font
Selected row color Solid blue Translucent blue (looks different on striped rows)
Range selection color Opacity 0.3, no inner borders Opacity 0.2, with inner borders
Row selection checkbox Centered in the cell Pushed to the top left
Inline edit input 28px tall, gray border Full row height, blue border and shadow

Differences of a few pixels that CSS can't fix (such as a header that is 1px taller, or a horizontal scrollbar that now extends under pinned columns) are documented in our README with the reason, and accepted.

How we proceeded

1. Build the foundation first (not used by any screen yet)

In this phase we only prepare the parts needed to build screens on v36. Every screen still runs on v21, so users see no change. We actually start using v36 in the next phase, "Migrate screen by screen".

Step What we did
1 Upgrade TypeScript from 4.8 to 5.9 (required by v36's type definitions)
2 Install v36 under aliased package names so it can coexist with v21
3 Scope the CSS at build time so v21 and v36 styles don't conflict (explained below)
4 Build a shared wrapper, AgGridV36, with defaults and visuals aligned to v21
5 Create v36 versions of the cell renderers, cell editors, filters, and column definitions by duplicating the originals

What "scope the CSS at build time" means

v21 and v36 use the same class names (such as .ag-row), so putting both on the same page makes each version's CSS hit the other's grid. To prevent that, when webpack loads AG Grid's CSS, we automatically add a condition to every selector.

/* Original CSS */
.ag-row { ... }

/* v36 CSS: applies only inside .ag-theme-v36 */
.ag-row:where(.ag-theme-v36, .ag-theme-v36 *) { ... }

/* v21 CSS: applies only outside .ag-theme-v36 */
.ag-row:not(:where(.ag-theme-v36, .ag-theme-v36 *)) { ... }
  • Wrapping the condition in :where() keeps specificity unchanged, so our existing override styles behave the same
  • The icon fonts also share a name, so the v36 font gets a -v36 suffix
  • The library itself is left untouched; the CSS is transformed on every build

This lets us ship releases where v21 and v36 screens are mixed.

2. Migrate screen by screen (this is where v36 goes live)

  • One screen = one ticket = one PR. The first list we migrated produced the mapping tables above, and later screens just look things up in them
  • Screens with many users or shown on the home screen keep the old version behind a feature flag so we can switch back
  • Every newly found difference is added to the mapping tables in the README

3. Turn the per-screen workflow into a template (harness)

Each step has a gate, and we don't move on until it passes.

  • Investigate: List where the screen uses v21 APIs, then sort each use into "covered by the table / uses a helper / behavior difference / new"
  • Implement: Build the v36 version. Mark temporary code with a fixed TODO marker (done when typecheck and lint pass)
  • Unit tests: Extract the rewritten logic into functions and test them
  • Screen E2E: Use Playwright to test the 15 checks shared by every list plus every operation specific to that screen. First inventory the screen's features in a table, then assign a test to every row
  • Compare with v21: When something looks like a bug, switch back to v21 and repeat the same steps. Every difference is either "fixed" or "documented in the README with a reason"
  • Feed knowledge back: Update the README, the E2E tests, and our notes so the next person avoids the same traps just by reading the README

4. Remove v21 at the end (consolidation)

Once every screen is on v36, we will remove everything we kept around for the migration (planned).

  • What gets removed
    • The v21 / v33 packages
    • The originals we duplicated for v36 (v21 cell components, column definitions, shared hooks, and so on)
    • The v21 versions of high-risk screens and their feature flags
    • The build-time CSS scoping, and v33's "load CSS only while displayed" workaround
  • How we avoid missing anything
    • All temporary code added during the migration carries the same marker comment (TODO: when removing v21…), so a single grep finds all of it
    • For screens with a feature flag, the flag file states when, what, and in which order to remove things
    • The top of the shared wrapper lists the duplicated originals to delete
  • Watch out for
    • Some originals (constants and components that don't depend on v21) are also imported by the v36 versions. Move them to the v36 side instead of deleting them

Why we chose this approach

  • Ship in small pieces, one screen at a time: Changing about 220 files at once makes review and debugging hard. If something breaks, only one screen is affected
  • Duplicate instead of modifying existing parts: Screens not yet migrated stay safe. v21 is removed all at once at the end
  • Feature flags for high-risk screens: If a problem shows up in production, we can switch back to v21 without reverting code

Ideas we drew on

  • Strangler Fig: Grow the new system alongside the old one and replace it gradually Martin Fowler - StranglerFigApplication
  • Branch by Abstraction: Put an abstraction in between (here, the shared wrapper and the switch components) and swap the implementation behind it step by step Martin Fowler - BranchByAbstraction
  • Parallel Change (expand / migrate / contract): Run old and new side by side (expand), move over (migrate), then remove the old one (contract) Martin Fowler - ParallelChange

Our process follows Parallel Change directly: "build the foundation first" is expand, "migrate screen by screen" is migrate, and "remove v21 at the end" is contract.

Pitfalls

  • Many differences don't cause type errors: Differences in column state or event source pass both typecheck and unit tests, and only show up when you use the screen
  • "v36 bug" that turned out to be the same in v21: We now always repeat the steps on v21 first. Quite a few bugs had been carried over from v21
  • Comparing visuals: Comparing getComputedStyle values was more reliable than comparing screenshots

For E2E we tried both Claude in Chrome and Playwright, and chose Playwright

At first we checked screens with Claude in Chrome, where an AI operates the browser, but partway through we switched to Playwright tests.

Playwright Claude in Chrome
Setup You have to write test code first You can start right away
Speed For a fixed set of steps, many times faster than driving the browser Slow, since it looks at the screen and acts one step at a time
Repeatability Runs exactly the same steps every time Doesn't always test the same way each time
Best for Running the same checks over and over across many screens, as in a migration Quick checks after a small bug fix, or exploring how a screen is built

A migration means running the same checks many times for every screen, so Playwright paid off even after the upfront cost of writing the code.

Note: This article covers only what we verified while migrating our own project. It may contain mistakes or details that differ between versions. When you migrate, please also check the official AG Grid documentation (the upgrade guide for each version and the API reference).

title: We looked up our new hostname four minutes too early and our resolver remembered that it did not exist
description:
In October we moved our stock service behind a new internal name, stock.internal, in a Route 53 private hosted zone. The cutover plan had two parts. The platform team's Terraform would create the record pointing at the new load balancer, and the client teams would deploy configuration that switched their services to the new name. The change window was ten o'clock.

The client deploys went out at five to ten. Terraform created the record at one minute past. For the next fifteen minutes, eleven of our nineteen client services, in two of our three VPCs, failed every call to stock with name not found, while the other eight worked perfectly against the same record.

Each client deploy had run a readiness check that resolved stock.internal before the record existed. The VPC resolver answered that the name did not exist and, as resolvers are supposed to, it cached that answer. How long a resolver keeps a negative answer is set by the zone's SOA record: the smaller of the SOA record's own TTL and its minimum field. In Route 53's default SOA the TTL is nine hundred seconds, so the resolver kept saying the name did not exist for fifteen minutes after it did. The eight that worked ran in a VPC where nothing had asked for the name before it existed, so its resolver had nothing to remember.

Nothing was broken, and every resolver in the path was doing what the standard tells it to do. Our plan had simply never considered that asking a question early is also an answer that gets remembered.

Records for a cutover are now created at least a day ahead, pointing at the old target, and the cutover itself changes the value of a record that already exists. A positive answer is cached for the record's own TTL, which we lower to sixty seconds the day before, so the switch lands in a minute. We also lowered the TTL on our private zones' SOA records to sixty seconds, so a negative answer that slips through costs a minute rather than fifteen. The cutover checklist begins with a lookup of every new name from inside the network, and it must succeed before any client deploy starts.

The plan asked whether the record would exist by ten. It never asked who would look for it before then.

– Sergey Shinder
