title: How to Audit Go Image Purchases Before Expiring Downloads Trigger Pages
description:
The useful page identifies the purchased original that a buyer cannot retrieve and the purchase that authorized its link. Start with a private original, a short presigned download window, and a durable purchase-to-link record. A green delivery dashboard cannot explain a missing entitlement.

Short answer: In a Node.js Express application, verify the purchase, presign the private original for a short window, record which purchase the link belongs to before returning it, and re-issue after checking entitlement when another download is needed. Keep that application contract stable when changing the provider behind the signing capability. The Go example below checks the image lookup boundary without pretending that a metadata response is a download credential.

Consider a hypothetical fintech media library that auto-tags licensed illustrations for search and sells their originals. Quality versus bandwidth is two decisions here: test whether a smaller tagging input preserves useful search detail, and fulfill a purchase with its original regardless of the derivative chosen for search. No accuracy or transfer savings are assumed.

What should an expiring download link record for a purchased original?

Use this exercise page: the original associated with purchase-1042 cannot be downloaded. That identifier is a fixture, not a customer story. The responder needs the purchase ID, original object reference, issuance ID, issuance time, and expiration time; otherwise the alert describes a symptom without identifying the access grant that needs investigation.

Ask what fired.

A page about expiry alone is suspect because expiration is intended behavior. A page about an issuance with no matching purchase record is different: support has lost the evidence needed to explain why access was granted. Work backwards from that distinction, through credential delivery and the audit commit, to the earlier signal that should have fired when the mapping could not be persisted. An aggregate success chart can remain reassuring while the purchase under investigation has no usable record.

Require the authenticated buyer to own the purchase, resolve the original on the server, and obtain a presigned URL for that private object. Persist the issuance mapping before returning the credential. If that commit fails, decline to deliver the credential and surface the failed issuance to the operator. This is an application policy; it does not assume a distributed transaction with the storage provider.

For the exercise, use a 300-second window. That is a design input, not a measured recommendation or a provider default. Choose the real window from legitimate download behavior and the sensitivity of the originals. Record a new issuance when reissuing; do not reinterpret an old audit record as an extension.

Keep originals private.

The audit mapping can reference an issuance ID without copying a live bearer URL into routine logs. Retain the purchase, object, and expiry relationship in access-controlled records after the credential expires. The access window and the support record serve different purposes.

2. Check the lookup boundary before trusting the delivery chart

Save the complete program below as main.go and execute it with the Go toolchain. Set INFRAI_API_KEY from your secret store, MEDIA_ORIGIN to the documented HTTPS API origin without a path, and IMAGE_ID to an image your application has already resolved from an authorized purchase. The origin is configuration so the example contains no vendor URL. Do not point this client at a returned presigned download URL: its bearer authorization belongs to the API request only.

This is a runnable image lookup check, not a complete Express handler or a signing implementation. It uses the verified lookup route, surfaces unsuccessful response bodies, and does not invent a presign request schema. A successful lookup is evidence about the media API boundary; it proves neither entitlement nor completed delivery.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    imageID := os.Getenv("IMAGE_ID")
    origin, err := url.Parse(os.Getenv("MEDIA_ORIGIN"))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if key == "" || imageID == "" || origin.Scheme != "https" ||
        origin.Host == "" || origin.User != nil ||
        (origin.Path != "" && origin.Path != "/") ||
        origin.RawQuery != "" || origin.Fragment != "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set the key, image ID, and a trusted HTTPS API origin")
    }
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(strings.TrimRight(origin.String(), "/") +
        "/v1/image/get/{id}", "{id}", url.PathEscape(imageID))
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 60 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("retry later after %d seconds", seconds)
                }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if at, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(at); wait > 0 {
                    if wait > time.Minute {
                        return fmt.Errorf("retry later at %s", at.Format(time.RFC3339))
                    }
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("media lookup status %d: %s",
                resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(data)))
        }
        fmt.Println("image lookup accepted; purchase and issuance checks still required")
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("lookup retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The retry budget is four attempts, with a 20s timeout per request and a 1 MiB response read limit. These are example limits, not provider guarantees. An explicit rate-limit delay longer than a minute returns control to the caller for later scheduling rather than sleeping indefinitely; a usable shorter delay is honored, and otherwise the client backs off exponentially. This example performs a read. It neither creates a link nor retries a purchase write.

Now apply the instrumentation change to the real issuance handler: distinguish lookup rejection, entitlement denial, failed audit persistence, and expected expiry. Count those decisions and attach the issuance reference to access-controlled events. Test that an audit commit failure prevents credential delivery. Also test the exact expiration boundary and a reissue by a buyer who no longer qualifies; a successful image lookup must not bypass either check.

The integration still needs its chosen signer's documented schema and durable storage. Do not turn a guessed JSON field into a production access boundary. Keep the signed URL out of the lookup client's authorization path, and let the buyer use the returned credential through the intended download flow.

For tagging, evaluate a derivative against a labeled sample before accepting lower bandwidth. Fine text or a small visual distinction in a fintech illustration might matter to search; that is a hypothesis to test, not a claimed model defect. Preserve the derivative-to-original relationship so a search hit resolves to the purchased original. MDN's format guide helps frame format selection, but it cannot establish search quality for this dataset.

3. Compare providers against the same purchase evidence

Infrai offers one key, one wallet, one bill and a single REST API with no SDK to install. Its unified API keeps the capability contract stable when swapping the vendor behind a capability, so the application code does not change with that swap. For the tagging and original-delivery workflow, the supporting advantage is a single API key across media and storage rather than separate credentials. The Go client above uses plain HTTP through the standard library. Buyer authorization and audit persistence still belong to the application; a common contract still needs provider-specific verification of the actual signed access.

The trade-off is another integration boundary to qualify. For a service that only needs to sign originals already stored in S3, direct S3 presigning is a better fit if avoiding that boundary matters more than a shared capability contract. The limitation of either choice is that signing alone cannot establish purchase ownership. A 20-second client timeout also limits each lookup attempt; it isn't a promise about end-to-end download time.

There are credible alternatives. Evaluate their access controls against the same purchase and reissuance tests instead of ranking a transformation demo as though it proves private-original fulfillment.

Option Where it merits evaluation Boundary to verify
Cloudinary A media workflow centered on image management and delivery. Check its documented private asset delivery mechanism, expiration behavior, and original-versus-derived resource selection.
imgix A workflow centered on image rendering and delivery from a source. Verify source protection and distinguish request signing from the purchase-specific expiration policy the application needs.
ImageKit A workflow combining image optimization and delivery. Evaluate its documented private-file and signed-URL configuration against the application's entitlement and reissuance rules.
Amazon S3 Originals already live in object storage and a direct presigned download meets the need. Verify effective expiry with the signing credentials, and keep purchase mapping in the application.

The first three deserve consideration where image handling is a substantial part of the application; a storage signer deserves consideration where controlled original delivery is the narrow requirement. None of these choices, by itself, records which purchase authorized a credential. Test that separately.

An existing Express handler can retain its purchase check, issuance record, and response responsibilities while delegating the provider call through an adapter. The Go check above makes one boundary observable; production acceptance needs an actual signed download test too. Refusing to conflate those two results makes the comparison less flashy and more useful to whoever receives the page.

4. Make the threshold pay for its false positives

Return to the exercise page. A broken purchase mapping is actionable at issuance time; ordinary expiry belongs in a buyer recovery flow that checks entitlement and issues a fresh link. A failed lookup needs its own diagnosis. Production paging thresholds require traffic context, and no measured incident rate is available here.

Do not page on every expired link.

The false-positive cost is responder attention: expected expirations generate noise, noise invites suppression, and suppression makes the missing audit commit harder to notice. The opposite mistake matters too, because returning a credential without its purchase mapping leaves support unable to explain that issuance. Decide which condition warrants a page by asking what the responder can repair, then review the threshold against legitimate reissues and mapping failures separately. A dashboard total that mixes them is a poor substitute for that decision.

Further reading

References for format selection and the provider-specific access boundaries discussed above:

  • MDN image file type and format guide: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Media/Formats/Image_types
  • Amazon S3 presigned URL documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Cloudinary media access control documentation: https://cloudinary.com/documentation/control_access_to_media
  • imgix securing assets documentation: https://docs.imgix.com/setup/securing-assets
  • ImageKit delivery URL security documentation: https://imagekit.io/docs/media-delivery-basic-security

title: Ferret: a rule engine with a mood, built spec-first in Kiro
description:
Written for the Kiroween 2026 hackathon (Frankenstein category). Demo: youtu.be/YyhL1DaMjWk · App, play money: ferret-amw8.onrender.com · Code, MIT, .kiro included: github.com/LeDenti/ferret

Lending rules are fixed. But after a default, a good lender gets more careful. I wanted a program that does the same thing without ever touching its rules. That program is Ferret, and this is how Kiro helped build it, including the parts that did not go smoothly.

The idea: a mood that scales, never decides

Ferret guards a small pool of play money that advances cash on invoices. Every request goes through twelve checks in a fixed order: duplicate invoice, analysis present, amounts, term, advance rate, concentration per debtor, absolute cap, liquidity. Each answer is a yes or a no with a stable reason, written to a field log.

On top of that sits a mood. A refused concentration or a default raises its stress; repayments and buybacks lower it; time makes it forget. The mood is calm, wary or feral. In the demo, one default takes the share a single debtor may hold from 30 % down to 25.5 %, and the longest term from 90 days down to 77. A 90-day invoice that a calm ferret would accept is now refused.

The one rule that matters: the mood changes the ceilings, never the rules. It never removes a check and never changes their order. It only scales two numbers.

The mechanism is borrowed from our research project XRPLife, where a model of the worm C. elegans runs on a public ledger. In that model, serotonin changes how much activity flows through the network, never which connections carry it. Ferret transposes that one idea to a rule book. It is a model, not a living worm, and no code from that project is reused.

Steering before anything else

The first thing Kiro wrote was not code but three steering files: product, tech and structure. They fixed the non-negotiables:

  • integer arithmetic only, no floating point anywhere near money;
  • zero runtime dependencies;
  • the reference/ folder is read-only for the agent;
  • the replay of the case file is the central test.

Writing these first paid off every time the agent was tempted to "help" by adding a library or touching the judge.

Four specs, 51 requirements

Ferret has four specs in .kiro/specs: mood (11 EARS requirements), invoice-pool (14, the twelve checks in their exact order), server (13) and field-log-ui (13). Each went requirements first, then design, then tasks, and only then code.

EARS forced precision where my notes were vague. A line straight from the invoice-pool spec, "WHEN deposit(lender, amount) is requested THE SYSTEM SHALL refuse with family zero_amount if amount ≤ 0", leaves no room for interpretation, and it maps one-to-one to a test.

A judge Kiro did not write

The part I am proudest of is not in Kiro at all, and that is the point. Before the engine existed, a Python reference implementation was written separately. It generated 120 scenarios, 4,926 random events in all, with the expected decision and the expected state after each one.

Kiro then wrote the TypeScript engine from the design. The first replay of the 4,926 events against it: zero mismatch.

Then something better happened. Four of the unit tests Kiro had written alongside the engine failed. The judge settled it in one command: the engine was right, the four tests were wrong about their own expectations. Without an independent judge, I would have "fixed" a correct engine to match wrong tests.

MCP: let the agent ask the judge

The judge is also exposed as an MCP server (.kiro/settings/mcp.json, tool replay_events). Instead of guessing what should happen after a deposit and an oversized advance, Kiro can ask. During the build it did exactly that, and got back "refuse, concentration_breached" with the effective ceilings.

Hooks and a reviewer agent

Three hooks in .kiro/hooks: run the tests whenever the engine changes, revert any edit under reference/, and keep the specs in sync with the code. A custom agent, immunologist, reviews changes for the three things that would quietly break Ferret: floating-point arithmetic, the mood reaching beyond the ceilings, and imports pointing the wrong way.

What did not go smoothly

  • The free tier is small. 50 credits a month, and a fifteen-minute throttle after a burst of large reads. The fix was discipline: short prompts, small read lists, one spec at a time, and never letting the agent open the 4 MB case file.
  • Non-interactive mode drafts in chat. Kiro CLI wrote nothing to disk until told, in so many words, to write to disk.
  • The UI needed three fixes after the first pass: a wrong operation name, a superfluous amount on withdrawals, and silent 400 errors. All three were caught by clicking through the app, not by the replay, which only covers the engine.

How I worked, disclosed

I did not drive Kiro by hand. On my instruction, an AI assistant (Claude Code) wrote the prompts to Kiro CLI, ran the tests between calls and committed the results. Kiro produced the code, the judge checked it, and I decided the scope, the rules and what to disclose. The README says the same.

What I take away

Spec mode is worth its cost when the spec is a contract with a judge. Requirements become tests, and a differential replay against an independent implementation ends every argument in one command. Vibe coding would have produced an engine faster, and left me unable to say why it was right.

Next for Ferret: two more "burrows" on the same engine, pay by evidence and a conditional escrow.

title: From Images to Grounded Edits: A Real-World Benchmark for Chinese Grammatical Error Correction in Handwritten Essays
description:
arXiv:2611.17966v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) is typically formulated as a text-to-text problem. While suitable for digital texts, this formulation falls short in real-world K-12 education, where AI-assisted corrections are expected directly on essay images, which are primarily handwritten and exhibit many irregularities. To bridge this gap, we introduce Grounded Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (G-CGEC), an image-to-grounded-edit task requiring systems to predict both corrections and their positions on essay images. We propose G-CGEC-Eval, a benchmark comprising real-world images of K-12 Chinese essays with fine-grained annotations. For evaluation, we adapt IoU-based metrics from object detection and propose a more tolerant alternative based on center-distance matching. Using this benchmark, we evaluate open-source and proprietary vision-language models under a direct single-pass setting, as well as settings with auxiliary components (OCR and character grounding) coordinated via pipelining or agentic harnessing. Results show that even top-tier proprietary models perform surprisingly poorly in the single-pass setting, while pipelining and agentic harnessing yield meaningful improvements. Notably, an error-type-based multi-agent workflow achieves the best performance, establishing it as the strongest baseline for future G-CGEC research. Through ablations and fine-grained analysis, we find the task remains far from solved, with linguistic error discovery and character-level grounding as the primary bottlenecks. This underscores the need for models that better integrate visual perception with linguistic reasoning and visual grounding.

title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
description:
arXiv:2611.17753v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.

title: Creating Steering Vectors via Input Optimisation
description:
arXiv:2611.17481v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Activation steering influences a language model's behaviour by adding a steering vector to its residual stream during generation, but it requires white-box access to modify the hidden states at every generation step. We introduce ActGCG, a modification of Greedy Coordinate Gradient which optimises a suffix to match the target activations obtained by adding a steering vector to the residual stream. We further introduce universal suffixes trained across many prompts at once, a model-translation step that rewrites the suffix into human-readable text midway through optimisation, and a soft-suffix variant to remove the discrete token space constraint. We study two behaviours: steering a model to answer in German, and anti-refusal steering for jailbreaking. For German, a discrete suffix reproduces the steering vector's behaviour almost perfectly and transfers well across prompts and models. For anti-refusal, the equivalence is weaker, succeeding under a phrase-avoidance metric but only partially under the stricter HarmBench classifier. Our results show that a steering vector's behaviour is reachable from the input, with no access to model internals at generation time, up to a loss that depends on the concept being steered.

title: Best cloud Android options for a two-person studio testing its own app (2026)
description:
I work with DuoPlus, so it's on this list and it's near the top. I'll say where it isn't the right pick, too.

Some context. A friend runs a two-person studio: one developer, one person doing everything else, including QA. They ship an Android app with a phone-number signup, and they kept running into the same three problems before every release: "does it still work on the older Android version our users have," "does the signup SMS actually arrive in the countries we launch in," and "who has the test phone right now." They asked me what to use instead of a drawer of second-hand phones. This is roughly the list I sent back, cleaned up.

I only describe the other products from their own homepages, which I re-read this morning (17 Nov 2026, Singapore time). No prices, because I didn't want to copy numbers that change.

1. Genymotion — if your testing is mostly scripted

I'll start with a competitor because it's honestly the most "QA-native" tool here. Genymotion offers Android virtual devices in the cloud and locally, and its homepage is built around test automation: integration tests, regression tests, and compatibility with AI agents for testing and development.

Fits: teams that already write automated tests and want to run them against Android virtual devices from anywhere. If you live in CI pipelines, look here first.

2. DuoPlus — if you test by hand, on real devices, across countries

https://www.duoplus.net/share/market

What made me suggest it for this studio: these are real ARM Android cloud phones (Android 10, 11, 12 and 15), and each one is its own isolated device environment, so the "old Android" phone stays the old Android phone and nobody's personal stuff ends up on it. You can set a proxy and region per device, with local environments in 150+ countries/regions, and DuoPlus also has cloud numbers that receive verification SMS, which is exactly what you need to test your own app's signup and OTP flow in a launch market. Sharing a phone with the other person is one click, and they open it already logged in. Root, bulk app install/uninstall/launch and an API are there when you want them. You get browser, desktop and mobile clients, and billing is per minute, which matters for a studio that tests in bursts.

Fits: small teams doing manual and exploratory testing, especially the "does signup work in country X" kind.

Drawbacks: it's not a test-automation framework, so if you want a CI-first device farm, Genymotion is the more natural starting point. And if what you need is iOS, this list won't help.

3. Redfinger — widest set of ways to connect

Redfinger runs a "100% native Android OS" and you can reach your phones from a Windows client, an Android APK, the web or iOS. The homepage mentions using it as a device simulator to see how software performs on mobile devices, next to gaming and business use.

Fits: someone who wants to check the app quickly from whatever device is in their hand.

4. VMOS Cloud — role permissions and system images

VMOS Cloud has a Team Hub with permissions and feature limits per role, a Synchronizer for bulk actions across devices, and an Image Market where you choose system image versions. App testing is listed among its use cases.

Fits: a studio that expects to grow and wants per-role limits early, or wants to pick specific system images.

5. Multilogin cloud phones — many locations

Multilogin's cloud phone page describes giving each profile its own phone, apps, location and IP, with cloud phone locations across 190+ countries, managed from one dashboard. The pitch is aimed at teams running many accounts rather than at QA.

Fits: teams whose main job is managing many app accounts, who also want to test in lots of locations.

6. LDCloud — phones that keep running

LDCloud's headline is 24/7 operation, unlimited multi-instance and one-click synchronized operation across devices, with cross-platform access. It's pitched mostly at AFK and cloud gaming.

Fits: long soak tests where you just want something running overnight. Less of a fit for careful per-country testing.

7. GeeLark — if your "app" is really social content

GeeLark pairs cloud phones for Android apps with browser profiles, and its homepage centres on social media marketing with AI content tools and automated posting.

Fits: marketing teams, not really QA. I include it because people ask.

What I'd tell a two-person studio

Pick by how you test, not by the feature list. If you write tests, start with Genymotion. If you test by hand and your painful bugs are "the SMS never came in Indonesia" or "it crashes on the older Android," a real cloud phone per test target with a proxy/region set per device saves a lot of guessing; that's where DuoPlus fit for my friend.

Whatever you choose, name each device after what it tests ("A12-ID-signup", not "phone 3"). It sounds trivial. It ended the "who has the test phone" question in about a day.

title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.17808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_\alpha$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.

title: Learn React by reading your own Framer site's code
description:
The fastest way for a Framer designer to learn React is to read a React project whose design you already know: your own site. Convert your published Framer site to code, run it locally, and trace each thing you built on the canvas (a component, a variant, a breakpoint, a CMS list) to the file that renders it. Because you know what every part should look like, you can focus on how the code expresses it, and every change you make shows up in the browser straight away.

This guide uses Deframer, which converts a published Framer site into a TypeScript project. Deframer is an independent tool and is not affiliated with, endorsed or sponsored by Framer. Use it on your own site, or one whose owner allows it.

Why your own site beats a tutorial

Tutorials teach React with to-do lists. That works, but the gap between a to-do list and a real website is wide. Your own site closes the gap from the other side:

  • You know the intent. You know the hero should stack on phones and the card should lift on hover, so you can tell whether you understand the code.
  • Framer already taught you the concepts. Components, variants, props (Framer's property controls), breakpoints and CMS collections all exist in React too, under similar names.
  • It's real. The project is a standard React app, so what you learn carries over to any React job.

Step 1: get the code running

  1. Convert your site with Deframer: paste the published address and keep the default framework, Next.js. Converting is free.
  2. To download, verify the site is yours by publishing a one-line meta tag in Framer's Site Settings, Custom Code. A verified download uses 1 credit ($10 as a single pack). See verifying Framer site ownership.
  3. Install Node.js (20.9 or later), unzip the project and run: 
npm install
npm run dev
  1. Open http://localhost:3000. That's your site, running from code on your machine.

Open the folder in an editor such as VS Code. Keep the browser and the editor side by side.

Step 2: learn the map

The project's README has a "Where to edit" table. These are the folders that matter while learning:

Framer concept Where it is in code
A page src/views/<page>.tsx plus <page>.module.css
The URL of a page src/app/<path>/page.tsx (a few lines that render the view)
Layout templates (nav, footer) src/layouts/
A design component src/components/<your folders>/
Color styles src/styles/tokens.ts, as CSS variables
Text styles src/styles/text/
CMS collections src/cms/<collection>.json
Code components you wrote src/code/

Components keep the folder names you used in Framer, and props and variants keep the names you gave them. A variant you called "Hover" or "Mobile Open" is called that in the code. What you get in a converted Next.js project tours every folder.

Step 3: five small exercises

Do these in order. Each one teaches a core React idea using something you designed.

1. Change some text (JSX)

Open the view for your home page and find a headline you wrote. Change the words and save; the browser updates. You've just edited JSX, React's HTML-like syntax. Notice how text sits inside elements, and how elements nest the way layers nest in Framer.

2. Change a color everywhere (CSS variables)

Open src/styles/tokens.ts and change one of your color styles. Every component that uses it changes. This is the same idea as a Framer color style, expressed as a CSS variable such as --token-....

3. Follow a component's props

Pick a component you reuse, such as a button. Find where a page uses it and look at what it passes in: a label, a link, a variant. Then open the component file and find where it reads those values. That's props: data passed from the parent, like property controls in Framer.

4. Read a variant

In the same component, look for its variants by name, such as variant === "Primary". Variants in React are usually just a prop that picks different styles or content. Hover and press states are written with motion/react, the animation library Framer's own animations grew from. Framer variants and hover states as React code explains the patterns.

5. Add a CMS item

Open a collection's JSON in src/cms/, copy one record, change its fields and give it a new slug. Restart the dev server if needed and visit its URL. You've just seen how data drives a list and a detail page: a component maps over records and renders one card per item.

Step 4: learn the concepts behind what you saw

Once the exercises feel natural, read the official React docs at react.dev with your project open. The sections on components, props, rendering lists, conditional rendering and state will each map to something you've already touched. When the docs show an example, find the equivalent in your site.

For routing and pages, read the Next.js docs on the App Router. Each folder in src/app is a URL, and each page.tsx is what that URL renders.

What to skip at first

Some parts of the project are there to reproduce Framer's runtime, and they're not where a beginner should start:

  • src/lib/deframer/: the small kit that replaces Framer's runtime. Useful later, distracting now.
  • src/vendor/: marketplace components as source, written by other people.
  • src/proxy.ts and next.config.ts: redirects and URL forms.

Treat them like a car's engine bay: know it's there, don't start learning to drive by opening it.

Use AI as a tutor, not a replacement

Tools like Cursor or Claude Code can explain any file in plain language. Ask "explain what this component does and which props it takes" rather than "change this for me". When you do let a tool edit, read the diff before you accept it. Editing a Framer site with Cursor or Claude Code has prompts and guardrails.

Keep designing in Framer if you like

Learning React doesn't mean leaving Framer. Many designers keep designing there and use the code to understand what developers will build, to prototype ideas faster in code, or to hand cleaner work to a team. If you want to understand the differences in depth, is Framer built on React? is a good next read, and which framework should your Framer site use? explains the other export options.

FAQ

Do I need to know JavaScript before starting?

It helps to know the basics, such as variables, functions and arrays, but you can learn them alongside. Your site gives you real examples of each.

Is the code readable for a beginner?

It's generated code, but it is formatted, uses human names for props and variants, and keeps your folders. Some parts are dense; start with views and components.

Will I break my live Framer site?

No. The code is a copy on your computer. Nothing you do in it changes the site Framer hosts.

Which framework should a beginner pick?

Next.js, the default. It has the most learning material and is what most React jobs use.

How much does it cost?

Converting and reviewing are free. Downloading your own site's code uses 1 credit with verification; a single credit costs $10. See pricing.

Originally published on the Deframer blog. Deframer converts a published Framer site into Next.js, Astro, React Router, TanStack Start, Vite, Nuxt or static HTML code.

title: Small Open-Weight Language Models for Crowd Decision-Making: Capabilities and Limits of Output-Level Fusion and Linguistic Aggregation
description:
arXiv:2611.17589v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Small open-weight language models can run crowd decision-making (CDM) on an institution's own infrastructure, which keeps the checkpoint, the inference settings and the opinions under its control. Their judgements vary across repeated queries; whether repeating and aggregating them, often through the 2-tuple linguistic representation, settles the decision rather than the labels is untested. Five open-weight models of 8-36B total parameters on one consumer GPU and a hosted reference classify 474 TripAdvisor reviews of four London restaurants ten times each; three open-weight models repeat the protocol on 600 reviews of twelve Madrid restaurants. Continuous evaluations preserve resolution: snapping each review leaves 5 distinct values against 21-65, and snapping at every level at most two collective values. Sensitivity to the participants persists once run-to-run variability is reduced: in London, redrawing the reviewers keeps the winner on 47-81% of replicas against 86-100% for redrawing the runs. With simultaneous intervals over every pair of alternatives under crowd resampling, no system on either corpus names a single winner: in London every system keeps all four restaurants as candidates, and in Madrid the candidate sets hold five to eight of the twelve. Extra runs and output-level fusion stabilize the winner but do not remove that sensitivity, and the fusion does not beat its best member. The three larger open-weight models name the hosted reference's London winner and at least match its per-review correlation with the reviewers' stars, so small open-weight models can support local CDM, reported as candidate sets with margins rather than forced rankings.

title: Toward Universal Translatability: On the Statistical Ontology of Generative AI
description:
arXiv:2611.17963v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper argues that the problem of translation functions both as a point of origin and as a normative horizon for contemporary generative AI. In current discourse around ''world models,'' their attainment is framed as the achievement of internal consistency, cross-modal alignment, and physical grounding. Taken together, these demands converge on an ideal of the model as a universal translation machine capable of establishing lossless correspondences across linguistic, visual, and physical representation spaces. I show that this ideal presupposes a metaphysical commitment that I call a statistical ontology: the belief that reality has an underlying, computable statistical structure that can be recovered through sufficient data and modeling, rather than being shaped and accessed through situated human interpretation and labor. Tracing this commitment back to Warren Weaver's 1949 Memorandum on machine translation, I outline how translation was historically recast as code deciphering and, later, as the alignment of probability distributions across structured outputs. Finally, I contrast this paradigm with approaches in Translation Studies that foreground opacity, power asymmetries, and the translator's positionality. I argue that generative AI's statistical ontology is pre-Kantian, pre-critical and obscures the infrastructures and human labor that make machine translatability---as alignment---possible in the first place.

title: Designing an owner portal residents will actually use
description:
An effective HOA or condo owner portal should make common tasks easy while protecting private information. Residents need clear access to their documents, account details, request statuses, and relevant notices. Developers should prioritize role-based permissions, understandable navigation, mobile usability, accessibility, and reliable notifications before adding features that make the interface harder to use.

Model permissions before building screens

An owner portal serves several user types.

Residents may view their own records. Directors may require additional association information. Administrative users may maintain data or process requests.

These permissions should be defined on the server, not merely hidden in the interface.

A simplified model might look like this:

User {
  id
  role
  unit_ids[]
  active
}

Document {
  id
  category
  visibility
  unit_id?
}

Request {
  id
  unit_id
  category
  status
  created_at
  updated_at
}

The application must verify both the user's role and their relationship to the requested record.

A resident changing an identifier in a browser request must not gain access to another unit's private information.

Organize the document library around user needs

A large collection of files is difficult to use when everything appears in a single list.

Group documents by purpose.

Possible categories include governing documents, meeting records available to owners, community policies, insurance information approved for distribution, and forms.

Each record should have a clear title, document category, and relevant version or approval information.

Search and filtering should operate only on documents the user is authorized to access.

Make request statuses understandable

Residents should not need to interpret internal workflow codes.

Instead of displaying technical labels, show plain-language statuses such as:

  • Submitted.
  • Under review.
  • More information needed.
  • Approved or declined.
  • Completed.

These examples should be adjusted to the actual process.

A status page should distinguish the current decision from general administrative progress.

For example, a maintenance request marked completed should not imply that an unrelated architectural proposal received approval.

A useful history shows when a status changed and any information the resident is permitted to see.

Build notifications around useful events

Notifications should provide meaningful updates rather than repeat information already visible on the dashboard.

Possible triggers include a document becoming available, an authorized status change, or a scheduled community notice.

Users should be able to manage optional notification preferences where permitted.

Avoid including sensitive account information in email subjects or other channels where it could be exposed.

Notifications should guide users back into authenticated views when private details are involved.

Design for phones and accessibility

Residents may access their portal from a phone while away from home.

The interface should work with small screens, touch input, and limited typing.

Accessible design also matters.

Use readable text, descriptive labels, visible keyboard focus, appropriate contrast, and understandable error messages.

Do not rely on color alone to communicate request status.

Forms should explain what information is required and preserve entered data when validation fails.

Test tasks, not just screens

A successful test is not simply whether the dashboard loads.

Ask whether an authorized resident can locate a community rule, understand a request outcome, or recognize an important notification without assistance.

Test expired sessions, permission changes, missing documents, and incomplete forms.

The portal succeeds when residents can complete ordinary tasks confidently and the application consistently protects information they should not see.

title: Protection-Oriented Assessment of Machine Learning-Based Fault Detection in Power Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.17872v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning (ML)-based fault detectors are increasingly proposed for power system protection, yet aggregate metrics can obscure the consequences of false and missed trips. We present a protection-oriented assessment of three ML detectors and a sequence-current reference on PROTECT-90, comprising 9,022 simulated fault episodes on a 90 kV double-circuit line. The assessment combines five window conditions, causal window-end labelling, episode-grouped cross-validation, and operating-point selection under a fixed security budget. It reports security, dependability, detection timing, decision margins, and episode-level nuisance assertions. Gradient-boosted trees, a convolutional neural network, and logistic regression achieve AUC-ROC values above 0.999, yet at a security budget of $10^{-3}$ their developed-fault missed-trip rates range from 0.007% to 1.99%. Post-clearing false-trip rates of approximately 0.12-0.16% per window coexist with nuisance assertions in 11.3-19.1% of episodes. Among the analysed physical descriptors, missed trips are most consistently associated with higher fault resistance within the sampled range. An analytical current proxy suggests a fault-current gradient only partly reproduced by waveform-derived current (rank correlation 0.62). No single topology state or faulted phase consistently dominates within the sampled domain. Because PROTECT-90 contains fault episodes only, security is assessed on pre-fault and post-clearing windows rather than independent non-fault disturbances.

title: Quantum Graph Neural Networks: Architectures, Trainability, and Applications
description:
arXiv:2611.17886v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum graph neural networks (QGNNs) apply parametrized quantum circuits to graph-structured data, with the aim of overcoming limits of classical graph neural networks in scalability, expressivity, and long-range information flow. Since the first Hamiltonian-based model in 2019, the field has produced many architectures, applications, and claims, but the evidence behind them has not been assessed systematically. This survey introduces a unified formalism that describes every QGNN as an encoder, a graph-conditioned circuit, observables, and an optional classical head, together with a circuit-level condition for permutation equivariance and a resource model for comparing costs. We organize the literature into five architecture families (convolutional, equivariant, message-passing and recurrent, Hamiltonian, and hybrid) and compare them by qubit cost, symmetry, scalability, and evidence. We then review symmetry and geometric inductive biases (permutation, rotation, and Lorentz), the results on expressivity, trainability, noise, and scalability, and applications in high-energy physics, chemistry, finance, healthcare, earth observation, and transportation. An audit of datasets and evaluation practices leads to a minimum reporting protocol. Our main finding is that the design space is rich and symmetry is the best-supported inductive bias, whereas the evidence remains thin: results are mostly simulated, on small graphs, at parity with classical models or with fewer parameters, and no advantage has yet been established on tasks over classical graph data. We identify five open challenges and a research agenda covering provable advantage, equivariant and geometric designs, fault-tolerant implementations, and shared benchmarks. The coverage extends through 2026 and emphasizes recent work.

title: I killed ARTEX on my lunch break
description:
I started Sentinels on a lunch break. It's a host intrusion detector for Linux, macOS and Windows, written in Rust and released under the MIT license.

It's meant to deal with automated attacks from tools such as ARTEX. The agent watches processes and connections on the machine and can stop a malicious process and its children. It can also quarantine files and disable supported startup entries associated with the attack. Those cleanup changes can be reversed.

The stopping times I'm seeing in internal tests are about 20 ms for rapid process chains and under 5 ms for selected tooling tests. I'll add the benchmark setup and results to the README.

You can use it on a single machine or run the fleet service yourself. Managed hosting is available too. AI analysis is optional; the default stop decision happens locally.

The repository has the source and installers. The manual covers setup and the response modes.

GitHub: https://github.com/gary23w/sentinels

title: MineralExp: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Experimental Design in Real-World Mineral Exploration
description:
arXiv:2611.17931v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In mineral exploration, verifying geological hypotheses relies on designing a variety of geochemical experiments. While large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate downstream geoscientific data analysis, a crucial upstream capability remains largely unexplored: automated geochemical experimental design, i.e., deciding which experiments to conduct before committing to costly laboratory work. Evaluating this capability of LLM agents is difficult for two reasons. First, geochemical experiments exhibit high methodological diversity and subjectivity: to test the same hypothesis, different geologists may choose different minerals and instruments, so no single protocol can serve as the reference answer. Second, open-ended experimental plans resist representation as structured labels, which makes objective scoring difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce MineralExp, a benchmark that reformulates geochemical experimental design as a hypothesis-based experiment selection problem, i.e., a multi-label classification problem. We abstract concrete instrument names and procedural details into a shared taxonomy of 19 experimental types across five mineral-system processes: Source, Transport, Deposition, Modification, and Preservation. This taxonomy yields deterministic multi-label targets while accommodating diverse experimental protocols. Constructed from published ore-deposit literature and verified by domain experts, MineralExp comprises 277 cases and 1,572 reference experimental plans. Given a geological hypothesis and initial context, an LLM agent selects the relevant tasks and generates concrete experimental plans, which are scored by multi-label classification metrics and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric. The experimental results show that current agents generally achieve high recall but low precision, tending to propose more experiments than are necessary to test the hypothesis.

title: How We Built an 8-Language Static Booking Site That Loads in Under 1 Second
description:
A private car transfer booking site doesn't sound like an interesting engineering problem until you try to serve it in eight languages and guarantee that no bad data ever reaches production. This is how we built navetteforyou.com, a Marrakech airport transfer site.

The stack: TanStack Router with file-based routing, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, Vite, deployed on Vercel as a fully static site. 624 HTML pages generated at build time with Bun, zero runtime server. Eight languages: English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese, and Arabic (RTL).

File-Based Routing With Locale Context

TanStack Router's file-based routing gives us 18 route files -- pages like /prices, /fleet, /faq, and dynamic segments like /transfers/$slug and /guides/$slug. Each slug resolves against locale-specific content:

export const Route = createFileRoute("/guides/$slug")({
  loader: ({ params, context }) => {
    if (!guideFor(params.slug, context.locale)) throw notFound();
    return null;
  },
});

English is unprefixed (/guides/marrakech-airport-arrivals), every other locale gets a prefix (/fr/guides/...). Eighteen route files times eight locales gives us 624 static HTML pages at build time.

The Entity Graph: JSON-LD as a Connected System

Most sites bolt on structured data as an afterthought -- one schema blob per page, unconnected. We took a different approach: every page references nodes in a shared entity graph, connected by @id references. The operator node is shared across two domains. The interconnected graph means answer engines (Google AI Overviews, Bing Copilot, Perplexity) can resolve "who operates this" without leaving the site's structured data.

The Static Price Check Gate

Before every deploy, a script scans all 624 built HTML pages, their embedded JSON-LD, the llms.txt file, and entity.json -- running 17,113 assertions. No amount under a floor price, no price on quote-only routes, no JSON-LD Offer under the floor. The regex handles Western digits, Arabic-Indic digits, and any thousands separator style. If any assertion fails, exit code 1, deploy blocked.

IndexNow and Arabic RTL

After every deploy, a script pings all 624 URLs to IndexNow (Bing, Yandex, Seznam, Naver). Supporting Arabic flips the entire layout. Performance is a side effect of static -- sub-second loads, near-perfect Lighthouse scores.

Wrapping Up

The interesting parts weren't the React components -- they were the systems around the site: a locale completeness gate, a 17,113-assertion price check, an interconnected entity graph, and a pipeline that turns 18 route files into 624 static pages. If you're building a multilingual static site, invest in the gates.

If you're ever in Marrakech and need a ride from the airport, that's what the site is for: navetteforyou.com

title: MySQL to BigQuery: A Hands-On Binlog Pipeline Through a BigLake Catalog
description:
A MySQL to BigQuery job tends to start as a nightly mysqldump, a file in a bucket and a bq load. It works for a while. Then an order status changes at lunch, the afternoon dashboard still shows the old one, and a customer who was deleted last week is still being counted.

The usual ways to get MySQL rows into BigQuery:

  • Datastream for MySQL: Google's managed change data capture (CDC) service. It reads the binlog and writes native BigQuery datasets, near real time by Google's description, with nothing for you to run. BigQuery is the only reader of what it writes.
  • Debezium, Kafka and a BigQuery sink connector: changes arrive in seconds, and you operate Kafka, Kafka Connect, Debezium and one sink per table.
  • Export, then bq load: a script, a scheduler and a staging bucket. Full reloads only, so updates and deletes never show up as changes.
  • Managed extract, load, transform (ELT) tools such as Fivetran, Estuary or Airbyte Cloud: nothing to host, freshness in minutes depending on the plan, and a second copy in BigQuery that you pay to move and store.

This post walks a fifth path. OLake Go, an open source (Apache 2.0) replication tool, reads the MySQL binary log and commits the rows as Apache Iceberg tables into BigLake, Google Cloud's Iceberg representational state transfer (REST) catalog. The files sit in your own Cloud Storage bucket, and BigQuery queries them by a four-part name with no dataset to create and no external table to declare.

I ran this against MySQL 8.4 in Docker and a bucket in us-central1, with OLake Go v1.1.0. The snapshot of 48 records took 37 seconds, and a change sync of 12 records took 55 seconds. All numbers below come from that run.

What the MySQL to BigQuery pipeline looks like

  • Source: a MySQL database shop with customers and orders, and the binlog on in ROW format
  • Pipeline: OLake UI from its Docker Compose install, one job in Full Refresh + CDC mode
  • Catalog and storage: a BigLake catalog named after a Cloud Storage bucket, holding Parquet data files and positional delete files
  • Readers: BigQuery first, then DuckDB 1.5.5 and Spark 4.0.1 with Iceberg 1.10.0 against the same tables

You need: Docker, a Google Cloud project where you can enable an API and create a service account, and about 30 minutes.

Step 1: MySQL with the binlog on

For a local test, start MySQL 8.4 with the four binlog settings on the command line:

docker run -d --name mysql_cdc -p 3306:3306 \
  -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=<root password> -e MYSQL_DATABASE=shop \
  mysql:8.4 \
  --server-id=1 --log-bin=mysql-bin --binlog-format=ROW \
  --binlog-row-metadata=FULL --binlog-expire-logs-seconds=604800

On a server you already have, the same lines go in my.cnf followed by a restart. On Cloud SQL, RDS, Aurora or Azure they are flags or a parameter group. On Cloud SQL, point-in-time recovery is what turns the binlog on.

Create the tables, or skip this and use your own:

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(100), email VARCHAR(200), city VARCHAR(100), tier VARCHAR(20),
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT, product VARCHAR(100), amount DECIMAL(10,2), status VARCHAR(20),
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id));

My run held 8 customers and 40 orders. Two of the customers, Liam Carter and Zara Ali, get updated in step 6, so add rows with those names if you want to replay my changes exactly.

Then the replication user and fresh statistics:

CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS 'olake'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY '<password>';
GRANT SELECT, REPLICATION SLAVE, REPLICATION CLIENT ON *.* TO 'olake'@'%';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

ANALYZE TABLE customers, orders;

SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('log_bin', 'binlog_format', 'binlog_row_metadata', 'server_id');
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'olake'@'%';

⚠️ ANALYZE TABLE is not optional on a fresh table. OLake Go splits the snapshot into parallel chunks from the row estimates in information_schema, and a table that was just loaded has none.

Seven days of binlog (604800 seconds) is the replay window. A job paused longer than that cannot find its saved position and needs a new full snapshot.

Step 2: The BigLake catalog on Google Cloud

There is no catalog to create by hand. BigLake makes one named after the bucket the first time OLake Go connects. You prepare four things in the console:

  1. APIs and services: enable the BigLake API.
  2. Cloud Storage: create a bucket in the region where BigQuery will run the queries. The bucket name becomes the catalog name in SQL, so keep it short.
  3. IAM and Admin, Service Accounts: create one for OLake Go, then grant BigLake Editor on the project and Storage Object User on the bucket. IAM stands for Identity and Access Management.
  4. Keys tab: Add key, Create new key, JSON. The file downloads once.

The two roles split the work. BigLake Editor lets the writer create namespaces and commit tables, and Storage Object User lets it write Parquet and metadata into the bucket.

Step 3: Start OLake UI and add MySQL 

curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-ui/master/docker-compose-v1.yml | docker compose -f - up -d

Open http://localhost:8000 and log in with admin / password.

Go to Sources, Create Source, MySQL. Leave Enable CDC on and the Initial Wait Time at its default. For connection details I used host host.docker.internal (the OLake containers reach MySQL through it), database shop, user olake, and SSL off.

Set up source tests the connection and then checks binlog_access, log_bin, binlog_format and binlog_row_metadata. A failing check is shown with its current and recommended value, so a wrong setting surfaces here and not halfway through a sync.

Step 4: The BigLake destination

Go to Destinations, Create Destination, Apache Iceberg, and pick BigLake as the catalog type.

Field Value
REST Catalog URI https://biglake.googleapis.com/iceberg/v1/restcatalog
BigLake Catalog Path gs://<bucket>, bucket root only
Authentication Type GCP
GCP Service Account JSON the whole key file from step 2
Catalog Name olake_iceberg
GCP Project ID your project ID
Enable Arrow Writes off

Click Create. The test calls the endpoint, creates the catalog on first contact, and writes and drops a test table. After that the catalog shows up under BigLake, Catalogs in the console.

⚠️ Leave the catalog in its default end-user credential mode. OLake Go 1.1.0 does not send the access delegation header that vended-credentials mode requires, and the test fails.

Step 5: The job and the first sync

Jobs, Create Job. Name it mysql_to_bigquery, pick a schedule, and select the source and destination. Under Advanced Settings, set Target Query Engines to Google BigQuery, Apache Spark and DuckDB.

That list decides the delete format. OLake Go offers only formats all three engines read, equality and positional deletes, and I kept Positional Deletes. Deletion vectors are left out because BigQuery reads them only in preview.

On the Streams page, tick both tables, keep Full Refresh + CDC and Upsert, then Create Job and Sync Now.

The first run copied 48 records (2.10 KB) in 37 seconds, container start included. The namespace is named after the job and the database, so it became mysql_to_bigquery_shop.

Step 6: Query in BigQuery, change rows, query again

In the BigQuery SQL editor, set the query location to the bucket's region, then use the four-part name:

SELECT id, name, city, tier
FROM `<project-id>.<bucket>.mysql_to_bigquery_shop.customers`
ORDER BY id;

SELECT status, count(*) AS n, round(sum(amount), 2) AS total
FROM `<project-id>.<bucket>.mysql_to_bigquery_shop.orders`
GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

No CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE, no metadata refresh. The namespace is the dataset and the bucket is the catalog.

Now make 12 changes in MySQL:

INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city, tier) VALUES
  ('Maya Patel', 'maya@example.com', 'Pune', 'silver'),
  ('Lucas Silva', 'lucas@example.com', 'São Paulo', 'bronze');
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product, amount, status) VALUES
  (9, 'Laptop', 1299.00, 'placed'), (9, 'Mouse', 25.50, 'placed'),
  (10, 'Monitor', 349.99, 'placed'), (3, 'Keyboard', 89.00, 'placed'), (7, 'Webcam', 79.90, 'placed');
UPDATE customers SET tier = 'gold'      WHERE name = 'Liam Carter';
UPDATE customers SET city = 'Abu Dhabi' WHERE name = 'Zara Ali';
UPDATE orders    SET status = 'delivered' WHERE id IN (1, 4, 7);

Sync Now again. The second run read 12 records (563 bytes) from the binlog in 55 seconds.

For customers the commit report in the sync log reads addedDataFiles=1, addedRecords=4, addedPositionalDeleteFiles=1, addedPositionalDeletes=2. Four rows went in (2 inserts plus the new versions of 2 updates), and one small delete file retired the 2 old versions. orders got 8 rows and 3 deletes.

Rerun the SELECT. Liam Carter is gold, Zara Ali lives in Abu Dhabi, the two new customers are there, and there is still one row per key.

Every table also carries _olake_id, _op_type, _olake_timestamp and _cdc_timestamp. _op_type is r for snapshot rows, c for inserts, u for updates and d for deletes.

Read the same tables from DuckDB

DuckDB attaches BigLake with a Google access token. In end-user mode it also needs its own storage credentials: a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) key for the same service account, from Cloud Storage, Settings, Interoperability.


INSTALL iceberg; LOAD iceberg;
INSTALL httpfs;  LOAD httpfs;
-- gcloud auth print-access-token, or a token minted for the service account
CREATE SECRET biglake_catalog (
  TYPE iceberg,
  TOKEN '<access token>',
  EXTRA_HTTP_HEADERS MAP {'x-goog-user-project': '<project-id>'}
);
CREATE SECRET biglake_files (TYPE gcs, KEY_ID '<hmac access id>', SECRET '<hmac secret>');
ATTACH 'gs://<bucket>' AS biglake (
  TYPE iceberg,
  ENDPOINT 'https://biglake.googleapis.com/iceberg/v1/restcatalog',
  SECRET biglake_catalog
);
SELECT id, name, city, tier FROM biglake.mysql_to_bigquery_shop.customers ORDER BY id;

DuckDB 1.5.5 returned the same 10 customers, and Spark 4.0.1 did too. The orders roll-up matched MySQL to the cent in all three engines: 16 delivered for 8659.68, 18 placed for 10522.26 and 11 shipped for 6397.25.

Tips from the run

  • decimal arrives as FLOAT64. OLake Go stores decimals as doubles. The sums still matched, but round at query time when exact decimal math matters.
  • datetime is read as UTC and shows up as TIMESTAMP. json, enum and time arrive as STRING.
  • Tables need a primary key. Without one, inserts replicate but updates and deletes have no row to match.
  • Watch metadata.json. BigLake rejects one above 1 MB, which a busy table reaches after a few thousand syncs. Expire snapshots and compact on a schedule.
  • Catalog tables are read from Parquet on every query. When a dashboard needs native BigQuery speed, load the hot slice into a native table on a schedule.

How the MySQL to BigQuery options compare

Method Freshness Updates and deletes Where the data lands What you run
Datastream near real time yes native BigQuery datasets nothing; a stream in the console
Debezium, Kafka, BigQuery sink seconds yes, in upsert mode Kafka, then BigQuery tables Kafka, Connect, Debezium, sinks
Export plus bq load hours to daily no native BigQuery tables a script and a scheduler
Managed ELT minutes, by plan varies a second copy in BigQuery nothing; per row or per GB pricing
OLake Go to BigLake CDC, schedule down to one minute yes, as row-level deletes open tables BigQuery, Spark and DuckDB read one Docker Compose stack

When BigQuery is the only reader and a managed Google service is what you want, Datastream is the shorter route. Writing open tables once pays off when Spark, DuckDB or a notebook needs the same rows, or when you want the files in your own bucket.

FAQ

What happens when someone adds a column in MySQL?

The next sync adds it to the table and commits the new schema to BigLake in the same commit, so BigQuery shows it on the next query. Widening changes such as int to bigint are applied. A narrowing or incompatible change fails the sync instead of corrupting the table.

Can the dataset have a different name than mysql_to_bigquery_shop?

Yes. The Iceberg DB field at the top of the Streams page sets the namespace before the first sync. By default it combines the job name and the source database.

Why not deletion vectors, if BigQuery can read them?

BigQuery reads deletion vectors only in preview, with a cap of 100,000 entries per query. Positional deletes are fully supported, and DuckDB and Spark read them as well. That is why the job resolves to positional deletes with these three engines.

What does the job cost to keep running?

Storage is Cloud Storage rates for the Parquet and delete files, and the catalog has no per-table charge. BigQuery bills queries by bytes scanned on demand or by slot time on an edition. OLake Go runs on whatever machine hosts Docker.

Where to go from here

  • Swap the Docker MySQL for your real server. Only how the binlog flags are set changes.
  • Put compaction and snapshot expiry on a schedule with Spark's rewrite_data_files and expire_snapshots through the same catalog.
  • The full guide, with the CLI configs, the Spark connection and the data type table, is on olake.io.

If one of these steps behaves differently for you, leave a comment with the error and I will update the post.

title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
description:
arXiv:2611.17338v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.

title: Learning Anisotropic Prediction Targets for Flow Models
description:
arXiv:2611.17767v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Flow-based generative models are trained on a hand-chosen prediction target, such as the velocity, the noise, or the clean data. This choice strongly affects training and sample quality. We introduce Anisotropic Flow Models (AnisoFlow), which replaces a fixed prediction target with a fully learnable one. AnisoFlow learns to scale the noise component of the target anisotropically, assigning a separate nonnegative weight to each direction in a jointly learned basis. A closed-form map recovers the velocity from the network's prediction, leaving the architecture, flow-matching loss, and sampler unchanged. Since recovery is exact, training optimizes the target purely to make it easier for the network to predict. We theoretically analyze the resulting prediction error and predict that the preferred noise weight in each direction scales near-linearly with data variance, in agreement with the weights learned empirically in pixel space. AnisoFlow improves FID from 1.90 to 1.55 over the JiT baseline on ImageNet 256$\times$256, by learning only the prediction target, without representation alignment or architectural changes. In pixel-space text-to-image generation, AnisoFlow improves image quality and, through better-conditioned velocity recovery, largely removes patch-seam artifacts under reduced-precision inference.

title: RSSA: Robust Semantic and Spatial Aligner for Collaborative Perception
description:
arXiv:2611.18023v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: V2X collaborative perception improves single-vehicle perception by aggregating multi-view features from collaborative agents. However, existing methods typically rely on simple spatial warping to align the collaborative features, which can cause semantic misalignment during fusion. Meanwhile, these deterministic warping-based methods are highly sensitive to the positional noises. In this paper, we propose a plug-in module called Robust Semantic and Spatial Aligner (RSSA), which performs semantic and probabilistic spatial transformations for robust feature alignment. Specifically, a Semantic Transformation (SemT) block modulates feature channels based on the observed relative pose to correct semantic inconsistencies. Subsequently, a Probabilistic Spatial Transformation (P-SpaT) block performs probabilistic warping by sampling from the Gaussian-modeled relative pose space. A Relative Transformation Augmentation (RT-Aug) strategy is further introduced to augment the relative poses and facilitate the training of the RSSA. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that RSSA improves the state-of-the-art methods by a large margin under the configuration of both clean and noisy positions.
