title: How to Hide PHP Source Code in 2026 (From a Developer Who's Been Doing It Since 2018)
description:
Back in 2018, when we started building PHPDEFENDER, the PHP protection market was basically a two-horse race. If you wanted to hide your source code, you used IonCube or SourceGuardian.

At the time, we started by offering IonCube-compatible encoding to help developers migrate away from the legacy tools. But over the years, we realized that "hiding PHP source code" is not a one-size-fits-all problem. The method you choose depends entirely on where your code is being deployed.

Here is the honest truth about the three main ways to protect PHP source code in 2026, based on 8 years of building encoding tools.

1. Obfuscation (The "False Security")
This is usually the first thing developers try. You change variable names to random characters, strip comments, and maybe run a base64_encode on a few strings.

It feels like you are doing something, but obfuscation is not encryption. Anyone with a basic understanding of PHP can use a decoder to get the logic back. It might stop a casual user, but it will not stop someone who actually wants to steal your code. For commercial software, it is a waste of time.

2. Loader-Based Encoding (IonCube, SourceGuardian, and PHPDEFENDER)
This is the traditional method. Tools like IonCube, SourceGuardian, and our own PHPDEFENDER Loader compile your PHP code into bytecode and encrypt it. To run the encoded files, the server must have a specific PHP extension (the Loader) installed.

Why it works: It offers the highest level of security. If you control the server, this is usually the fastest and safest option.

The Problem: If you are selling software to clients on shared hosting (cPanel, Plesk), you often cannot install custom extensions. If the loader is missing, your app crashes. And when a new PHP version is released, you have to wait for the encoder company to update their loader.

3. Loaderless Encoding (The 2026 Solution)
As more developers started deploying to restrictive shared hosting environments, we realized the industry needed a different approach. Around 2020, we started developing our Loaderless edition, and in 2026, it is finally a mature, production-ready solution.

Loaderless encoding compiles your PHP code into a protected format that runs natively, without requiring any server extensions.
Why Loaderless is the Modern Choice

No Server Dependencies: Runs on any standard PHP hosting environment.
PHP 8.5 Compatible: You don't have to wait for a loader update.
Full Licensing: You can lock the code to a specific domain, IP, or MAC address.

How to Choose

If you are distributing to clients you don't control, loaderless is the safest path. If you control the server, a loader-based approach (like our PHPDEFENDER Loader or IonCube) is perfectly fine.

At PHPDEFENDER, we actually offer both. We have our own PD Loader, IonCube-compatible encoding (for migration), and a fully Loaderless edition. That flexibility is why we built the platform in the first place.

You can test the loaderless workflow on your own app here and see which method fits your deployment best.

This article is based on real deployment experience with commercial PHP applications since 2018.

title: How to show regulators exactly which code handled your data
description:
To show a regulator exactly which code handled a piece of data, run the code in an attested hardware enclave and have it sign every result with a key that belongs to that exact code. On Lit Protocol, a Lit Action is identified by a hash of its source, and every action has its own signing key that the enclave derives from that hash. If the code changes by one character, the hash changes and so does the key. So a signed result is a receipt that names the code that produced it, and anyone can check it later without trusting you.

I will build a small screening check that returns signed receipts, and then go through how a regulator verifies one.

A check that signs its own receipts

This action screens a customer against a sanctions service and returns a receipt. The receipt is signed with the action's own key.

// screen-v1.js
async function main({ customerId, name, country, salt }) {
  const result = await fetch("https://screening.example.com/check", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ name, country }),
  }).then(r => r.json());

  const receipt = JSON.stringify({
    customerId,
    inputHash: ethers.utils.id(`${salt}|${name}|${country}`), // ties the receipt to the data that was screened
    outcome: result.match ? "match" : "clear",
    listVersion: result.listVersion,
    checkedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  });
  const signer = new ethers.Wallet(await Lit.Actions.getLitActionPrivateKey());
  return { receipt, signature: await signer.signMessage(receipt), signer: signer.address };
}

The screening URL stands in for whichever provider you use. The receipt leaves out the customer's name. It includes a hash of the name and country with a random salt that you keep, so you can store and share the receipt without the personal data, and later show which data was screened by revealing the salt.

Your service calls the action with a usage API key. Send the X-Privacy-Mode header so Lit's server does not write the request or the result to its logs.

SALT=$(openssl rand -hex 16)   # keep this with your private record for c-1042
jq -n --rawfile code screen-v1.js --arg salt "$SALT" '{code: $code, js_params: {customerId: "c-1042", name: "Jane Doe", country: "GB", salt: $salt}}' \
  | curl -s -X POST https://api.chipotle.litprotocol.com/core/v1/lit_action \
      -H "X-Api-Key: $USAGE_KEY" -H "X-Privacy-Mode: true" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @-

Store each receipt and signature wherever you keep audit records. A signed receipt cannot be edited without breaking the signature, so the storage itself does not have to be trusted.

How a regulator checks a receipt

You give the regulator the source file, screen-v1.js, and the receipts they want to look at. They can do the rest themselves.

First, they compute the code's hash. This call needs no account.

jq -Rs . screen-v1.js | curl -s -X POST https://api.chipotle.litprotocol.com/core/v1/get_lit_action_ipfs_id \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @-
# "Qm..."

Next, they look up the signing address for that hash. They can do this from their own Lit account by running a one-line action, Lit.Actions.getLitActionWalletAddress({ ipfsId }), with a usage key that is allowed to run it. The enclave derives the address from the hash, so every account gets the same answer. You can also publish the address next to the source, and the regulator can confirm it this way.

Then they check each receipt against that address.

import { ethers } from "ethers";
const recovered = ethers.verifyMessage(receipt, signature);
console.log(recovered.toLowerCase() === actionAddress.toLowerCase()); // true means screen-v1.js produced this receipt
// once you share the salt for a customer, this shows which data was screened
console.log(ethers.id(`${salt}|${name}|${country}`) === JSON.parse(receipt).inputHash);

That proves which code produced the receipt. To trust that the code ran where you say it did, the regulator also checks the enclave. Phala's Trust Center publishes a report for Lit's production enclave that verifies the Intel TDX hardware quote and the hash of the deployed server, and the verification guide explains each layer.

Changing the code

When you change the screening logic, you get a new file with a new hash and a new signing address. Old receipts still verify against the old address, and new ones verify against the new one. Keep every version of the source you have run, because each one is what a past receipt points to.

What this does not show

The receipt proves which code ran and what it returned. It does not show which account ran it, and it does not prove the screening provider gave a correct answer. Anyone can run a public action, so the input hash is what ties a receipt to your customer's data. A Lit Safe that needs 2 of its 4 signers approves the code that runs in Lit's enclave, and a release approved that way could sign with any action's key, so the receipt also depends on that approval process. The upgrade governance page explains how a new release is approved. If your regulator wants that decision with you, Lit is open source and you can run your own deployment.

Working with Lit

Lit works with regulated teams to set up checks that produce receipts like these. To talk about the data you handle and what your regulator needs to see, use the Lit contact form. Signing results with an action's own key is covered under patterns in the docs.

title: Soteria: Formally Verified Planning with Runtime Enforcement for Safe LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.17880v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents that execute multi-step tool calls must satisfy two objectives simultaneously: completing the user's task (utility) and conforming to domain policies and correctness constraints (safety). These objectives are in tension -- blocking an unsafe action prevents a violation but can leave the agent stranded with no principled way to recover. Existing approaches sacrifice one objective for the other. We introduce Soteria, a framework that reconciles safety and utility through verified hierarchical planning and runtime enforcement of specifications. Before execution, the agent generates a structured plan that is formally verified against the specifications prior to any tool invocation. During execution, the verified plan serves dual roles: it ensures that the agent takes specification-conformant trajectories and provides guidance when unsafe actions are blocked. Across multiple benchmarks covering a diverse range of tool-use tasks, Soteria achieves 1.7 times the average task success rate of the best baselines, with no violations of policy specifications, demonstrating that safety and utility need not be traded off.

title: GT-FENG: General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding in Language Models *Author(s)
description:
arXiv:2611.18279v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Whether a language model's answer is correct often depends on context: the same value can be right under one jurisdiction, date, or legal definition and wrong under another. We introduce GT-FENG (General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding), the first general framework to unify contextual/temporal correctness and rule-based error attribution across law, policy, and other rule-governed domains. GT-FENG checks answers against the applicable rules and identifies documented rules that match incorrect answers. It shows that when multiple rules give the same value, the answer alone cannot tell which rule the model used. In Medicaid income-limit answers from two models, documenting the asked state's own records reduces the number of wrong answers that match only other states' values by 68-78%, and more than half of stable wrong answers then match two or more documented sources. GT-FENG provides a foundation for evaluating language models in rule-governed domains and for future benchmarks and evaluation toolkits. We release GT-FENG as an open-source Python package, gtfeng.

title: SWAM: Saliency-Weighted Asymmetric Merging for Efficient Vision Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.18057v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve strong performance on image recognition tasks, yet their quadratic self-attention complexity over input tokens creates prohibitive computational costs for practical deployment. Token reduction methods offer a practical solution by progressively reducing the token sequence during the forward pass. We propose Saliency-Weighted Asymmetric Merging (SWAM), a training-based token merging framework that extends the Bipartite Soft Matching (BSM) with two saliency-aware mechanisms. We introduce a two-step matching formulation in which cosine similarity decides candidate pairs, while a multiplicative maximum saliency penalty regulates their selection for merging. We then further use asymmetric exponential saliency-weighted aggregation, which allows more salient tokens to contribute more strongly to the merged representation. A lightweight MLP-based saliency prediction module (75k parameters per stage, 1% of backbone parameters) supervised via attention rollout is trained end-to-end jointly with a DeiT-Small backbone using a composite cross-entropy, knowledge-distillation, and saliency-alignment objective. On CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet-100, under a conservative schedule that reduces tokens from 196 to 100 patch tokens, with the CLS token retained throughout, 27.5% FLOPs reduction and 1.35 times speedup, SWAM matches or exceeds baseline across the reported results. Under an aggressive schedule (196 to 70 tokens with the CLS token kept throughout, 33.8% FLOPs reduction, and 1.46 times speedup), accuracy gains are achieved on ImageNet-100 (+0.23%) with minimal losses on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet.

title: Adversarial Tracking: Attacks on Image Sensors for Object Tracking in Autonomous Vehicles
description:
arXiv:2611.17505v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Object tracking systems estimate the motion of surrounding vehicles by linking detected objects across video frames. In particular, Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) systems combine object detectors with motion prediction and data association to maintain object identities over time. However, neural network-based detectors are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that perturb input images, and their impact on downstream trajectory estimation is not fully characterized by detection accuracy alone. Therefore, this paper evaluates image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 detectors paired with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT tracking systems. The evaluation uses CARLA simulator and measures tracking quality through Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA), and Identification F1 (IDF1). Under image-specific attacks, HOTA for YOLOv3-based trackers declines from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%, while MOTA reaches -772.60% in the worst case. YOLOv4-based trackers exhibit greater robustness, while HOTA still declines to 25.06-26.86%. In addition, image-agnostic attacks can reduce the tracking accuracy using a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP), without generating a separate perturbation for individual frames.

title: Modelling EUDR Lot-to-Plot Traceability for Coffee: Plots, Lot Edges and GeoJSON Exports
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

If you build or integrate systems for coffee processors in Kenya, the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) is a lineage problem. From 30 December 2026, the EU operator that first places coffee on the EU market (usually the importer) must file a due diligence statement that includes the geolocation of every plot the coffee came from, plus the production period and supplier details. Micro and small operators follow on 30 June 2027.

The field data (plot points and polygons) is increasingly there. What usually breaks is the join between that data and the lots a factory, mill and warehouse actually move. Four design decisions matter:

  1. Plots as first-class entities, not grower attributes. A grower can farm more than one plot. Store plot with its own ID, a foreign key to grower, a geometry, area in hectares and a mapping date.
  2. Geometry rules enforced at write time. The guidance summarised by the European Coffee Federation: a GPS point with six decimal places is enough for plots up to 4 ha; plots above 4 ha need a polygon. Data must be exportable as GeoJSON.
  3. Lot composition as a recorded edge, not a reconstruction. When deliveries are pooled into a factory lot, or lots are bulked into a grade, write the edges (input, output, weight) at that moment. Lineage becomes a graph walk.
  4. Production period on the lot. The statement needs a date or time range of production (for coffee, the harvest season). Derive it from the min and max delivery dates and store it with the lot.

A minimal schema 

CREATE TABLE grower (
  grower_id     TEXT PRIMARY KEY,         -- same ID used in delivery, payment and mapping systems
  coop_id       TEXT NOT NULL,
  name          TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE plot (
  plot_id       TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  grower_id     TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES grower(grower_id),
  area_ha       NUMERIC(8,3) NOT NULL,
  geom_geojson  JSONB NOT NULL,           -- Point or Polygon, WGS84
  mapped_on     DATE NOT NULL,
  mapped_by     TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE delivery (
  delivery_id   TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  grower_id     TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES grower(grower_id),
  plot_id       TEXT REFERENCES plot(plot_id),   -- NULL = unknown plot: treat as a gap
  delivered_on  DATE NOT NULL,
  kg_cherry     NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE lot (
  lot_id        TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  stage         TEXT NOT NULL,           -- 'factory', 'milled', 'grade', 'bulk'
  season        TEXT,
  produced_from DATE,
  produced_to   DATE
);

-- Edges: deliveries into factory lots, and lots into downstream lots
CREATE TABLE lot_input (
  lot_id        TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES lot(lot_id),
  delivery_id   TEXT REFERENCES delivery(delivery_id),
  input_lot_id  TEXT REFERENCES lot(lot_id),
  kg            NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
  CHECK ((delivery_id IS NULL) <> (input_lot_id IS NULL))
);

Validating plot geometry 

def validate_plot(geom: dict, area_ha: float) -> list[str]:
    errs = []
    t = geom.get("type")
    def six_dp(x): return len(repr(float(x)).split(".")[-1]) >= 6
    if area_ha > 4 and t != "Polygon":
        errs.append("plot > 4 ha must be a Polygon")
    if t == "Point":
        lon, lat = geom["coordinates"]
        if not (six_dp(lon) and six_dp(lat)):
            errs.append("point needs 6 decimal places")
    elif t == "Polygon":
        ring = geom["coordinates"][0]
        if len(ring) < 4 or ring[0] != ring[-1]:
            errs.append("polygon ring must be closed with >= 4 positions")
    else:
        errs.append(f"unsupported geometry {t}")
    return errs

Add overlap checks between plots (in PostGIS, ST_Overlaps on a geometry column) and flag implausible areas against the recorded area_ha.

Walking the lineage

Given a bag's grade lot, a recursive query collects every delivery, and so every plot, upstream:

WITH RECURSIVE up(lot_id) AS (
  SELECT 'GRADE-AB-2026-0141'
  UNION
  SELECT li.input_lot_id FROM lot_input li JOIN up ON li.lot_id = up.lot_id
  WHERE li.input_lot_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT d.delivery_id, d.grower_id, d.plot_id, d.delivered_on, li.kg
FROM up
JOIN lot_input li ON li.lot_id = up.lot_id AND li.delivery_id IS NOT NULL
JOIN delivery d ON d.delivery_id = li.delivery_id;

Any row with plot_id IS NULL is a traceability gap you must resolve before the lot goes into an EU contract. Turn the distinct plots into a GeoJSON FeatureCollection for the buyer, with MIN(delivered_on) and MAX(delivered_on) as the production period.

Things that bite in practice

  • ID mismatch. Cooperative grower numbers, payment IDs and mapping-tool IDs often differ. Build the crosswalk once and enforce one ID.
  • Multi-plot growers. If the delivery only records the grower, all of that grower's plots end up in the lot's plot list. Capture plot at intake where you can.
  • Mixed lots. Decide whether unmapped deliveries are excluded from EU-bound lots, or tracked as a share. A lot with unknown inputs is hard to sell into the EU after the application date.
  • Bulking and blending at the mill. New references must keep their input edges. This is where most paper systems lose lineage.
  • Retention. Keep what you sent, when and to whom, and the buyer's statement reference, for at least five years.

Context and sources

Kenya is classified as low risk under the EU country benchmarking, which allows the operator simplified due diligence (no risk assessment or mitigation unless there are signals of risk). It does not remove the need for plot geolocation. In July 2026, the Kenya Coffee Platform told the EUDR Learning Community for Africa that about 90 percent of active coffee farmers had been mapped, and that the main remaining gap is traceability from cooperative level down to individual plots. That gap is a data model.

  • European Commission, EUDR overview and application dates: https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/forests/deforestation/eu-deforestation-regulation-eudr_en
  • European Coffee Federation, EUDR Due Diligence guidance (October 2026): https://www.ecf-coffee.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/ECF_EUDR_Due_Diligence_Guidance_Oct2026_FINAL.pdf
  • EUDR Learning Community for Africa, Session 1 minutes: https://eudrafrica.thecosa.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/EUDR-Learning-Community-for-Africa_Session-1-Meeting-Minutes-and-QA.pdf

The full 12-point operations checklist for cooperatives, mills and exporters, with an FAQ, is on the FactoraERP blog: https://factoraerp.com/en/blog/eudr-traceability-checklist-coffee-processors-kenya.

title: Why Your Sidebar Icons Look Inconsistent - Even at the Same Size
description:
You set every sidebar icon to 24 × 24.

The labels line up. The spacing is consistent. The colors match.

Yet the navigation still feels uneven.

One icon looks heavier than its neighbors. Another seems too small. A third has sharp corners beside rounded shapes.

Before adding more CSS overrides, check the artwork itself.

Identical dimensions give icons the same box. They do not guarantee the same visual size, weight, or drawing style.

Here is a practical way to find the mismatch and build a more coherent sidebar.

1. Check the drawing inside the box

This rule gives every SVG the same dimensions:

.sidebar-icon {
  width: 24px;
  height: 24px;
}

But the visible artwork may occupy very different amounts of that space.

Compare these two SVGs:

<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true">
  <circle cx="12" cy="12" r="10" />
</svg>

<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true">
  <circle cx="12" cy="12" r="7" />
</svg>

Both have a 24 × 24 coordinate system. Both can render inside a 24 × 24 CSS box.

The second circle still looks smaller.

Real icons introduce more variation:

  • Empty space around the artwork.
  • Tall, wide, or circular silhouettes.
  • Dense details or large open areas.
  • Shapes that extend close to the edges.

When an icon looks undersized, inspect its internal spacing before increasing its CSS dimensions.

2. Compare visual weight, not just stroke width

Two icons can use the same stroke width and still feel unbalanced.

A detailed gear contains more edges than a simple chevron. A solid shape may appear heavier than an outline. A wide symbol distributes its weight differently from a narrow one.

Review these properties together:

Property What to inspect
Fill style Outline, solid, or mixed
Stroke Thickness, line endings, and joins
Corners Rounded or angular construction
Detail Simple shapes or intricate drawings
Internal spacing How much of the box the artwork occupies

A single mismatch is easy to miss in a large preview. It becomes more obvious when the icons sit beside one another in navigation.

3. Choose icons as a group

Searching for each icon independently can produce a sidebar assembled from unrelated styles.

The home icon looks good.

The folder icon looks good.

The team icon looks good.

Together, they may not belong.

Start with the navigation concepts your interface needs:

Overview
Projects
Team
Settings
Search
Notifications
Help

Then compare candidate families against the whole list.

Check whether each family has suitable symbols for your actual actions. Choosing a family because you like one icon can create problems when you need the remaining six.

On SVGicons.com, you can search for the required concepts and browse individual sets to evaluate their coverage and visual style.

The useful question is:

Can this family support the navigation as a whole?

4. Give icons a stable place in the layout

Once the artwork is coherent, make the component predictable.

Here is a small example using a simple project symbol:

<nav class="sidebar" aria-label="Main navigation">
  <a
    class="sidebar-link"
    href="/projects"
    aria-current="page"
  >
    <svg
      class="sidebar-icon"
      xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
      viewBox="0 0 24 24"
      fill="none"
      stroke="currentColor"
      stroke-width="2"
      aria-hidden="true"
      focusable="false"
    >
      <rect x="4" y="4" width="6" height="6" rx="1" />
      <rect x="14" y="4" width="6" height="6" rx="1" />
      <rect x="4" y="14" width="6" height="6" rx="1" />
      <rect x="14" y="14" width="6" height="6" rx="1" />
    </svg>

    <span>Projects</span>
  </a>
</nav>

.sidebar {
  box-sizing: border-box;
  width: 16rem;
  max-width: 100%;
  padding: 0.75rem;
  background: #151f32;
}

.sidebar-link {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 0.75rem;
  min-height: 2.75rem;
  padding: 0.625rem 0.875rem;
  border-radius: 0.5rem;
  color: #c3cee1;
  text-decoration: none;
}

.sidebar-icon {
  display: block;
  width: 1.5rem;
  height: 1.5rem;
  flex: 0 0 1.5rem;
}

.sidebar-link span {
  min-width: 0;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}

.sidebar-link[aria-current="page"] {
  color: #b5c9ff;
  background: #263b68;
}

.sidebar-link:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #b5c9ff;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

Several details help:

  • flex: 0 0 1.5rem prevents the icon from shrinking beside a long label.
  • align-items: center centers the icon box against the text.
  • currentColor lets the drawing follow the link color.
  • The visible label supplies the accessible name, so the SVG is decorative.
  • The focus outline makes keyboard navigation visible.
  • Long labels can wrap without squeezing the icon.

The drawing attributes in this example suit a monochrome outline icon. Preserve the intended rendering when working with filled or multicolor artwork.

If labels wrap onto several lines, also check whether centered or top-aligned icons work better for your particular layout.

5. Review the source before adding another override

An occasional optical adjustment can be useful.

But a growing list of exceptions deserves investigation:

.icon-overview {
  transform: scale(0.91);
}

.icon-projects {
  transform: translateY(-1px);
}

.icon-team {
  transform: scale(1.13);
}

.icon-settings {
  stroke-width: 1.4;
}

Before adding another rule, check:

  • Did an icon come from a different family?
  • Did you accidentally mix outline and filled variants?
  • Does the artwork contain unusually large margins?
  • Is the symbol too detailed for its display size?

Scaling an icon normally changes its stroke and detail as well as its apparent size. It can improve one mismatch while introducing another.

Prefer a suitable source icon, then make small adjustments where the actual interface requires them.

6. Test inside the component

A large preview helps you inspect the drawing. Your users will encounter it inside a button, link, or navigation row.

Review the sidebar:

  • At its intended display size.
  • In default, hover, active, and keyboard-focus states.
  • Against each supported background.
  • With longer labels.
  • At narrow widths.
  • In collapsed navigation, if available.

Collapsed navigation needs particular attention.

Labels can make similar symbols easy to distinguish. Once the labels disappear, the same icons may become ambiguous.

Provide accessible names for icon-only controls and a way for sighted users to discover their meaning. For example, a tooltip should work on keyboard focus as well as hover.

A coherent appearance does not guarantee a clear meaning.

7. Record the selection rules

Make future additions easier by keeping a short note with the project:

Navigation icon rules

Family: [selected family]
Variant: Outline
Display size: 24px
Color: currentColor
Source: [source page]
License: [license and required notices]

The next developer should be able to find a compatible icon without guessing how the original selection was made.

Keep the relevant license information too. Finding icons through one website does not mean every set uses the same license.

Before shipping

Review the navigation as a group:

  • Does the selected family cover the required actions?
  • Are fill style, stroke, and corner treatment coherent?
  • Do the visible shapes feel balanced?
  • Do icons retain their dimensions beside long labels?
  • Are active and keyboard-focus states clear?
  • Are symbols understandable when labels disappear?
  • Can another developer identify the source and license?

Matching dimensions is a useful starting point. The final result depends on the drawings you choose and the components that display them.

For your next sidebar, list the actions first, compare the icons together, and test them at their actual size before committing.

You can use SVGicons.com to search across icon sets and compare candidates before integrating them.

Disclosure: I run SVGicons.com. This article shares a practical selection and integration workflow. The four-square SVG in the code example was created specifically for this explanation.

title: Tracing Knowledge and Reasoning in LLM
description:
arXiv:2611.17461v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.

title: How fintechs make sure no single employee can move funds
description:
To make sure no single employee or vendor can move funds, keep the signing key somewhere no person holds it, and make every payment pass rules that one person cannot skip or change. On Lit Protocol, the key lives inside a hardware enclave, and Lit's code never exports it. The payment rules are a JavaScript function, called a Lit Action, that runs in the enclave before every signature. The record of which rules apply to which wallet lives in a contract on Base, and you can make your own Safe multisig the only account the contract accepts rule changes from.

I will show a payment rule that needs two approvers for large payments, and then the setup that keeps any one person from changing it.

The payment rule

This action pays USDC on Base, and only to approved vendors. Payments up to 10,000 USDC go through on their own. Anything larger needs signatures from two of three named approvers, over the exact payment and before it expires.

// payments-v1.js
const USDC = "0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913";
const VENDORS = ["0xVendorOne...", "0xVendorTwo..."].map(a => a.toLowerCase());
const APPROVERS = ["0xAliceApprover...", "0xBobApprover...", "0xCarolApprover..."].map(a => a.toLowerCase());
const AUTO_LIMIT = 10_000_000000n; // 10,000 USDC, which has 6 decimals

async function main({ pkpId, payment, approvals }) {
  const { paymentId, to, amount, expires } = payment;
  if (typeof amount !== "string" || !/^[0-9]+$/.test(amount)) return { sent: false, reason: "amount must be a whole number string" };
  if (!VENDORS.includes(String(to).toLowerCase())) return { sent: false, reason: "not an approved vendor" };
  if (!(Number(expires) > Date.now())) return { sent: false, reason: "payment request expired" };

  if (BigInt(amount) > AUTO_LIMIT) {
    const message = JSON.stringify({ pkpId: pkpId.toLowerCase(), paymentId, to: to.toLowerCase(), amount, expires });
    const recover = sig => { try { return ethers.utils.verifyMessage(message, sig).toLowerCase(); } catch { return null; } };
    const signers = new Set((approvals || []).map(recover));
    if (APPROVERS.filter(a => signers.has(a)).length < 2) return { sent: false, reason: "needs two approvers" };
  }

  const provider = new ethers.providers.StaticJsonRpcProvider("https://mainnet.base.org");
  const wallet = new ethers.Wallet(await Lit.Actions.getPrivateKey({ pkpId }), provider);
  const usdc = new ethers.Contract(USDC, ["function transfer(address,uint256) returns (bool)"], wallet);
  const tx = await usdc.transfer(to, amount);
  return { sent: true, paymentId, hash: tx.hash };
}

Each approver signs the same message with their own wallet. The message names the wallet, the payment ID, the recipient, the amount, and the expiry, so an approval cannot be moved to a different payment or a different wallet. expires is a string holding a time in milliseconds, and amount is a string in USDC's smallest unit.

const message = JSON.stringify({ pkpId: pkpAddress.toLowerCase(), paymentId: "p-2291", to: vendor.toLowerCase(), amount: "25000000000", expires: "1792512000000" });
const signature = await approverWallet.signMessage(message);

The vendors, the approvers, the threshold, and the limit are written into the code. An action you approve can still return the key if its code does that, so review this file like any code that moves money. Lit knows the action by a hash of its code, so changing any of them makes a different action that the wallet will not run until someone adds it.

The action does not keep a record of past payments, so it cannot tell when the same approved payment is sent twice before it expires. Keep expiries short. For a stronger check, have the action look up the payment ID in your own ledger before it signs. The post on writing signing policies as code shows how to check your ledger from inside an action.

Keeping any one person from changing the rules

The payment service gets a usage API key that can run this action and nothing else. It cannot add a new action, add a wallet, or change the rules. If someone steals it, they can send payments of up to 10,000 USDC each to your approved vendors until the wallet is empty, and they cannot do anything else. So keep only a working balance in the wallet, along with a little ETH on Base for gas.

The account itself is the part to lock down. A new Lit account starts in API mode, where Lit holds the account's owner credential and relays your changes. Set up the wallet, the group, and the usage key first, with the calls in the API reference. Then convert the account to ChainSecured mode with a Safe as the owner. In the Lit dashboard, open the account menu, click Convert to ChainSecured, and connect the Safe. The Safe must already be deployed on Base, and its signers should be ready to sign within five minutes. After that, adding a new version of the rule or adding a wallet is a Safe transaction that needs your threshold of signers. No single employee can change the rules, and neither can any single person at Lit.

What this setup gives you and its limits

With this setup, a payment over the limit needs two people, and a change to the rule needs your Safe's threshold. Every change is a public transaction on Base that your auditors can read. The post on proving key custody to auditors goes through how they can check it.

A Lit Safe that needs 2 of its 4 signers approves the code that runs in Lit's enclave, and the same Safe can upgrade the account contract that stores your rules. Either change would be a public transaction on Base. If you need those decisions to sit with your own signers, Lit is open source and you can run your own deployment.

Working with Lit

Lit works with fintech teams to set up payment rules and account ownership like this. To talk about your payment flows and approvals, use the Lit contact form. The account modes are explained at developer.litprotocol.com/management/account_modes.

title: Vercel Sandbox starts up to 4x faster
description:
Vercel Sandbox now initializes up to 4x faster outside the Washington, D.C. (iad1) region when reused image data is served from a regional cache.

Initialization now reads cached image data close to where the sandbox runs, avoiding round trips to origin image storage in iad1 on cache hits. Regional caching supports managed and custom images backed by Vercel Container Registry, including snapshots based on those images.

In internal end-to-end benchmarks with Vercel Managed Images, startup time fell about 75% in Paris and from about 3.5s to 1.05s in Seoul. Regions closer to origin storage generally see smaller improvements because requests already travel a shorter distance.

Learn more in the Vercel Sandbox documentation.

Read more

title: SWIFT: Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning of Time-Series Foundation Models for Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2611.17915v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While current few-shot adaptation strategies for time series forecasting foundation models are predominantly dataset-centric, the necessity of obtaining an additional dataset for the finetuning process poses a significant hurdle for adoption. To address this constraint, we propose Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a novel forecasting adaptation framework that achieves fine-grained specialization by leveraging structural priors from the target instance's own history. This shift allows the fine-tuning process to be entirely transparent to the end-user, which significantly enhances the ease of adoption. To implement this framework, SWIFT synergizes Self-Retrieval for historical mining and Frequency-Aware Loss for spectral consistency, while employing Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion to balance adaptation with general knowledge preservation. Extensive experiments across four TSFM backbones and three long-history benchmark subsets validate SWIFT, yielding average MASE and WQL reductions of 6.41% and 4.83% across 24 combinations of four backbones and six Chronos Benchmark II datasets. To the best of our knowledge, SWIFT is the first framework to investigate sample-wise instance fine-tuning of time-series foundation models, specializing the model for an individual prediction window using only the corresponding forecasting sample's own observed history.

title: UI edge cases: A reference guide
description:
A practical reference guide for catching UI edge cases before they ship — organized by category, with how to test, how to detect them in the wild, and how to design a fix. With examples.

Introduction

One day my colleague and I were at a workshop in a client’s office about agentic workflows in UI Design and Development when suddenly the client asked us a very good question.

“If we, designers and developers, are left to check the AI’s code for all the small but important edge cases it might miss — why don’t we give a document or a list of UI edge cases to the AI to begin with?”

Indeed a very good question, so my colleague and I tasked ourselves with finding a document like this so we could send it to our client.

But we couldn’t find anything that was generic enough to fit every client and specific enough to include all the little cases we saw everyday. Between us we have more than 15 years of UI Design and Development background.

We did find a few documents that had some of the information we needed as well as some that were industry-specific like documents for the Military, Governments, Medical or Telecom.

In the end I was tasked with writing a comprehensive document and sending it to the client for approval and it did end up giving the agentic workflow better results in terms of code generation.

So in the name of sharing, I give here the full document paraphrased in human language with some of the more technical code left out to keep it as generic and readable as possible.

1. Content-Driven

Empty states

This can happen when there’s no data to show yet, zero search results, empty inbox, empty list — screen looks broken or unfinished with no explanation.

To test, load the page with a brand-new account or a filtered view that returns nothing, or manually clear a list’s data source.

The solution is to design and implement a dedicated empty state — icon / illustration, one-line explanation, a clear next action (e.g., “No projects yet — Create one”).

Text length extremes

Long names or titles that break the layout (overflow, wrapping into other elements), very short or single-character values might look off-balance.

We can use pseudo-localization or seed test data with a deliberately long string (e.g., “Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious International Holdings LLC”) and a 1 or 2 character string in every text field, like “I” or “OK”.

We can solve this by defining truncation rules per component (single-line ellipsis vs. multi-line clamp vs. wrap) and set max-widths.

Long unbroken strings

URLs, emails, or IDs don’t wrap, causing horizontal overflow or breaking the container. A user might paste a long URL or a 40+ character token into any field that renders user content.

We should decide whether to truncate mid-string (common for hashes / emails) with an ellipsis in the middle, or just allow wrapping.

Pluralization and zero counts

Wordings like “1 items” or “0 item” can read as broken or unpolished. Some languages have more plural forms than English (Russian, Arabic).

Force counts of 0, 1, 2, and a large number through any relevant component, test with a locale that has more complex plural rules if you plan to localize.

To solve this we need to explicitly copy-write the 0, 1, and many states rather than assuming one template covers all of them. On the development side, we can use an i18n library with proper pluralization.

Localization / i18n

Translated text can run up to 40% longer (German, Finnish) or even run shorter, breaking fixed-width buttons and labels. RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew) often need mirrored layouts while dates, numbers and currency formats vary.

We can pseudo-localize the UI (wrap strings with padding characters) to simulate expansion using a toggle with dir=”rtl” and browse the whole flow, try switching OS and browser locale when possible.

Design components with flexible widths, not fixed pixel widths for text containers, RTL “mirrored” variants for directional icons (arrows, chevrons and more) and “mirrored” interactions if relevant.
On the development side use logical CSS properties (margin-inline-start instead of margin-left) so RTL can be flipped automatically.

Missing media

Broken image links, users with no avatar, videos that failed to load — leaves a broken-image icon or an unintended blank space.

You can point an <img> src at a 404 URL (an address you know that doesn’t exist) to test this. Also test a user record with a null avatar field, a throttled network to successfully fail media loads.

Design a fallback state — initials-based avatar when image fails to load, or a generic placeholder image, a poster frame for a failed video.

2. State-Driven

Loading states

A blank screen or jarring pop-in while data loads — unclear if the app is frozen or if loading takes too long.

We can throttle network to “Slow 3G” in devtools and artificially delay API responses in a staging environment.

Design skeleton screens that match final content’s shape (not just generic spinners) for anything that takes >300ms and define a timeout state (“This is taking longer than usual”).

Error states

Network failures, validation errors, or partial failures (some data loaded, some didn’t) show up as a blank screen, console-only error, or generic “Something went wrong.”

Kill the network mid-request, mock a 500 / 403 / timeout response, simulate a request where only some of several parallel calls fail.

We should design distinct states per error type (network vs. permission vs. validation) with actionable recovery (a retry button, send bug report etc).

Interim / optimistic states

The gap between user action and server confirmation is either invisible (user might be unsure if it worked) or the UI update is later reverted, thus confusing the user.

We can add artificial latency and watch what the UI displays between click and response, we can force the server call to fail after an optimistic update to see the rollback behavior. Review any “like / save / delete” style interaction.

Define a clear pending visual, such as: subtle dimming, spinner on a specific element (not the whole page) and a clear rollback / error treatment if it fails / succeeds.

Permission / auth states

Logged-out views, session expiring mid-action, or insufficient permissions leads to silent failures or confusing redirects.

We can expire a session token manually and attempt an action, log in as a lower-permission role and attempt a restricted action, test deep-linking to a protected page while logged out.

Design a “session expired” interstitial that preserves the user’s in-progress work where possible, also design disabled / hidden variants for restricted actions with an explanation on hover or on tap.

Stale data

User might leave a tab open for hours, underlying data changes (deleted by someone else or otherwise updated elsewhere) and the UI still reflects the older state, leading to conflicting edits.

To test this — try to open the same record in two sessions, edit in one, then act on the other without refreshing.

We should design a “this has changed” banner with a refresh or merge actions rather than silently overwriting the tab, which can be jarring.

3. Input-Driven

Focus states

Keyboard-only users can’t tell what’s in focus. Focus can get trapped or lost when opening / closing modals or menus.

Try unplugging the mouse and navigate the entire flow with Tab / Shift+Tab / Enter / Space / Escape only.

Design a visible, high-contrast focus ring as a first-class state for every interactive element (don’t rely on browser defaults, but don’t remove it completely either).

Disabled / readonly variations

Disabled and readonly states might look identical, or aren’t visually distinguishable enough from enabled states, this can confuse users about why they can’t interact with some elements.

Try Placing a disabled, readonly, and enabled version of the same component side by side, or next to a simliar looking component, and see if a new user can tell them apart without any documentation (for example a primary disabled button next to an enabled secondary button).

Give the disabled and readonly states a distinct, documented visual treatment (for example: disabled = grayed + no cursor change. Readonly = normal color + lock icon).

Rapid / repeated input

Users might double-click a submit button and it shouldn’t fire duplicate requests (double charge, duplicate record, etc.), spamming a button or rapid resize / scroll causes jank or race conditions.

Try rapidly double-click and triple-click every button, hold down a resize handle and drag erratically, scroll-flick a long list repeatedly.

Show an immediate disabled / loading / read-only state on the button or input field the instant it was clicked.

Copy-paste

A pasted text can carry unexpected formatting, emojis, or control characters that break layout, validation, or storage.

Try to copy rich text from a Word doc or a webpage and paste it into every text input or text area. Paste emoji-heavy text and right-to-left text. Paste a string with null bytes or control characters.

Decide whether inputs even should accept formatting (a rich text field) or strip it (a plain text field) and be consistent per field type or style.

4. Layout / Responsive

Extreme viewport sizes

Very narrow screens (folded phones, for example) or very wide monitors (ultrawide, 3440px+) can break layouts designed for a “typical” resolution range.

Resize the browser window to its minimum and to full ultrawide width, you can use devtools device emulation for specific devices or screen sizes.

Design with min-width / max-width content in mind, don’t let a single-column layout stretch to a full-width column on an ultrawide display. Don’t let content collapse below a usable minimum either.

Zoom levels

Try zoom the browser to 200% or use OS text-scaling to break the layout, this can create overlapping texts and cut-off buttons.

Zoom browser to 200% (a WCAG requirement) and navigate the full flow. Increase or decrease OS-level text size setting.

Design with relative units in mind so text scaling doesn’t require pixel-perfect fixed layouts, otherwise near-sighted users may be unable to use your website.

Dynamic content changing dimensions

A component resizing based on content (for example: an accordion, a comment with a long reply) can push neighboring elements around unexpectedly, causing a layout shift.

Try to trigger the resize (expand accordion, load async content, change dynamic content) and watch for neighboring elements jumping, you can also check Lighthouse’s Cumulative Layout Shift score.

To accomodate this, please reserve space or use smooth height transitions rather than instant jumps. Consider whether the expanding element should overlay instead of pushing the content.

Nested scroll containers

Scroll-within-scroll creates ambiguous scroll targeting (users might scroll the page when they meant scrolling the inner panel, or vice versa).

Sticky elements can overlap or conflict, horizontally-scrollable components (carousels, tables) nested in a vertically-scrolling page can hijack diagonal trackpad / touch gestures, or unintentionally introduce page-level horizontal scrolling if content overflows without being contained.

We can scroll with our cursor at the boundary between inner and outer scrolling areas. We can test using a trackpad, a mouse wheel, and touch input separately (they can behave differently).

Also check for an unexpected horizontal scrollbar on the page itself by resizing the viewport narrower than the widest nested element.

Minimize nested scroll where possible. If necessary, give the inner scroll area a clear visual boundary so users can know which scroll will be captured. Avoid mixing scroll axes in adjacent / nested regions where possible.

Safe areas

Take into consideration notches, browser chrome, and virtual keyboards covering content or inputs, especially on mobile.

Test on an actual notched device (or simulator) in both orientations, also focus a text input near the bottom of the screen and check if the keyboard covers it or shifting the view to reveal it.

Try to keep critical content and actions out of the extreme edges. Design for a keyboard-visible state on forms when possible.

5. System / Environment

Dark mode / forced-colors / high contrast

Custom-styled components (checkboxes, radio buttons, focus rings) lose their custom styling or become invisible in forced-colors / high-contrast modes. Dark mode might reveal hardcoded colors that don’t adapt.

Toggle OS-level dark mode and Windows High Contrast Mode. Test with devtools prefers-color-scheme: dark / light.

Define a full dark-mode palette (not just an inverted light mode) and verify contrast ratios in both modes.

Reduced motion preference

Some users have stated preference for reduced motion and they still get full animations, which can cause discomfort or eye strain.

Try to enable “Reduce Motion” in OS accessibility settings and revisit all animated interactions in your site, does it still animate or do you see a fallback instead?

We should design a reduced-motion variant for key animations like cross-fading instead of slides and zooms, or instant state changes instead of complex movement.

Font-loading flash (FOUT / FOIT)

FOUT is the Flash of unstyled text and FOIT is the Flash of invisible text, both can happen while custom web fonts load, often times with a layout shift when the font swaps.

Throttle your network in devtools and reload the page. Compare fallback font metrics to the final font. Lighthouse flags font-display issues and layout shift from font swap.

We can try and choose a fallback font with similar x-height / width to the custom font to minimize the layout shift, or we can choose to hide the text itself until the font loads.

Offline / flaky connectivity

When a user is on a flaky network, the app might appear frozen or throws unhandled errors when the network drops or is intermittent.

Please use the devtools to simulate “Offline” mid-session. Use a network-throttling proxy to simulate packet loss or a flaky connection.

Design an offline banner / indicator and, if feasible, an offline-capable mode (view cached data, queue actions, local host etc).

Closing thoughts

I hope this list can be the bare-minimum standard of UI edge cases that are checked and taken care of, from localization to error states to offline mode, there’s no reason to leave them out anymore.

Next year I’m sure we’ll have more edge cases that will pop up once those are already fixed, I have high hopes for this industry that with the emergence of AI the standard for good software will only get higher.

If this list made you, or your AI, spit out more usable code or a better thought out product overall, please share this article online.

Thanks for reading, and I’d love to hear your experience in the comments, also if I missed any edge cases — please tell me and I’ll roll it into the next version of this article.

Sources

Apple Human Interface Guidelines — Patterns
Thinking like a developer, part II: design the edge cases
Edge Cases in UX/UI Explained
UX Edge Cases
Designing for Edge Cases: UX That Works When Things Go Wrong
20 Edge Case Examples in Software That Product Teams Miss

title: A mesh-free deep energy method for phase-field modeling of thermally driven brittle fracture
description:
arXiv:2611.17630v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Phase-field simulation of thermally driven fracture requires resolving localized crack bands whose paths are unknown in advance and thermal boundary layers whose thickness evolves during the transient. Neural energy-based computations of thermal fracture have so far started from defects placed in advance. This paper proposes a mesh-free deep energy method based on multiresolution neural representations that predicts spontaneous crack nucleation, crack spacing, and selective crack propagation and arrest under transient thermal loading. Two networks, each with its own multiresolution encoding, represent the displacement and phase fields and the transient temperature, and the mechanical energy and the incremental functional of the backward Euler heat equation are estimated on integration points redrawn at every iteration. Restricting irreversibility to the crack set, carrying the optimizer state across load steps and decaying the learning rates within each step help prevent spurious damage accumulation. On two notched plates the initiation peak loads agree closely with an independent finite element reference. On a quenched glass strip under an analytical temperature field the crack path changes from straight to oscillatory and then to branched, with an oscillation threshold close to the linear stability prediction. Under a prescribed boundary temperature a quenched ceramic slab forms a crack array of the type observed in experiment, with a spacing close to that of a published benchmark. On the slab and a quenched annulus the arrays are denser than those of a finite element computation on the same material field. No crack paths, nucleation sites or crack-adapted meshes are prescribed.

title: gspread APIError 429: Quota exceeded for 'Write requests per minute per user' (and the 3-layer fix)
description:
You loop over your data and write it to a Google Sheet, and after a few dozen calls:

gspread.exceptions.APIError: APIError: [429]: Quota exceeded for quota metric
'Write requests' and limit 'Write requests per minute per user' of service 'sheets.googleapis.com'

A time.sleep(1) did not fix it, or it fixed it and now the job takes hours. This is what is going on.

What Google counts

Google's Sheets API usage limits page lists, for both reads and writes: 300 requests per minute per project and 60 requests per minute per user per project. Read and write each have their own bucket. A batchUpdate request counts as one request, however many operations it contains. Google's advice for a 429 is exponential backoff. (Limits change, so check the page.)

Three consequences:

  • The unit is the request, not the cell. One cell and one 60,000-cell block both cost one request.
  • The binding limit for a script is usually the per-user one: 60 per minute. A service account counts as one user.
  • It is a speed limit per minute, not a ban. Without retry code a throttled job simply crashes.

The arithmetic

Writing a 5,000-row, 12-column table:

How you write it Requests Minimum time at 60/min
update_cell in a double loop 60,000 about 1,000 minutes
append_row in a loop 5,000 about 84 minutes
one block with ws.update 1 under a minute

Layer 1: make fewer requests (this fixes most 429s) 

import gspread

gc = gspread.service_account(filename="service_account.json")
ws = gc.open_by_key("YOUR_SHEET_ID").worksheet("Data")

rows = [["date", "usd"], ["2026-10-27", 1.115]]   # your whole table as a list of lists
ws.update(values=rows, range_name="A1", value_input_option="USER_ENTERED")   # one request

Note the argument order of gspread 6: values first, then the range. Also read once (ws.get_all_values()) and work in memory: every ws.cell() and ws.col_values() call is a request. To add rows below existing data in one request use ws.append_rows(rows, value_input_option="USER_ENTERED").

Layer 2: slow down on purpose

A well-batched job can still exceed 60 a minute when it touches many tabs. Keep a small sliding window and sleep when you are about to go over (55 calls per 60 seconds leaves headroom under the documented 60).

import time
from collections import deque

class PerMinuteLimiter:
    def __init__(self, max_calls=55, window=60):
        self.max_calls = max_calls
        self.window = window
        self.times = deque()

    def wait(self):
        now = time.monotonic()
        while self.times and now - self.times[0] >= self.window:
            self.times.popleft()
        if len(self.times) >= self.max_calls:
            time.sleep(self.window - (now - self.times[0]))
            return self.wait()
        self.times.append(time.monotonic())

limiter = PerMinuteLimiter()  # 55 calls per 60 seconds
# before every Sheets call: limiter.wait()

Layer 3: retry politely, with backoff and jitter 

import random, time, gspread

def call_with_backoff(fn, *args, tries=8, **kwargs):
    for n in range(tries):
        try:
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
        except gspread.exceptions.APIError as e:
            if e.code not in (429, 500, 502, 503, 504) or n == tries - 1:
                raise                                   # not retryable, or out of attempts
            time.sleep(min(2 ** n + random.random(), 64))

limiter.wait()
call_with_backoff(ws.update, values=rows, range_name="A1", value_input_option="USER_ENTERED")

Two details that matter:

  • Retry only what is worth retrying. A 403 "permission denied" or a 404 will never fix itself; retrying hides the real problem. e.code comes from the JSON error body; for a normal Sheets 429 it is the integer 429.
  • Wait longer than one quota window. A per-minute quota needs about a minute to recover. In my own test with one Cloud project, writes became possible again between under 10 and about 130 seconds after a burst (usually 40 to 60; about eight trials). A version that gave up after six retries (about 66 seconds in total) failed in three of those trials. Your numbers will differ, but eight retries with a 64-second cap is a safer default than three.

The jitter (the random.random()) stops many jobs from retrying at the same instant.

Estimate before you run

A job with more than about 50 requests per run needs a redesign, not more retries. Open the spreadsheet by ID (1 request), read each tab once, write each output block once, and put all formatting changes in one batchUpdate.

Free one-page checklist for the three things that most often kill a scheduled Sheets script (the 7-day invalid_grant, 429 Quota exceeded, duplicate rows): https://whop.com/whop-0bab/day-8-checklist-python-google-sheets-free/

Disclosure: I also sell a short fix pack with tested helpers for those three (EUR 9): https://whop.com/whop-0bab/python-google-sheets-fix-pack/, and a larger starter kit: https://whop.com/whop-0bab/python-google-sheets-running-on-autopilot-the-starter-kit/ . Everything in this post works without them.

title: VACO: Vertex-Aligned Decoding for Dense Hand Contact Estimation from a Single Image
description:
arXiv:2611.17755v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dense hand contact estimation from a single RGB image is a foundational primitive for dexterous manipulation and 3D interaction analysis. Direct predictors typically decode the entire per-vertex contact map from one shared query, leaving individual vertices ungrounded in the image and smearing contact across adjacent, non-touching surfaces. We present VACO, a vertex-aligned decoder in which each MANO vertex samples local image features at its projected location. A hand-reconstruction backbone, jointly trained for reconstruction and contact, predicts these locations at inference without an auxiliary reconstructor. Training uses noise-perturbed ground-truth projections and end-to-end feature adaptation to improve robustness and contact-sensitive features. A single VACO checkpoint sets a new state of the art on five benchmarks spanning hand-object, hand-human, hand-scene, and bimanual interactions. It improves F1 by +20.7 pp over the strongest prior direct predictor on Hi4D and generalizes to the held-out HOT3D and HOCap, with gains of +5.5 and +2.7 pp. The resulting contact predictions also improve downstream HOI reconstruction.

title: Decision Records So AI Context Doesn't Rot
description:
On one client project, an AI assistant helpfully "fixed" our queue setup three times in two months. Each time, a developer asked it to speed up a slow job, and each time it suggested moving the work from our dedicated Redis queue back to the database driver, because the database queue was simpler and the assistant saw a stray QUEUE_CONNECTION=database in an old .env.example. Nobody on the current team remembered why we had moved to Redis in the first place: a deadlock storm during a Black Friday import, two years earlier. That reason lived in a Slack thread and one engineer's memory. The code did not explain it, so neither the new developers nor the assistant could respect it.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every example against Laravel 11, Node 22, GitHub Actions and the adr-tools and MADR conventions. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi with 9+ years across PHP/Laravel, Vue, Node and .NET microservices, and through Loop Origin I maintain custom business applications where a lot of new code is now AI-assisted.

📚 Series Navigation — Maintaining AI-Written Code in Production

  • Part 1: Reviewing AI-Generated Pull Requests: A Checklist That Catches Real Bugs
  • Part 2: Characterization Tests Before You Refactor AI-Written Code
  • Part 3: Hallucinated Packages & Dependency Drift in AI-Assisted Code
  • Part 4: Static Analysis Gates: PHPStan, TypeScript Strict & Coverage in CI
  • Part 5 (This Post): Decision Records So AI Context Doesn't Rot
  • Part 6: Measuring AI Coding Impact With DORA Metrics, Not Vibes

Related earlier posts: Config & Feature Flags That Quietly Diverged Across Environments · Synthetic Checks & SLOs for the Paths Nobody Clicks

How do architecture decision records help with AI-assisted code?

Direct answer: An architecture decision record (ADR) is a short markdown file in the repo that explains one decision: context, choice, consequences and status. AI assistants and new developers only see what is in the codebase, so ADRs turn tribal knowledge into context they can read. Point your assistant's rules file at them and check in CI that big changes reference one.

Why context rots faster with AI in the loop

Before AI assistants, undocumented decisions decayed slowly. The person who made the choice usually reviewed the next change to that area. Now the volume of changes is higher, reviewers are stretched (Part 1), and the assistant generating the code has no memory of last year's incident. It optimises for what looks clean in the files it can see.

Typical decisions I have watched get silently reversed:

Decision Why it was made How it got undone Cost
Redis queues instead of database queues Deadlocks under bulk imports Assistant "simplified" the driver Repeat of the incident in staging
Money stored as integer cents Rounding errors in invoices New model used decimal(8,2) and floats in JS Penny mismatches in reconciliation
No ORM eager loading on the report endpoint; raw SQL instead N+1 timeouts on large tenants Refactor to Eloquent relationships 30s responses for the biggest client
Soft deletes disabled on audit tables Compliance: audit rows must never be hidden Trait added for "consistency" Audit gaps
Pinned PDF library version Newer version broke Urdu font shaping Dependency bump PR Garbled invoices

None of these were bad changes in isolation. They were bad because the reason was invisible.

Keep the format small enough that people actually write them

Long design documents do not get written for every decision, and nobody reads them. I use a trimmed MADR-style template that fits on one screen:

# 0007. Use Redis for queues, not the database driver

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2024-11-29
- Deciders: Ali, Hamza
- Supersedes: —
- Related code: config/queue.php, app/Jobs/Import/*

## Context
Black Friday product import (≈400k rows) caused InnoDB deadlocks on the
`jobs` table and stalled checkout. Database queue polling also added load
to the primary DB.

## Decision
All queues run on Redis (`QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis`) with Horizon.
The database driver is allowed only in local tests.

## Consequences
+ Imports no longer contend with checkout queries.
+ Horizon gives per-queue metrics and retries.
- Redis is now a hard dependency; it is monitored and backed up.
- Do NOT switch back to the database driver to "simplify" setup.

## Revisit when
Job volume drops below 1k/day or Redis hosting cost becomes material.

The "Revisit when" section is the one I added after years of maintenance work. It tells future readers, human or AI, under what conditions changing the decision is fine, so ADRs do not turn into permanent dogma.

Where ADRs live and how to number them

Put them next to the code, not in a wiki that drifts:

docs/
  decisions/
    0001-record-architecture-decisions.md
    0002-money-as-integer-cents.md
    0003-multi-tenant-by-tenant-id-column.md
    0007-redis-for-queues.md
    0012-pin-dompdf-for-urdu-shaping.md
    README.md   ← index: number, title, status, one-line summary

Never edit an accepted ADR to change the decision. Write a new one that supersedes it and update the old status to superseded by 0019. That history is exactly what explains why the code looks the way it does.

A tiny script keeps creation frictionless:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# bin/adr "Use Redis for queues"
set -euo pipefail
dir=docs/decisions
n=$(printf "%04d" $(( $(ls $dir | grep -E '^[0-9]{4}' | wc -l) + 1 )))
slug=$(echo "$*" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr -cs 'a-z0-9' '-' | sed 's/-$//')
file="$dir/$n-$slug.md"
sed -e "s/{{N}}/$n/" -e "s/{{TITLE}}/$*/" -e "s/{{DATE}}/$(date +%F)/" $dir/template.md > "$file"
echo "Created $file"

Point AI assistants at the decisions

Most AI coding tools read a project rules file: AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules, CLAUDE.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md and similar. I keep one short rules file and link the ADRs rather than copying them, so there is one source of truth:

# AGENTS.md (excerpt)

## Architecture decisions
Before changing queues, money handling, tenancy, audit tables or pinned
dependencies, read the matching record in docs/decisions/ and follow it.
If a change would contradict an accepted decision, stop and say so in the
PR description instead of changing it.

Key decisions:
- Money is integer cents everywhere (0002). Never use float for amounts.
- Tenancy uses a tenant_id column with a global scope (0003).
- Queues run on Redis + Horizon (0007).
- dompdf is pinned for Urdu shaping (0012). Do not bump without the PDF snapshot tests.

In practice this changed assistant behaviour more than I expected. When asked to speed up the import job, the assistant now proposes chunking and batch inserts instead of switching drivers, and it cites 0007 in its explanation. It is not magic; it is just context that used to be missing.

For decisions that can be checked mechanically, add a code comment pointing to the ADR at the exact spot people (and tools) will edit:

// config/queue.php
// See docs/decisions/0007-redis-for-queues.md — do not switch to 'database'.
'default' => env('QUEUE_CONNECTION', 'redis'),

Enforce it lightly in CI

I do not block every PR on documentation. I flag the risky ones. This GitHub Actions step fails when a PR touches protected paths without mentioning an ADR number in its description or adding a new ADR:

# .github/workflows/adr-check.yml
name: adr-check
on: pull_request
jobs:
  adr:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - name: Require ADR reference for protected paths
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.pull_request.body }}
        run: |
          changed=$(git diff --name-only origin/${{ github.base_ref }}...HEAD)
          if echo "$changed" | grep -qE '^(config/queue.php|config/database.php|app/Models/Concerns/Tenant|composer.json)'; then
            if echo "$changed" | grep -q '^docs/decisions/' || echo "$BODY" | grep -qE 'ADR[- ]?[0-9]{4}'; then
              echo "ADR referenced"; else
              echo "::error::Protected path changed. Reference an ADR (e.g. ADR-0007) or add one."; exit 1
            fi
          fi

Combine this with the static analysis gates from Part 4, for example a PHPStan rule or ESLint no-restricted-syntax that bans float casts on money fields, and the most important decisions are protected by both words and tooling.

What deserves an ADR (and what does not)

Write an ADR Skip it
Choice between two reasonable options that someone might reverse Formatting and naming conventions (use a linter)
Anything caused by a past incident One-off bug fixes with a good commit message
Pinned versions or unusual config Library choice with no real alternative
Data model rules (money, tenancy, deletes) Temporary experiments behind a flag
Security or compliance constraints Decisions fully expressed by a test

A practical rule: if you have explained the same decision twice in code review, write it down.

Backfilling decisions on an existing codebase

On inherited projects, I spend the first week writing five to ten ADRs from what I learn: incidents in the issue tracker, odd config values, pinned versions in composer.json and package.json, and comments like "don't touch this." Each one takes 15 minutes. This is often the most valuable part of a maintenance handover, and it is where Loop Origin's custom web application development engagements usually start. If you want a second pair of eyes on an inherited codebase, you can reach out here.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] docs/decisions/ exists with a one-screen template and an index README
  • [ ] Top 5–10 risky decisions backfilled (money, tenancy, queues, pinned deps, audit)
  • [ ] Each ADR has status, context, decision, consequences and "revisit when"
  • [ ] Superseded ADRs are kept and linked, never rewritten
  • [ ] AI rules file (AGENTS.md or equivalent) links key ADRs and says to stop on conflicts
  • [ ] Code comments point to ADRs at the exact config or class people edit
  • [ ] CI flags PRs touching protected paths without an ADR reference
  • [ ] Mechanical rules (no floats for money, etc.) enforced by static analysis too
  • [ ] New incident postmortems end with "ADR needed? yes/no"
  • [ ] ADR index reviewed quarterly for stale "revisit when" conditions

FAQs

Aren't ADRs just more documentation nobody reads?

Short ones get read, especially when code comments and the AI rules file point to them at the moment of change. The goal is one screen per decision, not a design document.

Should AI write the ADRs?

It is good at drafting from a Slack thread or PR discussion, and I often use it that way. A human who made the decision should still edit the context and consequences, because those are exactly the parts an assistant cannot know.

Do I need a tool like adr-tools or Log4brains?

No. A folder, a template and a ten-line script are enough. Tools help with rendering a site later, but they are not what makes ADRs useful.

How is this different from a README?

A README describes how the system works now. ADRs explain why it ended up that way and what was rejected. Both are useful; ADRs are what prevent well-meaning reversals.

Will the assistant really follow the rules file?

Usually, but not always. That is why the CI check and static analysis rules exist. Treat the rules file as guidance and the pipeline as enforcement.

How many ADRs is too many?

If the index has hundreds of entries nobody reviews, you are recording too much. Most business apps I maintain have 15–40 meaningful decisions.

Next in this series, Part 6 covers measuring AI coding impact with DORA metrics instead of gut feeling.

title: Building Arabic Order Forms: Labels, Phone Inputs, and Error Recovery
description:
Disclosure: This tutorial was drafted with AI assistance for the Dropsaas project. The example is a markup fragment, not a complete checkout or a claim about production conversion rates.

An Arabic order form needs more than right-aligned text. Customers may type Arabic names, Latin product codes, and phone numbers in the same flow. Make the meaning of each field explicit, then test mixed-direction content and error recovery.

Start with labels that remain visible

A placeholder disappears as soon as someone types. Keep a visible label and associate it with the input. This also gives the control an accessible name through standard HTML semantics. See the MDN label reference.

Here is a small starting fragment:

<div lang="ar" dir="rtl">
  <label for="buyer-name">الاسم الكامل</label>
  <input id="buyer-name" name="buyer_name"
         autocomplete="name" dir="auto" required>

  <label for="buyer-phone">رقم الهاتف</label>
  <p id="phone-help">أدخل رقمًا يمكن التواصل معك عليه لتأكيد الطلب.</p>
  <input id="buyer-phone" name="buyer_phone"
         type="tel" autocomplete="tel" dir="ltr"
         aria-describedby="phone-help" required>
</div>

The phone field uses left-to-right direction to make its digits and international prefix easier to inspect in an otherwise right-to-left layout. That is a design choice to test with your audience, not a universal rule for every input.

The fragment deliberately has no submission endpoint or pretend validation logic. It demonstrates field semantics. A production form still needs server-side validation, error handling, transport security, authorization where relevant, and a deliberate data-retention policy.

A telephone input does not validate every country's phone numbers

Using type="tel" does not automatically prove a number is valid or reachable. Its value is still text, and telephone formats vary. Check the MDN telephone input reference.

Choose validation based on the countries you actually support. Test spaces, an international prefix, local formatting, and Arabic-Indic digits if your normalization rules support them. Do not silently change an ambiguous number into a different one. Explain what the user should enter and show the corrected representation where appropriate.

A browser-side check helps someone fix an error quickly. Your server must still validate what it receives.

Give autocomplete useful hints

The example uses autocomplete="name" and autocomplete="tel". These tokens describe the expected information to the browser; they do not guarantee every browser will autofill the field. Consult the MDN autocomplete reference when mapping address and contact fields.

Avoid requesting unnecessary details just because a template contains those fields. For a cash-on-delivery order, map every required field to a real confirmation or fulfillment task. Ask the operations team which missing details actually prevent delivery.

Design error recovery before styling the error

Write an expected result for each failure scenario. If a required address field is missing, the message should identify the missing information. Valid information in the other fields should remain available so the customer does not have to start again.

Do not rely on a red border alone. Review keyboard navigation, focus behavior after submission, and how assistive technology encounters the error. Test the rendered page with the tools and devices your customers actually use; a static code review cannot verify the full experience.

Use a small test matrix

Scenario What to inspect
Arabic name and Latin phone number Reading order, alignment, and cursor behavior
Phone pasted with spaces Normalization and understandable feedback
Missing delivery area Specific error without clearing valid fields
Longer address on a narrow screen Wrapping and horizontal overflow
Repeated submission after a network problem Clear status and investigation of duplicate orders

Record the actual result and assign one next action per failure. A screenshot of an empty form is not a substitute for these scenarios.

Keep confirmation wording accurate

If the business calls to confirm an order, the success message should say so. Do not describe a recorded request as a dispatched parcel. Match interface wording to the actual order state and the next step handled by the team.

The most useful form improvement may be a clearer label, a preserved value after an error, or an honest success message. Fix a specific failure, rerun the same scenario, and document what changed.
