title: How to Build a Polymarket Market Maker with Rust
description:
Learn how to build a Polymarket market maker using Rust, inventory-aware quoting, bid-ask spreads, order management, and risk controls.

A market maker can buy at $0.48 and sell at $0.50, capture the two-cent spread, and still lose money.

The problem is rarely the spread calculation. It is what happens between the two trades.

Suppose your bid fills just before the market reprices to $0.44. Your ask at $0.50 is no longer competitive, and your inventory is worth less than you paid. You earned no round-trip spread. You simply bought into a falling market.

This is the central engineering problem when you build a Polymarket market maker: keeping quotes competitive without allowing inventory and adverse selection to overwhelm the expected spread revenue.

By Almach

Polymarket trading bots • Quantitative trading • Rust • Web3 infrastructure

Telegram: https://t.me/almachquant
YouTube: https://youtube.com/@almachquant
X: https://x.com/@almachquant
Polymarket: https://polymarket.com/@almach

The spread is revenue potential, not profit

Consider a hypothetical YES-token order book.

Quote Price Size
Best ask $0.52 800
Best bid $0.48 1,200

The quoted spread is:

spread = best_ask - best_bid
spread = 0.52 - 0.48
spread = 0.04

A market maker might submit a bid at $0.49 and an ask at $0.51, improving both sides of the existing market.

If both orders fill for equal quantities, the gross spread capture is $0.02 per matched share.

But that result assumes both executions occur. It also excludes applicable fees, inventory financing, price changes, and other costs.

A single-sided fill creates directional exposure. This is why market making cannot be reduced to continuously posting two limit orders.

Quote around a reservation price

A basic market maker starts with a fair-value estimate.

For a binary YES token, that estimate may come from a probability model, external reference data, or another research signal.

The model should produce a value between zero and one.

Instead of quoting symmetrically around fair value, an inventory-aware strategy adjusts its reservation price.

reservation_price = fair_value
                  - inventory_skew * net_inventory

bid = reservation_price - half_spread

ask = reservation_price + half_spread

Here, inventory_skew is a configurable risk coefficient, not a universal market constant.

If the bot holds too many YES shares, the reservation price decreases. Its quotes become less attractive for additional buying and more attractive for selling.

If inventory is negative, assuming short exposure is permitted and supported by the account's collateral and execution setup, the adjustment works in the opposite direction.

The goal is not to predict every price movement. It is to prevent repeated fills from pushing the portfolio into an uncontrolled position.

Implementing a quote calculator in Rust

The following Rust example calculates theoretical bid and ask prices using fair value, inventory, and a minimum spread.

It is a standalone quote model, not a complete Polymarket API client.

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Quote {
    bid: f64,
    ask: f64,
}

fn calculate_quote(
    fair_value: f64,
    inventory: f64,
    skew: f64,
    spread: f64,
    tick: f64,
) -> Option<Quote> {
    if !fair_value.is_finite()
        || !(0.0..=1.0).contains(&fair_value)
        || !inventory.is_finite()
        || !skew.is_finite()
        || skew < 0.0
        || !spread.is_finite()
        || spread <= 0.0
        || !tick.is_finite()
        || tick <= 0.0
    {
        return None;
    }

    let reservation = fair_value - inventory * skew;
    let half = spread / 2.0;

    let bid = ((reservation - half) / tick).floor() * tick;
    let ask = ((reservation + half) / tick).ceil() * tick;

    if !bid.is_finite()
        || !ask.is_finite()
        || bid <= 0.0
        || ask >= 1.0
        || bid >= ask
    {
        return None;
    }

    Some(Quote { bid, ask })
}

fn main() {
    let quote = calculate_quote(
        0.50,
        100.0,
        0.0001,
        0.02,
        0.01,
    );

    match quote {
        Some(q) => println!(
            "Bid: {:.2}, Ask: {:.2}",
            q.bid, q.ask
        ),
        None => println!("No valid quote"),
    }
}

For these hypothetical inputs, the result is:

Bid: 0.48, Ask: 0.50

The positive inventory shifts both quotes below the original $0.50 fair value.

A production implementation must obtain the market's permitted tick size, enforce valid price and order-size constraints, and check available balances before submitting orders.

Why quote cancellation matters as much as placement

A market maker operates in a changing order book. Its quotes become stale whenever fair value, inventory, spread, or market conditions change.

A sensible execution cycle is:

Receive market update
        |
Update fair value
        |
Reconcile inventory and open orders
        |
Calculate desired quotes
        |
Check exposure limits
        |
Cancel or amend stale orders
        |
Submit permitted replacements
        |
Reconcile acknowledgments and fills

Order acknowledgments are not equivalent to fills.

Similarly, sending a cancellation request does not prove that the order can no longer execute. The bot must account for fills that occur while cancellation is pending.

This race condition is particularly dangerous when replacing quotes: the old order and its replacement may both create exposure.

The inventory problem gets worse near resolution

Prediction-market contracts introduce risks that ordinary spot-market quoting models do not fully capture.

A YES token may trade near $0.50 for an extended period, then move sharply toward zero or one as new information arrives.

Inventory that appeared manageable under normal conditions can suddenly dominate the portfolio's risk.

A market maker therefore needs limits on individual token positions, total market exposure, correlated positions, and outstanding order quantities.

Near resolution or during abnormal volatility, widening quotes or withdrawing liquidity may be preferable to maintaining a constant spread.

The appropriate decision depends on the market rules, available liquidity, and model uncertainty.

Testing before deploying capital

Backtesting a market-making strategy using midpoint prices is insufficient.

A realistic simulator needs order-book updates, queue-position assumptions, partial fills, cancellation delays, transaction costs, and adverse selection.

A useful test asks whether the strategy remains viable when only its bid fills before a price decline, rather than assuming every buy is eventually matched with a profitable sell.

Operational testing matters too. Disconnect the market-data stream. Restart the process with outstanding orders. Introduce delayed acknowledgments and duplicate events.

The system should recover its actual positions and outstanding orders before resuming quoting.

A reliable Polymarket market maker is not the bot that posts the tightest spread. It is the one that knows when its quotes are no longer worth keeping in the market.

Trading-risk disclaimer: This article is educational. Market making involves inventory losses, adverse selection, liquidity risk, execution uncertainty, and market-resolution risk. Profitability is not guaranteed.

title: PostgreSQL: Relational Model, SQL, Normalization and ACID Properties
description:
Introduction

Databases are an essential part of modern application development. Almost every application needs a way to store, organize, retrieve, and manage information efficiently.

PostgreSQL is a powerful, open-source relational database management system (RDBMS) that helps developers manage structured data using SQL (Structured Query Language).

In this blog, we will explore the relational model, database keys, relationships, SQL joins, aggregate functions, normalization forms (1NF–3NF), and ACID properties.

1. Understanding the Relational Model

The relational model organizes information into tables consisting of rows and columns.

For example, an Employee Management System may contain an Employees table:

employee_id employee_name department_id
1 Ravi 101
2 Swaroop 102
3 Kiran 101

Here:

  • Table: A collection of related information.
  • Row: Represents a single record.
  • Column: Represents an attribute of the record.
  • Cell: Contains an individual value.

The relational model helps organize data and establish connections between different tables.

2. Database Keys: Primary Key and Foreign Key

Keys help identify records and establish relationships between tables.

Primary Key (PK)

A Primary Key uniquely identifies every record in a table.

Example:

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    age INT
);

The employee_id column uniquely identifies each employee.

A primary key must contain unique and non-NULL values.

Foreign Key (FK)

A Foreign Key establishes a relationship between two tables.

Example:

CREATE TABLE departments (
    department_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    department_name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    department_id INT REFERENCES departments(department_id)
);

Here, department_id in the Employees table references the Departments table.

Foreign keys help maintain referential integrity by ensuring that referenced records exist.

3. Types of Database Relationships

Relationships describe how records in different tables are connected.

One-to-One (1:1)

One record in a table is associated with one record in another table.

Example: One person has one passport.

One-to-Many (1:N)

One record in a table can be associated with multiple records in another table.

Example: One department can have multiple employees.

Many-to-Many (N:N)

Multiple records in one table can be associated with multiple records in another table.

Example: Multiple students can enroll in multiple courses.

A junction table is used to implement many-to-many relationships.

Example:

CREATE TABLE enrollments (
    student_id INT REFERENCES students(student_id),
    course_id INT REFERENCES courses(course_id),
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
);

4. SQL Joins

SQL joins combine information from multiple tables using related columns.

Consider two tables: Employees and Departments.

INNER JOIN

Returns only records that have matching values in both tables.

SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;

LEFT JOIN

Returns all records from the left table and matching records from the right table. Unmatched right-side values appear as NULL.

SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;

RIGHT JOIN

Returns all records from the right table and matching records from the left table.

SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
RIGHT JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;

FULL OUTER JOIN

Returns all records from both tables, including matching and unmatched records.

SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
FULL OUTER JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;

Joins are useful when application data is distributed across multiple related tables.

5. SQL Aggregate Functions

Aggregate functions perform calculations on multiple records and return a single result per group or query.

Important aggregate functions include:

  • COUNT(): Counts records.
  • SUM(): Calculates the total.
  • AVG(): Calculates the average.
  • MAX(): Returns the highest value.
  • MIN(): Returns the lowest value.

Example:

SELECT AVG(salary)
FROM employees;

This calculates the average employee salary.

GROUP BY

GROUP BY groups records with the same value.

SELECT department_id, COUNT(*)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id;

This query counts employees in each department.

HAVING

HAVING filters groups based on aggregate conditions.

SELECT department_id, COUNT(*)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;

This returns departments having more than two employees.

6. Database Normalization (1NF, 2NF and 3NF)

Normalization is the process of organizing database tables to reduce unnecessary duplication and improve data integrity.

It helps prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies.

First Normal Form (1NF)

A table satisfies 1NF when:

  • Every cell contains a single atomic value.
  • Each column contains values of a consistent type.
  • Each record can be uniquely identified.

Example of a table that violates 1NF:

Student Subjects
Ravi Java, Python

After normalization:

Student Subject
Ravi Java
Ravi Python

Each cell now contains one value.

Second Normal Form (2NF)

A table satisfies 2NF when:

  • It already satisfies 1NF.
  • Every non-key attribute depends on the whole candidate key, not just part of a composite candidate key.

For example, in a student-course enrollment table, student_name depends only on student_id, while course_name depends only on course_id.

We can separate the information into Students, Courses, and Enrollments tables.

This eliminates partial dependencies.

Third Normal Form (3NF)

A table satisfies 3NF when:

  • It already satisfies 2NF.
  • Non-key attributes have no transitive dependencies on candidate keys.

For example, employee_id determines department_id, and department_id determines department_name.

Instead of storing department_name repeatedly in the Employees table, we create a separate Departments table.

This reduces duplication and improves consistency.

Normalization Summary

  • 1NF: Removes repeating groups and ensures atomic values.
  • 2NF: Removes partial dependencies.
  • 3NF: Removes transitive dependencies.

Normalization is important because it helps maintain accurate and consistent data.

7. ACID Properties in PostgreSQL

ACID properties ensure reliable database transactions.

ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.

Atomicity

A transaction is treated as a single unit. Either all operations succeed or none of them are applied.

Example: During a bank transfer, money must be deducted from one account and credited to another.

Consistency

Every transaction must preserve database rules and constraints.

Example: A foreign key should not reference a department that does not exist.

Isolation

Concurrent transactions should not interfere with each other in ways that produce incorrect results.

Example: Two customers attempting to book the same available seat should not both successfully reserve it.

Durability

Once a transaction is committed, its changes persist even after a system failure, subject to the database's durability configuration.

Example: A successfully committed payment transaction remains recorded.

Example of a PostgreSQL Transaction 

BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 500
WHERE account_id = 1;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 500
WHERE account_id = 2;

COMMIT;

If an operation fails before committing, the transaction can be rolled back:

ROLLBACK;

Transactions help protect data and maintain database consistency.

8. Practical Implementation: Employee Management Database

To understand these concepts practically, we can create an Employee Management Database.

Create the Departments table:

CREATE TABLE departments (
    department_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    department_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

Create the Employees table:

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    age INT,
    salary NUMERIC(10,2),
    department_id INT REFERENCES departments(department_id)
);

Insert sample records:

INSERT INTO departments (department_name)
VALUES ('IT'), ('HR'), ('Finance');

INSERT INTO employees
(employee_name, age, salary, department_id)
VALUES
('Ravi', 23, 30000, 1),
('Swaroop', 22, 40000, 1),
('Kiran', 24, 35000, 2);

Retrieve employee and department information:

SELECT
    e.employee_name,
    d.department_name,
    e.salary
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;

This practical example demonstrates table creation, primary keys, foreign keys, relationships, data insertion, and joins.

9. Conclusion

PostgreSQL provides a strong foundation for managing structured application data.

Understanding relational models, database keys, relationships, SQL joins, aggregate functions, normalization, and ACID properties helps developers design reliable and maintainable databases.

These concepts are especially important when developing backend applications using technologies such as NestJS, Node.js, and PostgreSQL.

Learning these fundamentals prepares developers to work with real-world database systems and build applications with better data integrity, consistency, and reliability.

Key Takeaways:

  1. Relational models organize data into connected tables.
  2. Primary and foreign keys establish identity and relationships.
  3. SQL joins retrieve related information from multiple tables.
  4. Aggregate functions perform calculations on records.
  5. Normalization reduces duplication and improves data integrity.
  6. ACID properties ensure reliable database transactions.

Practice makes database concepts easier to understand. Start by creating tables, inserting records, writing joins, and experimenting with transactions in PostgreSQL.

title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
description:
Today, we are launching Vercel Security Review in public beta.

Security Review is a new capability in Vercel Agent, alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories.

Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings.

How it works

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works:

  1. You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project.

  2. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets.

  3. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request.

  4. You can fix findings by clicking Fix with Vercel Agent in the dashboard, or use the CLI to pull findings and have your own coding agent implement changes.

  5. When subsequent security reviews no longer detect a finding, it is marked as no longer detected in the dashboard, and the GitHub comment is closed.

Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment.

What the agent checks

The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. That process is how it catches logic flaws like missing authorization checks, which pattern-matching scanners miss.

Each review also applies your team’s security policies, which you can write in plain language and apply to specific projects or across your team. For example, a policy can require any endpoint that returns customer data to check that the requester owns it. You can also manage policies with the Vercel CLI, using vercel security policy.

How findings are tracked

Each new finding is checked against ones that have already been reported, so the same issue isn’t flagged twice. Every finding is tied to the deployment where it first appeared and changes are followed from there. That means that when a vulnerable change from a pull request is merged into your production branch, the finding is flagged in production as well.

When a later review no longer detects the issue in an environment, the agent marks the finding as no longer detected there.

Acting on findings

Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared.

Findings are listed in the Vulnerability view in the Security dashboard, where you can ask Vercel Agent to validate and commit fixes. Findings are also available via CLI, so you can fix vulnerabilities with your own coding agent.

Each new finding generates an audit log event, which Enterprise teams can send to their SIEM through Audit Log Drains.

Here is a demo of sample findings in the dashboard:

Fixing vulnerabilities with Vercel Agent

When Vercel Agent can fix a finding, you will see the option to click Fix with Vercel Agent on the finding page in the dashboard. After you click, the agent confirms the vulnerability still exists, then makes the smallest change that fixes it and updates the tests.

Say a developer pushes a change to an invoice download endpoint, and the lookup doesn't check which organization the invoice belongs to. Within seconds, Security Review flags that any signed-in user could download another organization's invoice by changing its ID. Vercel Agent's fix scopes the lookup to the user's organization:

Fixing vulnerabilities with your own coding agent

You can point your coding agent or other systems at the Vercel CLI to pull and fix vulnerabilities:

Findings in the dashboard also give you the ability to copy details as Markdown or JSON, making it easy to paste them into an agent conversation.

Every code change needs security review

Frontier AI models are making vulnerabilities far easier to find and exploit. Last month, researchers turned two decade-old flaws in PHP core into working remote code execution exploits with relatively little effort.

At the same time, agents are writing more of the code teams ship, and each handles security review its own way, or in many cases, not at all.

With Vercel Security Review, you can scan every push on every project for vulnerabilities by default, using the security policies you set.

What's next

Security Review starts with code pushed to GitHub. Next, we're bringing it to deployments from the Vercel CLI and v0, and to repositories that don't deploy on Vercel. We're also working on suggested fixes you can apply directly from the pull request.

Get started

Vercel Security Review is available today in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

To get started, enable Security Review in Vercel Agent Settings. You can choose to run Security Review on all projects, or only the ones you choose. To learn more, read the Changelog entry and the Security Review documentation.

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate, with model tokens at the provider's rate and no markup, plus $0.25 per million tokens.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026. Fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the rate above.

title: Alignment with Reflect-Reasoning: Learning How To Follow Principles
description:
arXiv:2611.17398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The appropriate governing norms and principles for the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) often depend on cultural context and deployment application. However, most alignment techniques focus on training models to conform to human preferences or constitutional principles specified at training time and subsequently fixed. In practice, many deployers rely on system prompting to implement contextual norms and guardrails at inference time. Prior work has shown that post-generation reflective reasoning with critique and revision can improve conformance compared to simple system prompting, but such methods are limited to the reasoning abilities inherent in the trained model. We introduce Reflect-Reasoning, a training method that teaches models how to reason about alignment to principles, rather than simply which principles to follow. Across five models, Reflect-Reasoning consistently outperforms both system prompting and explicit prompting strategies for in-context reflective reasoning. These improvements extend and generalize to entirely out-of-distribution domains of medical and financial principles. We additionally demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning reduces the occurrence of rare but serious principle violations. Finally, we show that Reflect-Reasoning does not erode the safety engineering of a model and is robust against jailbreaking attempts using adversarial constitutions. Overall, our results demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning is a scalable method for training constitutional alignment as a generalizable reasoning capability, enabling models to adapt to novel principles and produce transparent reasoning traces without additional fine-tuning.

title: Direction or Magnitude? Learning Scalars over Task-Calibrated Directions
description:
arXiv:2611.17784v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR, which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning.

title: Rethinking Visual Reasoning in Text-to-Image Reward Modeling
description:
arXiv:2611.17585v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reward models are a core component of modern text-to-image systems, serving as the objective for inference-time selection and RL-based post-training. A key prerequisite is visual understanding: to judge prompt adherence and ground aesthetic preferences, a reward model must bind attributes, resolve relations, and count reliably. We find that widely-used reward models perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning evaluations. Even when starting from strong vision-language backbones, preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities, and continual-learning baselines fail to mitigate a steep tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy. We propose a data-centric intervention that injects visual reasoning supervision into preference learning by flipping the pairing axis. To complement conventional human preference data (paired images under a shared prompt), we convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs that share the same image but differ in prompt, and train on the mixture. This yields a Pareto improvement in both visual understanding and preference prediction. Across inference-time best-of-n selection and RL post-training, the resulting reward model improves text-to-image generation on challenging compositional prompts (GenEval) by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively, outperforming HPSv3 which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.

title: Every MCP, Skills & Rules Config Path Across 15 AI Coding Agents (2026 Verified Reference)
description:
If you switch between Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, and a handful of newer agent CLIs on the same machine, you have probably hit the same quiet tax: every client stores MCP servers, Skills, model providers, and global instructions in a different file path, serialization format, and top-level key.

Symlinking a single config file across hosts seems clever until one CLI rewrites its startup fields and wipes your JSON, or rejects a key because it expects TOML instead of JSON.

This reference maps the verified local disk paths, root keys, formats, and gotchas across 15 AI coding agents, organized around what can actually be shared safely on a Mac.

Why Dotfiles Symlinks Break Across AI Coding Harnesses

Four schema incompatibilities make blind symlinking brittle:

  1. Incompatible root keys: Claude Code and Cursor expect mcpServers in JSON, Codex reads [mcp_servers.*] in TOML, and OpenCode nests entries inside mcp (not mcpServers) inside opencode.json.
  2. Mixed file formats: Current agent CLIs span JSON, TOML, JSON5 (with comments), and YAML.
  3. Runtime rewrites: Several clients write dynamic auth state or last-used model caches into the same config directory or file at startup.
  4. Separate surfaces on the same brand: Cursor IDE vs. Cursor CLI, Codex Desktop vs. Codex CLI, Antigravity Desktop vs. agy CLI, and Oh My Pi (OMP) vs. Pi do not share identical capabilities even when they live on the same laptop.

Group A — 6 Core Coding Agent Hosts (Verified Disk Paths)

These 6 clients are primary multi-agent coding harnesses with full MCP, Skill, hook, and local session directory structures:

Host (Surface) MCP Config Path & Format Model / Provider / Hooks Skill & Global Instruction Paths Key Gotchas
Claude Code CLI ~/.claude.json (JSON · key mcpServers) ~/.claude/settings.json (Hooks & provider env) ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md Supports user + project CLAUDE.md rules alongside native lifecycle hooks.
Codex (Desktop / CLI) ~/.codex/config.toml (TOML · [mcp_servers.<name>]) ~/.codex/config.toml, ~/.codex/hooks.json ~/.codex/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, ~/.codex/AGENTS.md Repo-level AGENTS.override.md or custom CODEX_HOME supersedes global instructions.
Cursor (IDE / CLI) ~/.cursor/mcp.json (JSON · key mcpServers) ~/.cursor/hooks.json ~/.cursor/skills/<name>/SKILL.md UI "User Rules" live outside documented filesystem files; .mdc rules require workspace project scope.
Antigravity Desktop ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json (JSON · key mcpServers) ~/.gemini/config/hooks.json ~/.gemini/config/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, ~/.gemini/config/rules Model selection stays inside Desktop UI; external tools should not rewrite private Desktop auth caches.
OMP (Oh My Pi CLI) ~/.omp/agent/mcp.json (JSON · key mcpServers) ~/.omp/agent/models.yml, ~/.omp/agent/config.yml, ~/.omp/agent/hooks/pre/ ~/.omp/agent/commands/*.md, ~/.omp/agent/AGENTS.md Respects .yaml siblings; avoid mixed legacy settings.json/models.json; subagents skip root AGENTS.md.
OpenCode CLI ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json (JSON · key mcp) ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json, ~/.config/opencode/plugins/ ~/.config/opencode/skills, ~/.config/opencode/commands/*.md Single JSON houses both providers and mcp (not mcpServers).

Group B — 9 Extended Coding & Assistant Clients

Beyond those 6 primary harnesses, 9 additional clients use distinct schemas and stricter boundaries:

Client MCP Config Path & Format Provider Config Skills / Instruction Paths Explicit Constraints
Claude Desktop ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json (JSON · mcpServers) Managed inside Desktop app (or .mcpb bundles) No managed global prompt directory Local MCP JSON / .mcpb extensions only; no session relay.
Gemini CLI ~/.gemini/settings.json (JSON · mcpServers) No external provider rewrite No managed global Skill folder Local MCP entries and snapshots only.
Grok Build CLI ~/.grok/config.toml (TOML · mcp_servers) Provider blocks read natively ~/.grok/skills, ~/.grok/AGENTS.md Global default model override is unsupported.
Kimi Code CLI ~/.kimi-code/mcp.json (JSON · mcpServers) ~/.kimi-code/config.toml (TOML) ~/.kimi-code/skills, ~/.kimi-code/AGENTS.md Split JSON MCP + TOML provider files.
MiniMax Code ~/.minimax/mcp.json (JSON · mcpServers) ~/.minimax/config.yaml (YAML) ~/.minimax/skills, ~/.minimax/AGENTS.md JSON MCP + YAML provider files.
Pi CLI ~/.pi/agent/mcp.json (JSON · mcpServers) ~/.pi/agent/models.json, ~/.pi/agent/settings.json ~/.pi/agent/skills, ~/.pi/agent/AGENTS.md Strictly separate from OMP; avoid rewriting hand-authored JSON5 configs.
Hermes Agent ~/.hermes/config.yaml (YAML · mcp_servers) ~/.hermes/config.yaml (custom_providers) ~/.hermes/skills, ~/.hermes/SOUL.md Global instructions target SOUL.md instead of AGENTS.md.
OpenClaw No native MCP sync ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json (JSON5 preserving comments · models.providers) ~/.openclaw/skills, ~/.openclaw/AGENTS.md Comments must be preserved in JSON5; native MCP syncing is unsupported.
agy (Antigravity CLI) ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json (JSON · mcpServers) Process env (GEMINI_API_KEY, GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL) + ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json ~/.gemini/config/skills, ~/.gemini/config/AGENTS.md Credentials belong in env/private profile rather than plaintext copies.

Two Practical Architectures Depending on Your Setup

Before reaching for extra tooling, match the approach to your OS and team constraints:

  1. Cross-platform teams (Windows / Linux / Intel Mac): Keep shared conventions in Git-committed CLAUDE.md + AGENTS.md ($0). It works across every OS without running a local background service.
  2. Single-Mac Apple Silicon (macOS 14.0+ arm64) developers switching across harnesses locally: If you want format-aware translation with pre-write diff checks, automatic rollback snapshots, macOS Keychain secret isolation, and /contextcore full-transcript session relay across the 6 core hosts, you can layer on Senrelay (qingsongcui/ContextCore) ($0, MIT License, no account required; does not support Windows, Linux, or Intel Macs, and public Beta builds need a one-time xattr -cr /Applications/Senrelay.app after brew install --cask qingsongcui/tap/senrelay).

For the full machine-readable config matrix and safety boundaries, see the canonical reference at senrelay.com/hosts.html.

title: Activation Steering the Nan-Shan in Typhoon
description:
arXiv:2611.17768v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Typhoon is an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella, in which Captain MacWhirr steers the steamer Nan-Shan directly into and through a catastrophic storm. The novella is a study of what happens when the scale of a phenomenon exceeds the practical and conceptual frameworks available to comprehend it and of the paralysis that sometimes follows a demand for action in such overwhelming circumstances. We chose the text of Typhoon to reflect on human culture's current AI moment. We prompt a large language model, seeded with Conrad's original language, to feed endlessly on its own output, and explore when and how the text becomes increasingly alien and unwieldy as time progresses, including deviations from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long periods of incoherent rumination. We employ methods from activation steering, including a novel adaptive steering method we introduce, to control the rhythm of the narrative and the model's digressions over long stretches of generation. The simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability of this steering showcases the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI, and the reality of a system that remains outside our comprehension and control.

title: What size_of could not tell me about a protobuf optimization
description:
While investigating Temporal Rust SDK issue #1653, I measured an enum that occupied 624 bytes inline. Boxing every variant brought a mirror of it down to 16 bytes.

That was an attractive number. It was also far from enough evidence to call the change a performance improvement.

The investigation became draft PR #1781. It contains a descriptor-driven boxing experiment and a runnable allocation probe. As of November 16, 2026, it remains open and incomplete. Here is what the measurements actually establish.

The handwritten enum, UpdateMsg, carries three generated protobuf message types: Acceptance, Rejection, and Response. My initial measurements used Rust 1.95.0 on aarch64-apple-darwin:

Representation Inline bytes
Original enum mirror 624
Only Rejection boxed 352
All three variants boxed 16

These are size_of results for that compiler, target, and resolved dependencies. They are not stable Rust ABI promises.

The enum needs enough inline space for its largest variant. Boxing the 624-byte Rejection removes that large inline value, but leaves the 352-byte Response. Boxing every variant leaves pointers and the enum's discriminant.

The missing part of the 16-byte result is the pointee. With every variant boxed, an acceptance needs a 320-byte heap object, a rejection 624 bytes, and a response 352 bytes. Adding the 16-byte enum gives nominal live storage of 336, 640, or 368 bytes respectively, before allocator overhead and separately allocated contents.

A rejection can therefore occupy more nominal storage than the original 624-byte enum slot. The smaller slot may still matter in some contexts, but the allocation has not disappeared. Neither have the backing allocations of strings, vectors, and maps; size_of does not include their contents.

Next I investigated selecting boxes from protobuf descriptors instead of maintaining a field-name list. This is a different experiment from manually boxing enum variants.

An early selector considered large message-valued oneof arms. It shrank Outcome from 304 to 24 bytes but left the UpdateMsg mirror at 624. The large rejection contained ordinary singular message fields, so optimizing only oneof arms did not remove the controlling size.

The later experiment also considers ordinary fields when the enclosing message exceeds a budget. Its approximate model uses estimated field sizes, minimum estimated savings, and an enclosing-message budget. The thresholds are experimental choices, not tuned defaults or an exact Rust layout model.

In the full protos pipeline, that version reduced the unchanged UpdateMsg mirror from 624 to 328 inline bytes. That result must stay separate from the manual 624-to-352 and 624-to-16 comparisons: each changes a different representation.

The public investigation document records those distinctions and the reproduction commands.

To look beyond layout, the standalone probe generates baseline and selected types from the same real proto import closure. It checks wire equality for four populated branches and measures construction plus Any encoding separately from decoding.

In those samples, rejection and failed-response paths gained an allocation; acceptance and successful-response paths did not. The measured allocation belongs to a selected field inside the generated structure. It is not the same operation as allocating an entire 624-byte Rejection in the initial manual experiment.

Even those allocation counts do not tell me the production outcome. I do not have production branch frequencies, payload distributions, replay measurements, or peak-memory data. A synthetic frequency table can show sensitivity to assumptions; it cannot supply the missing workload.

There was another important correction to the original intuition: Core immediately serializes UpdateMsg. Its outbox contains encoded protocol messages with Any bytes. A smaller temporary enum does not establish that the resident queue becomes smaller. That would require measuring the representation the queue actually holds.

Compatibility also remains work. Boxing changes generated Rust field types, which changes construction and conversion code. Focused checks and sample round trips passed, but the recorded all-feature lint attempt still had 45 Core type/conversion errors. Full workspace, server integration, and cross-platform validation remain incomplete.

The probe README also distinguishes its generation settings from the full SDK pipeline. A passing standalone experiment cannot substitute for those unfinished checks.

I can report a smaller inline representation and sample-specific allocation costs. I cannot yet report a runtime win. The next decision is about which generated API changes are acceptable and which real workload to measure—not how prominently to display the 16-byte number.

title: Can Large Language Models Optimize Pretrained Neural Network Weights? A Multi-Phase Empirical Evaluation of Gradient-Free Editing in YOLO26 Object Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.17789v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Direct weight editing offers a gradient-free alternative to fine-tuning pretrained detectors, but its generalization and the value of large language model (LLM) guidance remain uncertain. We evaluate five experimental phases using YOLO26 models and MS COCO, comparing deterministic scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, CMA-ES, structured interventions, real local-LLM proposals, failure-aware guidance, and hybrid LLM-CMA-ES against a matched random-policy control. Optimization uses native Ultralytics mAP50-95 on 1,000 COCO Val2017 images; selected candidates are assessed on a disjoint, previously examined 1,500-image subset, with COCO API AP50-95 reported separately where available. Increasing the CMA-ES budget from 8 to 250 evaluations raised development gains from +0.11 to +0.28 percentage points, while selection changes remained negative (-0.03 to -0.12 points); the 250-evaluation result uses one seed. The hybrid LLM approach showed no statistically established advantage over random-policy guidance (p = 0.612, 0.369, and 0.694 at budgets 8, 25, and 50). Five-seed YOLO26m replication yielded a COCO API AP difference of +0.004 points (95% CI: -0.026 to +0.034). Of 225 archived LLM proposals, 53 satisfy the final strict schema; early tensor-level execution cannot be fully verified. Genuine LLM-mediated weight editing is feasible, but the tested approaches did not demonstrate consistent transfer beyond the development subset or a measurable LLM advantage.

title: Your Tests Blocked System.exit With a SecurityManager and Java 25 Will Not Let You Install One
description:
The command line tool
called System.exit
when its arguments were wrong.

Fine in production.

Fatal in a test.

One call
and the whole test run
just stopped.

Years ago somebody solved it.

A small SecurityManager,
installed in the tests,
that threw an exception
whenever code tried to exit.

The test caught the exception,
checked the exit code,
and carried on.

Plenty of teams did the same.

Libraries were written for it.

Plugin hosts did something similar,
sandboxing code they loaded.

You have probably got one of these
somewhere
and forgotten it.

The Security Manager
was deprecated for removal
in Java 17.

You saw the warning.

So did everyone.

In Java 24,
JEP 486
switched it off for good.

You cannot enable it
at startup.

You cannot install one
while the program runs.

System.setSecurityManager
now throws
UnsupportedOperationException.

Java 25 is the long term release
that most teams on 21
are moving to now.

So for many codebases
this is not a future warning.

It is the next upgrade,
failing in the test suite
on day one.

Usually in a helper class
nobody has opened in years.

The good news
is that the real fix
was always the better design.

Do not call System.exit
deep inside your code.

Return an exit code,
or throw a specific exception,
and let main
be the only place
that ends the process.

Then the tests
call the logic, not main,
and check the code it returned.

No trick needed.

If you load code
you do not trust,
the answer is no longer
inside the same JVM.

Run it in a separate process
or a container,
with the operating system
drawing the limits.

The JDK team's position
is that the Security Manager
was rarely used for that anyway,
and expensive to keep.

Before you upgrade,
search for it.

SecurityManager.

checkPermission.

checkExit.

The java.security.manager flag
in your build files.

Count the hits.

That is the size
of the work
hiding behind a deprecation warning
you stopped reading five years ago.

A warning that says
for removal
is a date,
not an opinion.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
description:
arXiv:2611.17515v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22.
  In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

title: Turning a living-room photo into 'security footage' with the browser canvas
description:
Some templates earn their keep in the pre-processing. Our latest one — a "Santa caught on camera" clip — started as a prompt experiment: ask a video model for 1998-CCTV-style footage of Santa mid-delivery in your living room, and it politely ignores the style instructions. Art direction does not survive prompting; it has to be baked into the input image.

The grade happens in the browser

The moment a photo is picked, we run it through a canvas pipeline before anything uploads:

  1. draw the photo and desaturate it to luminance-only,
  2. push the contrast up,
  3. lay down per-pixel noise for the grain,
  4. burn a soft vignette into the corners.

The graded JPEG — not the original — is what the video model receives. A side effect we like: the thumbnail in the picker is pixel-identical to the model's input, so there is no "why does my clip look like that" mystery later.

Two prompt lessons we kept

You cannot prompt your way to a style; you can prompt your way to a line of dialogue. Write the line as spoken text and the model voices it — we verified transcriptions of names like "Leo" and "Aaliyah" survive the round trip. Write it as a whispered stage direction and you get no voice at all.

Because the spoken line contains the child's name, the name gets validated before anything renders: letters, spaces, hyphens, apostrophes, commas, periods and ampersands, up to 30 characters and 4 words. An invalid name greys out the generate button — nobody spends a credit on a clip that cannot say "Merry Christmas, [name]!".

The result

One room photo in, a short grainy clip out: Santa in the frame, the line spoken aloud, the whole thing looking like footage from a tape that has been in the attic since the nineties. It lives next to our Santa caught on camera template, and the classic version — Santa on stage, rapping your message — is at the personalized Santa video page.

Everything audio in our templates is original (we never bundle copyrighted songs), there is a free 6-second preview per account, and a full video is $3.99 one time — no subscription.

— AI Rap Video team

title: I Built an AI App. The Hardest Problems Had Nothing to Do With AI.
description:
I started building Knovum because I wanted a better way to work with my personal knowledge.

I wanted one workspace where I could collect notes, PDFs, web pages, images, audio, videos, and code — then search across them and ask questions without constantly switching between different apps.

That idea eventually turned into a much larger engineering project.

Knovum is an open-source, local-first AI knowledge workspace built with Tauri 2, Rust, Vue 3, SQLite, and LanceDB.

GitHub: https://github.com/madebyzan/knovum

While building it, I ran into problems that had little to do with writing prompts or calling an LLM API. Desktop application environments, native permissions, long-running media processing, task recovery, and source citations all required more engineering than I initially expected.

Here are some things I learned along the way.

1. What is Knovum?

Knovum is designed to bring different kinds of knowledge into one workspace.

Its main interface is an infinite canvas where users can organize and work with different types of content, including:

  • Notes and web pages
  • PDFs and Office documents
  • Images
  • Audio and video
  • Code and other text-based content

The goal is not just to store files. I also wanted the content to be searchable and useful in AI-assisted workflows.

Some of the capabilities include:

  • Keyword and semantic search
  • RAG-based question answering
  • Source references for retrieved information
  • OCR and audio transcription
  • Audio and video processing
  • Integration with external agents through MCP and ACP

Knovum follows a local-first approach. The application and its knowledge data are designed to remain on the user's device. Some processing can run locally, but when a user chooses a cloud model, the relevant task context is sent to that model provider.

I think that distinction matters. Local-first does not automatically mean every AI operation runs offline.

2. The technology stack

The project uses a combination of desktop, frontend, and backend technologies.

Layer Technology
Desktop framework Tauri 2
Backend Rust
Frontend Vue 3
Structured storage SQLite
Vector database LanceDB
Canvas format JSON Canvas
Embeddings Qwen3 Embeddings

I chose Tauri because I wanted a desktop application without shipping a full browser runtime as part of the app.

Rust handles native-side functionality and system integration, while Vue provides the application interface.

SQLite is used for structured data, and LanceDB supports vector-based retrieval.

The stack looks relatively straightforward on paper. The interesting problems appeared when these parts had to work together in a real desktop environment.

3. A desktop app does not run like your terminal

One of the first unexpected problems appeared on macOS.

A development command worked perfectly in my terminal, but launching the application through Finder or the Dock caused it to fail.

The problem was the environment.

An interactive terminal session and a GUI-launched desktop application do not necessarily inherit the same environment variables or executable paths.

In my case, the application could not reliably locate Node.js and npx.

I initially treated this like a dependency problem, but the underlying issue was how the application environment was initialized.

The fix involved resolving the interactive login shell environment and locating the absolute path to npx, rather than assuming the GUI process would inherit the same PATH as my terminal.

I also improved the error handling so that a missing dependency would produce a more useful error instead of an obscure failure.

Related PR: https://github.com/madebyzan/knovum/pull/153

My takeaway: Test desktop applications through the actual launch paths users will use. Running successfully from a development terminal is not enough.

4. Tauri permissions and plugin registration need to stay consistent

Another issue involved object storage functionality.

Some storage-related tests could not work correctly because the required Tauri capabilities and plugin setup were incomplete.

There were multiple pieces involved:

  • Capability configuration
  • Permission declarations
  • Plugin registration
  • Build configuration

The storage plugin was also missing from the relevant build.rs setup.

The confusing part was that these settings lived in different places. A feature could appear to be implemented in the application code while still being unavailable because the native-side configuration was incomplete.

I fixed the capability configuration, registered the missing plugin, updated permissions, and added a consistency test to make this kind of configuration problem easier to catch.

Related PR: https://github.com/madebyzan/knovum/pull/163

My takeaway: In a desktop application, configuration is part of the implementation. It deserves the same attention as application code.

5. Long-running audio processing is a memory problem, not just a timeout problem

Audio processing was another area that required a rethink.

The original audio separation approach used Spleeter. The processing path generated a large amount of intermediate STFT data, which created significant memory pressure.

Simply increasing the timeout would not have solved the underlying issue.

I moved the separation workflow to HTDemucs and changed the processing strategy:

  • Split longer audio into chunks of roughly one minute.
  • Use approximately four seconds of overlap between adjacent chunks.
  • Apply crossfading when combining the processed segments.
  • Raise the maximum supported processing duration to six hours.
  • Explicitly reject inputs that exceed the configured limit.

The chunk overlap and crossfade help reduce discontinuities at segment boundaries.

This was a good reminder that long-running media workflows need to be designed around memory usage, processing boundaries, and failure handling — not just execution time.

Related PR: https://github.com/madebyzan/knovum/pull/162

6. AI tasks should not silently change models during recovery

There is another problem that is easy to overlook when building an AI application.

Imagine a user submits a task using Model A. The task fails or needs to be retried later.

Meanwhile, the user changes the application's default model to Model B.

Should the retry use Model A or Model B?

I think the answer should be Model A.

The model choice is part of the original task configuration. A retry should not silently change the behavior of a task just because the global default changed in the meantime.

I updated the task flow so that the model selection is frozen when the task is submitted.

That makes retries and recovery more predictable.

Commit: https://github.com/madebyzan/knovum/commit/68cc5eb5d2aef418a9d58320c5a3021264b2104f

My takeaway: Persist the configuration that actually matters to a task. Do not rely on mutable global defaults when recovering previous work.

7. RAG citations need to point to something users can verify

Building RAG functionality also made me think more carefully about citations.

A vector search result is not necessarily a useful citation.

For example, when retrieving information from a PDF, users should ideally be able to locate the relevant page.

For audio, a timestamp is much more useful than a generic reference to the audio file.

For notes, a title and paragraph-level reference provide a better way to verify the answer.

There is also a less obvious issue: source content can change.

Suppose a document is updated after an AI-generated answer has been stored. The old citation may no longer point to the same content.

I do not think an application should continue presenting that reference as though it were still valid.

A more trustworthy approach is to recognize when a source has changed and mark the old reference as invalid or detached.

For me, this is an important part of making RAG useful beyond a demo.

The answer matters, but so does the user's ability to check where it came from.

8. The API bill became a significant part of development

Building Knovum also involved substantial AI development costs.

The API usage alone reached approximately 6,000–7,000 USD.

In addition, I paid for several development subscriptions and services:

  • Codex membership: over RMB 1,000
  • Qoder membership: approximately RMB 700
  • Gemini subscription: approximately RMB 60
  • Qoder API usage: approximately RMB 100

There were other tools involved as well, but I am not including those costs here.

These figures are development expenses, not production operating costs or business revenue.

I also cannot give a reliable total token count. Usage was spread across different providers, accounts, subscriptions, and API billing systems, so combining everything into one accurate token number would be misleading.

The more interesting question for me is not how many tokens I used. It is what that spending helped me build, what I learned from it, and how much iteration was required to get the application working.

AI coding tools can accelerate implementation, but they do not remove the need to understand the system being built.

They can help write code. They cannot automatically decide whether a retry should preserve its original model, whether a media-processing pipeline will exhaust memory, or whether a citation still refers to the correct source.

Those decisions still require engineering judgment.

9. What I learned

Looking back, a few lessons stand out.

First, desktop applications have their own class of problems.

Environment variables, native permissions, plugin registration, packaging, and GUI launch behavior are not minor details. They are part of the product.

Second, long-running workflows need explicit resource boundaries.

For media processing, chunking, overlap handling, memory usage, and input limits are more important than simply raising timeouts.

Third, AI tasks need predictable state.

Model selection, task configuration, retries, and recovery should behave consistently. A global setting should not unexpectedly rewrite the meaning of an existing task.

Fourth, RAG needs verifiable sources.

A generated answer is much more useful when users can navigate to the supporting page, timestamp, or paragraph — and when the application can recognize outdated references.

Finally, AI tools do not replace engineering fundamentals.

They can make development faster, but reliability still comes from understanding the full system and testing how its components behave together.

10. The project is still evolving

Knovum is still under development. There are plenty of things I want to improve, and I do not consider the current implementation finished.

The source code is available on GitHub:

https://github.com/madebyzan/knovum

It is released under the MIT License.

I would especially appreciate feedback from people who have worked on:

  • Tauri applications with complex native integrations
  • Local-first data architectures
  • RAG systems with source-level citations
  • Long-running audio and video processing pipelines
  • AI task orchestration and recovery

I am interested in practical feedback, especially around architecture and reliability.

One question for other developers: When building an AI application, what has turned out to be harder than you expected — the AI integration itself, or everything around it?

title: Learning nonlinear interactions and cross-feature couplings with product-unit residual networks
description:
arXiv:2611.18074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding nonlinear feature interactions is crucial in science and engineering, yet standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) often capture such interactions only implicitly, leading to entangled representations that can impair robustness and interpretability. We investigate complex-valued product-unit residual networks (CV-PURe) that integrate multiplicative product units with residual connections to explicitly model cross-feature couplings while stabilizing optimization. We conduct a systematic evaluation on an interaction-driven synthetic benchmark and real-world datasets and evaluate prediction together with input-level interaction recovery under a reproducible protocol. Across five data splits and five training seeds, CV-PURe achieves the lowest mean RMSE on four of six scientific benchmarks, reducing Friedman error by 53.9% relative to MLP. Its Friedman interaction maps assign 60.7% of total strength to the known interacting pair, compared with 31.0% for MLP. On a synthetic task containing third- and fourth-order products and 20 distractors, CV-PURe reduces RMSE from 0.1376 to 0.0797 relative to a complex-valued MLP and recovers all nine true pairwise projections in every training/sampling repetition. Bike Sharing experiments connect improved prediction to the contribution of temporal, calendar, and seasonal context through paired ablations of both PURe variants. Parkinsons Telemonitoring extends the context analysis to repeated measurements. Noise and learning-curve evaluations demonstrate sustained predictive gains under perturbed inputs and limited supervision, while inference measurements quantify computational cost. This article extends our ICCS 2026 paper, Modeling Nonlinear Feature Interactions with Product-Unit Residual Networks (doi:10.1007/978-3-032-29921-5_6).

title: Learning Word-Level Explanations of Text Reuse in Latin Literature with Little Annotation
description:
arXiv:2611.18319v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detecting an intertextual reference is only the first step; philologists also need to know how a later author reworked the source. We explain a reuse pair word by word: each word of the reusing passage is first aligned to its source word, then labeled with the operation that transformed it, such as a copy, a change of inflection, or a substitution. Such word-level operations are expensive to annotate, and only a few corpora annotated at this level exist for text reuse in Latin literature. We describe a procedure that needs only a limited number of annotations: synthetic pairs, built by applying known operations to Latin text, train a first model, and active learning chooses the pairs an annotator corrects. Among several architectures, a model that links and labels together performs best: a pointer network that, for every reuse word, chooses a source word and names the operation in the same step. We show that with active learning, 200 pairs chosen by uncertainty are enough for the model to match one trained on every annotated pair of the 1,490 references of the Loci Similes benchmark. We release our code, word-level predictions for all references, and an interactive demo.

title: My Capital One Interview experience. - Full-stack staff engineer.
description:
My experience with Capital One started with a recruiter call (They found me through LinkedIn - Canada based). The process took about four weeks. The first step was a ~10-minute screening with the recruiter, then a CodeSignal assignment with 4 questions:

  1. neighborSum - Pass: +300 points
    • https://codesignal.com/blog/example-codesignal-questions/ (Question 1: Array Manipulation)
  2. alternatingSort - Pass: +300 points
    • https://leetcode.com/discuss/post/2083038/codesignal-by-user0536yw-yyht/

  4. 1D Obstacle Placement & Collision Check - completed with the brute-force: +100 points
    • https://leetcode.com/problems/block-placement-queries/description/

Total points: 700 points. Enough to pass to the second round.

The second round was a video call system design interview. The question was, "Design a URL shortener." The interviewer was very professional and gave me the non-functional requirements up front:
URL shortening system

New system, internal only for internal employees
- Low volume of new URL creation 
- 2000 new URLs within the first 2 days   
- 500 new URLs per day steady state
- 5000 redirects per day, steady from day one
- North America only for MVP implementation
- 50,000 internal users

The interviewer made it clear that they wanted me to dive deep into how the short URL would be created, stored, and retrieved. He also asked me to explain my choice of database (SQL vs. NoSQL).

I didn't pass this interview because I fumbled the short URL creation details: e.g., sequential ID using Redis and then Base 10 ID to Base62. Or a truncated Hash function with collision checking. Plus, I couldn't explain the differences between SQL and NoSQL other than the classic "SQL is for structured data and strong consistency, and NoSQL is for unstructured data and massive scale"

After the interview, I decided to dive deeper into URL shorteners, and I wrote this article with lessons I read.
