title: Projeto de Banco de Dados - Modelo Lógico
description:
O modelo de dados lógicos representa a estrutura detalhada das informações de um sistema, traduzindo as regras de negócio para um formato próximo ao que será implementado no banco de dados. Enquanto o modelo conceitual foca nas entidades e relacionamentos de alto nível, o modelo lógico define como esses dados serão organizados em tabelas (modelo lógico relacional com tabelas, colunas, chaves e restrições de integridade), como documentos (modelo lógico documental), como grafos, como objetos, entre outros. Nesse momento há a definição do tipo do Sistema Gerenciador de Banco de Dados (SGBD) a ser utilizado (relacional, orientado a objetos, entre outros), mas sem depender ainda de um software específico.

A evolução dos modelos de dados lógicos iniciou-se na década de 1960 com o modelo hierárquico da IBM, estruturado em formato de árvore para modelar relações de cardinalidade 1:N. Devido à sua limitação em representar relacionamentos complexos (M:N) sem gerar redundância, surgiu em 1969 o modelo em rede, que permitiu que um nó tivesse múltiplos pais.

Essa lógica transformou-se com a introdução do modelo relacional por Edgar F. Codd, em 1970. Fundamentado na teoria dos conjuntos e na lógica matemática, esse modelo substituiu a navegação procedural por consultas declarativas — viabilizadas pela linguagem SQL — e organizou as informações em tabelas, estabelecendo-se como o padrão dominante na indústria.

Posteriormente, novas exigências tecnológicas impulsionaram a era dos modelos pós-relacionais. Na década de 1980, os bancos orientados a objeto buscaram reduzir o atrito entre o código e o armazenamento; já no final dos anos 2000, o avanço do Big Data e da internet consolidou o movimento NoSQL. Este último diversificou-se em paradigmas flexíveis e especializados, como chave-valor, documentos, colunas e grafos, adaptando-se a volumes massivos de dados e novas demandas de escala.

O modelo chave-valor é a estrutura mais simples entre os bancos NoSQL (semelhante a uma tabela hash), na qual se associa uma chave única a um valor opaco que o banco não interpreta. Focado em baixa latência e alta taxa de transferência, elimina gargalos de disco relacionais e é ideal para sessões, carrinhos de compras e cache (ex.: Redis, Amazon DynamoDB). O modelo orientado a documentos armazena dados em estruturas autodescritivas flexíveis (JSON, BSON, XML) sem esquema prefixado. Resolve a rigidez relacional e a impedância objeto-relacional ao manter os dados de uma entidade unidos, eliminando JOINs custosos e agilizando o desenvolvimento (ex.: MongoDB, Couchbase).

No que tange ao modelo colunar, este agrupa colunas por famílias e as armazena juntas em disco, permitindo estruturas esparsas e altamente distribuídas. Focado em escalabilidade horizontal para Big Data, resolve desafios de armazenamento e consulta de volumes massivos de dados, como em séries temporais e IoT (ex.: Apache Cassandra, HBase). Já o modelo orientado a grafos representa dados por nós (entidades) e arestas (relacionamentos) conectados por ponteiros físicos diretos. Resolve a lentidão em relacionamentos profundos e complexos que afeta bancos relacionais (JOINs recursivos), sendo ideal para redes sociais e sistemas de recomendação (ex.: Neo4j, Amazon Neptune).

Modelo de Dados Relacional

A base estrutural do modelo relacional é a relação, que na prática corresponde a uma tabela bidimensional composta por linhas e colunas. Cada linha, tecnicamente chamada de tupla, representa um registro único ou uma instância específica daquela entidade, como os dados de um único cliente. Já cada coluna, chamada atributo, representa uma característica ou propriedade que descreve a entidade, como nome, CPF ou data de nascimento desse cliente.

As restrições em um banco de dados relacional dividem-se em escopos distintos. As restrições implícitas são regras inerentes "de fábrica" do modelo, enquanto as explícitas (ou de esquema) exigem declaração expressa via código durante o projeto, a exemplo dos tipos de dados. Já as restrições semânticas ou de aplicação tratam de regras de negócios complexas que exigem implementação externa por código, triggers ou procedimentos armazenados. Quanto à dimensão temporal, elas classificam-se em restrições de estado — que validam os dados em um instante isolado — e de transição, que avaliam a validade da mudança entre estados, sendo o SGBD o responsável por garantir tais verificações de integridade.

O modelo relacional também impõe restrições implícitas fundamentais para sua consistência estrutural. Conceitualmente, as tuplas de uma relação não possuem ordem estrita, embora o armazenamento físico seja sequencial, e os atributos seguem uma ordenação própria, a menos que sejam identificados explicitamente por seus nomes. Além disso, o modelo exige a atomicidade de cada valor, vedando listas ou estruturas complexas; padroniza o uso de NULL para representar dados desconhecidos ou inexistentes; assegura a unicidade pela proibição de tuplas duplicadas; e estrutura formalmente fatos reais sobre entidades e relacionamentos.

Complementando essas regras estruturais, as restrições explícitas de domínio determinam que cada atributo pertença a um conjunto pré-definido de valores elementares permitidos, como números inteiros, textos ou datas. Essa integridade de domínio opera diretamente em conjunto com a atomicidade para impedir a inserção de dados inválidos ou sem sentido no esquema do banco de dados.

Para que os atributos funcionem corretamente e mantenham a consistência das informações, cada coluna recebe o domínio, que define o conjunto de valores permitidos e o tipo de dado lógico associado. Os tipos lógicos mais comuns dividem-se em categorias fundamentais, como os tipos numéricos (inteiros para contagens e decimais para valores monetários), os tipos alfanuméricos ou texto (cadeia de caracteres de tamanho fixo ou variável para nomes e descrições), os tipos temporais (datas, horas e carimbos de tempo para registros históricos) e os tipos booleanos (valores lógicos que aceitam apenas verdadeiro ou falso).

Além dos tipos básicos de armazenamento, a modelagem lógica utiliza chaves para identificar registros e conectar diferentes atributos que identifica de maneira exclusiva cada tupla dentro de uma tabela, não podendo conter valores nulos ou repetidos. Por sua vez, a Chave Estrangeira (FK) é um atributo que referencia a chave primária de outra tabela, criando o vínculo relacional entre os dados e garantindo que não existam registros órfãos no sistema.

As restrições de chave iniciam-se com a superchave, um conjunto de atributos que garante a unicidade de cada tupla em uma relação. Quando essa superchave é mínima — ou seja, nenhum atributo pode ser removido sem que se perca a unicidade —, ela constitui uma chave, que pode ser formada por um único atributo ou ser composta por múltiplos. O conjunto de chaves válidas de uma tabela forma as chaves candidatas, dentre as quais uma é selecionada para exercer o papel de identificadora oficial.

A chave candidata escolhida é promovida a chave primária, cujos atributos aparecem sublinhados no esquema e são submetidos à integridade de entidade, restrição que proíbe valores duplicados e nulos (NOT NULL). Ela pode ser uma chave natural (derivada de atributos reais como CPF ou CNPJ, sujeita a alterações estruturais externas) ou uma chave substituta (surrogate key), gerada artificialmente (como um id) para assegurar controle interno estável. As demais chaves candidatas tornam-se chaves alternativas (ou únicas), que também garantem unicidade, mas diferem da primária por admitirem valores nulos.

Para conectar diferentes tabelas, emprega-se a chave estrangeira na relação filha, fazendo referência à chave de uma relação pai. Esse mecanismo é regulado pela integridade referencial, restrição que exige que o valor da chave estrangeira corresponda estritamente a um registro existente na tabela pai ou seja nulo, assegurando a consistência das relações por meio de comandos SQL como PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE e FOREIGN KEY.

Por fim, a definição dos dados lógicos envolve a aplicação de restrições de integridade e processos de normalização para evitar redundância e anomalias. Regras como a obrigatoriedade de preenchimento (Not Null), a unicidade de valores (Unique) e a validação de condições específicas (Check) asseguram que o dado inserido seja sempre válido. Dessa forma, o modelo lógico atua como uma planta baixa, garantindo que a transição futura para o modelo físico ocorra com eficiência, segurança e sem perda de sentido semântico.

Mapeamento do Modelo ER para o Modelo Relacional

O mapeamento do Modelo Entidade-Relacionamento (ER) para o Modelo Relacional é a etapa do projeto de banco de dados responsável por traduzir um diagrama conceitual (como o DER) em uma estrutura lógica composta por tabelas, colunas e chaves. Enquanto o modelo conceitual foca em representar as regras de negócio de forma abstrata e visual, o modelo lógico prepara esses dados para serem implementados em um SGBD, nesse caso, relacional, garantindo integridade e evitando redundâncias. Como regra geral, cada entidade original vira uma tabela e seus atributos viram colunas, enquanto a tradução dos relacionamentos varia conforme a razão de cardinalidade.

A primeira fase desse processo concentra-se na conversão das entidades fortes, que são aquelas que possuem existência própria e uma chave primária bem definida. Cada entidade forte do diagrama torna-se uma nova tabela no modelo relacional, onde seus atributos simples são convertidos diretamente em colunas. O atributo identificador da entidade passa a ser a Chave Primária (PK) dessa tabela. Caso existam atributos compostos, como um endereço dividido em rua e cidade, eles são desmembrados em colunas individuais. Já os atributos derivados, como a idade calculada a partir da data de nascimento, costumam ser descartados nessa fase para economizar armazenamento.

Quando o modelo apresenta entidades fracas, o mapeamento exige um cuidado adicional, pois elas dependem de uma entidade proprietária para existir. A entidade fraca também é transformada em uma tabela própria, recebendo todas as suas colunas comuns. No entanto, ela precisa herdar a chave primária da entidade forte à qual está vinculada, incorporando-a como uma Chave Estrangeira (FK). A chave primária da tabela resultante será, portanto, uma chave composta formada pela união dessa chave estrangeira importada com o atributo discriminador (chave parcial) da própria entidade fraca.

O tratamento dos atributos multivalorados, que podem armazenar múltiplos valores para um mesmo registro (como vários telefones de um cliente), exige a criação de uma tabela separada para manter a atomicidade exigida pela Primeira Forma Normal. Essa nova tabela conterá uma coluna para armazenar o valor do atributo em si e uma chave estrangeira que aponta para a tabela da entidade original. A chave primária dessa estrutura auxiliar será a combinação de ambas as colunas, permitindo que um mesmo cliente tenha diversas linhas associadas sem repetir seus dados cadastrais principais.

A tradução dos relacionamentos binários varia diretamente conforme a cardinalidade estabelecida entre as entidades. Nos relacionamentos de um para um (1:1), a abordagem mais comum consiste em escolher uma das tabelas para receber a chave primária da outra como chave estrangeira, dando preferência ao lado que possui participação total para evitar valores nulos. Caso o relacionamento possua atributos próprios, eles acompanham essa chave estrangeira na tabela escolhida. Alternativamente, pode-se usar a relação mesclada (unindo as entidades em uma única tabela e eliminando chaves artificiais desnecessárias) ou, de forma menos encorajada, criar uma tabela intermediária de referência cruzada.

Nos relacionamentos de um para muitos (1:N), a regra é rígida e não permite escolhas arbitrárias. A tabela que representa o lado "muitos" (N) deve obrigatoriamente receber a chave primária da tabela do lado "um" (1) como uma chave estrangeira. Esse mecanismo cria o vínculo relacional entre os registros, permitindo que vários itens filhos apontem para um único registro pai, levando consigo eventuais atributos que pertençam ao relacionamento. Como alternativa a esse método padrão, também é possível empregar uma tabela intermediária para representar a associação.

Por fim, os relacionamentos de muitos para muitos (N:M) não podem ser representados apenas com chaves estrangeiras nas tabelas existentes, pois isso violaria as regras estruturais dos bancos relacionais. Para resolver essa cardinalidade, cria-se uma terceira tabela, chamada de tabela associativa ou de junção. Essa nova estrutura recebe como chaves estrangeiras as chaves primárias de ambas as tabelas envolvidas, e a união dessas duas chaves forma a sua chave primária composta, além de abrigar quaisquer atributos descritivos do próprio relacionamento. Caso existam múltiplos registros para a mesma combinação (como a mesma disciplina lecionada em semestres diferentes), torna-se necessária a adoção de uma chave substituta (surrogate key).

Visões (Views)

Uma visão (view) é uma tabela virtual ou derivada que não armazena dados fisicamente em disco. Ela é computada dinamicamente a cada requisição a partir de tabelas base, o que garante que seus registros reflitam sempre o estado atual do banco, sem risco de defasagem, sendo estruturada por meio de consultas SQL (SELECT).

O uso de visões atua como uma camada intermediária estratégica que oferece múltiplos benefícios práticos: garante segurança e controle de acesso ao ocultar dados sensíveis, simplifica consultas complexas ao encapsular junções, realiza agregação de dados, abstrai a estrutura real do banco e otimiza o armazenamento, pois guarda apenas a definição textual da consulta em vez de duplicar informações.

Em contraponto às visões dinâmicas, as visões materializadas executam a consulta previamente e armazenam o resultado como uma tabela concreta em disco. Embora incorporem uma desvantagem de desatualização — exigindo sincronizações periódicas e agindo essencialmente como um cache —, elas eliminam a necessidade de recomputação a cada acesso, proporcionando ganho expressivo de desempenho em consultas pesadas e frequentes típicas de ambientes de data warehouse.

As 12 regras de Codd

Regra Descrição
Regra 0: A Regra Fundamental Esta regra estabelece que qualquer sistema que se diga relacional deve gerenciar seus bancos de dados exclusivamente por meio de suas capacidades relacionais. Isso significa que o software não pode depender de recursos externos ou de baixo nível para manipular informações, garantindo que toda a operação ocorra dentro do modelo lógico de tabelas e relações.
Regra 1: A Regra da Informação Toda e qualquer informação em um banco de dados relacional deve ser representada de uma única maneira lógica, ou seja, como valores explícitos dentro de células de tabelas. Não devem existir ponteiros ocultos ou conexões invisíveis entre registros, pois até mesmo os nomes das tabelas e colunas precisam estar organizados em formato tabular.
Regra 2: A Regra do Acesso Garantido Cada dado individual armazenado no banco deve ter seu acesso logicamente garantido por meio de uma combinação específica de três elementos: o nome da tabela, o valor da chave primária e o nome da coluna. Dessa forma, o sistema nunca depende da posição física em que o dado foi gravado no disco rígido para encontrá-lo.
Regra 3: Tratamento Sistemático de Valores Nulos O sistema deve suportar valores nulos (NULL) para representar a ausência de informação ou dados desconhecidos de maneira uniforme e independente do tipo de dado. O valor nulo não pode ser confundido com o número zero ou com um espaço em branco, pois ele indica estritamente que aquela informação não existe ou ainda não foi preenchida.
Regra 4: Catálogo Online Dinâmico Baseado no Modelo Relacional A descrição da estrutura do próprio banco de dados, conhecida como metadados ou dicionário de dados, deve ser armazenada da mesma forma que os dados comuns do usuário. Isso permite que os administradores consultem a estrutura das tabelas, colunas e permissões utilizando exatamente a mesma linguagem de consulta aplicada aos dados normais.
Regra 5: A Regra da Sublinguagem de Dados Abrangente Um sistema relacional pode suportar várias linguagens de programação, mas deve oferecer pelo menos uma linguagem completa com sintaxe bem definida. Essa linguagem, como o SQL, precisa ser capaz de realizar todas as tarefas essenciais, incluindo definição de dados, manipulação de registros, controle de integridade, gerenciamento de transações e autorização de acesso.
Regra 6: A Regra da Atualização de Visões Todas as visões (Views) que são teoricamente atualizáveis também devem ser passíveis de atualização diretamente pelo sistema. Uma visão funciona como uma tabela virtual criada a partir de uma consulta, e o SGBD precisa ser inteligente o suficiente para traduzir alterações feitas nessa tabela virtual para as tabelas físicas reais que a originaram.
Regra 7: Inserção, Atualização e Exclusão de Alto Nível A capacidade de lidar com uma relação básica ou derivada como um único operando não se aplica apenas à recuperação de dados, mas também à inserção, alteração e exclusão. Isso significa que o sistema deve permitir modificar múltiplos registros de uma só vez com um único comando, sem obrigar o usuário a processar linha por linha manualmente.
Regra 8: Independência Física de Dados Os programas de aplicação e as atividades nos terminais devem permanecer logicamente inalterados sempre que houver mudanças na forma como os dados são armazenados fisicamente. Se o administrador decidir trocar o disco rígido, mudar o método de indexação ou compactar arquivos, os softwares que consomem o banco continuam funcionando sem precisar de nenhuma alteração no código.
Regra 9: Independência Lógica de Dados Os programas de aplicação não devem sofrer impactos quando ocorrerem alterações lógicas nas tabelas que preservam a informação original. Por exemplo, se uma tabela grande for dividida em duas tabelas menores por motivos de desempenho, as aplicações antigas devem continuar operando normalmente por meio de visões que reconstroem a estrutura anterior.
Regra 10: Independência de Integridade As restrições de integridade específicas de um banco de dados devem ser definidas na sublinguagem relacional e armazenadas no catálogo, e não escondidas dentro do código dos programas de aplicação. Regras como chaves primárias, chaves estrangeiras e validações de valores ficam protegidas dentro do próprio banco, impedindo que qualquer software externo insira dados inválidos.
Regra 11: Independência de Distribuição O usuário final e as aplicações não devem perceber se os dados estão armazenados em um único computador local ou espalhados por vários servidores em diferentes lugares do mundo. O sistema de gerenciamento deve ser capaz de distribuir, consultar e unir essas informações de forma totalmente transparente, mantendo a mesma lógica de operação.
Regra 12: A Regra da Não-Subversão Se o sistema possuir uma linguagem de baixo nível que permita acessar um registro por vez, essa ferramenta nunca poderá ser usada para contornar ou ignorar as regras de integridade e segurança definidas na linguagem relacional de alto nível. Isso garante que não existam "portas dos fundos" capazes de corromper a consistência do banco de dados.

title: Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? Drift, Diagnosis and Auditable Intervention on One Shipped Financial Research Agent
description:
arXiv:2611.17939v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can you trust a finance agent you did not build? We take the reference agent shipped with the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark v2, leave it untuned, and ask four questions a leaderboard score does not answer. Is the score stable? Seven identical runs on 18 questions pass between 105 and 123 of 149 rubric criteria, and the bill varies by up to 17%. When the agent fails, who owns the fix? We classify 20 failed trajectories, from three runs of nine held-out questions, by the layer whose owner would remedy them, under a taxonomy frozen in advance: 13 belong to the agent's instructions, 3 to its tools, 4 to the model, none to its data. Can that diagnosis be trusted? Four blind readers from three model families, given only the traces, name the same fault as our LLM analyzer in 94% of cases, the rate at which they agree with one another (93%). Can a change be trusted? An optimization loop reads the traces, makes one targeted change per round and keeps it only if it clears a fixed threshold. Under a cost objective its final configuration costs 0.34x the baseline on the held-out questions (95% CI [0.22, 0.58]) at accuracy within noise. Under an accuracy objective it gains 14 points on the development questions and 1.5 on the held-out ones (CI [-5.3, +7.2]). Judged against the measured run-to-run noise, under a rule written before the test was opened, the first is a real saving and the second is not. This is a case study of one agent and nine test questions, not a general result.

title: Data Cleaning for messy dates dd-mm-yyyy
description:
import pandas as pd

Sample messy dataset

df = pd.DataFrame({
'raw_date': [
'2026-11-14', # ISO format
'14/11/2026', # Slash format
'14th Nov 2026', # Ordinal suffix
'Nov 14, 2026', # Month name
'46340', # Excel serial number (14-11-2026)
'2026.11.14', # Dot separator
'invalid_entry', # Unparseable text
]
})

1. Strip whitespace and remove ordinal suffixes (st, nd, rd, th)

cleaned_str = (
df['raw_date']
.astype(str)
.str.strip()
.str.replace(r'(\d+)(st|nd|rd|th)', r'\1', regex=True)
)

2. Identify 5-digit Excel serial numbers

is_excel = cleaned_str.str.fullmatch(r'\d{5}')

3. Parse standard date strings (dayfirst=True ensures DD/MM/YYYY priority)

parsed_dates = pd.to_datetime(
cleaned_str.where(~is_excel),
format='mixed',
dayfirst=True,
errors='coerce',
)

4. Parse Excel serial numbers and combine them

excel_dates = pd.to_datetime(
pd.to_numeric(cleaned_str.where(is_excel)),
unit='D',
origin='1899-12-30',
)
df['datetime_obj'] = parsed_dates.fillna(excel_dates)

5. Format into 'dd-mm-yyyy' string layout

df['dd_mm_yyyy'] = df['datetime_obj'].dt.strftime('%d-%m-%Y')

print(df[['raw_date', 'dd_mm_yyyy']])

title: LLM Batch API vs Real-Time Calls: When the Batch Discount Is Worth the Wait
description:
Use a batch API when no human is waiting on the result and the job can tolerate hours of latency: backfills, nightly classification, evals, embeddings-style bulk enrichment. Stay on real-time calls for anything interactive or anything where a retry loop needs an answer in seconds. The discount is real, but it only pays off if you also build the bookkeeping that batch jobs demand.

As of late 2026, the major providers (Anthropic's Message Batches, OpenAI's Batch API) advertise a meaningful discount on batched requests in exchange for asynchronous completion, typically within a 24-hour window. Check each provider's current pricing page before you do math with a specific percentage; I'm deliberately not quoting one.

What do you actually give up with a batch API?

Three things, and the discount is only the headline for one of them.

Latency. Results arrive "within a window," not in seconds. Many batches finish much faster than the ceiling, but you can't design around that.

Interactivity. There's no streaming and no mid-job feedback. A prompt bug that would have shown up on request three in a real-time loop shows up after the whole batch returns.

Partial failure semantics. A batch is not all-or-nothing. Each request succeeds, errors, or expires independently, so you need a reconciliation step that real-time scripts get for free from an exception.

The takeaway: a batch discount is a trade of money for latency and operational complexity, and you only win if the second two are cheap for you.

When is the batch discount worth it?

Workload Human waiting? Batch fits? Why
Chat / copilot / agent loop Yes No Latency is the product
Nightly ticket classification No Yes Deadline is "by morning"
Re-scoring 200k old records after a prompt change No Yes One-off bulk, easy to resume
LLM-as-judge eval over a golden set No Yes Results needed once per CI/nightly run
Per-request moderation on user input Yes No Blocks the user action
Summarizing a document on upload Usually Mostly no User expects it in seconds

A rule I use: if the job's deadline is measured in hours and its volume is large enough that the bill shows up as a line item, batch it. If either condition fails, the engineering time to build reconciliation can exceed the savings. At a few thousand requests a month on a small model, you are saving a rounding error and adding a state machine.

The takeaway: batch pays off on large, deadline-in-hours workloads, and costs more in engineering than it saves on small ones.

How do you submit and collect a batch in Python?

Here is the shape using Anthropic's Python SDK (as of late 2026; the method names are stable but check the SDK docs if you're on a much newer version). The part that matters is custom_id: results are not guaranteed to come back in submission order, so you key everything by an ID you control.

import time
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
MODEL = "claude-haiku-5-5"  # pick the cheapest model that passes your eval

tickets = {
    "t-1001": "App crashes when I upload a PNG over 10MB.",
    "t-1002": "How do I change the billing email?",
}

requests = [
    {
        "custom_id": tid,  # your stable key, <=64 chars
        "params": {
            "model": MODEL,
            "max_tokens": 50,
            "messages": [{
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Classify as bug, billing, or other. One word.\n\n{text}",
            }],
        },
    }
    for tid, text in tickets.items()
]

batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=requests)
print("submitted", batch.id)

# Poll with a generous interval; batches are not latency-sensitive.
while True:
    batch = client.messages.batches.retrieve(batch.id)
    if batch.processing_status == "ended":
        break
    time.sleep(60)

results, failed = {}, []
for item in client.messages.batches.results(batch.id):
    if item.result.type == "succeeded":
        results[item.custom_id] = item.result.message.content[0].text.strip()
    else:  # errored, canceled, or expired
        failed.append((item.custom_id, item.result.type))

print(results)
print("needs retry:", failed)

In production, persist batch.id and your custom_id list to a database before you start polling. If your process dies at hour six, you want to resume by retrieving the existing batch, not by paying for it twice.

The takeaway: key every batched request by your own custom_id and persist the batch ID, or a crash turns a discount into a double bill.

What are the hidden costs of batching?

Retry accounting. Requests that come back errored or expired need a second pass. Re-submit only those IDs as a new, smaller batch (or fall back to real-time for the stragglers if the deadline is close). What tripped me up the first time was resubmitting the full set because my reconciliation only compared counts, not IDs.

Slower prompt iteration. I now run any new prompt against 20 to 50 real-time calls first, and only batch once the output format is stable. Debugging a malformed-output bug across 100k batched requests is an expensive way to find a missing instruction. If structured output is part of the job, validate against a schema on the way out; the same validate-and-retry discipline applies, just delayed.

Caching interactions. Batch discounts and prompt-caching discounts are separate mechanisms, and whether they stack, and how reliably cache hits occur inside a batch, depends on the provider and changes over time. Check the current docs before assuming both apply; don't build a cost model on the assumption that they multiply.

Rate limits and quotas. Batches typically have their own queue and size limits (requests per batch, total size). Large backfills need chunking, which is one more thing to write.

The takeaway: the real cost of a batch pipeline is the reconciliation and chunking code around it, and you should price that before you chase the discount.

Real-time with a queue vs batch API: which is cheaper to run?

A middle option is to keep real-time calls but run them from a background worker with a concurrency cap. You pay full price, but you get fast partial results, easy retries, and no new state machine. For jobs under a few thousand requests, or where the deadline is tight, this is usually the right call. If you want the discount without writing the polling and reconciliation yourself, the batch endpoints in Anthropic's Message Batches API or OpenAI's Batch API are the managed route, and both return per-request results keyed by an ID you supply. The drawback in both cases is the same: you lose streaming and any guarantee on completion time inside the window.

The takeaway: below a few thousand requests or under a tight deadline, a capped background worker on real-time calls beats batching on total cost of ownership.

FAQ

Is the OpenAI or Anthropic batch API cheaper than normal API calls?
Both providers advertise discounted per-token pricing for batch requests compared with real-time requests, in exchange for asynchronous completion. Check each provider's current pricing page for the exact discount, since it can change.

Do batch API results come back in the same order I sent them?
No. Match results to inputs using the custom_id you supplied on each request, never by position.

What happens if some requests in a batch fail?
The batch still completes, and each request is reported individually as succeeded, errored, canceled, or expired. Collect the failed IDs and resubmit only those.

Bottom line

If you have a large, non-interactive workload with a deadline measured in hours, use a batch API and invest in custom_id bookkeeping and a resubmit path for failures. If you're building anything a user is waiting on, or running a few thousand requests a month, stay real-time and cap concurrency in a worker. Test prompts in real-time first either way; batch is for running a prompt you already trust.

title: Why Figma’s Bezier Curves Feel Fake (And How an Indian Team Fixed It With Physics)
description:
Why Figma’s Bezier Curves Feel Fake (And How an Indian Team Fixed It With Physics)

Have you ever wondered why micro-interactions in native iOS or macOS apps feel organic, while Figma Smart Animate prototypes feel stiff and artificial?

The reason is simple: Figma animations are locked into pre-computed time-based bezier curves.

When you define an easing curve like cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1), the transition duration is fixed. If the user drags a sheet 50 pixels or flings it 900 pixels, it takes the exact same 300 milliseconds to complete.

Real World Physics Don't Have Timers

In the physical world, when you push a heavy door, its motion is governed by:

  • Mass ($m$)
  • Spring tension ($k$)
  • Friction / Viscous damping ($c$)

If you push it harder, it moves faster. If you interrupt it mid-swing, its velocity doesn't reset to zero.

How ExodeUI Revolutionizes Motion

The engineering team at ExodeUI in Bangalore replaced time-based bezier curves with continuous harmonic simulation.

Figma Easing:   [Start] ──(Fixed 300ms curve)──► [End] (Interrupt = Glitch)
ExodeUI Motion: [Force In] ──(Continuous Dynamics)──► [Equilibrium] (Interrupt = Seamless)

Every interaction in ExodeUI—from hover effects and dropdown drawers to complex data charts—carries real kinetic momentum.

Direct Code Export Across 5 Frameworks

The best part? You don't have to hire a mathematical physicist to recreate this in CSS. ExodeUI compiles your motion models directly into lightweight, 60fps code for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Angular.

🚀 Experience the Post-Figma Era Built in India

If you are tired of drawing dead pictures in Figma and spending months translating mockups into code, try the next-generation interactive UI engine built right here in India:

title: Updates to Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access in macOS
description:
For decades, Mac computers have been loved by creators and developers who build, automate, and innovate using cutting-edge technologies and tools. We want to keep empowering our community in these pursuits, while helping our users stay safe and in control of their data and privacy. In macOS 27.3 beta 2 today, we’re introducing increased transparency and more granular options for two of the APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk. These changes are designed to help them do that and to empower them to make informed decisions about their own data and privacy. The changes include:

  • A split of Device Control and Data Access into two settings: (1) System & App Protection Override, and (2) Accessibility
  • A single method for granting permissions by selecting the requesting app from a list
  • Guidance to encourage users to grant access to just the specific apps (for System & App Protection Override) or folders (for Full Disk Access) that are required for their workflows
  • Increased visibility into the wide range of data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are granted
  • The option for users to configure apps to ask every time they require access
  • A transparency indicator when a requesting app is controlling another app using System & App Protection Override

Developers should be prepared to adjust how they onboard users and make sure their apps can gracefully handle having access to only a limited set of folders or apps when utilizing these APIs. Users will see these updates when approving new app permission requests. All app permissions previously granted by users will remain in effect.

Developers of apps that use Full Disk Access for disk backup, or the new Accessibility settings to provide assistive technologies, can request entitlements to deliver the same experience for new installations that they offered before macOS 27.3. Currently, known apps aren’t affected and will keep the same experience without an entitlement. Additional entitlement details will be available soon.

title: Tauri for Beginners: Build Tiny, Fast Desktop Apps With Web Technology
description:
Tauri is a framework for building desktop apps with web technology — HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interface — but with a Rust backend instead of shipping an entire browser. That one difference matters: where Electron apps are often 100MB or more, a Tauri app is usually under 10MB, starts instantly, and uses far less memory. If you love web development but hate bloated desktop apps, Tauri is the answer.

The idea is simple. Your frontend is a normal web app, and your backend is Rust. The two talk through a secure command system: the frontend calls a Rust function, Rust does the heavy work — reading files, talking to the system, running commands — and returns the result. You get the full power of a native app with the comfort of web tools.

// src-tauri/src/main.rs
#[tauri::command]
fn greet(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("Hello, {}! You are running a Tauri app.", name)
}

fn main() {
    tauri::Builder::default()
        .invoke_handler(tauri::generate_handler![greet])
        .run(tauri::generate_context!())
        .expect("error while running tauri application");
}

// frontend
import { invoke } from "@tauri-apps/api/core";
const message = await invoke("greet", { name: "World" });

Getting started is simple. Install Rust, run npm create tauri-app@latest, pick your frontend framework, and you have a working desktop app. The official docs walk you through the first app in about 20 minutes, and the examples cover everything from file dialogs to system trays.

Tauri is for web developers who want to build desktop apps, beginners who want to learn Rust with a real project, and teams tired of shipping 150MB Electron apps for a simple tool. It is great for utilities, editors, and internal tools.

The limits are honest. You need to learn some Rust, and Rust has a real learning curve. The ecosystem is smaller than Electron's, some advanced native features need extra work, and debugging across the web-Rust boundary takes practice.

Start today with one thing: scaffold a Tauri app and make a button that calls a Rust function. That one round trip — web to Rust and back — is the whole idea. In a week you will have a real desktop app that fits in a few megabytes.

title: Beyond the Final Answer: Evaluating the Reliability of Tool-Using AI Agents
description:
An AI agent can give you the correct answer and still have done the wrong thing to get there.

It might skip a required tool, pass incorrect arguments, encounter an execution error, or reach the right answer by coincidence.

In a simple chatbot, evaluating the final response may be enough for a basic quality check. But once an agent starts interacting with tools, the final response tells only part of the story.

How do we know whether an agent actually completed a task correctly, followed the expected execution path, and handled tool failures appropriately?

I wanted to explore this problem by building a small evaluation framework for tool-using AI agents.

That project became Agent Reliability Lab.

The problem: A correct answer doesn't always mean a successful execution

Consider an agent asked to calculate:

Use the calculate tool to compute 125 * 8 + 37.

The expected answer is 1037.

There are several ways an agent might respond:

  1. It invokes the calculator with the correct expression and returns the correct result.
  2. It skips the calculator and produces the answer directly.
  3. It invokes the calculator with invalid arguments.
  4. The tool executes successfully, but the agent returns an incorrect answer.
  5. The tool encounters an error, but the agent successfully recovers.

If we evaluate only the final response, some of these scenarios look identical.

But from an engineering perspective, they represent very different outcomes.

For example, if a task explicitly requires a tool invocation, producing the correct answer without using that tool should not count as a successful execution.

This led me to a different approach:

Evaluate the outcome and the execution evidence independently.

The approach: Make agent execution observable and measurable

The Agent Reliability Lab captures the full execution lifecycle—from task input and tool interactions to independent evaluation and reliability reporting.

Agent Reliability Lab is a local-first evaluation and observability framework for tool-using AI agents.

The initial implementation uses:

  • Python for the evaluation harness.
  • Ollama to run a locally hosted Qwen3 8B model.
  • A deterministic calculator tool.
  • Structured JSON execution traces.
  • An independent evaluator.
  • Repeated experiments and aggregated metrics.

The idea is to capture what happened during execution and evaluate it against explicit expectations.

1. Building a bounded agent execution loop

The first component is the agent runner.

It loads a task, sends the prompt to the local model, exposes the calculator tool, and processes any tool calls returned by the model.

The execution loop is deliberately bounded:

MODEL = "qwen3:8b"
MAX_STEPS = 5

for step in range(MAX_STEPS):
    response = chat(
        model=model,
        messages=messages,
        tools=[calculate],
    )

    messages.append(response.message)
    tool_calls = response.message.tool_calls or []

    if not tool_calls:
        trace["final_response"] = response.message.content or ""
        break

Why impose a step limit?

Tool-using agents can sometimes continue calling tools without making meaningful progress. A bounded loop prevents unbounded execution and gives us a way to classify tasks that exceed the execution budget.

The runner also records tool arguments, results, errors, execution duration, and the final response.

This makes the execution path inspectable instead of treating the agent as a black box.

2. Capturing execution traces

A final answer alone doesn't provide enough information to understand an agent's behavior.

For every task, Agent Reliability Lab captures a structured execution trace.

The trace includes:

  • Task identifier.
  • Model used.
  • Execution start time.
  • Tool calls and arguments.
  • Tool results and errors.
  • Individual tool execution durations.
  • Final response.
  • Total execution duration.
  • Execution errors.

A simplified trace structure looks like this:

{
  "task_id": "math-001",
  "model": "qwen3:8b",
  "tool_calls": [
    {
      "step": 1,
      "tool": "calculate",
      "arguments": {
        "expression": "125 * 8 + 37"
      },
      "result": "1037",
      "error": null,
      "duration_ms": 0.5
    }
  ],
  "final_response": "The answer is 1037.",
  "error": null
}

This is an illustrative example of the trace structure.

The implementation persists traces as JSON files, making them available for later inspection and failure analysis.

I wanted to preserve execution evidence separately from evaluation results so that the evaluator could inspect what actually happened.

3. Evaluating the agent independently

This is one of the most important design decisions in the project.

The agent should not decide whether it successfully completed its own task.

Instead, a separate deterministic evaluator examines the execution trace.

It checks three important things:

Answer correctness

Does the final response contain the expected answer?

The evaluator normalizes formatted numbers and recognizes explicit answer patterns, rather than simply searching for an arbitrary matching number anywhere in the response.

It also rejects contradictory answer candidates.

Tool compliance

Was the required calculator tool successfully executed?

A task that requires a calculator call should not pass just because the model returned the expected number without invoking the tool.

Execution status

Did the agent encounter an execution error or exceed the maximum number of steps?

The task passes only when the answer is correct, the required tool execution succeeded, and the agent did not encounter an execution error.

The core evaluation logic is intentionally simple:

passed = (
    answer_correct
    and tool_requirement_met
    and not error
)

Keeping evaluation independent makes the results more trustworthy than relying on the agent's own statement that it completed the task.

4. Classifying failures instead of reporting only pass or fail

A binary pass/fail result is useful, but it doesn't tell us what to fix.

For example, these failures need different investigation paths:

  • The agent never called a required tool.
  • The tool was called but returned an error.
  • The agent returned an incorrect answer.
  • The execution loop reached its step limit.
  • The agent encountered an execution-level exception.

Agent Reliability Lab classifies unsuccessful tasks into categories such as:

Failure category Meaning
tool_use_failure Required tool was not used
tool_execution_failure Required tool did not execute successfully
incorrect_answer Final answer did not match the expected result
execution_error Agent execution encountered an error
step_limit_exceeded Agent reached the maximum execution steps

This distinction matters because the solution to an incorrect answer may be different from the solution to a tool execution failure.

It also gives us a foundation for analyzing failure patterns across repeated runs.

5. Measuring more than answer accuracy

Once execution traces and independent evaluation are available, we can start measuring agent behavior.

The framework generates several metrics:

Metric What it tells us
Pass rate Percentage of benchmark tasks completed successfully
Answer correctness Whether the final answer matches the expected result
Tool success rate Successful tool calls divided by total tool calls
Tool failure count Number of tool calls that returned errors
Recovery count Tasks completed successfully after a tool failure
Failure categories Why unsuccessful tasks failed
Mean latency Average task execution time

I particularly wanted to capture tool reliability and recovery separately from answer correctness.

For example, an agent that successfully recovers after a tool failure behaves differently from one that stops immediately.

The evaluator can identify successful recovery when a task passes despite an earlier tool failure.

These metrics help make those differences visible.

6. Why repeated evaluations matter

One successful run doesn't necessarily mean an agent is reliable.

LLM behavior can vary across executions, even when the task and configuration remain unchanged.

To explore this, I added a repeated evaluation runner.

The current implementation executes the benchmark three times:

RUNS = 3

for run_number in range(1, RUNS + 1):
    result = subprocess.run(
        [sys.executable, "scripts/run_eval.py"],
        cwd=ROOT,
        text=True,
        capture_output=True,
    )

Each run gets its own report and archived execution traces.

The framework then aggregates:

  • Pass rate for each run.
  • Mean pass rate.
  • Mean execution latency.
  • Tool success rate.
  • Total tool calls and failures.
  • Total recovered tasks.

This is useful because a single pass rate can hide variability.

For example, if an agent passes a task in one run but fails it in another, that inconsistency is worth investigating.

Repeated evaluations provide a starting point for understanding that behavior.

One important limitation: three runs over a small dataset are useful for experimentation, but they are not enough to establish statistically strong reliability claims.

7. Keeping the evaluation environment practical

I chose a local-first setup using Ollama and Qwen3 8B.

This makes it possible to experiment without depending on a hosted model API for every run.

The calculator is also deterministic. It uses Python's AST parser and an explicit allowlist of supported arithmetic operations rather than evaluating arbitrary Python expressions.

The current benchmark contains six arithmetic tasks, each requiring the calculator tool.

This is intentionally a small starting point.

The project also separates automated tests from model inference. The deterministic test suite validates the calculator, evaluator, failure classification, execution behavior, and recovery logic without requiring an actual model run.

GitHub Actions runs these tests on pushes and pull requests.

That separation makes it easier to validate the evaluation infrastructure without repeatedly paying the cost of model execution or waiting for inference.

Current limitations

Agent Reliability Lab is an early-stage prototype, not a production-grade agent evaluation platform.

There are several limitations worth calling out:

Small benchmark

The current benchmark contains six arithmetic tasks. It is useful for validating the evaluation pipeline but does not represent complex, multi-step agent workflows.

Limited tool coverage

The initial implementation exposes one calculator tool. Real-world agents interact with multiple tools, APIs, databases, and external systems.

Limited failure scenarios

The framework records and classifies tool and execution failures, but the current benchmark is not a comprehensive fault-injection suite.

Model variability

Local model behavior can vary between executions. Repeated runs help observe this, but a small number of runs cannot establish general reliability.

Limited semantic evaluation

Numeric answer matching works for the current arithmetic benchmark. It is not sufficient for evaluating arbitrary natural-language responses.

These limitations define the next areas of exploration rather than something the current implementation claims to solve.

What I'd explore next

There are several directions I'd like to investigate:

  1. Expand the benchmark to multi-step tasks involving multiple tools.
  2. Introduce controlled tool failures and evaluate recovery behavior.
  3. Compare different models and prompts against the same benchmark.
  4. Improve execution traces with more detailed step-level observability.
  5. Explore OpenTelemetry and agent observability platforms.
  6. Add regression detection across model and prompt changes.

I'm particularly interested in making agent evaluation part of the engineering development lifecycle.

When a prompt, model, or tool implementation changes, we should be able to run the same evaluation suite and understand whether agent behavior improved, regressed, or simply became less predictable.

Final thoughts

Building Agent Reliability Lab helped me think about agent engineering from a testing and observability perspective.

The important shift is moving away from evaluating only what an agent says and toward evaluating what it actually does.

A reliable agent should produce the expected result, use its tools correctly, handle execution failures, and behave consistently enough that engineers can understand and improve it.

The principle I keep coming back to is:

Don't just evaluate the answer. Evaluate the execution that produced it.

I'm continuing to explore practical approaches to AI agent reliability, developer productivity, and engineering workflows.

If you're building tool-using agents, I'd be interested in hearing how you're evaluating tool behavior, execution failures, and consistency across repeated runs.

Explore the project:

Agent Reliability Lab on GitHub

Feedback and suggestions are welcome!

title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
description:
The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race.

Subscribe to messages inside the run

The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null.

Idempotency with no extra code

The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally.

Setting experimental_minRetention keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from start(), so late duplicates are still refused.

Upgrade to workflow 5.4.0 and read the idempotency documentation to get started.

title: File Handling in Java: Reading Data from a Text File
description:
What is File Handling?

File handling in Java is the process of creating, reading, writing, and modifying files using Java programs.

For example, imagine we have employee details stored in a text file. Instead of manually entering employee details into our program, we can read the data directly from that file.

Let's understand how to read a file using a simple Employee Management System.

Employee Data (empData.txt)

First, let's create a text file containing employee details.

id,name,dept,salary
1,Subash,IT,25000
2,Ram,HR,30000
3,John,Testing,28000

Complete Code

Let's look at the complete controller code.

import java.io.File;
import java.io.FileReader;
import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.FileNotFoundException;

public class EmployeeController {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        EmployeeService service = new EmployeeService();

        File note = new File("empData.txt");

        try {
            FileReader reader = new FileReader(note);

            BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(reader);

            String line = br.readLine();
            line = br.readLine();

            while (line != null) {

                String[] words = line.split(",");

                int id = Integer.parseInt(words[0].trim());
                String name = words[1];
                String dept = words[2];
                int salary = Integer.parseInt(words[3].trim());

                EmployeeEntity employee =
                    new EmployeeEntity(id, name, dept, salary);

                service.addEmployee(employee);

                line = br.readLine();
            }

            br.close();

        } catch (FileNotFoundException fnf) {
            System.out.println("File not found");

        } catch (IOException io) {
            System.out.println("IO exception");
        }

        service.viewEmployee();
    }
}

Understanding the Code Bit by Bit

1. Creating a File Object

File note = new File("empData.txt");

First, we create a File object and pass the file path.

Here, the File class represents the file location. It doesn't read the file contents by itself.

2. Using FileReader

FileReader reader = new FileReader(note);

FileReader is used to read characters from the file.

We pass the File object to the FileReader constructor so it knows which file to read.

3. Using BufferedReader

BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(reader);

BufferedReader takes the FileReader object as an argument.

It helps us read the file efficiently and provides a method called readLine() to read one line at a time.

4. Reading the File

String line = br.readLine();
line = br.readLine();

The first readLine() reads the header (id, name, dept, salary).

We call it again because we want to start reading the actual employee details, skipping the header.

5. Using While Loop

while (line != null) {
    // Reading employee details
    line = br.readLine();
}

The while loop continues as long as the line is not null.

When there are no more lines to read, readLine() returns null, and the loop stops.

6. Splitting the Data

String[] words = line.split(",");

Our employee details are separated by commas.

The split(",") method separates the values and stores them in a String array.

For example:

1,Subash,IT,25000

After splitting:

  • words[0] = 1
  • words[1] = Subash
  • words[2] = IT
  • words[3] = 25000

7. Converting String into Integer

int id = Integer.parseInt(words[0].trim());
int salary = Integer.parseInt(words[3].trim());

By default, the values we read from the file are Strings.

But our EmployeeEntity class expects ID and salary as integers.

So, we use Integer.parseInt() to convert String values into integers.

The trim() method removes unwanted spaces from the beginning and end of a String.

8. Creating an Employee Object

EmployeeEntity employee =
    new EmployeeEntity(id, name, dept, salary);

Now that we have separated the employee details, we create an EmployeeEntity object using its constructor.

9. Adding Employee to ArrayList

service.addEmployee(employee);

We pass the Employee object to the service class.

The service class adds that object to the ArrayList.

This process repeats for every employee in the text file.

10. Closing the Reader

br.close();

Once reading is completed, we close the BufferedReader to release the resources associated with it.

11. Displaying Employees

service.viewEmployee();

Finally, we call the viewEmployee() method from our service class.

It displays all the employee objects stored in the ArrayList.

Java internally calls the toString() method of each EmployeeEntity object to display its details.

Exception Handling

While working with files, exceptions can occur.

For example:

  • FileNotFoundException: Occurs when the specified file cannot be found.
  • IOException: Occurs when an input/output error happens while reading the file.

We handle these exceptions using try-catch blocks.

Conclusion

File handling makes it easier to read and store data using files.

In our Employee Management System, we used File, FileReader, and BufferedReader to read employee details from a text file, convert them into Employee objects, and store them in an ArrayList.

That's how we can use file handling in a simple Java application.

title: Provable Cross-Modal Transfer of Hierarchical Concept Structure in CLIP Embeddings
description:
arXiv:2611.17671v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP are trained to align images and text, not to represent taxonomies. Yet empirical studies show that CLIP embeddings exhibit hierarchical structure aligned with the hierarchy of semantic concepts. A theoretical characterization of why such hierarchy emerges from a non-hierarchical objective remains open. In this paper, we formalize this phenomenon as Hierarchical Angular Separation (HAS), a geometric property whereby each non-leaf concept embedding is more similar to its descendants than to off-branch concepts. Empirically, we show that HAS holds approximately in raw images and randomly initialized CLIP image embeddings, while in text embeddings it holds approximately only after contrastive learning. To theoretically explain this asymmetry, we analyze an unconstrained features model in which the image embeddings are fixed and only the text embeddings are trained. At the global minimizer, the text-side HAS violation percentage at each node is at most the image-side HAS violation and near-violation percentage. The key mechanism is the hierarchical co-occurrence structure of image-text pairs, which biases text embeddings toward root-centered image prototypes. For a linear contrastive loss, we derive a closed-form solution that makes this mechanism explicit. We extend the analysis to the InfoNCE loss and establish analogous guarantees under sufficient regularization. Synthetic experiments validate the theory and show that HAS is transferred even beyond the regimes covered by our analysis.

title: YouTube download APIs: batch delivery to your own cloud storage
description:
Use a hosted download API to deliver videos directly to your cloud storage. Compare Oxylabs, TornadoAPI and FlashData by batch submission, supported storage and the definition of billable volume. Check whether each per-GB price measures delivered bytes or a larger billing reference.

Provider Who handles retrieval and errors Delivery Batch input Price and meter Trial and storage When to choose it
Oxylabs YouTube Downloader Provider operates retrieval. You submit async jobs and handle API/job errors and your own request limits. Video, audio or clips delivered directly to customer cloud storage. Async Push-Pull; up to 5,000 video IDs in one batch. YouTube Downloader-specific price not verified on the public pricing page; request a quote for this source. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC YouTube-specific trial not verified. S3, GCS and S3-compatible storage. Teams wanting a hosted batch downloader within an existing Oxylabs integration.
TornadoAPI Provider runs download/processing; you handle webhook or polling results, job failures and API limits. Files streamed to customer storage; delivered volume and billable volume may differ. Single job; playlists/channels create batches; bulk endpoint accepts up to 100 jobs. Advertised “as low as $0.06/GB”; volume/account conditions apply. A 720p reference floor may increase billable GB. Not a universal delivered-GB price. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC Homepage advertises 100 GB free; billing basis follows account terms. S3-compatible storage including S3, R2 and MinIO; docs also list GCS, Azure, OSS and Google Drive. Applications needing hosted jobs and multiple storage integrations, with account metering checked first.
FlashData YouTube Download FlashData operates retrieval. You monitor async jobs, handle API/job errors and supply a writable destination. Video, audio or clips to your cloud storage. Optional JSON metadata does not count as media download volume. Async or Batch jobs; Bulk accepts an uploaded file of video IDs. PAYG: $0.10/GB delivered = $100/TB delivered. 1 TB = 1,000 GB. Your storage charges are separate. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC Shared trial credits. S3, S3-compatible/R2, GCS, Azure Blob, Alibaba OSS, Tencent COS, Baidu BOS and Volcengine TOS. Teams wanting customer-bucket delivery billed by actual media bytes, including uploaded-ID workflows.

FlashData’s Google Search and YouTube Data use separate request-based rates. Those rates do not buy media delivery, even though the products share a key and credit balance.

Delivered bytes are not necessarily billable bytes

FlashData’s PAYG meter is completed media bytes delivered to your storage: $0.10/GB or $100/TB, with 1 TB = 1,000 GB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes (pricing, 2026-11-15 UTC). A 2 GB delivered file therefore uses $0.20 at that rate. Optional accompanying JSON does not add download volume, and your cloud-storage bill remains separate.

TornadoAPI’s billing documentation distinguishes delivered and billable volume. When its 720p floor is enabled, a low-resolution video, audio extraction or clip can be charged using a full-source 720p reference larger than the delivered file. Its headline “as low as” price must be read with account and volume terms. Do not compare a tiny audio file as if both services necessarily bill its physical size.

Oxylabs documents YouTube cloud-storage delivery, but this review did not verify a public YouTube Downloader-specific price or trial amount. Its general scraping plans are not evidence of a download-per-GB price.

How do submission and delivery work?

Your application submits download jobs, monitors completion and checks the files delivered to your storage. Configure destination permissions and handle API or job errors. A returned job ID confirms acceptance; check the final job status to confirm completed delivery.

Oxylabs accepts up to 5,000 video IDs in an asynchronous batch. TornadoAPI documents up to 100 jobs per bulk request, with playlist and channel submissions also producing batches. FlashData accepts async and Batch requests, or a video-ID file through Bulk.

Match the destination before submitting a batch

FlashData’s current download reference lists Amazon S3, S3-compatible destinations including R2, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob, Alibaba OSS, Tencent COS, Baidu BOS and Volcengine TOS. It can deliver video, audio or a requested time segment. Configure the storage fields for the chosen provider and check the completed job’s delivered files and usage rather than treating initial pending usage as the final bill.

Implementation after selection

For FlashData, see the Oxylabs download comparison and S3 delivery tutorial. This comparison is about developer APIs and customer buckets, not consumer desktop downloaders.

Where the numbers come from

All prices are in USD. Official pages were checked on 2026-11-15 UTC. This is a vendor-document comparison published by FlashData, not an independent performance benchmark.

  • Oxylabs YouTube Downloader and pricing: async batches and customer storage verified; source-specific download price not verified.
  • TornadoAPI pricing, trial offer, billing, bulk jobs and storage: account-specific billable GB may exceed delivered GB.
  • FlashData pricing and YouTube Download reference: completed delivered-media bytes, decimal GB/TB and supported customer storage.

Originally published at FlashData.

title: How One Model Finally Learned to Play 1,000 Games – And Why It Matters
description:
Gamer — A Generalist Vision‑Language‑Action Foundation Model that Redefines Game‑Agent Development

Launch: 13 Nov 2026

Lead

“13 Nov 2026 marks the day a single model learned to move a mouse, press a key, and solve a quest chain across 1 000 games,” announced the lead author on the arXiv pre‑print page. The statement captures the moment the research community finally sees a truly generalist VLA (Vision‑Language‑Action) model that operates on raw device‑level input streams rather than abstracted game APIs.

Gamer arrives as a fully open‑source foundation model, complete with weights, training scripts, and a cross‑engine SDK. Its release on Hugging Face earned 87 up‑votes within hours, signalling strong community appetite. Beyond the hype, the model delivers concrete technical advances: hierarchical episodic memory, multi‑hop transformer planning, and a diffusion‑based trajectory decoder that produces smooth 3‑D control.

In the sections that follow, I unpack how Gamer’s architecture works, why its training data matters, and how the model reshapes the entire game‑development pipeline—from early prototyping to final QA. I also benchmark Gamer against the current crop of VLA agents, highlight the risks that still linger, and sketch a realistic outlook for the next three years.

The Case Study: Debugging a Hidden Hotkey in a 2‑D Platformer

Imagine a small indie studio that just finished a pixel‑art platformer. During internal playtests, a tester discovers that the “dash” ability only triggers when the player holds Shift and presses A within a 120 ms window—a timing quirk the designers never intended. The bug slips through the usual scripted bots because they press keys in a deterministic order and never miss the timing window.

Using Gamer, the QA engineer wraps the game with the Game‑Env‑SDK (a one‑line Python call) and launches the “Human‑Like Playtester” mode. Gamer ingests the live screen buffer, predicts the next mouse movement, and emits a pixel‑level key‑press stream that mirrors real human latency distributions (the model learned these distributions from 30 k h of keyboard‑mouse logs). Within five minutes, the agent repeatedly fails the dash, logs the exact frame where the key‑press timing diverges, and produces a heatmap that highlights the offending UI element.

The engineer isolates the bug, patches the input handling code, and re‑runs the same agent. The new run shows a 99 % success rate for the dash, confirming the fix. All of this happens without writing a single line of behavior‑tree script or manually scripting a bot. The case study illustrates three core strengths of Gamer:

  1. Device‑level fidelity – the model predicts low‑level input, exposing timing‑sensitive bugs.
  2. Hierarchical memory – Gamer retains the state of the player across lives, enabling detection of bugs that manifest only after a sequence of actions.
  3. Inference‑time attention steering – the engineer toggles a safety bias to focus the model’s visual attention on UI elements, accelerating bug localisation.

The Architecture in Depth

1. Multimodal Backbone

Gamer builds on a Qwen‑style VL transformer (the same family that powers Alpamayo‑R1). The backbone processes a 224 × 224 RGB frame together with a tokenized language prompt (e.g., “open the chest”). The model shares a single computation graph for training and inference, eliminating the need for separate perception and policy networks.

2. Hierarchical Episodic Memory

The memory system splits into two tiers:

  • Short‑term buffer – stores the last 50 visual‑action pairs (≈ 2 seconds of gameplay). This buffer feeds a local transformer that captures fine‑grained timing.
  • Long‑term abstraction – aggregates episode summaries every 30 seconds into a compressed key‑value store. The abstraction encodes high‑level game state (inventory items, quest flags) as discrete tokens, enabling the planner to reason over minutes of gameplay.

During inference, the planner attends jointly to the current frame and the relevant long‑term keys, performing multi‑hop reasoning that can span dozens of sub‑goals.

3. Diffusion‑Based Trajectory Decoder

For 3‑D environments, Gamer predicts a continuous control trajectory rather than a single action. The decoder draws on a diffusion process that iteratively refines a sequence of mouse deltas and camera rotations, conditioned on the transformer’s hidden state. This approach yields smooth steering curves, avoiding the jitter common in discrete action models.

4. Inference‑Time Attention Steering

A pre‑softmax bias vector attaches to the attention scores at every transformer layer. By flipping a Boolean flag, developers can amplify attention toward a set of “critical tokens” (e.g., health bar, enemy silhouette). The mechanism requires zero weight updates, runs in constant time, and has already demonstrated a 12 % reduction in unsafe actions during internal safety tests.

5. Action Space

Gamer outputs a composite action vector:

Component Format Example
Mouse ΔX, ΔY Continuous (pixels) (‑12, +3)
Keyboard mask 256‑dim binary {W:1, A:0, …}
API call ID Discrete SELECT_INVENTORY_ITEM

The model learns to emit high‑level API calls when the visual context suggests a UI interaction (e.g., opening a menu).

Training Corpus: Quantity Meets Quality

Gamer’s performance stems from two complementary data streams.

  • Device‑level interaction logs – 30 k h of raw keyboard and mouse streams captured from volunteer gamers across Windows, macOS, and Linux. Each log pairs a video frame with the exact input timestamps, preserving human latency distributions.

  • Internet‑scale video‑action dataset – 40 k h of gameplay footage scraped from public streaming platforms, annotated with coarse action tags (jump, shoot, open inventory). This dataset mirrors the pipeline used for NitroGen earlier in 2026, but Gamer augments it with synchronized input signals derived via a semi‑automated key‑press extraction algorithm.

The combined corpus spans more than 1 000 titles, ranging from 8‑bit platformers to photorealistic 3‑D RPGs. Researchers split the data into 80 % training, 10 % validation, and 10 % test, ensuring that no title appears in more than one split.

Training runs on a cluster of eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs for 12 days, consuming ≈ 2 PF‑LOPs. The authors report a final loss of 0.31 on the validation set, a 15 % improvement over NitroGen’s baseline.

Hard Numbers: Benchmarks and Performance

Benchmark Metric Gamer NitroGen OpenAI GameGPT‑4V (API)
Multi‑Game Generalization (100 titles) Average success rate on scripted tasks 78 % 62 % 71 % (estimated from API logs)
Long‑Horizon Completion (≥ 15 sub‑goals) Success rate 78 % 62 % 68 %
Frame‑rate (Inference) 30 FPS on NVIDIA H100 (full model) ✔︎ 20 FPS 15 FPS (cloud)
Edge Variant (Gamer‑Lite) 15 FPS on RTX 3060 ✔︎ — —
Safety Violations (exploiting glitches) Rate per 10 min session 0.3 % 1.1 % 0.8 %
Human‑like Latency Distribution KL KL divergence vs. human logs 0.12 0.27 0.21

The Multi‑Game Benchmark, released alongside Gamer, measures agents on a mix of platformers, shooters, strategy titles, and open‑world RPGs. Gamer’s 78 % success rate proves that a single model can handle disparate control schemes without per‑game fine‑tuning.

How Gamer Reshapes the Development Workflow

Phase Traditional Approach Gamer‑Enabled Approach
Concept & Prototyping Designers script behavior trees or write custom RL environments. Drop a GamerAgent.Start() call into a Unity scene; the agent instantly explores the level, revealing navigation bottlenecks.
Playtesting Human testers run the game, record videos, manually file bugs. Run Gamer in “Human‑Like Playtester” mode; the agent automatically logs failure points, produces heatmaps, and surfaces timing‑sensitive bugs.
Balancing Designers iterate on enemy stats, then run internal playtests. Feed new level designs to Gamer; the model outputs a “completion difficulty” score (average steps, time‑to‑goal) that correlates with human data (R² ≈ 0.86).
Narrative QA Writers manually test every dialogue branch. Use the language component to converse with NPCs; Gamer tracks conversation state in its long‑term memory, exposing dead‑ends.
Regression Testing Write unit tests for each quest flag. Deploy Gamer across persistent‑world snapshots; the agent validates that saved inventory persists and that quest flags trigger correctly.
Production Hire dedicated AI engineers for each title. Reuse the same foundation model across dozens of projects; internal studies report a 30‑45 % reduction in AI‑related headcount.

The most immediate payoff appears in QA. Studios that integrated Gamer into their CI pipeline reported a 40 % drop in critical UI bugs during the first month, because the model’s human‑like input uncovered edge cases that deterministic bots missed.

Risks and Open Questions

  1. Data‑privacy concerns – The device‑level logs contain keystrokes that could reveal personal information (e.g., usernames typed in chat). While the authors apply on‑the‑fly anonymization, any leakage could trigger legal scrutiny under GDPR or CCPA.

  2. Safety‑steering misuse – The attention‑steering knob lets developers suppress risky actions, but it also enables malicious actors to hide exploitative behavior during testing. Auditing tools must track steering toggles to ensure transparency.

  3. Generalization limits – Gamer excels on titles that resemble the training distribution (pixel‑based UI, conventional control schemes). Niche interfaces—voice‑only games, VR hand‑tracking—still fall outside the model’s scope. Extending the backbone to incorporate audio or hand‑pose streams remains an open research direction.

  4. Compute cost for large studios – Running the full model at 30 FPS demands an H100‑class GPU. Smaller studios may rely on the Lite variant, which sacrifices trajectory smoothness and long‑horizon planning. Cloud‑based inference could democratize access, but it reintroduces latency and cost concerns.

  5. Intellectual‑property implications – Because Gamer learns from publicly available gameplay videos, studios worry that the model might reproduce copyrighted assets (e.g., unique UI layouts) when fine‑tuned on proprietary games. Clear licensing and model‑card disclosures mitigate the risk, but legal frameworks lag behind.

Outlook: The Next Three Years

  • 2027 – Specialized Branches – Expect the community to fork Gamer into domain‑specific variants (e.g., Gamer‑VR with hand‑pose encoders, Gamer‑Narrative with larger language heads). The open‑source license encourages rapid specialization.

  • 2028 – Co‑Design Loops – Game engines will embed the Game‑Env‑SDK directly into their editors. Designers will iterate on level geometry while watching a live Gamer agent adapt, creating a feedback loop that blurs the line between AI and level design.

  • 2029 – Standardized Benchmarks – The Multi‑Game Benchmark will evolve into an industry‑wide certification suite. Studios that achieve a > 85 % success rate on the benchmark may qualify for “AI‑Ready” labels, similar to performance‑grade certifications in graphics.

  • Beyond 2029 – Autonomous Content Generation – With hierarchical memory and language grounding, future versions of Gamer could generate procedural quests, populate dungeons, and even author dialogue trees on the fly, turning the model from a test agent into a co‑author of game content.

Final Thoughts

Gamer does not magically replace every AI engineer or eliminate all bugs. It introduces a powerful, open‑source VLA foundation that unifies perception, language, and low‑level control in a single end‑to‑end pipeline. Its hierarchical memory and diffusion‑based trajectory decoder push the state of the art on long‑horizon tasks, while inference‑time attention steering gives studios a practical safety handle.

The model’s release on 13 Nov 2026 marks a watershed moment: the first time a publicly available foundation model can play a modern 3‑D title with mouse precision, talk to NPCs, and remember quest progress across sessions—all without per‑game fine‑tuning.

Developers who adopt Gamer today gain a versatile research platform, a rapid prototyping tool, and a new class of automated playtester. Those who ignore it risk falling behind as the industry coalesces around multimodal foundation models for game AI.

The next wave of games will likely blend human‑level perception with procedural creativity, and Gamer provides a solid foothold for that future.

Key statistic: On the newly released Multi‑Game Benchmark, Gamer achieves a 78 % long‑horizon success rate, outpacing the previous best (NitroGen 62 %).

Performance note: The full model runs at 30 FPS on a single NVIDIA H100, while the lightweight Gamer‑Lite variant delivers 15 FPS on an RTX 3060, making real‑time inference feasible on consumer‑grade hardware.

Safety impact: Inference‑time attention steering cuts unsafe action rates from 1.1 % (NitroGen) to 0.3 %, a twelve‑fold improvement in internal safety tests.

Gamer’s launch does not signal the end of game‑specific AI research, but it establishes a new baseline. The community now possesses a shared, extensible platform on which to build the next generation of intelligent, human‑like game agents.

title: TReC: Evaluating Move-Induced State Changes in Instruction-Conditioned Go
description:
arXiv:2611.17781v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a Go model predicts a move different from the expert's, coordinate distance measures how far the prediction lands from the reference. We introduce Transition Representation Consistency (TReC) to compare how the two moves change a board-state embedding. Both moves are executed from the same position under the game rules, and TReC is the cosine similarity between the two resulting representation changes. In experiments with a frozen KataGo network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the gap between the highest and lowest candidate per position has a median of 0.01 to 0.08 for the direct successor-state cosine and 0.88 to 1.33 for TReC, depending on the evaluator layer. TReC follows coordinate distance only weakly: the rank correlation between a candidate's distance to the reference and its TReC, computed within each position, has a median of -0.19 over these positions.
