title: SQL Challenge : ROW_NUMBER() vs RANK() vs DENSE_RANK() – What's the Difference?
description:
SQL window functions are useful when working with employee rankings, sales reports and business data.


Three commonly used ranking functions are "ROW_NUMBER()", "RANK()" and "DENSE_RANK()". Although they look similar, they produce different results when multiple records have the same value.

If you want to understand SQL window functions in more detail, including "PARTITION BY", "LAG()", "LEAD()", running totals and interview questions, you can also explore this "SQL Window Functions and Analytic Functions Guide" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/window-functions-analytic-functions-sql-faq.html).

The Problem

Suppose you have an employees table containing employee IDs, employee names, departments and salaries.

emp_id| emp_name| department| salary
101| Amit| IT| 90000
102| Rahul| IT| 80000
103| Priya| HR| 80000
104| Neha| HR| 70000
105| Karan| IT| 80000
106| Sneha| HR| 65000

You need to compare the results of three SQL ranking functions when employees have equal salaries.

SQL Solution (Oracle)

SELECT
emp_id,
emp_name,
department,
salary,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id
) AS row_num,
RANK() OVER (
ORDER BY salary DESC
) AS salary_rank,
DENSE_RANK() OVER (
ORDER BY salary DESC
) AS dense_rank
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id;

Expected Output

emp_id| emp_name| salary| row_num| salary_rank| dense_rank
101| Amit| 90000| 1| 1| 1
102| Rahul| 80000| 2| 2| 2
103| Priya| 80000| 3| 2| 2
105| Karan| 80000| 4| 2| 2
104| Neha| 70000| 5| 5| 3
106| Sneha| 65000| 6| 6| 4

Understanding the Difference

  • "ROW_NUMBER()" assigns a unique sequential number to every row.
  • "RANK()" assigns the same rank to equal salaries and skips subsequent rank numbers.
  • "DENSE_RANK()" assigns the same rank to equal salaries without skipping rank numbers.

Your Turn

Suppose you want to find the top three distinct salary levels in each department, including all employees who share the same salary.

Which SQL ranking function would you use?

Share your answer in the comments!

For more practical SQL examples and interview preparation, explore the SQL window functions guide linked above.

sql #database #dataanalytics #programming

title: Analyzing Learning-Dynamics Across Loss and Prediction Choices for Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2611.17967v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Denoising generative models predict clean data ($x$), noise ($\epsilon$), or velocity ($v$), while training losses can be measured in any of these spaces. Although the resulting nine combinations are algebraically related, they can yield substantially different denoising accuracy and sample quality. We disentangle the effects of prediction and loss spaces. For a fixed prediction target, we show that changing the loss space is exactly equivalent to timestep reweighting and provide a heuristic analysis of how this reweighting affects generation quality. We then show that a rank-$m$ linear bottleneck compressing a $D$-dimensional noisy input imposes an irreducible squared-error floor of $D-m$ on noise and velocity prediction, whereas clean-data prediction can exploit low-dimensional data structure. Combining this bound with prediction-dependent error conversion yields distinct necessary conditions on bottleneck capacity. Experiments with U-Net and JiT across CIFAR-10, Imagenette, and ImageNet-256 support these theoretical predictions. Under compression, prediction choice strongly affects both denoising accuracy and sample quality, with noise-prediction errors closely matching the theoretical lower bound. Our results provide a quantitative understanding of how architectural bottlenecks interact with prediction and loss choices in denoising generative models.

title: CMC enrollment must authorize each certificate action, not just the connection
description:
CMC enrollment must authorize each certificate action, not just the connection

Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) carries certificate requests, responses, revocation, and status information inside CMS messages. The July 2026 revision in RFC 10002 modernizes the message structures, while RFC 10003 covers transport and RFC 10004 lists compliance requirements. A registration authority or certificate authority that only authenticates the HTTPS connection is missing much of CMC's security model.

CMC messages can be signed with CMS SignedData, authenticated with AuthenticatedData, or encrypted with EnvelopedData. A Full PKI Request can contain several controls, including identity proof, proof of possession, transaction identifiers, nonces, modification requests, and certificate acceptance. The receiver must verify the CMS signature before acting on those controls. RFC 10002 also requires a Full PKI Response when a request fails, remains pending, or needs to return information beyond the issued certificates.

That message model creates a useful audit boundary. The connection authenticates the transport peer. The CMS control authenticates the requested action at the PKI layer. A registrar should record which control caused an issuance, which transaction it belongs to, and whether the end entity accepted the result. This matters when an enrollment request crosses an RA, a CA, and one or more back-end signing services.

Bind the request to a transaction

RFC 10004 requires transaction IDs, sender nonces, and recipient nonces across end entities, RAs, and CAs. Their presence is not enough if the service does not preserve them. A CA should reject a response that does not match the outstanding request, and a client should reject a response that reuses a nonce or references an unknown transaction. If the RA stores only a certificate serial number, investigators lose the link between the approval and the request that produced it.

Proof-of-possession controls need the same treatment. A signed request can show that a key signed the request, while a POP link random value binds the key proof to the transaction. The server should treat a missing or stale POP witness as a failed enrollment, not as an optional hint. Batch requests add more state, so each response body and bodyPartID must map back to the correct request entry.

Separate approval from issuance

The end entity can ask for changes. The RA can modify a request or add extensions. The CA decides whether to issue the certificate. Keeping these decisions as separate records prevents a common failure where an account with permission to submit a request is also treated as an authority to approve it.

Certificate acceptance is another explicit action. When the CA asks for confirmation, the client sends a Full PKI Request containing the acceptance control, and the CA returns a confirming Full PKI Response. Automation should wait for that response before placing the certificate into service. Otherwise a rollback or a rejected certificate may still be deployed by a job that only saw the issuance response.

Operational checks

Inventory every CMC endpoint, including HTTP, email, and any other supported transport. Restrict algorithm policy at the CMS layer and reject unsigned controls when policy requires signatures. Keep request and response bodies long enough for incident review, but redact private-key archival material and other sensitive payloads. Alert on repeated badMessageCheck failures, unknown transaction IDs, nonce reuse, and a spike in pending confirmations.

Finally, test interoperability against the published CMC test cases and each vendor's supported control set. RFC 10004 describes requirements by role, and a product that calls itself CMC-compatible can still omit controls that another implementation depends on. Record the supported controls in the PKI service inventory so a later upgrade does not silently remove identity proof, POP, or acceptance handling.

References

  • RFC 10002: Certificate Management over CMS (CMC)
  • RFC 10003: CMC Transport Protocols
  • RFC 10004: CMC Compliance Requirements

title: JaRS: Contrast-Free Localization of Memorized Regions in Diffusion Models via Jacobian Row Sums
description:
arXiv:2611.18024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models sometimes memorize and reproduce regions of their training images, raising privacy and copyright concerns. We aim to localize these regions. Existing contrast-based methods use the diagonal of the denoiser Jacobian, which reflects the posterior variance of each pixel. However, a small diagonal entry is ambiguous: it signals either memorization or averaging over many neighboring pixels in smooth or predictable regions. To resolve this ambiguity, these methods subtract a reference map, which requires a second evaluation with a null prompt or an earlier checkpoint. Unconditional models have no null prompt, and earlier checkpoints are unavailable in general. We show that Jacobian row sums (JaRS), unlike the diagonal, separate memorization from local averaging without a reference map. Pairing JaRS with an image-level detection score that uses the same statistic at an early denoising step yields JaRS+. Across Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.1, Realistic Vision v5.1, and an unconditional diffusion Transformer (DiT), JaRS+ outperforms contrast-based localization methods.

title: Running Oracle SQL Developer without Oracle Java: Temurin to the rescue
description:
Connect with me: LinkedIn | X | GitHub

Oracle SQL Developer is still one of the most practical desktop tools for working with Oracle databases. It is free to download and use. The Java runtime that comes inside some of its downloads is a different story, and it is the reason many corporate laptops now show up in Java licence audits.

This post explains why that happens and how to run SQL Developer on Eclipse Temurin, the free and openly licensed OpenJDK build from the Eclipse Adoptium project, on both macOS and Windows. It also covers the two traps I fell into along the way, so you don't have to.

Why bother?

SQL Developer is a Java application. Oracle ships it in two flavours:

  • With a JDK included: the macOS ARM64 / x64 apps and the "Windows 64-bit with JDK 17 included" zip. These carry an Oracle JDK inside the application folder.
  • Without a JDK: the "Other Platforms" zip (the same file Oracle also lists as "Windows 32-bit/64-bit, requires JDK"). You bring your own Java.

The 24.3.1 bundles contain Oracle JDK 17.0.13. That version matters. Oracle's licence FAQ explains that Oracle JDK 17 was covered by the permissive No-Fee Terms and Conditions only up to 17.0.12 (September 2024). From 17.0.13 onwards, JDK 17 updates are under the Oracle Technology Network (OTN) licence, which is much narrower. You can confirm this on your own machine: the licence file inside the bundled JDK (jdk/legal/java.base/LICENSE) simply points to https://java.com/otnlicense.

Whether a JDK embedded in a free Oracle tool needs a separate licence for your use case is a question for your licensing team, not for a blog post. In practice, though, software-asset tools flag any Oracle JDK they find on disk, and the simplest way to make the finding go away is to not have one. SQL Developer runs happily on an OpenJDK build, so that is what we will do.

What you need

Component Version Where to get it
Oracle SQL Developer, no-JDK zip 24.3.1.347.1826 SQL Developer downloads ("Other Platforms"), or direct: sqldeveloper-24.3.1.347.1826-no-jre.zip (about 588 MB)
Eclipse Temurin JDK 17 (17.0.21 at the time of writing) adoptium.net, Temurin 17 releases

The same zip works on macOS, Windows and Linux. At the time of writing it downloads without an Oracle account sign-in.

To check your download, these are the values for the 24.3.1 zip I used:

SHA-256: 3390ef58972f1f255077c49e66b171b8664773bb16e37570a7ca16acc5afb8cb
MD5:     7de67da92e557e6cc3f8104c9fad951e

Why Temurin 17, and not 21 or the latest?

Oracle's release notes and installation guide for SQL Developer 24.3 name JDK 17 as the requirement. I tested the newest Temurin I had installed (JDK 27) out of curiosity, and it fails in two separate places:

  1. The JVM refuses to start: Unrecognized verification option: -Xverify:none. SQL Developer's ide.conf passes an option that has since been removed from Java.
  2. With that option commented out, startup fails again: java.lang.module.FindException: Module jdk.jsobject not found, required by javafx.web. Newer JDKs no longer ship that module, and SQL Developer's embedded JavaFX web component needs it.

You could patch your way around both, but you would be running an untested combination of a tool you depend on every day. Temurin 17 is supported, free, gets security updates, and just works. Use it only for SQL Developer if you like. It can sit alongside any newer JDK you already have.

macOS: step by step

Tested on macOS Tahoe (Apple Silicon) with SQL Developer 24.3.1 and Temurin 17.0.21.

Before you start: do not edit the Mac app bundle

Before the steps, here is the trap I fell into. If you already have the macOS SQL Developer app (the one with the JDK included), it is tempting to delete the jdk folder inside SQLDeveloper.app/Contents/Resources/sqldeveloper/ and point the app at Temurin. Don't.

The macOS app is code-signed, and the signature covers every file inside the bundle. Remove one folder and macOS reports the app as damaged, with an offer to move it to the Trash. That is exactly what happened to mine. Use the no-JDK zip below instead. It is a plain folder rather than a signed bundle, so you can arrange it however you like. Your existing settings and connections live in ~/.sqldeveloper, outside the app, and the new install picks them up as long as it is the same version.

Step 1: install Temurin 17

Option A, Homebrew:

brew install --cask temurin@17

The installer asks for your administrator password.

Option B, installer package: download the .pkg for your Mac (aarch64 for Apple Silicon, x64 for Intel) from Temurin 17 releases and double-click it.

Either way, the JDK lands in /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/temurin-17.jdk. To check it:

/Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/temurin-17.jdk/Contents/Home/bin/java -version

You should see OpenJDK Runtime Environment Temurin-17....

If you have newer JDKs installed, macOS keeps using the newest one as the default java. That is fine, because SQL Developer gets its own explicit setting in step 4.

Step 2: download SQL Developer without a JDK

From the SQL Developer downloads page, pick Other Platforms, or use the direct link from the table above. In Terminal:

mkdir -p ~/Downloads/sqldeveloper-no-jre
cd ~/Downloads/sqldeveloper-no-jre
curl -fLO https://download.oracle.com/otn_software/java/sqldeveloper/sqldeveloper-24.3.1.347.1826-no-jre.zip
shasum -a 256 sqldeveloper-24.3.1.347.1826-no-jre.zip

Compare the SHA-256 with the value above.

Step 3: unzip it 

cd ~/Applications
unzip -q ~/Downloads/sqldeveloper-no-jre/sqldeveloper-24.3.1.347.1826-no-jre.zip
ls ~/Applications/sqldeveloper

You should see folders such as ide, jdbc and sqldeveloper, and a sqldeveloper.sh script. There is no jdk folder, which is the point.

If you downloaded the zip with a browser rather than curl, macOS marks the files as quarantined. If SQL Developer later complains about libraries that "cannot be opened", clear the flag on this folder only, after you have verified the checksum:

xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine ~/Applications/sqldeveloper

Step 4: tell SQL Developer which Java to use

SQL Developer reads a per-user file, ~/.sqldeveloper/24.3.1/product.conf. Add a SetJavaHome line pointing at Temurin 17:

mkdir -p ~/.sqldeveloper/24.3.1
echo 'SetJavaHome /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/temurin-17.jdk/Contents/Home' >> ~/.sqldeveloper/24.3.1/product.conf
grep SetJavaHome ~/.sqldeveloper/24.3.1/product.conf

If the file already exists from an earlier install, make sure there is only one uncommented SetJavaHome line.

Step 5: start it 

bash ~/Applications/sqldeveloper/sqldeveloper.sh

The first start takes a little longer. The terminal shows a few warnings like the ones below. They are expected on JDK 17 and harmless:

OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM warning: Options -Xverify:none and -noverify were deprecated in JDK 13 ...
WARNING: System::setSecurityManager will be removed in a future release

Step 6 (optional): a proper app icon for the Dock and Spotlight

Starting from Terminal gets old quickly. This creates a small SQL Developer.app launcher in ~/Applications, with SQL Developer's own icon. You create it yourself on your own Mac, so macOS doesn't quarantine it, and it never touches the SQL Developer folder.

A="$HOME/Applications/SQL Developer.app"
mkdir -p "$A/Contents/MacOS" "$A/Contents/Resources"

cat > "$A/Contents/MacOS/sqldeveloper-launcher" <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
exec /bin/bash "$HOME/Applications/sqldeveloper/sqldeveloper.sh" >>"$HOME/.sqldeveloper/launcher.log" 2>&1
EOF
chmod 755 "$A/Contents/MacOS/sqldeveloper-launcher"

cat > "$A/Contents/Info.plist" <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>CFBundleName</key><string>SQL Developer</string>
  <key>CFBundleIdentifier</key><string>local.sqldeveloper.launcher</string>
  <key>CFBundlePackageType</key><string>APPL</string>
  <key>CFBundleExecutable</key><string>sqldeveloper-launcher</string>
  <key>CFBundleIconFile</key><string>sqldeveloper</string>
  <key>LSUIElement</key><true/>
</dict>
</plist>
EOF

cp ~/Applications/sqldeveloper/sqldeveloper/bin/SQLDeveloperIcons.icns "$A/Contents/Resources/sqldeveloper.icns"
open "$A"

Drag SQL Developer.app from ~/Applications onto the Dock to keep it there. While SQL Developer is running, the Dock shows the Java window's icon, not the launcher's.

Windows: step by step

Step 1: install Temurin 17

Option A, winget (from an elevated PowerShell or Terminal):

winget install EclipseAdoptium.Temurin.17.JDK

Option B, MSI installer: download the Windows x64 .msi from Temurin 17 releases and run it. The defaults add Java to PATH and associate .jar files. Set JAVA_HOME is an optional extra feature that SQL Developer doesn't need.

Temurin installs to C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\<package>, for example C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-17.0.21.9-hotspot. Check the exact folder name in File Explorer, because you will need it in step 4. To check it from a new terminal:

& "C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-17.0.21.9-hotspot\bin\java.exe" -version

Step 2: download SQL Developer without a JDK

From the SQL Developer downloads page, pick Windows 32-bit/64-bit (requires JDK) or Other Platforms. They are the same file. Avoid the "with JDK 17 included" download. In PowerShell:

$dir = "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\sqldeveloper-no-jre"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $dir | Out-Null
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://download.oracle.com/otn_software/java/sqldeveloper/sqldeveloper-24.3.1.347.1826-no-jre.zip" -OutFile "$dir\sqldeveloper-24.3.1.347.1826-no-jre.zip"
Get-FileHash "$dir\sqldeveloper-24.3.1.347.1826-no-jre.zip" -Algorithm SHA256

Compare the hash with the value above.

Step 3: extract it

Extract to a folder you own. A path without spaces avoids surprises, for example C:\Tools:

Expand-Archive "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\sqldeveloper-no-jre\sqldeveloper-24.3.1.347.1826-no-jre.zip" -DestinationPath "C:\Tools"

This gives you C:\Tools\sqldeveloper\sqldeveloper.exe, with no jdk folder.

Step 4: point SQL Developer at Temurin

Either of these works.

Option A, let it ask. Double-click C:\Tools\sqldeveloper\sqldeveloper.exe. When no Java is configured, it asks once for the full path of a JDK. Enter the Temurin folder from step 1, for example:

C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-17.0.21.9-hotspot

Option B, set it up front. Create or edit %APPDATA%\sqldeveloper\24.3.1\product.conf and add one line:

SetJavaHome C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-17.0.21.9-hotspot

In PowerShell:

$conf = "$env:APPDATA\sqldeveloper\24.3.1"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $conf | Out-Null
Add-Content "$conf\product.conf" 'SetJavaHome C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-17.0.21.9-hotspot'

Option A writes exactly this line for you, so you will find it in the same file afterwards.

Step 5: start it and add a shortcut

Run C:\Tools\sqldeveloper\sqldeveloper.exe. To pin it, right-click the running app in the taskbar and choose Pin to taskbar. Or right-click sqldeveloper.exe and choose Show more options > Send to > Desktop (create shortcut).

Check that you are really on Temurin

In SQL Developer, open Help > About and go to the Properties tab. Look for:

  • java.vendor: should read Eclipse Adoptium
  • java.home: should point to the Temurin folder

Tip: type java.v in the search box at the top of the Properties tab to filter the list.

Don't be alarmed by java.vm.specification.vendor = Oracle Corporation. That row names the owner of the Java specification, and every Java build reports it, Temurin included. What counts is java.vendor and java.vm.vendor.

On macOS you can also check from Terminal while SQL Developer is running:

ps -axo command | grep '[t]emurin-17.jdk'

Clean up the old Oracle JDK

Once the Temurin-based install works:

  • macOS: remove the old SQLDeveloper.app as a whole. Don't remove pieces of it, for the code-signing reason above. Then check /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines and /usr/libexec/java_home -V for any other Oracle JDKs.
  • Windows: delete the old SQL Developer folder that contains a jdk subfolder. Then check Settings > Apps for any "Java" or "Oracle JDK" entries.

Your connections, preferences and SQL history are stored in your user profile, not in the application folder. A same-version reinstall picks them up automatically. Still, export your connections first (right-click Connections > Export Connections) if you want a safety net.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Cause Fix
macOS: "SQLDeveloper is damaged and can't be opened. You should move it to the Trash." Files inside the signed .app were changed Reinstall using the no-JDK zip, and don't modify the .app
Unrecognized verification option: -Xverify:none Running on a JDK newer than 17 that no longer accepts the option (seen on JDK 27) Point SetJavaHome at Temurin 17
Module jdk.jsobject not found, required by javafx.web Running on a recent JDK that no longer ships jdk.jsobject (seen on JDK 27) Point SetJavaHome at Temurin 17
SQL Developer keeps asking for a JDK, or nothing happens on start SetJavaHome points to a folder that doesn't exist Fix the path in product.conf. It must be the JDK home: the folder that contains bin.
macOS: library "cannot be opened" after a browser download Quarantine flag on the extracted files xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine ~/Applications/sqldeveloper (after verifying the checksum)
Deprecation warnings in the terminal on start Normal on JDK 17 None needed

Summary

  1. Install Temurin 17.
  2. Download the no-JDK SQL Developer zip ("Other Platforms").
  3. Unzip it to a folder you own.
  4. Put SetJavaHome <temurin-17 home> in your per-user product.conf.
  5. Start it, check Help > About > Properties, and remove the old bundle.

Fifteen minutes, no Oracle JDK on disk, and the same SQL Developer you already know.

More from me: Oracle and OCI tools

If you work with Oracle and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), these open-source projects may save you some time too. Each has a write-up here on dev.to:

  • OCI draw.io Architect: a Claude Code plugin that generates draw.io OCI architecture diagrams from your Terraform configs or from a plain description. Repo on GitHub | Article: Generate OCI Architecture Diagrams from Terraform with One Claude Code Command
  • CIDR Atlas: a local-first CIDR inventory and allocation planner for OCI networks, built with Flutter, Dart and SQLite, with a desktop CLI. Repo on GitHub | Article: CIDR Atlas, a local-first CIDR planner for OCI networks

On a Mac? I also maintain a few native macOS utilities: RepoDeck (git status of all your repos in one dashboard), AltTab for macOS (Windows-style window switcher) and NoSleep (keep your Mac awake from the menu bar).

All of my projects are on GitHub, and my other articles are on my dev.to profile. For updates and new write-ups, follow me on LinkedIn or X. If this guide saved you an audit finding, a star on a repo or a follow here helps more people find it. And if you've run SQL Developer on Temurin on Windows or Linux, tell me how it went in the comments.

title: Why we don't offer a free database, and what we built instead
description:
TL;DR: A free container can be free because it sleeps when nobody is looking. A database cannot sleep, so every free database you will find comes with a clock, a pause button or a shared instance. That is why there is no free database here, and why we built a $1, 12-hour trial of the real managed add-on instead. The same logic applies to Redis and RabbitMQ.

The most common question we get after "is the free tier really free?" is "why is there no free database?". Fair question.

We give away containers, and a container without a database is half an app. The answer is about what can sleep and what cannot, and it is worth explaining, because it also explains why every free database you will find comes with a clock or a pause button.

Why a container can be free

A free container on SnapDeploy sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic, and the free tier is capped at 100 container-hours a month. Most free containers are awake for a few hours a month: they serve a demo, a portfolio, a side project someone opens now and then.

The rest of the time they use nothing. Sleeping is the whole trick.

It is what lets a free tier exist without an expiry date or a card, because a container nobody is looking at is not consuming anything.

Why a database cannot

A database cannot sleep the way a web container can. If Postgres is stopped when a request arrives, the app that depends on it fails: connection refused, then a pool of dead connections, then a timeout page shown to the visitor.

So a database has to run around the clock, and it needs persistent storage that survives restarts, backups that run whether or not you visited this week, and someone to answer when the connection string stops working. None of that stops when the project is abandoned after a weekend.

A free database is a promise to keep something running forever for every account that ever clicked "create", and we would rather not make a promise we would have to quietly break later.

How the others make "free database" work

Every free database we know of solves the same problem with one of three tricks. None of them is dishonest; they are just worth knowing before you build on one.

Trick Who What it means for you
Expiry Render: free Postgres expires 30 days after creation, with a 14-day grace period Fine for a demo; a calendar reminder for anything else.
Pause when idle Supabase: projects pause after 7 days without activity; Neon: compute suspends when idle and resumes on the next query, within 100 compute-hours a month The first request after a pause is slow or fails; your app needs retry logic.
Shared, capped instance MongoDB Atlas M0: 512 MB on a shared cluster, no expiry Genuinely free for small data; throttled throughput and no dedicated resources.

Neon and Atlas are good choices for a hobby app and we say so in our own guides. Their economics work because they built engines that can pause or share at a scale we do not operate at. We are a container host; we run stock PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and MongoDB on dedicated instances next to your containers, and a dedicated instance does not pause.

What we did instead

  • A $1 trial that is the real thing. The DB Sprint Pack is 12 hours of a full Mini-tier instance (PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8, MariaDB 11, MongoDB 7, Redis 7 or RabbitMQ 3) for $1, with persistent storage, daily backups and 50 connections. Not a throttled sandbox: the same instance you would pay for monthly, for long enough to find out whether it fits. Data is kept for 24 hours after the trial ends, and converting to a monthly plan re-attaches the same volume, so nothing is migrated.
  • Plain monthly prices. Mini is $29/month for the SQL engines and MongoDB, $12 for Redis, $14 for RabbitMQ, with the admin tools (pgweb, phpMyAdmin, mongo-express) and daily backups included. The prices are on one page, they do not change with usage, and they are the same for everyone.
  • No lock-in on the free side. A free container talks to Neon, Supabase, Atlas or any other database over a normal connection string. We would rather you use a good free external database than a bad free internal one.

What the $1 trial is for, in practice

  • A demo or a hackathon. Twelve hours covers a pitch, a workshop or a weekend build day, with a real Postgres instead of a SQLite file that vanishes on the next deploy.
  • Testing a migration. Restore a dump into a Mini for a dollar, run the app against it, and know whether the schema and the connection limits fit before you commit to a month.
  • Trying an engine you have not used. The same dollar buys MongoDB, MariaDB, Redis or RabbitMQ at the same size, with the browser admin tool attached, so the comparison is between engines, not between pricing pages.

What it is not for is production. The 12 hours end, the instance stops, and after the 24-hour grace period the volume is gone unless you converted. That limit is the point: it is what lets the trial be real rather than throttled.

The same logic for Redis and RabbitMQ

People sometimes ask why the cache is not free either, since Redis is "just memory". It is a process that has to be up at 3 a.m. when your container wakes and asks for a session, and a cache that sleeps is a cache that is empty when you need it.

Redis Mini is $12/month and RabbitMQ Mini $14/month for the same reason the databases are $29: they run whether or not you do. For an app that is idle most of the time, a serverless provider such as Upstash, which charges per command and has a free plan, is the better fit, and we say so in our Redis guide.

Would we ever add one?

Maybe, in the pause-when-idle form, if we build the engine work that makes it safe: a layer that holds connections while an instance resumes, so applications see a slow query rather than an error. That is a real project, not a pricing switch. Until then, the honest answer to "why no free database" is that a database cannot sleep, and free things on this platform are free because they can.

Current prices for every add-on are on the add-on pricing page; the compute free tier (4 containers, 100 container-hours a month, no card) is on the free tier docs page. Render, Supabase, Neon and Atlas limits are as published on their pages in September 2026.

title: My SVG Shows Up in the Browser but Not in React. Here's the Checklist I Use
description:
You open the .svg file in the browser and it looks perfect. You drop it into a React component and... nothing. No error, or a vague one, and an empty space where the icon should be.

The file is almost never the problem. Something between the file and the DOM is. Here is the order I check things in.

First, two quick checks. Open the console and look for a React warning. Then inspect the spot where the icon should be:

  • No <svg> or <img> element at all? It's the import or the component.
  • The element is there but blank? It's size, paint, or loading.

1. The import gives you a URL, not a component

Most bundlers turn import logo from "./logo.svg" into a URL string. Render that as <Logo /> and React gets a string where it expected a component.

  • Vite: add vite-plugin-svgr. In its current major version only imports ending in ?react become components: import Logo from "./logo.svg?react". A plain import stays a URL. For TypeScript, add /// <reference types="vite-plugin-svgr/client" />.
  • Create React App: the component is the named export ReactComponent; the default export is still the URL.
  • Next.js: without an SVG loader the import is an object with src, width, and height. <img src={logo} /> renders src="[object Object]". Use logo.src or next/image.

2. Raw SVG was pasted straight into JSX

JSX is not HTML. Some differences only warn (class, stroke-width), but these actually break the icon:

<svg style="fill:red">        // throws: style must be an object
<use xlink:href="#a" />        // Babel: namespace tags not supported
<!-- exported from Figma -->   // syntax error in JSX
<svg viewbox="0 0 24 24">      // lowercase, not treated as viewBox

Fixed versions: style={{ fill: "red" }}, href="#a", {/* comment */}, and viewBox.

3. No viewBox, or no size

If the element exists but takes no space, check its computed width and height.

  • Missing viewBox: a 512-unit drawing in a 24px box shows only its top-left corner. Some optimizer presets remove viewBox (SVGO 3's default preset does).
  • Zero or percentage size: width="100%" inside a parent with no width is zero.
  • Flex rows: give the icon a fixed width/height and flex-shrink: 0.
  • 1em sizing: inside a parent with font-size: 0, the icon disappears.

4. It's drawn, just in an invisible color

fill="none" with no stroke draws nothing. Outline icon sets rely on stroke, so removing stroke removes the icon. And currentColor takes the CSS color of the parent, so white text on a white button gives you a white icon.

5. Duplicate IDs in gradients, masks, and clip paths

IDs in inline SVG are global to the page. Render the same icon twice and every url(#id) points at the first copy. If that copy sits inside a hidden menu, the visible ones can lose their gradient or clip path. Generate a unique ID per instance with React's useId().

If the file loads but never draws

Check that the server sends image/svg+xml as the content type, and that your Content Security Policy allows the source you load it from.

I keep the full version of this checklist, with code for each framework and the MIME/CSP details, here: SVG Not Showing in React? Causes and Fixes. If you'd rather skip the attribute work entirely, I also built a free SVG to JSX converter that runs SVGR in the browser and keeps the viewBox (nothing is uploaded).

What's the weirdest reason an SVG went blank on you?

title: Safety Side Effects of Preventative Persona Steering: An Empirical Audit
description:
arXiv:2611.17620v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.

title: More of What You Say in Meetings Will Be Written Down by Software
description:
Join a call at many companies now and you will see a small notice that the meeting is being transcribed. When it ends, a summary appears in the chat, with a list of decisions and actions, sometimes before you have closed the window. The main video meeting tools all offer some version of this, and more organisations are switching it on by default.

That changes something quietly important about meetings. For years, a lot of what was said in them was gone the moment people left the room. Now more of it becomes searchable text that people who were not there can read, sometimes months later.

There are real benefits. People who missed the meeting can catch up. Colleagues working in their second language can check what was said. Actions are less likely to be forgotten. Used well, these tools can make meetings fairer.

But they also bring new habits worth learning early.

Read the summary, especially when you are named in it. Automated summaries can be wrong. They can attribute a point to the wrong person, turn a maybe into a decision, or miss the caveat that mattered most. If the summary says you agreed to deliver something by Friday and you did not, correct it in writing that day. Once a summary has been shared, people tend to treat it as the record.

Speak as if a stranger may read it later, because one might. That does not mean being dull or guarded. It means saying what you mean clearly, being careful with jokes about named people, and not discussing anyone's health or personal life in a meeting that is being transcribed.

Know where the off switch is, and when to ask for it. Some conversations, like personal matters, sensitive staffing discussions, or early ideas that need room to be wrong, are better held without a transcript. It is reasonable to ask at the start whether this one needs recording.

And if you chair meetings, take responsibility for the summary yourself. Check it, fix it, and send it on. The tool can write things down. Deciding what was really agreed is still a job for people.

– Asael Shinder

title: ECS 建站上线前，把“能打开”变成可交接的验收记录
description:
作者说明：本文由 YunECS Pro 所属团队整理，文末链接指向我们维护的独立技术指南，与阿里云官方没有隶属关系。

网站在自己的电脑上打开一次，只能说明一条访问路径在那个时间点成功。正式上线还需要回答：值班人员能否接管，数据能否恢复，用户失败时有没有告警，以及发布出现问题后能否回退。下面给出一套适用于小型 ECS 网站的验收方法。文中的例子是操作设计示例，不是已经完成的客户实测。

先写通过条件，再改配置

建立一张资源台账，至少记录账号主体、地域、可用区、实例标识、系统版本、应用版本、磁盘、域名与负责人。随后写清本次发布窗口、检查项目、通过条件和回退触发条件。例如，一个带询价表单的网站，需要验证的不只是首页状态码，还包括表单是否真正被后端接收、失败是否有日志、负责人是否收到通知。每条记录留下测试时间与证据，避免交接时只能依赖口头描述。

维护人员使用符合职责的 RAM 身份，提前验证常用管理通道和应急通道。应用访问云 API 时，评估实例角色与临时凭据，不要为了部署方便把长期高权限密钥写进代码库。台账可以保存身份用途和密钥保管负责人，不应保存密钥本身。

沿着真实请求路径验收网络

从应用本身开始检查：进程是否存活，监听地址与端口是否正确，本机请求是否成功。随后检查系统防火墙，再检查 ECS 实际关联的安全组。测试来源、协议、端口和方向必须对应同一次请求。管理端口只向必要维护来源开放；数据库和缓存按实际应用路径授权。

如果网站经过 CDN 或负载均衡，把用户到入口、入口到源站分开记录。浏览器访问成功可能是命中了缓存，不能直接证明源站健康。健康检查的来源与业务回源来源也可能不同，应按所用产品说明核对。每次仅修改已定位的问题，先保留原配置和维护连接，修改后使用新连接复测，排障结束处理临时规则。

域名与 HTTPS 要覆盖所有计划入口

核对 DNS 托管方、A 与 AAAA 记录、实际公网入口，以及根域名和使用中的子域名。对使用 IPv6 的访问者，只验证 IPv4 不够。证书检查覆盖域名、有效期和链，使用代理时还要分别检查对外 TLS 与回源连接。若部署 Nginx，可先做配置语法检查，再按维护流程重载，最后验证跳转、静态资源和接口。

测试表中应包含正常页面、缺失页面、HTTP 到 HTTPS 的跳转和主域名规范化。证书自动续期也需要负责人和失败告警。中国大陆地域承载网站时，应提前核实适用的备案要求，不能把服务器已经创建视为网站可以直接公开上线。

备份完成之后，还要证明能恢复

将代码、配置、数据库和上传文件分别列入保护范围，并为每一类数据确定恢复目标。磁盘快照与数据库一致性备份解决的问题不同：有快照不代表应用事务已经处于可恢复状态。发布前应保存备份标识、完成时间和一致性条件。

优先在隔离副本中演练恢复，检查应用版本、数据、挂载点、文件权限与外部依赖是否一起恢复。记录实际恢复时间，再判断是否满足业务要求。回滚原盘会覆盖快照之后的变更，因此需要事先约定新订单、新文件或数据库写入如何处理。只写“失败就回滚”无法指导值班人员处理数据。

让告警真的抵达一个人

确认 CPU、磁盘、网络和应用错误有持续数据，所需操作系统指标具备相应采集条件。除了实例指标，再从外部检查关键 URL。安排一次受控告警测试，验证通知到达、负责人响应、故障恢复后可以复核。阈值应结合业务基线，避免把演示阈值直接复制到生产。

最终上线记录应能回答：谁在什么时间，以哪个版本，通过了哪些功能测试；哪些问题尚未通过，由谁处理；何时需要回退，回退后怎样验收。需要逐项填写时，可使用我们整理的 ECS 上线检查清单。它适合作为验收起点，具体限制和操作前置条件仍需对照当前官方文档与自己的部署环境。

title: How to Pick Cron or Message Queue Delivery for Scheduled Cleanup
description:
Short answer: for scheduled data cleanup, use cron to run a recurring database scan until one batch can no longer finish comfortably inside its interval; add a message queue when you need bounded worker concurrency, independent retries, or isolation from slow downstream work. In either design, make the Postgres cleanup transition conditional and safe to repeat. The delivery mechanism can wake the work up, but the database must decide whether a held reservation is still eligible to expire.

For a customer-support system, the job is narrow: release reservations whose fixed hold window has ended. Don't begin with permanent deletion. Mark a row expired first, preserve enough information to audit the transition, and run physical retention as a separate policy. I've been paged for both missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, and the useful lesson is plain: a timer is not a completion guarantee, while a delivered message is not proof that the handler committed.

Start with the failure signal, not the scheduler

Define the invariant before choosing infrastructure: a reservation in held state may become expired after hold_expires_at, and repeating that attempt must not produce another business transition. That gives the operator something stronger than “cron ran at 02:00.” It gives a queryable outcome.

Track the age of the oldest overdue held reservation. Also track rows claimed, rows changed, batch duration, retry count, and the gap between hold_expires_at and expired_at. A run that reports success after changing zero rows can be healthy; a steadily growing overdue age cannot. Alert on the business lag, with the threshold tied to the support workflow's tolerance, rather than alerting merely because one trigger was late.

Duplicates deserve equal attention. A queue consumer may receive a message again after its visibility timeout, so the handler has to tolerate another delivery. Extending visibility can give long-running work more time, but it doesn't remove the need for an idempotent state change. If a handler calls a rate-limited downstream HTTP service, treat 429 Too Many Requests as backpressure and honor Retry-After when it is present; don't turn that response into a tight retry loop.

One detail changes the whole design: expiring the reservation and sending a customer notification are two separate effects. Commit the expiry in Postgres first. Represent any notification as durable follow-up work, preferably in the same transaction through an outbox record, so a process exit can't leave an untraceable gap between database commit and message publication.

Should scheduled data cleanup jobs use cron or a message queue?

Cron is the smaller operational system when a bounded query can find all overdue rows, each transition is quick, and a later run can catch anything missed by an earlier trigger. It is often the cheapest option in that situation because it reuses the database and scheduler already being operated. The catch is that a single scanning process becomes a poor fit when work duration is highly variable, downstream calls dominate runtime, or one batch needs more parallelism than the database should absorb at once.

A message queue earns its place when each reservation needs independently paced work, consumers need explicit concurrency limits, or retries must be isolated per item. It also adds moving parts: publication has to be durable, consumers need visibility-timeout discipline, poison work needs a terminal policy, and operators must watch both queue age and database lag. A queue is therefore not automatically the safer or cheaper choice. It shifts the failure boundary.

For this reservation case, the practical default is a hybrid only when scale requires it: a periodic scanner discovers eligible IDs and records outbox work, then queue workers perform bounded follow-up. The database transition remains conditional. Stick with the direct scanner when expiry is only a local row update and batches stay well within the operating window; choose queued workers when measured lag or downstream latency proves that isolation is needed.

I'm not sure where that boundary sits for your workload. Query plans, row counts, hold-window clustering, and downstream latency will resolve it; a vendor price table won't.

Make the reservation transition safe to repeat

The following Go program runs a bounded scan. It uses row locks with SKIP LOCKED, so overlapping workers can take different eligible rows, and the WHERE status = 'held' predicate makes a repeated attempt a no-op after the first commit. Set DATABASE_URL in the process environment and run it from the scheduler you already trust.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "os"
    "time"

    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"
)

const expireBatchSQL = `
WITH eligible AS (
    SELECT id
    FROM reservations
    WHERE status = 'held'
      AND hold_expires_at <= $1
    ORDER BY hold_expires_at, id
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    LIMIT $2
)
UPDATE reservations AS r
SET status = 'expired',
    expired_at = $1
FROM eligible
WHERE r.id = eligible.id
  AND r.status = 'held'
RETURNING r.id`

func expireBatch(ctx context.Context, db *pgxpool.Pool, now time.Time, limit int) (int, error) {
    rows, err := db.Query(ctx, expireBatchSQL, now, limit)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    changed := 0
    for rows.Next() {
        var reservationID string
        if err := rows.Scan(&reservationID); err != nil {
            return changed, err
        }
        changed++
    }
    return changed, rows.Err()
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    db, err := pgxpool.New(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer db.Close()

    started := time.Now()
    changed, err := expireBatch(ctx, db, time.Now().UTC(), 500)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("reservation_expiry changed=%d duration=%s\n", changed, time.Since(started))
}

Keep the transaction short. The code does no network I/O while locks are held, and its batch limit is a guardrail rather than a throughput promise. If more than 500 rows are overdue, the next invocation can claim another batch. If the cleanup interval is too slow to drain the backlog, first confirm the query plan and index for the eligibility predicate, then increase invocation frequency or worker count carefully while watching database lock time and lag. For queued follow-up, use the same reflex in the consumer: pass a stable reservation ID, attempt a conditional transition, acknowledge only after the database commit, and treat “zero rows changed” as an already-completed delivery rather than an error. Make the outbox identifier unique so retrying the scanner does not publish an unbounded number of logical copies. Consider the ugly timing window: worker A commits the expiry, loses its lease before acknowledgement, and worker B receives the same reservation. Worker B's conditional update changes zero rows, checks that the current state is already expired, and acknowledges. No second notification is implied merely by that duplicate delivery, because notification work has its own unique outbox key. If worker A instead loses its lease before commit, its transaction ends without a committed transition and worker B can perform the update. This distinction belongs in the runbook because an operator staring at two delivery log lines needs to know whether they represent two attempts or two customer-visible effects. Exactly-once language hides that question; an observable, repeatable state transition answers it.

Attempts are not effects.

Verify deployment and keep rollback boring

Before enabling writes, run the eligibility query in read-only mode against production-shaped data. Inspect its plan, estimate the largest expiry wave, and verify that rows with a future hold_expires_at, a non-held status, or an already populated expired_at remain untouched. Then enable a small batch and compare three counts: eligible before, changed during the run, and eligible after. Re-run the same IDs. The second transition count should be zero.

Deploy with a kill switch that prevents new claims without terminating in-flight database commits. During rollout, watch oldest-overdue age and batch duration together. Falling lag with stable database latency is the desired signal. Rising lag means capacity is inadequate; rising database latency means the cleanup is competing too aggressively. Pause, reduce the batch or concurrency, and reassess the plan.

Rollback is operational, not magical. Disable new claims first. Let current transactions finish, then verify the invariant and preserve the transition log. Automatically changing expired rows back to held can reopen reservations that support agents have already replaced, so restoration should be a reviewed business action based on recorded IDs and timestamps. This is why soft expiry belongs ahead of irreversible deletion.

Test the awkward boundaries too: two workers selecting at once, a retry after commit but before acknowledgement, a reservation updated by an agent at the cutoff, and a clock value exactly equal to hold_expires_at. Use a database-controlled or explicitly passed UTC timestamp consistently. Short test. Big payoff.

Use a decision rule the on-call can explain

Choose the direct scheduled scan when the work is a local conditional update, overdue rows are efficiently discoverable, missed triggers are recovered by the next scan, and the measured batch duration has comfortable headroom. It minimizes coordination and keeps diagnosis in one place.

Choose scanner-plus-queue when per-item work varies widely, downstream rate limits require pacing, independent retries matter, or database lag cannot be controlled with short batches. It is not suitable as a substitute for idempotency, nor does it repair an unsafe publish-after-commit gap by itself. Use a transactional outbox or another atomic handoff pattern for that boundary.

The cheapest architecture is the one that meets the delivery objective with the fewest failure modes your team must operate. For stale customer-support reservations, start with the conditional Postgres scan, measure business lag, and introduce queued delivery only in response to evidence. Keep the invariant unchanged across both designs. That makes migration dull — which is exactly what an expiry runbook should aim for.

References

  • AWS, “Amazon SQS visibility timeout”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • MDN, “429 Too Many Requests”: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429

Further reading

title: Electrocardiographic Imaging via Posterior Sampling under Operator Discrepancy
description:
arXiv:2611.17851v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface potentials, an ill-posed inverse problem. Diffusion posterior samplers combine a learned prior with an explicit forward operator that they assume to be accurate. In ECGI this operator is only an estimate, because the body changes with respiration and posture, and body composition such as subcutaneous fat is rarely known for an individual patient. The resulting operator discrepancy is structured and depends on the heart signal. We introduce OpDis-PS, a diffusion posterior sampler that models this discrepancy instead of treating it as signal-independent noise. OpDis-PS learns how the discrepancy depends on the signal, folds this into a corrected forward operator, and reconstructs with a fixed prior across all operator conditions. We study two realistic sources of discrepancy, changing lung conductivity and an added subcutaneous-fat layer. Across both, OpDis-PS reconstructs more accurately than classical regularization and learned predictors, with its largest gains on held-out cardiac pathologies.

title: PaperCritic: Training AI Reviewers to Assess the Soundness of Papers
description:
arXiv:2611.17834v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI conference submissions grow rapidly, AI reviewers are being considered as an alternative. However, simply imitating human reviewing is problematic because reviewing serves multiple purposes, including evaluating papers' soundness, interestingness, and clarity, the last two of which are subjective. In this work, we focus solely on evaluating soundness, the most important and objective criterion, and define the learning objective as jointly maximizing (1) precision, based on the soundness and substantiveness of review points, and (2) recall, the coverage of high-quality reference review points. Under this problem formulation, we construct a quality-labeled review point dataset, PaperSound-23K, using 1K ICLR submissions and 23K human-written and LLM-generated review points. Using this dataset, we train an AI reviewer model, PaperCritic, through reinforcement learning with the F1 score of precision and recall as the reward. Our experiments show that PaperCritic outperforms frontier models and models trained with other AI reviewer training methods on an in-domain test set. Surprisingly, learning to review ICLR submissions also transfers to reviewing Nature-family papers and even to out-of-domain reviewing tasks (e.g., code review, legal contract review, and feedback on story writing).

title: RiverScan: Learning to Accumulate on River Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.18005v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate runoff prediction across large river basins requires models to capture heterogeneous local hydrological responses and their accumulation downstream. River-network connectivity provides a natural structure for this task, but using it effectively requires learning how to combine contributions from subcatchments of different sizes. We frame this challenge as learning to accumulate and introduce RiverScan, a spatial operator based on area-weighted selective state-space recurrence. RiverScan recursively combines local temporal representations with accumulated upstream states in topological order. Contributing-area fractions account for subcatchment size, while learned retention controls how upstream information persists downstream. Experiments on 608 stations in the Danube basin show that RiverScan outperforms the evaluated temporal and graph baselines in overall predictive performance. Structural controls and ablations demonstrate that composing heterogeneous subcatchment representations in a manner aligned with hydrological accumulation substantially improves runoff prediction, with the benefits of correct topology growing along the river-network hierarchy. These findings establish physically structured accumulation as an effective inductive bias for hydrological modeling and motivate finer-grained, fully distributed AI-based hydrological models.

title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.17610v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

title: Robot Communication and APIs — Ch.12: API Case Studies [EN]
description:
STATERA Library · Series 08 · Volume 06 · Chapter 12 · EN
Source: https://github.com/Statera-Library/08_Vol_06_Robot_Communication_and_APIs/blob/main/Chapter_12_API_Case_Studies/Chapter_12_API_Case_Studies_EN.md

Volume 06 Robot Communication and APIs

12. API Case Studies

12.01 Hills Indoor AMR: REST / WebSocket API Architecture

Indoor autonomous mobile robots operate in environments where navigation, task execution, human interaction, and fleet supervision must be coordinated through interfaces that remain understandable to enterprise software. A practical architecture therefore separates transactional operations from continuously changing robot information. REST APIs provide a stable resource-oriented interface for commands and configuration, while WebSocket channels provide persistent bidirectional connections for real-time operational data.

The REST layer represents each AMR as a collection of resources such as robots, missions, maps, charging stations, tasks, diagnostics, and configuration profiles. Enterprise applications can retrieve robot information through GET requests, create missions through POST operations, modify permitted configuration through PUT or PATCH, and cancel appropriate resources through defined control endpoints. This resource abstraction prevents external systems from depending directly on internal ROS 2 nodes or hardware-specific interfaces.

A typical indoor AMR exposes identification, operational mode, localization state, battery status, current mission, fault information, and capability metadata through a robot resource. Mission resources contain destinations, waypoints, priorities, payload requirements, execution constraints, and lifecycle information. Separating robot resources from mission resources allows the API to preserve a clear distinction between the physical platform and the work assigned to that platform.

Mission creation is particularly suitable for REST because it represents a discrete transaction with a persistent result. A client may submit a transport request containing pickup and delivery locations, priority, payload information, and optional scheduling constraints. The server validates the request, creates a mission identifier, and returns an accepted or created response. The client can subsequently retrieve the mission resource without maintaining a continuous connection to the robot.

REST alone becomes inefficient when dashboards or fleet applications require rapidly changing information. Repeated polling for position, velocity, battery level, navigation state, obstacle conditions, and mission progress generates unnecessary HTTP transactions and introduces latency between an event and its observation. WebSocket complements REST by establishing a persistent communication channel through which the AMR or fleet server can publish operational changes immediately.

The WebSocket data model should use explicit event categories rather than transmitting arbitrary internal messages. Typical categories include robot.status, robot.pose, mission.progress, battery.status, navigation.state, safety.event, diagnostic.event, and connection.state. Every message should contain a robot identifier, timestamp, event type, schema version, and payload. This envelope structure makes real-time streams easier to validate, route, record, and evolve independently of individual robot implementations.

REST and WebSocket should share a common domain model. A mission created through REST must use the same mission identifier that appears in WebSocket progress events, while robot identifiers and state definitions must remain consistent across both interfaces. This avoids the architectural mistake of building separate command and monitoring models. The client can create a mission through REST, receive its identifier, subscribe to relevant WebSocket events, and track execution using the same semantic objects.

Inside the robot, an API gateway or edge service isolates external communication from the real-time control domain. REST requests are translated into validated high-level commands and delivered to mission management, navigation, charging, or diagnostic services. WebSocket publishers collect selected state changes from these services and transform them into external event schemas. Low-level motor commands, raw control loops, and safety-critical actuation remain outside the public API boundary.

This separation is essential because an enterprise API must never become the timing mechanism for motion control. HTTP and WebSocket communication can experience network delay, congestion, reconnection, or client failure. Navigation controllers, obstacle avoidance, emergency stopping, and motor control therefore continue locally with deterministic or bounded behavior. External APIs request intentions such as "execute mission" or "go to station," while onboard controllers determine how those intentions are safely executed.

Command semantics require explicit lifecycle management. After accepting a command, the system should distinguish states such as accepted, queued, executing, completed, canceled, rejected, and failed. Long-running operations should not keep an HTTP request open until physical completion. Instead, REST returns an operation or mission identifier immediately, and subsequent state transitions are available through resource queries and WebSocket events. This pattern scales better and provides clearer failure handling.

Idempotency is equally important because wireless communication can fail after a client sends a command but before it receives the response. Repeating a mission-creation request without protection could generate duplicate robot jobs. An idempotency key or client-generated request identifier allows the server to recognize retries and return the original result. Cancellation and configuration operations should similarly define whether repeated requests are harmless, rejected, or interpreted according to current state.

Indoor AMRs frequently move between wireless access points, enter elevators, pass through areas with weak coverage, or temporarily lose communication with the fleet server. WebSocket clients must therefore implement heartbeat monitoring, ping-pong mechanisms, timeout detection, exponential reconnection, and session recovery. Critical robot functions continue locally during interruption, while buffered operational events can be synchronized after connectivity returns according to retention and priority policies.

After reconnection, clients should not assume that every missed WebSocket event can be replayed. A robust design treats REST resources as authoritative snapshots and WebSocket messages as notifications of change. The client reconnects, retrieves the latest robot and mission states through REST, and then resumes event subscriptions. Sequence numbers or event offsets can additionally identify gaps when ordered event recovery is required for auditing or operational analysis.

Security must protect both interfaces consistently. REST endpoints should use HTTPS, while real-time connections use WSS. Authentication can be based on OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, signed tokens, certificates, or enterprise identity infrastructure according to deployment requirements. Authorization should distinguish monitoring, mission creation, mission cancellation, configuration, maintenance, and administrative privileges rather than granting every authenticated application unrestricted robot control.

Robot identity deserves separate treatment from human identity. Each AMR can possess a unique device credential or certificate, while operators and enterprise applications receive identities associated with defined roles. This allows the system to determine whether a message originated from a specific robot, fleet service, maintenance tool, WMS, or authenticated operator. Audit records can consequently associate important commands with their authenticated origin and execution result.

Safety-related events should receive higher semantic priority than ordinary telemetry. Emergency-stop activation, localization loss, blocked motion, protective-field activation, collision risk, hardware faults, and mission failures should be represented as structured events containing severity, source, timestamp, acknowledgement requirements, and recovery information. WebSocket delivery improves operational awareness, but reception of these messages must never replace the robot\'s local safety mechanisms.

Bandwidth management becomes important as fleet size grows. Publishing every pose update from every robot to every connected dashboard wastes network and server resources. Clients should be able to subscribe by robot, event class, fleet, or operational area, while the server applies appropriate update rates and change thresholds. High-frequency visualization data can be reduced independently from critical alarms, allowing one communication architecture to support both detailed diagnostics and large fleet supervision.

The architecture also provides a clean integration boundary for warehouse management systems, hospital logistics applications, building systems, elevators, automatic doors, and fleet management software. These systems interact with standardized mission and robot resources rather than directly controlling ROS 2 topics or vendor-specific navigation components. This abstraction supports replacement or upgrading of internal software while preserving stable interfaces for external applications.

Observability should cover both communication paths as one operational system. Useful measurements include REST request latency, response codes, authentication failures, mission submission rates, WebSocket connection counts, event throughput, reconnect frequency, dropped messages, queue depth, and end-to-end event latency. Correlating API requests with mission identifiers and robot identifiers allows engineers to trace a transaction from enterprise request through robot execution and final completion.

Version management should protect deployed integrations over the long service life of industrial robots. REST resources may use explicit API versions, while WebSocket event envelopes carry schema versions that allow consumers to interpret evolving payloads. Additive changes are preferable when possible, and deprecated fields should remain available during defined transition periods. Contract testing can verify that WMS, RMS, dashboards, and robot software remain compatible before deployment.

The combined REST-WebSocket pattern therefore creates a practical boundary between enterprise transactions and real-time robot observation. REST provides durable resources, explicit command semantics, configuration access, and recovery snapshots, while WebSocket provides efficient asynchronous status and event delivery. Together they form an API architecture suited to indoor AMRs without exposing safety-critical control loops or tightly coupling external applications to internal middleware.

In a production deployment, the most important architectural principle is not simply choosing two communication technologies, but assigning each technology the correct responsibility. REST governs stable resources and transactional intent; WebSocket distributes time-sensitive state changes; onboard software preserves autonomous and safe operation; and the API gateway enforces identity, policy, validation, and observability. This division creates an extensible foundation for individual AMRs, multi-robot fleets, and enterprise-scale robotic services.

12.02 Outdoor AMR gRPC-Based Real-Time Control API

Outdoor autonomous mobile robots operate across campuses, industrial yards, ports, construction sites, logistics facilities, and infrastructure corridors where communication latency and network quality can vary significantly. For these systems, gRPC provides a strongly typed, high-performance API layer based on Protocol Buffers and HTTP/2. It is particularly suitable for structured command exchange, continuous telemetry, mission coordination, and service-to-service communication between outdoor AMRs, edge servers, and fleet controllers.

The architecture should separate external mission-level communication from safety-critical onboard control. A remote fleet controller may request navigation toward a destination, initiate an inspection route, modify mission parameters, or retrieve diagnostic information through gRPC services. However, steering, traction control, obstacle avoidance, emergency braking, and other deterministic functions remain within the robot. The API communicates operational intent rather than directly closing real-time motor-control loops over an unreliable external network.

Protocol Buffers define the communication contract shared by the robot and external systems. Messages can describe robot identity, pose, velocity, localization quality, battery state, mission information, detected obstacles, system health, and command results using explicit field types. Compared with loosely structured payloads, this schema-driven approach reduces interpretation ambiguity and supports automatic client and server code generation for languages commonly used in robotic systems, including C++, Python, Java, and Go.

Unary remote procedure calls are appropriate for operations that naturally follow a request-response pattern. Examples include retrieving robot information, requesting current diagnostics, loading mission parameters, changing an operating mode, or querying supported capabilities. The client sends one structured request and receives one structured response. Deadlines should be defined for each call so that communication failure or an unavailable robot cannot leave a remote application waiting indefinitely for a response.

Server streaming becomes valuable when the fleet controller requires continuous information from an outdoor AMR. After establishing a subscription, the robot can stream pose, velocity, battery level, localization confidence, mission progress, safety state, and diagnostic information over a persistent HTTP/2 connection. This eliminates repeated polling and enables the receiver to process state changes as they arrive while preserving a clearly defined protobuf schema for every transmitted message.

Client streaming can support cases in which an edge or fleet system needs to transmit a sequence of related data to the robot service. Route segments, map updates, inspection parameters, or batches of operational information may be delivered as a stream and acknowledged after processing. This model should be used selectively because unrestricted continuous command transmission can create unnecessary coupling between remote infrastructure and the robot\'s autonomous execution layer.

Bidirectional streaming provides the most flexible gRPC communication model for interactive robot operations. The robot and supervisory system can exchange messages independently over the same logical connection, allowing commands, acknowledgements, state transitions, and operational feedback to coexist. A fleet controller can issue high-level updates while the AMR continuously returns execution status, but message semantics must remain explicit so that streaming convenience does not blur the boundary between supervision and safety-critical control.

A mission-oriented gRPC service can represent operations such as CreateMission, StartMission, PauseMission, ResumeMission, CancelMission, and GetMissionStatus. Mission messages may include mission identifiers, destinations, route constraints, priorities, payload information, operating zones, and execution policies. Long-running missions should return an acknowledgement or mission handle quickly rather than keeping a unary request active until physical completion. Progress is then reported through streaming status messages.

Outdoor localization requires richer state representation than a simple two-dimensional position. A telemetry schema may include GNSS coordinates, map-frame pose, heading, linear and angular velocity, localization source, covariance, GNSS RTK state, IMU status, and timestamp information. The API should identify coordinate frames and measurement units explicitly because ambiguity between geographic coordinates, local map coordinates, and robot-relative coordinates can cause serious integration errors in autonomous navigation systems.

Real-time communication also requires consistent time semantics. Each message should contain timestamps generated from a defined clock source, while sequence numbers can identify ordering and missing messages. Systems using GNSS, PTP, or other synchronization mechanisms can correlate robot telemetry with sensor data and server-side events more accurately. The API contract should distinguish measurement time from transmission or reception time so that network delay is not mistakenly interpreted as robot state delay.

Command processing should incorporate identifiers, deadlines, acknowledgements, and lifecycle states. A remote command may transition through received, validated, accepted, executing, completed, rejected, canceled, or failed states. The command identifier allows responses and telemetry to be correlated with the originating request. When a client retries after communication loss, the server should detect duplicate identifiers where appropriate rather than executing the same physical operation multiple times.

gRPC deadlines are especially important for outdoor robots because mobile networks can introduce unpredictable delays. Clients should specify how long a request remains meaningful, and servers should stop unnecessary processing when that deadline expires. Retry policies must consider command semantics carefully. Automatically retrying a read-only status query is generally safe, whereas automatically retrying a movement or mission command without idempotency protection could create duplicate physical actions.

The architecture must assume temporary network disconnection rather than treating connectivity as permanently available. Outdoor AMRs may move through radio shadows, transition between Wi-Fi and cellular networks, or experience congestion and packet loss. When connectivity disappears, the robot should continue executing locally permitted behavior according to mission and safety policies. Remote control services should detect connection loss, expose communication state, and reconcile mission status after connectivity is restored.

Flow control and backpressure are necessary when telemetry production exceeds the receiver\'s processing capacity. High-frequency pose, perception, or diagnostic streams should not consume unlimited memory or delay safety-relevant information. Telemetry services can define different update frequencies, subscription classes, or data priorities. High-bandwidth sensor information such as camera images and raw LiDAR data should generally use dedicated data paths rather than being mixed indiscriminately with essential command and state messages.

The gRPC API gateway or edge service forms a controlled boundary between external networks and internal robot middleware. It validates requests, authenticates clients, applies authorization policies, translates external protobuf messages into internal service commands, and exposes selected robot states. ROS 2, DDS, CAN, Ethernet-based controllers, or proprietary interfaces can remain behind this boundary, allowing external systems to use a stable API without becoming dependent on internal implementation details.

Security should use transport encryption and authenticated identities throughout the communication path. TLS protects gRPC traffic, while mutual TLS can authenticate both robot and server when stronger device identity is required. Certificates, tokens, or enterprise identity mechanisms can be combined with role-based authorization so that monitoring applications, fleet controllers, maintenance tools, and administrative services receive only the operations required for their responsibilities.

Remote motion-related commands require particularly strict authorization and validation. The server should verify operating mode, mission state, permitted geographic area, speed constraints, command freshness, and safety conditions before accepting an instruction. Even after validation, onboard safety logic retains final authority over physical motion. A valid API request therefore represents permission to attempt an operation, not an unconditional instruction that overrides obstacle detection, emergency stopping, or local safety constraints.

Health and diagnostic services can expose processor utilization, memory usage, network quality, battery condition, motor-controller state, localization health, sensor availability, thermal conditions, and active fault codes. Structured diagnostic messages allow fleet software to distinguish warnings from critical failures and identify whether degraded operation is still permitted. Streaming diagnostics can additionally support remote maintenance and predictive analysis without exposing unrestricted access to internal robot processes.

Observability should trace communication from the client request to robot execution. Useful measurements include RPC latency, deadline expiration, error status, active stream count, message throughput, reconnect frequency, authentication failure, command acceptance rate, and telemetry delay. Correlation identifiers can connect a fleet-level mission to individual RPC calls and onboard events, enabling engineers to determine whether an operational problem originated in networking, API processing, navigation, hardware, or mission logic.

The protobuf contract must also evolve without unnecessarily breaking deployed robots and fleet applications. Existing field numbers should remain stable, removed fields should be reserved, and compatible additive changes should be preferred. New capabilities can be introduced through optional fields or new RPC methods while older clients continue using the subset they understand. Automated compatibility and contract tests should verify communication between multiple robot software and fleet-server versions before field deployment.

Large outdoor fleets can place gRPC services behind redundant edge or fleet infrastructure, but connection ownership must be designed carefully because streaming sessions are long-lived. Service discovery, load balancing, health checking, and failover mechanisms should preserve robot identity and mission continuity. The system should distinguish temporary server migration from robot failure and prevent multiple controllers from simultaneously assuming authority over the same physical robot without an explicit coordination mechanism.

In a production outdoor AMR system, gRPC is therefore best positioned between high-level fleet supervision and autonomous onboard execution. Unary RPC supports discrete operations, server streaming delivers continuous telemetry, and bidirectional streaming enables interactive supervision when necessary. Protocol Buffers provide a stable typed contract, while deadlines, identity, security, observability, reconnection, and lifecycle semantics make the communication layer suitable for real operational environments.

The resulting architecture does not attempt to transform an external network into a deterministic robot control bus. Instead, it uses gRPC to create an efficient, strongly defined communication boundary around an autonomous machine. The fleet system communicates goals and policies, the robot reports state and execution results, and onboard controllers retain responsibility for immediate motion and safety. This separation enables outdoor AMRs to combine responsive remote integration with resilient local autonomy as deployments expand from individual robots to large heterogeneous fleets.

12.03 Mobile Manipulator Mission API Design Case
