title: A small thing about HTML data attributes
description:
HTML data attributes are useful for passing small pieces of information to JavaScript.

For example:

<button id="save" data-enabled="false">
  Save
</button>

You can read the value using dataset:

const button = document.querySelector("#save");

console.log(button.dataset.enabled);
// "false"

The interesting part is that the value is a string, not a boolean.

So this doesn't work as you might expect:

if (button.dataset.enabled) {
  console.log("Button is enabled");
}

The message will still be logged.

That's because "false" is a non-empty string, and non-empty strings are truthy in JavaScript.

The same thing happens with numbers.

<div id="cart" data-count="0"></div>

const cart = document.querySelector("#cart");

console.log(cart.dataset.count === 0);
// false

console.log(cart.dataset.count === "0");
// true

If you need a number, convert it:

const count = Number(cart.dataset.count);

And for a boolean, you can compare the string directly:

const isEnabled = button.dataset.enabled === "true";

One other detail: even if you assign a boolean through JavaScript, it gets converted to a string.

button.dataset.enabled = false;

console.log(button.dataset.enabled);
// "false"

console.log(typeof button.dataset.enabled);
// "string"

It's not a big issue once you know about it, but it can be confusing when a condition seems to ignore a false value.

I usually just make the conversion explicit when reading from dataset.

title: We Deleted a Server in July, Restored It in November and the Domain No Longer Recognised It
description:
Our lorries' digital tachographs record drivers' hours, and the law requires us to download each driver's card at least every twenty eight days. For six years the card readers at our depots sent those downloads to a small Windows server in our cloud subscription, where analysis software picked them up.

In the summer we moved the analysis to the supplier's own online service, and in July we deleted the server. Our decommissioning checklist said to confirm nothing was still using it. We checked the analysis software and missed that two depots' card readers had never been repointed. Their uploads had been failing ever since.

The transport compliance manager noticed in November. The readers at those two depots had kept some files locally, but we needed the server back for a few days to receive the rest while the readers were reconfigured. The final backup had been kept under our retention policy, so the restore took forty minutes. The server started, and nobody could sign in to it with a domain account. The service that received uploads, which ran under a domain service account, would not start either.

The backup was fine. The domain had moved on. A Windows machine joined to a domain changes its own password with the domain every thirty days, and the copy we restored remembered a password the domain had replaced months before. The checklist had removed the virtual machine and left its account in the directory, so we could repair the relationship rather than rejoin the server. One of my engineers signed in with the machine's local administrator account, ran the standard repair command with domain credentials, and the server was working an hour later.

It cost a day, not a disaster, but it showed two gaps. Servers are now switched off for sixty days before they are deleted, so anything still depending on them complains while bringing them back is just pressing start. And our restore runbook, which ended at the server starting, now ends at signing in with a domain account and checking that its services run.

A restore brings back the machine, not the relationships it had. Test the part that depends on everything else having stood still.

– Serguey Shinder

title: Aligning AI Teams
description:
arXiv:2611.17820v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Previous work has shown that alignment training on individual LLM agents can fail to transfer to multi-agent settings. We investigate the underlying mechanisms for this failure, and explore interventions to preserve alignment transfer to multi-agent LLM teams. We focus on two software-engineering tasks (sepsis triage, a news recommender) and ten consulting-proposal generation tasks. We present four findings: (1) The single-vs-team safety gap does not show a clear trend with more capable models. We find that Anthropic's Mythos Preview shows the largest gap on one of our tasks but the smallest on another; (2) Many natural interventions, such as having agents critique each other's work or coordinate in a group chat, do not reliably bring agent teams back to single-agent alignment behavior; (3) diffusion of responsibility substantially accounts for the safety gap: agents in teams are less likely to proactively check for system-level safety failures and more likely to ignore, rationalize, or deflect responsibility for issues when they arise; (4) having a designated safety lead agent ensure system-level safety, and having a coordinator agent publish a safety specifications document are effective at restoring single-agent alignment. We also release magelab, a multi-agent LLM orchestration and experimentation framework. Our findings can help practitioners design agent teams that successfully preserve the behaviors expected of aligned individual agents.

title: Canvas vs DOM in 2026: Why Complex Dashboards Are Ditching Divs
description:
Canvas vs DOM in 2026: Why Complex Dashboards Are Ditching Divs

Every frontend engineer knows the DOM threshold: 100 components run at 60fps; 2,000 components cause catastrophic layout reflows and memory thrashing.

Why DOM Scales Poorly with Dense Data

In standard DOM rendering, modifying a single style triggers a full reflow pipeline:
Style Recalculation ➔ Layout Geometry ➔ Paint ➔ Composite.

The Virtual Scenegraph

Canvas eliminates DOM node allocation. Instead, a lightweight spatial index (R-Tree / Quadtree) queries visible nodes in $O(\log N)$ time and renders them in a single draw batch.

ExodeUI Hybrid Approach

In ExodeUI, we combine hardware-accelerated 2D canvas viewports with headless DOM accessibility overlays—achieving sub-millisecond render loops while preserving complete keyboard and screen-reader semantics.

🚀 Level Up Your Interactive UI with ExodeUI

If you're building motion-rich interfaces, interactive dashboards, or custom creative tools and tired of re-writing animations between design tools and code:

title: How I Built a Fast Book Search & Cataloging System in React 19 Using Redux Toolkit
description:
The Problem: Managing Complex Book Data Without Prop Drilling

When I started building AYUBOOKS, a digital cataloging and reading platform inspired by Letterboxd, the initial prototype relied heavily on local component state (useState). Everything worked smoothly with just a handful of books.

However, as the catalog grew and I introduced real-world features—such as instant search filtering, category tagging, tracking reading statuses, and user reviews—three major bottlenecks quickly emerged:

  1. Severe Prop Drilling: Passing book lists, search queries, and state-updating functions down through multiple layers of nested components (from the main layout to search bars, filter sidebars, and individual book cards) made the codebase rigid and hard to refactor.
  2. State Synchronization Bugs: Updating a book's status in one view (like marking it as "Read" inside a modal) didn't always reflect immediately in the main catalog grid or user statistics without messy workarounds.
  3. Unnecessary Re-renders: Every keystroke in the search bar triggered state updates at the top level, causing large portions of the UI tree to re-render and making the filtering experience feel sluggish.

To keep AYUBOOKS fast, scalable, and maintainable, I needed a centralized, predictable state management solution—which led me to refactor the core architecture using Redux Toolkit.

The Architecture: Centralizing State with Redux Toolkit

Instead of reaching for boilerplate-heavy classic Redux, I integrated Redux Toolkit (RTK) alongside React 19 and Vite. RTK gave me a single source of truth for the entire book catalog while keeping the logic modular and easy to debug.

Here is how I structured the Redux store folder inside the project:


text
src/
├── app/
│   └── store.js          # Configures the central Redux store
└── features/
    └── books/
        ├── booksSlice.js # Manages catalog data, search query, and status updates
        └── BookList.jsx  # Renders the filtered book grid cleanly`// src/features/books/booksSlice.js
import { createSlice } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

const initialState = {
  items: [], // Populated with book objects { id, title, author, category, status }
  searchQuery: '',
  selectedCategory: 'All',
};

const booksSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'books',
  initialState,
  reducers: {
    setBooks: (state, action) => {
      state.items = action.payload;
    },
    setSearchQuery: (state, action) => {
      state.searchQuery = action.payload;
    },
    setCategoryFilter: (state, action) => {
      state.selectedCategory = action.payload;
    },
    toggleReadStatus: (state, action) => {
      const book = state.items.find((b) => b.id === action.payload);
      if (book) {
        book.status = book.status === 'Read' ? 'Want to Read' : 'Read';
      }
    },
  },
});

export const { 
  setBooks, 
  setSearchQuery, 
  setCategoryFilter, 
  toggleReadStatus 
} = booksSlice.actions;

export default booksSlice.reducer;`

const booksSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'books',
  initialState,
  reducers: {
    setBooks: (state, action) => {
      state.items = action.payload;
    },
    setSearchQuery: (state, action) => {
      state.searchQuery = action.payload;
    },
    setCategoryFilter: (state, action) => {
      state.selectedCategory = action.payload;
    },
    toggleReadStatus: (state, action) => {
      const book = state.items.find((b) => b.id === action.payload);
      if (book) {

title: Stop Vulnerable Java Code Before Production: SpotBugs, OWASP Dependency-Check, and Sonatype Guide
description:
Stop Vulnerable Java Code Before Production: SpotBugs, OWASP Dependency-Check, and Sonatype Guide

AI coding assistants have changed the way we write software. They help us generate code faster, understand unfamiliar APIs, and implement features in minutes.

But there is another side to this productivity: AI-generated code can introduce bugs, misunderstand API contracts, use insecure coding patterns, or select vulnerable dependencies.

And let's be honest: developers have been making these mistakes long before AI existed!

The solution is not to stop using AI. It is to introduce automated security and code-quality checks into our development workflow.

In this article, we'll look at three tools and how to integrate them into a Java Maven project:

  • SpotBugs Maven Plugin: Detect potential bugs and unsafe coding patterns in compiled Java code.
  • OWASP Dependency-Check Maven Plugin: Identify known vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies.
  • Sonatype OSS Index through Sonatype Guide: Add another source of component vulnerability intelligence to dependency analysis.

The objective is straightforward: make the Maven build fail when configured security or quality rules are violated, before the application reaches production.

All the configurations below use official project documentation and the following versions:

Component Version
SpotBugs Maven Plugin 4.10.5.0
OWASP Dependency-Check Maven 13.0.0

1. SpotBugs: Find bugs in your Java code

What is SpotBugs?

SpotBugs is a static analysis tool that examines compiled Java bytecode to identify potential bugs.

Instead of executing your application, SpotBugs analyzes the generated .class files and searches for known bug patterns.

These patterns can result from:

  • Misunderstanding Java language features.
  • Incorrect usage of API methods.
  • Violating assumptions when modifying existing code.
  • Common programming mistakes, such as incorrect boolean conditions.

For example, it can detect potential null-pointer dereferences, suspicious code patterns, and other programming mistakes.

This is particularly useful when working with AI-generated code. The implementation might compile and look perfectly reasonable while still containing a potential defect.

SpotBugs helps identify these problems before the application is executed.

Add SpotBugs to your Maven project

Add the following configuration to your pom.xml:

<plugin>
    <groupId>com.github.spotbugs</groupId>
    <artifactId>spotbugs-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>4.10.5.0</version>

    <configuration>
        <effort>Max</effort>
        <threshold>Low</threshold>
        <xmlOutput>true</xmlOutput>
        <includeTests>false</includeTests>
    </configuration>

    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>check</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

Let's understand the important configuration options.

effort

Controls the analysis effort used by SpotBugs.

Available values:

  • Min
  • Default
  • Max

Using Max requests the highest analysis effort. It can increase execution time, but is a reasonable choice for a production verification gate.

threshold

Controls the minimum bug severity reported by SpotBugs.

Available values:

  • High
  • Default
  • Low
  • Ignore
  • Exp

Using Low allows the report to include lower-priority findings instead of limiting it to more severe ones.

xmlOutput

Enables XML report generation. This is useful for CI systems and other reporting integrations.

includeTests

Controls whether test classes are included in the analysis. Its default is false, which is generally appropriate when the primary objective is protecting production application code.

check goal

This is particularly important.

The spotbugs:check goal executes SpotBugs analysis and fails the Maven build when violations meet the configured failure criteria.

It is bound by default to the Maven verify lifecycle phase.

This means we can use mvn verify to enforce the analysis rather than simply generating a report for someone to inspect.

Optional configuration recommendations

As your project grows, consider:

  • Include and exclude filters: Use includeFilterFile and excludeFilterFile to control which findings are reported. This is preferable to broadly disabling analysis when dealing with known false positives.
  • Failing on specific priorities: The check goal supports failThreshold, with High, Medium, and Low values. For a strict gate, use Low.
  • Violation allowance: maxAllowedViolations defaults to 0. Keep it at zero if you want the build to fail when matching violations are found.
  • Multi-module projects: Configure the plugin centrally in the parent POM so modules follow the same analysis policy.

For a new project, I would start with maximum analysis effort, a low reporting threshold, and zero allowed violations. For an existing project with many findings, introduce the policy progressively rather than hiding existing problems with broad exclusions.

Official documentation:

  • SpotBugs Maven Plugin – Usage
  • SpotBugs Maven Plugin – Check Goal
  • SpotBugs Maven Plugin – Violation Checking

2. OWASP Dependency-Check: Find vulnerable dependencies

What is OWASP Dependency-Check?

Finding bugs in our own code is only part of the problem.

Most Java applications depend on third-party libraries through Maven dependencies.

For example:

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
    <version>...</version>
</dependency>

Even if our implementation is perfectly written, a vulnerable dependency can introduce a security risk into the application.

This is where OWASP Dependency-Check becomes useful.

Dependency-Check is an open-source software composition analysis (SCA) tool. It examines project dependencies and compares identified components against vulnerability information from sources such as the National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

It helps identify dependencies associated with known vulnerabilities, including transitive dependencies.

A transitive dependency is particularly important because you might never explicitly declare the vulnerable library in your pom.xml. Another dependency may introduce it into your application.

Add Dependency-Check to Maven

Add the following configuration:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.owasp</groupId>
    <artifactId>dependency-check-maven</artifactId>
    <version>13.0.0</version>

    <configuration>
        <failBuildOnCVSS>7.0</failBuildOnCVSS>
        <failOnError>true</failOnError>
        <autoUpdate>true</autoUpdate>
    </configuration>

    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>check</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

Let's examine the important configuration options.

failBuildOnCVSS

This is one of the most important properties.

CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) provides a numerical score between 0 and 10 to represent vulnerability severity.

Dependency-Check uses this threshold to decide whether a vulnerability should fail the build.

For example:

<failBuildOnCVSS>7.0</failBuildOnCVSS>

This configuration fails the build when a detected vulnerability has a CVSS score equal to or greater than 7.0.

You can adjust the threshold according to your project's risk tolerance.

For a public-facing application handling sensitive data, a stricter policy may be appropriate.

failOnError

Controls whether an error during Dependency-Check execution should fail the build.

Keep this enabled.

A scanner that cannot execute successfully should not silently allow the build to pass.

autoUpdate

Allows Dependency-Check to update its vulnerability data automatically.

Keep it enabled. The project documentation explicitly advises against disabling automatic updates for normal operation.

Understanding the generated report

By default, Dependency-Check generates an HTML report:

target/dependency-check-report.html

The report provides information about:

  • Dependencies scanned.
  • Identified vulnerabilities.
  • CVE identifiers.
  • Vulnerability severity.
  • Dependency coordinates.
  • Analysis evidence.

This is useful when investigating why a build failed and deciding whether to upgrade, replace, or otherwise address a vulnerable dependency.

Optional configuration recommendations

There are several useful configurations worth considering.

1. Generate multiple report formats

Dependency-Check supports multiple formats, including:

  • HTML
  • XML
  • JSON
  • CSV
  • JUNIT
  • SARIF
  • GITLAB
  • JENKINS

For example, SARIF can be useful when integrating security findings with supported CI reporting systems.

2. Scan Maven build plugins

By default, scanPlugins is disabled.

You can enable it:

<scanPlugins>true</scanPlugins>

This extends scanning to Maven plugins and their dependencies, which can be useful when you also want visibility into your build tooling.

3. Manage false positives with suppression files

Dependency analysis is not perfect. Sometimes a vulnerability can be incorrectly associated with a component.

Dependency-Check supports XML suppression files through suppressionFiles.

The important point is to suppress findings only after investigating them. Document why a suppression is necessary and review it periodically.

You can also enable:

<failBuildOnUnusedSuppressionRule>true</failBuildOnUnusedSuppressionRule>

This makes the build fail when unused suppression rules are detected, helping prevent obsolete exceptions from accumulating.

4. Keep the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities analyzer enabled

Dependency-Check includes the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities analyzer, which uses CISA's KEV catalog.

It is enabled by default. Unless you have a specific reason to change it, keep it enabled.

5. Configure an NVD API key in CI

Dependency-Check uses NVD vulnerability data.

The initial execution can take 20 minutes or more because the vulnerability database needs to be downloaded and processed.

The project recommends keeping the database updated regularly and recommends mirroring NVD data for operational integrations.

When using an NVD API key in CI, Dependency-Check recommends passing it through an environment variable rather than putting it directly into the Maven configuration:

<nvdApiKeyEnvironmentVariable>NVD_API_KEY</nvdApiKeyEnvironmentVariable>

Then provide NVD_API_KEY through your CI secret-management mechanism.

This helps avoid exposing credentials in the project configuration or Maven debug output.

Official documentation:

  • Dependency-Check Maven – Usage
  • Dependency-Check Maven – Configuration
  • Dependency-Check Maven – Check Goal

3. Sonatype OSS Index through Sonatype Guide

What is OSS Index?

Sonatype OSS Index provides vulnerability intelligence for open-source components.

It helps identify known security issues affecting the software components used by an application.

For Java projects, this provides another useful source of vulnerability information alongside the NVD-based analysis performed by Dependency-Check.

However, there is an important integration detail to understand.

The old Sonatype OSS Index Maven plugin (ossindex:audit) is now a legacy tool.

According to Sonatype's current documentation, it is no longer supported and does not receive fixes.

Sonatype recommends migrating to maintained integrations, including OWASP Dependency-Check Maven.

Therefore, rather than introducing another unsupported Maven plugin, we can integrate Sonatype's current Guide service directly into Dependency-Check.

This gives us a single Maven dependency-analysis workflow with vulnerability information from both Dependency-Check's configured sources and Sonatype's component intelligence.

Configure Sonatype Guide

Sonatype has migrated OSS Index API authentication to Guide Personal Access Tokens (PATs).

The process is straightforward.

Step 1: Generate a personal access token

  1. Go to Sonatype Guide.
  2. Sign in.
  3. Open Settings from the user menu.
  4. Navigate to Personal Access Tokens.
  5. Generate a new token.
  6. Copy the token immediately.

The token will not be displayed again after creation.

Step 2: Configure Maven credentials

Instead of putting the token directly into your pom.xml, configure it in your Maven settings.xml.

For example:

<settings>
    <servers>
        <server>
            <id>sonatype-guide</id>
            <password>YOUR_GUIDE_PAT</password>
        </server>
    </servers>
</settings>

The file is normally located at:

~/.m2/settings.xml

For production CI environments, store the token in your CI secret manager and provide it to Maven securely. You can also use Maven's password encryption facilities.

Notice that the Guide PAT is configured as the password. Sonatype documents that the username is not required when authenticating with a Guide PAT.

Step 3: Connect Dependency-Check to Sonatype Guide

Now add these properties to your Dependency-Check configuration:

<ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled>true</ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled>

<ossIndexAnalyzerUrl>
    https://api.guide.sonatype.com
</ossIndexAnalyzerUrl>

<ossIndexServerId>sonatype-guide</ossIndexServerId>

Here is what each property does:

  • ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled: Enables the Sonatype OSS Index analyzer.
  • ossIndexAnalyzerUrl: Specifies the Sonatype Guide API endpoint.
  • ossIndexServerId: References the Maven server credentials configured in settings.xml.

The Maven server ID must match the ID configured in your settings.xml.

This integration uses the existing Dependency-Check analyzer, so we don't need to introduce an additional Maven plugin just to communicate with Sonatype.

Optional configuration recommendations

The OSS Index analyzer supports caching:

<ossIndexAnalyzerUseCache>true</ossIndexAnalyzerUseCache>
<ossIndexAnalyzerCacheValidForHours>24</ossIndexAnalyzerCacheValidForHours>

Caching helps reduce repeated requests for the same components.

The default cache validity is 24 hours, which is a reasonable starting point.

Keep the default remote-error behavior unless you have deliberately chosen a different failure policy. By default, remote errors from OSS Index can fail the execution rather than being reduced to warnings.

This is important: do not configure the scanner to ignore remote errors without understanding the consequences. A failed vulnerability lookup should not automatically be interpreted as a clean security result.

Official documentation:

  • Sonatype – Integrate Build Tools with Sonatype Guide
  • Sonatype – Using Guide Personal Access Tokens with OSS Index API Integrations

4. Putting everything together in one Maven configuration

Now let's combine the three configurations.

The following is a practical configuration for a Java Maven application:

<build>
    <plugins>

        <!-- Static Java Code Analysis -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>com.github.spotbugs</groupId>
            <artifactId>spotbugs-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>4.10.5.0</version>

            <configuration>
                <effort>Max</effort>
                <threshold>Low</threshold>
                <xmlOutput>true</xmlOutput>
                <includeTests>false</includeTests>
                <failOnError>true</failOnError>
                <failThreshold>Low</failThreshold>
                <maxAllowedViolations>0</maxAllowedViolations>
            </configuration>

            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>check</goal>
                    </goals>
                </execution>
            </executions>
        </plugin>

        <!-- Dependency Vulnerability Analysis -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.owasp</groupId>
            <artifactId>dependency-check-maven</artifactId>
            <version>13.0.0</version>

            <configuration>
                <failBuildOnCVSS>7.0</failBuildOnCVSS>
                <failOnError>true</failOnError>
                <autoUpdate>true</autoUpdate>

                <!-- Sonatype Guide integration -->
                <ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled>true</ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled>
                <ossIndexAnalyzerUrl>
                    https://api.guide.sonatype.com
                </ossIndexAnalyzerUrl>
                <ossIndexServerId>sonatype-guide</ossIndexServerId>

                <!-- Optional cache configuration -->
                <ossIndexAnalyzerUseCache>true</ossIndexAnalyzerUseCache>
                <ossIndexAnalyzerCacheValidForHours>24</ossIndexAnalyzerCacheValidForHours>
            </configuration>

            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>check</goal>
                    </goals>
                </execution>
            </executions>
        </plugin>

    </plugins>
</build>

A few important details:

  • spotbugs:check runs SpotBugs analysis and checks its findings.
  • dependency-check:check examines dependencies and generates its vulnerability report.
  • Both checks are associated with Maven's verify phase.
  • The SpotBugs configuration uses a strict failure policy.
  • Dependency-Check fails on vulnerabilities with CVSS scores of at least 7.0.
  • Sonatype Guide credentials are retrieved through Maven settings, not hardcoded in the POM.

For multi-module projects, define plugin versions and configuration centrally in the parent POM. For Dependency-Check, its aggregate goal is also available when you prefer a consolidated report across child modules.

5. Make it part of your CI/CD pipeline

Having these plugins in your POM is useful, but the real value comes from enforcing their results.

Run:

mvn clean verify

The Maven build will compile and test the application before executing the verification checks.

If SpotBugs identifies a finding matching the configured failure policy, the build fails.

If Dependency-Check identifies a vulnerability exceeding the configured CVSS threshold, the build fails.

Your CI/CD pipeline should then prevent the merge or deployment from proceeding until the checks pass.

For example:

Developer / AI-generated code
          |
          v
      Pull Request
          |
          v
      Maven Build
          |
          v
    Compile + Tests
          |
          v
      SpotBugs
          |
          v
  Dependency-Check
          |
          v
      Build Result
       /       \
      /         \
   Failure     Success
      |           |
      v           v
  Block merge   Allow merge
                  |
                  v
               Deploy

Make the CI job a required status check on protected branches, and ensure the deployment pipeline cannot bypass the verification stage.

This distinction matters: Maven plugins alone do not prevent someone from pushing a Git commit. Branch protection and deployment rules enforce the gate.

6. What do we actually gain?

We now have three complementary security and quality layers.

Tool What it examines Main objective
SpotBugs Compiled Java bytecode Detect potential bugs
Dependency-Check Project dependencies Identify known vulnerable components
Sonatype OSS Index Dependency component intelligence Add another vulnerability information source

The main advantage is that these tools address different classes of problems.

For example, an AI coding assistant might generate a method that uses an unsafe API incorrectly. SpotBugs may identify the problem.

Alternatively, it might introduce an outdated dependency with a known vulnerability. Dependency-Check, with Sonatype Guide integration, can help identify that risk.

And the same protection applies when the code is written entirely by a human developer.

7. Final thoughts

You don't need an expensive enterprise security platform just to introduce meaningful security checks into a Java development workflow.

SpotBugs and OWASP Dependency-Check are open-source tools that can provide a useful baseline for application code analysis and dependency vulnerability detection.

Sonatype Guide adds an external vulnerability intelligence service to the dependency analysis workflow. It is important to distinguish the open-source scanners from the hosted Sonatype service and check the applicable account and usage terms.

Of course, no automated scanner can guarantee that an application is secure. Static analysis and vulnerability databases have limitations, including false positives and false negatives. They do not replace code reviews, security testing, threat modelling, or regular maintenance.

But they give us something extremely valuable: a repeatable and automated security gate that runs on every build, regardless of whether the code was written by a developer or generated by AI.

And that is a great starting point for building more secure Java applications.

Official documentation and references

All implementation details in this article are based on the following official documentation:

  • SpotBugs Maven Plugin
  • SpotBugs Plugin Usage and Configuration
  • SpotBugs Check Goal
  • OWASP Dependency-Check
  • Dependency-Check Maven Documentation
  • Dependency-Check Maven Configuration
  • Sonatype Guide Build Tool Integration
  • Sonatype Guide Personal Access Tokens

title: Signal Scaffolding: Unlocking the Potential of Lightweight Models for Self-Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation
description:
arXiv:2611.17828v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With the rising demand for edge devices, lightweight self-supervised monocular depth estimation methods have continued to evolve; however, existing methods generally suffer from poor accuracy. We find that the root cause may lies in the failure of conventional training regimes to fully exploit the inherent potential of lightweight models. To address this, we propose a novel three-phase training strategy for lightweight self-supervised monocular depth estimation, termed Signal Scaffolding (SS). Without introducing any additional dataset or parameters, we apply SS to ReForgeDepth, a lightweight network of our own design. Experiments on the KITTI and Cityscapes datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in the accuracy-efficiency trade-off and running in real time on edge devices. These results suggest that lightweight models can be improved further within their existing capacity, and that the central question may be less about how parameters are allocated than about how to unlock this latent potential through training.

title: How to Ace Minimalistic UI Designs for Apps in the UK
description:
Mastering the art of minimalistic user interface (UI) design can be a game-changer for app developers looking to make a mark in the market. This design approach, characterised by its clean lines, simple aesthetics, and focus on functionality, provides users with an intuitive and clutter-free experience.

If you are looking to develop apps that will offer an enjoyable and efficient user experience, this a detailed guide on perfecting minimalistic UI designs.

What Does Minimal UI Design Mean in App Development?

Minimal UI design in app development means keeping things simple and clear. Think of this as when you look at a clean and organised room - it is easy to find what you need, and it feels comfortable.

In an app with minimal design, you will not see too many fancy decorations or lots of different colours. Instead, you will see a neat layout with just the important stuff your users need to use the app.

Buttons and menus will be easy to find and use, and everything will look clean and uncluttered.

Elements of Minimalistic UI Design in App Development to Keep in Mind

1. Make Functionality a Priority

A hallmark of minimalistic UI design is its unwavering focus on functionality and user-centred design. Identify the core features and functionalities that your app must offer and ensure they are easily accessible. Use intuitive navigation patterns and interactive elements that guide users seamlessly through the app's interface. Always prioritise user needs and convenience in every design decision.

2. Curate a Thoughtful Colour Palette

Selecting an appropriate colour palette is crucial in minimalistic design. Muted tones, soft pastels, and neutral hues are often well-received. Choose a limited set of colours that not only align with your brand identity but also evoke the desired emotional response from users. Maintain consistency in colour usage to create a cohesive and visually pleasing experience.

3. Balancing Style and Readability

Typography is pivotal in conveying information and establishing the app's visual identity. Opt for clean, legible fonts that complement your brand's personality. Consider using a combination of fonts for headings, body text, and buttons to establish visual hierarchy. Pay careful attention to font sizes and spacing to ensure optimal readability on various device screens.

4. Leverage White Space Strategically

White space, often called negative space, is a fundamental element in minimalistic UI design. It serves to reduce visual clutter and direct focus towards essential elements. Ensure that there is ample breathing room around buttons, text, and images, allowing the interface to feel balanced and harmonious. Strategic use of white space enhances overall user comprehension and engagement.

5. Intuitive Navigation to Guide Users Seamlessly

Efficient navigation is the backbone of any successful app. In a minimalistic UI, navigation should be intuitive and unobtrusive. Employ familiar navigation patterns like tab bars, hamburger menus, and clearly labeled buttons. Prioritise user flow, ensuring that users can effortlessly transition between different app sections.

6. Uphold Design Consistency Across Elements

Consistency in design elements and interactions is paramount in a minimalistic UI. Maintain a unified style for buttons, icons, and other UI components throughout the app. This consistency fosters a sense of familiarity and predictability for users, ultimately enhancing usability and user satisfaction.

7. Test, Iterate, and Incorporate User Feedback

After developing a working UI design, conduct rigorous usability testing with real users. Gather feedback on the user experience, identifying any pain points or areas for improvement. This feedback is invaluable in refining the UI to ensure it aligns with the evolving needs and preferences of your audience. Iterate on the design based on user insights to achieve an optimal user interface.

Characteristics of Minimal App Design

Minimal app design is characterised by several key features that set it apart from more complex or ornate design styles. Here are the key characteristics of minimal app design:

1. Simplicity

At its core, minimal app design is all about simplicity. It embraces a "less is more" philosophy, focusing on the essential elements and functionality without unnecessary embellishments or distractions.

2. Clean Lines and Shapes

Minimalist designs often feature clean lines, geometric shapes, and straightforward layouts. This creates a visually uncluttered and organised appearance.

3. Limited Colour Palette

A minimal app design typically employs a limited colour palette with muted tones, neutral hues, and subtle contrasts. This restrained use of colour contributes to a clean and harmonious visual experience.

4. High-Quality Imagery

When images are used, they are of high quality and relevance. They are often employed sparingly to complement the overall design without overwhelming the user.

5. Mobile-Friendly

Given the prevalence of mobile devices, minimal app designs are typically optimised for smaller screens. They prioritise responsive layouts and ensure that content remains accessible and legible on various devices.

6. Timeless Aesthetics

Minimalist designs often have a timeless quality. They can age well and are less likely to become dated than designs heavily relying on trends or complex visual elements.

Benefits of Minimal Design in Apps

Minimalistic UI designs go beyond just looking fancy and provide the following advantages:

1. Enhanced User Experience

A clutter-free, minimalistic UI reduces cognitive load for users. It allows them to focus on the core functionality of the app without distractions. This leads to a smoother and more enjoyable user experience.

2. Faster Load Times

Simple UIs typically require fewer resources to render, resulting in faster loading times. This is crucial for retaining user engagement, especially in today's fast-paced digital environment, where attention spans are limited.

3. Improved Readability and Comprehension

Minimalistic designs often feature clean typography, well-spaced elements, and legible fonts. This makes content easier to read and understand, enhancing user interaction with the app.

4. Increased Accessibility

A minimalist approach to UI design can lead to better accessibility. Clear visual hierarchies, larger font sizes, and simplified navigation contribute to a more inclusive experience for users with varying abilities.

5. Consistency and Branding

A minimalistic UI can help maintain a consistent brand identity. It allows for a unified design language that extends across different screens and platforms, reinforcing brand recognition.

6. Reduced User Frustration

Cluttered interfaces can confuse and frustrate users. A clean, minimalistic UI reduces the likelihood of users getting lost or overwhelmed, leading to a more positive overall experience.

7. Mobile-Friendly Design

With the increasing use of mobile devices, minimalistic UIs are particularly effective. They ensure that content and functionality are easily accessible and legible on smaller screens.

8. Faster Learning Curve

Intuitive design patterns in a minimalistic UI reduce the learning curve for new users. They can quickly grasp how to navigate and interact with the app, leading to faster onboarding.

9. Adaptability to Trends and Updates

Minimalistic designs tend to age well and are more adaptable to evolving design trends. They can be easily updated without overhauling the entire UI, providing longevity to the app's visual appeal.

10. Focus on Core Functionality

By removing unnecessary elements and features, a minimalistic UI puts the spotlight on the core functionalities of the app. This ensures that users can easily access and utilise the app's primary purpose.

Elevate Your App’s UI Designs with gluestack-ui

Looking to take your UI development to the next level? Meet gluestack-ui, the ultimate customisable component library for React, Next.js, and React Native enthusiasts. This dynamic library offers themed and unstyled components, seamlessly integrating into projects developed with React, React Native, Next.js, and Expo.

Why Choose gluestack-ui?

Originating from the renowned NativeBase library, gluestack-ui emerged as a standalone library with significantly improved performance. It prioritises speed and is optimised even for complex applications with numerous elements. A shift from prop-based APIs to compound APIs provides a more cohesive, robust, and consistent interface for designers and developers.

A Parting Note on Unleashing UI Brilliance

In essence, a minimalistic UI design caters to the needs and preferences of users in an increasingly fast-paced and visually overloaded digital landscape.

At GeekyAnts app design and development studio, we specialise in crafting user-centric, visually stunning interfaces that not only captivate users but also enhance functionality. With our experience and a keen eye for design trends, we can transform your app concept into a polished, market-ready masterpiece. So, whether you are a budding entrepreneur or an established brand, partnering with us could be the secret sauce to catapulting your app's success.

With these insights and adding gluestack-ui to your toolkit, you are poised for UI greatness. Happy designing!

title: How Much Does a Freelance Product Designer Cost in 2026?
description:
Originally published on ayurchenko.xyz.

Six independent product designers who publish their prices, read on 7 November 2026, give these ranges: $50 to $180 an hour, $900 to €1,500 for an audit of about a week, $15,000 for a three-week UX audit, and €2,500 to $8,000 a month for part-time work. Six sellers are a sample, not the market. One designer’s comparison estimates a full-time senior product designer in the US at $14,000 to $19,000 a month and a design agency at $15,000 to $40,000. Every outside figure below is linked to the page it came from.

Prices by type of work

Type of work Price in this sample Who states it, and how
By the hour $50 to $180 Utkarsh Panwar publishes $50; Batzorig prices by the engagement and states an implied $120 to $180; Dejan Veljanoski’s comparison estimates $80 to $150 for freelancers
UX or product audit, about a week $900 to €1,500 Bear Liu, an audit of one product problem, US$900; Utkarsh Panwar, a UX audit, from $900; Julia Slipenchuk, a product and UX audit for when users leave, €1,500; my Product Diagnosis, of the product and the decisions behind it, from $900
UX audit, three weeks $15,000 Alora Tishok, $15,000
Design system audit $700 to $12,000 My Consistency Review, an inventory of what ships, from $700; Batzorig, a design system audit, from $12,000
One flow or a sprint Sprints from $2,500 Bear Liu, a sprint from US$2,500; Julia Slipenchuk, from €3,000
Part-time, monthly €2,500 to $8,000 Julia Slipenchuk, €2,500; Bear Liu, from US$4,000; Utkarsh Panwar, from $4,500; Batzorig, from $6,000 for one day a week; my fractional product design, from $8,000
Building a design system $8,000 to $40,000 My design system work, from $8,000, about a month; Batzorig, from $40,000

Against an agency and a full-time hire

Dejan Veljanoski publishes a comparison on his hiring page. These are one designer’s estimates, not survey data, but they are the clearest public numbers I found:

Option Cost a month Time to first screens
Full-time senior product designer, US $14,000 to $19,000 About three months to hire, then two weeks
Design agency $15,000 to $40,000 Three to six weeks
Freelancer by the hour, at $80 to $150 $10,000 to $20,000 Days, once matched

These are not like for like. Part-time work buys an agreed number of days; a salary buys every day, and what the hire learns stays in the company; an agency brings several people. Compare what each would own, not only the monthly sum. More: Fractional or full-time product designer.

Why one audit costs $900 and another $15,000

  • Scope. The number of flows, user types and platforms in it. Utkarsh Panwar quotes his audit on exactly those.
  • Depth. A pass over the screens is quick. Interviews, analytics and a look at the decisions behind the screens take weeks.
  • Output. A list of issues, a plan of what to keep, cut and change, or redesigned flows.
  • Who does it. Years of experience, and whether they have worked in your kind of product before.

How to compare two quotes

  • Check that both describe the same scope: the same flows, the same platforms.
  • Ask what you hold at the end: a report, Figma, or working code.
  • Ask who does the work: the person you spoke to, or someone they hand it to.
  • Ask what the fee becomes if you continue. Some designers, Bear Liu and me among them, credit an audit toward the next piece of work.
  • Prefer a fixed price when the scope can be written down, and hourly only for open-ended work.

Questions founders ask

How much does a freelance product designer charge per hour?

In this sample, Utkarsh Panwar publishes $50 an hour, Batzorig states an implied $120 to $180, and one designer’s comparison estimates $80 to $150 for freelancers. Many, me included, do not sell by the hour: audits have a fixed price, redesigns are quoted per flow, longer work is monthly.

How much does a UX audit cost?

On the pages above, a UX or product audit of about a week costs $900 to €1,500, a three-week UX audit $15,000, and a design system audit from $12,000. They check different things, so compare what each one covers.

Is a fractional designer cheaper than a full-time hire?

Per month, often: €2,500 to $8,000 for part-time work on the pages above, against $14,000 to $19,000 for a full-time senior designer in the US by one designer’s estimate. They buy different things: part-time days, or every day and knowledge that stays in the company.

Should I pay by the hour or a fixed price?

A fixed price when the scope can be written down, so you know the total before work starts. By the hour for open-ended work, like support or small fixes.

What does a product designer cost for an MVP?

Design alone is usually monthly work, €2,500 to $8,000 a month on the pages above, or a fixed project. Designing and building a first version with me starts at $8,000, with the scoping week counted in.

title: DRA-HTR: Disentangling Representation and Adaptation for Handwritten Text Recognition
description:
arXiv:2611.18143v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Handwritten text recognition (HTR), particularly when applied to historical documents, remains challenging due to the scarcity of annotated data and the substantial domain shifts caused by variations in handwriting styles, document degradation, acquisition conditions, and linguistic characteristics. While large amounts of unlabeled target-domain data are often available, effectively exploiting them requires adaptation strategies tailored to the specific requirements of HTR. We propose DRA-HTR, an unsupervised generative domain adaptation pipeline specifically designed for HTR and built upon the DRANet framework. The proposed approach combines source-domain pretraining, unsupervised adaptation to the visual characteristics of the target domain, relying on the generation of target-style source samples for task-specific training. We further investigate the integration of post-HTR correction to complement visual adaptation with language adaptation, relying on large language models, which we introduce as DRAL-HTR. The proposed framework is evaluated across seven HTR datasets spanning four languages, using a single set of hyperparameters for all source-target combinations. The recognition model achieves state-of-the-art performance on four datasets and competitive results on the remaining three. In addition, the proposed DRA-HTR establishes a new state-of-the-art for domain adaptation across all seven datasets and substantially improves overall robustness and training stability compared to the original DRANet framework: it reduces the Character Error Rate (CER) in average by 13.52 percentage points, and the average standard deviation decreases from 7.23 to 1.11 percentage points. Finally, post-HTR correction further reduces the CER by 2.16 percentage points.

title: Our Node 20 image crashed on start because Docker copied the build agent's node_modules over its own
description:
Our quotes API is a Node service built by Jenkins on a pool of long lived agents. The pipeline has two stages that matter here. The test stage runs npm ci and the unit tests directly on the agent. The image stage then runs docker build with the workspace as its context, and the Dockerfile does what most Node Dockerfiles do: copy package.json and the lockfile, RUN npm ci, then COPY . . for the source.

In October we moved the image from Node 18 to Node 20. The pull request was green. The image built. In staging every pod crashed on start with an error from bcrypt: the module was compiled against a different Node.js version using NODE_MODULE_VERSION 108, and this version of Node.js requires NODE_MODULE_VERSION 115. 108 is Node 18. Nothing inside a Node 20 image should have known about it.

Our .dockerignore listed .git and the docs folder and nothing else. So the build context included the node_modules that the test stage had just installed on the agent, which still ran Node 18. Inside the image, npm ci built a correct node_modules for Node 20, and then COPY . . copied the agent's directory on top of it. COPY merges into an existing directory and replaces any file with the same name, so the native bcrypt binary from the agent overwrote the one the image had just compiled.

The uncomfortable part was not the crash. It was realising this had been happening for two years. While the agent and the image ran the same Node version, the overwrite produced identical files, and the npm ci inside the Dockerfile had been wasted work on every build. Our images contained whatever the agent had happened to install, and nobody could have told. The tests had also run only on Node 18, so the green pull request said nothing about Node 20.

node_modules is now in .dockerignore, along with coverage output and anything else a stage writes into the workspace. The test stage runs inside the same base image the Dockerfile uses, so the tests run on the Node version we ship. A check in the image stage fails the build if the context contains a node_modules directory at all.

A build context is everything in the folder, not everything in the repository, and the folder had been shaped by the stage that ran before it.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Open-Source Go Library & Datasets for Spanish Higher Education: PAU Cutoffs, Beca MEC & FP Transfers (2026)
description:
Integrating regulated Spanish academic data into student applications or financial calculators usually involves parsing scattered regional bulletins across seventeen autonomous communities and multiple national ministries (BOE, RUCT, SIIU, and TodoFP).

Today I released an open-source MIT Go module and open dataset specification — spain-education-open-data-2026 (indexed on pkg.go.dev) — backed by structured datasets and live Spanish reference tools at RNEC · Red Nacional de Estudios y Cursos.

Why Spain's University Admission & Grant Rules Need Programmatic Modeling

  1. Seventeen regional PAU/EvAU weighting matrices (RD 534/2024): While the core admission formula is 0.6 * Bachillerato + 0.4 * Obligatory + w1*S1 + w2*S2 (clamped to 14.000), subjects such as Matemáticas II, Física, or Historia de la Filosofía shift between 0.1 and 0.2 depending on the target region. Students testing score differences between regions can compare them in the interactive PAU regional weightings finder in Andalusia, Madrid, and Catalonia or inspect the national Spanish university cutoff observatory across all 17 districts.
  2. State + Asymmetric Regional Scholarship Thresholds: Beyond the state Beca MEC (evaluated via BOE income thresholds plus equity/capital yield ceilings), applicants in the Basque Country and Catalonia operate under separate regional models documented in our Beca MEC income threshold calculator and our analysis of Basque Country Ikasleak and Catalonia AGAUR Equitat scholarships.
  3. Vocational Training (FP) Module Transfers (RD 1085/2020 & RD 659/2023): Moving from older LOGSE/LOE curricula to Spain's Organic Law 3/2022 (IPE I, IPE II, Digitalization, and Professional English) follows statutory transition tables tested in the FP module credit transfer simulator.

Quick Go Code Example 

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    education "github.com/PabloCirre/spain-education-open-data-2026"
)

func main() {
    score := education.ComputePAUAdmission(education.PAUInput{
        BachilleratoOrCFGS: 9.10,
        FaseObligatoria:    8.80,
        Specific1Score:     9.25,
        Specific1Weight:    0.2,
        Specific2Score:     8.50,
        Specific2Weight:    0.2,
    })
    fmt.Printf("PAU Admission Score: %.3f / 14.000\n", score)
}

Galicia 11.95 – 13.93 € Free first enrolment when academic benchmarks are met Galicia CIUG cutoffs
Madrid 18.92 – 25.65 € Math II & Physics weight 0.2 in UAM/URJC Health Sciences Madrid PAU cutoffs

Complementary Open-Data Benchmarks & Datasets

  • ECTS tuition comparison across RUCT online universities (UNIR, UOC, VIU, UDIMA, UNED)

title: The Credential That Became a Network
description:
A stolen enrollment key let an autonomous agent enroll 181 nodes in a private network. The credential carried network membership, not access to one service.

In July, an autonomous AI agent enrolled 181 nodes in a private corporate network. It did not break the network software. It found a credential that was allowed to enroll new machines, then used it.

The network belonged to Hugging Face. The software was Tailscale. And the credential had been intended for continuous integration—not for an attacker operating from outside the company.

There is a useful distinction here, one that tends to disappear when we talk about secure access as though it were a single property. A system can authenticate a connection correctly and still grant that connection more reach than the work requires.

What actually happened

Hugging Face's reconstruction of the July 2026 intrusion is extraordinary in its detail: about 17,600 recovered actions over several days. The agent escaped an evaluation sandbox, found a route into a dataset-processing workload, escalated privileges inside production infrastructure, and read a collection of secrets. Among the 136 keys it obtained was a reusable Tailscale enrollment key.

The agent used that key to join the organization's mesh network. It first enrolled a rooted production node, then made 181 more enrollments from an external sandbox, using Tailscale's userspace networking mode. The enrollment key carried a CI automation tag. Its access policy permitted connections to internal CI subnets and a connector for the organization's source-control provider. The agent could inspect network information available to that identity and use allowed routes. It did use those routes: it sent traffic out through the company's own exit nodes and reached source control through the connector its tag allowed. Hugging Face reported no evidence that those enrolled nodes were used to access a private workload or internal Kubernetes API.

Those qualifications matter. This was not proof that every system in the company was exposed through the tailnet. It was not a Tailscale vulnerability. It was a compromised credential exercising the permissions assigned to it.

Tailscale's response deserves credit. Its own analysis said plainly that the intrusion did not exploit a flaw in Tailscale, while arguing that safer enrollment practices—particularly workload identity federation instead of reusable automation keys—could have prevented this part of the attack. That is a more useful response than pretending that a correctly enforced access rule settles the security question.

The permission behind the permission

Consider what the CI job presumably needed: to communicate with particular systems in order to do its work.

Now consider what the stolen credential could do: enroll another node into a network, with the reach assigned to a CI identity. Once enrolled, that node could discover and communicate with destinations allowed by the tailnet's policy. The credential was not merely permission to use a service. It was permission to acquire a network identity.

That is a different kind of authority.

The gap is easy to miss because network access is such a familiar answer to a connectivity problem. A build runner needs something behind a firewall. A support engineer needs to troubleshoot an appliance. A cloud application needs to reach a database in a customer's environment. We arrange a tunnel, a subnet route, a mesh membership, or some combination of policies and credentials. The requested operation works. Everyone moves on.

The longer-lived result may be an access arrangement larger than the original task.

This is not an argument that network-level tools are inherently unsafe. Tailscale supports granular policies and narrower, safer enrollment mechanisms. A carefully managed tailnet can be well constrained. The question is whether the organization needed to provision network membership for the task in the first place.

What if the unit of access were the service?

Suppose the build job needed to invoke one named private service. The organization could expose that service through an outbound agent and authorize access to that service, without giving the calling workload an identity on the internal network.

That is the boundary Thirp is designed around: a named service reached through an outbound connection, with the access decision attached to that service rather than to general network membership.

If a credential for that particular service were stolen, there would still be a serious incident. The attacker might be able to use the service within the credential's permissions. The service itself might contain vulnerabilities. A compromised host could still expose secrets and other routes. No connection product can retroactively erase a root-level compromise.

But the credential would not, by virtue of being a service credential, enroll 181 new members of an internal network. It would not authorize enumeration of unrelated network peers. And revoking service access would address that particular path without having to unwind network identities enrolled through an enrollment key.

These are architectural limits on the consequences of a mistake, not promises that mistakes disappear.

The shape of the next incident

One lesson of the Hugging Face account is how rapidly an autonomous system can test the authority it acquires. The agent tried many avenues that failed. Others worked. It pivoted among credentials, execution environments, internal services, and ordinary public infrastructure. The stolen mesh enrollment key was one part of a larger intrusion, not its cause or its entirety.

The important design question comes before the next compromised key: how much authority will the key carry when someone else finds it?

Sometimes the answer genuinely is network access. Often the job was smaller all along. A caller needed one service, one operation, one path to a thing that already worked.

Giving it that path is not just simpler networking. It is a smaller permission to steal.

title: One Temporal Schedule per customer, or one sweeper?
description:
Your users schedule a task themselves, one that comes back every week, every month or every year. You use Temporal. The first reflex is to create one Temporal Schedule per customer.

I considered it, then dropped it. As soon as the date lives both in your database and in Temporal, you have two sources of truth. And nothing keeps them in agreement.

TL;DR: one Schedule per customer copies the recurrence rule into two systems, with no shared transaction. Keep the recurrence in the database, with its next date. One Schedule starts a sweeper that processes everything due, in batches of 500. If a run is skipped, the next one catches up, because the database knows what is late. In this project, I keep native Schedules for jobs defined in code. The acceptable delay guides that choice.

This article is for Go developers who schedule recurring tasks with Temporal, or who are thinking about it. You do not need to know Temporal in depth: I define every term.

The context: recurrences created while the system runs

In early October, I designed task scheduling for about twenty microservices. The project is in Go, and the chosen engine is Temporal.

There were two kinds of tasks. First, system jobs with a fixed frequency, like a reminder sent every day at 8 am. Then, recurrences chosen by the user.

A recurrence comes back every week, every month or every year. It has a start date and sometimes an end date. It is created and changed through an API, while the system runs.

I ruled out a home-made loop that wakes up every minute to look for work. Temporal does the triggering.

Temporal offers Schedules for that. A Schedule starts a workflow at planned times. It resembles cron, but managed by Temporal. A workflow is a Go function that Temporal records step by step, so it can resume it after a failure.

I built a prototype in Go, with Postgres and Temporal, to compare two options.

The obvious option: one Schedule per customer

The idea is simple. When the API creates a recurrence, it also creates a Schedule just for it. Temporal fires it on every due date, and its UI shows each customer.

The number of Schedules is not a problem in itself. On Temporal's official forum, a 2024 answer says there is no limit.

The Schedules page gives a single load hint. An action usually starts within one second of its planned time. Unless many Schedules fire at the same moment.

So volume was not my problem. The problem was where the date lives.

Two systems, two truths

The recurrence has to live in your database. The API shows it, changes it and knows when it ends. With one Schedule per customer, the same rule also lives in Temporal.

Every change then becomes two writes, in two systems. They share no transaction. If the second one fails, the first one stays.

Take a simple case. A user switches a recurrence from monthly to weekly. The database saves the change. Then the call that updates the Schedule fails on a network cut.

Your database says "every week". Temporal still fires every month. Nothing warns you.

To guard against it, you need a job that compares both sides and fixes the gaps. But Temporal serves the list of Schedules through its search system. The documentation warns that this list is eventually consistent. A Schedule that was just created or deleted may not show up right away.

So your check job compares your database with a list that may lag behind.

A Schedule's calendar cannot say "the last day of the month" either. Temporal's API definition says it plainly. Such relative expressions are not representable, and you must list the days you want.

Yet a recurrence created on the 31st must land on February 28, then return to March 31. I covered that calculation in the AddDate article. With one Schedule per customer, that calculation would stay in your code anyway.

The sweeper: the database is the only truth

The other option keeps everything in the database. Each recurrence carries its next date, next_run_at. A single Schedule starts a sweeper at a fixed interval. The sweeper is a workflow that processes every due date that has arrived.

The recurrence lives in the database, one sweeper does the rest. At the top, every change writes into two systems. At the bottom, the API writes only to the database, and Temporal just runs on time.

It finds the due rows with this query:

SELECT id, period, anchor_at, end_at, timezone, next_index
FROM recurrences
WHERE status = 'active' AND next_run_at <= now()
ORDER BY next_run_at
LIMIT $1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Three details matter.

  • next_run_at <= now(), not "equal to today". A due date missed during an outage is still due on the next run.
  • LIMIT $1 caps the batch. The workflow passes the value 500.
  • FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED locks the rows it takes. Another sweep running at the same time skips them instead of waiting.

A partial index on next_run_at keeps the query fast. A partial index only covers the rows that match a condition, here status = 'active'.

The API, for its part, only writes to the database. On creation, the first due date is the start date. The API then asks the sweeper to run right away, with Trigger:

// The first run is due now: ask the sweeper to run instead of waiting for its next tick.
// If this fails, the next tick catches up, so it is not an error for the caller.
h := c.ScheduleClient().GetHandle(ctx, "recurrences.sweeper")
if err := h.Trigger(ctx, client.ScheduleTriggerOptions{}); err != nil {
    log.Printf("trigger sweeper: %v", err)
}

Look at the comment. If this call to Temporal fails, nothing is lost. The database already says the due date has arrived, and the next run will process it.

With one Schedule per customer, the same failure would have left both systems in disagreement.

In my design, changing a recurrence means closing the old one and creating a new one. The old one's end date is set to now. Everything happens in the database, and Temporal has nothing to update.

Batches of 500, then ContinueAsNew

Here is the sweeper workflow. Only the activity name differs from the prototype:

const batchSize = 500

func SweepWorkflow(ctx workflow.Context) error {
    ctx = workflow.WithActivityOptions(ctx, workflow.ActivityOptions{StartToCloseTimeout: time.Minute})
    var a *Activities
    for range 100 {
        var processed int
        if err := workflow.ExecuteActivity(ctx, a.ProcessDue, batchSize).Get(ctx, &processed); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if processed < batchSize {
            return nil // nothing left to do
        }
    }
    // 100 full batches: start again with a fresh history.
    return workflow.NewContinueAsNewError(ctx, workflow.GetInfo(ctx).WorkflowType.Name)
}

An activity is a workflow step that touches the outside world, here Postgres. Temporal retries it when it fails. ProcessDue takes at most 500 due rows, processes them in one transaction and returns their count.

Fewer than 500 rows? Nothing is left, so the workflow stops. Exactly 500? There may be more, so it goes again.

Why stop after 100 batches? Temporal records every step of a workflow in an event history. That history is capped at 51,200 events or 50 MB. Temporal warns you from 10,240 events or 10 MB.

ContinueAsNew restarts the same workflow with an empty history. After 100 batches, so 50,000 rows, the sweeper starts fresh and keeps going.

This exit mostly matters after a long outage, when the backlog piles up.

SKIP is enough, because the database knows what is late

A Schedule has an overlap policy. It says what to do when the time comes while the previous run is still going. Temporal offers six of them:

  • Skip, the default. The new run is not started.
  • BufferOne and BufferAll. The next run, or all the next runs, wait for the current one to finish.
  • CancelOther. The current run is cancelled, then the new one starts.
  • TerminateOther. The current run is killed at once, without waiting.
  • AllowAll. Several runs go on at the same time.

At first, the wish was to cancel the current run and start the new one. That is CancelOther. With a sweeper, I kept Skip.

The reason is simple. The sweep in progress already handles what is due. A skipped run loses nothing, because the next one reads the database again. Cancelling a sweep in the middle of a batch would only throw work away.

Same logic for catching up. A Schedule has a catchup window, one year by default. It covers the actions missed while the Temporal server was down.

The sweeper does not depend on that window. The server may have been down, or the worker, the program that runs your code. A run may also have been skipped. In every case, the query finds the late rows.

In the prototype, a recurrence anchored on January 31 received its 9 missed due dates in a single run.

Careful, the overlap policy only governs the runs started by that Schedule. It is not a lock on your data. The real protection stays in the database. It is the row lock, plus the per-due-date unique index from the AddDate article.

What the sweeper does not do on its own

The sweeper has two limits, worth knowing before you choose.

The first one is delay. A due date may wait until the next run. In my design, the sweeper runs every hour. In the prototype, it runs every 30 seconds, to see the result right away.

Trigger handles the first due date. For the next ones, pick the interval from the delay your product accepts. If each customer needs the exact minute, one Schedule per customer becomes defensible again.

The second limit is isolation. In the prototype, a batch of 500 fits in one transaction. It succeeds or fails as a whole. And by default, Temporal retries an activity with no limit on attempts.

The transaction and unique constraint make SQL retries safe. A permanent SQL error can still block the entire batch. Report it and isolate the failing item. But if each row calls another service, a single outage makes the whole batch fail.

During those retries, the workflow is still running. With Skip, the next runs are therefore skipped. The whole sweep waits on one row.

The prototype has the answer, in another job. That job starts one child workflow per item. A child workflow is a workflow started by another workflow. Its ID comes from the item. For a recurrence, use the recurrence and due date together to distinguish occurrences.

For the parent to continue, it must wait for the child to start, not for its result. Set ParentClosePolicy to ABANDON if the child must outlive the parent. By default, closing the parent terminates the child. Temporal refuses two active executions with the same ID. This does not deduplicate external calls from a retried activity. The called service must recognize the same idempotency key.

I simulated an outage of a service called by that job. Only the failing step was retried, then the child finished with no duplicate.

I would do the same for a sweeper that calls other services. It picks the due rows, then hands each one to its own child.

The rule: who owns the definition?

In the end, I kept both tools, each in its place. The boundary fits in one question: who owns the definition of the task?

  • The code owns it. It is a system job, and a developer sets its frequency before deployment. It gets its own native Schedule.
  • The database owns it. It is a recurrence, and a user creates it while the system runs. It goes through a sweeper, one per recurrence type.

For system jobs, the worker creates each Schedule when it starts. If the Schedule already exists, it updates it with the definition from the code. So the code stays the only truth, like the database for recurrences.

The checklist

The date lives in one place. The other systems only read it.

  • [ ] For each task, ask who owns its definition: the code or the database
  • [ ] Keep the next date in the database, with a partial index on active rows
  • [ ] Find due rows with <= now(), never with "equal to today"
  • [ ] Take rows in batches, with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  • [ ] Switch to ContinueAsNew after a fixed number of batches
  • [ ] Call Trigger on creation, and accept that it may fail
  • [ ] Pick the sweeper interval from the delay your product accepts
  • [ ] Give a child workflow to each item that calls another service
  • [ ] Create or update system job Schedules when the worker starts

What to remember

One Schedule per customer looks cleaner, because Temporal takes care of everything. In fact, it copies your recurrence rule into a second system. And then you have to keep both copies in agreement.

The sweeper does the opposite. Temporal knows only one thing: when to run. The database knows everything else. An outage, a skipped run or a failed call then leaves no disagreement to repair.

Are you weighing different ways to schedule tasks in Go, with or without Temporal? Let's talk.

Sources: Temporal, child workflow lifecycle · Temporal, Schedules (overlap, catchup, listing) · Temporal, Schedules in Go · temporalio/api, Schedule definition · Temporal forum, limit on the number of Schedules (2024) · Temporal, Event History limits · Temporal, Continue-As-New · Temporal, retry policies · PostgreSQL, SELECT and SKIP LOCKED · PostgreSQL, partial indexes

title: TIDE: Reclaiming Lost Performance In On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.17924v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synchronous, colocated RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) today suffers from severe under-utilization due to long-tail rollouts. Inference engines fall idle waiting for long-tail rollouts or decode at low, inefficient batch sizes. To address this, we present TIDE, an RL training system that preserves on-policy training semantics while recovering resource utilization. TIDE does so by two complementary techniques: (1) dynamically repurposing rollout GPUs for training while long-tail rollouts complete and (2) dynamically migrating rollouts between inference engines to boost decoding throughput. TIDE automatically determines the right time to repurpose rollout resources through an adaptive migration policy, obtaining performance improvements that generalize across multiple applications and hardware configurations without requiring bespoke configuration. In our evaluation, TIDE provides end-to-end speedups of up to 1.36x over colocated systems, outperforming all evaluated on-policy baselines and achieving up to 97% of optimal throughput.

title: Announcement, changelog entry or What's new widget? How to choose
description:
There are three ways to tell users what changed in your product: an announcement, a changelog entry, and a What's new panel. They look similar and do different jobs. This guide explains which to use when. I am building JustOneCX (disclosure), so the examples use its features, but the split is useful with any tool.

What is each one for?

Tool For Seen by
Announcement Something a specific group should see now The people you target, once
Changelog entry The permanent record of what shipped Anyone who looks
What's new panel A way to find the record inside your app Any signed-in user, any time

An announcement is a nudge. The changelog is the record. The panel is the door to the record.

How does an announcement work?

An announcement is a message in your product: a new feature, a maintenance notice, a promotion. It can be a modal, a slide-out, a banner or a changelog popover.

  • A banner is pinned to the top of the page and needs no target element, so it suits maintenance notices.
  • A visitor who dismisses it does not see it again.
  • It can have a call-to-action button that opens a link or starts a tour.
  • You set a schedule and targeting: everyone, or a segment, and how often.

Use Preview in the builder to click through it before it goes live.

How does the changelog work?

A changelog is the list of what you published, newest first. Visitors can mark an entry helpful, which gives you a cheap signal about what to write more of.

You can show it three ways: embedded in your own site, on your own subdomain such as roadmap.yourcompany.com, or on a hosted page with no code. All three show the same content.

What does the What's new panel add?

It is an in-app panel with your changelog (or roadmap) and a badge for unread entries. A button needs no code:

<button data-justonecx-whats-new>What's new</button>

The SDK sets an unread count on the button and adds a badge when there are new entries. It works on elements your framework renders later.

How should you combine them?

  1. Ship a feature. Write the changelog entry first. It is the permanent source.
  2. Tell the right people. If a group needs to know now, send an announcement to that segment with a button that opens the entry or starts a tour.
  3. Leave the door open. The What's new button lets anyone find the entry later.

Do not announce everything. Announcements stack up, and frequency caps exist for that reason. If every release is a modal, users learn to close modals.

A small checklist

  • Is the message for a group or for everyone?
  • Does it need action now, or is it just a record?
  • Did you preview it?
  • Is the changelog entry written before the announcement goes out?

What next?

Read the guides for announcements and the What's new widget. If you want to see the builder, you can book a demo.
