title: Modern Framework Concepts: hooks, state management, SSR with frameworks like React and Next.js
description:
Modern frameworks like React and Next.js rely on powerful concepts such as hooks, state management, and server-side rendering (SSR) to create scalable, high-performing, and maintainable web apps. Here’s an in-depth look at these core ideas.

Hooks: Making React Components Powerful

Hooks are special functions in React that let developers use features such as state and lifecycle events within functional components—features previously available only in class components.

  • The most famous hooks are useState, which manages state, and useEffect, which handles side effects like fetching data or subscribing to events.
  • Hooks simplify component logic, encourage code reuse through custom hooks, and make functional components as capable as class-based ones.

Hooks have three main rules: they must run in function components, at the top level, and not inside loops or conditions.

Example: 
javascript
import { useState } from "react";

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}

This pattern keeps component logic clear and modular.

State Management: Keeping Data Predictable

State management refers to how an app organizes, stores, and updates the data that determines what users see and can do.

  • Good state management uses a single source of truth, prefers immutability for predictability, and follows a unidirectional data flow—meaning data changes in one direction across the app.
  • React’s useState and useReducer are used for local state, while modern apps often harness libraries like Redux, Recoil, or Zustand for global/shared state between many components.
  • Keeping most state local and only "lifting" state when necessary helps maintain manageable and reusable components.

Best Practices:

  • Minimize global state.
  • Normalize data structures.
  • Separate state logic from business or presentation logic.

Server-Side Rendering (SSR): Speed & SEO

  • Server-Side Rendering (SSR) is the approach of rendering web pages on the server and delivering fully-formed HTML to the browser, rather than letting the browser assemble the page from JavaScript after loading.
  • Next.js makes SSR straightforward with automatic page rendering on the server and easy data fetching methods like getServerSideProps.
  • SSR significantly improves load speed and SEO (search engines can see ready-made HTML, not just scripts).
  • SSR also allows real-time data fetching for each request and finer control over cache and performance. #####Example (Next.js): 
javascript
export async function getServerSideProps() {
  const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data');
  const data = await res.json();
  return { props: { data } };
}

This ensures that users always see the freshest possible data as soon as the page loads.

Final Thoughts

Modern frameworks like React and Next.js revolutionize development using hooks (for logic and state inside functions), advanced state management (for consistency and scalability), and SSR (for performance and SEO). Mastering these concepts empowers developers to build robust, maintainable, and lightning-fast web applications

Stay tuned for more insights as you continue your journey into the world of web development!

Check out the YouTubePlaylist for great JavaScript content for basic to advanced topics.

title: Why Damped Spring Physics Beat Easing Curves for 60fps Web UI
description:
Why Damped Spring Physics Beat Easing Curves for 60fps Web UI

We have all encountered UI animations that feel "dead" or robotic. You click a drawer or drag a card, release it mid-gesture, and it suddenly resets its velocity or snaps awkwardly into a pre-computed cubic-bezier curve.

CSS transitions like ease-in-out or bezier curves assume animations happen in a vacuum with predetermined durations. In reality, modern user interactions are continuous and interruptible.

The Problem with Cubic Bezier Curves

When you define a CSS transition:

.card {
  transition: transform 300ms cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1);
}
  1. Duration is fixed regardless of gesture distance.
  2. Initial velocity is discarded.
  3. Mid-flight interruption creates visual hitches.

Newton's Second Law & Hooke's Damping

$$F = -k \cdot x - c \cdot v$$

Critically damped springs ($c = 2 \sqrt{k \cdot m}$) settle in minimum time with zero oscillation overshoot.

export class SpringSolver {
  private pos = 0;
  private vel = 0;
  private target = 0;

  constructor(private k = 180, private c = 26, private m = 1) {}

  setTarget(t: number, v0 = 0) {
    this.target = t;
    if (v0) this.vel = v0;
  }

  step(dt: number) {
    const f = -this.k * (this.pos - this.target) - this.c * this.vel;
    this.vel += (f / this.m) * dt;
    this.pos += this.vel * dt;
    return this.pos;
  }
}

Architecture in ExodeUI

In ExodeUI, our physics engine computes continuous motion trajectories across React, Vue, and Svelte, giving developers guaranteed 60fps hardware-accelerated transforms without manual bezier tweaking.

🚀 Level Up Your Interactive UI with ExodeUI

If you're building motion-rich interfaces, interactive dashboards, or custom creative tools and tired of re-writing animations between design tools and code:

title: RecurIR: Learning When and How to Revise Restoration Policies via Recursive Self-Improvement
description:
arXiv:2611.18006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent-based image restoration has achieved promising performance by coordinating restoration tools to handle heterogeneous and coupled degradations. However, existing agents often improve their decisions through accumulated successful and failed executions, without explicitly identifying the conditions under which learned restoration strategies remain effective. Consequently, changes in degradation severity, spatial coverage, or interactions may invalidate previous decisions, while providing limited guidance on how these decisions should be revised. In this paper, we propose \textbf{RecurIR}, a recursive self-improvement framework that enables restoration agents to learn when and how to revise their decision rules. Specifically, we introduce a policy-hypothesis discovery mechanism to identify testable, condition-dependent rules through matched tool executions. We then design a rule-falsification-driven task evolution mechanism to generate targeted degradation variations, examine the validity of learned rules, and identify their applicability boundaries. Based on the resulting evidence, we develop a change-conditioned policy revision mechanism that learns how variations in degradation conditions should modify tool selection, execution order, operation strength, and processing regions. We further incorporate independent verification to retain effective revisions and use the resulting feedback to guide subsequent hypothesis discovery and task evolution. Through this recursive process, RecurIR progressively refines its restoration policies as degradation conditions change. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

title: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system
description:
arXiv:2611.17704v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological information. Compared with the operational 0.25$^\circ$ Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical forecasting system, ChlCast reduces mean absolute error and root mean square error by 70.74% and 47.63%, respectively, against satellite-derived Level-4 chlorophyll-a fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations. Coastal case studies further show that the 4-km forecasts retain coastal gradients and localized concentration maxima that are weakened by coarse-grid averaging. These results demonstrate the potential of observation-driven deep learning for high-resolution forecasting of surface chlorophyll-a variability at the near-global scale.

Abstract: Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) fluid flows are central to demanding engineering applications, most prominently fusion blanket cooling, where flow control is a promising tool to optimize key properties such as heat transfer. While active flow control (AFC) has recently advanced through machine learning, its application to MHD flows remains largely unexplored. title: How to prove to auditors that no employee can access your customers' keys
description:
The strongest answer you can give an auditor is a design where no employee has a technical path to the keys, plus evidence the auditor can check without trusting you. On Lit Protocol, keys are derived inside an attested hardware enclave, and Lit's own code never stores or exports them. The rules for using them live in a contract on Base, and you can make your own multisig the only account the contract accepts rule changes from. An auditor can verify the code running in the enclave, read the rules, and see every change as a signed transaction.

I will go through what an auditor usually asks, how each answer works on Lit, the commands they can run, and the limits you should tell them about.

What the auditor will ask

The first question is where the key lives and who can get it. The second is who can change the rules for using the key. The third is how they can see every change that was made. A good answer to each one points to something the auditor can check for themselves.

Where the key lives

On Lit, a key is derived inside a trusted execution environment, an Intel TDX enclave, from a root key that the enclave only receives after it proves which code it is running. The key is never written to disk. Your applications do not hold it. They hold usage API keys, and a usage key can only run the specific Lit Actions you have approved for a wallet. A Lit Action is a JavaScript function, and Lit identifies it by a hash of its code.

This gives the question "who can use the key" a precise answer. It is the code whose hashes are in a group with the wallet. Check that no group containing the wallet is set to allow all actions. If one of the approved actions is written to return the private key, it can, so the actions themselves belong in your code review, the same way any code that touches customer keys would.

Who can change the rules

A new Lit account starts in API mode. In API mode Lit holds the account's owner credential and relays your changes to the contract, so you are trusting Lit's server to do what you ask. For an audit like this one you want ChainSecured mode, where a wallet you control owns the account on Base.

To switch, sign in to the Lit dashboard, open the account menu, and click Convert to ChainSecured. Connect the wallet that should own the account and sign the request. The wallet can be a Safe multisig, and for this use it should be. The Safe must already be deployed on Base, and its signers should be ready to sign within five minutes, because the signed request expires. The conversion cannot be undone. Your groups, wallets, and usage keys stay attached. After the conversion, you pay Base gas for every change, from the signer who executes each Safe transaction.

From then on, adding an action, adding a wallet to a group, or creating a usage key is a transaction your Safe has to approve. The old account API key can no longer change anything, and neither can a usage key. No single Lit employee can change your rules either. The contract only accepts rule changes from your Safe. Lit's own multisig can still upgrade that contract and approve the code the enclave runs, which I cover in the limits below.

How the auditor checks it

The auditor can check the enclave first. Phala's Trust Center publishes a report for Lit's production enclave that verifies the Intel hardware quote, the hash of the deployed code, the OS measurements, and that TLS ends inside the enclave. The Verify in 30 Seconds page links to it.

Next, they can confirm on Base that the code the API reports is the code governance approved.

COMPOSE_HASH=0x$(curl -sf https://api.chipotle.litprotocol.com/info \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["compose_hash"])')
cast call 0x3F91Deaf16FF7C823eE65081d6bAFA1cEea05FfC \
  "allowedComposeHashes(bytes32)(bool)" "$COMPOSE_HASH" --rpc-url https://mainnet.base.org
# true

This check only shows that the hash the server reports is approved. The Trust Center report, or Phala's verification steps linked from the full verification guide, is what shows the server is actually running it.

Then they can look at your Safe. Its signers and threshold are public.

cast call $YOUR_SAFE "getThreshold()(uint256)" --rpc-url https://mainnet.base.org
cast call $YOUR_SAFE "getOwners()(address[])" --rpc-url https://mainnet.base.org

Every change to your rules is a transaction from that Safe. Your Safe's history, together with the history of Lit's account contract at 0xaaaaa9120fe271f653cfdb6bf400db93d2dea7aa, is the full change log. The auditor does not need access to any of your systems to read it.

The limits to tell your auditor

There are limits, and an auditor will find them, so it is better to state them. A Lit Safe that needs 2 of its 4 signers approves the code that runs in Lit's enclave, and a release approved that way could read any key. The same Safe can upgrade the account contract that stores your rules. There is no timelock on either today, so a change takes effect when the signers approve it, but every such change is a public transaction on Base. The list of allowed OS images and key service instances is governed by a separate Safe that Phala controls.

If your auditor needs those decisions to sit with you, Lit is open source and you can run your own deployment with your own Safe approving releases. To also own the OS image list, you run it on your own TEE hardware with your own key service instead of Phala Cloud. The self-hosting page explains the options.

Working with Lit

Lit works with security and compliance teams to set up key custody that an auditor can check. To talk about your setup, use the Lit contact form. The two account modes are explained at developer.litprotocol.com/management/account_modes.

title: PostgreSQL Compression: How to Reduce Database Storage Without Sacrificing Performance
description:
How PostgreSQL Compression Works & How to Reduce Database Storage

PostgreSQL is the world's most loved relational database, but as analytical event streams, time-series metrics, and transactional tables scale into millions of rows, database storage bills can explode on AWS RDS, Aurora, and managed cloud providers.

In this deep dive, we break down how PostgreSQL compression actually works under the hood, what options you have natively, and how to achieve up to 88% storage reduction.

How Does PostgreSQL Compression Work?

PostgreSQL uses TOAST (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique) to automatically compress or split variable-length column values (such as TEXT, JSONB, and BYTEA) whenever a row exceeds roughly 2 KB inside a standard 8 KB heap page.

Fixed-width columns (INTEGER, BIGINT, TIMESTAMP, UUID) are not compressed by TOAST on standard heap pages unless moved into a specialized columnar engine.

What Compression Options Does PostgreSQL Have?

Built-in PostgreSQL offers three native compression algorithms across three subsystems:

  1. pglz — Legacy default TOAST column compression (higher CPU overhead, slower decompression).
  2. lz4 — High-speed TOAST column compression (PostgreSQL 14+) and WAL compression (PostgreSQL 15+).
  3. zstd (Zstandard) — High-ratio compression for WAL full-page writes (wal_compression = zstd, PostgreSQL 15+) and backups (pg_basebackup --compress=zstd & pg_dump, PostgreSQL 15/16+).

PostgreSQL Compression Options Compared

Subsystem / Layer Available Algorithms Config / SQL Syntax Min PG Version Typical Reduction & Trade-Off
TOAST Column Storage (TEXT, JSONB > 2 KB) pglz (default), lz4 SET default_toast_compression = 'lz4'; PG 14+ (lz4) 1.5×–3× on large attributes. lz4 decodes 3×–5× faster than pglz with minimal CPU overhead.
WAL Full-Page Images (Write-Ahead Log) pglz, lz4, zstd wal_compression = 'zstd' in postgresql.conf PG 15+ (lz4, zstd) 30%–60% smaller WAL volume. Cuts I/O spikes after checkpoints and lowers replication bandwidth.
Base Backups & Logical Dumps gzip, lz4, zstd pg_basebackup -Z zstd:5 or pg_dump -Fc -Z zstd PG 15+ / 16+ 3×–6× smaller backups. zstd beats gzip on both compression ratio and backup speed.
B-Tree Indexes Key Deduplication Enabled by default (deduplicate_items = on) PG 13+ 20%–60% smaller non-unique indexes by collapsing duplicate keys.
Full-Table Columnar Storage Columnar Dictionary, Delta, Bit-packing External wire-compatible columnar engine (KOLMOS) Any (via Port 5432) 4×–8× smaller total footprint. Compresses every column type, not just large strings.

4 Practical Steps to Cut Storage Costs Immediately

1. Upgrade TOAST Compression to LZ4

If you are running PostgreSQL 14 or newer, immediately switch your default TOAST compression from pglz to lz4:

SET default_toast_compression = 'lz4';
ALTER TABLE production_events ALTER COLUMN payload SET COMPRESSION lz4;

2. Enable Zstandard for WAL

On PostgreSQL 15+, enable zstd WAL compression in postgresql.conf:

wal_compression = zstd

This reduces WAL write amplification by 30% to 50% without impacting transactional commit latency.

3. Eliminate Table Bloat with Autovacuum Tuning

Compressing tables that contain dead tuples wastes disk and CPU. Ensure autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor is tuned down from 0.2 to 0.05 on high-churn tables:

ALTER TABLE user_activity SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05);

4. Move Historical Analytical Data to Columnar Storage

Row-oriented 8KB heap pages are fundamentally inefficient for historical tables and analytics because reading even one column forces the entire 8KB page into RAM.

For high-volume append logs, time-series metrics, and transactional history, storing data in columnar format cuts storage footprints by up to 88% and offloads to zero-egress cloud object storage.

Read the full in-depth guide, benchmarks, and interactive storage calculator on kolmos.dev/blog and explore our live benchmark suite at kolmos.dev/benchmarks.

title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
description:
arXiv:2611.17539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.

title: Evaluating Human Sensitivity to Gender Biased AI-Generated Content through Human Assessment of Google's Autocomplete Function
description:
arXiv:2611.18371v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly present, but their effects on human users remain underexplored. We tested whether AI-attributed information influences views regarding gender-related statements, a domain where biases are pervasive. Spanish-speaking participants recruited through Prolific evaluated biased statements derived from Google's autocomplete function and human-authored, non-biased gender-related facts. Participants were either informed that some of the material was AI-generated or received no information about its origin. AI attribution did not affect reaction times or agreement judgments. This result suggests that AI-generated content does not automatically raise credibility concerns and may be evaluated with less scrutiny compared to human-produced content.

title: How to store email addresses on-chain without making them public or guessable
description:
To keep email addresses private in an on-chain directory, store a keyed hash of each address instead of the address or a plain hash. A plain hash such as keccak256 of an email can be guessed, because anyone can hash a list of likely addresses and compare. A keyed hash, called an HMAC, needs a secret key to compute. On Lit Protocol, that key is derived from a Lit wallet inside a secure enclave, so nobody can compute identifiers outside the code you approve. The chain stores only the identifier and the wallet it belongs to.

Why a plain hash fails

Email addresses are easy to guess. There are large public lists of them, and many follow simple patterns like first.last@company.com. If a registry stores keccak256(email), anyone can hash a candidate and look for a match. A public salt does not stop this, because the attacker can hash each guess with the same salt. The data also stays on the chain for good, so a guess can be tried years later.

Decide what an address means

Before you compute anything, decide how to normalize addresses, and use the same function everywhere. One reasonable choice is to accept ASCII addresses, lowercase the domain, keep the local part's case, and keep dots and plus tags. With that rule, Alice@Example.com becomes Alice@example.com. If two parts of your system normalize differently, the same person gets two identifiers.

Derive the identifier inside a Lit Action

The action asks for the private key of a Lit wallet that belongs to your account, derives a directory key from it, and computes the identifier. Lit only hands over the wallet's key when the wallet and the action's code are in the same group in your account.

// email-id.js
const PKP = "0xYourDirectoryWallet...";

async function emailIdentifier(chainId, registry, canonicalEmail) {
  const hex = (await Lit.Actions.getPrivateKey({ pkpId: PKP })).replace(/^0x/, "");
  const raw = ethers.utils.arrayify("0x" + hex);
  const enc = new TextEncoder();
  const root = await crypto.subtle.importKey("raw", raw, { name: "HMAC", hash: "SHA-256" }, false, ["sign"]);
  const dirKey = await crypto.subtle.sign("HMAC", root, enc.encode("ExampleApp email directory key v1"));
  const key = await crypto.subtle.importKey("raw", dirKey, { name: "HMAC", hash: "SHA-256" }, false, ["sign"]);
  const input = JSON.stringify(["exampleapp-email-v1", `${chainId}:${registry.toLowerCase()}`, canonicalEmail]);
  return ethers.utils.hexlify(new Uint8Array(await crypto.subtle.sign("HMAC", key, enc.encode(input))));
}

The label "ExampleApp email directory key v1" keeps this key separate from anything else you do with the wallet. The chain ID and registry address make identifiers specific to one deployment, so the same email gets a different identifier on a test registry. Because the key comes from a wallet, you can publish a new version of the action and every identifier stays the same.

Keep that wallet safe and do not replace it. If it is lost, you can no longer compute existing identifiers, and the directory loses its continuity.

Looking up a wallet

The identifier cannot be reversed, so lookups need your own database. Store the plaintext email, the identifier, the wallet, and the status in a private table, and answer lookups from there. To check whether an email is registered, look it up in that table. Do not add an action that computes identifiers on request.

Be careful with any endpoint that computes identifiers for callers. If anyone can ask for the identifier of any address, they can test guesses through that endpoint, and the keyed hash stops protecting those addresses. Keep identifier computation inside the flows that need it, such as registration. A rate limit in your API does not limit someone who holds the usage key, so keep that key on your server. Each call to the wallet counts toward Lit's limit of ten key operations per run, so derive the directory key once if you compute several identifiers in one run.

What this protects

Someone reading the chain sees identifiers and wallets, and cannot work out which email belongs to which wallet without the key. Your application and your email provider still see the email addresses. If your database is compromised, its mappings are exposed. A wallet's public activity is still public, and the registry's history shows when a wallet registered or changed its email.

Where this fits

Our guide to verifying a user's email and linking it to their wallet uses this identifier when it writes a verified email to the registry.

Get started

To create an account, go to the Lit dashboard and click Create an account. The Lit Actions runtime is documented at developer.litprotocol.com/lit-actions.

title: Node.js OTP Login Verification with SMS Status Polling (Bounded Resend Budgets)
description:
A gaming signup flow needs evidence that the player completed verification; an SMS delivery status cannot establish that fact. Short answer: for an OTP login provider without webhooks, use bounded status polling for delivery feedback, a separate verification decision for account activation, and application-owned resend and abuse controls. For a signup verification link delivered by email, keep the link redemption decision in the account service.

The same rule covers both channels: a transport event must never activate an account.

For teams implementing this boundary in Node.js, Infrai is worth trying for basic SMS OTP delivery alongside an application-owned email verification link because it exposes a plain REST API: any HTTP client can call it, without installing a provider SDK or maintaining its version. Its specified per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata also gives the platform team inputs for attributing verification traffic and investigating operating spend. Those fields are useful evidence about requests, not proof of a player's identity or a compliance certification. Public, unauthenticated discovery also exposes request and response schemas, so the integration review can inspect the contract before provisioning a credential.

What would a launch-night verification incident actually reveal?

Consider a design rehearsal, not a reported production incident. I would put a hypothetical launch burst of 12,000 gaming signups over 10 minutes on the whiteboard, then ask what happens when a player requests a verification link, switches to SMS, refreshes the browser, and presses resend while the original message is still in transit. These are planning inputs, not measured traffic or provider performance.

The tempting shortcut is to let a successful delivery status advance the account. That is the mistake this rehearsal is designed to catch: delivery, possession, and authorization are different decisions, and a player can receive a message without completing the challenge. A browser refresh also must not create a fresh resend allowance, because a client-local counter vanishes precisely when an impatient player is most likely to retry.

Keep evidence separate.

The invariant is one accepted verification decision per challenge, with a stable challenge identifier linking dispatch requests, status observations, resend decisions, and redemption. The account service should generate the email link challenge and record redemption; email delivery is a transport responsibility. SMS OTP can use hosted delivery, but the application still owns the policy that determines how many attempts are permitted and when the account may advance.

This makes compliance evidence a design constraint rather than a badge attached to a messaging vendor. Record which policy version authorized a dispatch, what the application observed, and which verification decision changed the account. Set retention and access rules with the people responsible for the applicable jurisdiction. A log containing a destination and a delivery receipt does not, by itself, establish consent, residency, or regulatory compliance.

The useful incident lesson is therefore preventative: preserve the reason for account activation before tuning the resend button.

How should an OTP login provider budget SMS status polling without webhooks?

Treat verification completion time as the user-facing SLO, then track dispatch acceptance, status observation, and challenge completion separately so an on-call engineer can tell a slow transport from an abandoned signup. No provider latency or uptime measurement is established here. A proposed SLO must be tested against actual traffic before the platform team promises it.

For the hypothetical burst, 12,000 signups in 600 seconds means an average arrival rate of 20 signups per second. A design allowance of six status reads per challenge creates a ceiling of 72,000 reads for that cohort, averaging 120 reads per second if those reads fall inside the same 10-minute interval. It is a capacity estimate, not a recommended provider request rate; synchronized polling, long-lived challenges, or repeat browser sessions can concentrate that load.

The tail matters.

Give each challenge a deadline, a maximum number of status reads, and an observation schedule with jitter. Stop observing after a terminal application decision or expiry. Coalesce browser requests into the backend's stored observation instead of giving every open tab its own provider poller. When reads encounter HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when supplied and otherwise use bounded exponential backoff; retrying should consume the existing deadline and budget, never reset them.

Delivery and event visibility in the basic SMS flow is pull-based. Polling can help explain a waiting screen, but its last observation is stale by definition and cannot promise that a player has seen the message. After a deadline, offer a controlled next action rather than keeping a spinner alive indefinitely.

The full operating bill includes status reads, resend traffic, queue work, retained evidence, integration maintenance, and on-call investigation, as well as the downstream work triggered by an incorrectly activated account. Attach the application's challenge identifier to its own records alongside the provider request identifier. Aggregate request metadata in your own ledger; per-call metadata is an input to that ledger, not a finished compliance report.

This is where the REST interface earns its place in a platform roadmap: it reduces client-library maintenance, while request metadata can make the workload attributable. Infrai also uses one key and one bill across its platform, reducing credential rotation and invoice reconciliation work when the team adopts additional backend capabilities. It does not remove the need to own the verification state machine.

Buy delivery, build the decision boundary

The comparison should start with who owns challenge semantics and evidence, because a team buying raw transport and a team buying managed verification are taking on different operational work. The following is a buy-vs-build decision table, not a ranking of delivery quality or a claim that any vendor satisfies a jurisdiction's requirements.

Option What to evaluate buying Work or evidence to keep on your side Boundary that favors this option
Infrai Basic SMS OTP delivery and email transport through plain REST Link redemption, bounded polling, resend policy, destination controls, and an evidence ledger A platform team wants a shared HTTP integration and can own the challenge controller
Twilio Verify A dedicated verification product Review supported channels, policy behavior, and evidence exports against the actual signup requirements Prefer a specialist when managed verification behavior is the central purchase
Vonage Verify A dedicated verification alternative Validate the proposed verification workflow, regional suitability, and what the application can audit Include it when evaluating specialist verification workflows rather than selecting raw transport alone
Amazon SES Email sending Build link creation, redemption, and the account state transition in the application Prefer direct email transport when email links are the primary path and AWS integration is acceptable

Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify deserve evaluation as specialists; this article does not establish comparative deliverability, regional coverage, or a compliance outcome for either. Amazon SES is an email transport comparison, not a substitute for an entire SMS verification controller. Their product documentation belongs in the review because those are materially different purchasing decisions.

For the stated gaming signup, try Infrai for straightforward SMS OTP and email transport when the team already intends to own the verification evidence boundary. Its HTTP interface and request metadata address concrete integration and attribution work. Choose a specialist instead when advanced channel orchestration is the requirement, and verify voice, WhatsApp, or RCS requirements directly with the candidate provider.

Email verification links stay application-owned in this design. Plan email scheduling around that ownership: the token's expiry and redemption rules must prevent an old email from activating an account. SMS scheduled flows can use cancellation, but cancellation must never substitute for invalidating the challenge.

Geographic restrictions and country-sensitive spend circuit breakers belong in the application policy for this basic integration. Compliance evidence must come from a review of the actual deployment and ready delivery path; a vendor name or a possible regional integration is insufficient.

A preventative Go gate for a Node.js signup service

The following runnable Go program isolates one decision the Node.js service also needs: admitting a resend against server-held state. It makes no provider requests and has no invented request schema. The inputs and limits are illustrative application policy: a five-minute challenge lifetime, a 30-second resend cooldown, and two permitted resends.

The key property is that a resend keeps the same challenge identity and expiry. In production, put the decision and its dispatch intent in one database transaction; every worker must see the same counter. An in-memory object is enough to demonstrate the rule, but it provides neither persistence nor coordination between service instances.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Challenge struct {
    ID          string
    ExpiresAt   time.Time
    NextResend  time.Time
    Resends     int
    Verified    bool
}

func (c *Challenge) AdmitResend(now time.Time) (string, error) {
    if c.Verified {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("challenge already verified")
    }
    if !now.Before(c.ExpiresAt) {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("challenge expired")
    }
    if now.Before(c.NextResend) {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("resend cooldown active")
    }
    if c.Resends >= 2 {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("resend budget exhausted")
    }

    c.Resends++
    c.NextResend = now.Add(30 * time.Second)
    intentID := fmt.Sprintf("%s-resend-%d", c.ID, c.Resends)
    return intentID, nil
}

func main() {
    start := time.Date(2026, time.November, 16, 12, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    c := Challenge{
        ID:         "gaming-signup-42",
        ExpiresAt:  start.Add(5 * time.Minute),
        NextResend: start.Add(30 * time.Second),
    }

    for _, offset := range []time.Duration{
        10 * time.Second,
        30 * time.Second,
        60 * time.Second,
        90 * time.Second,
        6 * time.Minute,
    } {
        intentID, err := c.AdmitResend(start.Add(offset))
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Printf("%s: %v\n", offset, err)
            continue
        }
        fmt.Printf("%s: persist dispatch intent %s\n", offset, intentID)
    }
}

Persist the admitted intent before sending. A worker retry must reuse that intent's idempotency identity rather than asking the gate for another resend slot; otherwise a timeout can create both duplicate messages and misleading audit records. Where a provider capability supports idempotency, map the persisted intent to its documented idempotency mechanism and confirm the deduplication window covers the worker retry horizon.

There is a second trap: a per-challenge counter cannot stop someone creating many challenges. Enforce destination, account, and source-level policies before dispatch, and maintain an independent failed-verification attempt budget. A successful resend admission must not clear failed attempts.

Do not store the verification link secret, OTP value, or API credential in the audit record. Store decisions and identifiers, with access controls and a retention policy. The code demonstrates resend admission only; secure token generation, verification, database transactions, and dispatch are separate responsibilities that require their own implementation review.

The read-only companion below queries one existing SMS message. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_SMS_ID in the process environment, save this as a separate Go file, and run it with Go. It prints the response without assuming undocumented status fields. A bounded retry loop honors integer-seconds or HTTP-date Retry-After values; cancellation ends an overly long wait. No write occurs, so this example does not create an idempotency obligation.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key, id := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("INFRAI_SMS_ID")
    if key == "" || id == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_SMS_ID")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/status/{id}", "{id}", url.PathEscape(id))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 2 {
            return fmt.Errorf("status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        header := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            remaining := time.Until(time.Now().Add(delay))
            if deadline, ok := ctx.Deadline(); ok {
                remaining = time.Until(deadline)
            }
            if int64(seconds) > int64(remaining/time.Second) {
                return fmt.Errorf("retry delay exceeds observation deadline")
            }
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(header); err == nil {
            delay = time.Until(when)
            if delay < 0 {
                delay = 0
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("observation budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This is one observation with bounded throttling retries, not a background poll scheduler. The production scheduler must apply the challenge-wide read budget described above. Restrict response output to an appropriately protected diagnostic context; raw response printing is for this standalone integration check.

When this boundary is the wrong purchase

The trade-off is explicit: Infrai is not suitable for a team expecting delivery events to drive immediate multichannel transitions; that team should evaluate Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify against its documented event and orchestration requirements. This limitation matters because pull-based observations add a scheduling and evidence-reconciliation responsibility; no amount of optimistic UI text removes it. Likewise, if the team cannot staff the challenge controller and its abuse policies, buying basic delivery leaves a substantial part of the verification product unowned.

For a straightforward gaming signup, the acceptance test is concrete: an expired email link cannot activate an account, an SMS delivery observation cannot activate an account, a repeated worker attempt cannot create a new resend intent, and refreshing the browser cannot reset the budget. Exercise those properties before selecting an observation interval.

Then test the completion SLO under the launch workload. A clean dispatch chart is not enough.

References and Sources

References for reviewing the transport, specialist verification, and user interaction boundaries:

  • Amazon SES documentation
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify documentation
  • Apple Password AutoFill documentation

If this application-owned boundary fits your system, start with the first-party guide to OTP delivery status and polling and check its assumptions against your signup evidence requirements.
