title: I Audited My Own Site's Images. The srcset Reflex Was Wrong for Half of Them.
description:
Every responsive-image guide ends the same way: add srcset and sizes, you are serving desktop images to phones. I ran that advice against our own production site this morning, and it broke on our own numbers. Not because the advice is wrong, but because it skips the step that decides whether it applies.

Here is what I measured, how I measured it, and the order I now check things in.

The audit

21 URLs from the live sitemap.xml, fetched with a plain Node script (no browser, no build step, nothing installed). For every <img> tag I recorded srcset, sizes, width, height, loading, and then fetched each unique image to read its intrinsic dimensions straight out of the file signature (PNG IHDR, JPEG SOFn) and its delivered byte length.

The site-wide result:

Measured Value
Pages 21
<img> elements 187
Elements with srcset 0
Elements with sizes 0
<picture> / <source> elements 0
Unique images 69 (47 PNG, 15 JPEG, 7 unreadable)
Images served as WebP or AVIF 0
Images with a Cache-Control header 0

So yes: zero responsive markup, site-wide. That part of the standard advice applies to us completely.

But then I looked at where the bytes actually were.

The first surprise: the homepage was not the problem

The homepage has 61 image elements totalling 830 KB — and 59 of them carry loading="lazy". Only the 5 KB logo loads eagerly. First paint on the homepage is not paying for those images at all.

The page that is actually heavy is a service page:

Page HTML CSS JS Images Total Image share
digital-marketing.html 26.7 KB 77 KB 603.6 KB 4,737 KB 5,445 KB 87 %
graphic-design.html 27.5 KB 77 KB 603.5 KB 2,820 KB 3,528 KB 80 %
/ (homepage) 102.3 KB 0.7 KB 604.4 KB 830 KB 1,537 KB 54 %

digital-marketing.html has one lazy-loaded image. The five-card gallery that makes up most of its weight loads all six of its PNGs eagerly, on every visit, before anything scrolls.

If I had stopped at "homepage has lots of images", I would have fixed the wrong page. Measure eager bytes, not total bytes. loading="lazy" changes the answer completely, and it is invisible in a byte count that does not separate them.

The second surprise: on a phone, we are not over-serving

This is the step the standard advice skips, and it is arithmetic rather than opinion.

The gallery cards sit in .work-showcase, which is repeat(3, 1fr) above 1024 px, two columns at 641–1024 px, and one column at or below 640 px. The container is min(100% - clamp(28px, 6vw, 48px), 1280px), tightening to -32px under 1024 px and -24px under 480 px. Each card is aspect-ratio: 4/3 with the image at width: 100%; height: 100%; object-fit: cover.

So the CSS box — the thing a srcset is supposed to match — is:

Viewport Columns CSS box × DPR 2 × DPR 3
1440 3 413 × 309 826 1,239
1024 2 486 × 364 972 1,458
390 1 366 × 274 732 1,098

The source images are 1024 × 1536.

On a 390 px phone at DPR 3 — a modern iPhone or Pixel — the card needs 1,098 device pixels wide. Our source is 1,024. The phone is not receiving an oversized image; it is receiving a slightly undersized one.

On a 1440 px desktop at DPR 1, the card needs 413 and gets 1024. That is 2.5× the width, 6.1× the pixels, and it is real waste.

Same file, same site, opposite conclusions. srcset is a fix for the desktop case here and does nothing for the phone case. Which is the opposite of how the advice is usually written.

So the honest rule is:

Compute CSS box width × devicePixelRatio for each breakpoint you actually support. Only if the delivered width exceeds it meaningfully is srcset the right tool.

The third surprise: the codec was the whole story

Since dimensions were not the phone problem, I looked for what was. I re-encoded the six gallery PNGs with the same pixels and only changed the container, using System.Drawing at quality 80:

File As PNG As JPEG q80, identical 1024×1536 Ratio
dm-growth-01.png 1,944 KB 155.6 KB 12.5×
dm-strategy-01.png 635.5 KB 159 KB 4.0×
dm-ads-01.png 542.6 KB 152.1 KB 3.6×
dm-email-01.png 434.5 KB 169.5 KB 2.6×
dm-campaign-01.png 522.6 KB 215.3 KB 2.4×
dm-seo-01.png 499.1 KB 236.8 KB 2.1×

No pixels removed. No resolution changed. Just a container that suits photographic content instead of one that suits flat graphics.

Rolling the five visible gallery cards up: 4,080 KB as delivered, 592 KB as JPEG q80 at 2× the desktop CSS box — 85.5 % off. At the 390 px box, 493 KB — 87.9 % off.

That single number is bigger than every responsive-markup fix on this page combined.

The fourth surprise: resizing PNG made it worse

This one is the reason I am writing this up instead of just filing a ticket.

I generated a 972 px-wide PNG for the 1024 breakpoint, expecting a smaller file. dm-growth-01 went from 1,944 KB to 2,487 KB. It got 28 % bigger after losing 5 % of its pixels. The same thing happened at every other width: the 826 px PNG was 1,843 KB, and the 732 px PNG was 1,462 KB — all still above, or barely below, the original.

Lossless PNG pays for the resampling filter's new edge and gradient data. A photographic 3D render has no flat colour runs to exploit, so shrinking it can raise its entropy faster than it lowers its pixel count.

If you add srcset with PNG variants of a photographic image, you can make the page heavier while making the markup more correct. I would have shipped that if I had trusted the reflex instead of measuring.

The order I check in now

  1. Separate eager from total. loading="lazy" moves the answer. Count bytes that load before the first scroll.
  2. Compute the box, then multiply by DPR. Read the grid and aspect-ratio rules, don't eyeball a screenshot. If delivered width ≈ box × DPR, srcset buys you nothing.
  3. Change the codec before you change the markup. Same pixels, container swap. On our gallery this was 2.1×–12.5×.
  4. Then add srcset for the breakpoints where step 2 showed a real gap — for us, the desktop columns.
  5. Check Cache-Control last, but don't skip it. All 69 images on our site ship without it, so browsers fall back to heuristic freshness from Last-Modified. Nothing is cached deterministically.

The markup, for the case where it does apply

Once you know the box, srcset is short. The w descriptor plus sizes is the form I use, because it lets the browser do the DPR maths against a length it can measure:

<img
  src="dm-growth-01@732.jpg"
  srcset="dm-growth-01@413.jpg 413w,
          dm-growth-01@732.jpg 732w,
          dm-growth-01@826.jpg 826w,
          dm-growth-01@1024.jpg 1024w"
  sizes="(max-width: 640px) calc(100vw - 24px),
         (max-width: 1024px) calc((min(100vw - 32px, 1280px) - 20px) / 2),
         calc((min(100vw - 48px, 1280px) - 40px) / 3)"
  width="1024" height="1536"
  loading="lazy" decoding="async"
  alt="Growth marketing campaign visual">

sizes has to describe the layout, not the file. If your card is a 1fr column inside a min()-sized container with a gap, that is what goes in sizes. A wrong sizes is worse than no srcset, because the browser trusts it.

Two things that are easy to get wrong in this specific pattern:

  • object-fit: cover crops, so the visible pixels are not the whole file. Our source is 2:3 portrait into a 4:3 landscape box. Width governs the cover scale, so matching srcset to the box width is right — but if you instead sized by the area of the box you would under-serve badly.
  • Keep width and height as intrinsic pixel values even when you serve a smaller file. They are the aspect-ratio hint that prevents layout shift. Ours are correct today, which is the one thing this gallery already got right.

For genuine art direction — a different crop per breakpoint, not just a different size — that is <picture> with <source media>, and it is a different decision. We have zero <picture> elements and, on the evidence above, do not need them yet.

What I am not claiming

  • No field data. Chrome UX Report has said "not enough usage data" for this domain for months. Every figure here is a lab measurement on one machine, from one observation point, with no throttling and no synthetic monitoring.
  • Quality was not assessed. I measured bytes at q80. I did not run a visual A/B, so "q80 is acceptable for these images" is not a finding, it is an assumption to check before shipping.
  • WebP and AVIF were not measured. My toolchain had no encoder for them. They would very likely beat the JPEG numbers again, so treat 592 KB as a conservative floor, not the target.
  • The PNG inflation is one encoder's resize filter. HighQualityBicubic specifically. The general point — verify that a downscaled lossless variant is actually smaller — holds regardless.
  • 7 unreadable in the format tally means my header parser did not recognise them, not that they are broken.

We have a live site, and I found the wrong thing to fix by trusting a rule of thumb. Check the box before you check the markup.

Prepared with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy by Design Den Solutions. The measurements come from scripts run against our own production site on 17 November 2026; the audit and re-encode scripts and their JSON output are described in this article rather than attached.

We build and maintain responsive websites, and image weight is something we now measure before we recommend a fix. If your site's first load is heavier than you expected, that is work we take on: web development services — +91 98721 90965.

title: How to fix ITMS-91053 in React Native and Expo (with one command)
description:
You upload a React Native build to App Store Connect, and a few minutes later Apple sends an email with this subject:

ITMS-91053: Missing API declaration

If you've seen it, this post explains what it means, why React Native apps hit it so often, and how to fix it for good. If you haven't seen it yet, this is how to make sure you never do.

What Apple wants

Since May 2024, every iOS app has to explain why it uses certain APIs that could be used to identify a device. Apple calls them required reason APIs. There are five groups:

  • User defaults (simple key-value storage)
  • File timestamps (when a file was created or changed)
  • System boot time
  • Disk space
  • Active keyboards

Your app has to list each group it uses in a file called PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy, together with an approved reason code. If one is missing, Apple flags the upload.

Why React Native apps get caught

Your JavaScript never touches these APIs. Your libraries do. Storage, device info, file system, maps, video, Firebase, analytics: each one may use some of them in its native iOS code.

Some libraries ship their own privacy file. But React Native links most native code statically through CocoaPods, and as Expo's privacy guide points out, Apple doesn't reliably read those library files. The safe fix is to declare everything your libraries use in your app's own privacy file.

Doing that by hand means opening every native library in node_modules, searching its iOS code, picking the right reason codes, and repeating it every time you add or update a library.

Nobody does that. So I built a tool for it.

The fix: one command

rn-privacy is a free, open-source CLI. Run it in your app folder:

npx rn-privacy

In about a second it scans every native library in your app and lists:

  • which of the five API groups your app needs to declare
  • which libraries use each one
  • which libraries use them without declaring them anywhere (these are the ones that trigger ITMS-91053)

Then check your app and fix it:

npx rn-privacy check
npx rn-privacy ios --write

check tells you exactly what's missing. On one of my apps it said:

✗ Missing required reason API: Disk space (used by react-native-maps, GoogleMaps SDK)

ios --write then adds the missing entries for you:

  • Bare React Native: it updates ios/<YourApp>/PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy
  • Expo: it updates app.json

It only adds. Nothing already in your file is removed, and without --write it just shows what it would change.

Never get the email again

Add one line to your CI:

- run: npx rn-privacy check

Now when someone adds a library that needs a new declaration, your build fails, not your App Store upload.

Bonus: the store privacy forms

Both stores also ask what data your app collects: App Privacy in App Store Connect and Data safety in Google Play Console. Again, most of that data is collected by your libraries.

rn-privacy knows what popular SDKs collect (Firebase, Sentry, AdMob, Meta, Mixpanel, Amplitude, PostHog, Segment, RevenueCat, OneSignal, AppsFlyer, Branch and more) and drafts the answers for both stores:

npx rn-privacy report -o store-privacy.md

It also tells apart data your app can read (camera, location, contacts) from data it collects. Using expo-location doesn't mean you must declare location. You only declare it if you send it to a server.

What I found on real apps

Before publishing, I ran it on two production apps, one Expo and one bare React Native:

  • One had no privacy file at all, while its libraries used 4 of the 5 API groups.
  • The other was missing Disk space, needed by react-native-maps and the Google Maps SDK.
  • Several popular libraries used these APIs in their iOS code without declaring them.

Neither app had shown any warning. Both would have been flagged by Apple.

Reason codes cheat sheet

When a library doesn't give a reason, rn-privacy suggests the one most apps use. Make sure it matches what your app does:

  • CA92.1: User defaults, data only your app can access
  • 1C8F.1: User defaults, shared with your widgets or extensions
  • C617.1: File timestamps, for files inside your app
  • 3B52.1: File timestamps, for files the user picked
  • 35F9.1: Boot time, to measure time between events
  • E174.1: Disk space, checking there's room before saving files
  • 85F4.1: Disk space, showing free space to the user

Codes C56D.1 and 0A2A.1 are only for SDKs and must never go in an app's file. rn-privacy removes them for you.

Honest limits

  • It's a starting point, not legal advice. You're responsible for what you declare.
  • It can't see what your own code or server does with user data.
  • It knows the data practices of the libraries in its list. Others are still scanned for the five API groups.
  • It never turns on tracking settings for you. If you use ad SDKs, set that up yourself.

Try it

It's free, takes a second, and changes nothing unless you add --write.

  • ⭐ GitHub: https://github.com/yogesh2902/rn-privacy
  • 📦 npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/rn-privacy

This is my first open-source package. If a library you use is missing, or the tool gets something wrong, please open an issue.

Have you been hit by ITMS-91053? Which library caused it? Tell me in the comments 👇

title: Inside my React portfolio: a glassmorphic bento grid with generated project data
description:
My portfolio repository, rsume-site, is a React application built around a glassmorphic bento grid. The interesting part is not just the translucent cards. It is how the page separates its presentation from a generated content file, while keeping most of the interface in a straightforward component tree.

A small frontend stack

The package configuration uses React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Framer Motion, and Lucide icons. There is no application server in the implementation described here. The page imports its content from src/data/auto-content.json, rather than fetching the project list during rendering.

In src/App.tsx, the root component composes a background, floating decorations, a glass shell, and individual cards. A reusable GlassCard wraps its children in a motion element with an opacity and vertical entrance animation. Each card supplies its own delay, so the layout can appear in stages without repeating the animation configuration everywhere.

The cards cover a hero, three featured skill categories, projects, an Arka link, and contact information. The hero delegates its title and floating code brackets to separate components. That keeps those visual effects out of the main layout code.

Project data is separate from project presentation

I find the project selection logic worth making explicit. The application copies and sorts the project array, placing the configured Arka repository first and ordering the remaining entries by update time. The phone-shaped project previews then exclude Arka and take only two projects. A separate “View all” link points to the GitHub profile.

Those phone previews are illustrative UI compositions, not screenshots of the linked applications. They use gradients, translucent blocks, a project title, and a hover animation. This distinction matters when describing what a visitor is actually seeing.

The README documents a refresh command that updates the generated JSON:

npm run sync

It also says GitHub Actions refreshes projects daily and on main-branch pushes that touch the sync script. The page therefore consumes a saved snapshot of project metadata, not a live feed on every visit.

Running the frontend

The README lists these development commands:

npm run dev
npm run build
npm run lint

The package file confirms that the production build runs tsc -b && vite build. It also provides npm run preview. The README does not include a complete dependency-installation walkthrough, so those commands should not be mistaken for a fully documented setup sequence.

The limits of this version

Some content is intentionally fixed in code, including the featured skill categories and email contact. The LinkedIn QR image comes from an external QR-generation service. That introduces a network dependency even though the project data itself is bundled.

I would describe this version as a focused portfolio frontend, not a CMS or a real-time GitHub dashboard. This walkthrough is based on source inspection, not a fresh build or performance benchmark. The concrete takeaway is architectural: a generated data file can sit behind an expressive React layout without making the rendering layer responsible for synchronization.

title: TechInventory: cómo comprobar la recuperación de CouchDB con Docker, GitHub Actions y Azure
description:
Autor: Gabriela Estefania Cohaila Alvarado

El problema: conservar datos no demuestra que podamos recuperarlos

En la primera etapa de TechInventory usamos un volumen de Docker para que el inventario sobreviviera al reemplazo de contenedores. Esa persistencia depende del almacenamiento original: si desaparece la máquina o el volumen, también podemos perder la información.

Por eso esta continuación incorpora un respaldo físico cifrado y un ensayo de restauración. El criterio de aceptación es concreto: recuperar en otro volumen y comprobar que los documentos, sus revisiones y los permisos coincidan.

Los recursos públicos de esta construcción son:

  • Repositorio de la aplicación.
  • Script de respaldo y recuperación.
  • Prueba automatizada de recuperación exitosa.
  • Aprovisionamiento y despliegue automatizado en Azure.
  • Resultados de la demostración en Azure.
  • Video público de la construcción, con narración femenina en español y duración aproximada de 3:03.

Una decisión adecuada para nuestro alcance

El laboratorio utiliza un nodo de CouchDB y pocos datos sintéticos. Elegimos una copia física en frío: pausamos las escrituras de Express, obtenemos una referencia del contenido y detenemos CouchDB antes de copiar su volumen y configuración.

La documentación de CouchDB permite respaldar los archivos de base y recomienda conservar la configuración necesaria para restaurar el servicio. También admite replicación; sin embargo, una réplica que recibe eliminaciones o cambios equivocados no reemplaza por sí sola una copia anterior conservada.

Nuestra pausa es una decisión de simplicidad para el laboratorio. No significa que CouchDB obligue siempre a detener la base para respaldarla, ni demuestra alta disponibilidad. Para un servicio continuo habría que evaluar la consistencia, el tiempo permitido de interrupción y el mecanismo de captura apropiado.

Del volumen a un archivo protegido

El script backup.sh exige un archivo externo con la contraseña de cifrado y utiliza flock para impedir dos respaldos simultáneos. Luego conserva los datos físicos de CouchDB, su directorio etc y las variables necesarias para reconstruir la aplicación.

Después de la captura reinicia los servicios originales. El cifrado, la transferencia y el ensayo se realizan fuera de esa pausa. El paquete se cifra con GnuPG usando AES-256; la suma SHA-256 se calcula sobre el archivo cifrado.

Estas medidas cumplen funciones diferentes. El cifrado protege la confidencialidad del paquete, que contiene configuración sensible. La suma permite detectar cambios frente a una referencia confiable. Una suma pública que puede ser reemplazada junto con su archivo no prueba quién creó el respaldo.

El destino externo es un contenedor privado de Azure Blob Storage, separado del disco de la VM. La transferencia utiliza HTTPS y una autorización SAS temporal. La clave de cifrado debe conservarse por separado: ni el repositorio público ni el mismo almacenamiento de las copias deben ser su única ubicación.

La restauración como prueba automática

El ensayo comprueba primero el SHA-256, descifra el paquete y extrae su contenido nuevamente. Esto evita aprobar una restauración usando por accidente los archivos temporales originales en lugar del respaldo cifrado.

Después crea un proyecto Compose independiente con su propia red y volumen. Arranca CouchDB con la misma imagen de la captura y recupera allí los archivos. La instancia restaurada no publica puertos ni sobrescribe el volumen original.

La comparación incluye:

  • Cantidad de documentos.
  • Identificadores y revisiones de los equipos.
  • Hash del contenido de los documentos.
  • Hash del objeto de permisos _security.

Si los resultados difieren, el comando falla. El ensayo no se limita a comprobar que un contenedor esté encendido.

Integración en GitHub Actions

El workflow backup-drill.yml levanta una instancia real de CouchDB, construye la aplicación y agrega un equipo sintético. Genera una clave efímera y ejecuta el proceso de respaldo y restauración. Se dispara ante cambios pertinentes en main y también admite ejecución manual.

La ejecución pública del 16 de noviembre de 2026 terminó con PASS, coincidencia de documentos y revisiones, coincidencia de permisos y restauración aislada. Registró dos segundos para el tramo de recuperación del pequeño conjunto de prueba.

Este dato no es un RTO de producción: no incluye recuperar toda una infraestructura, descargar desde el almacenamiento remoto ni comprobar todos los accesos de usuarios. Las evidencias del workflow tienen retención limitada; el código permanece en el repositorio.

Qué se comprobó en la nube pública

La demostración se desplegó automáticamente en una VM Ubuntu de Azure for Students mediante Azure CLI y Docker Compose, con Caddy para HTTPS. La API respondió correctamente e identificó Apache CouchDB como base de datos.

La recuperación aislada en Azure comparó tres documentos y terminó con PASS. El tramo medido tardó seis segundos. Azure Blob Storage recibió el archivo cifrado de 24 897 bytes y su suma de 108 bytes. Ambos se descargaron a Cloud Shell y la suma devolvió OK.

Es necesario distinguir las dos comprobaciones: el ensayo completo restauró el archivo cifrado local; la descarga de Blob se validó por SHA-256 por separado. No afirmamos haber ejecutado un segundo ensayo completo desde esa descarga.

Los resultados también registran acceso público de blobs deshabilitado, HTTPS obligatorio y TLS 1.2 mínimo. La infraestructura fue temporal y se retiró tras conservar las evidencias para controlar los créditos académicos.

Frecuencia y retención: objetivos de operación

Para una operación continua proponemos copias diarias y previas a cambios relevantes, siete copias diarias y cuatro semanales, con pruebas periódicas desde el almacenamiento externo. Esa política es una propuesta: el laboratorio no demuestra semanas de ejecución ni un respaldo productivo diario ya programado.

Con una copia diaria válida, el objetivo de RPO sería aproximadamente 24 horas; depende de que el proceso se ejecute y su copia sea recuperable. El RTO debe medirse con datos y condiciones representativos. También harían falta alertas, custodia de claves y pruebas de acceso posteriores a la recuperación.

La construcción tampoco demuestra una estrategia 3-2-1 completa: no contamos con una tercera copia independiente verificada. El resultado útil de esta etapa es un mecanismo reproducible que exige evidencia de recuperación antes de considerar exitoso el respaldo.

Referencias

  • Apache CouchDB: Backing up CouchDB.
  • Microsoft Learn: autorización de Azure Storage mediante SAS.
  • TechInventory: implementación y evidencias públicas.

title: Measuring answer faithfulness in RAG: metrics that hold up
description:
Short answer: faithfulness in RAG means every claim the answer makes is supported by the retrieved context — not by what the model memorized. Three metrics hold up: a RAGAS faithfulness score for eval suites, a deterministic grounding check for CI, and a narrow LLM-as-judge for the edge cases neither catches.

The confusion I see most often: people conflate correctness and faithfulness. A correct answer can be unfaithful — the model happened to state the right fact from memory, not from the context you gave it. That's a different failure mode than getting it wrong, and it matters a lot when the retrieved context changes.

What does faithfulness actually measure — and what it doesn't?

Faithfulness answers: did the model only use what I gave it?

It says nothing about whether the retrieved context was right in the first place (that's context precision and recall), and nothing about whether the answer addressed the question well (that's answer relevancy). Three separate dimensions, easy to conflate.

The concrete definition: a faithful answer contains zero claims that require knowledge beyond the retrieved chunks to verify. If your context says "the return window is 30 days" and the model outputs "returns are accepted within 30 days" — faithful. If it outputs "returns are accepted within 30 days, free of charge" and your context says nothing about fees — the second half is unfaithful. It might even be correct. Doesn't matter.

How does RAGAS measure faithfulness?

RAGAS faithfulness works in two steps: decompose, then check.

Step 1 — decompose the answer into atomic statements. An LLM splits the answer into the smallest verifiable claims. "Returns are free within 30 days of purchase" becomes two statements: "returns are free" and "the return window is 30 days."

Step 2 — check each statement against the context. Another LLM call checks whether each statement is entailed by the retrieved chunks. The score is supported / total.

from ragas import evaluate
from ragas.metrics import faithfulness
from datasets import Dataset

# Your data: question, answer your RAG produced, and the contexts it retrieved
data = {
    "question": ["What is the return policy?"],
    "answer": ["You can return items within 30 days for a full refund, free of charge."],
    "contexts": [["Purchases may be returned within 30 days. No restocking fee applies."]],
}

dataset = Dataset.from_dict(data)
result = evaluate(dataset, metrics=[faithfulness])
print(result["faithfulness"])  # e.g., 0.5 — "free of charge" wasn't in the context

A score of 0.5 here means one of the two decomposed claims wasn't supported. The model said "free of charge" — that's consistent with "no restocking fee," but RAGAS decomposed them into separate verifiable statements and the LLM-as-judge for that specific claim didn't find the exact phrase. That's a known limitation of the decomposition step.

The practical threshold: score below 0.6 on a golden dataset question → manual review. Below 0.4 → hard failure. Above 0.8 → trust it.

How do you implement your own faithfulness scorer?

You don't always want RAGAS's decomposition step. Sometimes you want a scorer that maps exactly to your rubric. Here's the core:

FAITHFULNESS_PROMPT = """\
You are a strict factual auditor. Answer ONLY with a JSON object.

Retrieved context:
{context}

Generated answer:
{answer}

For each factual claim in the answer, decide:
  "supported": the claim is directly entailed by the context
  "unsupported": the claim cannot be verified from the context alone
  "contradicted": the claim conflicts with the context

Respond with:
{{"claims": [{{"text": "...", "verdict": "supported|unsupported|contradicted"}}], "faithfulness_score": 0.0-1.0}}
Score = supported_claims / total_claims. Contradicted claims count as unsupported."""

def faithfulness_score(answer: str, context_chunks: list[str]) -> dict:
    context = "\n---\n".join(context_chunks)
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
        max_tokens=400,
        temperature=0,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": FAITHFULNESS_PROMPT.format(
            context=context, answer=answer
        )}],
    )
    import json
    return json.loads(resp.content[0].text.strip())

# Usage in an eval loop
result = faithfulness_score(
    answer="Returns are free within 30 days. Standard shipping applies.",
    context_chunks=["Returns accepted within 30 days of purchase."],
)
# result["faithfulness_score"] = 0.5
# result["claims"][1]["verdict"] = "unsupported"  # "standard shipping applies" wasn't in context

Pin temperature=0 and the model version. When you upgrade the judge model, re-baseline your score distributions before trusting comparisons.

The grounding check: fast faithfulness proxy for CI

The LLM-based scorer costs tokens and takes ~500ms per call. You need something that runs on every PR without a bill. A grounding check gives you ~70% of the signal for free:

import re

def extract_facts(text: str) -> set[str]:
    """Extract numbers, percentages, timeframes — the claims most likely to hallucinate."""
    return set(re.findall(
        r'\b\d+(?:[.,]\d+)?(?:\s?%|\s?days?|\s?hours?|\s?months?|\s?\$)?\b',
        text, re.IGNORECASE
    ))

def grounding_check(answer: str, context_chunks: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Return specific facts in the answer that appear in no context chunk."""
    context_text = " ".join(context_chunks)
    context_facts = extract_facts(context_text)
    answer_facts = extract_facts(answer)
    return list(answer_facts - context_facts)

def test_refund_answer_grounded():
    context = ["The return window is 30 days from delivery date."]
    answer = "You have 30 days to return items. A $5 handling fee may apply."

    ungrounded = grounding_check(answer, context)
    assert not ungrounded, f"Answer claims facts not in context: {ungrounded}"
    # fails: {'$5'} — the model invented a fee that isn't in the source

This catches number hallucinations instantly. What it misses: semantic inversions ("returns are not accepted" when the source says they are), invented qualitative claims without numbers, and omissions. The LLM scorer handles those.

Combining the metrics in an eval suite

Don't pick one metric. Run the cheap check first, escalate to scored eval only when needed:

def full_faithfulness_eval(answer: str, context_chunks: list[str]) -> dict:
    # Layer 1: instant, free
    ungrounded = grounding_check(answer, context_chunks)
    if ungrounded:
        return {"verdict": "FAIL", "reason": f"invented facts: {ungrounded}", "score": 0.0}

    # Layer 2: scored, ~500ms
    scored = faithfulness_score(answer, context_chunks)
    score = scored["faithfulness_score"]

    if score < 0.6:
        return {"verdict": "FAIL", "reason": "faithfulness score below threshold", "score": score}
    if score < 0.8:
        return {"verdict": "REVIEW", "reason": "borderline faithfulness", "score": score}

    return {"verdict": "PASS", "reason": "", "score": score}

In CI: run only Layer 1. In your nightly eval suite: run both. Any REVIEW verdict feeds a Slack thread for a human — expect 2–5% of your eval set to land there, not 100%.

What faithfulness doesn't tell you

A score of 1.0 means the model said nothing beyond what the context contained. That's the ceiling. The floor — whether the context itself was right — is a retrieval problem: context precision (did the retriever pull relevant chunks?) and context recall (did it pull all the relevant chunks?). Faithfulness doesn't touch either.

It also doesn't catch omissions. If the source says "this product is for adults only" and the model writes a glowing summary with no age restriction, every claim in the summary may be supported by some chunk — faithfulness passes. The omission of a safety constraint is invisible to faithfulness scoring. You need a separate "completeness" rubric for that, targeted at your high-stakes fields.

The faithfulness + grounding check combo gets you ~90% of attribution failures. The other 10% — omissions, subtle re-framings, retrieval failures — need purpose-built checks for your domain.

If you want a working eval harness with grounding check, RAGAS integration, and a custom judge prompt already wired up, the free test lab has it. The full chapter on RAG eval design — including how faithfulness interacts with the other three RAGAS dimensions and when to weight them differently — is in AI Software Testing in Practice.

FAQ

What is answer faithfulness in RAG?
Faithfulness measures whether every factual claim in the generated answer is supported by the retrieved context — not by the model's training data. A faithful answer only asserts things the retriever actually returned. RAGAS defines it as: supported_claims / total_claims, where each claim is checked for entailment against the context.

How does the RAGAS faithfulness score work?
RAGAS faithfulness decomposes the answer into atomic statements, then uses an LLM to check whether each statement is entailed (supported) by the retrieved context. The final score is the fraction of statements that pass: 1.0 means every claim is grounded, 0.0 means none are. Scores below 0.6 almost always indicate real hallucinations worth reviewing.

What faithfulness metric should I run in CI versus a nightly eval?
Run a deterministic grounding check (keyword/number extraction against source chunks) in every CI build — it's free and instant. Reserve the RAGAS faithfulness score or an LLM-as-judge for your nightly eval suite; they cost tokens and take seconds per call. Never gate a PR solely on a probabilistic score.

title: Ping64|What I Learned When a Summer Intern Shadowed Me for a Week and Wrote Down Every Question
description:
A couple of months ago our team got a summer intern, and since I was the only one without back-to-back meetings, she got assigned to shadow me for a week. I expected to spend five days narrating ticket queues and explaining where we keep the documentation. What actually happened was stranger and more useful.

By Wednesday she had filled a notebook with questions I couldn’t answer quickly, and none of them were deep technical ones. She wanted to know why we have three different tools that all send alerts, and why resetting a single account involves four systems. Her outsider eyes saw friction I had stopped noticing years ago. I found myself apologizing for things I had never chosen, which was a slightly uncomfortable feeling.

The things she wrote down

One page of her notebook was titled things that seem weird, and it was brutal in the gentlest possible way. Why does the password reset flow email a temporary password instead of using the self-service portal? Why do we check two dashboards to confirm one alert? Why is the asset list a spreadsheet that stopped being updated in March? Each question had an answer, and each answer was basically history rather than logic.

I laughed at a few of those, then realized I had asked the very same questions in my first year. Somewhere along the way I stopped asking and started working around things instead. That’s the part that got my attention. The workarounds had become so normal that I forgot they were workarounds. They had quietly turned into the actual process, documented nowhere and understood by everyone.

Why the weirdness becomes invisible

Nobody designs a messy process on purpose. Each odd step exists because someone once had an urgent problem, patched it quickly, and moved on with their week. A tool bought during one bad quarter, a script written by someone who has since left, a checklist copied from a previous job. Individually, each of them is defensible.

The trouble is that veterans absorb the friction and stop seeing it, while new people see it clearly but lack the authority to change anything. An intern asking why is not a criticism of anyone on the team. It’s usually the cheapest audit you’ll ever get, and it walks out the door in eight weeks if nobody captures it. Most teams lose that window and never know they had it.

Some teams try consolidated platforms like Ping64 to reduce the daily busywork of multi-tool security stacks. I mention that as an observation about where the industry has drifted, not a pitch. When routine work spreads across too many tools, every handoff becomes a place where confused questions pile up.

What we changed after the week

  • We turned her notebook into a real backlog. Half the entries were fixed in a day; the rest became honest tickets with named owners.
  • I added a standing item to our onboarding checklist: write down everything that seems odd during your first month, with no filtering.
  • We killed one redundant alerting path entirely, something nobody had dared to touch for two years. It turned out nothing had depended on it since the migration.
  • The self-service password portal finally got fixed, which had been sitting in a pending state so long that everyone forgot it existed.
  • She also got a small deliverable out of it: a one-page map of which tool does what, written from a newcomer’s view. We still keep it pinned in the team channel.

What surprised me most

The intern wasn’t smarter than the rest of us, and I want to be clear about that. She just had fresh eyes and no history, which is a resource most teams waste completely. If your onboarding process mostly teaches people the workarounds, you’re spending that resource badly.

I noticed my own habits shifting afterward, too. When I hit a clunky step now, I try to ask whether I’m working around a problem or actually fixing it. It’s a small mental shift, but it catches a surprising number of quiet issues before they harden into permanent fixtures that nobody questions anymore. If nothing else, it makes my own tickets more honest about the real cause.

Closing thoughts

I went into that week expecting to teach a student some basics of the job. I came out with a list of process debt I’d been carrying for years without noticing it. Not a bad return on one week of coffee runs and screen sharing. The most valuable part was that the list came with fresh explanations attached, not just complaints.

If you get an intern, a new hire, or even a colleague visiting from another team, treat their confused questions as free consulting. Write them down before the freshness wears off. Future you will be quietly grateful, and so will the next person who joins.

References
https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final
https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/
https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world
https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/cybersecurity-education

title: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent
description:
arXiv:2611.17780v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. On its own, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, maintains its accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantized weights, and transfers zero-shot to Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB within 3.1 points of its native SQLite accuracy. Combined with Claude Opus 5.5 in a pre-registered confidence cascade over 227 questions on databases published after Opus's training cutoff, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all questions locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy. Finally, contamination probing shows that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema; however, its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas and reaches 95.6-97.4% on post-cutoff databases. Code and data: https://github.com/IAMIbrahimmemon/luthorsql

title: MacroGS: Macro-Pixel Shared Gaussian Primitives for Arbitrary-Scale Light Field Super-Resolutio
description:
arXiv:2611.17957v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Arbitrary-scale light field spatial super-resolution reconstructs high-resolution views at any requested scale from low-resolution multi-view observations. Gaussian primitives enable continuous reconstruction, but generating separate primitive sets for each view redundantly encodes shared scene structure across views and causes the primitive count grow linearly with the number of views. To avoid such redundancy, we propose MacroGS, a feed-forward decoder that jointly predicts a single shared Gaussian set per macro pixel rather than generating separate sets for each view. Disparity-dependent replacement and angle-conditioned appearance allow each set to be reused across all output views, keeping the predicted primitive count independent of the number of views at each requested scale. The decoder iteratively predicts per-primitive disparities, retrieves the corresponding multi-view features, and updates the primitive states. Gaussian splatting and residual refinement then reconstruct the output light field. Despite being learned without geometric supervision, the predicted disparities strongly correlate with underlying scene geometry. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that MacroGS integrates effectively with diverse light field encoders, improving reconstruction quality at fixed scales while achieving leading performance across most evaluated arbitrary-scale settings. The decoder also achieves speedups of approximately $2$-$10\times$ over state-of-the-art implicit light field decoders and $10$-$18\times$ over the view-wise Gaussian baseline.

title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say
description:
arXiv:2611.17639v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.

title: Method and Constructor
description:
Method Overloading, Constructor Overloading and Method Overriding in Java

Polymorphism is one of the important concepts in Object-Oriented Programming (OOP). It allows the same method name or interface to behave differently in different situations. Java supports polymorphism through method overloading and method overriding. Constructor overloading is another useful feature that provides different ways to initialize objects.

1. Method Overloading

Method overloading means creating multiple methods with the same name but different parameters within a class. The parameters can differ in number, data type, or order.

Example:

class Calculator {

    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }

    double add(double a, double b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}

Here, the add() method is defined three times with different parameters. Java automatically identifies which method to execute based on the arguments passed during the method call.

Important points:

  • Method names must be the same.
  • Parameters must be different.
  • Changing only the return type is not method overloading.
  • It is an example of compile-time polymorphism.

2. Constructor Overloading

Constructor overloading means creating multiple constructors within the same class with different parameters. It allows us to initialize objects in different ways.

Example:

class Student {

    String name;
    int age;

    Student() {
        name = "Unknown";
        age = 0;
    }

    Student(String n) {
        name = n;
    }

    Student(String n, int a) {
        name = n;
        age = a;
    }
}

Here, the Student class contains three constructors. When an object is created, Java selects the appropriate constructor based on the arguments passed.

For example:

Student s1 = new Student();
Student s2 = new Student("Arun");
Student s3 = new Student("Kumar", 22);

Each object is initialized differently.

Important points:

  • Constructor names must match the class name.
  • Constructors do not have return types.
  • Constructors can have different parameter lists.
  • Constructors cannot be overridden.

3. Method Overriding

Method overriding happens when a child class provides its own implementation of a method that is already defined in its parent class. It allows the child class to change the inherited method's behaviour.

Example:

class Animal {

    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal makes a sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    @Override
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

Here, the Dog class inherits the Animal class using the extends keyword. Both classes contain the sound() method, but the Dog class provides its own implementation.

Animal a = new Animal();
Dog b = new Dog();
a.sound();
b.sound();

Output:

Animal makes a sound
Dog barks

Although the reference variable is of type Animal, the actual object is Dog. Java executes the overridden method based on the actual object at runtime. This is called runtime polymorphism or dynamic method dispatch.

Important points:

  • Inheritance is required.
  • Method names and parameters must match.
  • The return type must be the same or covariant.
  • The @Override annotation helps identify overriding mistakes.

title: AWS WAF advanced rate-based rules are now available in AWS GovCloud (US), Thailand, and Mexico
description:
AWS WAF advanced rate-based rules are now available in the Asia Pacific (Thailand), Mexico (Central), AWS GovCloud (US-East), and AWS GovCloud (US-West) Regions. Customers in these Regions can now aggregate requests using custom keys and choose a 1 or 2 minute evaluation window in addition to the existing 5 and 10 minute options, the same capabilities already available in other AWS Regions.

A rate-based rule counts requests and applies an action, such as Block or CAPTCHA, when the request rate exceeds a limit you set. Previously, rate-based rules in these Regions could aggregate requests only by IP address and used a 5 or 10 minute evaluation window. Now you can aggregate by request components such as HTTP headers, cookies, query strings, URI paths, HTTP methods, and label namespaces, and combine up to five of them into a composite key. For example, you can limit login attempts per IP address and User-Agent pair, or per session cookie, which helps against attacks spread across many IP addresses. A shorter evaluation window detects request floods sooner, and a longer window catches slower, sustained attacks.

You can configure these options in the AWS WAF console, the AWS CLI and SDKs, and AWS CloudFormation. There is no additional charge for these capabilities, and standard AWS WAF pricing applies. Advanced rate-based rules are now available in all commercial AWS Regions where AWS WAF is available and in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, see Using rate-based rule statements in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

title: 30 stats every engineering leader should know about AI-era software quality
description:
Most statistics in this field do not survive being looked up. Take the claim that a production bug costs 100 times more to fix than one caught in design. It traces back not to a study, but to IBM internal course notes cited in a 1987 textbook, whose underlying data “could be as old as 1967” (The Register). It has been repeated for forty years as though it were research.

Every figure below names its source, its date and its sample, and links to somewhere you can check it. Each also carries a tag showing what kind of evidence it is. A peer-reviewed paper, a regulatory filing and a vendor’s customer survey are not equally strong, and you should not have to guess which one you are reading. Antidote sells autonomous verification, so read our own framing with the same scepticism.

The verification gap

1. 90% of software professionals now use AI, but 30% trust its output little or not at all.

23% trust it "a little" and 7% "not at all". Nearly 5,000 respondents worldwide.

Industry survey, Google-run · DORA 2025, Google

2. Only 6.6% of developers trust AI with important decisions.

The most common answer, at 48%, was "I trust it when I can easily verify the output". 14,304 answered the question, in a survey of more than 30,000 people across 169 countries, published October 2026.

Developer survey · Stack Overflow 2026

3. 96% of developers don't fully trust AI code to be correct, yet only 48% always check it before committing.

AI already accounts for 42% of committed code, and developers expect 65% by 2027. More than 1,100 developers, January 2026.

Vendor survey · Sonar

4. 70% of software leaders believe application quality is already suffering.

93% have adopted AI coding tools, and 40% generate more than 40% of their code with AI. Of 273 CTOs, CIOs, developers and QA directors, 86% are raising testing budgets by more than 11% this year.

Vendor survey · SmartBear

5. "Almost right, but not quite" is developers' biggest frustration with AI tools.

66% of 31,476 developers chose it, the most-selected of seven options. Runner-up: 45.2% say debugging AI-generated code takes longer. This is from 2025, the most recent edition to ask the question.

Developer survey · Stack Overflow 2025

6. AI-co-authored pull requests carry 1.7 times more issues than human ones.

10.83 issues per PR against 6.45, across 320 AI-co-authored and 150 human-only open-source PRs. Logic and correctness issues were 75% more common. Authorship was inferred, not confirmed.

Vendor analysis · CodeRabbit

7. AI-generated code introduces a known security flaw 45% of the time, no better than two years ago.

More than 95% of it is syntactically correct. Defences against cross-site scripting passed just 15% of the time. 150+ models, four languages, March 2026.

Vendor benchmark · Veracode

8. Code duplication is up 81% and refactoring has collapsed.

Duplicated blocks rose from 40.3 to 73.0 per million changed lines between 2023 and 2026. Moved or refactored lines fell from 21% of changes in 2022 to 3.8%. 623 million analysed changes.

Vendor telemetry · GitClear

What AI is doing to delivery

9. At teams with high AI adoption, incidents per merged PR more than tripled.

Up 243%, with monthly incidents up 58% and bugs per developer up 54%. Task throughput per developer rose only 34%. 22,000 developers across 4,000+ teams, two years of data to March 2026. It is a before-and-after comparison within teams, not a controlled experiment.

Vendor telemetry · Faros AI

10. Median time in code review rose 441%, and PRs merged with no review rose 31%.

Same teams, same comparison. The bottleneck has moved from writing code to checking it.

Vendor telemetry · Faros AI

11. Main-branch success fell to 70.8%, its lowest in over five years, before recovering to 78.3%.

Across 28.7 million workflows in September 2025, median teams' main-branch throughput fell 7% while feature-branch throughput rose 15%. By August 2026, across 22.1 million workflows, success had recovered to 78.3%.

Vendor telemetry · CircleCI 2026, CircleCI Q3 2026

12. Developers saving 10+ hours a week with AI fell from 68% to 26% in a year.

65% spend time correcting AI output that missed the original intent. Only 17% report a clear AI strategy across the delivery lifecycle. 1,560 respondents, self-reported.

Vendor survey · Atlassian via InfoQ

13. 87% were confident they could tell within 24 hours whether AI code caused an incident. Of those that had one, 34% couldn't.

Harris Poll, 1,528 developers and technology buyers, six countries, June 2026.

Vendor survey · GitLab

What the tests themselves cost

14. 84% of Google's pass-to-fail test transitions involved a flaky test.

That's against a steady background of about 1.5% of all test runs reporting a flaky result.

Company engineering data · Google Testing Blog, 2016

15. A quarter of Google's tests using the Android emulator were flaky.

25.46% of them, against a general finding that "the larger the test, the more likely it will be flaky".

Company engineering data · Google Testing Blog, 2017

16. Only 1.23% of Google's test targets ever found a real breakage.

In one month covering more than 4 billion test outcomes, 2.07% of 5.5 million targets both passed and failed. Only 1.23% remained once flaky targets were filtered out.

Peer-reviewed · Memon et al., ICSE-SEIP 2017

17. Up to half of all builds contain a flaky failure, and 86% of flaky tests only flake in CI.

The figure was 14% to 52% of builds, depending on the project, across five Microsoft projects over 30 days, and 4.6% of individual tests were flaky. Of 315 flaky tests re-run 100 times on a local machine, 86% never flaked there.

Peer-reviewed · Lam et al., ISSTA 2019

18. Two thirds of Mozilla's job failures were not real failures.

25,871 of 38,596 failures across nearly 2 million runs, each classified by hand rather than by heuristic.

Peer-reviewed · Lampel et al., ESEC/FSE 2021

19. Flaky tests outnumbered genuine failures four to one at Facebook.

In CI data where almost 99.9% of dependency-selected test targets passed.

Peer-reviewed · Machalica et al., ICSE-SEIP 2019

What failure costs

20. Poor software quality costs the US at least $2.41 trillion.

On top of that is about $1.52 trillion of accumulated technical debt, reported separately. A modelled estimate from 2022, with no later edition.

Consortium estimate · CISQ

21. The average US data breach now costs a record $11.5 million, and one in four malicious breaches is AI-enabled.

The global average is $4.99 million, up 12%, across 602 organisations breached between March 2025 and February 2026. AI-enabled attacks rose 56% in a year.

Vendor study · IBM via CFO.com, IBM X-Force

22. Downtime costs Global 2000 companies $600 billion a year, and every technology leader surveyed had an AI-related outage.

That's up 50% in two years, or roughly $300 million per company. Half cited incorrect AI-driven automation. 2,000 executives, 20 countries, 2026.

Vendor survey · Splunk, Cisco newsroom

23. 10 of 2025's 16 major cloud outages were caused by configuration or deployment changes.

Covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Cloudflare, mostly from official post-mortems. Two examples: a database permissions change took Cloudflare down for about five and a half hours in November 2025. AWS's October 2025 us-east-1 outage cost US companies an estimated $500–650 million.

Vendor analysis of post-mortems · Control Plane, Cloudflare, Parametrix via Insurance Edge

24. One bad update cost the Fortune 500 an estimated $5.4 billion, and Delta around $500 million on its own.

CrowdStrike, July 2024; the Fortune 500 figure excludes Microsoft and was modelled by an outage insurer. Delta reported $380 million of lost revenue and $170 million of extra non-fuel cost, offset by $50 million of unburned fuel, across 7,000 cancellations in five days.

Insurer model · Regulatory filing · Parametrix, Delta, SEC filing

25. UK banks logged 803 hours of unplanned outage in two years.

More than 33 days, across at least 158 incidents at nine institutions between January 2023 and February 2025, on their own returns to Parliament.

Parliamentary data · Treasury Committee, 2025

Customer and revenue impact

26. A 31% faster page lifted Vodafone's sales by 8%.

A genuine 50/50 A/B test with no visual or functional differences between versions. Around 34,000 visits per version per day, all paid media traffic.

Controlled experiment · Google web.dev

27. A 1.09% crash rate is enough for Google Play to flag your app.

Above that share of daily users experiencing a crash, an app crosses Google's "bad behaviour" threshold. For a single device model, the threshold is 8%.

Platform policy · Google Play Console

28. Shoppers cut spending after 47% of bad experiences.

Down 8 points year on year, but 58% in online retail and 62% in fast food. 20,000+ consumers, 14 countries, Q3 2025.

Vendor survey · Qualtrics XM Institute

Where the market is heading

29. Gartner expects 70% of enterprises to have AI-augmented testing tools by 2028.

Up from 20% in early 2025. From Gartner's first Magic Quadrant for AI-Augmented Software Testing Tools, October 2025.

Analyst forecast · Gartner, via Keysight

30. Only 15% of companies have scaled AI in quality engineering enterprise-wide.

43% are still experimenting and 30% have it in limited use cases. Gen AI non-adopters rose from 4% to 11%. 2,000+ senior executives, 22 countries.

Vendor survey · World Quality Report 2025-26

What this means

Read together, these numbers tell a consistent story. Writing code has stopped being the bottleneck; checking it now is. Developers say they trust AI when they can verify its output (2), but fewer than half verify it (3). Review queues have grown more than fivefold (10), more code ships with no review at all, and incidents per change are rising (9). Meanwhile the test suites meant to catch problems spend much of their time raising false alarms (14–19).

Most failures that reach users show up as behaviour: a broken checkout, a crash, a config change that takes a region down. So the useful question is not whether more code passes review, but whether what you are about to ship still works for the people using it. You can only answer that by checking real behaviour, with evidence, before every release.

Originally published on the Antidote blog. I work at Antidote, which sells autonomous verification, so read our framing with the same scepticism.

title: Troubleshooting Four AWS Networking Incidents
description:
This article documents four networking incidents I resolved in the Learn to Cloud networking lab, covering the investigation process, root causes, configuration changes, and verification steps.

The lab provides intentionally misconfigured AWS infrastructure, with issues involving private subnet internet access, internal DNS resolution, application connectivity, and network security rules.

I used the AWS CLI and Linux networking tools to investigate the deployed resources, identify the misconfigurations, apply fixes, and verify connectivity.

1. Lab Environment

The infrastructure consisted of four EC2 instances deployed within an Amazon VPC:

Component Purpose
Bastion host SSH access to the other instances
Web server Public application entry point
API server Private application service listening on TCP 8080
Database server PostgreSQL listening on TCP 5432

The application communication path was:

Web server → API server → PostgreSQL database

The environment also included:

  • A NAT gateway providing outbound internet access for private instances.
  • Amazon Route 53 with an internal.test private hosted zone for internal DNS.
  • Security groups controlling instance-level inbound and outbound traffic.
  • Network ACLs filtering traffic at subnet boundaries.

Terraform provisioned the infrastructure, while troubleshooting and configuration changes were performed against the deployed AWS resources using the AWS CLI.

The command examples below use variables instead of deployment-specific resource IDs and addresses.

2. Incident 1: Private API Unable to Access the Internet

Problem

The API instance was unable to establish outbound HTTPS connections. Requests to external services were timing out.

The instance was deployed in a private subnet and required outbound internet access through a NAT gateway.

Investigation

I inspected the NAT gateway and the route table associated with the private subnet.

aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways \
  --nat-gateway-ids "$NAT_GATEWAY_ID"

aws ec2 describe-route-tables \
  --route-table-ids "$PRIVATE_ROUTE_TABLE_ID"

The NAT gateway existed in a public subnet, but the private subnet's route table did not contain a default route pointing to it.

Root Cause

The private route table was missing the following route:

Destination Target
0.0.0.0/0 NAT gateway

Without this route, internet-bound IPv4 traffic from the private subnet had no path through the NAT gateway.

Resolution

I added the missing default route:

aws ec2 create-route \
  --route-table-id "$PRIVATE_ROUTE_TABLE_ID" \
  --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 \
  --nat-gateway-id "$NAT_GATEWAY_ID"

Verification

I repeated the HTTPS request from the API instance:

curl -4 --noproxy '*' -sS -o /dev/null \
  -w '%{http_code}\n' --max-time 10 https://example.com

Result: HTTP 200.

The API instance could establish outbound HTTPS connections through the NAT gateway while remaining in its private subnet.

Reference: AWS VPC Route Table Documentation

3. Incident 2: Internal DNS Resolution Failure

Problem

The application could not resolve the following internal service names:

  • web.internal.test
  • api.internal.test
  • db.internal.test

These hostnames were expected to resolve to the corresponding instances' private IPv4 addresses.

Investigation

I inspected the Route 53 private hosted zone and its DNS records.

aws route53 get-hosted-zone \
  --id "$HOSTED_ZONE_ID"

aws route53 list-resource-record-sets \
  --hosted-zone-id "$HOSTED_ZONE_ID"

The investigation confirmed that:

  • The internal.test private hosted zone existed.
  • The hosted zone was associated with the lab VPC.
  • The zone contained the default NS and SOA records.
  • The required application A records were missing.

Root Cause

The Route 53 private hosted zone did not contain A records mapping the application hostnames to their respective private IP addresses.

Resolution

I created the missing A records using Route 53 UPSERT changes.

DNS Record Target
web.internal.test Web server private IP
api.internal.test API server private IP
db.internal.test Database server private IP

Each record was configured with a TTL of 60 seconds.

Verification

I queried the VPC DNS resolver directly:

dig +short @169.254.169.253 web.internal.test A
dig +short @169.254.169.253 api.internal.test A
dig +short @169.254.169.253 db.internal.test A

All three queries returned their expected private IPv4 addresses.

I also checked DNS resolution through the instance's configured system resolver:

getent ahostsv4 api.internal.test

The command returned the API server's private address, confirming that internal name resolution was functioning.

Reference: AWS Route 53 Private Hosted Zones

4. Incident 3: Application Connection Timeouts

Problem

Two application connections were failing:

Source Destination Port
Web server API server TCP 8080
API server PostgreSQL TCP 5432

The services were running, but remote connections between the instances were timing out.

4.1 Web Server to API Connectivity

Investigation

The API health endpoint responded successfully when accessed locally on the API instance.

However, requests from the web server could not reach the API.

I inspected the security-group rules controlling communication between the two instances.

The required permissions were:

Security group Direction Traffic Peer
Web Outbound TCP 8080 API security group
API Inbound TCP 8080 Web security group

Security-group references have different meanings depending on rule direction. An inbound rule references an allowed source, while an outbound rule references an allowed destination.

Resolution

I corrected the application security-group rules to permit the required traffic from the web server to the API.

Verification

The API health endpoint was tested from the web server:

curl --noproxy '*' -fsS --max-time 5 \
  "http://${API_PRIVATE_IP}:8080/health"

The health check succeeded after the rules were corrected.

4.2 API Server to PostgreSQL Connectivity

Investigation

The API was also unable to establish a connection to PostgreSQL on TCP 5432.

An initial PostgreSQL readiness check returned no response.

I inspected the database service, listening sockets, host firewall, security groups, and subnet network ACL.

Check Finding
PostgreSQL service Running
Listening socket 0.0.0.0:5432 and [::]:5432
UFW host firewall Inactive
Database security group TCP 5432 permitted from API security group
Subnet network ACL Inbound rule 100 explicitly denied TCP 5432

PostgreSQL was listening on the required port and was not restricted to the loopback interface.

The database security group also contained a rule permitting TCP 5432 from the API security group.

The subnet network ACL, however, contained an explicit deny rule for the same traffic.

Root Cause

Network ACL rule 100 blocked inbound TCP 5432 traffic to the database subnet.

Unlike security groups, network ACLs are stateless and evaluate numbered rules in ascending order. An explicit matching deny prevents the traffic from reaching the instance, even when its security group permits the connection.

Resolution

I removed the blocking network ACL rule and configured the database security group to permit PostgreSQL traffic specifically from the API security group.

Broad database access permissions were removed after the required application connection was restored.

Verification

From the API instance, I tested TCP connectivity to the database:

nc -zvw3 "$DB_PRIVATE_IP" 5432

I also checked PostgreSQL readiness:

pg_isready -h "$DB_PRIVATE_IP" \
  -p 5432 -U labuser -d labdb -t 3

Both checks succeeded.

The required communication path between the web server, API, and PostgreSQL was restored.

Reference: AWS Network ACL Documentation

5. Incident 4: Restricting Network Access

Problem

The lab infrastructure contained overly permissive network access rules.

The objective was to restrict access to the required sources and ports without interrupting application connectivity or administrative SSH access.

Investigation

I reviewed the security-group permissions associated with:

  • Administrative SSH access through the bastion host.
  • SSH connections to private instances.
  • Web server to API communication.
  • API to PostgreSQL communication.
  • ICMP access to the web server.

Resolution

I configured the following access model:

Destination Traffic Permitted source
Bastion host SSH, TCP 22 My public IPv4 address (/32)
Web, API, and database SSH, TCP 22 Bastion security group
API server TCP 8080 Web security group
PostgreSQL TCP 5432 API security group
Web server ICMP Bastion security group

The narrower rules were added and tested before the corresponding broad permissions were removed.

This sequence preserved the required connections while reducing unnecessary network access.

Security groups combine applicable allow rules. Adding a restrictive rule does not override an existing broader allow rule, so the unnecessary permissions also had to be removed.

Verification

After updating the security groups, I reviewed the resulting permissions and tested the required connections.

The verification confirmed that:

  • Administrative SSH access remained available through the bastion.
  • Web-to-API traffic on TCP 8080 remained functional.
  • API-to-database traffic on TCP 5432 remained functional.
  • The intended network access restrictions were in place.

Reference: AWS Security Group Rules

6. Summary of Findings

The four incidents involved different components of the AWS networking configuration.

Incident Root cause Resolution
Private API internet failure Missing default route in private subnet route table Added 0.0.0.0/0 route to NAT gateway
Internal DNS failure Missing A records in Route 53 private hosted zone Created records pointing to service private IPs
Application timeouts Incorrect application traffic permissions and an explicit network ACL deny Corrected security-group rules and removed blocking ACL rule
Overly permissive access Security-group rules allowed unnecessary access Restricted access to required sources and ports

Each incident was investigated by identifying the affected source, destination, protocol, port, and relevant AWS networking components.

Configuration changes were followed by connectivity tests from the affected instances to verify that the original failures had been resolved.

The final configuration restored the required application communication paths and restricted network access to the intended sources.

Project repository: Teedex1/networking-lab

Lab credit: Learn to Cloud Networking Lab. The project supplied the training infrastructure and incident scenarios. This article documents the troubleshooting and configuration changes performed in the deployed AWS environment.

title: websandbox: the WebArena sites as small SQLite + Node servers that reset in milliseconds
description:
If you train or evaluate web agents on WebArena, a lot of the cost is the environment rather than the agent: five heavy stacks (Magento, Postmill, GitLab, Kiwix, OpenStreetMap) and resets that mean restarting containers.

I rebuilt the five WebArena sites as lightweight, self-hostable versions: a store with its back office, a forum, a code-hosting site, a wiki and a map. Each site is one SQLite database plus one small Node server. It boots in under a second and resets to its initial state in milliseconds (a rollback of a transaction that is never committed), so one machine can run dozens of independent copies of every site.

What is included:

  • All 812 WebArena tasks converted to these sites: 807 verified by browser runs, 5 dropped with the reasons documented.
  • 12,283 generated tasks from 217 templates, each template checked with UI runs.
  • Template-disjoint train and held-out splits (10,452 and 2,638 tasks), so no held-out template is seen in training.
  • Graders that check answers, URLs and site state.

The data (about 21 GB, the same underlying data as WebArena) is a Hugging Face dataset, and the code is Apache-2.0.

Code: https://github.com/junfengzh/websandbox
Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/junfengzhou/websandbox
Demo, one copy of each site reset hourly: https://websandbox.pystem.com

Feedback is welcome, especially from anyone running agent RL or evals on WebArena-style tasks.

title: A Full-Page Overlay That Only Covers a Card? Check the Parent for transform
description:
A share dialog is supposed to dim the whole page. You give the dimmed backdrop position: fixed and inset: 0. That combination usually covers the window. Instead, the dimming sits only on one card. The rest of the page stays bright and clickable.

The overlay is not broken. It is obeying a different containing block. A parent, often one with a small transform used to lift the card, has become the reference for fixed.

The layout

A card lifts a little on hover. The share overlay is rendered inside the card, because that is where the button lives.

<section class="card">
  <h2>Quarterly report</h2>
  <button type="button">Share</button>
  <div class="overlay">
    <div class="dialog">Share this file</div>
  </div>
</section>

.card:hover,
.card.is-open {
  transform: translateY(-8px);
}

.overlay {
  position: fixed;
  inset: 0;
  background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.4);
}

When the card is open, or hovered, the overlay covers only the card.

What we measured

We tested this in Chrome 156 on November 13, 2026. A 240 by 160 pixel card sat on an 800-pixel-wide page. The overlay used position: fixed; inset: 0.

  • With no transform on the card, or with transform: none, the overlay sat at the top left of the viewport and covered the window.
  • With transform: translateY(-8px), the overlay sat on the card. Its box matched the card's inner size, 236 by 156 pixels, which is the card minus its 2-pixel border.
  • The same card-sized result appeared with transform: translate(0, 0). A move of zero was enough.

That last case is the one that is easy to miss. A "do nothing" transform still counts.

Why fixed leaves the viewport

position: fixed is described, in everyday use, as "relative to the viewport." MDN's page on position gives the fuller rule. The containing block is the viewport, unless an ancestor has transform, perspective, or filter set to a value other than none. That ancestor then becomes the containing block. MDN also says that will-change: transform establishes a new containing block.

CSS Position Level 3 lists properties that can make a box a fixed-position containing block. It names transform, will-change, and contain.

Our Chrome tests matched those documents:

  • filter: brightness(1) (a visual no-op) pinned the overlay to the card.
  • will-change: transform did the same.
  • contain: paint did the same.
  • perspective: 500px did the same.
  • will-change: opacity did not. The overlay covered the viewport, as it did with no transform. That fits MDN, which names will-change: transform, not every will-change value.

The fix: move the overlay, or move the transform

The overlay has to live outside the element that creates the containing block.

The most direct approach is to render the overlay as a child of document.body, not inside the card. A UI library's "portal" does this. After the move, position: fixed; inset: 0 refers to the viewport again. That holds as long as no other ancestor on the way up has transform, filter, perspective, will-change: transform, or contain: paint.

If the lift effect is the only reason for the transform, apply it to an inner element, and keep the overlay outside that inner element:

<section class="card">
  <div class="card-face">
    <h2>Quarterly report</h2>
    <button type="button">Share</button>
  </div>
</section>

.card:hover .card-face,
.card.is-open .card-face {
  transform: translateY(-8px);
}

The card wrapper itself has no transform. An overlay that is a sibling of .card-face, or a child of body, is not trapped by the lift.

Do not rely on "resetting" the parent with transform: none if some other code then sets translate(0, 0). As our test showed, a zero translate still creates the containing block.

A short checklist

  • position: fixed; inset: 0 covers the window only when the containing block is the viewport.
  • Inspect ancestors for transform, filter, or perspective values other than none, for will-change: transform, and for contain: paint.
  • A zero translate, or a filter that does not change the look, is enough.
  • Move the overlay out of that ancestor, or move the transform onto an inner wrapper that does not wrap the overlay.

On MDN, position is marked Baseline widely available from July 2015, and transform from September 2015.

Sources

  • MDN, position: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/position
  • MDN, transform: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/transform
  • W3C CSS Positioned Layout Module Level 3: https://www.w3.org/TR/css-position-3/
  • W3C CSS Transforms Module Level 1: https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transforms-1/

PIXEL RECRUITING LLC introduces frontend and UI engineers to product teams that care about details like this one. We mean a modal that really covers the page, not only the card that opened it. We are a direct staffing partner for Mastercard in O'Fallon, MO. Learn more at pixelrecruiting.com.
